title: MAST CELLS REGULATE NEUROGENIC BLADDER REMODELING AFTER SPINAL CORD INJURY
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction (PD01)
authors: Joys Annika G. David, Christina Lepak, Lindsay Milich, Ping Wei, Iryna Crescenze, Dana McTigue
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction is a common and debilitating consequence of spinal cord injury (SCI) that reduces quality of life and increases risk for recurrent urinary tract infections and renal damage. While immunological and structural changes in the SCI-induced neurogenic bladder have been shown, their temporal progression remains unclear and no targeted therapies exist. We characterize the timeline of bladder remodeling after SCI in a murine model and identify mast cells as modifiable drivers of pathology. METHODS: To model bladder pathology without other major SCI complications, we induced a moderate T9 contusion in 12-week-old female mice. Bladders from SCI and sham-surgery (LAM) control mice were harvested at 1-70 days post-injury (dpi) for histology, qPCR, and bulk RNAseq. Based on our findings, we conducted an intervention study administering intraperitoneal mast cell stabilizer, cromolyn sodium, or saline from 10-17 dpi and assessed bladder histology post-treatment. RESULTS: SCI induced a biphasic immune response in the bladder: early neutrophil and macrophage infiltration peak within 7 dpi, followed by dendritic, B, and T cells increasing up to 30 dpi. Mast cells and their mediators exhibited an especially robust and sustained increase 10-70 dpi, demonstrated by our histological and gene expression analyses ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191256.04437.4c.01#F1)). Structurally, we found progressive collagen deposition accompanied by early and persistent upregulation of fibrotic mediator genes. Cromolyn reduced mast cell number and degranulation in SCI mice when administered during the initial period of mast cell increase. Importantly, mast cell modulation was sufficient to lower vesical collagen deposition, indicative of reduced fibrosis ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191256.04437.4c.01#F2)). CONCLUSIONS: Although the bladder is not directly injured by SCI, its immune dysregulation parallels inflammatory responses at the spinal cord lesion, suggesting systemic immune involvement in SCI-bladder pathology. Our findings identify mast cells as key regulators of fibrotic bladder remodeling after SCI and highlight their potential as a novel therapeutic target.

title: CD73 INHIBITS PYROPTOSIS AND ALLEVIATES AUTOPHAGY TO IMPROVE NEUROGENIC BLADDER REHABILITATION BY REGULATING A2BAR SIGNALING
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction (PD01)
authors: Guanqun Zhu
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Neurogenic bladder (NB) is a debilitating condition with no definitive and effective treatment currently available. This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential and mechanism of action of CD73 expressed by stem cells in repairing NB in rats. METHODS: ADSCs were engineered into three variants: CD73 knockdown (CD73-/ADSCs), control (CD73+/ADSCs), and CD73-overexpressing cells (CD73+/+ADSCs). Conditioned medium (CM) from each group was applied to RBTECs for 48 h to evaluate proliferation, migration, and inflammation. In vivo, male SD rats underwent bilateral pelvic nerve crush to induce NB and were divided into five groups: sham, NB untreated, CD73-/ADSCs, CD73+/ADSCs, and CD73+/+ADSCs. Labeled ADSCs were injected into the bladder wall. After four weeks, bladder function was assessed by cystometry, and tissues were analyzed histologically and molecularly. RESULTS: CD73 overexpression significantly enhanced ADP-to-adenosine conversion. Increased A2BAR, suppressed IKK activity, and reduced NF-κB phosphorylation, leading to decreased inflammation. In vivo, CD73+/+ADSC-treated rats showed markedly elevated A2BAR levels, improved bladder tissue regeneration, and superior cystometric performance compared with other groups. TUNEL assays revealed reduced apoptosis in CD73+/+ADSC recipients, while p-AKT expression was increased. A2BAR activation upregulated autophagy-related proteins (BNIP3, ULK1, LC3A/B) via the ERK1/2–ULK1 pathway, promoting cellular homeostasis. Pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-6 were significantly decreased. Additionally, HIF1-α negatively regulated CD73 via the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, indicating a feedback mechanism in inflammatory conditions. CONCLUSIONS: Overexpressing CD73 in ADSCs enhances adenosine production, activates A2BAR, and simultaneously suppresses inflammation and promotes autophagy. These dual effects significantly improve bladder tissue regeneration and functional recovery in NB rats.

title: SELECTIVE ANDROGEN RECEPTOR MODULATION RESTORES DETRUSOR CONTRACTILITY AND PROTECTS SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS FROM HYPOXIC INJURY
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction (PD01)
authors: Hao-Chih Yang, Dong-Ru Ho
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Detrusor underactivity (DU) lacks effective pharmacologic therapy. Androgen receptor (AR) signaling regulates smooth muscle function and stress resistance. We investigated whether LGD-4033 (SARM) could improve bladder contractility in ischemia-induced DU and protect smooth muscle cells from hypoxia. METHODS: Female rats (n=3-5/group) underwent bilateral iliac artery ligation to induce DU. Groups received vehicle, LGD-4033 (10 mg/kg/day), enzalutamide (10 mg/kg/day), or combination for 4 weeks. Cystometry measured maximum voiding pressure (Pmax). Bladder tissue underwent Western blot analysis. Human bladder smooth muscle cells (HBdSMC) were exposed to hypoxia (1% O2) with LGD-4033 (0-1000 μM) for 24 h. RESULTS: DU reduced Pmax by 57% vs control (0.447±0.226 vs 1.048±0.071). LGD-4033 produced 8.2-fold improvement over DU (3.674±0.745, p<0.001), exceeding control by 250%. Enzalutamide completely blocked SARM effects (0.408±0.055), confirming AR-dependence. Western blot showed modest MYH11 upregulation without stress marker activation. In vitro, low-dose LGD-4033 (15.625-31.25 μM) enhanced HBdSMC survival under hypoxia (110-112% vs 95%, p<0.05), while higher concentrations (>62.5 μM) showed cytotoxicity. CONCLUSIONS: SARM dramatically restores bladder contractility in ischemia-induced DU via AR-dependent mechanisms. Direct cytoprotective effects on hypoxic smooth muscle cells provide mechanistic insight. The dual action of functional restoration and cell protection supports SARMs as a promising therapeutic for DU.

title: BLADDER NECK SPARING DURING ROBOT-ASSISTED RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY: ASSOCIATION BETWEEN POSTOPERATIVE LOWER URINARY TRACT FUNCTION AND NERVE DENSITY IN THE BLADDER NECK REGION
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction (PD01)
authors: Yuki Harigane, Junya Hata, Akari Hiraguri, Tomoyuki Kumekawa, Syunta Makabe, Kei Yaginuma, Ryo Tanji, Ruriko Takinami, Yuichi Sato, Hidenori Akaihata, Soichiro Ogawa, Motohide Uemura, Yoshiyuki Kojima
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Bladder neck sparing (BNS) during robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) has been reported to enhance early recovery of lower urinary tract function by maintaining the anatomical structures related to urinary continence and voiding control. However, the detailed distribution and histological characteristics of the nerves surrounding the bladder neck remain incompletely understood. Because parasympathetic fibers are densely distributed in this region, their preservation may contribute to the favorable outcomes associated with BNS. This study aimed to quantify nerve density around the bladder neck and clarify its association with postoperative urinary function following RARP. METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated 152 patients (mean age 67.4±5.2 years) who underwent RARP with technically feasible BNS, defined as complete urethral isolation with preservation of circular smooth muscle fibers. Histological analysis of the prostate base was performed using S100 immunostaining to identify nerve distribution and tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS), and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) staining to distinguish sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers. Nerve density in anterior and posterior bladder neck regions was semiquantitatively graded on a three-point scale and correlated with postoperative parameters, including 1-hour pad test, maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax), voided volume, postvoid residual (PVR), International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), and Overactive Bladder Symptom Score (OABSS), assessed at 1, 3, 6, 9, and 12 months postoperatively. RESULTS: Posterior bladder neck nerve density was significantly greater than anterior (p<0.05) and predominantly parasympathetic (TH–/nNOS+/VIP+) (p<0.05). Higher posterior nerve density was associated with improved 3-month pad test results, higher Qmax at 6 and 9 months, and lower PVR at 3 and 9 months (p<0.05). No significant relationships were found between nerve density and IPSS or OABSS, nor between anterior density and any parameter. CONCLUSIONS: A higher parasympathetic nerve density posterior to the bladder neck appears to enable more effective preservation of detrusor-innervating fibers during BNS, supporting early recovery of urinary continence and voiding function after RARP. These findings highlight the anatomical basis of functional preservation and emphasize the importance of meticulous posterior bladder neck dissection in achieving optimal postoperative outcomes.

title: NEUROGENIC LOWER URINARY TRACT DYSFUNCTION: CONTEMPORARY PATIENT OUTCOME WHILE ADHERING TO AUA/SUFU GUIDELINES
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction (PD01)
authors: Rakayle Crawley-Searuggs, Fahima Mohamud, Angelo Gousse
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (NLUTD) results from abnormal bladder, bladder neck, or urethral sphincter function secondary to neurologic disease. The AUA/SUFU risk-stratified framework classifies patients as low (LR), moderate (MR), or high risk (HR) to guide management and surveillance. Using a large single-institution database, we evaluated outcomes following application of this framework in a contemporary NLUTD cohort. METHODS: After IRB approval, records of 980 patients with NLUTD managed between 2010–2025 were retrospectively reviewed; 884 had complete data. Based on AUA/SUFU criteria, 9% (n=79) were HR, 18% (n=158) MR, and 73% (n=645) LR. Median age was 52, median follow-up of 82 months, 54% male, and 46% female. Etiologies included multiple sclerosis (MS) 32% (n=283), cerebrovascular accident (CVA) 25% (n=221), spinal cord injury (SCI) 21% (n=185), lumbosacral disk disease (LSDD) 16% (n=141), and Parkinson’s disease 4% (n=35). RESULTS: Bladder management included intestinal reconstruction (10%), indwelling catheter (5%), intermittent catheterization (18%), and spontaneous voiding (67%). HR/MR patients underwent annual renal US or CT and renal function testing; urodynamics (UDS) and cystoscopy were done as indicated. LR patients received studies only when necessary. Surgical interventions among HR patients included augmentation cystoplasty (38%), bladder neck closure/continent catheterizable channel (25%), incontinent diversion (12%), artificial urinary sphincter (6%), and sphincterotomy (4%); 17% underwent combined reconstruction or suprapubic (SP) catheter placement. Among MR patients, 7.5% had reconstruction, 67% received medical therapy (MT; anticholinergics and/or β3-agonists) with OnabotulinumtoxinA (BTX), and 25% MT alone. LR patients required no surgery; 33% MT+BTX, 67% MT alone. Sacral neuromodulation was not utilized. No patient developed renal deterioration, renal failure, or recurrent febrile UTI under AUA/SUFU-guided management. Overall, 89% achieved satisfactory continence. CONCLUSIONS: NLUTD patients can be effectively managed using the AUA/SUFU framework, maintaining stable renal function, low UTI rates, and high continence and QoL. Multi-institutional validation is warranted.

title: INTRADETRUSOR BOTULINUM TOXIN A FOR OVERACTIVE BLADDER SYMPTOMS IN PATIENTS WITH MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS WHO ARE VOIDING: LONGITUDINAL EXPERIENCE
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction (PD01)
authors: Briana Hay, Tasha Posid, Courtenay Moore, Iryna Crescenze
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive disease that is linked to neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (NLUTD). Intravesical onabotulinumtoxin A (BTX-A) injections are frequently used to treat NLUTD in patients with MS; however, long-term outcomes data, particularly among patients who void spontaneously, remain limited in this population. The purpose of this study is to describe dose escalation and failure patterns over time in patients with multiple sclerosis that are spontaneously voiding and examine predictors of treatment failure. METHODS: Our retrospective, observational cohort study included 50 patients with MS who were treated with BTX-A at a single tertiary referral center during a 10-year period (2014-2024). Data on dose, dose escalation, and treatment failure were collected retrospectively from medical records. Treatment failure was defined as discontinuation of BTX-A due to limited or no benefit, bothersome side effects, including urinary retention and urinary tract infection (UTI), or initiation of an alternative treatment. Logistic regression was used to examine predictors of failure. RESULTS: A total of 50 patients were included and mean follow up time was 2.80 years (SD 3.04). Among patients receiving more than one injection, 36.4% increased dose after a mean time of 1.54 years (SD 1.27). Of the 43 patients with adequate follow up, 53.5% failed BTX-A treatment with a mean time to failure of 1.21 years (SD 1.58). Type of MS and functional status were significantly associated with failure, with progressive MS (p=0.007) and lower functional status (p=0.025) being more common among those who failed. Progressive MS independently predicted treatment failure after adjusting for gender, years from diagnosis, Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), and initial dose (OR 18.0, 95% CI 1.7–187.0, p=0.015). CONCLUSIONS: Due to the progressive and evolving nature of MS, most patients will require dose escalation and are likely to experience BTX-A treatment failure over time. Patients with progressive MS and low functional status are at a greater risk for BTX-A failure and should be counseled accordingly. Providers must set realistic expectations with patients and be prepared to escalate dose and provide alternative treatment options. | | | --- | | |

title: VOIDING SYMPTOMS AND SEXUAL DYSFUNCTIONS IN PATIENTS SUFFERING FROM MIGRAINE WITH AND WITHOUT AURA: DATA FROM A HIGH VOLUME TERTIARY ACADEMIC CENTRE
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction (PD01)
authors: Antonio Luigi Pastore, Andrea Fuschi, Paolo Pietro Suraci, Yazan Al Salhi, Damiano Graziani, Manfredi Bruno Sequi, Fabio Maria Valenzi, Onofrio Antonio Rera, Cosimo De Nunzio, Riccardo Lombardo, Antonio Carbone
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Migraine is a pervasive neurobiological headache disorder that is caused by increased excitability of the central nervous system (CNS). Migraine represents one of the most disabling medical disorders. The diagnosis is based on the headache's characteristics and associated symptoms. Migraine without aura is the most common form of migraine in both children and adults, while 15% to 33% of migraineurs experience aura. Aura is a fully reversible, gradual focal neurological phenomenon involving most commonly visual, sensory, speech and/or motor symptoms. This study investigated the correlation between migraines (with or without AURA) with Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (LUTS) and Sexual Dysfunctions (SD). METHODS: This study enrolled patients referring to neurological outpatient clinic, suffering from migraine. The patients were divided into control group (patients with no prior diagnosis of migraine) and migraine group. This latter group was further subdivided into two subgroups based on the presence or absence of AURA. All patients were investigated with self-administered questionnaires (IPSS, SF.OAB-q, IIEF-5, MSHQ, ICIQ-FLUTS, ICIQ-UI, FSI, MIDAS). Subjects with other neurological disorders, prior pelvic and/or prostatic surgery, in treatment whit alpha-blocker and/or antimuscarinic drug, and aged <18 and >50 y.o. were excluded from the study. RESULTS: We prospectively enrolled 295 patients and divided these subjects into Group C (control) and Group M (migraine) with 149 (101 females, 48 males) and 146 (95 females, 51 males) subjects, respectively. Group M was subdivided into group Ma (migraine withaura) and Group Mw (migraine without aura), composed of 52 and 94 patients, respectively. The mean age was comparable between the two groups (34.3 y.o. Group C; 33.8 y.o. Group M). In Group C, no significant correlation between migraine and urinary orsexual dysfunction was reported. Statistically significant differences were found in Group M. Particularly, a significant correlation was found between the MIDAS score and the SF-OAB-Q, IEEF-5, and FSI scores. Higher MIDAS scores were directly correlated with higher SF-OAB-q and lower IEEF-5 and FSI scores. IPSS was also higher in Group M, even no statistically significant (6.2 p=0.12). The mean MIDAS score in Group Ma was 15.4 and 16.3 in Group Mw. In group Ma, the mean SF-OAB-Q, IEEF-5, and FSI scorewere 28.1, 17.4, and 19.2 and 26.9, 18.2 and 20.3 in Group Mw, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: This study shows for the first time that a correlation between urinary symptoms and sexual dysfunction with migraine exists. Especially, a statistically significant correlation was found between OABq and MIDAS score. Furthermore, OAB and SD were found to be more prevalent in patients suffering from migraine with aura.

title: UPPER URINARY TRACT PROTECTION AND PATIENT CLASSIFICATION FOLLOWING SACRAL NEUROMODULATION IN NEUROGENIC BLADDER WITH HYDRONEPHROSIS: A MULTICENTER STUDY WITH 2-YEAR FOLLOW-UP
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction (PD01)
authors: Peixian Chen, Hao Huang, Hai Huang
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Previous studies have demonstrated the efficacy of sacral neuromodulation (SNM) for neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (NLUTD), but the therapeutic effect on upper urinary tract has not been clearly defined. We aimed to investigate the protective effect of SNM on the upper urinary tract in patients with NLUTD. METHODS: We included NLUTD patients with hydronephrosis who underwent SNM in two hospitals from September 2018 to March 2025. Preoperative clinical data of the patients were collected, including age, gender, disease duration, urinary symptoms, and the degree of hydronephrosis. During the follow-up period, we mainly compared the urinary diary and the degree of hydronephrosis before and after treatment to assess the improvement of symptoms. RESULTS: We included 89 patients, with a permanent implantation rate of 69.6%. Preoperative ultrasound examination revealed 84 sides of mild hydronephrosis, 26 sides of moderate hydronephrosis, and 45 sides of severe hydronephrosis. Based on the urodynamic results and cluster analysis, patients were divided into three categories. The first category included patients with both storage and voiding phase dysfunction, whose bladders were characterized by low compliance, DO, and DSD, with response rate of 76.7%. The second category included patients with storage phase dysfunction, whose bladders were characterized by low compliance, low capacity, and sensitive bladder, with response rate of 75%. The third category included patients with voiding phase dysfunction, characterized by low compliance with a high volume of residual urine, with response rate of 61.3%. The median time of the follow-up was 24 (14, 43) months. Sacral neuromodulation could effectively improve the hydronephrosis (p<0.001) and urinary symptoms (p<0.001), with a long-term efficacy rate of 87.3%. Specifically, in 112 sides of hydronephrosis, 74.1% (83/112) was alleviated, 45% (49/106) was cured, and 18.8% remained stable. CONCLUSIONS: Sacral neuromodulation can effectively protect the upper urinary tract function of NLUTD patients after permanent implantation, with stable long-term effects, especially for patients with low compliance, detrusor overactivity (DO), and DSD.

title: IMPACT OF CHRONIC SPINAL CORD INJURY SEVERITY ON URINARY BLADDER AUTONOMIC ACTIVITY
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction (PD01)
authors: Jagadeesh Thippeswamy, Merlin Mamachan, Paul Lu, Mahadevan Rajasekaran
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Anticholinergic agents are commonly prescribed to manage bladder dysfunction following spinal cord injury (SCI); however, their long-term effectiveness may be limited by chronic changes in bladder muscarinic signaling. Previous studies in rats have shown transient impairment of muscarinic responses after SCI (PMID: 18599189; 22386753), but the persistence and severity dependence of these effects remain unclear. This study investigated the long-term impact of mild, moderate, and severe SCI on carbachol-induced bladder contractility three months post-injury. METHODS: Female Wistar rats underwent thoracic (T9) contusions of mild (200 kdyn) or moderate (250 kdyn) severity, or complete transection (severe SCI). Sham-operated animals served as controls. Bladder pressure was continuously monitored via telemetry before and immediately after SCI. After three months, bladder strips (n=4 per group) were evaluated for KCl (80 mM)– and carbachol (10-8–10-4 M)–evoked contractions using an in vitro organ bath system (Radnoti). Data were analyzed using an Acqknowledge MP150 setup. RESULTS: Severe SCI caused an acute increase in bladder pressure post-injury ( Figure 1A). At three months, KCl-induced contractile force decreased with injury severity—by ∼14% (mild), 36% (moderate), and 56% (severe) compared to controls. Carbachol dose–response curves showed rightward shifts and reduced maximal contractile effects (Emax), most pronounced after severe injury (1.69±0.09 g vs. 4.38±0.35 g in controls; Figure 1B-F). CONCLUSIONS: Chronic SCI produces severity-dependent reductions in muscarinic-mediated bladder contractility, suggesting long-term alterations in receptor regulation or downstream signaling. These findings indicate that standard antimuscarinic therapies may be less effective in chronic, severe SCI and underscore the potential of alternative pharmacologic targets—such as β3-adrenergic or purinergic pathways—to manage bladder function after chronic SCI.

title: MULTI-CENTER ANALYSIS OF BLADDER MANAGEMENT AND QUALITY OF LIFE IN ADULTS LIVING WITH SPINA BIFIDA
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction (PD01)
authors: Blayne Welk, Rose Khavari, Rano Matta, Sean Elliott, Antoine Khoury, Iryna Crescenze, David Ginsberg, Evgeniy Kreydin, Zhina Sadeghi
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Bladder management in spina bifida frequently includes intermittent catheters and bladder reconstructive procedures, however the impact of these factors on bladder-related quality of life and symptom burden in adults with spina bifida is unknown. METHODS: The Neurogenic Bladder Research Group initiated a multi-institutional, prospective cross-sectional study of adults with spina bifida; the primary objective was to examine the differences in bladder specific QOL and symptom burden across different bladder management methods. Standardized data collection, with medical record review was carried out at each center. Results of the interim analysis are reported. The validated Neurogenic Bladder Symptom Score-SF (NBSS) was used (range 0 (best)-32 (worst)). Ordinal (NBSS bladder specific QOL question) and linear (NBSS-SF total score) regression models were used. RESULTS: We recruited 81 patients (60% female) with a mean age of 34 (standard deviation (SD) 13). Almost half (48%) had a college degree and 55% were non-ambulatory. Bladder management included: voiding+/-CIC (16%), CIC (64%), indwelling catheter (12%), and continent/incontinent urinary diversion (6%); 30% had a catheterizable channel into native bladder, and 36% had a bladder augmentation. The mean NBSS-SF total score was 11 (SD 6). Bladder-related QOL was good (62%), mixed (29%) and poor (9%).Bladder management technique was not associated with bladder-related QOL (p=0.13) or NBSS-SF total score (p=0.90). Among people that used CIC, age, sex, frequency of catheters, independent CIC and use of incontinence pads were not significantly associated with bladder-related QOL (p=0.42). However, independent CIC (p=0.04) and use of incontinence pads (p<0.01) were significantly associated with a worse NBSS-SF total score. Examining the impact of prior bladder surgery, age at reconstructive surgery, catheterizable channel, and bladder augmentation were not significantly associated with bladder-related QOL (p=0.19) or NBSS-SF total score (p=0.44). CONCLUSIONS: In a diverse group of adults with spina bifida, bladder management and reconstructive surgery was not significantly associated with bladder symptoms or QOL. Ongoing work will explore the interaction with bowel, psychosocial and cognitive symptoms.

title: AUGMENTATION CYSTOPLASTY VERSUS BOTULINUM TOXIN A IN NEUROGENIC DETRUSOR OVERACTIVIY: A CROSS-SECTIONAL COMPARISON OF SYMPTOMS, QUALITY OF LIFE, AND DECISION REGRET

title: IMPACT OF THE ANTIREFLUX IMPLANTATION’S SITE FOR CONTINENT CUTANEOUS URINARY DIVERSION: NATIVE BLADDER VERSUS ENTEROCYSTOPLASTY
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction (PD01)
authors: Ophelie Decombe, Pierre Lecoanet, Adrien Montazeaud, Julie Lienard, Olivier Larmure, Vladimir Gomola, Lory Hage, Pascal Eschwège, Jean-Louis Lemelle, Charles Mazeaud, Nicolas Berte
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: In patients who cannot perform intermittent self-catheterization via the urethra, continent cutaneous urinary diversion (CCUD) represents a valuable alternative, often associated with enterocystoplasty (EC). The CCUD is created using the appendix or the ileum, which can be implanted into the native bladder (NB) or the EC using various surgical techniques. This study aimed to evaluate postoperative outcomes and functional results of CCUD according to these two surgical approaches. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, single-center study that included patients who underwent CCUD creation between 1991 and 2020. Clinical characteristics were compared using _Fisher_’s exact test and the _Mann-Whitney_ test. Postoperative complications were analyzed using _Kaplan-Meier_ survival curves and compared using the _Log-rank_ test. RESULTS: A total of 94 patients were included (60 children, 34 adults): 74 (79%) CCUD were implanted into the native detrusor (NB group), and 20 (21%) onto the anterior wall of the enterocystoplasty (EC group). Early complications occurred on average at 7.5 days \[7–11.5\], with an overall rate of 5%. Forty patients (42%) experienced at least one long-term complication (e.g., leakage, stenosis, kinks), with no significant difference between groups. Survival analysis revealed no significant difference in overall surgical revisions (NB: 42%, EC: 46%; p=0.51) or endoscopic revision. However, the EC group had significantly more frequent subfascial revision procedures (p=0.005) and less frequent superficial stoma revision (p=0.02), but this was not significant on multivariate analysis. At the end of follow-up (median: 12 years \[7–21\]), 82% of patients remained continent (NB: 83%, EC: 75%). CONCLUSIONS: A short and straight abdominal segment of the CCUD appears to reduce complication rates, as recommended by the technique involving implantation into a detrusor flap. However, reservation of the native bladder may contribute to persistent overactivity. The study is limited by its low external validity and the heterogeneity of patient characteristics, which may reduce statistical power. Nevertheless, the results reflect a real-life experience with a complex and uncommon surgical procedure. Implantation of the conduit into the native bladder seems to be associated with better long-term continence outcomes and fewer subfascial revisions despite multiple confounding factors. Further studies are needed to refine surgical techniques and reduce complications.

title: PRECLINICAL FEASIBILITY OF CONTINUOUS BLADDER VOLUME MONITORING USING WEARABLE NEAR-INFRARED SPECTROSCOPY VERSUS ULTRASOUND IN YUCATAN MINIPIGS
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction (PD01)
authors: Aram Kim, John Thomas Stoffel, Hyeong Gon Kim, Sehwan Kim
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Patients with neurogenic bladder lack reliable tools for continuous bladder volume monitoring, leading to overdistension and catheter-related complications. This study evaluated whether a wearable near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) patch estimates bladder volume as accurately as portable ultrasound. Secondary objectives were to assess reproducibility under varied attachment conditions and tissue safety in a Yucatan minipig model. METHODS: In an AAALAC-accredited facility, two female Yucatan minipigs underwent repeated, controlled bladder filling under general anesthesia. A wearable NIRS patch and a portable ultrasound scanner were tested at matched time points. Primary endpoints were Pearson correlation (r) with infused volume and mean absolute error (MAE), with 95% confidence intervals estimated by cluster bootstrap. Secondary endpoints included reproducibility across attachment pressure/position and histopathology. RESULTS: Across eight infusion cycles in the smaller and fifteen in the larger animal, NIRS tracked bladder volume closely (r=0.97–0.99) with MAE similar to ultrasound. In head-to-head testing: small animal—NIRS MAE 23.1±4.7 mL, r=0.98±0.01 vs ultrasound 32.5±12.2 mL, r=0.95±0.04; large animal—NIRS 31.1±9.7 mL, r=0.98±0.00 vs ultrasound 30.4±14.5 mL, r=0.99±0.01. Accuracy improved with firm fixation, while inferior displacement increased error. Histopathology confirmed no device-related inflammation or tissue injury. Limitations include small sample size, anesthesia, saline infusion, and species differences limiting extrapolation. CONCLUSIONS: A wearable NIRS patch provided ultrasound-comparable accuracy with continuous, noninvasive monitoring in animal models. The finding suggests that a wearable NIRS based monitoring could help people with neurogenic bladder empty at the right time and avoid overfilling or infections.

title: SMART, REUSABLE CATHETER SYSTEM FOR LONGITUDINAL URINARY MONITORING AT THE POINT OF CARE
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Neurogenic Voiding Dysfunction (PD01)
authors: Erika C. Solano, Zhi Dou, W. T. Al-Shaibani, Abdullah Obeidat, Riadh Al-Haidari, Neda Sezgin, Rania Adam, Willow Denker, Mark J. Schadt, Souvik Paul, Kara Allanach, Daniel Wollin, Mark D. Poliks
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Driven by the needs of individuals with spinal cord injury (SCI) who rely on intermittent urinary catheterization, CathBuddy, Inc. developed the Aurie System—a reusable catheter platform with a cleaning and disinfection unit to ensure safe reusability. Building on this, we present a Smart Catheter integrating reusable pressure (P), temperature (T), and pH sensors for real-time urodynamic monitoring, with Near Field Communication (NFC) data transfer at the point of care. Longitudinal bladder P monitoring offers clinical-level insight into bladder dynamics, while monitoring urinary T and pH may support early detection of catheter-associated urinary tract infections. By combining multimodal sensing, wireless communication, and accessible technology, this Smart Catheter aims to enhance independence, reduce long-term healthcare costs, and support personalized, patient-centered care for individuals SCI patients. METHODS: Commercial P and T sensors were selected based on biocompatibility, low power, and compact packaging, and integrated into a 3D-printed catheter tip made with biocompatible elastomers. Custom potentiometric pH sensors were built using Pt/Ir and Ag wires, as the working (WE) and reference (RE) electrodes, respectively, forming an electrochemical cell. The WE surface was activated to create iridium oxide sites, and open circuit potentiometry (OCP) measured voltage shifts from hydronium ion activity. The pH sensors were calibrated using standard pH buffers, while integrated P and T sensors were validated in a customized bladder model against reference instruments. RESULTS: The customized testing setup successfully demonstrated integration and reliable data transmission from the P and T sensors. The potentiometric pH sensors exhibited near-Nernstian behavior across a physiologically relevant pH range (4.5–8.0), validating their suitability for urinary monitoring. Sensor robustness and reproducibility were demonstrated, and functionality was retained after multiple cleaning and disinfection cycles following Aurie’s standardized procedures. CONCLUSIONS: This work validates a multimodal Smart Catheter capable of measuring P, T, and pH with wireless data transfer. Sensors maintained stability, reproducibility, and responsiveness after repeated sterilization, confirming feasibility for reusable point-of-care urinary monitoring.

title: IS HUNNER LESION-INTERSTITIAL CYSTITIS/BLADDER PAIN SYNDROME (HL-IC/BPS) A B CELL-DRIVEN AUTOIMMUNE DISEASE? A COMPREHENSIVE, POPULATION-BASED ANALYSIS OF AUTOIMMUNITY AMONGST A LARGE COHORT OF HL-IC/BPS PATIENTS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis (PD02)
authors: R. Christopher Doiron, Rebecca J. Griffiths, J. Curtis Nickel, Timothy P. Hanna, Akihiro Nakamura, Tiziana Cotechini
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: We explored whether the observed propensity for widespread autoimmunity amongst interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) patients might be driven by the Hunner lesion (HL) cohort and their propensity for B cell-driven autoimmune diseases (BCDAD), which would support a B cell-driven etiopathogenesis of this inflammatory phenotype. METHODS: We used administrative datasets from the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES) to create a population-based cohort of female patients with HLs who were treated with fulguration in the province of Ontario, Canada over a 10-year period. Our control group were age-matched women undergoing surgery for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). We evaluated the relative rate (RR) of concomitant BCDADs and non-BCDADs amongst the HL cohort compared to controls. RESULTS: Our cohort includes n=953 cases of HL-IC/BPS compared with n=953 age-matched SUI controls. All BCDADs examined in this analysis were significantly more likely to be present in the HL cohort, including multiple sclerosis (MS), systemic lupus erythema (SLE), and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (see Table 1). Some non-BCDADs examined – including Crohn’s, ankylosing spondylitis, and Still’s disease – were also significantly increased amongst the HL cohort. Several additional non-BCDADs showed no differences between the groups, including psoriasis, giant cell arteritis, and polymyalgia rheumatica. Important limitations include lack of a non-HL IC/BPS control group, and the RR reported for SLE may represent an overestimate, as this is a composite diagnostic code and includes other, albeit more rare rheumatologic diagnoses. CONCLUSIONS: Our population-based analysis of B cell-driven autoimmune diseases amongst a large cohort of Hunner lesion patients supports a B cell-driven autoimmune etiopathogenesis of this inflammatory phenotype of IC/BPS. | | | --- | | |

title: THE FIRST PROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY COMPARING FULGURATION OF BIOPSIED HUNNER LESIONS (HLS) TO BLADDER BIOPSY AND FULGURATION OF NON-HL INTERSTITIAL CYSTITIS/BLADDER PAIN SYNDROME
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis (PD02)
authors: Molly McIntyre, Tiziana Cotechini, J. Curtis Nickel, R. Christopher Doiron
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Several cohort studies comparing fulguration of Hunner lesions (HLs) with active control groups has led to it being recommended as an effective treatment option for HL-interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) in several clinical guidelines. All such studies lacked a placebo control or a non-HL control group. We report for the first time, a HL fulguration trial, with a non-HL control group undergoing bladder biopsy and fulguration. METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, part of a larger investigation evaluating the immunologic microenvironment of the urothelium in HL-IC/BPS vs non HL-IC/BPS patients, patients underwent cold cup biopsy under general anesthetic; HL and biopsy site were fulgurated in the HL arm while non-HL subjects underwent biopsy site fulguration. Completed symptom questionnaires at baseline and at 3 months post-treatment were compared between the groups. RESULTS: 16 HL-IC/BPS and 15 non HL-IC/BPS patients were enrolled. Of these, complete baseline and 3-month Interstitial Cystitis Symptom Index (ICSI), Interstitial Cystitis Problem Index (ICPI) were collected from 15 HL-IC/BPS and 9 non HL-IC/BPS patients. Six patients from each cohort also had full Genitourinary Pain Index (GUPI) data for analysis. Baseline scores were not significantly different between groups. At three months follow-up, HL patients demonstrated a significantly greater improvement than non-HL: ICSI decrease of –5.9 (±5.3) vs –0.6 (±3.4) (p=0.009) and ICPI –6.9 (±5.5) vs –0.6 (±3.8) (p=0.009). The GUPI outcomes similarly showed greater improvement in the HL arm though this difference was not statistically significant (see Table 1). CONCLUSIONS: Our findings confirm fulguration is an effective treatment of HL-IC/BPS, for the first time comparing improvements in pain and urinary symptoms to a non-HL control group, who underwent limited ablation of their urothelium. These findings more broadly confirm the real existence of HLs as painful, focal inflammatory lesions within the bladder. | | | --- | | |

title: URINARY PROTEINS STRATIFY SEVERE AND NON-SEVERE PATIENT PHENOTYPES OF UROLOGIC CHRONIC PELVIC PAIN SYNDROME (UCPPS): A MAPP RESEARCH NETWORK STUDY
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis (PD02)
authors: John W. Froehlich, Ted Lee, Tanya Logvinenko, Barnali Das, Adrie van Bokhoven, Marsha Moses, Richard S. Lee
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The pain and urological severity of urologic chronic pelvic pain syndrome (UCPPS) is currently determined by patient questionnaires. An objective and non-invasive molecular test that scales with urinary and/or pain severity would improve management of UCPPS. In this study, we quantify and validate the varying urinary proteome in the UCPPS subpopulation with severe symptom scores, as compared to non-severe subjects. METHODS: Quantitative urinary proteomic analysis of 81 UCPPS subjects was performed. Patients were stratified into “severe” (n=37) and “non-severe” (n=44) subpopulations based on summing pain and urinary severity scores which were derived from the GenitoUrinary Pain Index (GUPI) questionnaire. RESULTS: Utilizing quantitative urinary proteomics, a total of 118 proteins were significantly altered (p<0.05) between the severe and non-severe UCPPS subpopulations. Over 40% of all differentially expressed urinary proteins were regulated by one or more of TGFB1, KRAS, or TNF, implicating these as putative key regulators of UCPPS severity. We developed a model utilizing logistic regression and 4-fold cross validation to identify a panel of 5 proteins with a ROC AUC of 0.928 to predict severe and non-severe UCPPS subpopulations. A parallel analysis of the proteomics data using a decision tree analysis performed similarly. CONCLUSIONS: UCPPS patients with severe pain and urinary symptoms have differentiating quantitative proteomic changes in urine compared to UCPPS patients with less severe symptoms. These markers may be used as an objective measure of severity of UCPPS. These changes impact the activation status of proinflammatory signaling. A subset of these differentially regulated proteins can differentiate severe and non-severe UCPPS patients with high sensitivity and specificity. Informatic analysis of the quantitatively altered urinary proteome implicates specific upstream regulators that could be evaluated as therapeutic targets to minimize UCPPS symptoms.

title: COMPREHENSIVE PROFILING OF URINARY EXTRACELLULAR VESICLE MICRORNAS IDENTIFIES NOVEL DIAGNOSTIC BIOMARKERS FOR IC/BPS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis (PD02)
authors: Fumihiko Urabe, Eriko Kasuya, Mana Nakata, Yue Ogihara, Akira Furuta, Taro Igarashi, Shota Kawano, Takahiro Kimura
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) is characterized by chronic pelvic pain with urinary symptoms, yet diagnosis remains challenging due to reliance on subjective assessment and cystoscopic findings. A reliable, objective biomarker could standardize diagnosis and enable earlier intervention. Extracellular vesicle (EV)–associated microRNAs (miRNAs) are stable in biofluids and have shown promise as disease-specific biomarkers. We conducted comprehensive urinary EV miRNA profiling to identify novel diagnostic markers for IC/BPS. METHODS: We prospectively collected urine samples from 8 patients with Hunner-type IC (HIC), 2 with BPS, and 10 controls without lower urinary tract symptoms. HIC/BPS diagnoses followed the Japanese IC/BPS guideline and were confirmed cystoscopically. Urinary EVs were isolated using a nanowire-based device, and miRNA expression was analyzed with a 3D-Gene Human miRNA Oligo Chip covering 2,632 miRNAs. Quality control yielded 485 miRNAs for analysis. Leave-one-out cross-validation and ROC analysis identified candidate miRNAs with area under the curve (AUC) ≥0.85 and accuracy ≥0.85. Associations with clinical scores (O’Leary–Sant indices, VAS) were assessed via Pearson correlation. RESULTS: Principal component analysis and heatmaps showed distinct clustering of HIC, BPS, and controls ( Figure 1A,B ). Two urinary EV miRNAs—miR-375-5p and miR-6766-5p—met selection criteria, with AUCs of 0.89 and 0.86, and cross-validated accuracies of 0.90 and 0.85, respectively, for differentiating IC/BPS from controls. In HIC vs control analysis, miR-375-5p achieved AUC 0.86 (sensitivity 0.88, specificity 0.90) and miR-6766-5p AUC 0.86 (0.88, 0.80) ( Figure 1C ). No significant correlation was found between candidate miRNA expression and symptom or quality-of-life scores. BMI showed no association with miRNA levels. CONCLUSIONS: This first comprehensive urinary EV miRNA profiling in IC/BPS identified two novel candidates—miR-375-5p and miR-6766-5p—with high diagnostic accuracy. These biomarkers could offer a rapid, non-invasive, objective diagnostic tool for IC/BPS, reducing diagnostic variability and enabling earlier treatment. Validation in larger, multi-center cohorts is warranted.

title: INTEGRATION OF SINGLE-CELL AND SPATIAL TRANSCRIPTOMIC ANALYSES REVEALS PATHOGENIC MECHANISMS IN INTERSTITIAL CYSTITIS/BLADDER PAIN SYNDROME
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis (PD02)
authors: Michael J. Koo, Jihwan Lee, Sihyun Sung, Taekmin Kwon, Kyu Sung Lee, Kwangjin Ko
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) is a chronic inflammatory bladder disorder characterized by pelvic pain and urinary dysfunction that severely impairs quality of life. However, the underlying pathogenic mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study aimed to elucidate the cellular and molecular architecture of Hunner-type IC/BPS by integrating single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomic analyses of patient bladder tissues. METHODS: Bladder tissues were surgically obtained from IC/BPS patients (n=8) and healthy controls (n=2). Single-cell transcriptomic profiling and spatial mapping were conducted to identify cell-type-specific alterations. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) used Hallmark gene sets from MSigDB, and Gene Ontology (GO) analysis was performed via the DAVID database. Cell clusters and subpopulations were annotated based on marker gene expression ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.06#F1)), and spatial gene expression patterns were integrated to examine immune–stromal interactions and smooth muscle remodeling ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.06#F6)). RESULTS: A total of 24 transcriptional clusters were identified, comprising 12 distinct cell types including epithelial, immune, and stromal populations ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.06#F1)). Compared with normal bladder tissue, Hunner lesions exhibited marked infiltration of Th17 cells ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.06#F2)) and enrichment of pro-inflammatory and autoimmune-related pathways ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.06#F3)), suggesting an activated autoimmune microenvironment. Among smooth muscle cell (SMC) subtypes, one IC-enriched cluster showed transcriptional signatures of a phenotypic shift from contractile to synthetic states ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.06#F4)). Pseudotime trajectory analysis revealed that a transition from contractile to synthetic phenotype in this subtype ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.06#F5)). Collectively, these findings delineate an immune–stromal crosstalk tha contributes to the chronic inflammatory and fibrotic features of IC/BPS. CONCLUSIONS: Integration of scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics provided a comprehensive single-cell map of the IC/BPS bladder microenvironment. Coordinated alterations in Th17 cells and SMCs suggest that autoimmune activation and aberrant muscle remodeling contribute towards pain and dysfunction in Hunner-type IC/BPS. These insights reveal key cellular targets for future immunomodulatory or anti-fibrotic therapies.

title: MOLECULAR CHARACTERIZATION OF CHRONIC INFLAMMATORY DISEASES OF THE URINARY BLADDER BASED ON NEXT-GENERATION RNA SEQUENCING AND DIGITAL IMAGE ANALYSIS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis (PD02)
authors: Yoshiyuki Akiyama, Jimpei Miyakawa, Masafumi Horie, Tetsuichi Saito, Tomonori Minagawa, Haruki Kume, Yukio Homma, Yi Luo, Daichi Maeda
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to elucidate distinct cellular and immunological characteristics associated with chronic inflammatory conditions of the urinary bladder, including Hunner-type interstitial cystitis (HIC), bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG)-related cystitis, follicular cystitis (FC), and chronic bacterial cystitis (CBC), by next-generation RNA-sequencing and digital image analysis. METHODS: Mucosal bladder biopsies of HIC (n=21), BCG cystitis (n=13), FC (n=5), or CBC (n=3) were subjected to RNA sequencing and quantitative polymerase chain reaction for key genes involved in adaptive immune responses. Digital immunohistochemical quantification was performed to evaluate and compare the degree of urothelial denudation and the density of infiltrating T-lymphocytes, B-lymphocytes, mast cells, and plasma cells. RESULTS: HIC specimens exhibited a markedly distinct transcriptional profile ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.07#F1)), with 3,566 differentially expressed genes and enrichment of 116 biological processes particularly associated with microbial response and heightened autoimmunity with Th1/Th17 axis polarization. HIC samples showed significantly increased levels of mRNA expression for genes associated with Th1-immune responses (specifically, IL12A/B, IFNG, and TBX21). Histologically, the density of IL-17-positive cells, epithelial denudation, and plasma cell ratio were significantly higher in HIC bladders than other types of cystitis, while there was no difference in the densities of lymphoplasmacytic and mast cells, or in B cell ratio between the groups ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191260.74872.fd.07#F2)). CONCLUSIONS: HIC inflammation is characterized by increased plasma cell infiltration in the context of a Th1/17-polarized immune environment, coupled with epithelial denudation. These findings provide a platform for development of novel treatment strategies, and facilitate basic research into the pathophysiology of this enigmatic disease.

title: CORNEAL CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY AS A DIAGNOSTIC TOOL FOR DETECTING SMALL FIBER NEUROPATHY IN PATIENTS WITH CHRONIC PELVIC PAIN SYNDROME
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis (PD02)
authors: Artem Loktev, Natalia Krotova, Olga Malinina, Maria Sizova
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CPPS) is a challenging condition that has a major impact on the quality of life of both men and women. CPP is a multifactorial disorder where pain may originate in any of the urogynecological, gastrointestinal, pelvic musculoskeletal, or nervous systems and usually unknown etiology. Corneal confocal microscopy (CCM) is a novel technique allows for the quantification of small fibers located near the center of the cornea. CCM is noninvasive and fast, and might be a useful method to confirm small nerve fiber pathology. Our objective was to assess corneal small nerve fiber morphology in patients with CPPS and to determine the prevalence of Small fiber neuropathy (SFN) in patients with CPPS using CCM. METHODS: This was a cross-sectional observational study aimed at evaluating corneal small nerve fiber morphology in patients with CPPS and determining the prevalence of SFN in this population. The study included 27 patients with CPPS who were either unresponsive to initial treatment or had comorbid pain syndromes, along with 10 healthy controls. All participants completed standardized questionnaires assessing symptoms of CPPS, including a neuropathic pain questionnaire, to map clinical characteristics. Corneal imaging was performed using in vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM). Measurements of corneal nerve thickness and dendritic cell density were conducted by a single ophthalmologist blinded to the clinical diagnosis. Outcome Measures: Corneal stromal nerve thickness (quantified in micrometers). Dendritic cell density (cells per square millimeter). Prevalence of SFN based on IVCM findings. RESULTS: In patients with CPPS, the mean stromal nerve thickness was 4.8±1.0 micrometers, which was significantly lower than that of the control group (6.0±1.3 micrometers, p=0.01). Dendritic cell density was significantly higher in patients with CPPS: 10±2 vs. 3±1 in controls (p=0.01). 73% of patients with CPPS showed evidence of SFN as measured by CCM. Comorbid conditions such as chronic prostatitis, irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia and others were frequently observed in patients with CPPS. CONCLUSIONS: Small fiber neuropathy plays an important role in the pathogenesis of chronic pelvic pain. Corneal confocal microscopy is a useful non-invasive method to diagnose SFN in patients with CPPS. The results emphasize the potential of CCM as a tool for early diagnosis and monitoring of SFN, as well as for studying the pathophysiological mechanisms of chronic pain. The lack of changes in the microscopic picture in the background of treatment indicates the need for further studies to identify possible pathogenetic links between SFN and CPPS.

title: ANTLER STEM CELL EXOSOMES AMELIORATE INTERSTITIAL CYSTITIS VIA MITOCHONDRIAL COMPONENT TRANSFER TO REPROGRAMMING MACROPHAGE POLARIZATION
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis (PD02)
authors: Junlong Huang, Zheng Liu, Wenshuang Li, Bolong Liu, Xiangfu Zhou
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Interstitial cystitis (IC) is a chronic inflammatory bladder disease lacking effective treatments. Exosomes from antler stem cells (ASC-Exos), derived from regenerating deer antler tissue, exhibit immunomodulatory properties, but their mechanisms in IC remain unclear. METHODS: An IC rat model was established via intravesical LPS/protamine sulfate instillation and treated with ASC-Exos. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated through pain threshold testing, urodynamics, histopathology, and immunofluorescence. Fluorescently labeled ASC-Exos were tracked in vivo. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) identified cellular targets and transcriptional changes. Mitochondrial transfer was assessed using MitoTracker labeling and confocal microscopy. Mitochondrial function was measured via mtDNA copy number, membrane potential, oxygen consumption rate, ATP production, and mitochondrial ROS. Macrophage polarization was evaluated by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence. Co-culture systems assessed ASC-Exos-treated macrophage effects on epithelial repair. Macrophage depletion confirmed their therapeutic necessity. RESULTS: ASC-Exos significantly ameliorated IC pathology, reducing inflammation, restoring barrier integrity, and alleviating pain and voiding dysfunction. Fluorescence tracking showed preferential ASC-Exos uptake by bladder macrophages. ScRNA-seq identified macrophages as predominant infiltrating immune cells with markedly downregulated oxidative phosphorylation genes and mitochondrial respiratory pathways in IC. ASC-Exos transferred mitochondrial components to macrophages, restoring mitochondrial function (increased mtDNA, membrane potential, oxygen consumption, ATP; decreased mitochondrial ROS). This mitochondrial rescue promoted M1-to-M2 macrophage polarization, reducing pro-inflammatory and increasing anti-inflammatory markers. ASC-Exos-treated macrophages enhanced epithelial cell migration, proliferation, and tight junction expression. Macrophage depletion abolished therapeutic effects. CONCLUSIONS: ASC-Exos alleviate IC by transferring mitochondrial components to dysfunctional macrophages, restoring metabolic homeostasis and reprogramming M1-to-M2 phenotype, thereby promoting epithelial repair. This establishes ASC-Exos as a novel mitochondrial transfer-based cell-free therapy for IC.

title: THERAPEUTIC EFFICACY OF CAPACITIVE-RESISTIVE MONOPOLAR RADIOFREQUENCY IN PATIENTS WITH CHRONIC PELVIC PAIN SYNDROME: A RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis (PD02)
authors: Olga Malinina, Ulyana Boreiko
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Capacitive-resistive monopolar radiofrequency (CRMRF) therapy at a frequency of 448 kHz is a non-invasive technology that delivers energy to tissues via specialized electrodes. It effectively alleviates pain through both thermal and non-thermal mechanisms. Non-thermal effects promote tissue regeneration by stimulating mesenchymal stem cell proliferation and exert anti-inflammatory actions, potentially via modulation of cytokine expression (e.g., MCP-1, IL-4). Thermal stimulation enhances blood flow, oxygen delivery, and metabolic clearance, thereby reducing ischemic pain . METHODS: A total of 150 patients (100 females, 50 males) diagnosed with myofascial pain syndrome, pudendal neuralgia, interstitial cystitis, chronic prostatitis, or endometriosis were enrolled. Participants completed standardized questionnaires including:Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for pain intensity (0–10) Sexual Quality of Life-Female Version (SQOL-F) or Male Version (SQOL-M) Pelvic Pain and Urgency/Frequency Symptom Scale (PUF) International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) – for male participantsPatients were randomly assigned to two groups:Intervention group : CRMRF therapy (8 sessions every 5–7 days) targeting the suprapubic and perineal regions using capacitive (10 min) and resistive (15 min) modes, combined with supervised physical therapy. Intensity was gradually increased from level 1 to 5 based on treatment progress. Control group: Supervised physical therapy only. RESULTS: In the intervention group, significant improvements were observed compared to the control group: Pain reduction : Mean VAS score decreased from 7.34±1.28 to 2.82±1.19 vs. 7.49±1.17 to 4.51±1.12 in the control group (p<0.05) Sexual Quality of Life : Significant improvement in SQOL scores indicating enhanced sexual satisfaction and overall well-being Symptom burden : Improvement in PUF and IPSS scores suggesting reduced urinary urgency/frequency and better functional outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: The addition of CRMRF therapy to standard physical therapy significantly improves pain relief, sexual function, and overall quality of life in patients with chronic pelvic pain syndromes. These findings support its integration into multidisciplinary management protocols aligned with current international urological congress standards for patient-centered care.

title: TO REMOVE, RECONSTRUCT, OR RETAIN? EVALUATING SURGICAL MANAGEMENT OF THE NATIVE BLADDER IN PATIENTS WITH INTERSTITIAL CYSTITIS/BLADDER PAIN SYNDROME
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis (PD02)
authors: Angeleque S. Hartt, Nooshin Tafazoli, Chiyuan Amy Zhang, Ashu Mohammad, Zoe Gan, Amy D. Dobberfuhl
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) is a chronic, debilitating condition characterized by bladder pain and urinary urgency in the absence of infection or other identifiable causes. Although conservative management with lifestyle modification and pharmacotherapy provides relief for many patients, a subset remains refractory to these interventions. For these individuals, surgical options such as substitution cystoplasty or urinary diversion with or without cystectomy may be pursued. This study examines over three decades of surgical cases at Stanford Hospital to characterize patient demographics and quantify postoperative pain outcomes, aiming to identify patterns and differences in recovery across surgical approaches. METHODS: This single-institution, IRB-approved retrospective cohort study included patients with IC/BPS identified by CPT code who underwent substitution cystoplasty or urinary diversion at Stanford Hospital over the past 30 years. A REDCap database identified 58 patients, of whom 49 were confirmed to have a true diagnosis of IC/BPS upon direct chart review. These patients were categorized into three surgical treatment groups: (1) total cystectomy with urinary diversion, (2) supratrigonal cystectomy with substitution cystoplasty, and (3) urinary diversion without cystectomy. Excluded cases were used as a matched non-diseased cohort for comparative outcome analysis. De-identified clinical data were analyzed descriptively and through multivariable logistic regression using SPSS software. RESULTS: Of the 58 patients included in this study, the average age ranged from 54–60 years with comparable BMIs across study groups (26.6–30.7 kg/m). Baseline symptom severity did not differ significantly based on available chart data (ICSI 14.6–15.5, p=0.84; ICPI 10.7–13.7, p=0.80). Chronic overlapping pain conditions (COPs) were also comparable between groups (p=0.75). Postoperative pain improvement was reported across all surgical cohorts without statistically significant differences noted amongst the different types of surgical intervention (p=0.37). Most patients discontinued urologic IC/BPS pain medications postoperatively, though no difference was observed between treatment groups (p=0.63). Race, however, was found to be statistically different between treatment groups (p=0.011). CONCLUSIONS: The findings demonstrate that patient demographics, baseline symptom severity, and postoperative outcomes were largely comparable across surgical treatment groups for IC/BPS. While pain relief and medication discontinuation were commonly observed following surgery, no statistically significant differences were detected between the different surgical interventions. The only factor that differed significantly between groups was race, which may warrant further investigation to assess potential sociodemographic or access-to-care disparities, as well highlight a limitation in our homogenous study cohorts. Overall, these results suggest that each surgical approach yielded similar postoperative outcomes, supporting the interpretation that surgical selection may be tailored based on clinical presentation and patient preference rather than expected differences in efficacy.

title: ARE THERE UROLOGICAL CONSEQUENCES TO MEDICINAL KETAMINE? A FIVE-YEAR MULTI-INSTITUTIONAL ANALYSIS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis (PD02)
authors: Atieh Ashkezari, Akiva Grimaldi, Joshua Wang, Robert Moldwin
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ketamine is an FDA-approved anesthetic and analgesic now used for treatment-resistant depression. Though medically indicated, it is also misused recreationally, where chronic exposure causes bladder inflammation, fibrosis, and upper tract injury. These findings raise concern for long-term urologic effects in therapeutic use. We evaluated the 3- and 5-year incidence of urinary diagnoses and procedures following medicinal ketamine exposure using a large, multi-institutional dataset. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was performed using the TriNetX Research Network (2000–2020). Adults aged 18–50 years with substance use disorder diagnoses (ICD-10: F10–F19) were included. To isolate medicinal rather than recreational exposure, patients with F16 (hallucinogen-related disorders), which includes illicit ketamine, were excluded. Because TriNetX aggregates data from hospital-based populations, both cohorts consisted of individuals with substance-related conditions rather than healthy controls. Cohort A included those prescribed ketamine (RxNorm 6130) within one year before a substance use diagnosis; Cohort B comprised matched controls without ketamine exposure. Propensity-score matching (1:1) on 21 demographic and clinical covariates yielded 51,198 patients per arm. Incident urologic diagnoses and procedures were evaluated at 3 and 5 years using risk ratios (RR, 95% CI). RESULTS: After matching, 102,396 patients were included (mean age 34.7±8.3; 56% male). Medicinal ketamine users had higher risks of multiple urinary diagnoses and procedures at both 3 and 5 years. Greatest increases were seen for neurogenic bladder and urinary retention, while cystitis and voiding difficulty showed smaller but significant elevations. Effect sizes persisted, though slightly attenuated over time, suggesting sustained rather than progressive risk. Full estimates are shown in Tables 1 and 2. CONCLUSIONS: Within a hospital-based, substance-diagnosed population, exposure to medicinal ketamine was associated with modest but sustained elevations in bladder-related diagnostic and procedural coding over 3 to 5 years. Although causality cannot be inferred and dosing patterns were not available, these findings align with prior literature showing that urinary effects from ketamine appear related to cumulative exposure rather than isolated use. Considering that legitimate medical indications, such as chronic pain and treatment-resistant depression, may involve ongoing administration rather than single doses, continued evaluation of the long-term urologic safety profile of therapeutic ketamine is warranted. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: ELEVATED PSYCHIATRIC COMORBIDITY AND POLYGENIC RISK FOR DEPRESSION IN INTERSTITIAL CYSTITIS/BLADDER PAIN SYNDROME
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis (PD02)
authors: Catherine Astrid Brownstein, Elicia Estrella, Ashish Jain, Madelyn Weisenhahn, Melissa Fernandes, Emma Deaso, Kamil E. Barbour, Liang Sun, David Glahn
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) is a chronic pain condition with significant psychiatric comorbidity. However, systematic psychiatric evaluation of individuals with IC/BPS using gold-standard diagnostic interviews has not yet been performed. Therefore, we conducted the first study integrating Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 (SCID-5) assessments and genome-wide polygenic risk scoring (PRS) to evaluate whether psychiatric comorbidity in IC/BPS reflects psychosocial effects of chronic pain or shared genetic vulnerability. METHODS: Forty-three individuals with clinically confirmed IC/BPS completed the SCID-5 to establish DSM-5 psychiatric diagnoses. Two genotyped cohorts of individuals with clinically confirmed IC/BPS (IC1: n=88; IC2: n=76) were analyzed using the Illumina Global Screening Array and imputation to the 1000 Genomes reference. Polygenic risk scores (PRS) for depression and anxiety traits were computed using validated Polygenic Score Catalog models and compared to matched European-ancestry controls using Wilcoxon tests with false discovery rate (FDR) correction. RESULTS: Among 43 participants completing the SCID-5 (43% of those invited to participate), 55% met criteria for an anxiety disorder and 42.5% for a depressive disorder, with Panic Disorder (27.5%) and Major Depressive Disorder (20%) most prevalent; 15% reported suicidal ideation attributable to IC/BPS. PRS analysis revealed significantly higher genetic risk for ‘Recent feelings of depression’ (PGS001899; adjusted p=0.04) in IC1. Though significance did not survive correction for multiple testing for any other PRS, the direction of effect was consistent across cohorts with PRS distributions elevated for _Major depression_ (PGS000193; _IC1_), _Seen a psychiatrist for nerves, anxiety, tension or depression_ (PGS000141; _IC2_), and _Depression_ (PGS000145; _IC2_). CONCLUSIONS: IC/BPS is associated with significant psychiatric morbidity and genetic susceptibility to depression, indicating a shared biological pathway between affective regulation and pain perception. These findings support integrating psychiatric screening and cognitive behavioral therapy into IC/BPS management. Incorporating PRS into clinical risk assessment may enable precision stratification and improved outcomes in urologic care.

title: PARAURETHRAL INJECTION OF HYALURONIC ACID FOR THE TREATMENT OF RECURRENT POSTCOITAL CYSTITIS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis (PD02)
authors: Tatiana Lukomnik, Olga Malinina
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Postcoital cystitis (PC) impacts patients' quality of life. Current treatment strategies, primarily antibiotic prophylaxis, are associated with increasing antimicrobial resistance and various side effects. Periurethral hyaluronic acid injections have emerged as an alternative treatment option for women. Our study examines the efficacy and cost-effectiveness of periurethral hyaluronic acid (HA) injections for reducing the frequency of PC episodes. To evaluate the effectiveness of periurethral injection of a bulking gel in reducing the frequency of postcoital cystitis episodes over a 12-month follow-up period compared to a control group. METHODS: The study included 318 women with postcoital cystitis and a positive O'Donnell-Hirschhorn test, treated between 2018 and 2025. The study group (n=268) received combination therapy (standard treatment and paraurethral injections of a hyaluronic acid-based filler). The control group (n=50) received antibiotic therapy alone. Paraurethral injections of gel (1–2 ml) were performed using fan-shaped movements from the 6 o'clock position. This technique created a "gel cushion" that elevated the external meatus and distal urethra, thereby limiting their mobility and preventing injury during sexual intercourse. Follow-up examinations were performed at 3, 6, and 12 months after the injection. RESULTS: In the combination therapy group, postcoital cystitis recurred for the first time after 12 months in only 47 patients (17.5%), as the gel biodegraded, requiring repeat filler injections. Quality of life (UDI 6 and PISQ-12 questionnaires) improved in 82.5% of patients (p<0.05). In the control group, postcoital cystitis recurred for the first time after 3 and 6 months in 47 patients (94%), requiring repeat antibiotic therapy. Quality of life improved in 3 patients (6%). No complications were observed. CONCLUSIONS: The results of this study will enable the widespread adoption of an effective, minimally invasive, and safe treatment method for postcoital cystitis associated with urethral dystopia. This will serve as an alternative to both long-term antibiotic therapy and invasive surgical interventions. This will improve treatment adherence and quality of life for millions of women.

title: ANALYSIS OF NOVEL GENETIC FACTORS CONTRIBUTING TO LL-37 RESISTANCE IN CLINICALLY ISOLATED UROPATHOGENIC _ESCHERICHIA COLI_
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Interstitial Cystitis (PD02)
authors: Swami P. Sadanala, Namrata V. Sawant, Eesha Desai, Joseph Boll, Philippe E. Zimmern, Nicole J. De Nisco
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The human cathelicidin, LL-37 is a broad-spectrum cationic antimicrobial peptide that defends the urinary tract against infection. Escherichia coli (UPEC) is the most common causative agent of UTI, and some strains have developed resistance towards LL-37, causing severe and recurrent infections. UPEC strains likely employ a diversity of mechanisms to resist LL-37 but few have been characterized. Recurrent UTI isolate EcPNK007 exhibits extreme resistance to LL-37 (MIC>32 μM), but this resistance is independent of previously identified mechanisms. The goal of this work was to determine the mechanistic basis for LL-37 resistance in rUTI UPEC to better understand how UPEC subverts host defenses. METHODS: A transposon mutant library of LL-37-resistant EcPNK007, a UPEC strain isolated from a postmenopausal woman with active rUTI, was constructed using the Himar1 mariner transposon system. Genomic DNA was isolated from the transposon library grown in LB and LB with 16 μM LL-37 and subject to Illumina sequencing to identify genes essential for LL-37 fitness in EcPNK007. Markerless gene deletions were performed using the Lambda Red system. SDS-EDTA growth inhibition assays were performed to assess outer membrane (OM) integrity. Broth microdilution LL-37 susceptibility testing was performed to quantify LL-37 minimum inhibitory/bactericidal concentrations (MIC/MBC) of single and double gene mutants to define epistatic relationships between genes required for LL-37 resistance. RESULTS: Tn-seq identified 69 genes required for growth in 16 μM LL-37. Top hits included genes encoding proteins involved in OM integrity (ybjX, nlpD), drug efflux (yqjA), and global gene regulation (phoPQ). Isogenic ΔphoP, ΔybjX, ΔyqjA, ΔnlpD, PNK007ΔphoPΔybjX, PNK007ΔphoPΔnlpD, and PNK007ΔphoPΔyqjA mutants demonstrated >3 log10 reduction in the presence of 16 μM LL-37. Mutant strains showed similar MIC/MBCs to LL-37 sensitive strains (<8 μM). Deletion mutants ΔphoP, ΔnlpD, ΔamiC, and ΔyqjA, showed significant SDS-EDTA sensitivity, highlighting their critical role in OM integrity. Finally, epistasis analysis of LL-37 resistance genes revealed that while ybjX and yqjA are regulated by phoP, amiC and nlpD are part of a different, yet to be defined, regulatory pathway in EcPNK007. CONCLUSIONS: Genes critical for rUTI UPEC fitness in LL-37 were identified and found to contribute to OM integrity, revealing enhancement of OM integrity as a critical LL-37 resistance mechanism. Epistasis analysis revealed multiple regulatory pathways are involved in rUTI UPEC LL-37 resistance and identified the contribution of both Pho-dependent and Pho-independent regulatory mechanisms to LL-37 fitness.

title: ROBOTIC PARASTOMAL HERNIA REPAIR OF ILEAL CONDUIT: KEYHOLE TECHNIQUE WITH NOVEL MESH COLLAR MODIFICATION
session: Upper Tract Reconstruction I (V01)
authors: Sean P. Elliott, James V. Harmon
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Parastomal hernia repair has low success rates in the literature. Recurrence rates range from <20% for Sugarbaker technique to >30% for keyhole technique. However, these data may not apply to urinary conduits as there are few urinary conduits in these series. We are concerned that the Sugarbaker technique could cause renal obstruction in urinary conduits. Concerns with the existing keyhole technique include the risk of sliding hernia and the risk of the permanent mesh triangle flaps eroding into the conduit. We sought to modify the keyhole technique to address these shortcomings. METHODS: We have developed a mesh collar that is absorbable on both the inner and outer face. We demonstrate how we create this collar and secure it to the keyhole mesh. We then demonstrate the technique for robotic implantation. We review our success in all patients undergoing this procedure (with our without a collar) in the last 18 months. Success was defined as no recurrence on cross-sectional imaging. RESULTS: Among 7 patients undergoing robotic parastomal hernia repair of a urinary stoma with a keyhole technique, 6 were in ileal conduits and one in a Mitrofanoff. We performed the keyhole without a stomal collar in 4 (including the one Mitrofanoff) and with a stomal collar in 3. Success rates by cross sectional imaging are 100% but follow-up is limited to 6 months. There were no complications. CONCLUSIONS: Robotic parastomal hernia repair of urinary stomas is a minimally invasive option that helps minimize further injury to the fascia. A keyhole repair is feasible and safe. The addition of a mesh collar may help reduce recurrence rates. The innovative double-sided feature of the collar may help reduce the risk of erosion into native bowel and the conduit.

title: SINGLE-PORT ROBOTIC URETEROENTERIC STRICTURE REPAIR
session: Upper Tract Reconstruction I (V01)
authors: Wattanachai Ratanapornsompong, Sutthirat Sarawong, Amr Elbakry, Jeffery S. Lin, Lee C. Zhao
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ureteroenteric strictures (UES) are a significant complication following urinary diversion and often require surgical reconstruction. This video aims to illustrate ureteroenteric stricture repair using the single-port (SP) robotic platform and to demonstrate non-transecting techniques—specifically side-to-side anastomosis and Y-V plasty—that preserve ureteral vascularity. METHODS: Representative cases were performed using the SP robotic platform via a transperitoneal approach. Key operative steps included stricture exposure, flap creation, and anastomosis under near-infrared fluorescence guidance. Non-transecting techniques were applied for short or moderate strictures with preserved ureteral mobility, while complex cases were managed with bowel flaps. Outcomes were evaluated for perioperative parameters, complications, and stricture-free rates. RESULTS: Twenty-eight SP robotic UES repairs were performed. Median operative time was 189 minutes and median blood loss 20 mL. The median stricture length was 2 cm (range 1–10). Median hospital stay was one day, with five day-case surgeries. Minor complications occurred in 21.7% and major in 13%. At a median 23-month follow-up, the overall success rate was 96.4%. CONCLUSIONS: Single-port robotic ureteroenteric stricture repair using non-transecting and selective flap techniques is safe, precise, and effective. The SP platform facilitates minimally invasive reconstruction with high success and low morbidity. | | | --- | | |

title: ROBOTIC URETEROCALICOSTOMY FOR COMPLEX PROXIMAL URETERAL STRICTURES: SURGICAL EXPERIENCE AND TECHNICAL CONSIDERATIONS
session: Upper Tract Reconstruction I (V01)
authors: Yishun Y. Huang, Xiang X. Wang, Xinfei X. Li, Kunlin K. Yang, Xuesong X. Li
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This video is to demonstrate the surgical technique and clinical outcomes of robotic ureterocalicostomy (UC) for complex proximal ureteral strictures in our institution, particularly in patients with congenital anomalies and a history of prior urinary tract reconstruction. METHODS: Between January 2024 and February 2025, four patients underwent UC in our institution. The procedure involved mobilization of the distal ureter and lower pole of the kidney, carefully avoiding the collecting system and renal vessels. A fan-shaped proximal ureter was prepared for anastomosis, followed by opening of the dependent lower calyx and mucosa-to-mucosa anastomosis with 4-0 barbed sutures. In one patient with congenital megaureter and a history of ureteroneocystostomy, a combined side-to-side ureteroneocystostomy was performed to address distal ureteral stricture. The video showcases the technical subtleties, such as hemostatic control and preservation of the renal vasculature. RESULTS: All patients had a history of prior upper urinary tract reconstruction. Three had congenital anomalies, including renal malrotation with horseshoe kidney, congenital ureteropelvic junction obstruction, and congenital megaureter. The remaining patient, although without anomalies, had undergone multiple prior interventions for ipsilateral ureteral calculi. The mean operative time was 160.25±24.22 minutes, with a median estimated blood loss of 30 mL (range 20–30). During a median follow-up of 16 months (range 8–22), all patients achieved clinical success, and no Clavien–Dindo grade ≥II complications occurred. Representative cases demonstrated patent anastomoses, unobstructed drainage, and favorable functional outcomes on follow-up imaging. CONCLUSIONS: Preliminary clinical results indicates that robotic ureterocalicostomy is a safe, effective, and feasible reconstructive option for managing complex upper urinary tract obstructions. It provides new treatment methods and approaches for patients with congenital malformations or previous failed repairs in clinical practice. However, large-sample, and long-term studies are still needed.

title: SINGLE PORT ROBOTIC TOTAL URINARY TRACT RECONSTRUCTION AFTER PELVIC CRUSH INJURY
session: Upper Tract Reconstruction I (V01)
authors: Audra Garrigan, Lucas Wiegand
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This video details a total urinary tract reconstruction of a patient following pelvic crush injury using the da Vinci Single Port Robot System. The objective of this video is to demonstrate that the SP system enables concurrent ureteral reimplantation and posterior urethroplasty. METHODS: Surgical video detailing SP robotic repair.
