The patient was then monitored for several months with post operative imaging to evaluate for successful repair. RESULTS: The patient had an uneventful postoperative course. Following discharge, he has been observed for several months without evidence of recurrence. The patient had no post operative hydronephrosis and is voiding spontaneously successfully. CONCLUSIONS: The SP robotic system enabled concurrent bilateral ureteral repair and posterior urethroplasty allowing for a successful reconstruction. SP can be a useful tool when treating a patient after trauma to provide access to complex and difficult to reach areas.

title: SINGLE-PORT ROBOTIC-ASSISTED TRANSVAGINAL RETROPERITONEAL URETERAL REIMPLANTATION: EARLY EXPERIENCE
session: Upper Tract Reconstruction I (V01)
authors: Aleksandra Walasek, Wattanachai Ratanapornsompong, Sutthirat Sarawong, Amr Elbakry, Lee Zhao
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Single-port robotic-assisted transvaginal retroperitoneal ureteral reimplantation represents a novel, minimally invasive technique for managing distal ureteral strictures in female patients. This approach provides direct retroperitoneal access without entering the peritoneal cavity, potentially reducing morbidity and expediting recovery. METHODS: Between January 2024 and September 2025, the transvaginal approach was attempted in six female patients undergoing robotic ureteral reimplantation. The retroperitoneal space was entered through an anterolateral vaginal fornix incision using a small SP access port. The ureter was dissected along the external iliac and superior vesical vessels and reimplanted into the bladder using a refluxing technique. RESULTS: The mean age was 48 years (range 42–62), and five patients had a history of prior abdominal surgery. In three patients with prior surgery and iatrogenic ureteral injury, conversions to the robotic low anterior approach was necessary—two due to dense scarring at the ureteral stump preventing safe dissection, and one due to a higher-than-anticipated ureteral injury necessitating a transperitoneal ileal ureter. No intraoperative complications occurred; one converted case required blood transfusion. The mean operative time for the transvaginal cases was 195 minutes and all were discharged within 24 hours. At a mean follow-up of 6.5 months (1–19), all patients were hardware-free, symptom-free, and had no obstruction on imaging. No sexual dysfunction or major complications were observed. CONCLUSIONS: Single-port robotic-assisted transvaginal retroperitoneal ureteral reimplantation is a feasible and safe technique for distal ureteral reconstruction, offering minimal invasiveness and rapid recovery with excellent short-term outcomes. Surgeons offering this technique should be facile with alternative approaches, as previous surgery with iatrogenic ureteral injury can lead do dense fibrosis and distortion of the anatomy, necessitating conversion.

title: ROBOTIC RIGHT TO LEFT TRANSURETEROURETEROSTOMY WITH A LEFT URETERAL REIMPLANT IN BILATERAL URETERAL STRICTURE DISEASE
session: Upper Tract Reconstruction I (V01)
authors: Elisabeth Rindner, Daniella Portal, Michael Markel, Nathan Shaw
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Reconstructive urologic surgery is typically the gold standard for definitive management of complex bilateral ureteral strictures. In this video, we present a case of a robotic right to left transureteroureterostomy with a left ureteral reimplant in a patient with stage IV endometriosis who subsequently developed bilateral ureteral strictures. METHODS: Patient was placed in supine position. Robotic ports were placed in a standard fashion. The peritoneum was divided at the level of the right iliac vessels to expose the retroperitoneal space. The right hydronephrotic ureter was identified and transected at the level of the strictured segment. Then, the proximal landing point on the left ureter was identified. A tunnel was created under the sigmoid colon to pass the right ureter to the proximal mid left ureter. The distal most aspect of the left ureter was identified for the neocystotomy and the anterior peritoneum was incised to expose the bladder. A left posterior dome cystotomy was made and the left ureter was reimplanted into the bladder. A ureterotomy was made in the left ureter and an end to side ureteral anastomosis was made between the right and left ureter to form the transureteroureterostomy. A ureteral stent was placed and both a peritoneal flap and omental tissue were placed over the distal suture lines. A drain was placed and the robot was undocked. RESULTS: Total operative time was 316 minutes. Estimated blood loss was minimal. The patient was discharged on post operative day (POD) 3. The foley was removed on POD7. Patient’s post operative course was complicated by two hospital admissions for urinary tract infections. The patient’s stent and left nephrostomy tube were removed at 5 weeks after confirmatory retrograde pyelogram demonstrated a well healed and patent ureteral anastomosis. The right nephrostomy tube was removed after 7 weeks. CONCLUSIONS: This video features key components of robotic bilateral ureteral reconstruction. Our approach demonstrated that it is feasible to perform robotic concomitant distal and proximal ureteral reconstruction without compromising vascularity and without the need for more complex ureteral reconstruction methods, which can be associated with higher morbidity.

title: ROBOTIC APPENDICEAL ONLAY FLAP FOR SALVAGE URETEROPLASTY AFTER FAILED BUCCAL MUCOSA GRAFT
session: Upper Tract Reconstruction I (V01)
authors: Raeesa Islam, Kristen Duncan, Sammy E. Elsamra
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: § A 65-year-old female presented with severe right hydronephrosis, recurrent right ureteral stones secondary to a proximal ureteral stricture and was therefore taken to the operating room for a Single-Port right ureteroplasty with buccal mucosal graft and omental wrap. However, she represented three more times with right flank pain, hydronephrosis, and more stones. Retrograde pyelogram at the time of a ureteroscopy for stone surgery revealed a UPJ obstruction proximal to the buccal graft site. She underwent laser endopyelotomy and ballon dilation. She recovered well initially but then returned once more with the same symptoms. She had a nephrostomy tube placed and then diagnostic testing with antegrade nephrostogram, retrograde pyelogram and cystogram. There was evidence on these imaging studies of a distal ureteral stricture. She was booked for a robotic right ureteral reimplant with psoas hitch. However, once she was in the OR and her distal ureter was dissected, it appeared normal. Ureteroscopy was performed at this time which confirmed the suspicion that the distal ureter was indeed patent. In fact, the flexible ureteroscope was able to traverse the entire ureter. However, proximally at the site of the buccal mucosal graft and omental wrap, there was tortuosity and kinking of the patent ureter. METHODS: Though the ureter was patent and the ureteroscope could easily navigate and ascend to the renal pelvis, we suspected that these kinks were the cause for her functional obstruction. We excised the omentum that was wrapped around the right ureter. We also mobilized the lower pole and lateral aspect of the kidney. We then incised the ureter and detubularized it for roughly 7 cm, essentially the entire proximal ureter. We identified the appendix and isolated its origin off the cecum. A robotic 8 mm staple load to ligate off the appendix from the cecum with care to preserve the ileocecal artery. The appendix was aligned over the detubularized portion of the ureter and identified which orientation would be proper (in this case the distal tip was placed most cephalad). We then detubularized the appendix. We sewed the appendix onto the detubularized portion of ureter using 4-0 Vicryl suture in multiple locations to anchor it in place and then using 3-O STRATAFIX in a running fashion to perform the anastomosis. We performed ureteroscopy once more to confirm the ureter was straight, without stricture, without kinking, and the repair was watertight. We placed an 8 French by 24 cm double-J stent over a wire, left a 15 Blake drainand closed in standard fashion. RESULTS: The patient was discharged on POD2 after she passed trial of void and JP was removed. She was discharged with the nephrostomy to drainage as she was having right flank pain, although the opening pressure was low. After 2 weeks, antegrade nephrostogram confirmed patency with the stent and nephrostomy tube was removed. The stent was removed after 6 weeks. Two months out from surgery, patient is doing well without any flank pain, hydronephrosis, AKI, UTIs, or stones. CONCLUSIONS: Appendiceal onlay flap is a good salvage option for long right ureteral reconstruction.

title: TECHNICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR ROBOTIC CYSTECTOMY WITH INTRACORPOREAL URINARY DIVERSION IN CONGENITAL INTESTINAL MALROTATION
session: Upper Tract Reconstruction I (V01)
authors: Rainjade Chung, Michael Lesgart, Benjamin J. Croll, Tamir Sholklapper, Zafardjan Dalimov, Shivaram Cumarasamy, Abigail Keller, Randall A. Lee
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Congenital intestinal malrotation is a rare anatomical abnormality that affects up to 1:500 live births who ultimately have symptomatic malrotation. Malrotation results from abnormal rotation of the gut during embryogenesis. During normal development, the gastrointestinal tract rotates 270 degrees as it migrates into its final position in the abdomen. Congenital intestinal malrotation results when the full rotation is not completed. As a result, the mesentery is narrowed, and the surgeons should expect the large intestine to be on the patient’s left and the small bowel on the right ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191264.83903.71.08#F1)). Our objective was to describe technical considerations when approaching intracorporeal diversion in a patient with congenital intestinal malrotation. METHODS: The patient was a 77 yo male with HGT1 bladder cancer who had failed and exhausted multiple therapies including BCG induction x2, gemcitabine/docetaxel induction x1, pembrolizumab, and nadofaragene firadenovec. He consented to undergo robotic radical cystectomy with intracorporeal urinary diversion. RESULTS: The operative time was 6 hrs 38 mins with an estimated blood loss of 100 ccs. Postoperatively, the patient developed an ileus on postoperative day 4, which resolved with an NGT and TPN. He was discharged home on postoperative day 14. His final pathology was pTisN0 with negative surgical margins. CONCLUSIONS: Congenital intestinal malrotation should not preclude patients from receiving an intracorporeal ileal conduit diversion. The primary consideration is staying oriented and recognizing that the intestinal anatomy will be atypical. In cases of incomplete malrotation the large intestine is positioned predominantly on the left, the ileocecal junction lies near the midline, and the small intestine occupies the right side of the abdomen. Most importantly, the conduit should be rotated in a counterclockwise direction rather than clockwise, to prevent ischemic complications.

title: SINGLE PORT ROBOTIC NON-TRANSECTING PYELOPLASTY IN RENAL TRANSPLANT
session: Upper Tract Reconstruction I (V01)
authors: Carlos Casanova-Martín, Aleksandra Walasek, Alejandra Gómez-Villanueva, Luis Martínez-Piñeiro, Lee C. Zhao
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ureteral obstruction occurs in 2-10% of renal transplant patients, with ureteric ischemia accounting for around 90% of cases. Management of Ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO) in transplant recipients presents unique challenges due to altered anatomy, compromised vascular supply, and the need to preserve graft function. Single-port robotic surgery offers enhanced visualization and precision while minimizing surgical trauma. Non-transecting techniques may reduce ischemic injury in transplanted kidneys with already compromised blood supply. METHODS: Patient Presentation: A 69-year-old female with a complex medical history including diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, treated hepatitis C virus infection, and end-stage renal disease underwent deceased donor renal transplantation in June 2022\. The immediate post-transplant period was complicated, requiring surgical re-exploration and revision. One year post-transplant (June 2023), the patient developed hydronephrosis of the transplanted kidney requiring percutaneous nephrostomy tube (PCNT) placement for urinary drainage and preservation of graft function. Surgical Technique: A single incision was placed to access the transplanted kidney in the iliac fossa. The ureteropelvic junction was carefully dissected and exposed with meticulous preservation of periureteral tissues to maintain vascular supply. A non-transecting technique was employed, utilizing a longitudinal incision through the stenotic segment following the Heineke-Mikulicz principle. The spatulated anastomosis was performed with running absorbable suture, and a double-J ureteral stent was placed for internal drainage. RESULTS: The patient tolerated the procedure well without intraoperative complications. The postoperative recovery was excellent, with the patient being discharged home within 24 hours of surgery. The patient has remained free of urinary tract infections since the procedure. Renal function has been preserved with serum creatinine remaining stable and similar to her pre-obstruction baseline values throughout the follow-up period. Resolution of hydronephrosis was achieved, and the patient has maintained good graft function. CONCLUSIONS: Single-port robotic non-transecting pyeloplasty is a safe, effective option for UPJO in renal transplant recipients, achieving successful reconstruction with preserved function and minimal morbidity.

title: UPPER URINARY TRACT RECONSTRUCTION FOR THE TREATMENT OF URETERAL STRICTURE IN A DUPLEX COLLECTING SYSTEM: OUR EXPERIENCE
session: Upper Tract Reconstruction I (V01)
authors: Yixuan Huang, Xinfei Li, Liqing Xu, Honggang Ying, Guanpeng Han, Shihao Liu, Zhihua Li, Kunlin Yang, Xuesong Li
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: A duplex collecting system (DCS) is a relatively common anatomical anomaly that may remain asymptomatic; however, when complicated by ureteral stricture it can lead to hydronephrosis, recurrent urinary tract infection, and loss of renal function. Upper Urinary tract reconstruction can relieve obstruction while avoiding resection of a renal moiety and maximising renal preservation. Given the variability and unpredictable anatomy inherent to DCS, reconstruction demands individualised strategies and presents distinct operative challenges. We aimed to describe our surgical strategy and report clinical outcomes of upper urinary tract reconstruction in adult patients with DCS complicated by ureteral stricture. METHODS: Between January 2014 and March 2025, 15 patients with a DCS underwent laparoscopic or robot-assisted upper urinary tract reconstruction for ureteral stricture. Clinical success was defined as symptom-free/relief, no radiographic re-obstruction, and stable/improved renal function. Post-operative complications were graded using the Clavien–Dindo classification. RESULTS: Fifteen patients were included, involving 18 kidneys and 26 ureters. Aetiologies were predominantly congenital anomalies (11/15, 73.3%), with prior radiotherapy in 2 (13.3%), and one case each of ureteric polyp and tuberculosis (6.7% each). Moiety involvement affected the upper moiety in 2 (13.3%), the lower moiety in 5 (33.3%), and both moieties in 8 patients (53.3%). Procedures were laparoscopic in 5 (33.3%) and robot-assisted in 10 (66.7%); one laparoscopic case converted to open, with all others completed minimally invasively. Median operative time was 154 (range 75–340) minutes. One Grade II complication occurred (6.7%); there were no ≥Grade III events. At a median follow-up of 24 months (range 6–48), clinical success was achieved in all patients (15/15, 100%). We consider that the reconstructive strategy should be tailored to the location, length, and number of ureters involved. The vast majority of UPJO involves only the lower moiety; both pyeloplasty and pyeloureterostomy are viable options depending on the specific anatomy. For distal strictures, ureteric reimplantation is generally preferred, with psoas hitch and Boari flap as additional techniques when indicated. When distal stricture involves both ureters, we typically perform separate reimplantations. If the two ureters are strictured at different levels, a combined approach of ureteroureterostomy plus ureteric reimplantation is feasible. Finally, ileal ureter replacement represents the solution for long-segment strictures. CONCLUSIONS: Minimally invasive upper urinary tract reconstruction appears safe and effective for ureteral strictures in DCS, with high clinical success and low complication rates. Larger, multi-centre cohorts with extended follow-up are required to validate durability and refine patient selection.

title: BILATERAL URETERAL STRICTURE: TOTAL URETERAL REPLACEMENT WITH CECAL APPENDIX – VIDEO-ASSISTED TECHNIQUE DESCRIPTION
session: Upper Tract Reconstruction I (V01)
authors: Ignacio Arenas Norton, Nicolas Rosiere, Javier Ruiz, Leandro Asen, Otilia Blain, Francisco Imaz, Danel Alberti, Felicitas Lopez Imizciz, Cristian Sager, Gomez Yesica, Carol Burek, Juan Pablo Corbetta, Santiago Weller
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Extensive ureteral strictures represent a major therapeutic challenge in pediatric urology. In selected cases where conventional reconstructive techniques prove insufficient, the use of the cecal appendix as a ureteral substitute constitutes a viable—though uncommon—alternative in the pediatric population. The objective of this video is to describe the key technical aspects of ureteral replacement using the cecal appendix in a pediatric patient with severe right ureteral stricture secondary to BK virus infection. METHODS: We performed a Video showing step by step of a combined approach in a complicated patient. RESULTS: A 15-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia in remission and unrelated bone marrow transplantation developed BK virus infection, resulting in bilateral ureteral stenosis, renal insufficiency, and pelvicalyceal dilatation. He underwent multiple endourological procedures and an initial surgery consisting of left-to-right transureteroureterostomy with right vesicoureteral reimplantation (Psoas Hitch technique). Due to progressive hydronephrosis and functional deterioration, retrograde pyelography confirmed recurrence of right ureteral stenosis, prompting the decision to perform ureteral replacement using the cecal appendix. The procedure began in the Valdivia–Galdakao position with a transabdominal laparoscopic approach aimed at identifying the right ureter and the cecal appendix, optimizing access and allowing for a targeted open approach. Through a minimal incision, conventional open dissection was completed, identifying the previously exposed structures. The stenotic right ureter was resected, the appendix was divided with closure of the cecal stump, and a term-to-term anastomosis was constructed—proximally to the right renal pelvis and distally to the bladder. Simultaneously, the left transureteroureterostomy was reconstructed by anastomosing it to the appendiceal graft using 5-0 PDS sutures. Bilateral 5 Fr double-J stents, Foley and suprapubic catheters, and an abdominal drain were placed. The postoperative course was uneventful; bladder catheters were removed on postoperative day 5 and the drain on day 7. CONCLUSIONS: The cecal appendix represents a valuable option for ureteral replacement in patients with long or complex strictures where other reconstructive techniques have failed. Its successful application requires careful preoperative planning and advanced reconstructive urology expertise. This case highlights the feasibility and usefulness of this technique in highly complex clinical scenarios.

title: ROBOTIC ASSISTED LAPAROSCOPIC RETROPERITONEAL NON-TRANSECTING URETERONEOCYSTOSTOMY WITH ONLAY BUCCAL MUCOSAL URETEROPLASTY
session: Upper Tract Reconstruction I (V01)
authors: Wasin Saengthongpithak, Thitipat Hansomwong
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ureteric stricture is one of the most common complications after stone surgery. The more episodes of stone interventions a patient undergoes, the greater risk of accumulated ureteric injury. When multiple strictures are encountered, it a near impossible to perform a single reconstructive surgery with reliable outcomes. This suffers our patients, and may lead to loss follow-up, subsequently, infectious complications and progressive renal function loss. This recording demonstrates robotic-assisted, laparoscopic retroperitoneal non-transecting ureteroneocystostomy with onlay buccal mucosal ureteroplasty. Utilizing advantages of robotic surgery, precise dissection and port versatility to perform a two-field ureteric stricture correction using a single set of cannula placements. METHODS: A 72-year-old male recurrent stone former underwent multiple open and endourologic stone surgeries. He later developed multi-segmental ureteric strictures. Repeated endoscopic procedures results a failure. He was subsequently referred to Siriraj Hospital for definitive reconstruction. RESULTS: The operation a success. The robotic surgical system enabled a minimally invasive retroperitoneal approach, allowing meticulous ureteric dissection while preserving its blood supply. A side-to-side, non-transecting ureteroneocystostomy and a buccal graft upper ureteroplasty were performed simultaneously. Console time was 1 hour and 30 minutes for ureteroneocystostomy and 1 hour and 10 minutes for buccal graft ureteroplasty. There were no major postoperative complications, and estimated blood loss was 50 milliliters. Postoperative opioid use was minimal. The Foley catheter was retained for 5 days, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 6. 1-month postoperative ultrasound showed no residual hydronephrosis, and a 3-month postoperative ureteroscopy revealed patent anastomoses and a viable buccal mucosal graft. The DJ stent was removed just before ureteroscopy. CONCLUSIONS: Robotic-assisted laparoscopic retrperitoneal non-transecting ureteroplasty is a viable surgical option for patients with multiple ureteric strictures. It allows same-incision, simultaneous, multi-segmental ureteric reconstruction with high precision in perfusion preservation. Retroperitoneal approach minimizes bowel-related complications and shortens recovery time. The use of buccal graft provides a tension-free anastomosis and may ultimately reduce patient suffering from repeated corrective surgeries in the future.

title: THE SUMMIT STUDY: A REAL-WORLD, PROSPECTIVE, MULTI-CENTER STUDY TO EVALUATE THE PERFORMANCE OF THE OPTILUME BPH CATHETER SYSTEM IN MEN WITH SYMPTOMATIC BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA (BPH)
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Mario Bitar, Naeem Bhojani, Hazem Elmansy, Patel Premal, Ahmed Zakaria, Malek Meskawi, Edward Matsumoto, Kevin C. Zorn, Bilal Chughtai, Katherine Lajkosz, Dean Elterman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Optilume BPH Catheter System (Urotronic, Inc./Laborie Medical Technologies, Plymouth, MN, USA) is an FDA-approved, minimally invasive drug-coated balloon dilation device developed for the treatment of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). It has demonstrated symptom improvements comparable to other minimally invasive surgical therapies (MISTs). In this study, we evaluated functional and patient-reported outcomes, including maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax), quality of life (QoL), post-void residual volume (PVR), and responses to a validated symptom questionnaire. METHODS: This prospective, single-arm, multicenter, open-label study was conducted across five Canadian sites to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of the Optilume BPH System in treating LUTS secondary to BPH. Functional and sexual outcomes were assessed in 30 catheter-free patients at baseline, on the day of treatment, and at 3-, 6-, and 12-month follow-up visits. RESULTS: Thirty patients were treated for symptomatic BPH using the Optilume BPH system between July 2022 and August 2025. The mean age was 63.1 ± 7.0 years, and the average prostate volume was 45.9 cc (IQR: 33.7–63.1). The mean procedure duration was 23.4 ± 4.3 minutes, with a median of 21.5 minutes (range: 17.0–31.0). Symptom severity, measured by the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), improved markedly from 23.4 ± 5.1 at baseline to 12.2 ± 6.0 at 3 months, 11.0 ± 6.6 at 6 months, and 10.8 ± 7.5 at 12 months. The IPSS quality-of-life score decreased from 4.7 ± 1.3 at baseline to 2.2 ± 1.6 at 6 months and 2.0 ± 1.6 at 12 months. Sexual function outcomes remained stable, with the MSHQ-Function score changing minimally from 8.3 ± 3.8 at baseline to 7.9 ± 4.0 at 12 months (p=0.955), and the MSHQ-Bother score from 1.9 ± 1.7 to 2.2 ± 1.5 (p=0.972). Similarly, the IIEF total score showed no significant difference, from 43.7 ± 21.3 at baseline to 42.0 ± 23.0 at 12 months (p=0.13). Median maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax) improved from 8.7 ± 3.7 ml/s at baseline to 15.5 ± 7.5 ml/s at 6 months and 14.7 ± 6.9 ml/s at 12 months (p=0.003). Post-void residual volume (PVR) decreased from 95.7 ± 79.1 ml at baseline to 60.3 ± 49.0 ml at 6 months and 63.1 ± 41.6 ml at 12 months. PSA levels remained stable from baseline (1.7 ± 1.6 ng/mL) to 12 months (1.7 ± 1.8 ng/mL). The mean postoperative catheterization duration was 2 days. CONCLUSIONS: Throughout the 12-month follow-up period, patients demonstrated significant and sustained improvements in urinary outcomes and validated symptom scores. Sexual function remained stable, indicating that urinary benefits were achieved without compromising sexual health. These results affirm the findings of the prior EVEREST and PINNACLE studies.

title: EFFECT OF A VIRTUAL HOME HOSPITAL PATHWAY ON LENGTH OF STAY AND RECURRENT PRESENTATIONS IN SEPTIC STONE PATIENTS
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Matthew Mancuso, Patrick Albers, Sabrina Pattar, Nathan Hoy
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Hospital capacity constraints have underscored the importance of safely expediting patient discharge without compromising care. Traditionally, patients with septic stones remain hospitalized until clinical stability is achieved and culture-directed oral antibiotic therapy can be initiated. However, most patients stabilize within 24–48 hours after source control, yet remain admitted for intravenous (IV) antibiotics and monitoring. To address this, a Virtual Home Hospital (VHH) pathway was introduced on December 16, 2024, enabling early discharge with continued physician oversight, remote vital monitoring, laboratory follow-up, and home-based IV antibiotic administration until rationalization was completed. Our primary objective was to assess for length of hospital stay (LOS). Secondary objectives included assessing the safety of the pathway via rates of re-presentation to hospital, re-admission rates, and the number of subsequent unscheduled healthcare interactions after discharge. METHODS: This retrospective study analyzed 64 patients diagnosed with a septic stone at the University of Alberta Hospital before VHH implementation compared to 18 patients after, of which 15 (83%) were enrolled in the VHH pathway. Collected data included patient demographics, drainage method and laterality, incidence of positive blood cultures, and ICU admission. Statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS software. RESULTS: No significant differences between age or gender were noted. ICU admission occurred in 13% of pre-pathway patients, with none in the VHH group. Positive blood cultures were seen in 45% of pre-pathway patients and 28% of VHH patients (p=0.18). Following implementation, mean LOS was 3.7 days in the pre-pathway group vs. 2.6 days in the VHH group (p=0.17). The mean duration of VHH admission was 14.5 days, with total antibiotic treatment shortened from a mean of 13.3 days in the pre-pathway group to a mean of 10.4 days in the VHH group (p<0.001). No significant differences were observed in pre-and post-pathway groups for emergency or clinic re-presentations prior to definitive stone surgery (p=0.58 and p=0.28, respectively). CONCLUSIONS: Preliminary results suggest that a Virtual Home Hospital pathway is a feasible and safe approach for managing septic stone patients who stabilize rapidly after source control. Post implementation of the VHH pathway, there was a significantly shorter duration of antibiotic treatment which may be secondary to closer outpatient follow-up and antibiotic rationalization. Though no significant difference was noted with respect to LOS, this may be a result of the limited sample size of the post implementation group.

title: EVALUATION OF TESTES WITH MICRO-ULTRASOUND IN MEN WITH NON-OBSTRUCTIVE AZOOSPERMIA
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Matthew Mancuso, Phil V. Bach, Brian Wodlinger, Andrea Matte, Stacey Broomfield, Adam Kinnaird, Paul Shin
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: There remain significant limitations in prognostication and pre-operative surgical planning for men with non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA). Micro-ultrasound (microUS) is a high-resolution device that resolves down to 70 microns, permitting the visualization of seminiferous tubules and their contents. The primary objective of this study is to examine imaging differences in testicular seminiferous tubules using microUS in men with NOA versus in those with normal spermatogenesis. A secondary objective will be the correlation between microUS results and findings at microsurgical testicular sperm extraction (microTESE) in men with NOA. METHODS: This study is a prospective multisite Phase 2 trial at Shady Grove Fertility in Washington, and at the University of Alberta in Edmonton. The trial includes≥20 men with azoospermia and investigative findings consistent with a diagnosis of NOA (elevated FSH and small testicular volumes) and≥20 men with normal spermatogenesis (proven fertility). The ExactVu high-resolution microUS is used to systematically scan each testis in a predetermined grid, searching for isolated tubular ectasia. Imaging differences will include both quantitative measures of tubule diameter, density, and echogenicity as well as qualitative descriptions of the imaging features observed. RESULTS: 28 men with NOA have been evaluated with microUS. Seven men have had surgical exploration for sperm, either prior to or after scanning. Of these, 4 men have yielded sperm, and 3 have yielded no sperm. When examining the reflection and attenuation of the microUS images across these scanned men, differences distinguishing testicular areas with sperm from those without sperm have emerged. Applying Downshift and Nakagami Omega distributions, these areas can be visually represented with heatmaps in which blue areas correlate to architecture patterns in those with sperm, while yellow areas correlate to those without sperm ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191268.85865.a2.03#F1)). Imaging characteristics from men with normal spermatogenesis are currently pending. CONCLUSIONS: MicroUS imaging characteristics appears to be able to differentiate testicular tubules with and without sperm. MicroUS may have a future role in surgical planning and may help optimize results of microTESE in real time using point of care imaging during surgery.

title: EXPANDING SAME-DAY-DISCHARGE AQUABLATION BPH SURGERY OUTCOMES IN AMBULATORY SURGICAL CENTERS: UPDATED LARGEST EXPERIENCE OUTCOMES OF 350 CONSECUTIVE CASES
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Kevin C. Zorn, Adel Arezki, Peter Gilling, Neil Barber, Bradley Gill, Juan Justo Quintas, Silvia Secco, Tiago Rodrigues, Bilal Chughtai, Brian Helfand, Augustin Saibi, Rakan Alhaidey, Mana Almuhaideb, Rahul Mehan, Dean Elterman, Feras Al Jaafari
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) surgery is increasingly transitioning to outpatient and ambulatory surgical center (ASC) environments. Aquablation, s robotic, waterjet-based, image-guided resection has demonstrated consistent safety and durability. Our group first reported the feasibility of same-day-discharge (SDD) Aquablation in 40 men in 2023\. Herein, we present an updated analysis of the largest, most contemporary cohort of 350 consecutive ASC Aquablation procedures with extended follow-up to 12 months. METHODS: A retrospective review was performed of 350 consecutive men undergoing Aquablation for symptomatic BPH between June 2023 and September 2025 at a single high-volume ASC. Standardized intraoperative and postoperative protocols included general anesthesia, adjunctive focal bipolar hemostasis, 24F Rusch 3-way catheter with 50 cc balloon, and bladder irrigation with 3 L saline. Same-day discharge was targeted for all patients following hemodynamic stability, hematuria control, and pain <4/10 VAS. Functional and uroflow parameters were assessed preoperatively and at 3, 6, and 12 months. RESULTS: Mean age was 67.5 years and mean prostate volume 122 ml (41–320); 62% had median lobes and 54% were in retention. Mean operative time was 64 min, with 3.6 passes and 36 min of adjunct bipolar cautery. SDD was achieved in 97% (338/350), with 1.5% overnight stays for pre-planned travel and 1.5% for transient hematuria. Mean postoperative recovery time was 3.8 h and Foley removal at 5.2 days. Thirty-day complications were minimal: ER visits 2.5%, hematuria requiring irrigation 1.4%, reoperation 0.5%, infection 0.8%, transfusion 0.5%, and transient stress incontinence 0.5%. At 3, 6, and 12 months (n=320, 290, 202), mean IPSS improved from 30.3 to 7.3, 5.3, and 4.6; QOL from 5.3 to 0.7, 0.6, 0.6; and Qmax from 5.0 to 24.2, 26.1, 23.9 ml/s. Mean PVR decreased from 431 ml to 43–46 ml. Mean TRUS prostate volume decreased ~67%, with stable SHIM and MSHQ-Function/Bother scores. Retrograde ejaculation occurred in ~10%. CONCLUSIONS: This largest series to date confirms that SDD Aquablation in an ASC setting is safe, effective, and durable up to 12 months. Symptom and flow improvements mirror hospital-based series, with low complications and preservation of sexual function. | | | --- | | |

title: GLOBAL PROSTATE RESEARCH DISPARITIES: A 25-YEAR BIBLIOMETRIC ANALYSIS OF AUTHORSHIP EQUITY AND DISEASE FOCUS
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Pritish P. Kendrekar, Ansh M. Bhatia, Hasim Bakbak, Archan Khandekar, Gurpremjit Singh, Ahmad Abdelaziz, Jonathan E. Katz, Robert Marcovich, Hemendra N. Shah
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Equitable representation in scientific research is essential to ensure worldwide relevance of disease insights and clinical practice. This study analyzed global patterns in prostate research from 2000 to 2025 to evaluate disparities in authorship contribution and research focus across countries stratified by income level. METHODS: We conducted a bibliometric analysis of Scopus-indexed prostate publications on May 27, 2025. Metadata including publication year, journal, language, document type, authors, affiliations, access status, and author keywords were extracted. Affiliations were assigned to World Bank income groups: high-income countries (HIC), upper-middle-income (UMIC), lower-middle-income (LMIC), and low-income (LIC). Publications were categorized as benign or malignant based on title, abstract, and keywords. Authorship inequality was assessed using Lorenz curves and Gini coefficients. Temporal trends were analyzed using the Mann\\x{2013}Kendall test, and associations between income group and disease type using Pearson's chi-square test. RESULTS: A total of 89,406 publications from 160 countries were included. HICs produced 78.8% of total authorship and 78.0% of corresponding authorship, whereas LICs contributed only 0.09% and 0.11%, respectively. International collaborations accounted for 16.6% of publications, yet 87.9% were driven by HIC authors, with LIC involvement only 0.22%. From 2000 to 2024, HIC representation decreased from 96.6% to 66.9%, with significant increases in UMIC and LMIC participation (p<0.001) ( Table 1). Malignant prostate research dominated the literature (79.9%) compared to benign disease (14.2%), with benign research declining over time. Income distribution and disease-type inequality modestly improved, though LIC progress remained minimal ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191268.85865.a2.05#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: Despite an encouraging rise in global participation, HICs continue to dominate prostate research which remains highly focused on malignancy. Strengthening collaboration in LMICs and LICs is critical to advancing equitable global scientific progress. | | | --- | | |

title: THE WASHOUT STUDY: EARLY PROACTIVE INTERVENTION IN EMERGENCY HAEMATURIA REDUCES LENGTH OF STAY, MORTALITY ANDREADMISSIONS
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Nikita R. Bhatt, Kevin Byrnes, Simona Ippoliti, Raghav Varma, Bing Jie Chow, Quentin Mak, Nikki Kerdegari, Aqua Asif, Arjun Nathan, Alexander Ng, Anna Ireland, Joanne Cresswell, Yazan Qaoud, Luke Lavallee, Amrut Phonde, Kumar Madhavan, Piyush Bhargav Sarmah, Molly Nichols, James Green, Ahmed Ahmayda, Graeme Maclennan, Kevin Gallagher, Sinan Khadhouri, Veeru Kasivisvanathan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: There are currently no evidence-based guidelines for the management of emergency haematuria. As a result, clinical practice maybe highly variable and dependent on several factors, including anecdotal clinician judgement, clinician experience, hospital-level resource, and patient comorbidities. The WASHOUT study aimed to investigate variations in the management of emergency haematuria and evaluate impact of variation on patient outcomes. METHODS: A prospective, international, multi-centre cohort study was conducted using the British Urology Researchers in Surgical Training(BURST) collaborative model, incorporating patient and public involvement. The primary outcome was length of stay (LoS) measured from the date of admission to the date of discharge in days. Key secondary outcomes included overall mortality, and readmission to hospital after index admission. Patients were followed up for 90 days. Outcomes were analysed using appropriate statistical models adjusted for relevant covariates. Poisson regression models estimated adjusted relative risk of increased LoS and logistic regression was used to estimate adjusted relative risk of mortality and readmission. RESULTS: Data from over 8,500 patients across 382 centres over a 12-month period, were included. An increase in the number of days between admission and definitive management was significantly associated with increasing LoS and an increased risk of readmission, and death (OR 1.02) (p=0.00). _On comparative analysis, patients with >2 days between admission and completion of_ _management had an average LoS increase of 5.6 days, a 2.5% greater probability of_ _death within 90 days, and a 3.1% greater probability of readmission after adjustment_ _for covariates._ Other factors independently associated with prolonged LoS and increased mortality included frailty, sepsis, upper tract obstruction, and the need for intensive care. Mortality was also higher among patients who did not undergo imaging in the emergency department, lacked a definitive diagnosis during admission, or had malignancy as the underlying cause of haematuria. Higher 90-day readmission rates were observed among patients with a history of radiotherapy, those receiving antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, patients without prior hospital admissions, and those with longer initial hospital stays. CONCLUSIONS: WASHOUT is the first study to evaluate factors influencing outcomes in patients presenting with emergency haematuria. Based on our findings, we propose patients with emergency haematuria should have emergent imaging on admission and intervention within 2 days of admission if the haematuria has not settled by conservative measures within this time frame. There is an urgent need for evidence-based guidelines to standardise and expedite the investigation and management of emergency haematuria, and improve patient outcomes.

title: COMPARING HOUNSFIELD UNITS, VICKERS HARDNESS, AND SURGEON-PERCEIVED FRAGMENTATION SUSCEPTIBILITY BETWEEN COHORTS OF PURE URIC ACID AND CALCIUM OXALATE MONOHYDRATE CALCULI
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Gavin Hughes, Jonguk Lee, Abbas Hammoud, Rachel Wong, Panagiotis L. Papalazarou, Kiran Iyer, Kyra White, Kate Hardman, Rory Shan, Yu Zou, Mohamad Bakerberjaoui, Nikhile Mookerji, Brian Carrillo, Monica Farcas
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Higher Hounsfield units (HUs) predict higher energy requirements in shockwave lithotripsy; however, it is unclear how HUs relate to mechanical hardness, a variable many believe is an important stress–strain mechanical proxy in the context of laser lithotripsy and percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL). In this study, our team investigated the relationship between HUs and Vickers Hardness (HV), and whether the operator’s perception of fragmentation difficulty during PCNL correlates with true mechanical hardness. METHODS: Fifteen PCNL-derived stones from St. Michael’s Hospital, Toronto, met inclusion criteria as 100% calcium oxalate monohydrate (COM) (n=8) or 100% anhydrous uric acid (UA) (n=7), as determined by Fourier Transform Infrared spectroscopy. Mixed stones were excluded to remove compositional confounding. Postoperatively, the primary surgeon was asked to provide a global rating of fragment difficulty using the ultrasonic lithotripter from 1 to 10, with 1 being the easiest and 10 being the most difficult to fragment. All stones underwent ultrasonic cleaning, air-drying, resin embedding, and sequential grinding and polishing to 1 µm to expose an internal cross-section. HV measurements were performed using the LECOLM310 microindentation system at 0.5 kgf load for 10s per indentation. HUs were obtained by aggregating pre-operative CT axial slices for each stone. RESULTS: No association was found between HUs and HV in UA stones (r=0.10, p=0.82); however, in COM stones, HUs correlated inversely and strongly with HV (r=−0.91, p=0.002). Further, we found a positive (r=0.37) but non-statistically significant (p=0.21) correlation between perceived fragmentation difficulty and mean Vickers hardness. CONCLUSIONS: Utilizing HUs as a proxy for mechanical hardness should not be done in isolation and must be interpreted in the context of stone composition. For COM stones, higher HUs reflect denser, preferentially oriented crystallites with reduced organic matrices, conditions that promote cleavage-controlled microcracking under indentation. Consequently, HUs, a volumetric voxel average, can increase as HV, a localized, defect-sensitive measure, decreases. More critically, our results indicate that Vickers hardness does not, in practice, reliably align with the surgeon's perception of fragmentation difficulty, prompting further analysis from our group, including microCT and nanoindentation.

title: EFFECT OF HIGH-FAT DIET ON RADIATION RESPONSE IN BLADDER CANCER: AN _IN VIVO_ STUDY
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Rakan Al Haidey, Jose Mansure, Fatima Inigo, David Labbe, Eva Michaud, Wassim Kassouf
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Obesity and high-fat diets (HFD) have been associated with tumor progression, immune modulation and reduced responsive to various therapies, including radiotherapy (RT). However, their specific influence on radiation response in bladder cancer remains underexplored. Our objective was to investigate the impact of a HFD on tumor growth and RT efficacy in a murine model. METHODS: 60 mice were randomized to a HFD or control diet (CTL) following acclimatization. They were subsequently injected with subcutaneously in the flank, with the MB49 murine bladder cancer cell line. Upon tumor volumes (TV) reaching 0.15cm3, mice were further stratified to either receive a single fraction of 10 Gy radiation to the tumor versus observation, yielding 4 cohorts: HFD-RT, HFD-Control, CTL-RT and CTL-Control. TV and mice body weight (BW) were monitored at regular intervals until TV reached 2.0cm3. Shapiro-Wilk Test was used to assess normal distribution. Pairwise Mann-Whitney U analysis done using R-Studio Software Version 12.1 2024. RESULTS: RT significantly decreased TV in the CTL group (CTLRT vs CTLCTL: 820.3 ± 505.4 mm3vs 1467.9 ± 734.8 mm3, p0.028) confirming the effect of a single fraction of 10Gy. However, in the HFD cohort, no statistical difference noted between the treatment and control arm (HFDRT2 vs HFDCTL: 1397.0 ± 600.8 mm3vs 1390.9 ± 740.4 mm3, p=0.86) elucidating the notion that HFD possibly increases tumor resistance to RT, which was also observed when comparison between the HFDRT and CTLRT shows a statistical difference in TV (p0.038).Despite expectations, HFD alone did not result in a greater BW at endpoint compared to the CTL (p0.78). However, BW loss following RT was significant in the control fed mice (CTLRT vs CTLCTL, p0.012), while no significant change in BW was observed in the HFD treated with RT compared to their respective controls. (HFDRT vs HFDCTL, p0.28), These results may suggest that the high-fat diet potentially mitigates the BW loss typically induced by radiation therapy. CONCLUSIONS: A HFD appears to attenuate the therapeutic efficacy of RT in an in vivo bladder cancer murine model. These findings suggest the hypothesis that dietary factors modulate tumor response to radiation and may have implications for treatment strategies in patients.

title: A COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF PROSTATIC URETHRAL LIFT AND WATER VAPOUR THERMAL THERAPY FOR BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA ON POST-PROCEDURAL MEDICATION CESSATION AND UNPLANNED READMISSIONS
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Kelly Hei Yiu Tsang, Athena Yan Hiu Lee, Brian Wai Hei Siu, Chi Ho Leung, Jeremy M. H. Ho, Yvonne Y. Y. Chan, Jeremy Yuen Chun Teoh, Peter Ka Fung Chiu, Ka Lun Lo, Chi Fai Ng, Janice H. C. Wong, Alvina Yiu, Justin Y. T. Leung, Jonathan Man, Yihong Zhou, Chris Ho Ming Wong, Alex Q. Liu, David Ka Wai Leung, Steffi K. K. Yuen, Chi Hang Yee
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Minimally invasive surgical therapies (MIST) are increasingly adopted for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) due to their favorable safety and functional preservation profiles. This study aims to compare the drug-free status and complication rates of Prostatic Urethral Lift (PUL) and Water Vapour Thermal Therapy (WVTT). METHODS: We identified patients aged 50 years or older with prostate volumes of 30-80 cc who underwent either PUL or WVTT from January 2021 to December 2024. To ensure comparability, the cohorts were matched using 1:3 propensity score matching. Additional multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted on the entire pre-matched population. The primary outcome is the attainment of a drug-free status, defined as the discontinuation of both alpha-blockers and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors at the 6-month follow-up. The secondary outcome is unplanned readmissions within 30-day post-procedure. RESULTS: The analysis included 421 eligible patients (363 WVTT; 58 PUL). Baseline characteristics of the patients before and after matching are summarized in Table 1. Following propensity score matching (174 WVTT; 58 PUL), the PUL procedure was associated with a significantly greater likelihood of achieving drug-free status at 6 months compared to WVTT (weighted OR: 2.62, \[95% CI: 1.22-5.61\], p=0.013). This association persisted in the multivariable regression analysis (adjusted OR: 2.41 \[95% CI: 1.31–4.58\], p=0.006). There is no statistically significant difference in 30-day readmission rates between the groups in either the propensity score (p=0.097) or multivariable analysis (p=0.123), possibly due to the low number of readmission events (WVTT: 30; PUL: 5). Both MIST options exhibited an excellent safety profile, with no reinterventions recorded within the first year. Subgroup analyses consistently demonstrates superior drug-free outcome for PUL in patients with prostate size >50cc (OR 3.68, 95% CI 1.50–9.02, p=0.004), catheter-dependent patients (OR 2.54, 95% CI 1.13–5.70, p=0.024), and in cases without median lobe treatment (OR 2.53, 95% CI 1.18–5.43, p=0.018). CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates a statistically significant advantage for PUL over WVTT in enabling patients to discontinue BPH medications at six months, positioning PUL as a compelling MIST option with comparable safety progile for patients prioritizing cessation of medication. | | | --- | | |

title: PREDICTIVE MODELLING OF FUNCTIONAL OUTCOMES IN HOLEP VERSUS MONOPOLAR TURP: A RANDOMIZED TRIAL WITH ROC AND MULTIVARIATE STATISTICAL ANALYSIS IN LARGE-VOLUME BPH
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Katamreddy Prajeeth Reddy, Venkateshen Palanisamy, Kothapalli Sushmitha, Thalapathi S. Raja, Vivek Meyyappan, Velmurugan Palaniyandi, Hariharasudhan Sekar, Sriram Krishnamoorthy
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Large-volume BPH (>60 g) poses operative challenges due to bleeding and incomplete resection risk during monopolar TURP. HoLEP offers a size-independent, hemostatic alternative. This randomized trial compared HoLEP and monopolar TURP in prostates >60 g, incorporating ROC-based predictive modelling of postoperative voiding outcomes. METHODS: A prospective, block-randomized study included 120 men with symptomatic BPH and prostate volume >60 g, randomized to HoLEP (n=60) or monopolar TURP (n=60). Primary endpoints were perioperative hemoglobin change, catheterization duration, and hospital stay. Functional outcomes (Qmax, PVR, IPSS) were assessed at 1, 3, and 6 months. ROC analysis evaluated ΔQmax as a predictor of successful voiding. Multivariate regression adjusted for age, prostate volume, and baseline Qmax. RESULTS: Baseline demographics and symptom indices were comparable. HoLEP demonstrated reduced hemoglobin drop and shorter catheterization and hospitalization (mean stay 1.5 ± 0.4 vs 2.3 ± 0.6 days; p<0.01). Operative duration was modestly longer with HoLEP (81.6 ± 9.7 vs 74.9 ± 10.3 min; p=0.03). At 6 months, both groups improved significantly, with greater improvement in the HoLEP group (ΔQmax 10.2 ± 3.6 vs 7.9 ± 3.1 ml/s; p=0.02). HoLEP independently predicted higher postoperative flow (β=0.39; p=0.01) and reduced PVR (β=–0.35; p=0.02). ROC analysis showed stronger predictive accuracy for HoLEP (AUC 0.83; 95% CI 0.75–0.90; p<0.001) than TURP (AUC 0.70; 95% CI 0.61–0.81; p=0.01). Optimal ΔQmax cutoff≥14 ml/s yielded sensitivity/specificity of 82%/76% for HoLEP versus 69%/64% for TURP. CONCLUSIONS: In prostates >60 g, HoLEP demonstrates superior perioperative safety and improved early urinary flow outcomes compared with monopolar TURP, with equivalent symptom relief. Multivariate and ROC-based modelling confirms HoLEP as a more reliable predictor of durable voiding success in large-volume BPH. HoLEP represents a robust, size-independent therapeutic option in centers with established expertise.

title: LEVEL OF CIRCULATING CELL-FREE DNA IN URINARY BLADDER CANCER AFTER TRANSURETHRAL RESECTION OF BLADDER TUMOUR: A PROSPECTIVE OBSERVATIONAL STUDY
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Sivaraman C, Shanky Singh, Rani Ojha, Ravimohan S. Mavuduru, Aditya P. Sharma, Girdhar S. Bora, Sudheer K. Devana, Santosh Kumar, Uttam K. Mete
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) is the standard diagnostic and therapeutic procedure for bladder cancer. However, concerns regarding tumour cell dissemination during surgery persist. Circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) has emerged as a promising minimally invasive biomarker for cancer detection, treatment response, and post-treatment surveillance. This study aimed to measure changes in cfDNA levels before and after TURBT in patients with newly diagnosed primary bladder cancer and to correlate these changes with tumor grade, stage, and pathological characteristics. METHODS: This prospective observational pilot study was conducted at a tertiary care center in northern India from July 2022 to December 2023. Fifty patients with newly diagnosed primary bladder tumours scheduled for TURBT and undergoing complete endoscopic resection were enrolled. Peripheral blood samples were obtained preoperatively and 2 hours postoperatively. cfDNA was extracted using a commercially available plasma DNA extraction kit, and concentrations were quantified using a standard spectrophotometric method. Statistical analysis utilized paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test, while associations with clinicopathologic variables were evaluated using Spearman correlation and chi-square tests. RESULTS: The median pre-TURBT cfDNA level was 4.18 ng/mL (IQR 1.90–8.80), and the median post-TURBT level was 4.20 ng/mL (IQR 2.18–9.46), with no significant overall change. Significant increases in cfDNA were observed in patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer (p<0.0005), high-grade tumors (p<0.0007), and stage II–III disease (p<0.05). No significant association was observed between cfDNA change and operative duration >60 minutes. The cohort consisted primarily of older males, most presenting with painless gross hematuria and common risk factors such as smoking and occupational exposures. CONCLUSIONS: cfDNA levels appear influenced predominantly by tumor biology, including grade and stage rather than the TURBT procedure itself. cfDNA demonstrates potential as a non-invasive biomarker reflecting tumor aggressiveness and may complement histopathologic assessment in bladder cancer management. Larger studies are warranted to validate its clinical utility.

title: DIAGNOSTIC PERFORMANCE OF 68GA-PSMA-PET AND MPMRI FUSION BASED TARGETED-COGNITIVE BIOPSY IN PATIENTS WITH SUSPECTED PROSTATE CANCER: A PILOT STUDY
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Sanjay Kumar, Rohit Gupta, Amlesh Seth, Rakesh Kumar, Seema Kaushal, Sanjay Sharma, Siddharth Jain, Manoj Kumar
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate cancer (PCa) diagnosis remains challenging due to the limited specificity of PIRADS 3–5 lesions on multiparametric MRI (mpMRI), often leading to unnecessary biopsies. Improved imaging techniques that enhance lesion characterisation and localisation could optimize biopsy yield. This pilot study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of 68Ga-PSMA-PET and mpMRI fusion-based cognitive targeted biopsy in detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) for improving biopsy accuracy. METHODS: This prospective observational study was conducted at AIIMS, New Delhi,between July 2022 to August 2025. A total of 66 patients with suspicious lesions (PIRADS≥3) on multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) and elevated prostate-specific antigen (PSA) of more than 4 and less than 20 ng/ml were enrolled after informed consent. Patients with clinically palpable disease on DRE, prior prostate surgery or pelvic radiation were excluded. All enrolled patients underwent PSMA PET/CT also before biopsy followed by software based fusion of PSMA-PET CT and MpMRI. All the patients underwent targeted biopsy based on MpMRI and fused PSMA-PET/MR image suspected lesions along with systematic 12 core TRUS fusion biopsy. The primary objective was to evaluate the accuracy of fused PSMA-PET/MRI image targeted biopsy in diagnosing clinically significant prostate cancer, secondary objective includes overall cancer detection accuracy. RESULTS: The study included 66 male patients with suspected prostate carcinoma and serum PSA levels between 4-20 ng/mL. The mean age was 63 ± 6.8 years and mean serum PSA was 8.05 ± 4.4 ng/mL. Imaging assessments using fused 68Ga PSMA-PET/MRI reveals notable diagnostic performance, particularly for clinically significant prostate cancer. The modality exhibits a high sensitivity of 96 %, specificity of 79 % and a positive predictive value (PPV) of 76.4 %. The negative predictive value (NPV) was 96.8 %, indicating that fused 68Ga PSMA-PET/MRI targeted biopsy has a high sensitivity for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer than MRI targeted alone. These results suggest that 68Ga PSMA-PET/MRI fusion could be an effective tool for guiding targeted biopsies in patients with elevated PSA levels and suspected prostate cancer. CONCLUSIONS: Our study underscores the clinical potential of 68Ga-PSMA-PET/MRI fused image as a powerful diagnostic tool in the evaluation of patients with suspected prostate cancer. By integrating the molecular specificity of PSMA-PET with the superior anatomical resolution of multiparametric MRI, this hybrid approach enables more accurate differentiation between clinically significant and insignificant prostate cancers, reducing the number of unnecessary biopsies and minimizing patient morbidity, procedural risks, and healthcare costs. The high negative predictive value (NPV) observed with fused 68Ga-PSMA-PET/MRI targeted biopsy supports its role as a reliable pre-biopsy triage modality. Moreover, in resource-limited settings where integrated PET/MRI systems are not readily available, software-based fusion of PSMA-PET/CT and mpMRI represents a feasible and cost-effective alternative for targeted biopsy guidance.

title: EFFECTS OF ORAL VITAMIN D SUPPLEMENTATION IN AN EXPERIMENTAL MODEL OF PEYRONIE’S DISEASE
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Leonardo Seligralopes, Renan T. Jost, Ligia A. M. A. Demello, Giuliana Petri, Nuha A. Dsouki, Monica A. Sato, Sidney Glina
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Despite several proposed treatments, the underlying molecular mechanisms of fibrosis and potential modulatory therapies of Peyronie's Disease (PD) remain unclear. Recent evidence suggests that vitamin D (vitD) may play a regulatory role in extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammation, and fibrosis, offering a potential therapeutic pathway for PD. We aimed to evaluate effects of vitD supplementation in an experimental model of PD. METHODS: Thirty-six male Wistar rats were divided into groups: control (G1), induced PD and placebo (G2) and induced PD plus oral vitD supplementation (G3). PD was induced by TA injection of autologous plasma according to a validated model. VitD was administered orally for 8 or 18 weeks, corresponding to the acute and chronic phases. Collagens I and III were quantified by Picrosirius Red staining and VitD receptor expression was evaluated by immunohistochemistry. RESULTS: During the acute phase, type I collagen content did not differ significantly among groups (p=0.91), nor did type III collagen (p=0.54). In the chronic phase, Group 1 showed lower collagen I (12.4 ± 8.4%) and higher collagen III (38.7 ± 6.4%) compared to G2 and G3, though not statistically significant (p=0.27). In the chronic phase, G2 exhibited a higher type I/III collagen ratio compared to treated group (G3), indicating a more fibrotic tunical pattern, whereas vitD administration may be associated with a shift toward a less fibrotic, more regenerative matrix profile. ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191268.85865.a2.18#F1)) VitD receptor expression did not differ significantly among groups in the acute phase; however, in the chronic phase, both mean H-score and stained area percentage were significantly higher in Group 3 than in Groups 1 and 2 (p<0.05), indicating upregulated vitD receptor expression ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191268.85865.a2.18#F2)). CONCLUSIONS: VitD supplementation was associated with upregulation of VitD receptor expression and a reduced type I/III collagen ratio in the tunica albuginea, suggesting attenuation of chronic fibrosis and preservation of a more regenerative matrix profile. These findings support a potential antifibrotic role of vitD in PD.

title: FINASTERIDE 1 MG: SILENT IMPACTS ON MALE FERTILITY DESPITE PRESERVED HORMONAL BALANCE
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Nilson Marquardt Filho, Thiago Afonso Teixeira, Lucas Gabriel Fraga, Josias Siqueira Torres Filho, Lucas Vasconcelos Sanvido, João Pedro Gismondi, Ana Flávia Quiarato Lozano, Bruno Chiesa Gouveia Nascimento, Jorge Hallak
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Finasteride, a type-2 5α-reductase inhibitor, is prescribed for benign prostatic hyperplasia and androgenetic alopecia. Effects on male fertility remains uncertain. This study aimed to assess the impact of finasteride 1 mg/day on semen parameters, hormonal profiles, sexual function, and psychological status in men of reproductive age. METHODS: This retrospective, cross-sectional case-control study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (No. 92540525.0.0000.0068) and included 465 men aged 18–60 years (69 finasteride users and 396 controls). Semen analyses followed WHO 2021 criteria. Hormones measured included total and free testosterone (TT, FT), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), estradiol (E2), sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), prolactin (PRL), cortisol, and dihydrotestosterone (DHT). Metabolic (glucose, HbA1c, lipids, 25-hydroxyvitamin D) and thyroid parameters were also assessed. Sexual and psychological status were evaluated using the International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF-15), quantitative Androgen Deficiency in the Aging Male (qADAM), Male Sexual Quotient (MSQ), Beck Depression and Anxiety Inventories (BDI, BAI), Hamilton Anxiety Scale (HAM-A), and Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS). Univariate comparisons and multivariate linear regression were adjusted for covariates. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05. RESULTS: Mean age 41.9 ± 8.4 years; BMI 27.1 ± 3.9 kg/m2. Finasteride users had similar metabolic and hormonal profiles, except for higher HDL cholesterol (49.7 ± 8.7 vs. 46.1 ± 10.6 mg/dL; p=0.025). Mean duration of finasteride treatment was 73.5 ± 72.0 months. Semen quality was reduced in finasteride users: sperm concentration 55.6 ± 58.3 vs. 90.6 ± 93.8 ×106/mL, total sperm count 151.9 ± 205.1 vs. 254.1 ± 258.9 ×106/ejaculate, and total motile sperm count 72.6 ± 79.8 vs. 166.6 ± 182.9 ×106(all p0.001). Sperm morphology Kruger (2.0 ± 2.7 vs. 3.9 ± 4.0%) and WHO criteria (9.0 ± 8.2 vs. 14.9 ± 9.7%). Multivariate regression confirmed finasteride as an independent predictor of lower sperm concentration (=−26.9; p=0.025), total sperm count (=−72.9; p=0.031), total motile sperm count (=−75.7; p=0.002), and sperm morphology (=−4.18; p=0.002). DHT was lower (0.17 ± 0.20 vs. 0.58 ± 0.49 ng/mL; p0.001), but TT, FT, FSH, LH, and E2 were similar between groups. Questionnaire analyses showed mild, nonsignificant declines in erectile function and vitality. Sexual satisfaction, mood, urinary, and stress scores were comparable. CONCLUSIONS: Finasteride 1 mg/day reduces significantly sperm production and morphology without affecting endocrine, sexual, or psychological function.

title: COMPENSATED HYPOGONADISM AND SPERM DNA FRAGMENTATION IN MEN WITH SICKLE CELL DISEASE: IMPACT ON SEMEN PARAMETERS
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Ana Paloma R. Ribeiro, Ricardo B. Tiraboschi, Jean Carlos C. Zambrano, Caroline Silva, Rodolfo Pimenta, Lidiane J. Lisboa, Bruno Nascimento, Eduardo Miranda, Carlos A. Molina, Cristiano M. Gomes, Jose Bessa, Jr
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Men with sickle cell disease (SCD) may have impaired fertility due to chronic systemic burden, vaso-occlusive injury, and treatment-related toxicity, even when conventional semen parameters appear normal. Hormonal alterations and oxidative stress can compromise spermatogenesis and sperm DNA integrity. Compensated hypogonadism, defined by normal testosterone with elevated LH, may represent early endocrine dysfunction, but its impact on sperm DNA fragmentation (DFI) in SCD is poorly characterized. We aimed to evaluate semen parameters, sperm DNA integrity, and hormonal profile in adult men with SCD, focusing on the association between compensated hypogonadism and unfavorable seminal outcomes. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study including 37 adult men with SCD (median age 38 years; IQR 29–44) followed at a reference hematology center. Semen analysis was performed according to WHO 2021 guidelines. DFI was measured by flow cytometry using a validated protocol. Serum total testosterone, FSH, LH, and AMH were assessed. Structured interviews collected demographic, clinical, and reproductive data. Compensated hypogonadism was defined as total testosterone >300 ng/dL with LH≥9.4 mIU/mL. Statistical analyses included correlation tests and subgroup comparisons between eugonadal and compensated hypogonadal men. RESULTS: Of 37 participants, 25 (67.5%) completed semen analysis; four declined for religious reasons. Median sperm concentration was 23.4 million/mL, median DFI was 28% (IQR 12–49), and median strict morphology was 1%. All men had total testosterone >300 ng/dL, while 30% met criteria for compensated hypogonadism. This subgroup showed significantly lower total motile sperm count (median 3.45 vs 26.4 million; p<0.05) and higher DFI (49.5% vs 15%; p<0.01). DFI was moderately and significantly correlated with strict morphology (r=–0.57; 95% CI –0.82 to –0.14; p=0.013). Given the small sample size, no clear pattern emerged regarding hydroxyurea exposure and semen parameters or DFI. CONCLUSIONS: Despite normal serum testosterone, compensated hypogonadism in men with SCD was associated with poorer semen quality and markedly higher sperm DNA fragmentation, indicating that reproductive dysfunction may occur before a measurable decline in circulating testosterone. These findings support routine reproductive evaluation and early fertility counseling in men with SCD, even in the absence of overt hypogonadism, and highlight the potential role of DFI assessment beyond standard semen analysis.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE–DERIVED TUMOR VOLUME IN MULTIPARAMETRIC MRI: VALIDATION AND MULTIMODAL APPLICATIONS FOR NODAL AND EXTRACAPSULAR EXTENSION PREDICTION IN PROSTATE CANCER
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Ignacio Eltit, Ignacio Rojas, Alfredo Aliaga, Gabriela Ramírez, Mario Fernández, Alberto Bustamante, Renato Souper, Hugo Otaola, Pablo Bernier, Rodrigo Pinochet, Marcelo Orvieto, Andrés Labra
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Tumor volume is a key prognostic factor in prostate cancer, associated with extracapsular extension (ECE), nodal invasion (pN+), and recurrence. Artificial intelligence (AI) applied to multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) enables objective and reproducible volume quantification, potentially improving preoperative risk stratification. This study aimed to validate AI-derived tumor volume against histopathology and evaluate its integration into multimodal predictive models for nodal and extracapsular extension. METHODS: A retrospective cohort of 102 patients who underwent radical prostatectomy with extended pelvic lymph node dissection and preoperative mpMRI and PSMA PET/CT between 2021–2024 was analyzed. Tumor volume was automatically calculated from mpMRI using a convolutional neural network–based segmentation algorithm integrated into the mdprostate© platform (Mediaire GmbH, Germany). Pathological volume was obtained from surgical specimens. Correlation between AI-estimated and pathological volumes was assessed with Pearson and Spearman coefficients. AI-derived variables (tumor volume and tumor density \[tumor\ volume/prostate volume\]) were integrated into two logistic regression models: (1) a nodal model, combining tumor density and PET-PSMA SUVmax, compared with the Briganti nomogram; and (2) an ECE model, incorporating MRI-based ECE status, AI-derived tumor density, and SUVmax, benchmarked against mpMRI alone. Model performance was evaluated by AUC, calibration, and diagnostic metrics using SPSS v29.0. RESULTS: AI-derived tumor volume strongly correlated with pathological volume (r=0.71; ρ=0.68; p<0.001), with a systematic underestimation (bias –5.8 ml). In multivariable analysis, tumor density (OR 1.15; p=0.03) and SUVmax (OR 1.06; p=0.02) were independent predictors of nodal invasion. The multimodal nodal model achieved an AUC of 0.870 (95% CI 0.801–0.940), outperforming Briganti (AUC 0.740) and reducing indicated lymphadenectomies by ≈6% at equivalent sensitivity (97%). For ECE prediction, MRI ECE (OR 7.77; p<0.001), tumor density (OR 1.13; p=0.03), and SUVmax (OR 1.06; p=0.02) were independent predictors. The AI-based model outperformed mpMRI (AUC 0.823 vs 0.761), reducing false negatives from 29.2% to 21.7% and false positives from 19.2% to 13.7%, improving surgical planning accuracy in ≈7% of patients. CONCLUSIONS: AI-derived tumor volume is a validated quantitative biomarker that enhances the prediction of nodal and extracapsular extension when combined with MRI and PET-PSMA parameters. This multimodal approach supports more individualized and precise surgical decision-making. Prospective multicenter validation is warranted before clinical implementation.

title: EPIDEMIOLOGY AND REGIONAL VARIATION IN PROSTATE CANCER INCIDENCE AND TREATMENT IN HUNGARY
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Ádám Lénárt, Áron Soós, Dániel Reibl, Célia Blasszauer, Ida Komka, András Horváth, Áron Bécsi, Michael S. Leapman, Pawel Rajwa, Shahrokh F. Shariat, Péter Hegyi, Tibor Szarvas, Péter Nyirády, Tamás Fazekas
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate cancer (PCa) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality among European men. Most epidemiological evidence originates from Western countries, yet substantial variation may exist in smaller nations such as Hungary due to differences in population risk, screening, and treatment practices. We therefore conducted a comprehensive national assessment of PCa epidemiology and management in Hungary. METHODS: Data from the National Health Insurance Fund, Hungarian Central Statistical Office, National Cancer Registry, and WHO were used to calculate crude, age-specific, and age-standardized incidence and mortality rates. County-level analyses assessed regional variation in incidence and the use of radical prostatectomy (RP) and definitive radiotherapy (RT). Analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism. RESULTS: Between 2001 and 2022, the crude incidence of PCa in Hungary increased from 55.7 to 102.3 cases per 100,000 men, with a peak observed in 2017, followed by a transient decline. Since 2012, age-standardized incidence rates have remained stable, whereas crude rates continued to rise gradually. Age-specific incidence increased steadily with advancing age, peaking at 642 cases per 100,000 men aged≥80 years in 2022. The largest relative contribution to total cases occurred in the 60–69-year age group. Regionally, Budapest showed the highest crude incidence (113 per 100,000). County-level data revealed wide regional variation, with RP rates ranging from –37% to +51% and RT rates from –38% to +72% relative to the national mean. Some areas, like Komárom-Esztergom County, fell well below average in both RP (–27%) and RT (–37%). RP and RT rates reached about 20% and 15% of the national prostate cancer incidence, respectively. While age-standardized mortality declined from approximately 60 to 40 deaths per 100,000 men (annual percent change: –0.97% per year; 95% CI: –1.49% to –0.46%), crude mortality increased gradually, and age-specific mortality remained stable across all age groups. The age-standardized mortality-to-incidence ratio remained around 0.33 (2012-2022), temporarily exceeding 0.40 during COVID-19. CONCLUSIONS: PCa in Hungary is underdiagnosed, with most cases detected at older ages and stark regional variation, which may reflect differences in healthcare access. Limited screening and uneven availability of curative treatments lead to delayed detection and lower intervention rates outside wealthier regions. These findings underscore the need for further research to clarify drivers of variation and to support efforts toward earlier detection and broader access to high-quality PCa care in Hungary.

title: TESTOSTERONE RESPONSIVENESS AS A PREDICTIVE BIOMARKER OF SUCCESSFUL SPERM RETRIEVAL IN NON-OBSTRUCTIVE AZOOSPERMIA
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Oussama G. Nasrallah, Baraa Al Jardali, Mohammad Fawaz, Bilal Alameddine, Bassel G. Bachir
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether testosterone responsiveness to pre-operative hormonal therapy predicts successful sperm retrieval (SSR) after microsurgical testicular sperm extraction (micro-TESE) in men with non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA), and to define hormonal and operative parameters that may improve surgical outcomes. METHODS: A retrospective review of 77 NOA patients who underwent micro-TESE was performed. Demographic, clinical, and hormonal data (FSH, LH, testosterone, estradiol, prolactin, TSH) were recorded pre-and post-hormonal therapy (oral or injectables). The testosterone response (ΔT=post – pre testosterone) and therapy route (oral vs. injectable) were correlated with SSR, operative time, and IVF outcomes. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors of SSR. RESULTS: The overall SSR rate was 46.7%. Patients with positive retrieval had significantly higher post-therapy testosterone (771 vs 464ng/dL; p=0.003), greater ΔT (478 vs 245ng/dL; p=0.026), and shorter operative time (99 vs 121 min; p<0.001). Oral hormonal regimens achieved higher SSR than injectables (56.8% vs 33.3%; p=0.054). On multivariable analysis, both post-therapy testosterone and ΔT independently predicted SSR (p<0.05). Pregnancy and live-birth rates after successful retrieval were 41.6%. CONCLUSIONS: Dynamic testosterone response following hormonal therapy serves as an independent predictor of sperm retrieval success in NOA. Incorporating ΔT into pre-operative evaluation may help identify candidates most likely to benefit from micro-TESE. These results support testosterone responsiveness as a true biomarker for precision fertility surgery.

title: A COMPOSITE BIOMARKER APPROACH TO WITHHOLD NEOADJUVANT CHEMOTHERAPY IN SELECT MUSCLE-INVASIVE BLADDER CANCER PATIENTS
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Joep J. De Jong, Marla Johnson, James Proudfoot, Inge Ede Kruijff, Jaco Kraan, Elai Davicioni, John Martens, Nick Beije, Ewan A. Gibb, Arno van Leenders, Joost L. Boormans
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) prior to radical cystectomy (RC) is recommended for muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). However, we propose a composite biomarker approach of circulating tumor cell status and gene expression to select patients in whom NAC may be omitted. METHODS: Transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) samples were collected from patients with cT2-T4aN0-N1M0 MIBC who were included in the prospective CirGuidance study (NL3954), in which circulating tumor cells (CTC) were enumerated using the CELLSEARCH® system. Expression profiling was performed using the validated Decipher Bladder genomic subtyping classifier to determine luminal and non-luminal molecular subtypes (Veracyte, Inc.). The luminal favorable subtype was determined using a lncRNA-based classifier (de Jong et al. 2019 and 2024). The primary endpoint was cancer-specific mortality (CSM), calculated from the date of study inclusion to the date of bladder cancer related death. RESULTS: In the CirGuidance study (n=231), most patients (n=213; 92%) underwent RC without NAC, while (n=18) received NAC plus RC. Among RC-only patients, CTCneg status (n=172) was associated with a two-year CSM of 21% versus 41% in CTCpos patients (Gray’s test, p=0.01). No significant differences were observed in the distribution of molecular subtypes between CTCpos or CTCneg patient subgroups. Within CTCneg patients treated with RC alone, 2-year CSM was 14% in luminal (n=77, 36%) versus 25% in non-luminal (n=136, 64%) whereas in CTCpos patients it was 38% and 44%, respectively. Among 18 NAC plus RC treated patients, non-luminal subtype (n=10) had a two-year CSM of 11%, whereas in luminal subtype it was 27%, similar to outcomes when treated with RC alone. Importantly, the lncRNA-based luminal favorable classifier identified 26 patients with luminal favorable subtype among CTCneg patients with 0% CSM at two years (MVA p=0.02) when treated with RC alone. CONCLUSIONS: We identified a biomarker-defined subgroup of MIBC with more favorable outcomes after RC alone. These findings support the future prospective validation of CTC and molecular subtyping as a tool to guide NAC selection.

title: BEYOND THE SCALPEL: EVALUATION OF THE PACLITAXEL DRUG-COATED-BALLOON AS AN ALTERNATIVE TO OPEN URETHROPLASTY AT A TERTIARY REFERRAL CENTER: TWO YEAR FOLLOW-UP DATA
session: Global Gateway Posters Day 1 (GG01)
authors: Susanne Sylvia Ohnesorge, Henriette Veibyholm
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Patients with recurrent bulbar urethral stricture≤3 cm have been offered treatment with Paclitaxel Drug-Coated-Balloon (DCB) as an alternative to open urethroplasty at our centre since December 2022. The objective of this study is to evaluate the success rate of DCB treatment. METHODS: All patients treated with DCB from December 2022-March 2024 were included in this retrospective single-centre study. All patients follow a standardized treatment and follow-up (FU). All patients were evaluated with retrograde urethrogram and urethroscopy at baseline and when indicated during FU. We record IPSS score, USS-PROM, IIEF-5, and uroflowmetry preoperatively, and at FU at 3-, 12-month and annually up to 5 years postoperatively. The primary endpoint is the need for retreatment. Secondary endpoints include changes in Qmax, residual urine, IPSS score, USS-PROM, quality of life and erectile function. RESULTS: 111 men with a median age of 42 years (range 18–82) were included. 100 patients (90%) had a bulbar stricture, 11 (10%) had a bulbomembranousstricture. Prior treatments included direct vision internal urethrotomy (DVIU) (N=102), urethroplasty (N=15), and 15% of the patients performed Clean Intermittend Catheterization (CIC)/selfdilatation at some point. Etiology was mostly idiopathic or unknown (N=95), and median stricture length was 10 mm (range 2–32). Median Qmax at baseline was 8.1 (2.1-30). Adverse events following treatment included haematuria (20%), including one transfusion-requiring haemorrhage (Hb 12 to 7), urinary tract infection (3.6%), and transient urinary retention after catheter removal (1%). All 111 patients have completed the 12-month FU. Median Qmax at 3-month FU was 21.5 (7.3-50) and 19 (4-50) at 12-month FU. Recurrent strictures, confirmed by urethrography, were found in 42/111 (38%) patients. Median time from treatment to recurrence was 12 months (4-24). So far, 39 of these have undergone retreatment: 29 urethroplasty, 5 redo-DCB, 1 DVIU, 4 simple dilations. Nine out of ten patients retreated with conservative methods had soft, short strictures. The rate of freedom from repeat intervention for all 111 patients after a median FU-time of 23 months (14-34months) is 62%.
