abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Elective surgery cancellations negatively affect the healthcare system leading to increased healthcare costs, adverse patient outcomes, and decreased scheduling efficiency. Social determinants of health (SDOH) are increasingly being recognized as dominant non-medical factors contributing to these effects. The goal of this study was to determine what demographic and SDOH factors are associated with elective surgery cancelations. METHODS: Patients scheduled for an elective surgery with a pediatric general surgeon or urologist between 10/2022 and 2/2024 were retrospectively reviewed. Patients admitted prior to surgery or whose surgery was cancelled >3 days before were excluded. Patient age, sex, race, ethnicity, primary language, insurance, area deprivation index, and SDOH questionnaire responses were compared between the surgery as scheduled and surgery cancelled cohorts with univariate and multivariate analyses. RESULTS: Of the 3,158 scheduled elective pediatric general or urological surgeries, 2,718 (86%) went as scheduled and 440 (14%) were cancelled. Cancellations disproportionately affected younger patients (4 vs 9 years, p<0.001), males (81% vs 57%, p<0.001), those with public insurance (65% vs 51%, p<0.001), and those of Hispanic/Latino ethnicity (11% vs 2%, p<0.001), Table 1. There was no significant difference in the day of week the surgery was scheduled or primary language spoken between the two cohorts. Cancellations were more likely among patients with positive SDOH screens (18% vs 12%, p=0.002), especially in those with transportation barriers and childcare needs, Table 1. On multivariable analysis, transportation barriers were associated with an almost threefold increased odds of cancellation (OR 2.9, p=0.002), and public insurance also significantly increased cancellation risk (OR 1.7, p=0.001). Interestingly, patients reporting difficulty "making ends meet" were less likely to cancel (OR 0.17, p=0.019). CONCLUSIONS: SDOH factors including public insurance and transportation barriers were associated with elective pediatric surgery cancellations. Younger, male, Hispanic/Latino children and those with positive SDOH screens are at highest risk. These factors may be used to systematically screen patients and create targeted presurgical outreach interventions to help mitigate cancellation rates. | | | --- | | |

title: THE IMPACT OF COMMUNITY-LEVEL SOCIOECONOMIC DISTRESS ON STONE BURDEN, PREVENTION, AND QUALITY OF LIFE IN PATIENTS WITH NEPHROLITHIASIS
session: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Jackson Cabo, Rochelle Kofman, Zelle Bannister, Mira Keddis, Mitchell R. Humphreys, Karen L. Stern
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Social determinants of health such as income and gender contribute to disparities in stone-related quality of life and timely management. The impact of community level socioeconomic disadvantage on nephrolithiasis-related quality of life and disease burden remains understudied. METHODS: We performed a nationwide cross-sectional survey of adult ResearchMatch registrants with kidney stones. Socioeconomic disadvantage was assessed using Distressed Community Index (DCI) with DCI≥75 defined as a disadvantaged community. Disease burden, preventative management, quality of life, and patient-reported barriers to care were compared between distressed and not distressed communities. Stepwise multivariable linear regression assessed the association between DCI and Wisconsin Stone Quality of Life (WISQOL). RESULTS: 126 of 938 respondents (13.4%) were from distressed communities. Individuals from distressed communities had lower WISQOL scores (83 vs. 87.5, P=0.005), were more likely to miss 5+days of work due to stones (17.5% vs. 8.4%; P=0.003) and were more likely to report barriers to making preventative dietary changes ( Table 1). Rates of completing of a 24-hour urine study (41.3% vs. 40.0%; P=0.77) and rates of seeing a dietician (15.9% vs. 12.1%; P=0.25) were similar between high and low DCI groups. On multivariable analysis ( Table 2), after controlling for demographics and emergency care utilization, DCI was inversely correlated with WISQOL score (β=-0.08,-0.13--0.03, P=0.003), however, addition of income to the model abolished the relationship between DCI and quality of life. CONCLUSIONS: In this study, stone-formers from socioeconomically distressed communities had greater work disruption, increased barriers to preventative management, and poorer stone-related quality of life. However, the relationship between DCI and WISQOL score was attenuated after controlling for income, highlighting a need for urologists to account for cost when recommending preventative regimens for nephrolithiasis. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: COMMUNITY-BASED KNOWLEDGE-TO-ACTION TRANSLATION TO IMPROVE EARLY DETECTION OF PROSTATE CANCER AMONG BLACK INDIVIDUALS
session: Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Sung Min Kim, Jenney Lee, Yohali Burrola-Mendez, Dante' Morehead, Marty Chakoian, Michael Ware, Kojo Ward, Floyd Gossett, Vida Henderson, Patricia Egwuatu, Burcu Darst, John Masembe, Erika Wolff, Yaw Nyame
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Black prostate cancer (PCa) patients are 120% more likely to die compared to average US population, which is the largest racial disparity in cancer-related death in the US. In our previous work, Black men cited lack of awareness and knowledge to support shared decision making (SDM) with primary care providers (PCPs) as barriers to PCa screening and care. The objective of this study was to design a patient-centered, culturally relevant toolkit to improve the knowledge and awareness of PCa screening among Black Americans. METHODS: We convened a working group (WG) of Black PCa survivors and community advocates, clinicians, researchers, and health communications specialists. During monthly meetings, the WG followed Graham’s Knowledge-to-Action framework to synthesize information from: 1) peer-reviewed literature on the use of SDM aids; 2) interviews conducted by our research team with Black individuals regarding barriers and facilitators to access PSA testing; and 3) community input on PSA testing and PCa early detection. We then facilitated four iterative design sessions with the WG to develop recommendations for toolkit content, framing, and format. RESULTS: With the WG, we designed a framework with a comprehensive set of resources to increase knowledge and awareness of PSA testing for early detection of PCa among Black individuals, with detailed recommendations on the content, framing, and format. Recommendations encompass: 1) comprehensive interactive web-based information about PCa risk and screening; 2) printable SDM documents that present evidence-based information about the use of PSA testing to guide conversations between Black individuals and their PCPs; and 3) educational videos focused on PCa basics and dispelling common misconceptions about PCa risk and screening, with content delivered by Black PCa survivors and providers. CONCLUSIONS: This study addressed the need for a community-developed approach to increasing knowledge and awareness about PCa screening and early detection in an accessible, culturally relevant, and accurate manner. We used a collaborative process that centered the experiences of Black PCa survivors and advocates in the design of a toolkit that can facilitate SDM discussions between Black individuals and their PCPs for use of PSA testing for PCa screening. | | | --- | | |

title: COUNTRY ROADS AND CANCER CARE: COMPARING MEASURES OF TRAVEL BURDEN AMONG PATIENTS WITH BLADDER CANCER
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Jacqueline C. Fannin, Andrew Trimble, Elaine Mattox, Samuel G. Deem
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Travel distance affects access, treatment, and outcomes, yet methods to measure burden vary. Comparing zip code centroid-based and network-based is essential to accurately assess geographic barriers to care. The aim of this study was to assess agreement on two measures of travel distance, zip code centroid-based network-based travel distance, and among patients with bladder cancer at a single tertiary medical center. METHODS: Patients diagnosed with bladder cancer by transurethral resection of bladder tumor between January 1, 2018, and December 31, 2022, were retrospectively identified from electronic health records. Demographic and clinical variables were abstracted by chart review. Travel distance was estimated using two approaches: centroid-based ZIP code calculations (ArcGIS) and network-based routing (Google Maps). Agreement and misclassification between approaches were analyzed, and association with patient demographics and survey-reported transportation concerns were evaluated. RESULTS: The average percent difference between network-and centroid-based travel distances was 38.8% (95% CI, 34.6–42.9%). Bland–Altman analysis demonstrated poor agreement with proportional systematic bias between the two methods of determining travel distance, showing a median bias of 5.7 (range, 2.39–87.7) between the two methods. Use of centroid-based distances led to 25.6% misclassification of patients based on travel bands. Misclassified patients were significantly more rural compared to appropriately classified patients (94.9% vs 84.3%, p<0.001). Patients who reported that transport was a high concern on the survey were more likely to be further away from the facility (33.4 vs. 17.0 miles, p=0.02) and located in travel bands 3 and 4 (64.9% vs 33.7%, p=0.03) as indicated in the network-based distance methods. CONCLUSIONS: Centroid-based travel distances underestimate the true travel distance and lead to patient misclassification, particularly among rural populations. Neither method was able to identify specific patient groups or treatment outcomes based on travel distance. Patient-reported survey responses indicated that patients with high concern regarding transportation did not include a specific patient demographic, but transport concern was reported higher in patients who were further away from the facility using network-based method of travel distance.

title: SOCIOECONOMIC VULNERABILITY PREDICTS MORTALITY AFTER RADICAL CYSTECTOMY
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Fionna Sun, Kezia Reji Thomas, John P. Quezada, Soutik Ghosal, Max Stempel, Tracey L. Krupski, Jennifer M. Lobo
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Radical cystectomy (RC) remains the cornerstone treatment for muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) but carries substantial morbidity and mortality. Traditional risk models emphasize clinical variables while overlooking community-level disadvantage. The Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) quantifies such vulnerability across four domains: socioeconomic status (RPL-1), household composition and disability (RPL-2), minority status and language (RPL-3), and housing and transportation (RPL-4). This study evaluated whether SVI or its component domains independently predict mortality after RC for MIBC. METHODS: A retrospective review of 144 patients who underwent RC for T2-stage MIBC was performed using an IRB-approved institutional database. Cox proportional hazards models assessed overall and cause-specific mortality, adjusting for age, sex, race, neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC), Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), travel time to UVA, and SVI (overall and domain-specific, derived from CDC 5-digit zip code data). Models were selected by Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). Cause-specific analyses distinguished bladder cancer–related mortality from non-cancer mortality. RESULTS: Median follow-up was 931 days (IQR 433–1,478). Mortality occurred in 31% of patients: 18% attributed tometastatic MIBC and 13% other causes. Median time to death was 307 days (IQR 147–602). The best-fit model included sex, travel time, and RPL-1; RPL-1 was significantly associated with higher mortality (HR 5.84, 95% CI 1.60–21.4, p=0.008). Cumulative incidence plots showed greater bladder cancer–related mortality overall. On subset analysis, RPL-1 predicted non-cancer mortality (HR 9.93, 95% CI 1.32–74.6, p=0.026) but not cancer-specific mortality (HR 3.99, 95% CI 0.73–21.9, p=0.110). CONCLUSIONS: The SES (RPL-1) domain—encompassing unemployment, lack of high school education, uninsured status, and poverty—emerged as an independent predictor of mortality after RC. Patients from socioeconomically vulnerable communities experienced excess overall and non–cancer mortality, suggesting deaths driven by structural inequities rather than tumor biology. Integrating SVI domains into perioperative risk models may enhance prognostication and guide targeted interventions to reduce disparities and improve survivorship.

title: COUNTY-LEVEL POVERTY AS A PREDICTOR FOR PROSTATE CANCER MORTALITY IN MISSISSIPPI
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: James J. Loome
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Mississippi has the second highest prostate cancer mortality rate of any state in the USA. Our state also faces significant socioeconomic challenges. Since poverty has been identified as a social determinant of health that may influence cancer outcomes, we explored how this relationship exists on the county level. Our county-level analysis underscores local-access disparities that the AUA seeks to address nationwide. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional using county-level data from Mississippi. Poverty rates (percentage of residents living below the federal poverty line) and age-adjusted prostate cancer mortality rates (2018–2022) were examined for 73 counties with complete data. Simple linear regression was used to evaluate the association between poverty and prostate cancer mortality. RESULTS: Regression analysis demonstrated that county-level poverty was a significant predictor of prostate cancer mortality (=99.92, 95% CI 53.00–146.84, p=0.000065). This result corresponds to an estimated increase of ~10 deaths per 100,000 for each 10% increase in poverty rate. The model explained 20.3% of the variation in prostate cancer mortality across counties (R2=0.2025). We found that Leflore, Bolivar, and Sunflower counties, all within the Mississippi Delta region, had the highest prostate cancer mortality rates. CONCLUSIONS: Counties with higher poverty rates generally experienced higher prostate cancer mortality. These findings highlight the role of socioeconomic determinants in cancer outcomes and suggest that targeted interventions in high-poverty areas may help reduce disparities in prostate cancer mortality across Mississippi, as well as the rest of the nation.

title: BUILDING SUSTAINABLE RECONSTRUCTIVE UROLOGY CAPACITY IN THE UNDERSERVED AREA OF THE PHILIPPINES: A COLLABORATIVE GLOBAL SURGERY MENTORSHIP MODEL
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Michael E. Chua, Robert Christopher Doiron, Kurt McCammon, Ellen Chong, Maria Carmela Lapitan, Joal Patrick Aldana, Diosdado Limjoco, Josefino Castillo, Dennis Serrano, Manuel C. See, IV
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Reconstructive urology restores function for patients with congenital, traumatic, infectious, and iatrogenic conditions, yet capacity-building in low-and middle-income settings often relies on brief visits that rarely shift local practice. We report a mentorship approach linking the University of Toronto, Eastern Virginia Medical School, and Queen’s University with two Philippine hospitals—St. Luke’s Medical Center (SLMC) and Philippine General Hospital (PGH). Objectives were to: (1) institute a year-round program anchored by a single, concentrated in-country teaching week; (2) deliberately move host teams toward higher-complexity reconstruction while preserving safety; and (3) evaluate feasibility, clinical outcomes, educational gains, and milestones for stepped autonomy. METHODS: From 2022–2024, monthly virtual boards standardized case selection, imaging, perioperative optimization, and resource readiness. This preparation led to one 6–7-day annual on-site session at SLMC/PGH where 2–3 visiting faculty and 1–2 trainees worked side-by-side with local surgeons. A prospective log captured case mix, operative duration, length of stay (LOS), and complications (Clavien–Dindo). Trainee learning was measured with 0–10 Likert scales (comfort; technical understanding) before and after the teaching week. The curriculum emphasized progressive complexity (e. g., redo hypospadias; long-segment/pan-urethral graft urethroplasty; augmentation cystoplasty; continent catheterizable channels; ileal ureter). Ethics approvals and temporary privileges were secured in advance; there was no industry or external funding, and outcomes were tracked prospectively. RESULTS: Thirty-three patients underwent surgery (median age 23 years; IQR 12.5–41.5); 33.3% were pediatric, and 84.8% had major reconstructive procedures. Median operative time was 240 minutes; median LOS was 2 days. Overall complications were 15.1%, including one major event (Clavien–Dindo≥III). Forty-five residents participated. Self-reported comfort increased from 2.51 to 6.93 and technical understanding from 5.18 to 8.84 (both p<0.001). The case portfolio advanced in complexity year-over-year while maintaining acceptable safety. Program success criteria include: each site independently performing predefined index reconstructions with≥2 credentialed local surgeons; outcomes approximating published benchmarks; rising independent volumes;≥80% clinic retention at 6–12 months; and emergence of a trainer-of-trainers. Sustained achievement for two consecutive years prompts tapering to remote support only. CONCLUSIONS: A continuous mentorship framework with a single, intensive annual on-site week can accelerate safe transfer of complex reconstructive skills while preserving local ownership. Early experience at SLMC/PGH demonstrates feasibility, meaningful educational improvement, and stable perioperative outcomes amid increasing complexity. The model is lean, scalable, and aligned with health-system priorities on workforce and quality, offering a practical route from joint cases to autonomous local expertise.

title: PERCEIVED BARRIERS TO LGBTQ+ INCLUSIVITY FOR UROLOGY TRAINEES
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Pedro Silva, Luis Campos Pinheiro, Luis Severo, João Cunha, Miguel Gil
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Inclusive healthcare training environments are essential to equitable urological practice. This review synthesizes available evidence on barriers to LGBTQ+ (lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer/questioning, and other sexual and gender minority) inclusivity perceived by trainees in urological surgical programs, identifying key educational and institutional gaps that limit preparedness to deliver competent LGBTQ+-affirming care. METHODS: A systematic search using Pubmed, Embase and Scopus examining LGBTQ+inclusivity among urology trainees and program directors. Study designs included seven cross-sectional surveys, two reviews, and one abstract encompassing residents, fellows, and applicants across U. S., Canadian, and international settings. Extracted data covered educational curricula, clinical exposure, institutional support, and geographic or demographic disparities. RESULTS: All ten studies reported measurable barriers. Educational: Six studies cited limited didactic exposure to transgender or LGBTQ+ care and five identified an absence of structured curricula. One national survey found 59.5% of applicants lacked any clinical or didactic exposure to genital gender-affirming surgery. Clinical: Eight studies documented insufficient hands-on experience; only 42% of programs had institutional transgender health initiatives. Trainees expressed low confidence counseling LGBTQ+ patients and reported uneven exposure across training levels. Institutional: Eight studies noted absent faculty expertise, limited administrative support, or fragmented interdepartmental collaboration. Program director attitudes and regional policies influenced inclusion of LGBTQ+ content. Geographic & Demographic: Barriers varied by American Urological Association region, gender, and training level; female residents and LGBTQIA+ applicants reported greater interest but less opportunity for transgender-care training. CONCLUSIONS: Educational, institutional, and structural barriers continue to impede LGBTQ+ inclusivity in urology training. Addressing these requires development of standardized curricula, expansion of clinical exposure through dedicated transgender health modules, and faculty development in culturally competent care. Reducing geographic and demographic inequities will help ensure future urologists deliver equitable, patient-centered care to LGBTQ+ populations.

title: DISPARITIES IN OUTCOMES FOR GENDER MINORITIES WITH ADVANCED PROSTATE CANCER
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Folaju Oladipupo-George, Katy-Anne Burr, Ching Hao Chen, Alice Cotton, Tet Yap
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Advanced and metastatic prostate cancer (PCa) in sexual and gender minority (SGM) patients remains largely understudied. Current treatment frameworks focus on cisgender men, leaving insufficient guidance for treating those who have undergone (testosterone-suppressing) gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT). This literature review aimed to evaluate advanced/metastatic PCa therapy in gender minority (GM) patients, compare treatment outcomes with cisgender men and identify gaps in GM care. METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines we searched PubMed, Embase, Medline and PsychInfo databases in October 2025, using MeSH terms for “sexual and gender minorities”, “advanced”, “metastatic” and “prostate cancer”. Studies met inclusion criteria if they assessed incidence of advanced/metastatic PCa in GM patients, prior gender affirmation and treatment outcomes. Quality assessment was performed using JBI checklists-studies included were either moderate or low-moderate in quality, with limitations frequently related to sample size and lack of comparison. Qualitative data extraction was conducted using NVivo. RESULTS: Of 62 articles screened, eight met the inclusion criteria. From these, excluding single case reports, two studies reported on a total of 57 GM patients combined and another (ongoing) plans to have ultimately enrolled 333 participants, although cisgender and GM participants are not separately tallied. Records suggest an increased proportion of metastatic PCa at diagnosis in GM patients, despite a much lower general incidence rate of PCa. One study suggested an association with GAHT and biochemical recurrences and bone metastases. These likely contribute to the reported higher mortality rate after PCa diagnosis in GM patients, compared to cisgender patients. However, treatment outcome data was generally indirect and incomplete. CONCLUSIONS: PCa appears more likely to be advanced or metastatic in a GM patient, with very limited report on treatment outcomes. Despite this, outcomes are well documented for cisgender men. Our findings highlight an inequity in available evidence and exemplify the need for further data collection, such as prospective case series with follow-ups on GM patients with advanced or metastatic PCa. A better understanding of reported disparities will help reduce outcome inequalities, improving care. | | | --- | | |

title: IMPACT OF PROSTATE CANCER ON PARTNERS: COMPARING EVIDENCE BETWEEN SEXUAL AND GENDER MINORITY POPULATIONS AND NON-MINORITY POPULATIONS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Victoria Richards, Arisma Arora, Ching Hao Chen, Alice Cotton, Tet Yap
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate cancer (PCa) impacts not only the patient but their intimate partners, influencing sexual satisfaction and relationship quality. Research has largely focused on heterosexual and cisgender couples, leaving gaps in the understanding of how PCa affects sexual and gender minority (SGM) patients’ partners. This study aimed to compare current evidence on PCa’s impact on SGM patients’ partners’ sexual health versus non-SGM partners and identified key gaps in research. METHODS: A systematic search of PsycINFO, Medline and Embase databases was conducted in October 2025 for full-text articles published in English. Included studies focused on sex and relationships and partners’ experiences. Excluded studies included an intervention rather than focusing on the initial affect of PCa on patients and partners. Extracted data included patient characteristics, SGM status, relationship characteristics, partners’ sexual satisfaction and relationship impact. Findings were thematically synthesised to identify key factors affecting partners of SGM versus non-SGM patients. RESULTS: Of the 1969 records screened, five studies were included in the review. Three studies included non-SGM populations, and two included SGM populations. Non-SGM partners were assessed using validated tools such as SKIPPP-F. No validated assessment tools were reported by studies of partners of SGM patients. Five key factors impacting partners’ sexual health included: partner involvement, communication, sexual function and intimacy, emotional/relational adjustment, and partner wellbeing. SGM partners reported worse outcomes in all domains. Both SGM and non-SGM patients and partners reported that their sex life was worse post-treatment, along with loss of intimacy and lower satisfaction with sex and relationships. However, sex was perceived as more important in gay relationships compared to non-SGM relationships. CONCLUSIONS: PCa significantly affects partners’ sexual satisfaction and relationship quality in both SGM and non-SGM populations. However, partners of SGM patients experience more exclusion from care and higher relational strain. This highlights the need for inclusive clinical practice and validated assessment tools that specifically address the experiences of SGM patients and their partners to improve sexual and relational outcomes. | | | --- | | |

title: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF THE ONLINE RESOURCES FOR SEXUAL AND GENDER MINORITIES ADDRESSING SEXUAL CONSEQUENCES OF TREATMENT IN BREAST, ANAL, CERVICAL AND PENILE CANCER
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Katy-Anne Burr, Ching-Hao Chen, Alice Cotton, Tet Yap
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Information on the sexual side effects of cancer treatments has been well researched within the heterosexual population. However, less is known about the sexual side effect burden on sexual and gender minority (SGM) groups. Limited understanding of SGM sexual practices among healthcare professionals, combined with patients’ fear of discrimination, drives many SGM patients to seek information online. After conducting previous research into SGM specific prostate cancer resources, we aimed to explore digital resources in breast (BCa), anal (ACa), penile (PCa), and cervical cancer (CCa). METHODS: We conducted this review according to PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO CRD42024628689). A novel search was conducted of Google and YouTube in April 2025, with 21 key search terms. Online resources were included if they published sexual side effect information specific to SGM populations after BCa, ACa, PCa or CCa treatments. The AACODS checklist was used to assess resource quality. Data extracted from resources included: sexual side effect coverage, the inclusion of transgender (TG) information, ease of use, and quality of information. RESULTS: Eighteen websites and one YouTube channel met inclusion criteria. Eight resources for BCa, seven for ACa, two for CCa and two for PCa. Across all cancers, Cancer Council provided the highest-quality resources, offering inclusive, well-structured materials with comprehensive side-effect coverage and TG representation. Breast Cancer Network Australia and Young Survival Coalition (YSC) also performed strongly for BCa, with YSC uniquely highlighting identity and relationship challenges post-treatment. Macmillan scored well for accessibility and ease of use through its multilingual and audio features, but often lacked depth in side-effect detail. Overall, PCa materials were the weakest, showing minimal side-effect detail and poor inclusion of TG perspectives. CONCLUSIONS: There is a lack of SGM-specific online resources discussing sexual outcomes after BCa, ACa, CCa, and PCa treatment. This absence may impact SGM patients’ ability to make informed treatment decisions. Future research should examine the sexual effects of all cancer treatments in SGM patients to inform inclusive resources covering all sexual side effects and practices. Further work should also assess the accessibility and usability of online resources to ensure equitable patient access. | | | --- | | |

title: INVISIBLE BARRIERS: MISGENDERING, BIAS, AND CARE AVOIDANCE IN UROLOGICAL PRACTICE
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Pedro Silva, Luis Campos Pinheiro, Miguel Gil, João Cunha, Luis Severo
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Transgender and gender-diverse patients frequently encounter discrimination in medical care, yet urology remains one of the least studied specialties regarding inclusivity. This systematic review analyzed the types, prevalence, and impact of discrimination experienced by transgender patients in urology care settings, aiming to identify actionable targets for improving equitable access and provider competency. METHODS: A semantic systematic search using Pubmed, Embase and Scopus. Twelve studies (2019–2025) met inclusion criteria: 6 qualitative, 5 cross-sectional, and 1 longitudinal cohort, encompassing over 31,000 transgender and nonbinary participants across urology, gynecologic, sexual health, and general clinical contexts. Data extraction followed PRISMA-adapted protocols emphasizing urology specific discrimination, care avoidance, and provider behavior. RESULTS: Prevalence of Discrimination: 23% avoided urologic care due to fear of mistreatment. 33% were asked to educate providers about transgender health. 15% experienced invasive or inappropriate questioning. 26% reported misgendering; 59% cited insufficient provider training; 18% noted absence of affirming imagery or language. 68% delayed or avoided healthcare following prior negative experiences. Patterns Identified: Interpersonal bias: Misgendering and assumptions about anatomy were common in both general and gender-affirming urology clinics. Structural discrimination: Administrative misclassification, lack of inclusive documentation, and insurance barriers were recurrent. Provider deficits: Only 27% of patients were asked their preferred terminology for anatomy. Intersectionality: Older, biracial, and disabled participants faced disproportionately higher denial rates (up to 8% for trans-specific care). Contextual factors: Hospital settings showed higher gender insensitivity than community-based or academic centers. Urology clinics reported more frequent discomfort during genital examinations than non-surgical specialties. CONCLUSIONS: Discrimination in urology care for transgender patients is prevalent, multifaceted, and driven by both interpersonal and structural factors. Fear of misgendering, inadequate provider training, and administrative barriers directly contribute to delayed presentation and reduced trust in urologists. These findings underscore the urgent need for trans-affirming training programs, inclusive documentation systems, and explicit EAU guidelines addressing gender diversity in urological care.

title: REDEFINING PROSTATE CANCER CARE IN TRANSGENDER PATIENTS: DIAGNOSTIC GAPS, SCREENING INEQUITIES, AND HORMONE RELATED BIASES
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Pedro Silva, Luis Campos Pinheiro, Miguel Gil, João Cunha, Luis Severo
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate cancer risk persists in transgender women despite gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT). Hormonal suppression alters PSA levels and tissue morphology, complicating diagnosis. This review synthesized current evidence on prevalence, diagnostic accuracy, and oncologic outcomes in transgender patients receiving GAHT. METHODS: A semantic systematic review using the Pubmed, Embase and Scope databases was conducted and 12 studies (2006–2025) were selected including >140 000 transgender women and gender-diverse individuals. Extracted variables included PSA kinetics, histopathology, recurrence risk, and screening access disparities. RESULTS: Epidemiology & Risk: Prostate cancer incidence in transgender women on GAHT was 0.20 standardized incidence ratio (SIR) compared with cisgender men, equivalent to a 2.56-fold lower overall risk. Prevalence: 0.62 % (n = 589/95,460; _JAMA Oncol 2024_). Despite lower incidence, recurrence risk was higher among GAHT users (OR 1.83 for biochemical recurrence; OR 3.96 for bone metastasis). Diagnostic Challenges: PSA suppression: GAHT lowers PSA by 1.1–1.3 ng/mL (p < 0.001), making standard biopsy thresholds unreliable. Histopathology: Estrogen and antiandrogen therapy induce atrophic and metaplastic nuclear changes, leading to under-recognition or over-grading when hormone history is not considered. Access disparities: Only 23 % of transgender women aged ≥ 50 years ever underwent PSA screening; rates were lower in Black and non-binary individuals (OR 0.51, 95 % CI 0.25–1.01). Anatomical barriers: Post-vaginoplasty access limits digital rectal examination and biopsy feasibility. Healthcare Delivery & Awareness: Provider training deficits identified in 7/12 studies; only two national guidelines explicitly mention prostate screening for transgender patients. HIV-positive individuals were more likely to be screened (OR 3.61, 95 % CI 1.28–10.19). No standardized PSA cut-off or imaging protocol exists for transgender women. Oncologic Outcomes: PSA at diagnosis often underestimated disease burden; cases diagnosed at higher stage (T3+) were reported in long-term estrogen users. Survival data remain limited, but recurrence patterns suggest biologic differences driven by prolonged hormonal modulation. CONCLUSIONS: Prostate cancer in transgender women represents a diagnostic blind spot in modern urology. Hormone-induced PSA suppression and tissue remodeling obscure early detection, while inconsistent screening practices amplify health inequities. Despite lower incidence, evidence of increased recurrence risk warrants tailored PSA thresholds, modified biopsy algorithms, and multidisciplinary pathways integrating urology, endocrinology, and transgender health services. Development of EAU-endorsed guidelines is essential to ensure equitable, evidence-based care for all patients with prostates—regardless of gender identity.

title: BASELINE REPRODUCTIVE AND SEXUAL HEALTH KNOWLEDGE AMONG UNDERGRADUATE STUDENTS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Kunal Jain, Esha Jain, Ruben Blachman-Braun, Premal Patel
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Many undergraduate students are newly sexually active adults with unsafe sexual practices. We sought to assess undergraduate students' knowledge and attitudes on reproductive and sexual health. Our aim was to identify variables associated with knowledge deficiencies. METHODS: A novel, cross-sectional questionnaire was created with local expert input. The survey was distributed online from January to March 2021 at two universities in Manitoba, Canada, through student unions. Local ethics board approval was obtained, participation was voluntary, and data was anonymized. Chi-squared, Kruskal-Wallis, and univariable and multivariable-adjusted logistic regression analyses were used. P-value<0.05 was considered statistically significant. RESULTS: There were 309 respondents out of approximately 28,816 possible undergraduate students (n=309, response rate 1.1%). Of the respondents, 239 (77.3%) were females, 146 (47.2%) were≥22 years old, 49 (15.9%) were from a high socioeconomic status (SES), and 264 (85.4%) were from Manitoba. The overall mean knowledge score was 65.5%, with averages of 71.7% for STIs, 65.6% for infertility, and 59.2% for contraception/family planning. On multivariate analysis, higher knowledge scores were associated with identifying as female (male OR: 0.39, 95% CI: 0.18–0.87; p=0.021), older age (age 21 OR: 6.04, 95% CI: 1.78–20.49; p=0.004 and≥22 years OR: 4.07, 95% CI: 1.35–12.26; p=0.012), and university attended (University of Manitoba OR: 1.97, 95% CI: 1.11–3.49; p=0.021). On subgroup analysis, family SES was associated with higher STI knowledge scores (OR: 2.19, 95% CI: 1.07–4.48; p=0.032). Few felt that their post-secondary education on contraception/family planning (26.2%), STIs (34.6%), and infertility (4.5%) was adequate. CONCLUSIONS: Undergraduate students face unique barriers in obtaining adequate reproductive and sexual health knowledge. Younger males who attend smaller universities, and possibly those from lower SES, may be at greater risk of negative outcomes. We highlight the need for improved access to education and supports to assist students in making more informed decisions.

title: IMPROVED ACCESS TO PERI-OPERATIVE EDUCATION FOR PATIENTS UNDERGOING RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Claire L. Haas, Tasha L. Posid, Claire L. Postl, Patrick Di Meo, Karen L. Meade, Robert Rogers, Shawn Dason, Ahmad Shabsigh, Akshay L. Sood, Geoffrey Box, Michael Gong
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Radical prostatectomy is associated with well-documented adverse effects on urinary and sexual function, often accompanied by anxiety, depression, and reduced quality of life. Patient adherence with post-operative exercises and self-management of symptoms is critical for optimal recovery. We created the Prostatectomy Care Companion Application (PCCA), a digital education program embedded in the electronic health record, to provide a standardized pathway that included instructional videos and handouts accessed through EPIC’s MyChart application. Our objective was to evaluate patient engagement with the application. METHODS: Patients enrolled from November 2022 to July 2025 were evaluated for initial and continued engagement with the PCCA program. Educational video topics included PCCA introduction, prostatectomy procedure, pelvic rehabilitation, sexual health, and pre-and post-operative expectations. Primary outcomes included patient enrollment in the PCCA and ongoing engagement with app content over time. Retrospective review of app usage logs was performed to evaluate patterns of enrollment and interaction across months of prostatectomy. RESULTS: 349 patients were identified: Engagement with the application has increased over time (see (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191272.33670.20.22#F1)) with a >1.5-fold increase (approximately 15% to 30% engagement) after the onboarding of a Pathway Coordinator in Fall 2024. As of July 2025, engagement was almost 50% of all patients offered this resource. Initial engagement appeared to promote continued use, as 97.6% of patients who activated the PCCA remained active at their last appointment. CONCLUSIONS: Through this initiative, we developed a library of standardized, evidence-based educational materials for prostatectomy patients, underwent iterative review by our clinical team, and were integrated into our preoperative application pathway. These findings highlight the PCCA’s value in enhancing patient engagement and facilitating access to comprehensive post-surgical care.

title: SOCIAL PREDICTORS OF NO SHOWS AT AN URBAN, SAFETY-NET UROLOGY CLINIC: A MIXED EFFECTS MODEL STUDY
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Lynn Leng, Pablo A. Suarez, Mubarak A. Momodu, Jules Benjamin Greenfield, David B. Bayne
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Clinic non-attendance negatively affects patient outcomes and disrupts clinic workflow. This study aims to identify predictors of patient no-shows at an urban, safety-net urology clinic. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study including all scheduled patients and appointments from April 2024 to April 2025 was conducted. Patient sociodemographic factors (SDOH; including education, employment, insurance, social support, etc.) were abstracted from EPIC reports. The primary outcome was clinic attendance. Continuous and categorical variables were analyzed using student’s T-test and chi-square, respectively. A multivariate mixed-effects logistic regression model was performed to adjust for covariates. RESULTS: Among 6,945 scheduled appointments, 1,752 (25.2%) were no-shows. On univariate analysis, select significant factors associated with no-shows included women gender (odds ratio \[OR\] 0.84, 95% confidence interval \[CI\] 0.73-0.98), non-Hispanic Black race (OR 1.57, CI 1.33-1.89), Asian/Pacific Islander race (OR 0.50, CI 0.42-0.61), inactive patient portal (OR 2.06, CI 1.84-2.30), divorced (OR 1.59, CI 1.31-1.92), single (OR 1.64, CI 1.44-1.86), non-English language (OR 0.67, CI 0.59-0.74), interpreter needed (OR 0.67, CI 0.60-0.76), assigned primary care provider (OR 0.56, CI 0.48-0.67), unemployment (OR 1.50, CI 1.33-1.77), new visits (OR 2.23, CI 1.99-2.51), procedural visits (OR 0.77, CI 0.63-0.92), history of being unhoused (OR 2.43, CI 2.10-2.82), lead days (OR 1.00, CI 1.00-1.003), historical no show rate (OR 1.09, CI 1.08-1.10), and social vulnerability index (OR 1.18, CI 1.11-1.25). On multivariable analysis, history of being unhoused (OR 2.29, CI 1.53-3.42), patient portal inactivation (OR 1.84, CI 1.37-2.47), social worker on file (OR 1.33, CI 1.02-1.72), new visits (OR 1.47, CI 1.26-1.72), procedural visits (OR 0.64, CI 0.49-0.83), historical no show rate (OR 1.11, CI 1.09-1.13), and lead days (OR 1.00, CI 1.00-1.01) remained significant. CONCLUSIONS: Predictors of urologic clinic no shows were history of being unhoused, historical no-show rate, new visits, assigned social worker, inactive patient portal, and increased time from appointment scheduling, of which the latter two are intervenable. This study offers upstream solutions for improving attendance for a safety-net clinic and healthcare access for urologic patients. | | | --- | | |

title: NATIONAL TRENDS AND DISPARITIES IN SURGICAL MANAGEMENT OF NEUROGENIC BLADDER
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Stephanie Chan, Frances Kazal, Gregory Joice
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Neurogenic bladder (NGB) includes a heterogeneous group of patients with impaired bladder control. Surgical management ranges from continent procedures that preserve urinary control to incontinent diversions. Prior studies report NGB treatment disparities but are limited to single institutions or specific NGB etiologies. We examined national trends and disparities in continent versus incontinent urinary diversions among NGB patients. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional analysis using the National Inpatient Sample from 2016 to 2022. ICD-10 codes were used to classify NGB patients by congenital or acquired etiologies (e. g. cerebral palsy, spina bifida, multiple sclerosis, paraplegia). Outcomes included continent (bladder augmentation, neobladder, continent catheterizable channels, artificial urinary sphincter) or incontinent procedures (ileal conduit, vesicostomy, cutaneous ureterostomy, colon conduit, sphincterotomy). Patient demographics, comorbidities, and hospital characteristics were compared by diversion type. Multivariable analyses identified predictors of incontinent diversions. RESULTS: A total of 312,486 patients with NGB were identified, including 19,539 with congenital and 133,700 with acquired etiologies. Among these, 1,564 admissions involved a continent or incontinent urinary diversion, with 60% receiving incontinent procedures. Patients undergoing incontinent diversions were older and more likely to have public insurance. Hospital characteristics did not differ by diversion type. On adjusted analysis, NGB etiology was not associated with diversion type. Independent predictors of incontinent diversion included older age, male sex, public insurance, lower household income, and pre-existing colostomy. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings highlight the influence of demographic and socioeconomic factors on surgical management of NGB. As the first national study covering a wide range of NGB etiologies and inpatient treatments, these results underscore disparities in access to continent urinary diversions and the need for strategies to ensure equitable care for all NGB patients. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: BARRIERS TO ELECTRONIC HEALTH RECORD M-ISI QUESTIONNAIRE COMPLETION IN UROLOGY PATIENTS: THE IMPACT OF AGE AND SOCIAL VULNERABILITY
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Raviraj Rege, Carl Ceraolo, Soumya Konar, David Song, Elisabeth Hayward, Rajat Jain, Scott Quarrier
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Collecting patient-reported outcomes (PROs) through electronic health record (EHR) patient portals (ePP) helps clinicians better understand patients’ experiences while streamlining workflows. However, these digital tools can unintentionally amplify disparities in participation. We evaluated demographic and social factors associated with M-ISI completion. METHODS: This was a single-center retrospective study of all adults with diagnoses of incontinence, LUTS, BPH, elevated PSA, or prostate cancer who were distributed M-ISI via ePP at an outpatient urology clinic from June 2019 to June 2025. M-ISI was sent 7 days before the visit. Completion rates were analyzed at patient and encounter levels. The CDC Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) by ZIP code served as a neighborhood-level socioeconomic measure. Statistical comparisons were performed using Wilcoxon rank sum, chi-square, and multivariable logistic regression tests. RESULTS: EHR record data identified 24,746 unique patients and 166,028 encounters when M-ISI was distributed. Completion rate was 22.1% by encounter and 44% by patient. Completers were younger (71.3 ± 10.8 vs 72.9 ± 13.7 yr, p<0.001) and lived in less vulnerable areas (median SVI 32.5 vs 46.2). Non-completers were more likely non-White (7.7% vs 16.4%) and Latinx (1.1% vs 2.6%, both p<0.001). In multivariable analysis, older age (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.986–0.988), female sex (0.85, 0.82–0.87), non-White race (0.49, 0.47–0.51), Latinx ethnicity (0.61, 0.54–0.68), and high social vulnerability (SVI≥75: 0.67, 0.64–0.70) independently predicted lower completion (all p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Despite automated EHR ePP distribution, M-ISI was completed in one in five encounters. Older age and higher social vulnerability were major barriers to completion, highlighting the need for alternative delivery methods and interventions to promote inclusive patient evaluation. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: PELVIC FLOOR DISORDERS ARE COMMON AND BURDENSOME AMONG WOMEN WITH BLADDER CANCER
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Nicolle Acuna, Adam Williams, Elena Cortizas, Kendra Boyd, Katherine Amin, Raveen Syan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Pelvic floor disorders (PFDs) disproportionately affect women with bladder cancer (BC), yet they are underassessed and undertreated, despite a significant impact on quality of life (QOL). The Survivorship and Pelvic floor InterventioNs (SPIN) study was created for women with BC (newly diagnosed, undergoing treatment, or previously treated) to receive PFD care from a urogynecologist. This study aimed to describe the prevalence and severity of PFDs among women enrolled in SPIN. METHODS: Women were recruited to SPIN during urologic oncologist visits. Participants completed validated questionnaires prior to their initial visit, including the Pelvic Floor Distress Inventory (PFDI-20), Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI), Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), and a series of questions assessing the relationship between PFDs and BC treatments. Descriptive statistics summarized patient characteristics and scores. Group comparisons used Wilcoxon rank-sum, with significance set at p<0.05. RESULTS: Of 33 women enrolled, 25 completed their baseline surveys (median age 68 years, IQR 63–73; 93.9% White, 54.5% Hispanic). Baseline PFD burden was substantial: UDI-6 scores (subset of PFDI-20 examining urinary bother) had a median score of 41.7 (IQR 25, 45.8) and PFDI-20 score 70.8 (IQR 52.1, 97.9). 54.5% reported overactive bladder (OAB) symptoms and 48.5% stress urinary incontinence (SUI). Women with SUI had higher urinary distress than those without (UDI-6: 41.7 vs 0, p>0.01). Sexual dysfunction was prevalent (80%) with median FSFI 5.0 (IQR 3.6, 19.6). Perceived stress was moderate to high (median PSS 20.5, IQR 18.5–23). 29.2% reported oncologist discussion of sexual health impacts, 41.7% reported discussions of bladder symptom impacts, while 50% of participants reported no discussion of treatment effects. CONCLUSIONS: Baseline findings reveal a significant burden of PFDs among women with BC, with 50% of patients reporting these symptoms were not assessed during oncologic visits. This highlights the need for multidisciplinary care to improve QOL and outcomes for female BC patients. | | | --- | | |

title: A DEDICATED UROGYNECOLOGIC PROGRAM FOR WOMEN WITH BLADDER CANCER ALLOWS FOR MARKED IMPROVEMENT IN PELVIC FLOOR DISORDERS AT 3 MONTHS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Nicolle Acuna, Adam Williams, Elena Cortizas, Kendra Boyd, Katherine Amin, Raveen Syan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Women with bladder cancer (BC) often experience pelvic floor disorders (PFDs) that are overshadowed by their cancer treatment priorities, however they can severely impact patient quality of life (QOL). The Survivorship and Pelvic floor InterventioNs (SPIN) study was created for women with BC (newly diagnosed, undergoing treatment, or previously treated) to receive PFD care from a urogynecologist. This study assesses if participants demonstrate improvement in PFDs symptoms between baseline and three-month follow-up by participating in SPIN. METHODS: Women with BC were recruited during their urologic oncologist visits. Participants completed validated questionnaires prior to their initial visit, including the Pelvic Floor Distress Inventory (PFDI-20), Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI), Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), and a series of questions assessing the relationship between PFDs and BC treatments. Descriptive statistics summarized participant characteristics and questionnaire scores. Paired Wilcoxon signed-rank compared baseline and 3-month results, with significance defined as p<0.05. RESULTS: 13 women completed both baseline and 3-month assessments. At baseline, participants demonstrated significant symptom burden with a median UDI-6 (subset of PFDI-20 examining urinary bother) score of 37.5 (IQR 29.2, 45.8), PFDI-20 score of 81.3 (IQR 66.7, 103.1), FSFI score of 5.0 (IQR 4.2, 25.5), and PSS of 18 (IQR 11, 21). After three months, urinary distress decreased substantially (UDI-6 20.8, IQR 0, 37.5; p=0.0137), overall pelvic floor distress improved (PFDI-20 37.5, IQR 18.8, 87.5; p=0.0105), and sexual function increased (FSFI 13.4, IQR 5.2, 29.6; p=0.0034). Perceived stress decreased from baseline to 3-months \[PSS 10 (6.5, 15), p=0.0020\]. CONCLUSIONS: Enrollment of women with BC in a structured urogynecologic program addressing PFDs (SPIN) significantly improves PFD symptom bother. We propose that all women with BC be offered automatic referral to urogynecologic care to help improve PFD symptom burden and QOL.

title: BRIDGING THE GAP IN RURAL URINARY INCONTINENCE CARE: PROVIDER PERSPECTIVES AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF AN EDUCATIONAL URINARY INCONTINENCE CARE INITIATIVE
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Grace Powderly, Morgan Loy, Julia Long, Trevor Diepenbrock
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary Incontinence (UI) is an extremely prevalent condition across all demographics that can significantly affect a patient’s quality of life. However, the proportion of those with UI who seek care remains low, indicating the existence of barriers to care. Currently, there is a gap in research evaluating rural UI care. This study explored provider-identified barriers to rural UI care, aiming to reduce disparities through the creation of an educational packet — the Urinary Incontinence Care Initiative. METHODS: This cross-sectional study surveyed rural medical providers in Northeast Missouri. Rurality was established by county using the Health Resource & Service Administration’s definition of ‘fully rural.’ The survey assessed providers’ views and practices in UI management and evaluated perceived barriers to care. Based on the results, an educational packet was created and distributed to 57 rural medical practices. RESULTS: Among 38 respondents, 21 providers met criteria for further analyses. The majority were physicians (17, 81.0%). Most providers agreed or strongly agreed they feel comfortable diagnosing (20, 95.2%) and treating UI (17, 81.0%). Around half always screen UI patients for depression (12, 57.1%). One-third reported never sharing online resources with UI patients (7, 33.3%). Physicians were more likely to inform patients of community resources than nurse practitioners (P=.012). Lack of support and care resources, low patient health literacy, and limited access to secondary care providers were the top-tanked barriers to UI care. The majority of providers expressed interest in educational materials on community resources (11, 68.6%), online resources (11, 68.6%), and a UI screening tool (10, 62.5%). CONCLUSIONS: Rural providers feel comfortable managing UI; however, many believe patients lack necessary support and care resources. The UI Care Initiative was created to increase awareness of available resources and reduce educational barriers. This packet included evidence-based materials for providers (UI screening tool, treatment algorithm, referral list) and for patients (UI education, pelvic floor exercises, community and online resource guide). Overall, the packet aimed to address the identified disparities in rural UI care.

title: BRIDGING THE GAP AT CUTLER CENTER FOR MEN: EARLY OUTCOMES FROM A COMPREHENSIVE, NAVIGATION-BASED MODEL OF PREVENTIVE CARE
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Ramy Abou Ghayda, George Gheordunescu, Randy A. Vince, Sophie L. Elias, Jennifer Muehle, Thriaksh Rajan, Lee Ponsky
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Men experience shorter life expectancy and higher rates of preventable illness, in part due to lower healthcare engagement. To address this gap, University Hospitals (UH) launched the Cutler Center for Men (CCM) – a free, multidisciplinary, male-focused program offering personalized navigation, preventive alerts, and community engagement. This received media attention and was featured in the New York Times. We evaluated the program’s impact on healthcare utilization, clinical outcomes, and community engagement among enrolled men versus non-members within the same health system. METHODS: We conducted a propensity-matched observational study comparing 1,270 CCM members to 3,810 non-member men matched by age, comorbidities, race, income, insurance, and prior healthcare use. Primary outcomes included annual primary care visits, prostate cancer screening, diabetes control (A1c <8%), influenza vaccination, and outpatient visit frequency. Program-level metrics included enrollment growth, care coordination, and community outreach. RESULTS: Between September 2023–2024, 3,300 men enrolled in CCM (30% annual growth), accounting for 15% of all new UH Urology Institute encounters. Members demonstrated a 55% increase in overall encounters post-enrollment, 82% PCP assignment, and a Net Promoter Score of 84—nearly double national healthcare benchmarks. After adjustment, members were 70% more likely to receive prostate cancer screening (95% CI 1.47–1.96, p<0.05), 37% more likely to complete an annual primary care visit (95% CI 1.16–1.63, p<0.05), and 36% more likely to achieve diabetes control (A1c <8%) (95% CI 1.18–1.57, p<0.05). No difference was found in influenza vaccination. Community events and social engagement more than doubled compared with baseline. CONCLUSIONS: Enrollment in a dedicated men’s health center significantly improved preventive care utilization, chronic disease control, and healthcare engagement. These data demonstrate that a free, system-integrated, gender-specific model can effectively close gaps in men’s health outcomes. The CCM’s navigation-based framework represents a replicable, outcomes-driven blueprint for health systems seeking to promote male population health improvement.

title: SURGICAL GLOVE SIZING DISPARITIES AMONG OPERATING ROOM STAFF: A MULTI-INSTITUTIONAL ANALYSIS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Improving Access and Outcomes Across All Populations I (IP01)
authors: Mimi V. Nguyen, Sabrina Mehari, Gwen Grimsby
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Use of commercialized surgical instruments tailored to male subjects has been shown to impact both ease of instrument use and result in more injuries in the operating room (OR) for female users. Furthermore, improper glove sizing can impair dexterity and safety in surgery. We investigated whether female surgical staff were more likely to wear incorrectly sized sterile gloves and identified predictors of mismatch. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional survey study of surgical personnel at Phoenix Children’s and Mayo Clinic Arizona. Participant demographics, usual glove size worn, and hand dimensions were collected. Correct sterile glove size was determined using the ProtexisTM PI manufacturer’s guide based on hand width. Mismatch was defined reported glove size differing from the recommended size. Independent-samples t-tests and chi-square tests were used for univariate analysis. Binary logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of incorrect sizing. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05. RESULTS: Among 124 surgical staff, 36 (29%) wore an incorrect sterile glove size. There were no differences in mean age, sex, or ethnicity between those who wore correct vs incorrect gloves (p=0.61-0.73). Staff with mismatched gloves had greater mean hand width (9.25 ± 0.75 cm vs 8.67 ± 0.74 cm; p<0.001), and circumference (20.74 ± 2.08 cm vs 19.66 ± 2.68 cm; p=0.04). On multivariable analysis, male sex strongly predicted correct glove fit (OR 11.6, p=0.002), while greater hand width predicted mismatch (OR 0.08, p<0.001). Among those with mismatched gloves, Hispanic participants were more likely to wear gloves that were too small (37.5% vs 7.1%; p=0.03). CONCLUSIONS: Nearly one-third of surgical staff wore incorrectly sized sterile gloves. Female staff remained disproportionately affected even after adjusting for hand dimensions, suggesting current glove designs better accommodate male hand proportions. Most mismatches resulted from oversizing. These findings highlight ergonomic and equity gaps in glove design. Expanding glove size ranges and refining fit standards could enhance comfort, dexterity, and safety in the OR. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: METABOLOMICS ANALYSIS IDENTIFIES SERUM BIOMARKERS PREDICTING RISK OF INTRAVESICAL TUMORRECURRENCE AFTER INTRAVESICAL BACILLUS CALMETTE–GUéRIN THERAPY (BCG) IN PATIENTS WITHNON-MUSCLE INVASIVE BLADDER CANCER
session: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I (IP02)
authors: Makito Miyake, Kota Iida, Nobutaka Nishimura, Kazuki Miyazaki, Yuki Oda, Takuto Shimizu, Yusuke Iemura, Kiyohide Fujimoto
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Evidence on metabolomics research and metabolomics-based biomarkers predicting treatment outcomes is still limited in bladder cancer. Here, weexplored serum metabolites which were potentially associated with risk of intravesicalrecurrence after intravesical BCG therapy. METHODS: Two independent cohorts, discovery cohort (n=23) and validation cohort (n=40),were included in this study. Blood was taken before induction BCG therapy (pre-BCG blood;both discovery cohort and validation cohort) and after 6 doses of BCG (post-BCG blood; onlydiscovery cohort). Metabolome analysis of serum samples was conducted using capillaryelectrophoresis time-of-flight mass spectrometry. The endpoint was intravesical recurrence-freesurvival, which was analyzed with the Kaplan–Meier estimates, the log-rank test, and Coxproportional hazard model. RESULTS: Of 353 metabolites quantified, nine (2.5%) including four amino acids and four (1.1%) werefound to be upregulated and downregulated, respectively. Heatmap of hierarchical clusteringanalysis for the fold-changes of serum metabolites differentiating 10 recurrent cases and 13non-recurrent cases in the discovery cohort. The higher number of metabolites showing highfold-change were observed in the non-recurrent cases as compared to the recurrent cases( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191276.85430.b0.01#F1)). A metabolome response-based score model using 16 metabolites including threonine and N6,N6,N6-trimethyl-lysine well stratified the risk of post-BCG recurrence. In addition, pre-BCG metabolome-based score models using six metabolites, octanoylcarnitine, S-Methylcysteine-S-oxide, theobromine, carnitine, indole-3-acetic acid, and valeric acid weredeveloped from the discovery cohort. Univariate and multivariate analysis confirmed highpredictive accuracy in the validation cohort and combination cohort ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191276.85430.b0.01#F2)). CONCLUSIONS: We demonstrated that numerous types of serum metabolites were altered inresponse to intravesical BCG therapy and developed high performance and non-invasive scoremodels which well differentiates risk of post-BCG recurrence.

title: DYNAMIC PREDICTION OF RECURRENCE AND PROGRESSION RISK IN NON-MUSCLE INVASIVE BLADDER CANCER USING CONDITIONAL SURVIVAL: A SEER-MEDICARE ANALYSIS
session: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I (IP02)
authors: Chia-Xhen Chang, Agustin Perez-Londoño, Jamil Almohtasib, Sumedh Kaul, Aaron Fleishman, Simon Kim, Aria F. Olumi, Peter Chang, Andrew Wagner, Boris Gershman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Predicting recurrence and progression risk in non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) is essential for counseling and risk-adapted management. However, conventional models do not account for the change in baseline risk over the time. We therefore examined the conditional survival free of recurrence and progression among older adults with NMIBC to develop a dynamic risk prediction model. METHODS: We identified patients aged 66-89 years with a diagnosis of Ta/Tis/T1 cN0 cM0 bladder cancer treated with TURBT from 2000-2017 in the SEER-Medicare linked database. The conditional recurrence-free (RFS) and progression-free (PFS) survival were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Associations of baseline characteristics with RFS and PFS at pre-specified landmark times were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards models. RESULTS: A total of 39,862 patients were included. Of these, 26,339 (66%) had Ta, 11,758 (29%) had T1, and 1765 (4%) had Tis disease. Median follow-up was 65 months. Baseline 60-month RFS and PFS were 0.39 and 0.85 respectively. Given a 6-, 12-, 24-, 36-, 48-, and 60-months event-free survivorship, the 60-month RFS and PFS were 0.52, 0.62, 0.73, 0.78, 0.82, 0.85 and 0.86, 0.87, 0.89, 0.90, 0.90, and 0.91 respectively ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191276.85430.b0.02#F1)). Conditional RFS rapidly improved within the first 24 months, then plateaued. When stratified by T stage, patients with T1 disease demonstrated the greatest improvement in conditional RFS. On multivariable analyses, T stage and tumor grade were less predictive of RFS with longer landmark times. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with NMIBC, the risks of disease recurrence and progression decrease with longer event-free intervals. These observations are most pronounced among those at highest risk, as evidenced by tumor stage and grade. Dynamic risk prediction can improve patient counseling and risk-adapted management during follow-up.

title: PROSPECTIVE OPEN-LABEL STUDY TO EVALUATE THE SAFETY AND EFFICACY OF INTRAVESICAL SUSTAINED-RELEASE GEMCITABINE DOCETAXEL COMBINATION (NDV-01) IN HIGH-RISK NMIBC: UPDATE WITH 9-MONTH COMPLETE RESPONSE DATA
session: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I (IP02)
authors: Mahmoud Abbas, Boris Chertin, Max Kates, Raj Pruthi, Scott White, Paul Greene, Hila Kfir, Avigdor Gordon, Dan Touitou, Moyad Beibooh, Ilan Z. Kafka, Ofer Z. Shenfeld, Dmitry Koulikov, Ariel Mamber, Michael Pasherstnik, Ala Eddin Natsheh, Yair Lotan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Sequential intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel (Gem/Doce) represents a promising option to treat patients with high-risk NMIBC – including those who are BCG-naïve, -exposed and -unresponsive. Gem/Doce is not available in a sustained-release formulation, limiting intravesical exposure. NDV-01 an investigational intravesical agent designed for sustained release of Gem/Doce continuously over a 10-day period. NDV-01 does not require a specialized pharmacy or hood. NDV-01 may also help overcome the burdens to patient and to provider of traditional Gem/Doce. METHODS: The study is a phase 2, single-arm, open-label trial of NDV-01 in subjects with HG NMIBC. Subjects were given 6 bi-weekly instillations followed by monthly maintenance instillations through month 12. Complete response (CR) was defined as a negative cystoscopy, cytology, and biopsy (if indicated). The first assessment for CR was evaluated at 3 months. Subjects with a non-CR at 3 or 6 months were eligible to be reinduced with an additional 6 bi-weekly course of therapy. Disease assessments for CR were also performed at 6, 9, and 12 months. Twenty-five patients have reached the first disease assessment (3-months follow-up) and are included in the per-protocol efficacy analysis. Twelve patients are pending their first response assessment.) All 36 patients who have received >=1 treatment are included in the safety analysis. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics of the 36 enrolled subjects (of a planned 70 patients) are shown in Table 1. All patients were ECOG 0-1. Of the 36 patients who received >=1 dose of NDV-01, 22 (61%) had a TRAE (62% dysuria, 9% asymptomatic positive urine culture, 7% hematuria). No patient had >=Grade 3 TRAE and no patients discontinued treatment due to AEs. Response rates in the 25 patients who received >=3-month disease assessment are shown in Table 2. Two subjects have reached 12-month assessment, and both have a CR. No patient had progression to muscle invasive disease, and no patient has undergone a cystectomy. Of patients with BCG-UR disease, the CR for the 11 participants who had >=3 -month assessment were: CR anytime (10/11 (91%)); 3-month (9/11(82%), 6-month (7/9(78%)), and 9-month (7/8(88%)). CONCLUSIONS: NDV-01 is a novel sustained formulation of Gem/Doce for intravesical use. NDV-01 provides excellent 9-month safety and efficacy in patients with high-risk NMIBC -- including those who are BCG-naïve, -exposed and -unresponsive. The study remains ongoing to provide longer term follow-up and a larger sample size. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: ADVANCED-2 (COHORT A): PRELIMINARY EFFICACY AND SAFETY DATA IN BCG-NAÏVE PARTICIPANTS WITH HIGH-GRADE NON-MUSCLE INVASIVE BLADDER CANCER
session: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I (IP02)
authors: Mark Tyson, Gautam Jayram, Myroslava V. Doronina, Brian Mazzarella, Alexander Sankin, Jacqueline Zummo, Carla Beckham, Eppie Brown, Khushboo Belani, Claire Middleton, Andrea Di Figlia, Brian Desch, Chen Quin Lam, Neal Shore
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: There continues to be a significant unmet need for safe, effective, and bladder-sparing treatment options for patients with non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), and this need is more pronounced in patients who are unable to receive Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG). TARA-002 is a lyophilized biological preparation for intravesical instillation containing inactivated cells of Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A, type 3) Su strain. TARA-002 rapidly enters cancer cells, activating TLR2 and NOD2 to trigger innate immunity, inflammation, and potential immunogenic cell death. This abstract presents interim efficacy and safety data of TARA-002 from the BCG-naïve cohort of the ADVANCED-2 study. METHODS: ADVANCED-2 (Cohort A) is an ongoing Phase 2, open-label study to evaluate the safety and efficacy of intravesical TARA‑002 in adults ≥ 18 years with high-grade (HG)-NMIBC CIS (±Ta/T1) who are BCG-naïve. Key exclusion criteria include penicillin allergy; history of ≥ T2 bladder cancer, nodal, or metastatic disease; and concomitant prostatic or upper tract urothelial involvement. Each participant is treated with intravesical TARA-002 induction (6 weekly doses), reinduction (if disease persists at 3 months) and maintenance (through 24 months). Response is assessed every 3 months for 2 years. Long-term follow-up is conducted up to 60 months. Safety is monitored throughout the study. The primary endpoint is HG complete response (CR) at any time. The key secondary endpoint is duration of response at 12 months. RESULTS: As of October 24, 2025, 31 BCG-naïve participants (median age: 71.0; range: 45 to 89) have been enrolled. The majority of BCG-naïve participants are White (93.5%, 29 of 31), male (80.6%, 25 of 31), and non-Hispanic (90.3%, 28 of 31). The majority of participants had a baseline ECOG score of 0 (83.9%, 26 of 31) and baseline diagnoses of CIS only (58.1%, 18 of 31). TARA-002 demonstrated 72.4% (21 of 29) HG CR at any time in evaluable participants. The 6-month CR was 66.7% (18 of 27), the 9-month CR was 61.1% (11 of 18), and the 12-month CR was 42.9% (6 of 14). Most treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were mild and transient. No participants experienced drug-related serious AEs (SAEs) or drug-related TEAEs leading to withdrawal or death. CONCLUSIONS: Preliminary data suggest that TARA-002 monotherapy is well-tolerated and produces clinically meaningful rates of initial CR coupled with durability of response in BCG-naïve HG NMIBC with CIS (±Ta/T1) through twelve months of treatment. Updated efficacy and safety data will be provided based on evaluable time points at the time of the presentation.

title: COST-EFFECTIVENESS ANALYSIS OF SASANLIMAB PLUS BCG FOR HIGH-RISK NON-MUSCLE INVASIVE BLADDER CANCER (NMIBC): ANALYSIS FROM CREST
session: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I (IP02)
authors: Daniel D. Joyce, Vidit Sharma, Grace Ratcliff, Sam S. Chang, David F. Penson, Vignesh T. Packiam, Girish Kulkarni, Kevin M. Wymer, Stephen A. Boorjian
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The phase 3 CREST trial demonstrated that combining sasanlimab, a subcutaneous checkpoint inhibitor, with BCG (s+BCG) improved event-free survival compared to BCG alone for patients with BCG-naïve high-risk NMIBC. However, patients treated with s+BCG experienced higher rates of ≥ grade 3 treatment-related adverse events (AE), including 15.7% with ≥ grade 3 immune AE, and the cost of checkpoint inhibitors is substantial. We used a Markov model to weigh the costs, toxicities, and efficacy of s+BCG to further investigate its utility. METHODS: We used a decision-analytic Markov model to compare s+BCG to BCG alone for BCG-naïve high-risk NMIBC. Efficacy and toxicity model probabilities were extracted from the CREST trial. Cost data for sasanlimab were extrapolated from subcutaneous nivolumab pricing ($24,225/dose), as sasanlimab is not currently FDA approved. The model used a U. S. Medicare payer perspective with a lifetime time horizon. One-way and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were performed to vary all model inputs across biologically plausible ranges. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) were compared using a willingness to pay threshold of $100,000/quality-adjusted life year (QALY). RESULTS: Over a patient’s lifetime, the combination of s+BCG resulted in 0.03 additional QALYs (6.11 vs 6.08) at an additional cost of $191,666 relative to BCG alone. Combination therapy was found not to be cost effective over a lifetime horizon (ICER=$6,440,594). On one-way sensitivity analysis ( Figure), the combination of s+BCG became cost-effective only if the per dosing price of sasanlimab was reduced by > 90% (to $1244/dose) from the existing pricing of a currently available subcutaneous checkpoint inhibitor. The combination therapy was cost effective in 0% of 100,000 Monte Carlo simulations in probabilistic sensitivity analyses at $100,000/QALY. CONCLUSIONS: At anticipated pricing consistent with currently available immunotherapy, sasanlimab is not cost effective as a combination therapy with BCG relative to BCG alone for patients with high-risk NMIBC. Further efforts are needed to improve the efficacy/toxicity profile of novel therapies in this disease space, while continued scrutiny of the healthsystem cost implications of new agents remains warranted.

title: PROGNOSTIC OUTCOMES COMPARING UPFRONT RADICAL CYSTECTOMY AND PRIMARY BCG THERAPY IN VERY-HIGH RISK NON-MUSCLE INVASIVE BLADDER CANCER: AN UPDATED ANALYSIS IN THE MODERN BCG ERA
session: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I (IP02)
authors: Sagar Patel, Zhouxuan Li, Joseph Black, Wei Qiao, Mikael Rauf, Taeweon Lee, Kelly Bree, Charles Guo, Byron Lee, Colin Dinney, Neema Navai, Ashish Kamat
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The European Association of Urology (EAU) has defined very-high risk (VHR) non–muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) as a subgroup of NIMBC with very high rates of local recurrence, progression to muscle-invasive disease, and metastasis for whom upfront radical cystectomy (RC) is recommended. This study aimed to compare survival and progression outcomes among VHR patients treated with primary Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) therapy versus upfront RC in the modern era of bladder sparing approaches. METHODS: We performed an IRB-approved retrospective review of consecutive patients diagnosed with NMIBC from 2000 to 2023 to identify patients meeting 2021 EAU VHR criteria: high-grade T1 with or without carcinoma in situ (CIS), high-grade Ta with CIS, lymphovascular invasion (LVI), prostatic urethral involvement, or variant histology. Additional risk factors (tumor volume, multifocality, and age at diagnosis) were incorporated into the EAU classification. Overall survival (OS) and cancer-specific survival (CSS) was defined from diagnosis to death; progression-free survival (PFS) was defined as the interval from diagnosis to disease progression, or death. Survival outcomes were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared via the log-rank test. RESULTS: Among 285 patients with VHR NMIBC, 166 underwent primary BCG therapy and 119 underwent upfront RC, with a median follow-up of 51 months (IQR 28–83). Variant histology was more prevalent in the RC group (43% vs 17%, p<0.001) while T1 (P=0.202), CIS (P=0.125), LVI (P=0.169), and prostatic urethral involvement (P=0.535) were similar across both groups ( Table 1). 5-year OS (82% vs 76%, P=0.71), CSS (96% vs 95%, P=0.67), and PFS (71% vs 70%, P=0.59) did not differ significantly between BCG and RC cohorts, respectively ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191276.85430.b0.06#F1)). Outcomes remained comparable across all EAU-defined VHR subgroups and were unaffected by the number or type of VHR risk factors (p>0.05). CONCLUSIONS: In the modern BCG era, patients with VHR NMIBC experience comparable survival and progression outcomes with primary BCG therapy versus upfront radical cystectomy. Bladder-sparing management with intravesical BCG should be offered as an option even for patients meeting EAU VHR criteria.

title: HOLMIUM LASER EN BLOC RESECTION VS MONOPOLAR TURBT FOR BLADDER TUMORS >3 CM: A PROSPECTIVE RANDOMIZED TRIAL—INTERIM ANALYSIS
session: Bladder Cancer: Non-invasive I (IP02)
authors: Maykon W. A. P. Pereira, Alexandre Iscaife, Leopoldo A. R. Filho, Fabio P. Gallucci, Katia R. M. Leite, Leonardo Cardili, William C. Nahas
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Monopolar TURBT fragments the specimen, complicates pathological assessment and may increase the risk of understaging. Prior RCTs largely enrolled tumours ≤3 cm, limiting applicability to larger lesions. We aimed to compare safety and specimen quality between holmium laser en bloc resection (HoLEBT) and monopolar TURBT (RTUb) for tumours larger than 3 cm. We previously conducted a pilot study (2018–2019) of HoLEBT with morcellation for bladder tumours >3 cm. In that cohort, detrusor muscle was present in all specimens and no intra- or peri-operative complications were recorded. These findings provided the rationale for a definitive randomised trial comparing HoLEBT with monopolar TURBT to clarify the optimal endoscopic approach for large bladder tumours. Objectives: To compare HoLEBT with monopolar TURBT regarding presence of detrusor muscle in the specimen assessment, intra- and peri-operative complications, and oncological outcomes. METHODS: Prospective, single-centre, single-blind, randomised (1:1) trial (planned n=100): HoLEBT (n=50) versus monopolar TURBT (n=50). The protocol received Institutional Review Board approval and was registered in ReBEC (RBR-67npwrk) and on ClinicalTrials. gov (NCT05833997). Key inclusion criteria: bladder tumours >3 cm confirmed by CT/MRI within 3 months before randomisation. Exclusion criteria: prior bladder cancer; radiological suspicion of ≥pT2 disease, N+ or M+; urethral stricture; previous chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Central pathology review was pre-specified; patients with pT1 undergo re-TURBT at 30–60 days. Primary endpoints: detrusor muscle representativeness in the specimen.
