Median follow-up was 365 days for UroLift and 127 days for Optilume. Primary outcomes were new-onset ED and EJD within one year post-procedure. Risk differences, relative and odds ratios, and Kaplan-Meier survival analyses were used. RESULTS: After excluding those with baseline ED, new-onset ED occurred in 6.76% of UroLift patients and 2.78% of Optilume patients, with Optilume associated with significantly lower risk (RR 0.412, 95% CI 0.259–0.655; ARR 3.97%; p=0.0001). Twelve-month ED-free survival was 92.25% for UroLift vs. 93.46% for Optilume (log-rank p=0.2730, HR 0.764, 95% CI 0.472-1.238; p=0.3487). Among patients without baseline EJD, new-onset EJD occurred in ≤10 patients per group with no significant difference in risk (RR 0.979, 95% CI 0.409–2.344) or one-year EJD-free survival (UroLift 99.22% vs Optilume 99.86%; log-rank p=0.0848; HR 0.194, 95% CI 0.024–1.553). CONCLUSIONS: Both UroLift and Optilume demonstrate low rates of new-onset ED and EJD at 12 months. Although UroLift had a higher absolute ED incidence, survival analysis showed no significant difference. EJD was rare across both procedures. Both Optilume and UroLift are viable options for men prioritizing sexual preservation with Optilume potentially preferred in those who are at an elevated baseline risk for ED.

title: PRESERVATION OF SEXUAL FUNCTION WITH UROCROSS EXPANDER - A NOVEL NON-PERMANENT PROSTATIC EXPANDER FOR LUTS/BPH
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Kevin T. Mcvary, Ricardo Gonzalez, Dean Elterman, Daniel Rukstalis
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Many treatments for LUTS/BPH have negative effects on sexual function. Data from a prospective, randomized, double-blind, sham controlled study evaluating the Urocross Expander was evaluated to determine the impact of treatment with this novel technology on sexual function. The Urocross Expander is a novel MIST that combines mechanical urethral dilation with urethral reshaping using a non-permanent nitinol device removed after 6 months. METHODS: 240 subjects were randomized in a 2:1 fashion to receive the Urocross or Sham (160:80). Baseline measures included assessments via the International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF) and Men’s Sexual Health Questionnaire – Ejaculatory Dysfunction (MSHQ-EjD). Men were queried regarding history of ErectileDysfunction (ED) at the baseline (BL). RESULTS: Baseline IIEF and MSHQ-EjD were similar between the Urocross and Sham arms for sexually active subjects (IIEF 16.0±6.3 vs 16.5±5.9, MSHQ-EjD 8.2±3.3 vs 8.9±3.2). A total of 132 men randomized in the Urocross Arm claimed they are sexually active at BL. Men with active sexual activity reported overall better score of IIEF from BL, with the average IIEF score improved from 16.0 (n=132) at baseline to 17.7 (n=67) at 1yr post treatment, indicating a categorical change from “Mild to Moderate ED” to “Mild ED” ( Figure 1A). At 7mo post-treatment (1mo post-retrieval), men with severe ED improved the most and men with no ED before surgery are maintained at the BL level ( Figure 1B). Men with active sexual activity also report overall better score of MSHQ from BL through 12 months. MSHQ score has an average of 2.0 improvement at 12mo (6mo post-retrieval), regardless of their history of ED or not. CONCLUSIONS: Treatment with Urocross resulted in significant symptom relief while preserving erectile and ejaculatory function. These results offer support for the use of Urocross in men seeking treatment for LUTS/BPH who are concerned with preserving sexual function.

title: EJACULATION-PRESERVING BLADDER NECK SIMMETRICAL INCISION AT 3 AND 9 O’CLOCK: INSIGHTS FROM A LARGE MULTICENTER EXPERIENCE

title: MORCELLATION SAFETY CHECKLIST SIGNIFICANTLY REDUCES ERRORS AND ENHANCES TEAM COMMUNICATION DURING HOLEP
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Phillip Huffman, Dan Gralnek, Margaret Knoedler, Ali Antar, Matthew Grimes, Gray Roberge, Emily Serrell, Christopher Manakas
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Holmium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate (HoLEP) requires a critical multi-step transition from enucleation to morcellation. Despite high surgical volume, we experience preventable errors with morcellation device assembly, fluid management, and suction setup. Surgical checklists can improve consistency, reduce omissions, and facilitate communication among surgical teams. This study evaluates the impact of a novel safety checklist on morcellation errors, troubleshooting, efficiency, and complications. METHODS: We perform HOLEP using the Piranha morcellator in three distinct operating room (OR) settings, each with unique staffing pool and no dedicated teams for HOLEP. A team of physicians and staff developed a ten-item Morcellation Safety Checklist (MSC) as a “read-do” checklist (Fig.1) designed to be used before the start of morcellation. Baseline outcomes data were recorded with post-HOLEP REDCap surveys measuring morcellator efficiency, assembly or irrigation errors, pauses for troubleshooting, and complications. Prior to MSC implementation, OR staff at all three sites were engaged to ensure readiness and compliance. The MSC was attached to each morcellator and added to surgeon preference cards. Post-implementation surveys assessed impact of MSC on performance and safety outcomes. RESULTS: From September to October 2025, morcellator performance data were collected for 88 consecutive HOLEPs (43 pre-MSC and 45 post-MSC) performed by five surgeons at three facilities. Morcellator errors were reported in 44% of HOLEPs (19/43) pre-MSC compared to 17% (8/45) post-MSC implementation. Use of MSC corrected 12 morcellator setup errors in six cases prior to beginning morcellation. Irrigation fluid out errors occurred in 6.97% (3/43) pre-MSC and were eliminated (0/45) post-MSC. Pauses for troubleshooting were reduced from 21 pre-MSC to 13 post-MSC. Morcellator efficiency was not impacted by MSC: 7.7g/min pre-MSC vs. 6.4g/min post-MSC (p=0.18). No morcellator complications were reported in either group. CONCLUSIONS: Adoption of an MSC provides a standardized framework for the complex, team-based transition from enucleation to morcellation, independent of surgeon or site. The MSC reduces morcellator errors, reduces troubleshooting, and promotes safety and team engagement without sacrificing efficiency. This low-cost intervention may be implemented to improve morcellation safety.

title: EFFECT OF LOCAL ANESTHETIC-ELUTING FOLEY CATHETER(FREE-FOLEY) ON URETHRAL PAIN AND DISCOMFORT AFTER HOLEP: A RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Hwanik Kim, Young Jun Uhm, Ki-Hyuck Moon, Jae Hoon Chung, Cheol Young Oh, Byoungkyu Han
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is common in middle-aged and older men and often requires surgical treatment. Following surgery, a large-bore (18–20 Fr) Foley catheter must be maintained to ensure adequate drainage, which invariably causes severe urethral pain and catheter-related bladder discomfort (CRBD). Systemic analgesics alone may be insufficient to relieve this localized discomfort, and their use is limited in elderly patients due to systemic side-effect risks. This study evaluated whether a Free-Foley catheter that continuously elutes 2% lidocaine can effectively reduce post-operative urethral pain and discomfort and decrease systemic analgesic use. METHODS: In a prospective, multicenter, randomized, double-blind trial, 108 male patients aged 50–79 undergoing HoLEP were allocated to either the experimental group (FreeFoley with 2% lidocaine solution, 1 ml/hr infusion) or the control group (FreeFoley with normal saline, 1 ml/hr). Pain and discomfort were assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) at postoperative recovery and at catheter removal. Primary outcomes included differences in VAS scores and systemic analgesic use. Secondary outcomes included catheter-related complications and patient satisfaction. RESULTS: 108 patients were analyzed. VAS scores were significantly lower in the experimental group compared to control group along the perioperative course (the day of surgery: 3.01 ± 1.60 \[experimental group\] vs 4.07 ± 1.65 \[control\], p<0.001; the day of catheter removal 2.35 ± 1.26 \[experimental group\] vs 3.03 ± 1.25 \[controls\], p<0.001). Analgesic requirement was also markedly reduced (5.6% vs 27.8%, p<0.001). No significant differences were observed in catheter-related complications or satisfaction. CONCLUSIONS: The anesthetic-eluting Foley catheter effectively reduces postoperative urethral pain and discomfort, as well as analgesic requirements, without increasing catheter-related complications. | | | --- | | |

title: A RANDOMIZED, PLACEBO-CONTROLLED TRIAL EVALUATING TADALAFIL 5 MG FOR MANAGEMENT OF EARLY STORAGE SYMPTOMS AND ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION AFTER HOLEP
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Mohammed M. Aljabiri, Nasr El-tabey, Ahmed Shehab-El-Din, Mahmoud Laymon
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To test whether short-term tadalafil (5 mg daily) started on the day of HoLEP improves early postoperative sexual function deterioration and storage urinary symptoms versus placebo. METHODS: Prospective, parallel-group, randomized, placebo-controlled trial at a tertiary center (NCT05955001). Men≥40 y with BPH/LUTS scheduled for HoLEP were randomized 1:1 to tadalafil or placebo for 3 months starting from the day of surgery. Primary outcome was IIEF-15 orgasmic function at 3 months. Secondary outcomes included IIEF-15 total with its domains,MSHQ-ejaculatory (1, 3, 6 months), urinary outcomes including IPSS total, storage subscore, and IPSS-QoL (2 weeks, 1, 3, 6 months). Analyses were available-case, baseline-adjusted ANCOVA (adjusted mean difference, AMD; two-sided α=0.05) with supportive longitudinal models. RESULTS: A total of 160 screened; 144 randomized (tadalafil 73; placebo 71). At 3 months, 130 (90.3%) contributed primary data. During treatment, sexual outcomes favored tadalafil. At 1 month, IIEF-15 total was higher (AMD +22.7, 95% CI +15.1 to +30.3; p<0.001); domains also favored tadalafil, including erectile function (AMD +8.15; p<0.001). For the primary endpoint, orgasmic function showed superiority at 1 month (AMD +2.7, 95% CI +1.6 to +3.8; p<0.001) and 3 months (AMD +2.3, 95% CI +1.4 to +3.2; p<0.001), with convergence by 6 months after discontinuation. Urinary outcomes improved in both groups after HoLEP; baseline-adjusted differences already favored tadalafil at 2 weeks for IPSS total (AMD−5.67; p<0.001), storage (AMD−2.98; p<0.001) and IPSS-QoL (AMD−0.71; p<0.001), persisted at 1 and 3 months (e. g., IPSS total AMD−4.97 and−2.62, both p≤0.002), and were no longer evident at 6 months. By 6 months, both arms remained significantly better than baseline for IPSS total, storage, and QoL. Adverse events with tadalafil were infrequent (headache 6.4%, musculoskeletal pain 6.5%, dyspepsia 5.1%); three patients discontinued. Thirty-day complication rates were similar between groups. CONCLUSIONS: Tadalafil 5 mg daily, begun on the day of HoLEP and continued for 3 months, provides a transient, clinically meaningful early benefit in sexual function (including the preregistered orgasmic domain) and in storage-predominant LUTS, with group differences dissipating after therapy stops. These data support short-term PDE5I therapy to bridge the vulnerable early postoperative period.

title: EXAMINING THE EFFECTS OF PREOPERATIVE BOWEL FUNCTION ON HOLMIUM LASER ENUCLEATION OF PROSTATE (HOLEP) OUTCOMES
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Kyle P. Tsai, Nabila Khondakar, Perry Xu, Amir Patel, Jenny Guo, Alyssa McDonald, Allaa Fadl-Alla, Amy Krambeck
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The relationship between bowel and bladder function is well-described, however the association between bowel function and outcomes from benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) surgery is not well characterized. We sought to investigate the association of preoperative bowel function on urinary recovery after holmium laser enucleation of prostate (HoLEP). METHODS: We performed a prospective cohort study and recruited patients undergoing HoLEP by a single surgeon at a high-volume center between Dec 2023 and Sep 2024. Preoperative bowel function was evaluated using the validated Constipation Scoring System (CSS) and Vaizey Incontinence Score (VIS) patient questionnaires. Primary outcomes include change in International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) and Michigan Incontinence Severity Index (MISI) scores at 3 months. Statistical analysis was performed using Pearson correlations and linear regression as appropriate. RESULTS: We enrolled 120 patients, with 93 patients completing 3-month follow-up included in the analysis. Mean age was 71.1 and mean preoperative prostate size was 102.2g. Forty-four (47%) patients had history of prior urinary retention. Mean preoperative CSS and VIS were 2.9 and 1.2, respectively. Mean preoperative IPSS total and quality of life (QoL) scores were 18.0 and 4.3. Mean preoperative MISI severity and bother were 5.2 and 1.7. Postoperative IPSS total, QOL, and MISI bother scores improved by 12.0, 2., and 0.6 respectively, while MISI severity worsened by 0.3. Higher CSS scores were correlated with higher VIS scores (r=0.452, p<0.001) and less improvement in postoperative IPSS total scores (r=-0.211, p=0.043). Higher VIS was associated with less improvement in MISI severity (r=-0.261, p=0.012). On linear regression controlling for age, BMI, prostate size, and history of urinary retention, higher VIS continued to be predictive of less improvement in MISI severity (β=-0.308, p=0.013). Higher CSS was associated with decreased change in IPSS total scores however did not reach statistical significance (β=-200, p=0.083). CONCLUSIONS: Patients with higher degree of self-reported preoperative constipation and bowel incontinence appear to have less improvement in urinary symptoms after HoLEP, suggesting that optimization of bowel function may help maximize BPH surgery outcomes. | | | --- | | |

title: COMPARATIVE EFFICACY AND OUTCOMES OF HOLMIUM AND ITS MOSES 1.0 AND MOSES 2.0 PULSE MODULATION LASER MODES IN PATIENTS UNDERGOING HOLEP FOR TREATING LUTS IN BPH PATIENTS WITH TRAINEE INVOLVEMENT
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Juanita Velasquez Ospina, Sabika Sadiq, Ansh Bhatia, Haşim Bakbak, Maggie Meyreles, Ahmad Abdelaziz, Archan Khandekar, Jonathan Katz, Robert Marcovich, Hemendra N. Shah
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Moses™ pulse modulation was developed to enhance the efficiency of Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) by optimizing energy delivery to tissue. While studies have compared either Moses 1.0 (M1) or Moses 2.0 (M2) with standard Holmium (SH), direct comparisons across all three platforms remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate perioperative and functional outcomes among SH, M1, and M2 HoLEP performed in an academic setting with trainee involvement. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed all men who underwent HoLEP between June 2022 and May 2024 at a single academic institution. Patients were categorized by laser platform: SH, M1, or M2 based on OR where case was performed. All patients were kept overnight for observation and planned to be discharged next day after voiding trial. Baseline demographics, perioperative parameters, complications, and functional outcomes up to 6 months were analyzed using ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis tests, with p<0.05 considered significant. RESULTS: A total of 389 patients were included (SH n=206; M1 n=126; M2 n=57). Baseline characteristics were comparable among groups ( Table 1). Median operative times were 105 (80–157) for M1, 100 (37–163) for M2, and 95 (73–115) minutes for SH (p=0.25), and median resected prostate weights were similar (85 g vs 79 g vs 84 g respectively, p=0.44). Median hospital stay was slightly longer with Moses lasers (1.6 days each) than with SH (1.4 days, p<0.001). Hemoglobin drop and transfusion rates were low and did not differ significantly among groups, and rates of acute urinary retention and urethral stricture were similarly infrequent. Continence recovery at 4–6 weeks was comparable among groups (73.2% M1 vs 81.0% M2 vs 73.8% SH, p=0.60). At 6 months, IPSS, Qmax, and PVR improvements were significant within each group but comparable across modalities. CONCLUSIONS: HoLEP was safe and effective across all laser platforms. Perioperative and functional outcomes were comparable, with similar continence recovery, hemoglobin drop, and transfusion rates. No clinically meaningful differences were observed among technologies. Thus, laser selection should be guided by institutional availability and surgeon preference rather than expected outcome differences. | | | --- | | |

title: EARLY APICAL RELEASE IN HOLMIUM LASER ENUCLEATION OF THE PROSTATE. IS IT WORTH IT? A META-ANALYSIS AND META-REGRESSION ON PERIOPERATIVE AND POSTOPERATIVE OUTCOMES
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Marco Antonio Andrade, Rafael Baldissera-Cardoso, Danilo Oliveira Amaral, José Arnaldo Shiomida Cruz, Artur De Oliveira Paludo, Mauro Weiss, Milton Berger, Henrique Rodrigues, Andre Kives Berger, Nicole Miller
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Holmium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate (HoLEP) is a standard surgery for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), but early continence issues persist. Early Apical Release (EAR), often with en-bloc enucleation, aims to release apical mucosa early, reducing sphincter strain and functional risks. Evidence for its benefits is limited, with varying techniques among urologists. This meta-analysis compares EAR to standard HoLEP on efficacy, safety, operative times, and complications. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane through April 2025 for studies comparing EAR vs standard HoLEP. Followed PRISMA; extracted data from reports; assessed quality per Cochrane. Outcomes: operative time, American Urological Association Symptom Score (AUASS) at 3 months, Clavien-Dindo (≤2 and≥3a), overall complications, postoperative incontinence (<30 days and 1–3 months). RESULTS: Six studies were included, comprising 3,538 patients (1,440 EAR and 2,098 standard). There was no significant difference in AUASS at 3 months (MD-0.10; 95% CI-1.42 to 1.22; p=0.88; I2=75%) or operative time (MD-0.09 minutes; 95% CI-11.51 to 11.33 minutes; p=0.99; I2=93%). No statistically significant difference was observed in early postoperative incontinence, both within 30 days (OR 0.33; 95% CI 0.10–1.03; p=0.06; I2=90%;) and at 1–3 months (OR 0.38; 95% CI 0.13–1.14; p=0.09; I2=67%). However, EAR was associated with significantly higher rates of complications: Clavien-Dindo≤2 (OR 1.44; 95% CI 1.11 to 1.87; p=0.006; I2=0%), Clavien-Dindo≥3 (OR 2.53; 95% CI 1.24 to 5.17; p=0.01; I2=0%), and overall complications (OR 1.46; 95% CI 1.18 to 1.79; p=0.0004; I2=0%). Meta-regression showed that prostate size (=-0.0891, p=0.015) and incontinence definition varying from 0-2 pads (=-3.2059, p=0.001) significantly moderates the treatment effect on incontinence risk, explaining part of heterogeneity. CONCLUSIONS: EAR was not superior to non-EAR standard techniques. Moreover, EAR was associated with a significantly higher overall complication rate, including both Clavien-Dindo grade≤2 and≥3 complications. No significant differences were observed between the techniques regarding symptom relief or operative time. These findings suggest that familiarity with both approaches may be beneficial to optimize patient outcomes and tailor the surgical strategy to individual clinical scenarios.

title: HOLEP FOR LARGE AND MEGA GLANDS: REAL-WORLD OUTCOMES AND EVIDENCE OF SIZE-ENHANCED EFFICIENCY
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Yadong Lu, Elisabeth Hayward, Aaron Saxton, Carl Ceraolo, Soumya Konar, Nitin Sharma, Rajat Jain, Scott Quarrier
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While not formally standardized, the term “mega gland” is most applied to prostates larger than 200cc on preoperative imaging. Mega gland prostates are traditionally perceived as technically challenging for holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) due to increased vascularity, difficult planes, and instrument length limitations. This study evaluates perioperative and postoperative outcomes of HoLEP for mega glands compared with large glands (120–200cc) in a contemporary real-world cohort. METHODS: We conducted a single-center, retrospective analysis of patients who underwent HoLEP for glands≥120cc between January 2021 and June 2025. Patients were categorized into large (120-200cc) and mega (>200cc) gland groups. Baseline characteristics, intraoperative parameters, and postoperative outcomes were compared using Wilcoxon rank-sum, Pearson’s chi-square, and Fisher’s exact tests on R (v4.4.3). RESULTS: Out of 602 HoLEPs performed during the study period, there were 208 patients with large gland prostates and 35 with mega gland prostates. Baseline characteristics were broadly similar between groups, though mega glands demonstrated higher baseline PSA (9.9 vs 5.6 ng/mL, p=0.001). Operative time was longer for mega glands (114 vs 96 min, p=0.003), as expected. However, enucleation speed (2.8 vs 1.6 g/min, p<0.001) and energy efficiency (0.8 vs 0.5 g/kJ, p<0.001) were significantly higher in mega glands, despite similar enucleation times. Postoperatively, length of stay was slightly longer (1.0 \[1.0–1.0\] vs 1.0 \[1.0–2.0\] days, p=0.011) for mega group. No significant differences were observed in catheter duration, failed void trial, ED visits, readmission, or 3-month PROM evaluation (MISI, p=0.248; IPSS, p=0.533). CONCLUSIONS: Although large prostates have traditionally been viewed as technically challenging, our data suggests a volume threshold beyond which HoLEP becomes more efficient, with higher enucleation speed and energy efficiency in glands >200 ml. This highlights HoLEP as a size-enhanced procedure—not merely size-independent—achieving excellent perioperative and functional outcomes. Further work is needed to define this efficiency threshold more precisely and explore its clinical implications. | | | --- | | |

title: PERIOPERATIVE OUTCOMES AND PREVALENCE OF URETHRAL STRICTURES DURING SURGERY FOR BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA: RESULTS FROM THE GRAND STUDY
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Nikolaos Pyrgidis, Gerald Bastian Schulz, Philipp Weinhold, Yannic Volz, Iason Papadopoulos, Christian Stief, Julian Marcon, Patrick Keller
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Limited data exist on the prevalence of urethral strictures during surgery for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). We aimed to analyze their perioperative outcomes and trends. METHODS: The German Nationwide Inpatient Data (GRAND) registry was used to identify male patients diagnosed with urethral stricture who underwent surgery for BPH between 2005 and 2022. Multivariable regression analyses were performed to compare perioperative morbidity. RESULTS: A total of 1,367,065 BPH surgeries were performed in Germany. Of them, 150,356 had a relevant concomitant urethral stricture (11%). Their median age was 72 years (interquartile range: 66-78). Patients with urethral stricture during BPH surgery underwent an internal urethrotomy in 113,501 (75%) cases, a dilation of the urethral stricture in 29,848 (20%) cases, or a meatoplasty in 7,007 (5%) cases. The annual prevalence of relevant urethral strictures during BPH surgery has decreased from 11,329 (7.5%) cases in 2005 to 5,900 (3.9%) in 2022. Compared to patients with no urethral stricture, those with urethral strictures during BPH surgery displayed higher rates of postoperative incontinence (4.5% versus 3.6%) and reoperations (1.2% versus 0.8%). On the contrary, they were associated with lower rates of perioperative acute urinary retention (9.3% versus 9.8%). CONCLUSIONS: Urethral strictures during surgery for BPH display a high prevalence and may affect perioperative outcomes.

title: PLASMA-KINETIC ENUCLEATION OF THE PROSTATE (PKEP): SAFETY AND EFFICACY IN PATIENTS ON ANTIPLATELET AND ANTICOAGULANT THERAPY
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Ben Sionov, David Yagudaev, Mubarak Dahamshy, Itay Sagy, Alexander Tsivian
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Discontinuation of anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy prior to surgery carries an increased risk of thromboembolic events, while continuation raises concerns about perioperative bleeding. Plasma-kinetic enucleation of the prostate (PKEP) is a minimally invasive and effective technique for the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). The aim of this study was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of PKEP in patients receiving antiplatelet (AP) or anticoagulant (AC) therapy. METHODS: Data were retrospectively reviewed for patients who underwent PKEP between March 2023 and July 2025. All patients underwent preoperative transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) evaluation to assess prostate size. Demographic characteristics, intraoperative parameters, and postoperative outcomes were analyzed. RESULTS: Among 116 operated patients, 64 (Group A) were on anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy, and 52 (Group B) were not. Patients in Group A were older. No significant differences were found in prostate size, resected tissue weight, or operative time ( Table 1). Most patients were catheterized preoperatively, and all were catheter-free within a median of 0.5 days postoperatively in both groups (p=0.39). The mean IPSS decreased from 24 to 9.2, with an average improvement of 14.8 points, showing no intergroup difference (p=0.7). Postoperatively, 4 patients in Group A and 3 in Group B required blood transfusions (6.2% vs. 5.7%, p=0.91). One patient in each group required endoscopic coagulation for hemostasis. The overall complication rate did not differ significantly between groups (20.3% vs. 19.2%, p=0.88), despite the higher mean age in Group A ( Table 2). CONCLUSIONS: PKEP is a safe and effective procedure even in patients maintained on anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy. The surgery can be performed without discontinuation of blood thinners, achieving significant symptomatic improvement without an increased risk of bleeding or major complications. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: SINGLE LATERAL LOBE SPARING HEMI-HOLMIUM LASER ENUCLEATION OF THE PROSTATE (HEMI-HOLEP) OUTCOMES COMPARED TO STANDARD WHOLE-GLAND HOLEP
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Jenny N. Guo, Amir S. Patel, Perry Xu, Nabila Khondakar, Julio Meza, Amy E. Krambeck
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: There is limited data on outcomes of holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) in patients with prior pelvic XRT given potential risks of poor wound healing and incontinence. The objective of this study was to investigate post-operative outcomes of a novel approach, hemi-HoLEP, in which we spare the smaller of the two lateral lobes to avoid a circumferential epithelial defect. METHODS: We retrospectively identified 11 hemi-HoLEP patients and propensity-score matched with a 3:1 ratio to 33 whole-gland HoLEP controls based on age and prostate specimen weight. All HoLEP patients had at least 3 months of follow up. Statistical analysis was performed using t-tests, Fisher’s exact test, and Chi-squared tests (p<0.05). RESULTS: Hemi-HoLEP patients were more likely to be actively in urinary retention prior to surgery (64% vs 24%, p=0.043). Average specimen weight was 13g in the control cohort and 17g in the hemi-HoLEP cohort (p=0.5). Enucleation time was significantly shorter in the hemi-HoLEP cohort (13.3 vs 16.9 minutes, p=0.031). All hemi-HoLEP patients planned for same-day trial of void (TOV) passed their same-day TOV (8/8, 100%). There were no incidences of urethral stricture or bladder neck contracture in either group. Complications and medical visits at 90 days post-operatively were similar amongst both groups (p>0.05). Hemi-HoLEP patients had increases in their Michigan Incontinence Symptom Index (M-ISI) bother scores post-op compared to pre whereas control patients showed slight decreases (0.27 vs-0.39, p=0.04). Post-operative outcomes are summarized in Table 1, and differences in AUA Symptom Score and M-ISI scores are listed in Table 2. CONCLUSIONS: We describe outcomes of a novel approach to treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia after pelvic XRT using hemi-HoLEP. Although our series is limited, hemi-HoLEP patients had similar post-operative outcomes to standard healthy controls. Based on these results, we noted that hemi-HoLEP is a viable treatment option for post-XRT benign prostatic hyperplasia patients. Larger, prospective studies are needed to better understand these findings. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: COST-EFFECTIVENESS OF CONTEMPORARY BPH SURGICAL OPTIONS FOR GLANDS 30-80CC: INSIGHTS FROM A MICROSIMULATION MODEL
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Kelly Lehner, Kevin Wymer
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: BPH surgical options vary significantly in regards to costs and outcomes, as do individual patient priorities. Herein, we performed a comprehensive cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) for BPH procedures, assessing sensitivity to variations in weighting of different outcomes. METHODS: Using a microsimulation model, a CEA was performed comparing HoLEP, TURP, WVTT, PUL, RWT, iTIND, and Optilume. Model probabilities were based on published values, and effectiveness was calculated using post-operative complication severity, sexual function, and urinary symptom scores (IPSS). The model was performed from a U. S. Medicare payer perspective, with quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) used to assess cost-effectiveness at a willingness-to-pay threshold of $100,000/QALY. Univariate and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were performed. RESULTS: Over a patient’s lifetime, HoLEP resulted in the highest QALYs (12.25), followed by iTIND (12.02) and WVTT (11.98). Lifetime BPH costs per patient ranged from $6,557 (WVTT) and $8,431 (HoLEP) to $13,327 (PUL). HoLEP was most cost-effective (ICER $6,931). However, the probability and utility value (effectiveness) of post-operative ejaculatory dysfunction significantly impacted model outputs. In addition, the cost-effectiveness of HoLEP was dependent upon relatively high post-HoLEP urinary symptom utility values as well as longer life expectancy ( Figure 1-2). CONCLUSIONS: Using currently published data, HoLEP is the most cost-effective option for patients with a gland size 30-80cc. However, ejaculatory-preserving therapies (e. g. WVTT, PUL, iTIND) become favored if higher patient priority is given to antegrade ejaculation. Similarly, HoLEP is only cost-effective at longer life expectancy (>10 years), and with high symptom improvement. Such findings highlight the benefit of HoLEP on a systems-level, while also emphasizing the imperative of surgical selection driven by individual patient priorities.

title: THREE-YEAR REINTERVENTION OUTCOMES AFTER REZUM VS UROLIFT: A TRINETX COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Pin Chun Chen, Yu-Cheng Lu, Allen W. Chiu, Chen‑Hsun Ho, Chih-Wei Wu, Yu-Hsuan Shao
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Rezum and UroLift are minimally invasive options for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), yet head-to-head long-term data are sparse. We examined three-year reintervention rates for both treatments in a large real-world cohort. METHODS: From the TriNetX US Collaborative Network, we identified men ≥40 years who underwent Rezum or UroLift between January 2018 and December 2020 via CPT codes. Patients were followed for three years for subsequent urologic procedures. Propensity score matching balanced baseline factors, and Cox proportional hazards models compared reintervention risk overall and by age strata. RESULTS: We included 3,231 patients (Rezum 792; UroLift 2,439). After matching, overall reintervention risk was similar (HR 1.19; 95% CI 0.82–1.73). Among patients ≥65 years, Rezum showed a significantly lower reintervention rate than UroLift (HR 0.60; 95% CI 0.37–0.97). In those aged 40–64 years, rates were similar (HR 1.49; 95% CI 0.87–2.55) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191280.81177.3f.21#F1)). Within the Rezum cohort, younger patients (40–64 years) had higher risk than those ≥65 years (HR 2.12; 95% CI 1.15–3.93), whereas no age-related difference was observed after UroLift (HR 0.85; 95% CI 0.62–1.17) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191280.81177.3f.21#F2)). CONCLUSIONS: Rezum was associated with fewer three-year reinterventions than UroLift in adults ≥65 years, while outcomes were comparable in those aged 40–64 years. These findings suggest patient age may influence the durability of minimally invasive BPH therapies and should be considered during treatment selection.

title: MATCHED COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF ROBOT-ASSISTED SIMPLE PROSTATECTOMY (RASP) VERSUS HOLMIUM LASER ENUCLEATION (HOLEP) FOR LARGE (>100 ML) BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA (BPH): EXPERIENCE FROM A HIGH-VOLUME CENTER
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Attilio Barretta, Angelo Mottaran, Sara Tamburini, Pietro Piazza, Edoardo Beatrici, Nicolas Carl, Francesco Prata, Mario De Angelis, Natali Rodriguez Penaranda, Francesco Pepillo, Alessio Guidotti, Vincenzo Cavarra, Claudio Brancelli, Rocco Papalia, Edward Lambert, Ruben De Groote, Geert De Naeyer, D'Hondt Frederiek, Riccardo Schiavina, Alexandre Mottrie
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: In men with large benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH; >100 ml), both robot-assisted simple prostatectomy (RASP) and holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) represent established treatment options. Comparative data remain scarce and often limited by baseline imbalances. We aimed to provide a matched comparative analysis of peri-operative and functional outcomes between RASP and HoLEP in a high-volume centre. METHODS: We analysed data of 468 patients with symptomatic BPH due to large (>100 ml) prostate glands who underwent RASP (n=206, 44%) and HoLEP (n=262, 56%) at OLV Hospital, Aalst (Belgium) between 2011 and 2024. A 1:1 propensity-score matched (PSM) cohort was generated to reduce baseline imbalances. Pre-, intra-, and post-operative data were collected, with complications graded according to Clavien–Dindo (CD). Functional outcomes were assessed by International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax), and post-void residual volume (PVR) at immediate, 6-, and 12-month follow-up. RESULTS: At baseline, age, BMI, IPSS, Qmax and PVR were comparable (all p>0.05), whereas RASP patients presented with larger prostate volume, higher PSA, and higher Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) (all p<0.05). Median operative time was longer for RASP (130 vs. 110 min; p<0.001), while length of stay (LOS) was shorter after HoLEP (2 vs. 3 days; p<0.001). Intra-operative complication rates were similar (14% vs. 15%), but major Clavien–Dindo (CD) grade III–V events occurred only in HoLEP (0% vs. 8.3%; p=0.016). At 6 months, both groups showed an improvement of maximum flow rate (Qmax +14 vs. +14 ml/s; p=0.8), a reduction of PVR (−73 vs. −53 ml; p=0.3), and a decrease of IPSS (−17 vs. −17; p=0.9). At 12 months, Qmax was +11 vs. +13 ml/s (p=0.2), PVR −74 vs. −55 ml (p=0.2), and IPSS −18 vs. −18 (p=0.8) for RASP and HoLEP, respectively. Functional outcomes and complication rates are shown in (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191280.81177.3f.22#F1). After PSM, a balanced cohort of 144 patients (72 vs. 72) was obtained. In this analysis, functional outcomes remained equivalent and peri-operative differences were confirmed. CONCLUSIONS: Both RASP and HoLEP provided equivalent functional improvements in large BPH. HoLEP was associated with shorter length of stay, whereas RASP showed longer operative time. After PSM, results were confirmed, supporting both as effective options depending on patient profile and expertise.

title: MULTI-INSTITUTIONAL OUTCOMES OF ROBOT-ASSISTED SIMPLE PROSTATECTOMY: A RETROSPECTIVE STUDY BY THE ERUS SCIENTIFIC RECONSTRUCTIVE WORKING GROUP
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Yasmin Heiniger, Severin Lautenschlager, Beat Foerster, Simone Crivellaro, Charles-Henry Rochat, Christian Schwentner, Christian Wagner, Christopher Hiertsiefer, Julia Heinzelbecker, Esra Yilmaz, Toni Franz, Jens-Uwe Stolzenburg, Matthias Saar, Jennifer Kranz, Pieter Uvin, Paolo Umari, Bernardo Rocco, Antonio Andrea Grosso, Francesco Porpiglia, Ugo Pinar, Geert Denaeyer, Alba Farré, Héctor Ayllón, Madeleine Eriksson, Hubert John
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Management of large-volume prostate adenomas remains challenging in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). This study evaluated surgical techniques, perioperative outcomes, functional results, and complication rates of robot-assisted simple prostatectomy (RASP) in a multi-institutional cohort. METHODS: a retrospective analysis included patients who underwent RASP between January 2013 and July 2024 at 17 centers in Europe and the United States. Functional outcomes including uroflowmetry, post-void residual volume (PVR), International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), and Quality of Life (QoL), were evaluated at 6 weeks and 1 year postoperatively. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05 (paired t-test). Postoperative complications were assessed at 30 and 90 days. Surgical techniques were systematically analyzed and video-validated. RESULTS: a total of 1345 patients underwent RASP. Median age was 70 years (IQR 65–76), median prostate volume 140 ml (IQR 110–180). Median operative time was 144 min (IQR 116–180) with median blood loss of 300 ml (IQR 150–440). Functional outcomes are shown in Table 1. Clavien–Dindo ≥ III complications occurred in 41/1344 (3%) at 30 days and 6/1218 (0.5%) at 90 days. Regarding surgical technique, 1196/1345 (89%) were treated with the DaVinci multiport system, 94/1345 (7%) with the SinglePort, and 55/1345 (4%) with the Hugo-RAS system. A transperitoneal approach was used in 1023/1345 (76%) and an extraperitoneal in 321/1345 (24%). Transvesical access was applied in 719/1344 (54%) and transcapsular in 625/1344 (46%). Standard enucleation was performed in 1151/1345 (86%), urethra-sparing in 186/1345 (14%). After standard enucleation, no closure of the prostatic fossa was performed in 363/1151 (32%), posterior vesico-urethral reconstruction (180°) in 297/1151 (26%), and full vesico-urethral reconstruction (360°) in 441/1151 (38%). CONCLUSIONS: Robot-assisted simple prostatectomy provides significant improvements in urinary function and quality of life for patients with large-volume prostatic adenoma, with low perioperative morbidity and stable outcomes at 1 year. Despite variations in surgical techniques across centers, postoperative outcomes were consistent throughout this large multi-institutional cohort. | | | --- | | |

title: RESIDENT SURGICAL LEARNING CURVE FOR ROBOTIC-ASSISTED SIMPLE PROSTATECTOMY
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Ali A. Nasrallah, Raymond Che, Vincent Yang, Zain Akbar, Cole Nipper, Corey Able, Joseph Sonstein, Joseph N. Sreshta
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Learning curves for fully trained urologists performing robotic-assisted simple prostatectomy (RASP) are well described, but data on trainees are limited. We aimed to characterize the learning curve of multiport RASP among urology residents. METHODS: Consecutive RASP cases performed by three urology senior residents (2021–2024) were retrospectively reviewed. Metrics included operative time, percent prostate enucleated, IPSS improvement, and Clavien–Dindo ≥2 complications. Moving average curves and best-fit trendlines were used to assess performance over time. RESULTS: Eighty-seven cases were analyzed (Resident A=25; B=27; C=35). Median patient age was 68 years (IQR 62–72), prostate volume 108 cc (90–131), and preoperative IPSS 25 (18–27); 62% were catheter-dependent. Median operative time was 136 min (116–159), decreasing from >160 min to ~120 min after 15 cases before plateauing. Percent prostate enucleated increased from ~50% to 70% after 15 cases. Median IPSS improvement was 80% (66–85) with stable grade ≥2 complication rates (9 events, 10%). (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191280.81177.3f.24#F1) depicts aggregated moving-average curves. CONCLUSIONS: Residents achieved proficiency in multiport RASP after approximately 15 cases, as reflected by improved operative time and extent of enucleation. Functional outcomes and complication rates remained stable across experience levels, suggesting early attainment of safety and efficacy.

title: EFFICACY OF ROBOT-ASSISTED SIMPLE PROSTATECTOMY IN PROSTATIC ENLARGEMENTS: A COMPARATIVE STUDY ABOVE AND BELOW 150 GRAMS
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Ibrahim C. Aykanat, Arif Ozkan, Ahmet Gurbuz, Ersin Koseoglu, Baris Esen, Serdar Madendere, Abdullah Erdem Canda, Mevlana Derya Balbay, Tarik Esen, Yakup Kordan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robot-assisted simple prostatectomy (RASP) is a minimally invasive alternative to open surgery for large benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). We compared perioperative and functional outcomes of RASP in patients with large (<150 g) versus very large (≥150 g) prostates. METHODS: A retrospective single-center analysis was performed. Fifty-eight patients underwent RASP, stratified by prostate weight into Group 1 (≥150 g, n=39) and Group 2 (<150 g, n=19). RESULTS: All cases were completed robotically with no conversion to open surgery. Group 1 had higher PSA (9.7 vs 5.6 ng/mL, p=0.037) and longer operative time (148.5 vs 121.8 min, p=0.019) than Group 2, while estimated blood loss, length of stay, and catheterization time did not differ significantly. Pre- and postoperative IPSS, Qmax, and PVR were comparable between groups (all p>0.05). All patients showed significant improvements in symptoms and voiding parameters: mean IPSS decreased from 22.8 to 7.4, Qmax increased from 9.0 to 20.5 ml/s, and PVR decreased from 136.3 to 37.1 ml (all p<0.001). Improvements in IPSS, Qmax, and PVR were similar in Group 1 vs Group 2 (ΔIPSS 16.3 vs 14.1, p=0.361; ΔQmax +11.6 vs +11.1 ml/s, p=0.912; ΔPVR −120.2 vs −75.1 ml, p=0.076, respectively). Continence and erectile function outcomes were similar between groups; one patient (<150 g) developed new-onset mild stress incontinence managed conservatively, and no new erectile dysfunction occurred. Antegrade ejaculation was preserved in 10/51 sexually active patients (19.6%), without a group difference (p=0.982). Complications were infrequent and two Group 1 patients developed urethral strictures; all other complications were Clavien grade I–II. CONCLUSIONS: RASP is a safe and effective treatment for large prostate adenomas (≥150 g), providing symptom relief and urinary function improvement comparable to outcomes in smaller glands. While operative time was longer for larger prostates, perioperative morbidity and overall outcomes did not differ between groups. These findings support the use of RASP as a viable minimally invasive alternative to open surgery even for prostates above 150 g. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: COMPARING OUTCOMES OF SINGLE-PORT VS MULTI-PORT ROBOT-ASSISTED SIMPLE PROSTATECTOMY: A PROSPECTIVE SINGLE-CENTER EXPERIENCE
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Alfredo Bove, Rocco Simone Flammia, Aldo Brassetti, Umberto Anceschi, Gabriele Tuderti, Maria Consiglia Ferriero, Riccardo Mastroianni, Simone D'Annunzio, Flavia Proietti, Leonardo Misuraca, Costantino Leonardo, Giuseppe Simone
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robot-assisted simple prostatectomy (RASP) is an established option for the surgical management of large benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). The recent introduction of single-port (SP) robotic platforms aims to further minimize surgical invasiveness. However, comparative data between SP and conventional multi-port (MP) RASP are still limited. This study aimed to compare perioperative and functional outcomes between SP and MP RASP performed at a single high-volume referral center. METHODS: A prospective cohort of men undergoing RASP for symptomatic BPH with prostate volume >80 ml was analyzed. All procedures were performed according to either a transvesical or transcapsular approaches, without retrigonization. Baseline, perioperative, and functional variables, including age, BMI, ASA score, indwelling catheter, prostate volume, surgical approach (transvesical vs transcapsular), BPH6 achievement and OAB recovery (defined as: an OABq-SF improvement ≥11 points, absence of postoperative pharmacologic treatment for urgency and a postoperative ICIQ-SF score <6) were compared between SP and MP procedures. Continuous data were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test, and categorical variables using the Fisher exact test. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05. RESULTS: A total of 93 patients were included: 89 (96%) underwent MP-RASP and 4 (4%) SP-RASP. SP patients were slightly younger and had smaller prostates (median 93 vs 116 g, p=0.08) ( Table 1). No significant differences were observed in operative time (110 vs 100 min, p=0.59), length of stay (3 vs 3 days, p=0.24), or BPH6 achievement (25% vs 54%, p=0.34). OAB recovery was achieved in 100% of SP and 73% of MP cases (p=0.57) ( Table 2). CONCLUSIONS: Single-port RASP achieved perioperative and functional results comparable to those of multi-port surgery in this prospective cohort. Despite the limited sample size, these findings suggest that the introduction of the single-port platform does not jeopardize outcomes of RASP. Larger multicenter studies are needed to confirm these early results and to better define the role of the Single port surgery in the management of large BPH. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: A LONGITUDINAL ANALYSIS OF PSA FOLLOWING ROBOTIC-ASSISTED SIMPLE PROSTATECTOMY
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Gabriel F. Rodrigues, Dylan Buller, Ilene Staff, Tara McLaughlin, Kevin Pinto, Laura Olivo Valentin, Joseph Tortora, Stuart Kesler, Joseph Wagner
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Aging men are at risk for prostate cancer (PCa) and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Men undergoing robotic assisted simple prostatectomy (RASP) for BPH may be on active surveillance for low grade PCa, have PCa identified incidentally on RASP pathology, or have a delayed PCa diagnosis post-operatively. Unlike radical prostatectomy, RASP preserves the peripheral zone, leading to detectable but poorly defined normative PSA values. This leads to difficulty distinguishing PSA reflecting benign remnant tissue from clinically significant (cs) PCa. We evaluated PSA trends in patients following RASP to inform post-RASP PCa screening and surveillance. METHODS: We identified all patients who underwent RASP at our institution from 5/1/2015 to 9/30/2023. Patients having (1) no PCa; (2) non-csPCa (GG1); or (3) csPCa (≥GG2) were compared for post-operative PSA metrics using Kruskal Wallis and Fisher Freeman Halton tests. RESULTS: PSA data were available for 214/288 patients who underwent RASP. 171 had no diagnosis of PCa, 29 had non-csPCa, and 14 had csPCa. Significant differences in PSA and PSA change emerged over time. PSA values among groups did not differ significantly within the first 12 months, but did at 12-24 months (p=0.048) and >24 months post-RASP (p=0.012). Highest median post-RASP PSAs were observed in the csPCa group (p=0.001). The median time to reach post-RASP PSA nadir was shortest for the csPCa group (189 days), followed by non-csPCa (293 days) and benign groups (430 days) (p=0.015). Data are summarized in Table 1. CONCLUSIONS: We present the first detailed analysis of longitudinal PSA trends after RASP in men with and without PCa. While pre-RASP PSA and the initial post-RASP PSA nadir did not differ significantly among groups, the time to nadir did. Patients with clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) reached their PSA nadir faster, likely due to earlier PSA rise from recurrence, whereas the benign group reached nadir later as PSA declined with natural fluctuations and resolution of postoperative inflammation. Among groups, those with csPCa demonstrated the highest PSA at 12-24 months of follow-up, a trend which continued when PSA was assessed beyond 24 months. Our findings suggest that a single early post-RASP PSA value is insufficient for men who would benefit from continued PSA monitoring. Instead, serial PSA monitoring beyond one year may be necessary to effectively identify patients with underlying csPCa who warrant further investigation. Furthermore, these data can provide a reference for urologists and patients when interpreting post-RASP PSA values. | | | --- | | |

title: PREDICTORS OF SAME-DAY DISCHARGE TRIFECTA FOLLOWING SINGLE PORT TRANSVESICAL ROBOTIC SIMPLE PROSTATECTOMY: A REPORT FROM THE SINGLE PORT ADVANCED RESEARCH CONSORTIUM (SPARC)
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Nicolas A. Soputro, Jacob Hershenhouse, Anastasia Mavridis, Jacob O'Hara, Claudia Ramirez Marcano, Shada Sinclair, Graham Kupsaw, Ruben Sauer Calvo, Narmina Khanmammadova, Jewel Bamby, Mehr Nasir-Moin, Sean Horan, Kennedy E. Okhawere, Gabriela Nieto-Blanco, Sarah Duncan, Abdulrahman Al-Bayati, Rui M. Bernardino, David I. Lee, Ruben A. Olivares, Mohamed Eltemamy, Kshitij Hemal, Srinivas Vourganti, Zeyad R. Schwen, Ketan K. Badani, Andrew Wagner, Peter Chang, Mutahar Ahmed, Michael D. Stifelman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the incidence and predictors of same-day discharge trifecta following Single Port (SP) Transvesical Robotic Simple Prostatectomy (RASP), defined as outpatient surgery without postoperative complications or readmission. METHODS: A retrospective review of the prospectively maintained, IRB-approved SP Advanced Research Consortium (SPARC) database identified 503 patients who underwent SP-RASP. Only Transvesical procedures with ≥3 months follow-up were included. Baseline clinicodemographic, perioperative, and postoperative variables were collected, with inferential statistics as presented. Postoperative complications within 90 days were classified according to Clavien-Dindo, with major complications defined as grade ≥3a. Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of trifecta achievement. RESULTS: Of 220 eligible patients, outpatient surgery was achieved in 54.6%. Postoperative complications occurred in 23.9%, and readmission in 4.6%, yielding a trifecta outcome in 59.5%. Trifecta and non-trifecta groups were similar in age, body habitus, prostate volume, LUTS severity, and uroflowmetry results. Patients achieving trifecta had lower comorbidity burden (median CCI 3 vs. 4, p=0.003), shorter operative time (median 165 vs. 191 min, p<0.001), lower intraoperative blood loss (median 75 vs. 100 ml, p<0.001), and were less likely to require continuous bladder irrigation (0.8% vs. 14.3%, p<0.001). On multivariate analysis, lower comorbidity burden (OR 0.767, 95% CI 0.590–0.990, p=0.043) and shorter operative time (OR 0.992, 95% CI 0.987–0.999, p=0.002) independently predicted trifecta success. CONCLUSIONS: The same-day discharge trifecta after SP Transvesical RASP can be achieved in over half of patients. Nevertheless, while lower comorbidity burden and shorter operative time were identified as independent predictors of success, larger cohort data remain necessary to further enhance our best-practice patient selection and to guide perioperative planning. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: DEVELOPMENT OF A HIGH-FIDELITY SURGICAL TRAINING MODEL FOR SINGLE-PORT ROBOT-ASSISTED TRANSVESICAL SIMPLE PROSTATECTOMY (SP-RASP)
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Madison Brookfield, Ahmed Ghazi, Avinash Dhimal, Lauren Shepard, Ian Spears, Juliet Han
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: SP-RASP has emerged as a unique regionalized robotic approach for the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia. Due to the unique anatomical orientation of this procedure, surgeons encounter steep learning challenges such as limited triangulation and single-port instrument articulation. To address the need for realistic training modalities, this project was aimed to develop and validate a high-fidelity model that can replicate the tactile and visual properties of the key procedural steps in SP-RARP. METHODS: A 120-gm prostate adenoma, prostate capsule, bladder, and surrounding pelvic anatomy were reconstructed from patient imaging data. Polyvinyl alcohol hydrogel was molded into 3D printed casts to create each structure separately. Hydrogels of varying formulations were made to mimic the texture of each organ and crosslinked using a freezing process to recreate realistic dissection planes. 5 experts and 5 novices defined by caseload performed key procedural steps under standard robotic visualization: bladder entry, prostate dissection, and vesicourethral anastomosis. The realism of the model was then evaluated by experts with a post-surgery questionnaire that assessed the anatomical realism, tissue handling, and educational value. Performance metrics (adenoma resected, resection efficiency, and errors) were compared between both groups. RESULTS: Ten total surgeons, 5 novices and 5 experts, rated the model via a survey. The survey responses were rated on a five-point scale: 5=Strongly Agree, 4=Agree, 3=Neutral, 2=Disagree, and 1=Strongly Disagree. On average, novices rated the model’s replication of human anatomy at 4.5, while experts rated it at 4.2. Similarly, novices gave the model’s educational value an average rating of 4.9, compared to 4.7 from experts. Further breakdown of these results is depicted in Figure 1A. Figure 1B displays the anatomical model during the main steps of the procedure. Feedback revealed that participants wanted the surgical planes to be more difficult to distinguish and separate. CONCLUSIONS: The custom hydrogel-based model for SP-RASP provides a reproducible and realistic platform for skill enhancement and surgical practice in SP-RARP. Its high fidelity, reproducibility, and ability to differentiate in performance make it a promising addition to SP robotic surgical education.

title: IMPLEMENTATION OF MINI-HOLEP (MILEP) IN VERY LARGE PROSTATES: A PROPENSITY SCORE–MATCHED STUDY
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology I (IP03)
authors: Tomer Mendelson, Omri Schwarztuch Gildor, Adi Kidron, Tomer Bashi, Karin Lifshitz, Yotam Veredgron, Ofer Yossepowitch, Mario Sofer
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Mini-HoLEP (MiLEP) using a 22-Fr resectoscope has been shown to have several advantages over the conventional 26-Fr system. However, its implementation in treating very large prostates (≥150 cm3) has been scarcely reported. We aimed to characterize the feasibility, safety, and perioperative outcomes of MiLEP in patients with prostates ≥150 cm3. METHODS: A retrospective review of all 635 HoLEP procedures performed in our institution after MiLEP introduction (September 2022–August 2025) revealed a cohort of 135 (21%) procedures performed in prostates ≥150 cm3. Of these, 96 were done with a 26-Fr instrument and 39 with MiLEP. Propensity score matching (1:1) on age, ASA class, prostate volume, and presence of an indwelling catheter yielded two matched comparison groups of 29 patients each. Statistical analyses were performed using univariable and multivariable models. RESULTS: Post-matching baseline characteristics are shown in Table 1; univariable comparisons appear in Table 2. Compared with standard HoLEP, MiLEP was associated with a significantly lower need for meatal dilation (p=0.001), better intraoperative preservation of body temperature (p=0.009), and higher tissue-removal efficiency (p=0.013). Multivariable models confirmed and strengthened these findings. No case required conversion from MiLEP to standard HoLEP; conversely, two procedures were converted from HoLEP to MiLEP—one for an anterior urethral stricture and one due to a penile prosthesis. Complication rates were similar between groups. CONCLUSIONS: We report, for the first time, expanding MiLEP use to prostates ≥150 cm3, demonstrating feasibility, safety and effectivity. MiLEP's previously documented advantages were reproduced in the ≥150 cm3 population. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: ASSISTANCE OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL-BASED AI AGENT IN PREOPERATIVE COMMUNICATION REDUCES ANXIETY OF PROSTATE CANCER PATIENTS AND WORKLOAD OF CLINICIANS: A PROSPECTIVE, RANDOMIZED, PHASE II TRIAL
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Zheng Liu, Hua Xu, Bo Dai
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Preoperative communication is crucial in reducing patients' anxiety but demands considerable effort from clinicians. This study aims to evaluate whether AI agent-assisted preoperative communication reduces patient anxiety, and decreases clinician workload compared to standard communication. METHODS: We developed an AI agent using DeepSeek-R1 for preoperative communication, based on clinical guidelines and our institute's experience. Patients with newly diagnosed prostate cancer scheduled for radical surgery at our center were enrolled, excluding those with severe mental illness or cognitive dysfunction. Upon admission, patients were randomized at the ward level into control and AI agent-assisted groups. Both groups immediately received baseline emotional and cognitive assessments such as GAD-7 and B-IPQ. Specific questions of the two groups were collected via our AI agent. The AI agent-assisted group then received personalized responses from our AI agent, validated for scientific accuracy before delivery. Both groups then received preoperative communication from clinicians blinded to group assignments and underwent emotional and cognitive assessments again. Clinicians' workload was assessed using NASA-TLX. Primary endpoints were GAD-7 scores and NASA-TLX results. Secondary endpoints included other emotional (VAS-A, I-PANAS-SF), disease cognition scales (APAIS, B-IPQ), patient satisfaction, and communication time for clinicians. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials. gov (NCT07082049). RESULTS: From Feb to Aug 2025, a total of 245 patients were randomized into control (n=124) and AI agent-assisted (n=121) groups. The two groups of patients totally asked 3,294 questions, averaging 13.94 questions per patient. These questions covered various aspects of surgery, including anesthesia, perioperative care, and management. Patients in the AI agent-assisted group experienced notably lower anxiety levels compared with the control group, with decrease in GAD-7 scores (median (IQR): 3.5 (2.0-5.0) vs. 7.5 (6.5-9.0), p<0.001). Clinician workload was notably reduced in the AI agent-assisted group, with lower NASA-TLX scores (median (IQR): 38.0 (24.5-52.5) vs. 57.0 (37.0-77.5), p<0.001) and remarkable nearly half the communication time compared to the control group (11.7 mins vs. 20.9 mins, p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: AI-assisted preoperative communication significantly reduces patient anxiety, enhances disease perception, and decreases clinician workload, identifying previously unaddressed patient concerns.

title: PREDICTING 1-YEAR ERECTILE FUNCTION RECOVERY AFTER ROBOTIC-ASSISTED RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY FROM RAW SURGICAL VIDEO VIA AN AUTOMATED, ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-BASED SYSTEM
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Jasmine Lin, Xi Li, Nicholas Matsumoto, Cherine H. Yang, Peter Wager, Alvin C. Goh, Geoffrey A. Sonn, Christian Wagner, Andrew J. Hung
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Surgical outcomes vary widely as a function of surgeon performance, but the specific aspects of surgical performance that define outcomes are not well understood. We implement “Frame-to-Outcome” (F2O), an end-to-end artificial intelligence (AI) system, to identify metrics that predict erectile function (EF) outcomes after robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) from raw surgical video. METHODS: We analyzed 130 videos of RARPs by 30 surgeons from 4 international hospitals. Patients with clinically localized prostate cancer and EF sufficient for intercourse prior to surgery were included. F2O uses frame-level classification and spatiotemporal modeling to convert video of the nerve-sparing step into a sequence of standardized surgical gestures, where each gesture represents the smallest meaningful interaction between instrument and tissue. F2O-predicted gestures were then evaluated with effect size analysis to discern the features (e. g. gesture frequency, duration) associated with EF recovery at 12 months (defined as Sexual Health Inventory for Men score >17), where a positive effect size denotes higher value in the EF recovery group. Results were compared with features derived from human-annotated data. For overlapping features, we report mean absolute difference in effect sizes and Pearson correlation coefficients with corresponding p-values. RESULTS: In our data, 44/130 patients (33.8%) recovered EF at 12 months while 86/130 (66.2%) did not. F2O correctly predicted EF recovery with mean accuracy of 0.75 (95% CI 0.70-0.81). EF recovery was positively associated with higher frequency (d=0.26, p=0.13) and duration (d=0.31, p=0.06) of spread gestures and negatively associated with frequent energy cut gestures (d=-0.26, p=0.16). When comparing gesture features against those derived from our prior work using human annotated data, effect size directions were concordant with small mean absolute difference (0.13) and strong correlation (r=0.97, p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: F2O generates gesture features from surgical video to accurately predict 12-month EF outcomes after RARP, without need for human effort. While prior effort to quantify surgical performance using gestures has been limited by scalability due to reliance on human annotators, F2O enables fully automated processing of surgical video to correctly predict outcomes.

title: A NON-INVASIVE MRI-BASED MULTIMODAL FUSION DEEP LEARNING MODEL (MF-DLM) FOR PREDICTING OVERALL SURVIVAL IN BLADDER CANCER: A MULTICENTER RETROSPECTIVE STUDY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Xiao Yang, Qiang Lu, Qiang Cao, Lingkai Cai
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Accurate prognosis prediction in bladder cancer (BCa) is crucial for personalized treatment. This study aimed to develop and validate a non-invasive model using MRI for predicting the overall survival (OS) in BCa patients. METHODS: This retrospective multicenter study included 1131 BCa patients from eight institutions. We developed a multimodal fusion deep learning model (MF-DLM), leveraging a cross-attention mechanism to integrate four key preoperative data modalities: 3D deep learning features using a modified 3D ResNet50 network, 3D radiomics features, morphological MRI features, and clinical features. Patients were stratified into low- and high-risk prognostic groups based on MF-DLM scores, and model interpretability was evaluated using SHAP and Grad-CAM. RESULTS: The MF-DLM demonstrated excellent performance in predicting overall survival (OS), achieving higher C-index values than pT stage (training: 0.902 vs. 0.793, p<0.001; validation: 0.864 vs. 0.757, p=0.014; external test: 0.841 vs. 0.760, p=0.047). In addition, MF-DLM-based low-risk group demonstrated significantly longer OS in the training, validation, and external test sets (p<0.001). In the adjuvant therapy (AT) cohort, high-risk patients had significantly worse prognosis compared with low-risk patients (p<0.0001). Additionally, high-risk pT3/4 patients exhibited no statistically significant OS difference between those who received AT and those who did not (p=0.18), whereas low-risk pT3/4 patients experienced significantly improved OS with AT (p=0.0059). Besides, the low-risk group had better OS than the high-risk group in neoadjuvant therapy cohort (p=0.0032). CONCLUSIONS: The MF-DLM can reliably predict OS in BCa patients and provide additional prognostic stratification beyond pT and pN stages. Furthermore, MF-DLM-based risk groups can identify patients most likely to benefit from perioperative therapy.

title: DEVELOPMENT AND VALIDATION OF A DEEP LEARNING TOOL FOR AUTOMATED READING OF FLUORESCENCE CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY IMAGES IN RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Lixiang Fang, Nikhil Mayor, Anna Silvanto, Aiman Haider, Alexander Light, Archana Gopalakrishnan, Ricardo Almeida-Magana, Eoin Dinneen, Greg Shaw, Martin J. Connor, Taimur T. Shah, Hashim U. U. Ahmed, Francesca Fiorentino, Mathias Winkler
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Fluorescence confocal microscopy (FCM) is a more feasible alternative to the NeuroSAFE procedure for intraoperative margin assessment in radical prostatectomy (RP) with reasonable diagnostic accuracy. However, FCM images still require interpretation by a pathologist in a time of increasing workforce pressure. We aimed to develop and validate an AI model capable of distinguishing benign from malignant tissue on FCM images in RP, enabling real-time intraoperative decision-making without reliance on a pathologist. METHODS: FCM images from 153 patients were obtained from the IP8-FLUORESCE study using the Histolog Scanner. Pathologist-annotated regions containing cancer/benign tissue were used to create a dataset of 275 images reflecting real-world class imbalance (tumour 13%, benign 87%). A modified deep learning architecture was developed using the established ResNet50 convolutional neural network. To optimise performance on minority (tumour) classes, we applied modified focal loss, balanced data sampling, and classier head with dropout. A supervised learning approach was used. The model was trained on 80% of the data and tested on the remaining 20%. External validation was performed using 46 annotated margins (23 tumour, 23 benign) from an independent dataset. To improve explainability, gradient-weighted class activation maps (Grad-CAMs) were applied to highlight areas the model had identified as suspicious for cancer. RESULTS: On internal testing, our model achieved 87.5% (47.4-99.7) sensitivity, 97.9% (89.2-100.0) specificity, and AUC of 0.98 (93.1-100.0) for cancer detection. The model performed well on external validation: 91.3% (73.2-97.6) sensitivity, 73.9% (53.5-87.5) specificity, and AUC 0.83 (0.74-91.4). Grad-CAM heatmaps accurately localised malignant glands, highlighting features consistent with pathology assessment (Fig1). CONCLUSIONS: Our AI-driven deep learning model demonstrated high accuracy for classifying RP surgical margin status in a realistic, imbalanced dataset. Grad-CAMs provide interpretable visual outputs for clinicians. This approach has the potential to streamline the use of FCM for intraoperative margin assessment and limit reliance on pathologists. The study was limited by the small number of positive cases. Prospective clinical evaluation on larger datasets is required.

title: GENERATING NATURAL-LANGUAGE SURGICAL FEEDBACK DIRECTLY FROM VIDEO BY EXTRACTING ESSENTIAL COMPONENTS: INSTRUMENT, ACTION, TARGET TISSUE
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Rafal Kocielnik, Firdavs Nasriddinov, J. Everett Knudsen, Jeanine Kim, Peter Wager, Anima Anandkumar, Andrew J. Hung
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Surgeons-in-training need consistent feedback, but expert coaches are not always available. We built a machine-learning pipeline able to watch surgical videos and automatically generate relevant, coaching-style comments. The key to our approach is representing the variability of trainer feedback in a standardized format: instrument, action, and target tissue (IAT triplet). METHODS: We use a dataset of 33 robot-assisted urology surgeries with ~4.2k video-to-text pairs of trainer-trainee dialogue and employ a large language model (LLM) to extract IAT triplets from human feedback transcripts, grouping similar terms and normalizing inconsistent delivery. We then train a surgery-specific video-based model (PeskaVLP) to predict triplets by combining visual content, estimated motion of instruments, and provided procedure/task context ( Fig. 1.1a). Using the IATs predicted from the video to guide an LLM (1.1b), we generate coaching-style natural language feedback. We evaluate our approach in a 5-fold cross-validation setup, reporting AUCs for predicting IAT components from video. We further assess how well generated feedback matches actual trainer delivery by using a published 1-5 content alignment rubric (higher is better) ( Fig. 1.3) and estimating ratio of important words captured (ROUGE) and word-level mistakes (WER). RESULTS: When predicting IATs, adding instrument motion and procedure/task context improved performance over baseline model for each component ( Figure 1.2a), raising AUCs for Instrument (0.65→0.73); Action (0.58→0.61); Tissue (0.70→0.79) compared to video alone. For feedback, using the extracted IAT triplets to condition LLM generation produced trainer-style feedback that scored better on the alignment rubric 2.17→2.44 (+12%) due to better preservation of core actionable guidance (examples in 1.3). Crucially, the proportion of acceptable outputs (score ≥ 3) increased from 21% to 42%, and word-level metrics improved as well (WER ↓~31%, ROUGE ↑~64%), see 1.2b. CONCLUSIONS: By anchoring our model’s interpretation of surgical video around explicitly defined IAT triplets and using those to guide language generation, we produce feedback whose content and complexity is more aligned with real-world trainer delivery. Future work will improve the triplet abstraction and control delivery style, such as urgency or encouragement.

title: THE UROFLOW TRIAL: FIRST-IN-CLASS REAL-WORLD COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF A SMARTPHONE-BASED AI UROFLOWMETRY APP VERSUS STANDARD CLINIC UROFLOWMETRY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Kenneth Omar Cintron-Cartagena, Javier Castillo-Ortiz, Millie Lopez-Inostroza
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Uroflowmetry remains the cornerstone of objective lower urinary tract evaluation, yet its clinical utility is limited by access, repeatability, and clinic follow up adherence. Artificial Intelligence Enhanced digital home uroflowmetry offers scalable, patient-centered remote monitoring of physiologic voiding in a more natural environment. We compared its performance against gold-standard clinic uroflowmetry, in a real world setting where reproducibility and clinic–home uroflowmetry concordance remain unexplored. METHODS: A total of 170 patients from five centers were enrolled to be part of a prospective cohort trial. All (100%) completed baseline clinic uroflowmetry; 140 (82.4%) also performed at least one remote AI uroflowmetry “MenHealth App”. At 4 week follow-up, only 50 (29.4%) returned for repeat clinic testing, whereas 82.4% engaged with remote AI monitoring (3,586 total remote uroflow tests).For comparative analysis, clinic uroflowmetry (n=50 with follow-up) was compared against MenHealth remote uroflowmetry (n=141 flows). Median Qmax, Qavg, voided volume, and flow time were assessed with Mann–Whitney U tests, while Spearman correlations were performed between objective measures, symptom scores, and quality-of-life (QoL) domains. RESULTS: AI Uroflowmetry “MenHealth” demonstrated reduced variability across repeated measures, with tighter clustering and greater internal consistency compared to clinic uroflowmetry. In paired data (n=50), clinic parameter reproducibility was strong (r=0.79 for flow time), but “MenHealth” achieved greater stability in repeated recordings, supporting the value of frequent at-home sampling. The MenHealth App captured physiologic voiding patterns through mobile uroflowmetry across the day, in contrast to conventional single-timepoint clinic testing, demonstrating lower values for Qmax (16.6 vs 33.9 ml/s), Qavg (9.4 vs 11.6 ml/s), and voided volume (212 vs 312 ml; all p<0.001). MenHealth App demonstrated that Voided volume correlated strongly with Qavg (ρ=0.778, p<0.001) and flow time (ρ=0.796, p<0.001). Symptom scores correlated with QoL (ρ=0.551, p<0.001). QoL differed significantly by age group (p=0.004), peaking in middle-aged/early elderly participants. CONCLUSIONS: AI-driven home uroflowmetry achieved higher compliance than clinic uroflowmetry and captured physiologic voiding patterns through mobile uroflowmetry across the day, in contrast to conventional single-timepoint clinic testing. These findings support AI-based home uroflowmetry as a novel urological tool to expand access, adherence, and equity in urologic care.

title: DEVELOPING AN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE MODEL FOR INTRAOPERATIVE IDENTIFICATION OF URINARY STONE COMPOSITION
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Kunal K. Hanchate, Chase Mallory, Subhash Nerella, Rohan Bagulwar, Parisa Rashidi, Vincent G. Bird
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Determination of urinary stone composition guides diagnosis and management. To date, there is no study exploring artificial intelligence (AI) for endoscopic urinary stone identification or how deep neural networks can identify and predict stone patterns. We aimed to evaluate the efficacy of an AI model to identify stone composition based on intraoperative endoscopic imaging and use heatmaps to visualize stone patterns indicative of composition. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of intraoperative images of patients undergoing ureteroscopy or percutaneous nephrolithotomy from 03/2023 to 10/2025. In- and ex-vivo images of stones were catalogued. Stone type was classified by dominant composition (>70%). Our model included a deep neural network utilizing a Vision Transformer and Pubmedbert model to process image and metadata text. Domain-adversarial training was utilized with a gradient reversal layer to learn endoscope invariant image features representing stone composition. Heatmaps were generated to visualize maximal image feature activation during prediction. Model performance was evaluated through precision, recall, and F1 score (harmonic mean of recall and precision). RESULTS: A total of 229 patients were included, comprising 2,324 images. Pure stone compositions accounted for 87% (n=200) of data. Table 1 depicts model performance across pure compositions. The model demonstrated strong performance in identifying calcium oxalate stones (F1 score: 0.88) and moderate performance in identifying infectious stones (F1 score: 0.59) and calcium phosphate stones (F1 score: 0.53). Lower performance for other compositions was demonstrated, likely attributable to small sample size. Heatmaps of calcium oxalate and uric acid stones are depicted in (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191284.35857.1d.07#F1). CONCLUSIONS: We developed a novel AI model to identify stone composition based on intraoperative endoscopic imaging, illustrated visually via heatmapping. Our model demonstrates strong performance among well-represented compositions and underscores the need for rare stone type representation, with heatmaps highlighting stone patterns for future studies. | | | --- | | |

title: REAL-TIME IMAGE-GUIDED ROBOT-ASSISTED PARTIAL NEPHRECTOMY: DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY OF THE BISTOURY-CLINICAL PROSPECTIVE TRIAL
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Francesco Prata, Clemente Lauretti, Rosaura Morfino, Guido Manni, Antonino Capillo, Daniele Di Noto, Marco Chessari, Marco Massenzi, Paolo Soda, Loredana Zollo, Rocco Papalia
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The BISTOURY-CLINICAL trial was conceived as the translational phase of a multi-step research programme focused on AI-driven 3D navigation. This prospective clinical protocol aims to evaluate the feasibility, safety, and workflow integration of real-time image-guided robot-assisted partial nephrectomy (RAPN) performed with the Hugo™ RAS platform. The study also establishes a standardized methodological framework for multimodal data acquisition, synchronization, and validation, forming the technological basis for future autonomous and adaptive robotic systems. METHODS: This is a prospective, single-centre, observational trial enrolling 30 consecutive patients scheduled for RAPN. Eligibility criteria are displayed as follows: patients aged ≥18 years with solitary, localized renal masses eligible for partial nephrectomy, adequate renal function, and no prior ipsilateral surgery. The methodological design consists of four sequential phases: (1) Preoperative phase: acquisition of contrast-enhanced CT scans, automated segmentation and 3D patient-specific model generation; (2) Intraoperative phase: synchronized acquisition of endoscopic video and optical tracking data, enabling dynamic registration and augmented-reality visualization within the surgical field; The intraoperative technological framework integrates intraoperative 3D reconstruction based on monocular videos (BodySLAM), and a deformable registration pipeline (CPD+OpVD) for dynamic alignment between preoperative and intraoperative models (3) Postoperative phase: anonymised integration of all data streams for quantitative evaluation of spatial alignment accuracy, temporal stability and workflow feasibility, as well as qualitative assessment of surgeon orientation and usability via structured questionnaires; (4) Simulation and cross-validation phase: replication of selected procedures in a controlled robotic simulation environment to benchmark system performance and refine algorithmic components. Primary endpoints are system feasibility (no procedural delay >5 min), registration accuracy (<5 mm RMS error), and real-time performance stability (≥20 fps). RESULTS: The clinical phase has begun, and the first two RAPN procedures have been successfully performed using the Hugo™ RAS platform. In these cases, the CPD+OpVD pipeline achieved an average RMSE reduction of 51.03 ± 10.78% relative to rigid registration, with a mean computational time of 1.22 ± 1.16 s per endoscopic frame. CONCLUSIONS: These promising preliminary results demonstrate the potential of real-time deformable registration for image-guided robotic surgery and encourage the continuation of clinical experimentation toward an integrated AI-assisted surgical workflow.
