title: CONVOLUTIONAL NEURAL NETWORK FOR CT-GUIDED KIDNEY STONE IDENTIFICATION AND NEEDLE PATH PLANNING IN PERCUTANEOUS NEPHROLITHOTOMY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Maher Abdessater, Ramy Touma Sawaya, Oussama Nasrallah
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) is the standard treatment for renal stones larger than 2 cm but demands accurate access tract planning to prevent injury to surrounding organs. Although preoperative CT scans offer crucial anatomical information, their interpretation remains manual. This study aimed to create an artificial intelligence (AI)–driven application employing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to automatically detect kidney stones and generate safe needle trajectories for PCNL planning. METHODS: A dataset of 1,942 de-identified CT images was collected and segmented using 3DSlicer and TotalSegmentator to delineate the kidneys, collecting systems, vasculature, bowel, and musculoskeletal structures. A convolutional neural network (CNN) utilizing the YOLOv8 architecture was trained to detect kidney stones, determine spatial coordinates, calculate stone size and distance from the skin, and produce optimized percutaneous access trajectories. The generated outputs were integrated into an interactive interface that displayed annotated CT slices, visualized trajectories, and provided quantitative data such as puncture angle, needle length, and confidence scores. RESULTS: The AI application was successfully developed, enabling seamless integration between non-contrast CT imaging and automated segmentation. It consistently processed all CT datasets, automatically detecting kidneys, collecting systems, renal stones, and surrounding organs. The algorithm produced quantitative stone measurements with associated confidence scores and generated a virtual percutaneous access path connecting the skin to the stone’s center, calculating both puncture angle and needle length. Additionally, an alert feature identified cases where critical structures such as the pleura or colon were in close proximity. CONCLUSIONS: The proposed AI system shows the potential for automated kidney stone detection and trajectory planning in PCNL. Further validation will evaluate its accuracy, user performance, and relationship with intraoperative results.

title: DEEP LEARNING–BASED PREDICTION OF SURGICAL NECESSITY IN GRAY-ZONE BLADDER OUTLET OBSTRUCTION USING URODYNAMIC PRESSURE–FLOW SIGNALS: A PROSPECTIVE MULTICENTRE STUDY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Ahmet Karakeci, Fatih Demir, Ahmet Keles, Fatih Mehmet Celik, Burak Caliskan, Asif Yildirim, Irfan Orhan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To prospectively evaluate a deep learning model for predicting the need for surgical intervention in men with persistent lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) and equivocal bladder outlet obstruction (BOOI 20–40), a group in which standard urodynamic parameters are often inconclusive for guiding management decisions. METHODS: This multicentre prospective study enrolled 265 men with persistent LUTS despite medical therapy across two tertiary centres (2024–2025). Patients underwent pressure–flow urodynamics with detrusor pressure and flow signals sampled at 100 Hz and converted to time–frequency spectrograms. The reference standard for surgical indication was determined by blinded consensus of three senior urologists (κ=0.86) integrating cystoscopy and 6-month outcomes, independent of model outputs. A 104-layer stacked residual network (SR-Net) was trained and validated using 10-fold cross-validation. Model performance was assessed using a confusion matrix, reporting accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values. Comparisons with expert interpretation of conventional urodynamic parameters (Qmax, BOOI, PdetQmax) used the McNemar test, and spectral energy differences were evaluated by Mann–Whitney U (p<0.05). RESULTS: Baseline characteristics are shown in Table 1. The cohort (mean age 67 ± 8 years) exhibited severe LUTS (mean IPSS 26.9 ± 3.4), reduced Qmax (9.7 ± 8.2 ml/s), and elevated PVR (173 ± 158 ml). Spectrograms showed higher spectral energy density among surgery-indicated patients (p<0.05). The SR-Net achieved 74.7% accuracy (95% CI 69.2–80.2), sensitivity 73.3%, specificity 76.1%, PPV 75.4%, and NPV 74.2% ( Table 2). The confusion matrix ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191284.35857.1d.10#F1)) demonstrated 102 true positives, 96 true negatives, 35 false positives, and 32 false negatives. Expert prediction reached 73.1% accuracy (95% CI 67.5–78.7) with no significant difference (p=0.58). At 6 months, 89% of conservatively managed patients improved without surgery. CONCLUSIONS: The SR-Net model analyzing urodynamic spectrograms achieved moderate accuracy (74.7%) for predicting surgical benefit in men with equivocal BOO, comparable to expert interpretation. While feasible, its modest gain and reliance on invasive testing limit clinical adoption. External validation and integration with non-invasive parameters are warranted before clinical use. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: A TIERED AI-ENHANCED CURRICULUM FOR UROLOGY RESIDENTS: INTEGRATING CHATGPT TO IMPROVE GUIDELINE ADHERENCE AND CLINICAL REASONING
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Manfredi Bruno Sequi, Fabio Maria Valenzi, Andrea Fuschi, Paolo Pietro Suraci, Yazan Al Salhi, Onofrio Antonio Rera, Alice Antonioni, Damiano Graziani, Filippo Gianfrancesco, Giuseppe Candita, Giorgio Martino, Paolo Benanti, Giovanni Di Gregorio, Luca Erra, Gaia Vivarelli, Salvatore Viola, Hila Rogozinski, Cosimo De Nunzio, Antonio Franco, Antonio Carbone, Antonio Luigi Pastore
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Traditional urology training often provides fragmented exposure to guideline-based management, leading to variable progression from diagnostic reasoning to advanced clinical decision-making. The expansion of the EAU Guidelines further increases the challenge of ensuring consistent, evidence-based education. AI tools may help bridge this gap by providing adaptive, interactive, and structured learning experiences tailored to different residency stages. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of a tiered AI-assisted curriculum on knowledge improvement, guideline adherence, and clinical reasoning among urology residents. METHODS: A single-center study was conducted over an 8-week period, involving 14 urology residents participating in a structured program. The curriculum was organized into 3 progressive learning levels. The initial stage focused on the fundamentals of diagnostic criteria, risk stratification, LUTS/BPH management, urolithiasis, and urinary infections. Intermediate modules were based on oncological guidelines. The final stage emphasized the management of multimodal and refractory cases, perioperative strategies, and complication handling. Residents used ChatGPT through interactive case discussions simulating clinical reasoning and required justification of diagnostic and therapeutic choices. Pre- and post-intervention assessments evaluated guideline-based knowledge and decision accuracy. Self-reported confidence was measured using a Likert scale. All AI responses were reviewed by faculty for clinical accuracy and Guideline adherence. RESULTS: Completion of the program led to a significant overall improvement in knowledge, with mean scores increasing from 66.9% to 86.7% (p<0.01). The most pronounced gain was observed among senior residents, who demonstrated a 27.1% increase in performance for complex case management. Confidence rose from 3.0 to 4.5 (p<0.01). Improved clarity in diagnostic reasoning (85.7%), stronger understanding of algorithms (78.6%), and greater time efficiency in clinical decision-making (71.4%) was reported. Faculty confirmed high guideline consistency (94.8%) across ChatGPT outputs, with minor inaccuracies in 7.2% of responses, involving risk stratification nuances and therapeutic sequencing in advanced disease. CONCLUSIONS: The tiered ChatGPT-enhanced curriculum effectively improved residents' knowledge, guideline adherence, and confidence across all levels of training, highlighting the potential of AI-assisted education to standardize learning in urology. Limitations were observed, including occasional oversimplification and dependence on the user's ability to formulate precise clinical prompts. While AI cannot replace expert supervision, its integration into structured residency programs may serve as a valuable adjunct to traditional mentorship.

title: FEASIBILITY OF AI-SYNCHRONIZED ROBOTIC RESPIRATORY COMPENSATION INDEPENDENT OF ACTIVATION TIMING IN LITHOTRIPSY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Sung Yong Cho, Jae Chul Kim, Kyu Seob Song, Dong Geol Lee, Dong Ho Lee, Joon Hwan Kim, Dong Soo Kwon, Jose Carlo Elises, Hyo Myung Lee
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Compensating for respiratory motion can substantially improve the precision of robot-assisted intrarenal laser lithotripsy. In Zamenix, using this function requires the operator to manually press a dedicated action button at the precisely defined target instant shown on the flexible ureteroscope display during respiration-driven renal motion. Because timing is influenced by user experience, scope position, and dynamic intrarenal conditions, the button is not always pressed at the optimal moment. In this study, we assessed how precisely operators could identify and click the target instant and compared this with the start-time detection performance of an AI-assisted respiratory-synchronization model. METHODS: We assembled a validation set of 20 ureteroscopic videos recorded at multiple intrarenal sites and environments in eight pigs, each containing 5–6 respiration cycles. These videos were evaluated by eight urologists familiar with intrarenal procedures. Participants independently viewed the randomized videos and pressed a timing-logging button to mark the target moment for respiratory-motion compensation. To obtain each participant’s near-optimal click per video, the task was repeated in two rounds. For the AI-assisted synchronization model, we prepared a training set—distinct from the validation set—of respiration-induced renal-motion videos and trained the model to detect the same target timing. RESULTS: Timing error was defined as the time difference (ms) between the target timing and the click. Across 1,909 total clicks from eight participants on 20 videos, the mean error relative to the target timing was 453.98 ± 194.86 ms. We generated just over 100 image-sequence samples (short clips) per video as inputs to the AI-assisted synchronization model, enabling it to locate the target timing. Across 2,478 samples, the overall mean error was 70.22 ± 141.72 ms, with erroneous detections observed in 0.44% (11 samples). CONCLUSIONS: These findings support the operational feasibility of integrating AI-assisted synchronization into robotic respiratory-motion compensation to improve urologists’ working conditions. We confirm the potential for AI assistance to enable more effective and consistent use of the compensation feature, reducing inter-user variability, which is expected to help improve outcomes in robot-assisted RIRS.

title: LEVERAGING DEEP LEARNING FOR OPTICAL BIOPSY: MALIGNANCY PREDICTION FROM FLUORESCENCE CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY OF PROSTATE BIOPSIES
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Salim K. Younis, Karim Daher, Mohamad Watfa, Nicholas E. Heller, Lin Wang, Sahil Patel, Abdulrahman Al-Bayati, Samarpit Rai, Nicolas Soputro, Rui Miguel Marques Bernardino, Rishi Jonnalagadda, Gabriela Diaz, Jacob M. Knorr, Riccardo Autorino, Ruben Olivares, Zeyad R. Schwen, John Weaver, Jane Nguyen, Christopher J. Weight, Jihad Kaouk
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Conventional histopathology requires fixation, embedding, and staining, delaying diagnosis and limiting same-day decision-making. Fluorescence confocal microscopy (FCM) enables rapid, label-free imaging of fresh, unfixed tissue with near-histologic resolution. However, interpretation remains expert-dependent and subject to variability. We developed a weakly supervised deep learning framework to predict malignancy directly from FCM images of prostate biopsies, aiming to assess the feasibility of automated diagnostic support during tissue acquisition. METHODS: Fresh prostate biopsy cores were scanned using an FDA-cleared FCM system. Final histopathology served as the reference standard. Each slide was divided into overlapping tiles, and a multiple-instance learning (MIL) architecture was trained using weak (core-level) labels without manual region annotation. A Top-K pooling strategy focused learning on the most informative tiles within each biopsy core. Model performance was evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation with patient-level grouping to prevent data leakage. Primary metrics were the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and average precision (AP). RESULTS: A total of 62 FCM slides from 52 patients, comprising 198 prostate biopsy cores (98 malignant, 96 benign), were analyzed. Each slide corresponded to a biopsy location containing an average of 3.25 cores. The deep learning model achieved a mean AUC of 0.81 ± 0.08 and AP of 0.85 ± 0.09 across folds. Heatmap visualizations localized high-probability regions consistent with malignant glandular morphology on FCM images when reviewed by an expert genitourinary histopathologist. CONCLUSIONS: Weakly supervised deep learning can distinguish malignant from benign prostate biopsy cores using fluorescence confocal microscopy of fresh tissue. This proof-of-concept study demonstrates the potential of AI-driven optical biopsy to accelerate prostate cancer diagnostics and support same-session clinical workflows.

title: BRINGING DEPTH PERCEPTION BACK TO ROBOTIC SURGERY: AI DIFFUSION-BASED STEREO RECONSTRUCTION FROM MONOSCOPIC SURGICAL VIDEO
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Nicholas Matsumoto, Ujjwal Pasupulety, Peter Wager, Andrew J. Hung
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Surgical video recordings are conventionally monoscopic (mono), limiting depth perception for postoperative review and surgical training. In contrast, intraoperative robotic console view provides stereoscopic cues critical for spatial understanding. We adapted a stereo video generation framework that converts standard mono surgical videos into stereoscopic format for immersive visualization on 3D/VR displays. METHODS: The AI-based framework comprises two stages: depth-based video splatting and stereo video inpainting ( Fig. 1a). First, per-frame scene geometry is estimated using a mono video depth model. The left-eye video is then warped into a right-eye viewpoint through depth-based splatting, yielding an occlusion mask to identify regions that need to be filled in. Next, a diffusion-based video inpainting model fills occluded areas conditioned on the warped frames and masks, producing a photometrically coherent right-eye sequence. Since we have true stereo videos (both right and left eye recordings) in this dataset, quantitative image fidelity was assessed against ground-truth right-eye videos using peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index (SSIM), and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS). RESULTS: From 12 robotic cases with stereo video (median duration 38.9 min at 30 fps), we utilized one eye’s video (left) to generate the other eye (right), resulting in 12,912 stereo pair frames. Generated right-eye views achieved a mean PSNR of 14.95 ± 0.91 dB, SSIM 0.26 ± 0.03, and LPIPS 0.48 ± 0.03 . While the PSNR and LPIPS meets the standard for perceptual quality (PSNR > 13, LPIPS < 0.5) and confirms the visual realism of the output, the lower SSIM (where SSIM > 0.7 is generally considered robust) reflects the difficulty of applying generative stereo synthesis to the surgical domain. CONCLUSIONS: A depth-guided splatting and diffusion-based inpainting framework can reconstruct realistic stereo video from mono endoscopic recordings, enabling immersive visualization for retrospective review and surgical education. While quantitative metrics reflect the inherent difficulty of dynamic surgical scenes, this work establishes a reproducible foundation for applying generative stereo synthesis in clinical video workflows and novel VR-based surgical training.

title: FROM CYSTOSCOPY TO CYSTECTOMY: ENHANCING UROLOGIC SURGICAL TRAINING WITH CHATGPT ACROSS THE FULL SPECTRUM OF PROCEDURES
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Manfredi Bruno Sequi, Fabio Maria Valenzi, Andrea Fuschi, Paolo Pietro Suraci, Yazan Al Salhi, Onofrio Antonio Rera, Alice Antonioni, Damiano Graziani, Filippo Gianfrancesco, Giuseppe Candita, Giorgio Martino, Paolo Benanti, Giovanni Di Gregorio, Luca Erra, Gaia Vivarelli, Salvatore Viola, Hila Rogozinski, Giorgia Tema, Cosimo De Nunzio, Antonio Carbone, Antonio Luigi Pastore
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Contemporary urologic surgical training faces increasing challenges due to reduced operative exposure, complex surgical techniques, and time-limited learning environments. ChatGPT, an advanced large language model developed by OpenAI, offers an innovative, real-time educational tool that enhances preparedness, procedural understanding, and clinical decision-making. This study aimed to assess the impact of ChatGPT on knowledge acquisition and confidence among urology residents across a comprehensive range of urologic interventions. METHODS: A prospective study was conducted involving urology residents in high-volume academic training programs. Over a 6-week period, participants engaged with ChatGPT modules tailored to core urologic procedures: cystoscopy, rigid and flexible URS, nephrostomy placement, ureteral stenting, TURP, TURBT, RIRS, HoLEP, PCNL, ECIRS, prostate biopsy, orchiectomy, laparoscopic nephrectomy, laparoscopic pyeloplasty, laparoscopic cystectomy and prostatectomy, RARP, RAPN, and RARC. Each module included step-by-step walkthroughs, simulated intraoperative challenges, complication management, and guideline-based decision-making. Participants completed pre- and post-module multiple-choice knowledge assessments and self-reported confidence evaluations (5- point Likert scale), followed by a satisfaction and feedback survey. RESULTS: A total of 27 Residents participated in the study. Post-intervention analysis revealed improvement in procedural knowledge, with mean test scores increasing from 62.1 to 81.5% (p<0.01). Confidence in performing or assisting procedures improved from a baseline mean of 2.8 to 4.2 (p<0.01). ChatGPT was rated “useful” or “very useful” by 77.7% of participants; 85.18% expressed willingness to integrate it into their study routine. The most appreciated features were the model's clarity in procedural sequencing, adaptability to different training levels, and its utility in reinforcing intraoperative decision-making. The most common limitation was the lack of anatomical visuals (70.37%) and oversimplification of complex cases (33.3%). The faculty review confirmed high content relevance and clinical coherence, with minor factual inaccuracies found in 10.1% of AI responses. CONCLUSIONS: ChatGPT proved to be an effective cognitive training tool across a wide range of urologic procedures, significantly improving both procedural knowledge and trainee confidence. Its flexibility and accessibility make it a promising supplement to traditional surgical education, particularly in resource-limited or high-volume training environments. While it cannot replace hands-on experience or expert mentorship, its integration into structured curricula could enhance the standardization and scalability of urologic education. Future studies should evaluate long-term retention, clinical applicability, and outcomes in multi-institutional settings.

title: AI-SKALPEL: AI-SEGMENTATION OF KIDNEY ANATOMY AND LITHIASIS FOR PRECISION AND ENHANCED LEARNING
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Leo C. Chen, Jun Ma, Bo Wang, Kenneth T. Pace
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: 3D visualization of surgical anatomy using virtual reality or 3D printed models has been shown to improve surgical outcomes, trainee performance, and reduce the rate of complications. However, creation of 3D models requires significant effort to manually annotate the relevant anatomy for each individual patient. While artificial intelligence (AI)-based methods can dramatically improve annotation efficiency, existing segmentation models for kidney stones and the collecting system are either proprietary, not publicly available, and/or require contrast enhanced CT scans. We thus aimed to develop an open source AI segmentation tool capable of delineating kidney stones and the collecting system on non-contrast CT scans. METHODS: 2,000 publicly available CT scans and radiology reports (AMOS-MM dataset) were evaluated for kidney and ureteral stones. Stone size, volume, and Hounsfield units were calculated, and the presence of hydronephrosis was noted. Manual segmentation was performed to delineate all stones, and a subset of scans with hydronephrosis had bilateral collecting systems annotated in an iterative fashion. Segmentations were used to train Residual Unet models to automatically delineate the stones and collecting systems. Pseudomasks were generated for surrounding organs (colon, spleen, liver, lungs, bony structures) based on previously published work. RESULTS: A total of 174 non-contrast CT scans with 537 kidney/ureteral stones were identified in the AMOS-MM training cohort. Of these, 106 scans had at least one ureteral stone. Mean stone size and volumes were 4.6 mm and 255 mm3. There were 42 stones over 1 cm and 11 stones over 2 cm in size. Hydronephrosis was present in at least one collecting unit in 46 scans. AI segmentation was robust with an average Dice score of 0.97 for the collecting system and median normalized surface distance (NSD) of 0.93 for kidney stones on a held-out test set. Average manual segmentation times per scan were 4.8 minutes for stones and 30.4 minutes for the collecting systems, compared to average AI inference times of 3 seconds for stones and 26 seconds for the collecting systems. CONCLUSIONS: We describe AI-SKALPEL, a freely available AI-segmentation tool for kidney stones and the collecting system. Work is ongoing to validate the model on private, retrospective clinical cohorts.

title: FIRST FULLY AUTOMATED, MULTI-MODAL, LARGE-LANGUAGE-MODEL–DRIVEN PROSTATE CANCER REGISTRY INTEGRATING BIOPSY, MRI, OPERATIVE, AND PATHOLOGY REPORTS
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Salim K. Younis, Kristina Dortche, Sahil Patel, Rishi Jonnalagadda, Rikhil Seshadri, Haya Abusafieh, Daniel Jevnikar, Mohamad Watfa, Gabriela Diaz, Karim Daher, Gagandeep Fervaha, Betty Wang, Sean McSweeney, Jacob M. Knorr, Riccardo Autorino, Ruben Olivares, Robert Abouassaly, Zeyad R. Schwen, Nicholas E. Heller, Jihad Kaouk, Christopher J. Weight
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Manual registry development in prostate cancer remains limited by fragmented diagnostic, imaging, operative, and pathology data. Prior automation efforts targeted single report types or relied on rule-based systems. We developed and validated a locally deployed large language model (LLM) framework that unifies these four domains into a structured, patient-centric registry. METHODS: Reports from 1,179 prostate cancer patients were retrieved from Epic Clarity, including biopsy pathology, prostate MRI, robotic radical prostatectomy operative notes, and surgical pathology. All reports were processed on institutional GPU servers using the locally deployed Qwen3-8B model. Domain-specific prompts were designed for each report type to mirror reporting conventions and output structured JSON. Twenty-seven key variables were extracted across diagnostic, imaging, intraoperative, and pathologic domains. Records were linked by MRN and procedure episode to form a longitudinal dataset. Concordance with manually curated references was evaluated using Cohen’s κ, intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), percent agreement, and mean absolute deviation (MAD). RESULTS: A total of 3,426 reports were processed. Complete linkage across all four domains was achieved in 1,157 of 1,179 patients (98.1%), verified through one-to-one MRN alignment with no mismatches. Median performance across 27 variables was κ=0.93, ICC=0.95, and 97.5 percent agreement. According to interobserver reliability benchmarks, these values correspond to “almost perfect” and “excellent” agreement ranges typical of expert human raters. CONCLUSIONS: This study establishes the first fully automated cross-domain large-language-model prostate cancer registry integrating biopsy, MRI, operative, and pathology data within institutional infrastructure. Using domain-specific prompts and structured JSON outputs, it achieved near-complete longitudinal linkage and expert-level concordance while preserving institutional governance. This provides a scalable blueprint for real-time outcome tracking and next-generation AI-assisted prostate cancer research. | | | --- | | |

title: FROM DATA TO DECISIONS: DEVELOPMENT OF MACHINE LEARNING MODELS AND AN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE APPLICATION TO PERSONALIZE CARE IN INFLATABLE PENILE PROSTHESIS SURGERY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Muhammed A. M. Hammad, David W. Barham, Justin C. Schneider, Jonathan Prunean, Elia Abou Chawareb, Dan Han, Babak Azad, David Swerdloff, Jake A. Miller, Robert Andrianne, Arthur L. Burnett, Kelli Gross, Georgios Hatzichristodoulou, James M. Hotaling, Tung-Chin Hsieh, James M. Jones, Aaron Lentz, Vaibhav Modgil, Daniar Osmonov, Sung Hun Park, Ian Pearce, Paul Perito, Hossein Sadeghi-nejad, Maxime Sempels, Alfredo Suarez-sarmiento, Jr, Koenraad Van Renterghem, Nicholas J. Warner, Matthew Ziegelmann
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: We developed and deployed a web-based, real-time risk calculator for predicting intraoperative, postoperative non-infectious, and infection-related complications following inflatable penile prosthesis (IPP) surgery. The platform enables transparent, multi-center validation and comparative endpoint assessment of machine-learning based risk models. METHODS: Using a multicenter dataset of 5,815 IPP procedures, machine learning models were developed in Python 3.13. Two feature sets were engineered: a Gamma set (pre-operative variables) and a Sigma set (combined pre- and intra-operative variables). Data preprocessing utilized Scikit-Learn pipelines with ten classifiers tested, including Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and Bernoulli NB. Given low complication rate (<7%), class imbalance was addressed using weighting and resampling techniques with 240 configurations evaluated (80 per target). Final models included Logistic Regression for intraoperative events, Random Forest for non-infectious complications, and Gradient Boosting for infection prediction. Trained models were serialized and deployed through Next. js frontend and FastAPI backend to allow real-time web access. RESULTS: The calculator generates individualized risk estimates in 0.62 ± 0.03 seconds across all endpoints. Model recall for intraoperative, non-infectious, and infectious complications was 74%, 75%, and 79%, respectively. Output visualization displays predicted complication probabilities derived from model distributions, allowing users to explore differences between high- and low-risk patient profiles. Stratification demonstrated stepwise increases in infection probability among patients with multiple comorbid risk factors. Technical performance, data privacy, and security were verified; multi-center prospective validation is ongoing. CONCLUSIONS: This open-access IPP complication risk calculator provides a transparent, real-time platform for individualized complication prediction. The tool’s risk estimates align with published multi-institutional complication rates and facilitate external validation across institutions without compromising data privacy. Broader adoption will allow refinement of predictive performance and integration into future clinical decision-support systems for prosthetic urology.

title: AI-ASSISTED STONE PREVENTION: A PATIENT-CENTRIC ASSESSMENT OF LLM PERFORMANCE ON URINE STUDY INTERPRETATIONS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Aleem Khan, Jared Winoker, Stephen Jackman, Kyle Spradling
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Use of large-language models (LLMs) has increased exponentially in recent years. While much study is currently focused on adoption of artificial intelligence technologies for providers, there remains a paucity of data on the state of current commercially available platforms available to the public. As there is not currently a consensus on how patients should be counseled on use of these platforms, there remains a need to assess real-world performance of these technologies from a patient perspective. This study intends to assess the accuracy and readability of common AI platforms on interpretation of 24-hour urine studies and their provided dietary recommendations. METHODS: A series of 4 hypothetical 24-hour urine study results were created to personify 4 classic patient archetypes for recurrent kidney stone formers (low fluid intake, high urinary calcium oxalate, hypocitraturia, high uricosuria). Each table was uploaded to 3 commercially available AI models (Gemini, Perplexity, ChatGPT) with the same prompt requesting interpretation of the uploaded results and dietary recommendations to prevent kidney stone formation. Each generated response was then compared to AUA Nephrolithiasis Medical Management Guidelines for accuracy (with inaccuracies classified as major or minor) of interpretation and dietary recommendation. Reading comprehension of each response was then calculated using both the Flesch-Kincaid Reading Level (FKRL) and Simple Measure of Gobbledygook (SMOG) indices to assess readability. RESULTS: Of the 4 archetypes, all 3 AI models accurately interpreted the 24-hour urine studies in diagnosis of the underlying metabolic risk factors associated with recurrent nephrolithiasis. ChatGPT had 2 minor inaccuracies when providing dietary recommendations for the high uric acid and hypocitraturia patients, while the remaining AI models did not have any inaccuracies in dietary recommendations. Mean FKRL (9.58 Gemini vs 11.26 Perplexity vs 7.86 ChatGPT, p<0.001) and SMOG indices (12.03 Gemini vs 12.08 Perplexity vs 10.01 ChatGPT, p<0.001) were significantly different between the 3 AI models, with ChatGPT having the easiest level of comprehension and Perplexity having the most difficult. CONCLUSIONS: Current commercially available AI platforms are able to accurately assess 24-hour urine study results and overall provided appropriate dietary recommendations. ChatGPT did provide the easiest/lowest required reading comprehension for responses for each prompt while Perplexity had the most difficult. Further studies are needed to better inform urologists on how to counsel patients on using these technologies.

title: PATHOLOGICAL CHARACTERISTICS AND CAUSE-SPECIFIC DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY OF A DEEP LEARNING MODEL FOR FALSE-POSITIVE PHOTODYNAMIC DIAGNOSIS OF BLADDER CANCER
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Shinkuro Yamamoto, Wonjik Kim, Hirokazu Nosato, Ryu Shigehisa, Atsushi Ikeda, Hideo Fukuhara, Satoshi Fukata, Keiji Inoue
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: False-positive (FP) findings in photodynamic diagnosis (PDD) arise from biological and optical factors, including tangent illumination, inflammation, non-neoplastic epithelial alterations, and chromosomal instability in premalignant mucosa. These FP mechanisms complicate intraoperative decision-making and may result in unnecessary resection. Building on our previous study demonstrating the feasibility of a deep learning (DL) model for distinguishing true and false positives, we analyzed its cause-specific diagnostic performance according to pathological background and compared its accuracy with that of expert urologists. METHODS: A total of 1,192 intraoperative PDD-positive cystoscopy images (486 true positives, 706 false positives) from Kochi Medical School Hospital were used to train a ResNet-50–based DL model fine-tuned with PDD data. Performance for distinguishing true and false positives was previously reported at AUA2024 (accuracy 64.3%, sensitivity 60.9%, specificity 66.7%). An independent test dataset of 153 images (104 false positives) was used for pathological differentiation. FP lesions were categorized as: (1) inflammation, (2) non-neoplastic epithelial alterations (reactive atypia, squamous metaplasia, or mild dysplasia), or (3) no pathological findings. The diagnostic accuracy of the DL model was compared with that of 17 expert urologists. RESULTS: Among 104 false-positive images, the DL model correctly identified FP lesions with accuracies of 60.0% for inflammation, 75.0% for non-neoplastic alteration, and 67.9% for no pathological findings, all comparable to or exceeding expert urologists (52.9%, 61.8%, and 57.3%, respectively). The DL model effectively identified false-positive lesions across different pathological backgrounds. CONCLUSIONS: The DL model showed reliable accuracy in distinguishing pathological causes of PDD false positives and performed at an expert level across all categories. This pathological stratification highlights the biological heterogeneity of PDD false fluorescence and represents a step toward AI-assisted fluorescence imaging for optimized bladder cancer surgery and early lesion detection.

title: COMPARATIVE VALIDATION OF AI-ASSISTED MRI SCREENING PATHWAYS IN THE IP1-PROSTAGRAM STUDY
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Nikhil Mayor, Antony W. Rix, Aarti Shah, Nikita Sushentsev, Luca Rosso, Natalia Klimowska-Nassar, Henry Tam, Heminder Sokhi, Mathias Winkler, David Eldred-Evans, Anwar R. Padhani, Hashim U. U. Ahmed
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Several studies have evaluated MRI as an upfront or sequential screening tool for prostate cancer, with variable PSA thresholds and biopsy criteria assessed. However, screening MRI can be challenging to interpret consistently. AI decision support systems (AI-DSS) may have a role in standardising assessment which could improve the balance of harms and benefits of screening with MRI. We retrospectively validated the Lucida Pi AI-DSS on the IP1-PROSTAGRAM cohort, comparing its performance with 3 MRI-based screening pathways. METHODS: 371 men with complete records from IP1-PROSTAGRAM were included. Men underwent Prostagram™ MRI, ultrasound and PSA, with systematic biopsy for any positive test and targeted biopsy if positive imaging. 159 (42.9%) underwent biopsy, detecting 15 (4.0%) GG ≥2 and 19 (5.1%) GG1 cancers. Alternative pathways were modelled using (P1) MRI for all; (P2) MRI if PSA ≥1; and (P3) MRI if PSA ≥3. In each pathway, a radiologist PI-RADS score of ≥3 and ≥4 was compared with AI-DSS. Outcomes: biopsy recommendation rate, GG ≥2 and GG1 detection, benign biopsy rate (GG0), and 3 derived utility metrics: selectivity (GG ≥2/GG1), efficiency (GG ≥2/\[GG1+GG0\]), and selective biopsy avoidance (GGx \[no biopsy\]/GG0). RESULTS: AI-DSS maintained or improved GG ≥2 detection whilst reducing biopsy rates in most scenarios. In P1, AI-DSS achieved similar GG ≥2 yield (11/371, 3.0%) to PI-RADS ≥3 (3.5 %) and ≥4 (3.0 %), with fewer biopsies (9.2% vs 16.7% and 9.7%), GG1 cases (1.1% vs 1.9% and 1.3%), and benign biopsies (5.1% vs 11.3% and 5.4%), improving almost all utility metrics. In P2, AI-DSS maintained GG ≥2 detection (11/371, 3.0%) relative to PI-RADS ≥3 (3.0 %) and ≥4 (2.7%), reducing biopsy rates compared with PI-RADS ≥3 (8.4% vs 11.1%), with a modest increase compared with PI-RADS ≥4 (7.0%), and the lowest GG1 yield (0.5%). In P3, only 9% of men progressed to MRI, yielding 6/371 (1.6%) GG ≥2 cancers and missing half of all GG ≥2 cases; here, AI-DSS offered no additional benefit. CONCLUSIONS: On population screening data, AI-DSS achieved equivalent or superior detection of clinically significant prostate cancer compared with MRI/PSA pathways whilst reducing biopsy rates and overdiagnosis. The benefit was greatest for screening pathways using upfront MRI without a PSA threshold or following PSA≥1. The small dataset and low number of events is a limitation. | | | --- | | |

title: PERFORMANCE OF A LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL IN PREDICTING CLINICAL MANAGEMENT FOR NEW PROSTATE CANCER AND KIDNEY STONE VISITS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Craig Cronin, Maria Carolina Rodriguez Steube, Mark N. Alshak, William Azar, Arun Rai
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Electronic medical record platforms are developing proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) tools to enhance clinical decision making, such as Epic’s advanced reasoning tool. However, limited research has evaluated the accuracy of existing, publicly available large language models (LLMs) within urology. This study assessed the ability of GPT-5 to predict appropriate next steps in clinical management for new patients evaluated for prostate cancer or kidney stones at Johns Hopkins Hospital. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed new patient clinic visits for a provider specializing in prostate cancer and one in kidney stones. Basic demographic data, past medical and surgical histories, relevant laboratory values, and relevant imaging reports were extracted for all visits. For 10 prostate cancer visits, biopsy findings available at the time of the appointment were included. For 10 kidney stone visits, prior stone histories were extracted. These variables were entered into a HIPAA-secured version of GPT-5 using a standardized prompt to generate next-step management recommendations. Each response was independently evaluated by a senior urology resident, blinded to data extraction, and graded for accuracy on a 5-point Likert scale (1=inaccurate, 5=fully accurate) relative to the provider’s documented clinical plan. Descriptive statistics summarized accuracy scores, and a Mann-Whitney U test compared mean accuracy between visit types. RESULTS: Across 20 new patient visits, GPT-5-generated clinical recommendations achieved high accuracy (median 5 \[interquartile range 4-5\]). Accuracy was comparable between prostate cancer and kidney stone visits (mean 4.2 ± 0.92 vs 4.7 ± 0.48; p=0.76). The LLM received a perfect score for a prostate cancer visit where it appropriately recommended deferring biopsy given a negative MRI and low malignancy risk. Minor discrepancies involved suggesting follow-up digital rectal exams or laboratory tests not discussed by the clinician. For kidney stone visits, most deductions stemmed from minor medication adjustments or screening recommendations tangentially related to the presenting concern. CONCLUSIONS: LLMs can generate accurate and contextually appropriate management recommendations for new urology patients using pre-visit data. Performance was particularly strong for kidney stone evaluations and remained high even in prostate cancer cases that typically require nuanced, patient-directed decision making. Remaining inaccuracies largely involved unnecessary testing or minor screening recommendations, which may be reduced through targeted prompt refinement and broader variable collection.

title: CAN AI JUDGE URODYNAMIC STUDY QUALITY? VALIDATION USING THE BRISTOL UTRAQ SCALE
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: João Oliveira, Margarida Henriques, Luis Vale, Carlos Ferreira, Joao Silva, Tiago Antunes-Lopes
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urodynamic studies (UDS) are essential tools for evaluating lower urinary tract dysfunction, but the reliability of the decisions based on them depends critically on the technical quality of the recordings. The Bristol Urodynamic Trace Quality (UTraQ) scale was developed to provide a framework for assessing the technical adequacy of UDS. Artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) have recently become widely available and have shown potential across several areas of healthcare. While their performance in interpreting UDS remains limited, given the complexity of waveform analysis, quality assessment mainly relies on written or structural information, potentially making it a more suitable application for these models. This study aimed to evaluate the performance of an LLM (ChatGPT) in applying the Bristol UTraQ scale, and to compare its scoring with that of an expert. METHODS: The 50 most recent UDS performed at our centre, up to 30 September 2025, were included from patients who consented to participate. For each examination, anonymised images of the filling and pressure-flow phases were submitted to ChatGPT (version 5) using a structured prompt to answer all 24 UTraQ items. All AI outputs were automatically stored in a database. An experienced urodynamicist, blinded to the AI results, independently scored the same studies. Only comparable items (excluding 999) were analysed, and percentage agreement and Cohen's κ were calculated globally and by domain (pre-filling, filling, voiding). RESULTS: Fifty UDS were analysed. According to the expert, the median UTRAQ score was 77.8% (IQR 72.2–80.0%), indicating overall acceptable but suboptimal technical quality. The most frequent deficiencies were patient position not indicated (item 11: 19/49 studies), missing start/end of voiding markers (item 20: 48/48), and absence of the Qmax marker (item 22: 48/48). Pre-filling items were almost universally satisfactory. A total of 863 comparable item pairs were evaluated. The overall agreement between ChatGPT and the expert was 90.5%, with a Cohen's κ of 0.74 (substantial). Agreement was highest in the pre-filling domain (97.7%; κ=0.91), high but asymmetric in the filling domain (88.8%; κ=0.09), and lower in the voiding domain (82.5%; κ=0.65), largely reflecting systematic absence of voiding markers. CONCLUSIONS: ChatGPT applied the Bristol UTraQ scale with high agreement to an expert urodynamicist, demonstrating strong reproducibility in structured technical evaluation. As UTRAQ scoring relies primarily on identifiable written or symbolic elements rather than waveform interpretation, LLMs appear reliable to support this task. AI-assisted quality assessment may provide a fast, standardised, and objective approach for audit and training in urodynamics. Future developments combining textual and signal-based analysis could further advance automated urodynamic quality control.

title: REAL-TIME AI-BASED SMOKE REMOVAL IN LAPAROSCOPIC SURGERY: FIRST IN-VIVO FEASIBILITY STUDY
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Wayne Poll, M. Carmen Mir
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Visual clarity is essential for safety and efficiency in minimally invasive surgery (MIS). However, surgical smoke generated by electrocautery often obstructs the operative field, contributing to interruptions, prolonged procedure time, and increased risk of complications. While artificial intelligence (AI)-based smoke removal methods have shown promise in offline analyses, real-time clinical application has not yet been demonstrated. This study presents the first documented in-vivo demonstration of real-time AI-powered smoke removal during laparoscopic surgery, using a system called CLARIS by vopemed. METHODS: In August 2025, a feasibility session was performed in a live porcine model undergoing laparoscopic nephrectomy. Surgical smoke was generated via monopolar electrocautery, with trocar valves closed to create dense smoke conditions. The laparoscopic video signal was routed through the CLARIS console, which processed the feed and displayed the desmoked image to the surgeon. Frames were retrospectively analyzed using Dark Channel Prior (DCP) and Fog Aware Density Evaluator (FADE), two referenceless smoke metrics. Higher values indicate greater smoke density. RESULTS: CLARIS operated continuously with no interruptions or frame instability for 30 minutes, processing a total of 18,139 frames at 1080p and 20 fps. The original video feed showed an average DCP of 1.25 ± 0.35 and average FADE of 61.47 ± 20.73, which improved by 12.8% and 31.2%, respectively, following CLARIS processing (1.09 ± 0.33 and 42.32 ± 15.98). The operating surgeon qualitatively reported improved visibility during smoke events, noting clearer tissue contrast and more defined anatomic structures, such as kidney edges. Dissection could be performed without interruption for smoke evacuation. No adverse events occurred, and integration required no workflow modifications. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates the first in-vivo application of real-time AI-based smoke removal during laparoscopic surgery. CLARIS integrated into the existing technical stack, maintained stable operation, did not disrupt workflow, and improved contrast by removing smoke. Future work will improve the model's performance and validate it across multiple surgeons, procedures, and setups to assess generalizability and clinical impact.

title: KTGROW-ML: A NOVEL, MACHINE-LEARNING-BASED, MODEL TO PREDICT THE FUTURE GROWTH OF KIDNEY TUMORS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Simon W. White, Hersh Chandarana, Rajesh Ranganath, William C. Huang, Madhur Nayan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The detection of small kidney tumors has risen dramatically and often presents a diagnostic and management dilemma due to their heterogenous biology. Estimating future kidney tumor growth could enable more personalized management by reducing unnecessary interventions for indolent lesions and optimizing active surveillance frequency. The objective of this study was to develop and evaluate KTGrow-ML, a machine-learning (ML)-based prediction model to estimate the future growth of a kidney tumor. METHODS: We used electronic health record data from a large healthcare network to identify patients with serial size measurements for a suspicious kidney tumor or complex kidney cyst in radiology reports between 2011 and 2025. Tumor characteristics were extracted using our previously validated large language model (LLM)-based approach. The dataset was randomly split into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets. Supervised ML models were developed to predict tumor size at 6 and 12 months and compared against two baselines: recent-slope extrapolation and per-patient linear trend. Model performance was assessed using root mean squared error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and R2. Feature importance was evaluated using SHAP values. RESULTS: We identified 496,732 radiology reports with potential descriptions of a kidney tumor. Of these, the LLM classified 46,334 as having a kidney tumor with size dimensions. After applying inclusion criteria, 19,059 reports from 6,550 unique patients were analyzed. Median age was 68.6 (interquartile range (IQR) 58.9-76.8), 43.5% were female, and median tumor size was 2.20 cm (IQR 1.50-3.60). All ML models significantly outperformed both baselines for 6- and 12-month predictions (Figure 1, p0.05). The best-performing model, Elastic Net regression (KTGrow-ML), achieved a 6-month RMSE of 1.14 (95% CI 0.41–1.16), MAE 0.54 (0.25–0.56), and R2 0.77 (0.76–0.95); and a 12-month RMSE of 1.14 (0.60–2.39), MAE 0.51 (0.47–1.31), and R2 0.61 (−2.93–0.89). Current tumor size was the most influential predictor followed by size at diagnosis. CONCLUSIONS: We developed KTGrow-ML, a novel ML model to predict the future growth of kidney tumors. Our model significantly outperforms baselines and if further validated, could be used to reduce overtreatment of indolent tumors and personalize active surveillance schedules.

title: TOWARDS CLINICAL TRANSLATION OF A REAL-TIME, ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI)-ASSISTED CYSTOSCOPY SYSTEM FOR BLADDER CANCER DETECTION
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Calvin C. Zhao, Max Siauw, Liang Qiu, Timothy J. Lee, Kathleen E. Mach, Joseph C. Liao
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: White light cystoscopy is the cornerstone of bladder cancer detection and surveillance; however, challenges remain, including identification of carcinoma in situ, multifocal tumors, and distinguishing cancerous and benign lesions. Computer-vision artificial intelligence (AI) models for tumor detection have strong potential to overcome these limitations. This study aims to address the clinical translation hurdles related to workflow compatibility and usability by integrating an AI-assisted cystoscopy system in clinical settings. METHODS: We developed an end-to-end AI-assisted cystoscopy system featuring a compact, custom-built video processing hub measuring 377 mm × 330 mm × 82 mm ( Fig. 1) and an intuitive graphical user interface for integration with standard endoscopy towers. The hub supports up to four HDMI connections, enabling real-time switching between various video inputs via a front-panel control. Equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 5060 graphics card, the system provides real-time AI inference displayed as toggleable, low-latency overlays. A foot pedal allows the operator to quickly cycle through or deactivate AI overlays. For procedural safety, a hardware bypass button ensures the primary video feed remains uninterrupted in the event of a system error. A 14-question usability survey was designed to assess clinician user experience, focusing on interface usability and utility ( Fig. 2). RESULTS: The platform was successfully deployed in 4 operating room and 3 clinic cystoscopy procedures. Survey feedback from 4 physician users confirmed the system was user-friendly and minimally disruptive to workflow. Reported limitations include noticeable system latency during transurethral resection and false positive detections of non-cancerous lesions, such as resection beds. CONCLUSIONS: This pilot study demonstrates a feasible, user-centric platform for integrating AI into cystoscopy. Future efforts will focus on optimizing latency and gathering broader clinician feedback across diverse clinical settings.

title: DEVELOPMENT AND INTERNAL VALIDATION OF MACHINE-LEARNING MODELS TO PREDICT ADVERSE PATHOLOGICAL FEATURES IN UPPER TRACT UROTHELIAL CARCINOMA USING DATA FROM THE ROBUUST 3.0 COLLABORATIVE
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Philipp Korn, Soum Lokeshwar, Giacomo Musso, Karim Daher, Linhui Wang, Zhenjie Wu, Alireza Ghoreifi, Hooman Ebrahimi, Hooman Djaladat, Alex Kutikov, Randall Lee, Lin Lin, Vitaly Margulis, Alessandro Veccia, Riccardo Bertolo, Alessandro Antonelli, Gabriele Tuderti, Flavia Proietti, Giuseppe Simone, Andrea Mari, Luca Lambertini, Andrea Minervini, Alex Stephens, Carlo Silvani, Alfonso Santangelo, Firas Abdollah, Takashi Yoshida, Hidefumi Kinoshita
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Reliable preoperative identification of adverse pathological features in upper tract urothelial carcinoma remains challenging and upstaging on final pathology occurs in up to 60% of patients. Current guidelines differ in preoperative risk stratification, and most established risk factors are mainly based on postoperative findings. We aimed to develop and internally validate machine-learning (ML) models for preoperative prediction of muscle-invasive (≥pT2) and node positive disease (pN+) in UTUC. METHODS: Patients who underwent radical nephroureterectomy or distal ureterectomy without neoadjuvant chemotherapy from the multi-institutional ROBUUST 3.0 registry were identifed. Routinely available preoperative variables, including demographics, biopsy pathology (grade, variant histology, cytology), clinical features (cT-stage, cN-stage, tumor size, hydronephrosis, multifocality, serume creatinine) were processed with missing data imputed using Hyperimpute. Four classifiers (elastic-net logistic regression, random forest, LightGBM and SVM-RBF) were optimized via five-fold cross validation and hyperparameter optimization via Optuna. A logistic meta-learner combined base models into a stacking ensemble. Performance was evaluated using area under the curve (AUC) and Brier score in an 80/20 train-validation split. RESULTS: A total of 3584 patients with extirpative surgery and 1596 patients who additionally underwent lymph-node dissection were identified. Muscle-invasive disease was present in 1979 (55.2%) of cases, and node-positive disease in 1595 (31.6%) cases. The stacking model achieved the best discrimination for pN+ prediction (AUC 0.78 \[95% CI: 0.72\ – 0.83\], Brier 0.16), while for ≥pT2 prediction random forest outperformed other single learners and the stacking ensemble (AUC 0.66 \[95% CI: 0.63 – 0.70\], Brier 0.23) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191284.35857.1d.27#F1)). Significant predictors for pN+ disease were cT-stage, cN-stage and cytology. Significant predictors for >pT2 were cN-stage, creatinine and tumor size. CONCLUSIONS: Machine-learning models achieved robust accuracy for predicting nodal metastases but only moderate discrimination for muscle-invasive disease, underscoring the limitations of accurate preoperative primary tumor staging. External validation is needed to confirm clinical utility and inform preoperative risk-stratification and multimodal approaches to treatment.

title: APPLYING ADVANCED PROMPT ENGINEERING TECHNIQUES TO GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE MODELS FOR ANALYZING DIAGNOSTIC QUALITY IN RETROGRADE URETHROGRAM IMAGES
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Omer A. Choudhary, Eli Ferrara, Jin Kyu Kim, Michael Chua, Rano Matta, Amanda Hird, Robert Nam, Sender Herschorn, Sarah Neu
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Retrograde urethrograms (RUGs) are the main imaging method for evaluating urethral stricture disease. However, diagnostic quality varies with technical and anatomical factors, making consistent evaluation essential for patient management. Conventional artificial intelligence (AI) image analysis requires large datasets, which is costly and time intensive. Advanced prompting of generative AI models may offer a faster, data-efficient alternative. Our objective was to evaluate the effectiveness of advanced prompting in accurately assessing RUG quality. METHODS: We reviewed a random sample of 233 RUGs from 2010-2024 at a tertiary care centre. De-identified RUG images were labeled by a trained reviewer as diagnostic (good quality) or non-diagnostic (poor quality), with classifications verified by a reconstructive urologist. The labeled dataset was then used to evaluate a Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT)-4o AI model for automated RUG quality assessment. Using advanced prompting strategies like multishot, negative, and chain-of-thought prompting, we developed an internal GPT-based AI tool to classify each RUG as diagnostic or non-diagnostic with reasoning. To assess performance, 75 randomly selected RUGs were analyzed under two conditions: 1) with advanced prompting and 2) without any prompting (unprompted baseline). RESULTS: Mean age at RUG was 52.52 ± 18.50 years. Based on reviewer assessment, 164/233 (70.4%) studies were diagnostic and 69/233 (29.6%) non-diagnostic. The prompted model achieved first-pass accuracy of 53/75 (70.7%) and improved to 61/75 (81.3%) after an unguided “try again” prompt ( Table 1). False positives occurred in 12/75 (16.0%) and false negatives in 10/75 (13.3%). In contrast, the unprompted model reached 33/75 (44.0%) accuracy with 8/75 (10.7%) false positives and 34/75 (45.3%) false negatives. Advanced prompting performed well in identifying urethral kinks but occasionally misclassified images with obscured urethral length due to x-ray vignetting. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that advanced prompting improves the model’s ability to assess the diagnostic quality of RUGs, primarily by reducing false negatives. Future refinements, like a mixture-of-experts approach where specialized GPT-based agents evaluate individual quality factors and report back to a main model, can enhance accuracy and reliability. | | | --- | | |

title: AMBIENT LISTENING TECHNOLOGY IN AN OUTPATIENT UROLOGY CLINIC: IMPACT ON PROVIDER SATISFACTION AND RETURN ON INVESTMENT METRICS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Ernest A. Morton, Christopher Holland, Bryan Blanchette, Prachi Chopde, Drew Marchione, Vikram M. Narayan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ambient listening technology (ALT) leverages large language models (LLMs) to transcribe and structure patient–provider conversations into clinical documentation. Several vendors now provide ALT solutions for health systems. By removing extraneous information, highlighting salient points, and reorganizing dialogue, ALT can generate complete and concise notes. This may enhance the patient–provider relationship by reducing the documentation burden and improving electronic medical record (EMR) usability. We evaluated the impact of ALT implementation in an outpatient academic urology practice, focusing on clinical productivity and provider EMR use. METHODS: ALT was deployed across our institution’s (Emory Healthcare, Atlanta, GA) outpatient clinics beginning September 2023, using services from a third-party vendor (Abridge AI, Inc.). Data were collected from the Epic Systems Signal dashboard to assess provider time in the EMR and monthly charges from September 2023 through October 2024. All urology providers were included, regardless of ALT adoption status. RESULTS: By October 2024, 20 of 36 eligible providers (56%) were classified as high-volume ALT users, defined as using ALT for at least 50% of clinic notes. These providers used ALT in 72% of encounters on average. Overall, 35/36 (97%) providers trialed ALT at least once. Compared with non-users, high-volume users demonstrated reductions of 3.97 hours/month in note-writing time and 7.70 hours/month in total EMR time. Billing analysis showed a modest increase in coding level (mean 0.10 higher per month) but a substantial difference in charges: high-volume ALT users generated an additional $191 per encounter, averaging over $48,000 in increased monthly charges per user. They also produced 189.85 more relative value units per month compared with non-users. Of 36 providers surveyed, 13 responded. Among respondents, 53% agreed or strongly agreed that ALT improved productivity, and 70% reported perceived improvements in provider wellness. CONCLUSIONS: Implementation of ALT in outpatient urology clinics was associated with decreased EMR documentation time, increased clinical productivity, and higher billing-related outputs. Provider-reported benefits further suggest ALT may enhance efficiency and wellness in academic practice.

title: MODERNIZATION OF A HISTORICAL PROSTATE CANCER REGISTRY USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: A TALE OF TWO LLMS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Surgical Technology & Simulation: Artificial Intelligence (IP04)
authors: Michael K. Wang, Peter Galatowitsch, Julian Diaz-Cabo, Jamie O’Byrne, Eric Li, Brian Linder, Eugene Kwon, Bradley Leibovich, Vidit Sharma, Matthew Gettman, Matthew Tollefson, Jeffrey Karnes, Stephen Boorjian, Abhinav Khanna
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Since 1986, the Mayo Clinic Prostate Cancer Registry has followed over 30,000 men who underwent radical prostatectomy. Historically, data abstraction was performed by nurse abstractors, a labor intensive process. Recent advances in LLMs may provide an opportunity to modernize data collection, reduce human abstraction burden, and improve registry efficiency. We report the results of LLM data abstraction for surgical pathology data in the Mayo Clinic Prostate Cancer Registry. METHODS: Original unstructured surgical pathology reports were obtained for patients undergoing surgery from 2018-2022. LLM prompts for 13 pathology variables were developed, each run independently through two independent LLMs (Google Gemini Flash 1.5 and 2.0), and refined until the two LLMs achieved a >90% concordance. Consensus and individual LLM outputs were then compared to historical registry data collected by a trained and experienced nurse-abstractor. Discrepancies were adjudicated by a team of humans to determine the ground truth ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191284.35857.1d.30#F1)). Accuracy was compared using Fischer’s exact test. RESULTS: A total of 3210 patients were included. The dataset was split into training (2022, n=404), internal validation (2021, n=710), and test subsets (2018-2020, n=2096). Median consensus LLM error rate was 0.09% (IQR 0.03-0.16%), as compared to median human error rate of 2.81% (IQR 1.83-3.17%; p<0.01, (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191284.35857.1d.30#F2)). Notably, each individual LLM had a three times higher error rate compared to consensus LLM (Gemini 1.5 0.27% (IQR 0.09–0.34%), Gemini 2.0 0.30% (IQR 0.17%-0.48%)). Total estimated time for human data abstraction for all 13 variables in the entire cohort was 294 hours, as compared to 9 hours for our LLM pipeline. CONCLUSIONS: LLM data abstraction employing a consensus vote across two LLM models consistently yielded higher accuracy than human or single LLM abstraction alone. A dual LLM architecture holds promise in improving data abstraction efficiency and reducing errors, and should be considered for integration into all prospectively maintained longitudinal clinical registries.

title: HIGHER CONUT (CONTROLLING FOR NUTRITIONAL STATUS) SCORES ARE ASSOCIATED WITH COMPLICATIONS AFTER RADICAL NEPHRECTOMY BUT NOT ONCOLOGIC OUTCOMES
session: Kidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP05)
authors: Michael K. Wang, Eric Li, Tae-Hee Kim, Chloe Shi, Maddy Dorr, Matthew Tollefson, Stephen Boorjian, Jeffrey Karnes, Bradley Leibovich, Abhinav Khanna, Vidit Sharma
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Controlling Nutritional Status (CONUT) scores assess the nutritional-immune status of patients using albumin, cholesterol, and lymphocyte. Prior studies of patients undergoing radical nephrectomy (RN) for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) found that patients with high CONUT scores have worse overall survival (OS), cancer specific survival (CSS), and progression free survival (PFS), though these studies lacked comprehensive risk adjustment in their models. Further, no studies have examined the CONUT’s relationship with RN complications. Here, we examine the CONUT’s association with oncologic outcomes and 90 day complications after RN. METHODS: We queried our prospectively maintained nephrectomy registry for patients undergoing RN for RCC with available CONUT data. Kaplan Meier curves and multivariable Cox regression were performed for OS, CSS, and PFS for patients with clear cell RCC who had Mayo PFS and CSS scores. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression evaluated CONUT’s association with 90 day any and high grade complications. RESULTS: Among 486 patients (median follow up 7.3 years), 167 patients (34%) had a CONUT score of ≥3 (immune-nutritional depleted). Patients with high CONUT scores had higher Mayo PFS scores compared to those with low CONUT scores (8.0 vs 6.0, p<0.001). On univariable analysis, CONUT scores ≥3 were associated with worse OS (HR 1.8), CSS (HR 2.7), and PFS (HR 1.6), p<0.05 ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191288.32814.7d.01#F1), Table 1). After adjusting for Mayo PFS and CSS scores, higher CONUT scores were not associated with worse OS, CSS, and PFS. For any and high 90 day complications, a CONUT score of ≥3 was associated with more any (OR 2.2) and high grade (OR 2.4) 90 day complications on univariable analysis. This was maintained on multivariable analysis for any 90 day complications (OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.1-3.1, p=0.03). CONCLUSIONS: While patients with high CONUT scores were more likely to have aggressive disease and experience complications after RN, they were not more likely to experience oncologic events after adjusting for Mayo PFS and CSS scores, suggesting that the prior literature demonstrating this effect may be suffering from incomplete risk adjustment.

title: RADIOMIC TUMOR CONTACT SURFACE AREA PREDICTS POST-OPERATIVE COMPLICATIONS AND LOCAL RECURRENCE OUTCOMES FOR PATIENTS UNDERGOING MULTIFOCAL PARTIAL NEPHRECTOMY
session: Kidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP05)
authors: Eric V. Li, Michael K. Wang, Madeline Dorr, Greg J. Michalak, Cole J. Cook, Timothy L. Kline, Stephen A. Boorjian, Bradley C. Leibovich, Abhinav Khanna, Vidit Sharma
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The management of multifocal synchronous renal masses with partial nephrectomy (PNx) is a rare scenario, with sparse data to inform complication and local recurrence risk. We previously developed an Artificial Intelligence (AI) tumor segmentation model that distinguishes kidney tumor from normal renal parenchyma and quantifies several radiomics measurements. Herein, we evaluate clinical and radiomic variables associated with post-operative complications and oncologic outcomes for patients receiving multifocal PNx. METHODS: Patients who underwent planned multifocal unilateral or bilateral PNx between 2000-2024 were queried from a prospective nephrectomy registry. Our AI algorithm used contrast-enhanced CT imaging to measure tumor contact surface area (CSA), endophycity, and centricity ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191288.32814.7d.02#F1)). CSA was quantified cumulatively and by CSA of largest renal mass. Multivariable logistic and Cox regression analysis evaluated factors associated with 30-day post-operative complications and local recurrence free survival (LRFS), respectively. RESULTS: Of 155 patients, 66 underwent bilateral PNx and 89 underwent multifocal unilateral PNx with median 2 tumors removed (IQR 2-3) and median tumor size 2.6 cm (IQR 1.6-3.9). After adjusting for number of tumors and unilateral vs bilateral PNx, cumulative CSA was associated with 30-day complications (OR 1.07 per 1000 voxels, 95% CI 1.02-1.12, p=0.007, (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191288.32814.7d.02#F2)). After adjusting for unilateral vs bilateral PNx, both cumulative CSA (HR 1.07, 95% CI 1.03-1.11, p=0.001) and CSA of largest renal mass (HR 1.08, 95% CI 1.02-1.15, p=0.007) were associated with LRFS with median follow up 9.5 years (IQR 6.3-12.8). Endophycity and centricity were not associated with complications or LRFS. CONCLUSIONS: Cumulative CSA was associated with 30 day post-operative complications, and both cumulative CSA and CSA of largest mass were associated with local recurrence. This AI tool may have potential applications for patient selection, surgical planning, and risk stratification for post-operative complications and oncologic outcomes among patients planned for complex PNx.

title: ROBOTIC PARTIAL NEPHRECTOMY DEFINES A NEW STANDARD FOR SAFETY AND RECOVERY: A COMPREHENSIVE ANALYSIS OF 1,441 CASES ACROSS THREE SURGICAL APPROACHES
session: Kidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP05)
authors: Husny Nasim Mahmud, Laufer Menachem, Dorit E. Zilberman, Barak Rosenzweig, Orith Portnoy, Dotan Zohar
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To comprehensively compare clinical outcomes and define the safest, most effective standard of care, we analyzed 1,441 partial nephrectomies (PN) performed via robotic (RAPN), laparoscopic (LPN), and open (OPN) approaches at a single tertiary center. METHODS: A retrospective review of 1,441 consecutive PNs (544 RAPN, 349 LPN, 548 OPN) from 2000-2025 was performed. We analyzed general recovery metrics (Length of Stay \[LOS\], same-day discharge, transfusion rates) across the entire cohort. To ensure a valid comparison and neutralize historical selection bias, a primary complication analysis (Urine Leak \[UL\] and Renal Artery Pseudoaneurysm \[RAP\]) was performed on a core, modern sub-cohort of 785 patients (2012-2022). This sub-cohort was confirmed to have no significant difference in baseline RENAL nephrometry scores across all three arms (p=0.55). Multivariable logisticregression (MVA) was used to identify independent predictors for major complications. RESULTS: Analysis of the full cohort (N=1,441) demonstrated clear advantages for RAPN in recovery metrics. The median length of stay for RAPN was 2.9 days, markedly shorter than 7.24 for LPN and 8.04 for OPN (p<0.001), with 25% of RAPN patients eligible for same-day discharge (vs. <5% for LPN/OPN). Blood transfusion rates were also significantly lower for RAPN (3.2%) compared to LPN (10.6%) and OPN (14.4%) (p<0.001). In the modern, complexity-matched cohort (N=785), RAPN demonstrated superior safety. The overall Urine Leak (UL) incidence was 2.4%, but the rate for RAPN was substantially lower at 0.75% (vs. 3.7% OPN, 4.91% LPN; p=0.03). Similarly, the Pseudoaneurysm (RAP) incidence was 2.1% overall, with RAPN again showing the lowest rate at 1.0% (vs. 3.4% OPN, 3.3% LPN; p=0.04). On Multivariable Analysis (MVA), the surgical approach emerged as a powerful, independent predictor for both complications. Compared to RAPN as the reference, both LPN (OR 6.8, p=0.007) and OPN (OR 5.2, p=0.014) independently predicted higher UL rates. The LPN/OPN approaches, along with operative time, were also the only independent predictors for RAP (p<0.05). While median operative time was longer for RAPN (169 min) vs. LPN (122 min), one-year eGFR preservation was similar across all groups (p=0.53). CONCLUSIONS: In this large-scale comparative analysis, RAPN demonstrates superior perioperative recovery (shorter LOS, fewer transfusions) and superior safety (significantly lower rates of UL and RAP). After rigorously adjusting for confounders in a modern cohort with comparable tumor complexity, RAPN remains an independent protective factor against major complications. These data reinforce RAPN as the standard of care for nephron-sparing surgery.

title: NEPHROMETRY SCORES AS PREDICTORS OF TRIFECTA, PENTAFECTA, AND POSTOPERATIVE RENAL FUNCTION FOLLOWING ROBOTIC PARTIAL NEPHRECTOMY
session: Kidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP05)
authors: Nicolas A. Soputro, Abdulrahman Al-Bayati, Lin Wang, Karim Daher, Samarpit Rai, Salim K. Younis, Rui M. Bernardino, Riccardo Autorino, Christopher J. Weight, Jihad Kaouk
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the utility of tumor size, RENAL, PADUA, and SPARE Nephrometry Scores (NSs) in predicting the likelihood of achieving trifecta and pentafecta outcomes, as well as the risk of postoperative acute kidney injury (AKI) and kidney disease progression at 12 months following RAPN. METHODS: Retrospective review was performed on IRB-approved, prospectively maintained database to identify 1787 consecutive cases of primary, non-metastatic small renal masses who underwent RAPN between 2011 and 2024. All pre-operative radiological images were reviewed by a single resident physician, who characterized all tumors based on the NSs. Trifecta outcome was defined as cases with warm ischemia time <25 minutes, negative surgical margin, and absence of complications. Pentafecta included the trifecta outcomes with the addition of >90% renal function preservation and absence of kidney disease progression at 12 months. Logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were completed to determine the predictive ability for the tumor size and each of the NS. RESULTS: Trifecta and pentafecta were achieved in 52.7% and 22.2%, respectively. All three NSs were established as statistically significant predictors of trifecta, pentafecta, and postoperative AKI, with all demonstrating comparable yet limited predictive performance (AUC 0.573–0.645). Notably, tumor diameter (AUC 0.649–0.665) was shown to outperform the NSs in predicting the likelihood of achieving trifecta and pentafecta, as well as the risk of AKI. None of the scoring systems were identified as independent predictors of kidney disease progression at 12 months. CONCLUSIONS: Although lower RENAL, PADUA, and SPARE NSs were significantly associated with achieving surgical success and reduced risk of AKI, their predictive performance was modest and consistently outperformed by a simpler and more objective measure, such as tumor diameter. Future studies remain necessary to re-evaluate the broader clinical utility of NS in predicting surgical and functional outcomes, in addition to its original purpose as standardized tools for the anatomical characterization of renal tumors.

title: MACHINE LEARNING–BASED PREDICTIVE MODEL FOR TRIFECTA ACHIEVEMENT IN ROBOT-ASSISTED PARTIAL NEPHRECTOMY
session: Kidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP05)
authors: Boran Aksakal, Tunkut S. Doganca, Nicolas A. Soputro, Ilter Tufek, Ali R. Kural
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To develop and internally validate a machine learning-based nomogram for predicting trifecta achievement in patients undergoing robot-assisted partial nephrectomy (RAPN). METHODS: This retrospective single-center study included patients who underwent RAPN between 2011 and 2025 at a tertiary academic hospital. Trifecta was defined as the presence of negative surgical margins, warm ischemia time ≤25 minutes, and absence of perioperative complications in the same patient. Preoperative and intraoperative variables were selected based on the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) logistic regression. Selected predictors were incorporated into a multivariable logistic regression model to construct a nomogram. Decision curve analysis (DCA) and area under the curve (AUC) were calculated to evaluate the model performance. RESULTS: Among 426 patients included, trifecta was achieved in 87.7%. Of the 15 perioperative variables initially evaluated with LASSO, five were retained as significant predictors. In multivariable logistic regression, trifecta failure was independently associated with longer operative time (OR 1.014, 95% CI 1.008–1.021; p<0.001), higher blood loss (OR 1.002, 95% CI 1.001–1.003; p<0.001), entry into the collecting system (OR 4.151, 95% CI 2.237–7.702; p<0.001), and perioperative blood transfusion (OR 24.226, 95% CI 7.385–79.477; p<0.001). On the other hand, posterior tumor location was in favor of trifecta achievement (OR 0.435, 95% CI 0.206–0.919; p=0.029). The model demonstrated good discrimination (AUC 0.792, 95% CI 0.738–0.845), acceptable calibration (bootstrap-corrected slope 0.91, intercept 0.13), and DCA indicated higher net benefit than treat-all/none strategies for thresholds of 0.10–0.75. CONCLUSIONS: This LASSO-guided, clinically interpretable nomogram predicts trifecta achievement after RAPN with strong internal validity. Given the association between trifecta status and favorable long-term renal and oncologic outcomes, this tool can support perioperative risk assessment, surgical planning, and patient counseling.

title: PERSONALIZED PREDICTORS OF RENAL RECOVERY AFTER PARTIAL NEPHRECTOMY
session: Kidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP05)
authors: Lucia Salerno, Pietro Scilipoti, Francesco Trevisani, Bettiga Arianna, Mattia Longoni, Alessandro Bertini, Chiara Re, Giacomo Musso, Ithaar Derweesh, Francesco Cei, Giuseppe Rosiello, Federico Belladelli, Ciro Piccolo, Natasha Disabato, Gaetano Ficarra, Aurora Campugiani, Martina Montesano, Roberto Bertini, Andrea Salonia, Francesco Montorsi, Alessandro Larcher, Umberto Capitanio
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Renal function recovery after partial nephrectomy (PN) results from a multifaceted interplay of modifiable and non-modifiable factors such as amount of spared parenchyma, ischemia duration, patient comorbidities, renal anatomy, and surgical approach. We aimed to delineate the non-linear relationship between ischemia time and renal function recovery, and to identify subgroups more vulnerable to ischemic injury. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 491 patients who underwent PN at a tertiary referral center. Renal function was assessed preoperatively and at 12 months after surgery, and the relative variation in estimated glomerular filtration rate (ΔeGFR%) was computed. Locally weighted scatterplot smoothing (LOWESS) curves were applied to explore non-linear trends between ischemia time and postoperative ΔeGFR across clinical and surgical subgroups. RESULTS: Median age was 61 years (IQR: 52–69), and 68% were male. Hypertension (48%) and diabetes mellitus (10%) were the most frequent comorbidities, while 2.2% of patients had a solitary kidney. Median ischemia time was 17 minutes (IQR 13–22). At 1 year, the median ΔeGFR was –6.5% (IQR –16 to -0.15). As illustrated in the LOWESS analyses, patients with hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, or a solitary kidney exhibited a steep decline in renal function beyond 20 minutes of ischemia, whereas those without such comorbidities showed a flatter curve, suggesting greater tolerance to ischemic insult. Tumour location and surgical approach had negligible influence: both subgroups displayed a stable ΔeGFR% for ischemia durations below 20 minutes, followed by a steeper decline thereafter, particularly among patients with non-inferior pole tumours or those undergoing open surgery. CONCLUSIONS: Renal function recovery after PN is shaped by a nuanced interaction between ischemia time, surgical technique, and patient comorbidities. Recognizing the unique sensitivity of hypertensive, dyslipidemic, and solitary-kidney patients can guide personalized surgical planning and postoperative monitoring. Integrating patient-specific risk profiles with surgical metrics may optimize functional preservation and long-term renal outcomes.

title: SHORT- AND LONG-TERM FUNCTIONAL OUTCOMES IN A LARGE COHORT OF PN PATIENTS MANAGED WITH PROLONGED ISCHEMIA
session: Kidney Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP05)
authors: Carlos Munoz-Lopez, Eran Maina, Nityam Rathi, Kieran Lewis, Jayant Siva, Akira Kazama, Angelica Bartholomew, Rebecca Campbell, Jihad Kaouk, Samuel Hawood, Jianbo Li, Steven C. Campbell
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Previous studies suggest irreversible renal functional decline begins after 25-30 minutes of clamp time during partial nephrectomy (PN), and hypothermia is protective.
