abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Single-use flexible ureteroscopy (fURS) devices often involve tradeoffs between scope diameter, optical quality, and mechanical durability. The HugeMed HU30M is a novel single-use, 6.3-French flexible ureteroscope. Its smaller diameter may reduce trauma and the need for ureteral pre-stenting but has a potentially greater risk of mechanical breakdown. We aim to evaluate the performance outcomes of this device for primary and complex fURS. METHODS: Consecutive fURS cases using the HU30M were analyzed from 4/2025 to 10/2025. Selection criteria for use were either 1) primary fURS without pre-stenting or dilation, or 2) complex cases with increased risk of mechanical device damage (>15 mm total, >10 mm inferior pole stone burden, or bilateral fURS). Surgeons rated device performance after each case on a 1-5 Likert scale for optical quality (5=similar to Karl Storz FLEX-XC), maneuverability (5=able to perform complete renoscopy), and mechanical durability (5=no visible or functional breakdown). Up and down maximum deflection was assessed before and after use. RESULTS: We performed 59 fURS cases using 62 HU30M devices on 75 renal units. Of the 59 cases, 43 (73%) were primary fURS, 27 (46%) for large stone burden, and 16 (27%) were bilateral. Primary fURS was achieved in all cases. In 58 (98%) cases, surgeons reported that the HU30M would acceptably replace their default fURS device (Boston Scientific LithoVue in 66% cases, FLEX-XC in 32% cases). Average performance ratings of the HU30M were 4.0 (SD 0) for optical quality, 4.9 (SD 0.5) for maneuverability, and 4.7 (SD 1.0) for durability (Figure). There were no significant differences in surgeon ratings based on indication for use (all p>0.05). Complete 270° up and down deflection was observed before use for all 62 scopes. After use, up and down deflection was 270° for 60 (97%) and 56 (90%) scopes, respectively. Of the 7 devices with deflection loss, all cases involved large stone burden requiring prolonged deflection. Of these, 2 were critical breakdowns causing case interruption and device replacement. CONCLUSIONS: A novel 6.3-French single-use flexible ureteroscope was successfully deployed for both primary and complex fURS in 100% of cases with a critical breakdown incidence of only 3%. Based on performance outcomes comparable to reusable digital devices, surgeons reported that the HU30M could replace their default fURS device in 98% of cases.

title: COMPARISON BETWEEN URETERORENOSCOPY WITH LITHOTRIPSY ALONE VERSUS COMBINATION WITH HYDROGEL FOR KIDNEY STONE REMOVAL: INTERIM RESULTS
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Thomas Amiel, Matthias Jahnen, Florian Kirchhoff, Michael Straub
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Residual fragments after flexible ureteroscopy (fURS) remain a relevant issue in endourological stone management. Even small clinically insignificant residual fragments can serve as a nidus for recurrence, making the achievement of zero residual fragments a key therapeutic goal. The MediNiK® hydrogel method was developed to enhance fragment retrieval and improve the stone-free rate (SFR). METHODS: This single-center, comparative study reports the interim results of an ongoing investigation including patients undergoing fURS for renal calculi. Patients were divided into two groups: URS alone (Group 1, n=30) and URS + MediNiK® (Group 2, n=30). All procedures were performed using disposable flexible ureteroscopes and a thulium fiber laser (TFL) for lithotripsy. A standard ureteral access sheath (UAS) without suction was used in all cases. In the MediNiK® group, a biocompatible hydrogel was applied intrarenally after laser fragmentation to encapsulate and facilitate retrieval of residual stone fragments. ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191292.44613.d7.08#F1) illustrates the application of the hydrogel methode). Postoperative non-contrast CT was performed in all patients to assess the SFR, graded as A (complete clearance), B (≤ 2 mm fragments), or C (2.1–4 mm fragments). Demographic and operative data, SFR, need for second-look URS, and perioperative complications (Clavien-Dindo) were analyzed. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups (median age 57 vs 59 years; BMI 25.5 vs 26 kg/m2). Median stone size was 11 mm in the URS group and 12 mm in the MediNiK® group (stone volume 402 vs 625 mm3). A higher proportion of patients in the MediNiK® group achieved complete clearance (Grade A=94%) compared to URS alone (66%). Including Grade B fragments, total clearance reached 97% vs 69.5%. The second-look URS rate was lower with MediNiK® (3% vs 13.5%). Operative time was slightly longer (87 vs 76 min), while readmissions and complications were comparable. CONCLUSIONS: These interim findings suggest that the MediNiK® hydrogel method may improve stone-free outcomes and reduce the need for secondary procedures, without increasing perioperative morbidity. Further data from the ongoing study will clarify its long-term safety and efficacy in achieving zero residual fragments.

title: ARE SGLT2 INHIBITORS A NEW RISK FACTOR FOR URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS AFTER URETEROSCOPY IN DIABETIC PATIENTS?
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Nicola Fazaa, Reut Shashar, Etan Eigner, Melissa Atallah, Ameer Nsair, Michael Mullerad, Gilad Amiel, Oleg Goldin, Yoel Soloveichik, Yoav Stabholz, Omer Sadeh
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary tract infection (UTI) following ureteroscopy (URS) is a frequent complication, particularly among diabetic patients. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), increasingly used for diabetes and heart failure, induce glucosuria that may predispose to infection. We aimed to determine whether SGLT2i use increases the risk of postoperative UTI after URS. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study of diabetic patients who underwent URS between 2018 and 2024 at a tertiary medical center. Patients were included if SGLT2i was used prior to surgery. The primary endpoint was postoperative UTI or fever >37.8°C within 30 days. Multivariate logistic regression and propensity score matching were performed to identify independent predictors. RESULTS: Among 1,220 diabetic patients, 213 (17.5%) were treated with SGLT2i. Post-URS UTI occurred more often in SGLT2i users (21.1% vs 12.1%, p<0.001). On univariate analysis, SGLT2i use was associated with higher UTI risk (odds ratio \[OR\] 2.36). A positive preoperative urine culture was the strongest predictor of postoperative UTI across both groups (OR 4.05). Propensity-matched analysis confirmed the independent link between SGLT2i use and postoperative UTI (OR 2.18). ICU admission was rare but twice as common among SGLT2i users (0.02% vs 0.01%). CONCLUSIONS: SGLT2i therapy independently increases the risk of postoperative UTI in diabetic patients undergoing URS, particularly among those with preoperative bacteriuria. Awareness of this risk may support more tailored perioperative infection prevention strategies or, temporarily placing the patient on alternative medications.

title: REASSESSING AMERICAN UROLOGICAL ASSOCIATION GUIDELINES: IMPACT OF A 72-HOUR ANTIBIOTIC PROPHYLAXIS REGIMEN FOLLOWING URETEROSCOPY
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Justine Lam, Ajay Macherla, Keerthana Danasekaran, Jason Fairbourn, Rajat Jain
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Current AUA Guidelines recommend single-dose perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis (ABX PPX) only for uncomplicated, non-infected ureteroscopy (URS) for urolithiasis. However, clinical observation suggests higher rates of post-stent removal UTI than current literature estimates of 3%. We instituted a novel prophylactic ABX course for 72 hours at the time of stent removal at home. This study aimed to (1) determine the post-stent removal UTI rate and (2) evaluate whether a 72-hour ABX PPX regimen reduces infection risk compared to single-dose perioperative ABX. METHODS: We retrospectively studied adults undergoing ureteral stent removal via string following URS by one urologist from 2/1/2022 to 2/29/2024 (STUDY00010773). The NO-ABX cohort received standard single-dose perioperative ABX, while the 72HR-ABX cohort received a novel 72-hour regimen starting 24 hours before removal. Subjects were identified via CPT code. Exclusion criteria included positive preop urine culture, infection-related stones, history of recurrent UTI, or PPX ABX given immediately postoperatively for any reason. The primary endpoint was UTI within 7 days post-stent removal. Fisher’s exact test was used to compare infection rates between cohorts (p<0.05). RESULTS: Of 669 subjects screened, 171 met inclusion criteria for uncomplicated, non-infected URS (NO-ABX: n=145; 72HR-ABX: n=26). There were no differences in demographics, BMI or Diabetes prevalence between groups ( Table 1). Post-stent removal UTI occurred in 15.2% (22/145) of patients in the NO-ABX group and 0% (0/26) in the 72HR-ABX group. Fisher’s exact test demonstrated a statistically significant difference between groups (p=0.028; odds ratio=0, 95% CI 0.00–0.94). CONCLUSIONS: At our institution, post-stent removal UTI rates were lower among patients who received prolonged antibiotic prophylaxis. These preliminary findings suggest a possible benefit of extended antibiotic duration in reducing post-stent infection risk and may help inform evidence-based post–stent removal antibiotic stewardship. | | | --- | | |

title: STRATIFICATION AND MANAGEMENT OF PERSISTENTLY POSITIVE URINE CULTURES IN UROLOGICAL STONE SURGERY
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Joshua Harvey, Ang Li, Ilya Sobol
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Standard practice for urological stone surgery involves a single preoperative urine culture with antibiotic treatment if positive. Our enhanced protocol includes re-culturing after treatment. This study evaluates whether this approach is justified by examining the prevalence of persistent positive cultures despite antibiotics, identifying risk factors for persistence, and determining if our protocol improves outcomes or could be optimized through patient risk stratification. METHODS: A retrospective review analyzed 224 patients with positive preoperative urine cultures who underwent urological stone surgery under a single surgeon. All patients received antibiotic treatment with re-culture prior to intervention. Persistent positivity was defined as any growth >10K on subsequent urine culture. Risk factors were assessed using univariate and multivariate logistic regression. Secondary outcomes included immediate and 30-day postoperative sepsis rates. The study findings informed the development of a risk scoring tool to identify patients most likely to benefit from this targeted management approach. RESULTS: Despite antibiotic therapy, 28.6% of patients demonstrated persistent positive cultures. Notably, 65.6% of persistent cases showed an organism shift between initial and re-culture. Significant risk factors in univariate analysis included history of urosepsis (OR=5.01, p=0.0011), multi-drug resistant organisms (MDRO) (OR=4.38, p=0.0029), recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) (OR=3.07, p=0.0003), and presence of indwelling devices (OR=2.51, p=0.0028). Multivariate analysis revealed that history of UTIs (OR=2.47) and presence of indwelling devices (OR=1.81) were the only independent predictors that remained significant. The persistent positive and the treated groups demonstrated similar sepsis within 24 hours of surgery (3.13% vs 2.50%) and after 30 days (4.69% vs 3.13%). CONCLUSIONS: The frequent shift in organisms among persistently positive cultures underscores the limited reliability in single preoperative culture to guide therapy. Notably, our stratified management approach maintained comparable sepsis rates despite treating a high-risk cohort, suggesting that risk-based stratification with tailored interventions can effectively mitigate infectious complications in urological stone patients. Further prospective validation of our risk-stratification tool is warranted to confirm the efficacy and to optimize resource utilization across diverse practices settings.

title: INTRARENAL ANTIBIOTIC IRRIGATION DURING PCNL REDUCES POSTOPERATIVE INFECTIONS AND ELIMINATES SEPSIS IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS: A MATCHED COHORT STUDY
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Pengbo Jiang, Kriselle Madamba, Bruce M. Gao, Jonathan Badin-Castro, Harel C. Sims, Seyed Amiryaghoub M. Lavasani, Elliott Freudenburg, Gustavo Gryzinski, Aymon Ali, Jaime Landman, Roshan M. Patel, Ralph V. Clayman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Despite use of oral and parenteral antibiotics, percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) may still be complicated by a host of infectious complications: urinary tract infections (UTIs), systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), and urosepsis. Patients with diabetes mellitus, history of recurrent UTIs, positive preoperative urine cultures, or indwelling urinary devices are especially at risk. We evaluated the impact of intraoperative intrarenal antibiotic augmented irrigation on postoperative infection rates in this high-risk population. METHODS: A retrospective matched cohort study was conducted using a prospectively maintained PCNL database (2020-2024) of over 600 patients. Fifty high-risk cases receiving genitourinary (GU) irrigant (40 mg neomycin base, 200,000 units polymyxin B sulfate per 3 L saline) were matched 1:1 to saline controls ( Table 1). The primary endpoint was 30-day symptomatic UTI; secondary endpoints included SIRS, sepsis, infection-related readmission, infection-related prolonged hospital stay, and emergency department (ED) visits due to UTI. Multivariable logistic regression was performed. RESULTS: At < 30 days postoperative, the fifty patients receiving GU irrigant had fewer postoperative symptomatic UTI events than the control group (6% vs. 34%, p=0.001). Secondary outcomes were almost all more sanguine among the GU irrigant patients: • SIRS criteria: 16% vs. 48% (p=0.001) • Sepsis: 0% vs. 16% (p=0.006) • Infection-related readmission: 6% vs 16% (p=0.200) • Infection related prolonged length of stay: 0% vs. 20% (p=0.001) • ED visits for UTI: 6% vs 16% (p=0.200) In the adjusted complete case model (n=99), GU irrigant remained independently protective against UTI within 30 days (adjusted OR 0.11; 95% CI 0.03–0.44; p=0.002). CONCLUSIONS: Among high-risk PCNL patients, intrarenal neomycin/polymyxin-B irrigation was associated with significantly fewer infectious complications. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: DOES DOPPLER ULTRASOUND REDUCE PERIOPERATIVE BLEEDING COMPARED TO B-MODE ULTRASOUND IN ULTRASOUND-GUIDED PERCUTANEOUS NEPHROLITHOTOMY? A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Luiz G. S. Gimenez, Carlos A. Battagello, Alexandre G. Silva, Fabio C. Vicentini, Alexandre Danilovic, Giovanni S. Marchini, Fabio Torricelli, Artur Brito, Rodrigo Perrella, Eduardo Mazzucchi, William C. Nahas
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) remains the gold standard treatment for large renal stones and can be safely guided by ultrasound (US). However, it is associated with significant perioperative bleeding, with transfusion rates ranging from 5-15% in contemporary series. We aimed to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate if the use of Doppler US can reduce bleeding during PCNL compared to B-mode US. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, searching Medline, Embase, Scopus, Cochrane Library and Web of Science from inception to September,27 2025, for comparative studies evaluating PCNL guided by B-mode versus Doppler US. Study risk of bias was assessed using the ROBINS-I and RoB-2 ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191292.44613.d7.15#F1)). Primary endpoint was blood transfusion rate (BTR). The protocol was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251147765). Statistical analysis was performed using Review Manager 5.4.1 (Cochrane Collaboration). RESULTS: Of 3821 studies, 7 met the inclusion criteria comprising 1,993 patients were included, with 49.6% receiving Doppler US PCNL. There was no difference in age, sex and body mass index (BMI) between groups. The mean stone size was 28.9 mm vs 28.5 mm (p=0.55) for Doppler US and B-mode US, respectively. Doppler US significantly reduced BTR (OR 0.24, 95% CI 0.12–0.48, p<0.0001, (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191292.44613.d7.15#F2)) and hemoglobin decrease (MD -5.01 g/L; 95% CI -8.22, -1.81; p=0.002). Subgroup analyses showed consistent BTR reduction with Doppler US in both randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-RCTs ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191292.44613.d7.15#F2)), with similar effect sizes regardless of study design. Furthermore, there was no statistically significant difference in operative time (MD -1.0 min; 95% CI -3.04, 1.04; p=0.34). CONCLUSIONS: In conclusion, Doppler US PCNL has a lower BTR and lower hemoglobin decrease than B-Mode US PCNL with no increased operative time. Therefore, Doppler US PCNL may be a viable strategy to reduce perioperative bleeding in selected patients.

title: CLINICAL PREDICTORS OF EFFECTIVE RENAL ANGIOEMBOLIZATION AFTER PCNL PROCEDURES
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Razvan Cosmin Petca, Razvan Ionut Popescu, Ionut Nedelcu, Razvan Alexandru Danau, Youssef Salaheddin, Viorel Jinga
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) is the standard first-line treatment for large renal calculi. Although instrument miniaturization and technical improvements have been achieved, postoperative bleeding remains a significant complication. This study aims to identify predictive factors associated with the success or failure of selective angioembolization following PCNL. METHODS: This prospective study enrolled 51 patients who underwent selective angioembolization for post-PCNL hemorrhage between January 2020 and January 2025. Demographic, clinical, and procedural variables were documented, including age, BMI, stone size and location, puncture site, number of access tracts, comorbidities, and preoperative use of anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy. Hematologic parameters, such as pre- and postoperative hemoglobin levels, hemoglobin drop, and transfusion requirements, were evaluated. Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics. The study received institutional ethics committee approval and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. RESULTS: Among the 51 patients included, 13 experienced primary angioembolization failure, stratifying the cohort into two groups: Group I, with successful embolization, and Group II, with recurrent or persistent bleeding requiring reintervention (procedural failure). Patient characteristics, including BMI and comorbidities, showed significant differences only for ischemic heart disease (18.42% in Group I vs. 53.84% in Group II, p=0.034) and preoperative anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy (21.05% vs. 69.23%). Although stone size did not correlate with outcome, higher failure rates were observed in patients with multiple stones and staghorn calculi (p=0.019). One of the most relevant predictive factors was the number of punctures and dilation tracts created during PCNL, with multiple tracts present in 46.15% of Group II (p=0.006). Intraoperative transfusion did not influence success; however, lower postoperative day 1 hemoglobin levels and increased postoperative transfusion requirements were strong predictors of embolization failure (p=0.0012 and p=0.0009, respectively). Variability in embolic agents used may also have contributed to outcome differences. CONCLUSIONS: Angioembolization is the most effective method for postoperative hemorrhage following PCNL. Medical history, procedural complexity, and postoperative monitoring are critical factors in the prompt detection of embolization failure.

title: URETEROSCOPY IN PATIENTS RECEIVING SYSTEMIC ANTICOAGULANTS: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS OF SAFETY, EFFICACY, AND PERI-OPERATIVE MANAGEMENT
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Donnacha Hogan, Stefanie M. Croghan, Bhaskar Somani, Olivier Traxer, Andreas Skolarikos, Rob Geraghty, Lazaros Tzelves, Niall F. Davis
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the safety and efficacy of ureteroscopy (URS) in patients receiving systemic anticoagulant (AC) therapy, including vitamin K antagonists and direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), and to compare outcomes with non-AC controls. The PICO framework was used to formulate the research question: In adults undergoing URS for stone disease, does continuation, interruption, or bridging of AC compared with non-anticoagulated or interrupted therapy influence peri-operative bleeding, thromboembolic events, and stone-free rates (SFR)? METHODS: A systematic review of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus identified studies reporting URS outcomes in patients on AC. The review adhered to PRISMA standards and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251154766). Data were extracted for peri-operative management strategy, bleeding and thromboembolic events, transfusion requirements, and SFR. Antiplatelet-only cohorts were excluded. Quantitative results were pooled, and comparative data were summarised where available. Risk of bias for non-randomised studies was evaluated independently by two reviewers using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS). RESULTS: Eleven studies were included published between 1998 and 2024 with a total of 770 AC patients and 10,099 controls. The pooled rate of clinically significant bleeding ranged from 3% to 15%, with the lowest rates when AC was withheld and the highest when continued through surgery. In comparison, non-AC control groups demonstrated bleeding rates of 1–3% (OR 5.67 (95% CI 1.48-21.7, p=0.011). Transfusion requirements were < 1% overall, and no study reported mortality. Thromboembolic complications were extremely rare—only one deep-vein thrombosis (0.1 %) was identified after temporary interruption. Stone-free rates averaged 88–94%, comparable to non-anticoagulated cohorts. Registry data indicated a modest rise in hospitalisation (4.3% vs 3.2%, p=0.02) among anticoagulated patients but no excess emergency visits (10.1% vs 9.4%, p=0.42) or re-operations. Across studies, outcomes were most favourable when AC was paused pre-operatively without bridging, and when contemporary holmium:YAG laser lithotripsy and controlled irrigation techniques were employed. On NOS assessment, seven studies were of moderate and four of low quality, with primary risks arising from retrospective design and variable bleeding definitions. CONCLUSIONS: URS can be performed safely in patients on AC therapy, though continuation during the peri-operative period increases bleeding risk compared with both interrupted therapy and non-AC controls. Temporary cessation without bridging minimises haemorrhagic and thromboembolic complications while maintaining high SFR. Current evidence supports an individualised, guideline-based approach to peri-operative AC, but larger prospective studies are needed to define optimal management across specific drug classes.

title: POST-OPERATIVE TRAJECTORIES OF PAIN INTERFERENCE AND INTENSITY AFTER URETEROSCOPY FOR NEPHROLITHIASIS IN YOUTH: A PKIDS STUDY
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Yuntong Sun, Jonathan S. Ellison, Brian Augelli, Jing Bi-Karchin, Jing Huang, Gregory E. Tasian, David I. Chu
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Youth with nephrolithiasis frequently undergo ureteroscopy to treat their stones, yet post-operative recovery courses are variable. We assessed the trajectories of pain interference and pain intensity following ureteroscopy and examined clinical predictors of trajectory group membership, hypothesizing that stone size would be significantly associated with trajectory group. METHODS: Participants aged 8-21 years from 31 centers in North America who underwent ureteroscopy between 2020 and 2023 as part of a prospective observational study were included. Outcomes of post-operative pain interference and pain intensity were evaluated at baseline and at weeks 1, 3, and 6 using Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System questionnaires. Group-based trajectory models were used to identify distinct recovery patterns. Classification trees identified predictors of trajectory group membership. RESULTS: Among 823 participants undergoing ureteroscopy (median age 15.6 years; 65% female), 667 had stents which were removed a median of 5 days post-surgery. Four distinct trajectory groups were identified for each outcome (see Figure). The groups included: High Stable Pain, Gradual Improvement, Rapid Rise and Recovery, and Early Pain with Recovery. For pain interference, the four groups were equally divided among the cohort. For pain intensity, nearly a third of the cohort were in each of the High Stable Pain and Early Pain with Recovery groups. For both pain interference and intensity, significant clinical predictors of group membership were age, baseline pain interference/intensity scores, baseline anxiety, and largest stone size. CONCLUSIONS: We identified distinct recovery trajectories for pain intereference and intensity after ureteroscopy with variable prevalences in our cohort. We also found significant clinical factors associated with group membership for pain interference and intensity. These findings highlight the heterogeneity in recovery and underscore the need for personalized pain management strategies.

title: WIDESPREAD PAIN AT NON-UROLOGIC PAIN SITES IS ASSOCIATED WITH GREATER STENT-ASSOCIATED SYMPTOMS AFTER URETEROSCOPY
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Maximilian Jentzsch, Navya Gunaje, Sarah Holt, Nayan Shah, H. Henry Lai, Charles Scales, Hussein Al-Khalidi, Naim Maalouf, Ziya Kirkali, Alana Desai, Jonathan Harper
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Most patients undergoing ureteroscopy (URS) for urinary stones receive ureteral stents, which can result in pain and urinary symptoms. Presence of pre-operative chronic pain conditions is associated with worse symptoms. Here we evaluated the association between pre-op pain at non-urologic body sites and post-op stent-associated symptoms (SAS). METHODS: The STENTS cohort is the largest multi-center prospective cohort study evaluating SAS to date. Participants completed a body map marking pain locations pre-operatively. We divided participants into 4 pain location categories: no pain sites, only expected urological pain sites (e. g., left flank pain for left stones), 1-2 non-urologic sites, 3+ non-urologic sites. ANOVA models were used to compare SAS across baseline, post-operative day (POD) 1-9, and 30 days post stent removal. SAS measures of interest included PROMIS pain intensity, pain interference, and urinary symptoms assessed by LURN SI-10. For POD 1-9, repeated measures mixed effects models with clinical site as random effect were used to evaluate the association of pre-operative pain distribution category on each SAS. Covariates included age, sex, depression, chronic pain, and baseline pain intensity. RESULTS: 462 participants were included in the analysis with a mean age of 50 years (SD 17) and 47% females. At baseline, 46% did not report any pain sites, 19% had pain at expected urologic sites only, 22% at 1-2 non-urologic sites, and 13% at 3+ non-urologic sites. SAS varied between baseline pain distribution categories at multiple time points, particularly for the outcomes of pain intensity and pain interference (Fig). Multivariable mixed effects models demonstrated higher SAS with 3+ pain sites at baseline (Table). CONCLUSIONS: Pain at multiple, non-urologic body sites is associated with higher SAS, particularly pain intensity and pain interference. These findings highlight an association between pre-operative complex chronic pain at surgically unrelated sites and post-op SAS.

title: OUTCOMES OF IMMEDIATE VERSUS DELAYED ENDOSCOPIC TREATMENT FOR PREGNANCY-ASSOCIATED UROLITHIASIS: PROSPECTIVE CONTROLLED TRIAL
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Pavel Y. Nizin, Sergey Vladislavovich Kotov, Roman Alexandrovich Perov
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Symptomatic upper urinary tract obstruction during pregnancy often requires urgent intervention. While ureteral stents may bridge patients to postpartum care, definitive ureteroscopy during gestation is increasingly feasible. Evidence comparing these approaches remains limited. METHODS: Single-center randomized prospective trial, 2018–2022; n=119. Patients were assigned to primary antepartum ureteroscopy or serial stenting with postpartum ureteroscopy. Outcomes included stone-free rate, operative parameters, and stent-associated morbidity. RESULTS: Stone-free rates were comparable (96.6% vs 96.7%). Antepartum ureteroscopy demonstrated significantly shorter operative time (median 60 vs 97 minutes, p=0.002). Stent-related morbidity was substantially higher in the delayed-treatment cohort, including encrustation, migration, and reflux pyelonephritis (63% incidence, p<0.001). Overall Clavien-Dindo complication profiles were similar. CONCLUSIONS: Primary ureteroscopy during pregnancy is safe, effective, and minimizes cumulative stent-related morbidity. When feasible, definitive treatment during gestation may optimize clinical outcomes and reduce infectious and mechanical stent complications.

title: THE RATE OF REPEAT SURGICAL INTERVENTION AMONG BRUSHITE STONE FORMERS AT A SINGLE INSTITUTION
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Kyle Berst, Cheney Hurley, Timothy Chow, Melissa Swee, Chad Tracy, Ryan Steinberg
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Brushite (calcium monohydrogen phosphate) stone formers are notorious for requiring high rates of surgical intervention for large stone burdens and stone recurrence even after removal. The actual rate and timing of repeat surgeries has not been reported. We sought to assess the rates of repeat surgical therapy among brushite stone formers at our institution. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, IRB-approved, single-institution review of all patients with any amount of brushite on stone analysis from January 2014 to June 2024. Patient demographics, medical histories, procedures, lab results, medications, and 24-hour urine chemistries were collected. All percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) procedures were done in prone split leg position. Ureteroscopy (URS) procedures were performed without the assistance of a suction (sheath or scope). Repeat surgery was defined as a procedure on the same side as the initial surgery >=3 months after the index surgery (or either side in the case of bilateral). Descriptive statistics were generated and Chai squared analysis was used to assess differences in rates of repeat surgery (p<0.05). RESULTS: We identified 119 brushite stone formers (40% male) with a median age of 37 years (IQR 27-53). Median follow-up was 3.9 years (IQR 0.7-8.5). 61 (51.3%) patients reported prior stone removal at another institution. 98 patients (82%) underwent initial stone surgery at our institution: 36 PCNL, 61 URS, and 1 SWL. 40 (41%) patients required a repeat surgery at a median of 22.8 months after the index procedure. After initial PCNL, 12 patients (33%) required 3 PCNL and 9 URS; after initial URS, 28 (46%) patients required 24 URS, and 4 PCNL. There was no difference in repeat surgery rates based on the index procedure (p=0.22). CONCLUSIONS: In light of aggressive initial stone removal, brushite stone formers have high rates (41%) of repeat surgery, with over half occurring within 2 years of the index case. URS was the most utilized salvage procedure. This data provides discrete data for patient counseling on the risk of recurrent surgery and underscores the importance of aggressive stone prevention.

title: ASSESSING STONE VOLUME IS VALUABLE FOR SURGICAL PLANNING IN PEDIATRIC UROLITHIASIS
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Rostyslav Nakonechnyy, Andrii Nakonechnyi, Dmytro Shevchuk, Taras Vivcharivskyi
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Pediatric urolithiasis requires a meticulous approach to selecting the optimal treatment strategy. While guideline-based treatment selection utilizes maximum stone diameter, this linear measurement inadequately reflects the true volume. Volume may more accurately determine stone burden in pediatric patients. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of treatment methods for pediatric urolithiasis based on stone volume and to determine its prognostic value on stone-free rate (SFR). METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted on patients aged 1 to 17 years treated for single urinary tract stones at a single center January 2023 to June 2025. Stone volume was calculated using data from non-contrast computed tomography using 3D Slicer software \[Panthier F, et al. World J Urol. 2021\]. Ultrasound-guided Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) was used as the first-line treatment for all patients, followed by semirigid or flexible ureteroscopy (URS) for those requiring subsequent intervention. Patients were divided into three volumetric groups: Group I 100 mm3, Group II 101-200 mm3, and Group III 201-370 mm3. The maximum linear size of the stones did not exceed 20 mm. Treatment efficacy was assessed by the SFR 3 months post-procedure on ultrasound. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS, using Kruskal-Wallis tests to identify group differences, and Spearman's correlation analysis for relationships between variables. RESULTS: The study included 72 patients, 39 (54.2%) boys and 33 (45.8%) girls. There were 37 patients in group I (51.4%), 21 in group II (29.2%), and 14 in group III (19.4%). The overall SFR was 93.1%. Group I achieved a 100% SFR, Group II achieved 90.5%, and Group III achieved 78.6%. Re-interventions (URS) were required for 10 (47.6%) patients in Group II and 8 (57.1%) patients in Group III. We identified a positive correlation between stone volume and the number of repeat surgical interventions (ρ=0.489, p<0.001), as well as between patient age and stone volume (ρ=0.243, p=0.04). The Kruskal-Wallis test showed a statistically highly significant difference in treatment outcomes (single intervention, re-intervention, residual fragments) depending on stone volume across the three groups (H=14.738, p=0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Stone volume is a key predictor of treatment success for pediatric urolithiasis and directly correlates with the need for re-interventions. For stones with a volume up to 100 mm3, ESWL as a first-line treatment demonstrates maximum efficacy. With an increase in stone volume, the likelihood of requiring additional procedures to achieve a stone-free status significantly increases.

title: PREDICTORS OF FAILURE AFTER ENDOSCOPIC MANAGEMENT OF IATROGENIC URETERAL STRICTURES
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Stefano Moretto, Olivier Traxer, Alberto Saita, Bhaskar K. Somani, Evangelos Liatsikos, Esteban Emiliani, Andreas Skolarikos, Leye Ajayi, Amelia Pietropaolo, Steeve Doizi, Vincent De Coninck, Panagiotis Kallidonis, Tarik Emre Sener, Eugenio Ventimiglia, Daniel Pérez-Fentes, Pietro Acquati, Frederic Panthier, Luca Villa, Iulia Andras, Mauro Ragonese, Anil Shrestha, Senol Tonyali, Lazaros Tzelves, Nicolò Maria Buffi
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Iatrogenic ureteral strictures (IUS) represent a challenging complication of endourological stone treatment, often requiring complex reinterventions with high failure rates. This study aimed to identify risk factors associated with treatment failure after endoscopic management of IUS. METHODS: This retrospective multicenter study included adult patients who underwent endoscopic treatment for IUS following prior ureteroscopic management of urolithiasis. Failure was defined as the need or reintervention after primary IUS treatment. Potential predictors were grouped into: baseline patient characteristics, features of the initial stone procedure, and stricture and treatment-related characteristics. Univariate logistic regression was performed to identify variables associated with failure(p<0.15). Statistically and clinically relevant variables were included in a multivariate Firth logistic regression model to adjust for small-sample bias. Effect sizes were reported as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI); p<0.05 was considered statistically significant. RESULTS: Of 101 patients, 63 (62%) had successful outcomes and 38 (38%) required reintervention. Descriptive characteristics are summarized in Table 1. Treatment approaches included balloon dilation alone (n=43), laser endoureterotomy alone (n=31),combined laser + balloon (n=21), and ureteral dilators (n=6). At univariate analysis, only three variables met criteria for multivariate modeling: residual stone fragments at the stricture site, proximal IUS location, and the use of balloon dilation alone (compared to combined laser and balloon treatment).In the multivariate model, residual fragments (OR 7.41; 95% CI 2.25–26.3; p=0.001) and balloon dilation alone (OR 3.70; 95% CI 1.10–13.9; p=0.041) were independently associated with failure. Proximal IUS location showed a trend toward significance (OR2.50; 95% CI 0.90–7.10; p=0.074). CONCLUSIONS: Endoscopic treatment of IUS results in a considerable failure rate (38%). The presence of residual fragments from previous lithotripsy and the exclusive use of balloon dilation, when compared to combined laser and balloon approaches, emerged as independent predictors of recurrence. Proximal IUS may also carry a higher risk of failure. Prospective studies are warranted to refine risk stratification and treatment strategies. | | | --- | | |

title: POSTOPERATIVE COMPLICATIONS FOLLOWING FLEXIBLE URETEROSCOPY. AN INSTITUTIONAL SERIES OF 1,389 CASES
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Eugenio Alessandria, Andrea Bosio, Glauco Bertello, Claudia Gozzo, Luca Micai, Eugenia Vercelli, Alessandro Bisconti, Paolo Gontero
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to evaluate the incidence of postoperative complications (PCs) following flexible ureteroscopy (RIRS) for stone treatment in an unselected Institutional series. METHODS: We analyzed data from our prospectively maintained RIRS for stone treatment institutional database (June 2014 to December 2024). The primary outcome was the overall incidence of PCs, classified according to the modified Clavien-Dindo system for RIRS, within 90 days from the intervention. The secondary outcome was the identification of factors associated with PCs. Descriptive statistics were performed to assess associations between clinical variables and PCs. RESULTS: A total of 1,389 RIRS procedures were included. Most patients were male (61%, 847/1,389), with a mean age of 56 ± 14 years and a mean BMI of 26 ± 5. The mean stone size was 11.9 ± 5.5 mm. Almost half of the patients had multiple stones (42.7%, 593/1,389). Preoperative urine culture was positive in 18.3% (254/1,389), and a preoperative stent was present in 38.3% (532/1,389). The mean operative time was 69.4 ± 30 minutes. Overall, PCs occurred in 11.5% of cases (160/1,389). Minor complications (Clavien grade I–II, mainly fever and urinary tract infection) occurred in 6.7% (93/1,389), while Clavien grade III complications occurred in 4.0% (56/1,389), mainly due to urgent stent placement (for stent dislodgment or renal colic). Clavien grade IVb complications (urosepsis) were rare, occurring in 0.6% (8/1,389). Three patients (0.2%) died within 90 days after the procedure (Clavien grade V). One of these patients died due to septic shock, while two patients died of myocardial infarction after being discharged. When comparing patients with and without complications, the rate of PCs was significantly higher in patients with stones >10 mm (16.9% vs. 11.3%, p=0.01) and was associated with a lower stone-free rate (62.5% vs. 72.7%, p=0.02). Other characteristics — such as sex, diabetes mellitus, ASA score, positive preoperative urine culture, and multiple stones — did not reach statistical significance when comparing patients with and without complications. CONCLUSIONS: In this large Institutional cohort, postoperative complications following RIRS occurred in about 1 in 10 patients, with the majority being minor and self-limiting. Patients with postoperative complications had significantly larger stone size and worse SFR. These data underline the importance of proper patient selection and preoperative risk assessment.

title: CONSTRUCTION AND VALIDATION OF AN OMICS-GUIDED DRUG-COATED URETERAL STENT FOR TARGETED THERAPY OF URETERAL STRICTURE
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Quan Liao, Shiyong Qi
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ureteral stricture represents a challenging urological condition that often leads to hydronephrosis and renal function impairment. While drug-eluting stents have been proposed as a solution, existing approaches often rely on empiric selection of antiproliferative agents, lacking precision tailored to the specific molecular signature of ureteral strictures. This strategy may pose risks of off-target effects. Consequently, there is a pressing need to develop a novel, targeted therapeutic strategy grounded in a deep understanding of the disease's molecular mechanisms. METHODS: RNA sequencing was performed on stricture tissue samples from 5 patients with ureteral strictures and 5 normal tissues. The LINCS L1000 database was queried with the disease-specific gene signature to identify potential therapeutic compounds. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis confirmed the critical role of the JAK-STAT pathway. A novel dual-layer coaxial stent was developed. The core therapeutic layer was fabricated by conjugating the identified small-molecule drug, thalidomide, to form a stable PLGA-TK-PEI matrix. The outer layer was coated with pDNA encoding STAT3-specific shRNA via classical adsorption. A rabbit model of ureteral stricture was employed for in vivo validation. Hydronephrosis was monitored by ultrasound, and harvested ureteral tissues were analyzed by histology and RNA-seq to evaluate fibrotic progression and pathway modulation. RESULTS: Transcriptomic analysis revealed significant activation of the JAK-STAT signaling pathway. LINCS database screening thalidomide as a candidate capable of reversing the disease signature. Given STAT3's pivotal role, we supplemented the approach with STAT3 shRNA for targeted inhibition. Histological assessments demonstrated that the stent exhibited a reduction in ureteral fibrosis. RNA-seq analysis of rabbit tissues confirmed the therapeutic mechanism, which was consistent with the initial findings from human patient samples. CONCLUSIONS: In conclusion, this study successfully demonstrates a translational "omics-to-therapy" pipeline. By integrating patient-derived transcriptomic data with bioinformatic drug discovery, we rationally developed a novel coaxial stent for the synergistic delivery of thalidomide and STAT3 shRNA. This targeted strategy effectively mitigated ureteral fibrosis and hydronephrosis in preclinical models by specifically inhibiting the JAK-STAT pathway, offering a promising and precise therapeutic approach for preventing ureteral stricture recurrence.

title: ASSOCIATION OF STENT-ASSOCIATED SYMPTOMS WITH ACCEPTABILITY OF FUTURE STENT PLACEMENT: RESULTS FROM STENTS
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Nayan Shah, Navya Gunaje, Sarah Holt, Maximilian Jentzsch, Alana Desai, Naim Maalouf, Charles Scales, H. Henry Lai, Hussein Al-Khalidi, Ziya Kirkali, Jonathan Harper
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The STudy to Enhance uNderstanding of sTent associated Symptoms sought to better understand stent associated symptoms (SAS) in patients who had ureteral stents placed after ureteroscopy (URS) for urinary stones. This study analyzes the association between postoperative pain intensity, pain interference, and urinary symptoms with patient acceptability of future stent placement. METHODS: This prospective, observational cohort study included those undergoing URS with stent placement for stone treatment across 4 centers. Participants completed SAS surveys on post-op day 1 and 3, and at time of stent removal they completed the ureteral stent symptom questionnaire which included a “global question” assessing their attitude towards future stent placement. Multivariable ordinal logistic regression including patient characteristics and SAS was used to examine the association of post-op pain intensity, pain interference and urinary symptoms with patient acceptability of future stent placement. RESULTS: 424 participants (mean age 49.5 ± 16.9 years, 46% female) were included. Global question scores are shown in the Figure. Greater pain intensity, pain interference, and urinary symptoms were all associated with decreased acceptability of future stent placement ( Table). Younger age was associated with decreased acceptability in all models. When urinary symptoms were adjusted for, female sex was associated with decreased acceptability of future stent. CONCLUSIONS: In patients with ureteral stent placement after URS for urinary stone disease, greater pain intensity, pain interference and urinary symptoms during the immediate post-operative period were all associated with decreased acceptability of future stent placement.

title: PIGTAIL SUTURE STENT VS CONVENTIONAL DOUBLE J STENT – A RANDOMIZED, SINGLE-BLIND, PROSPECTIVE CLINICAL TRIAL
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Luigi A. Lorenzetti, Fabio C. Vicentini, Giovanni S. Marchini, Alexandre Danilovic, Fabio M. Torricelli, Carlos A. Batagello, Artur H. Brito, Rodrigo Perrella, William C. Nahas, Eduardo Mazzucchi
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Double J (DJ) stents are a valuable tool after ureteroscopy. However, they are associated with significant morbidity, symptoms and decline in quality-of-life (QoL). Despite advancements in design and materials, these issues remain. We aim to evaluate QoL and safety of a Pigtail Suture Stent (PSS). METHODS: Patients undergoing flexible ureteroscopy for kidney stones under 2 cm were randomized to receive either a Pigtail Suture Stent (PSS) (7Fr x 16 cm) (JFill - Rocamed, Monaco) or a conventional DJ stent (6Fr x 26 cm). 148 patients will be included in the randomization (N). Randomization occurs by the end of the procedure when the stent is to be placed and surgeons are blinded until then. Patients remain blind throughout the study. QoL is assessed using the Ureteral Stent Symptom Questionnaire (USSQ) domains for pain, urinary symptoms, and total score at 4 time points: one day before surgery; on the first postoperative day (PO); before stent removal (between 7- 10th PO) and 14 days after stent removal. The USSQ is applied by a blinded nurse. Efficacy and safety were evaluated with an ultrasound at 4-7th PO, serum creatinine and urine culture after stent removal and a non-contraste computer tomography (NCCT) scan on the 30th PO. RESULTS: 56 patients completed the study so far and were analyzed. Demographic data including BMI, age, gender, stone characteristics, and surgical parameters were comparable between groups. On the PSS group, two patients (6,5%) experienced proximal stent migration requiring an additional ureteroscopy for retrieval (Clavien 3b), while the DJ group had no such complication (0%). Distal migration occurred in one PSS group patient (3.2%), with no incidents in the DJ group. Emergency room visits due to stent-related symptoms happened in 12.9% of the PSS group and 16.0% of the DJ group, with no cases of sepsis or catheter exchanges in either group. No statistical difference in the USSQ scores was observed in the four time points. Nevertheless, baseline symptoms were higher in the PSS group, indicating a less substantial increase in post-stent placement symptoms compared to the DJ group (Table 1). CONCLUSIONS: The PSS seems to be a safe and effective device. Its complication rate is consistent with the literature. It maintained an effective drainage of the upper urinary tract without requiring conversion to a standard DJ Stent. While no statistical difference in QoL was observed, further analyses may demonstrate differences, with baseline QoL tending to similar with randomization or with scores analysis adjusted for baseline.

title: URETERAL STENTING FOR ACUTE OBSTRUCTION. IS URETEROSCOPIC STONE REMOVAL ALWAYS NEEDED?
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Ibragim Mamaev, Gadzhimurad Saipulaev, Sergei Kotov
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Spontaneous passage of ureteral stones with an internal stent is a well-studied phenomenon today. Although the standard tactics for patients with small ureteral stones that do not tend to pass with a stent is surgical. The fact of passive dilation of the stented ureter is beyond doubt, due to which spontaneous passage of the stone can be expected after stent removal. The aim of the study is to assess the probability of spontaneous passage of a ureteral stone up to 4 mm in size after removal of an internal ureteral stent. METHODS: The study included 74 patients who underwent emergency drainage of the urinary tract with an internal stent. Exclusion criteria: urinary tract abnormalities, diabetes mellitus, multi-drug resistant bacteria, and sepsis preceding drainage. Native CT was performed in all patients within 2-3 weeks after stent placement. In patients who had solitary ureteral stone up to 4 mm in size cystoscopy was performed and the ureteral stent was removed. Patients were instructed to monitor the possible stone passage. Medical expulsive therapy was not prescribed. RESULTS: The average duration of drainage was 20.3 (7-34) days. Solitary ureteral stone ≤ 4 mm was diagnosed in 30 patients. Stone location: upper third - 8 (26.6%) patients, middle third - 3 (10%), lower third - 19 (63.3%). Most of patients (26) noted spontaneous stone passage. In 23 patients (76.6%) it was observed within 24 hours after stent removal, in 3 (10%) patients - within 48 hours. None of this patients had renal colic, 4 (15.4%) of them noted episode of urinary frequency. In 4 patients (13.4%) no stone passage was observed. All of them had renal colic. These patients underwent ureterolithotripsy. Most of them (3 of 4 patients) had a stone in the upper third of the ureter. The duration of observation before lithotripsy was 72 hours. Repeated emergency drainage was not required in any case. CONCLUSIONS: Spontaneous asymptomatic passage of ureteral stones was observed in 86,7 % (26 of 30) patients within 48 hours after stent removal. Preliminary results of our study demonstrate the option of avoiding surgical intervention in selected patients with distal ureteral stones ≤4 mm.

title: DO ENDOUROLOGISTS EXPERIENCE WORK-RELATED OCCUPATIONAL INJURY? A GLOBAL SURVEY OF SURGEON HEALTH AND SAFETY
session: Stone Disease: Surgical Therapy (Including ESWL) I (IP06)
authors: Jose Agudelo Bodington, Ali A. Antar, Margaret A. Knoedler, Michael E. Korostensky, Daniel Gralnek, Linda Shuang, Emily Serrell, Stephen Y. Nakada
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Endourology requires prolonged lead use, static posture, repetitive wrist/shoulder motion, and fluoroscopy exposure. Musculoskeletal injury and radiation exposure could contribute to burnout and early retirement across surgical fields, yet data specific to endourologists are limited. We sought to characterize global occupational injury burden, surgeon perception of risk, and use of mitigation strategies. METHODS: A 16-item anonymous survey was distributed globally to the Society of Endourology members (8/24–10/31/23). The primary outcome was surgeon concern regarding occupational hazard. Secondary outcomes were: presence of orthopedic, visual, neurologic, or auditory symptoms; whether surgeons attributed these to their career; and use of protective strategies. ANOVA, chi-square, and Spearman correlation were performed. RESULTS: 196 endourologists responded (global distribution: North America 49%, Asia 16%, Europe 16%; university practice 59%). Major concerns (“some or very concerned”) included: radiation exposure (79%), orthopedic injury (77%), and neurologic issues (56%). Despite near-universal lead apron and thyroid shield use (95% and 85%), adoption of other protective equipment was low: lead glasses (26%), lead gloves (5%), and hearing protection (7%). Orthopedic sequelae were reported by 45%; 91% believed these symptoms were caused or likely caused by their career. Visual complaints were common (63%), yet most did not attribute them to occupational exposure, suggesting risk under-recognition. Concerns did not differ by age, case volume, or years in practice. CONCLUSIONS: This first global survey demonstrates that nearly half of endourologists already experience orthopedic injury, and most are concerned about radiation exposure, yet adoption of preventive measures remains low. Perception of risk does not correlate with experience, indicating an opportunity for targeted ergonomic and radiation-safety interventions. Surgeon health is a patient-safety issue; specialty-wide changes in ergonomics training and OR workflow are needed to improve surgeon career longevity.

title: THE MILES TRIAL: PROSPECTIVE RANDOMIZED TRIAL OF SAFETY AND EFFICACY OF MINIMALLY INVASIVE VERSUS STANDARD LASER ENUCLEATION OF THE PROSTATE
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Vladislav Petov, Camilla Azilgareeva, Andrey Bazarkin, Alim Dymov, Yulia Li, Temirlan Karakotov, Roman Sukhanov, Leonid Chuvalov, Mikhail Enikeev, Magomed Gazimiev, Leonid Rapoport, Felipe Figueiredo
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Endoscopic enucleation of the prostate (EEP) is standard treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). A smaller resectoscope in minimally invasive laser enucleation (MiLEP) may reduce stress urinary incontinence (SUI) and urethral stricture compared with standard EEP. The aim of the study is to compare the efficacy and safety of MiLEP versus standard EEP. METHODS: This is an ongoing prospective randomized trial with IRB approval. Men with BPH (30–150 сс), severe LUTS (IPSS ≥20) and Qmax ≤15 ml/s are being randomized (1:1) to MiLEP (22 Ch) or standard EEP (26 Ch). Both arms use a thulium fiber laser with pulse modulation (FiberLase U-MAX; 2 J × 40 Hz). Enucleation is performed using the en bloc technique. SUI is defined as urine leakage requiring ≥1 pad/day. The primary endpoint is SUI after catheter removal; secondary endpoints are perioperative, functional outcomes and complication rate. RESULTS: 77 patients underwent MiLEP and 78 – standard EEP. Baseline characteristics were comparable, including age (p=0.34), prostate volume (p=0.52), IPSS (p=0.14), and Qmax (p=0.36). Operative time (p=0.26) as well as enucleation and morcellation durations did not differ (p=0.17 and 0.14); enucleation and morcellation efficiencies were comparable (p=0.4 and 0.06). Tissue weight was 34 \[25–42\] vs 35 \[27–42\] g (p=0.19). Median catheterization was 1 day (p=0.6) and length of stay 3 days (p=0.7) in both arms. Functional outcomes improved significantly in both groups, with no significant intergroup differences ( Table 1). Minor (Clavien–Dindo I–II) complications were comparable: 21.7% in MiLEP vs 28.0% in standard EEP (p=0.74). SUI after catheter removal was less frequent with MiLEP (6.5% vs 29.5%; p=0.04); at 3 months, continence was 100% after MiLEP vs 87.2% after standard EEP (p=0.23). Urethral stricture at 3 months was 1.3% vs 6.4% (p=0.06). Bladder neck contracture was 5.1% after standard EEP (p=0.15). CONCLUSIONS: MiLEP provides comparable perioperative and functional outcomes to standard EEP with a significant reduction in early SUI. Longer follow-up and expanded enrollment are required to prove the observed trends in urethral complications. | | | --- | | |

title: MULTICENTER 24-MONTH OUTCOMES OF RIVERMARK FLOSTENT: THE RAPID-II STUDY
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Peter Chin, Javier Sanchez, Peter Gilling, Flavio Ordones, Wikus Vermeulen, Joseph Ischia, Dean Elterman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Rivermark FloStent™ is a catheter-free device therapy for BPH that integrates with a standard flexible cystoscope for outpatient delivery. The RAPID-II clinical trial is an ongoing ethics-approved multi-center single-arm early feasibility intended to evaluate the safety and efficacy profile of the FloStent System. METHODS: The initial study cohort is fully enrolled and currently in the follow-up phase. Study implantations were performed in an outpatient setting at four centers in Australia, New Zealand, and Mexico. Various types of reusable (Olympus, Storz) and single-use (Ambu) cystoscopes were used for implantation. RESULTS: 55 subjects (age 64.5 ± 9.3 yr) with mean prostatic volume 47.9 ± 14.6 ml were implanted. Implantation success rate was 100%. No patient required a post-procedure catheter. Baseline IPSS score was 23.4 ± 4.7, and was reduced by 11.6 ± 7.3 and 9.9 ± 7.2 points at the 12-month and 24-month timepoints, respectively . Notably, a clinically significant IPSS reduction of 8.3 ± 7.1 was seen at the 2-week timepoint. QOL scores followed the favorable trend of IPSS scores, being reduced by 3.0 ± 1.4 and 2.6 ± 1.2 points at the 12-month and 24-month timepoints. At 12 months, Qmax increase was 2.1 ± 0.6 ml/sec and PVR reduction was 18.6 ± 18.9 ml. Measures of sexual function (IIEF-5 and MSHQ-EjD) remained stable throughout the follow-up period. Current device tolerability rate is 89.1% (number of patients who have the device removed due to symptomatic dissatisfaction, divided by the total number implanted). All device retrievals and exchanges have been performed with standard cystoscopic equipment, accessories, and techniques. The most common adverse events have been transient irritative LUTS. CONCLUSIONS: The Rivermark FloStent™ has demonstrated good clinical performance with rapid recovery and a durable treatment effect in a multi-center early feasibility study. Placement and retrieval with standard urological equipment has been demonstrated. Ongoing evaluation of clinical performance is underway, in the form of a randomized double-blinded sham-controlled pivotal clinical study.

title: MEDICAL TREATMENT OF BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA AFTER BLADDER OUTLET PROCEDURES
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Mahir Maruf, Andrew Gabrielson, Chloe Michel, Naren Nimmagadda
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: One benefit of outlet procedures for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is discontinuing medical therapy for obstructive lower urinary tract symptoms. However, medical therapy may be necessary again if there is significant regrowth of BPH tissue. We aimed to determine the rate of starting alpha blockers or 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (5ARi) after Laser enucleation of the prostate (LEP), Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), Photoselective vaporization of the prostate (PVP), Prostatic Urethral Lift (PUL), Transurethral water vapor thermal therapy (WVTT), and Robotic Waterjet Treatment (Aquablation). METHODS: The TriNetX Research Database was queried for men 35 years or older with the diagnosis of BPH (ICD 10: N40) without neurogenic bladder (ICD 10: N31) who underwent any of the following procedures between 2005 and 2025: LEP (CPT 52649), TURP (CPT 52601), PVP (CPT 52648), PUL (CPT 52441), WVTT (CPT 53854), or Aquablation (CPT 0421T). We investigated the initiation of alpha-blockers or 5-ARIs at least 3 months after the index outlet procedure. Primary outcomes were rate and time-to-first new alpha-blocker or 5-ARI between procedure groups. Kaplan Meier method with log-rank test was used to assess differences in time-to-first alpha-blocker prescription after index outlet procedure using LEP as a reference. RESULTS: At the index procedure, 14,269 underwent LEP, 50,644 TURP, 23,702 PVP, 7,372 PUL, 3,653 WVTT, and 4,897 Aquablation. The median time to new alpha-blocker therapy was not reached in the LEP group, 7.1 years in the TURP group, 7.9 years in the PVP group, 3.7 years in the PUL group, 3.4 years in the WVTT group, and not reached in the Aquablation group ( Figure). The 5-year probabilities of new alpha-blocker therapy in the LEP, TURP, PVP, PUL, WVTT and Aquablation groups were 28%, 43%, 40%, 58%, 57%, and 27% respectively ( Table). CONCLUSIONS: Patients who had LEP had a significantly lower rate of starting alpha-blockers after surgery compared to TURP, PVP, PUL, and WVTT. However, these rates were similar to Aquablation.

title: DOWNSTREAM EFFECTS: THE RATE OF POST-PROCEDURAL URETHRAL STRICTURE RATE AFTER AQUABLATION IS HIGHER THAN PREVIOUSLY REPORTED
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Jessica J. Pryor, Kelley J. Zhao, Connor J. McPartland, David S. Han, Samuel J. Ivan, Jay Simhan, Steven Sterious
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prior reports describe a 5% rate of urethral stricture (US) after Aquablation®, most commonly affecting the fossa navicularis. We observed US rates higher than previously described, and sought to further categorize presentation, surveillance, and management of these patients. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed a prospectively maintained database of patients undergoing Aquablation® from February 2019 to September 2025. Patients were assessed at 6-weeks, 3-months, and annually thereafter. The primary outcome was US, which was diagnosed on office cystoscopy, performed for new-onset or worsening LUTS – and confirmed on fluoroscopic imaging. Secondary outcomes included time to US diagnosis, postoperative IPSS, and perioperative factors previously associated with US. Univariable analysis was used to compare stricture and non-stricture cohorts. RESULTS: Across 193 patients with median follow-up 9.6 months (range 1-78.6 months), the post-procedural US rate was 8.3% (16/193) with 68.8% (11/16), 12.5% (2/16), and 12.5% (2/16) affecting the fossa navicularis, penile urethra, and bulbar urethra, respectively. Mean stricture length was 2 cm (range 0.5-6.0 cm), and 69% of patients underwent substitution urethroplasty for definitive repair. No patients had a prior history of US or radiation. The median time from Aquablation® to stricture diagnosis was 3.5 months (range 1-20 months). Stricture patients had a greater 3-month post-operative IPSS (median 12.5, IQR 8 - 18.25) compared to the non-stricture cohort (median 7.0, IQR 4-12, p<0.01). Stricture patients had statistically significantly longer traction time (21.0 vs 19.0 hours, p<0.01) and indwelling catheter duration (3.5 vs 2.0 days, p<0.01) than non–stricture patients. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, 8.3% of Aquablation® patients developed US, higher than prior reports. US was associated with longer traction duration and indwelling catheter duration. With longer follow up, time to diagnosis ranged from 1-20 months, suggesting surveillance over time is necessary. IPSS may aid in surveillance for postoperative US, but a high index of suspicion remains necessary. Multi-institutional investigations are needed to validate the US rate following this increasingly popular bladder outlet procedure. | | | --- | | |

title: PERIOPERATIVE AND TRIFECTA OUTCOMES OF SINGLE PORT TRANSVESICAL ROBOTIC SIMPLE PROSTATECTOMY: A REPORT FROM THE SINGLE PORT ADVANCED RESEARCH CONSORTIUM
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Nicolas A. Soputro, Jacob O'Hara, Anastasia Mavridis, Jacob Hershenhouse, Shada Sinclair, Claudia Ramirez Marcano, Graham Kupsaw, Ruben Sauer Calvo, Jewel Bamby, Mehr Nasir-Moin, Sean Horan, Kennedy E. Okhawere, Gabriela Nieto-Blanco, Sarah Duncan, Abdulrahman Al-Bayati, Rui M. Bernardino, Ruben A. Olivares, Mohamed Eltemamy, Kshitij Hemal, Srinivas Vourganti, Zeyad R. Schwen, Ketan K. Badani, Andrew Wagner, Peter Chang, Mutahar Ahmed, Michael D. Stifelman, Simone Crivellaro, Jullet Han
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To report the perioperative and functional outcomes of Single Port (SP) Transvesical Robotic Simple Prostatectomy (RASP). METHODS: A retrospective review was completed on the prospectively maintained, IRB-approved database of the SP Advanced Research Consortium (SPARC) to identify 503 patients who underwent SP-RASP. Only procedures performed with the Transvesical approach were included. Baseline clinicodemographic, perioperative, and postoperative variables were collected. Trifecta was defined as the absence of postoperative complications, urinary continence, and maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax) >12 ml/s at 3 months. RESULTS: A total of 492 patients were included, with a median age of 70.6 years (IQR 65 – 76), BMI of 27.4 kg/m2 (IQR 24.8 – 30.4), prostate volume of 124 ml (IQR 96 – 169), and 42.7% having a history of previous abdominal surgery. All procedures were completed successfully, with a median operative time of 178 minutes (IQR 144 – 220) and with a median estimated blood loss of 100 ml (IQR 50 – 150). Postoperatively, 96.5% did not require continuous bladder irrigation, 67.4% were discharged home the same day, and 85.7% experienced no postoperative complications. The median Foley catheter duration was 6 days (IQR 4 – 8). At 3 months, 92.5% were continent, with a median IPSS reduction of 78.3% (IQR 47.6 – 88.1) and Qmax improvements of 75.1% (IQR 35.7 – 327.9), corresponding to an overall trifecta rate of 82.4%. CONCLUSIONS: Transvesical SP-RASP is a safe and effective minimally invasive treatment option for large-gland benign prostatic hyperplasia, featuring high rates of outpatient surgery, low morbidity, minimal risk of transient urinary incontinence, and excellent early functional outcomes.

title: REAL-WORLD OUTCOMES OF AQUABLATION FOR BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA: A COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF THE INTERNATIONAL COLLABORATIVE AQUABLATION RESEARCH UROLOGY SOCIETY (ICARUS) DATABASE, WATER AND WATER-II TRIALS
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Nick Lee, Adel Arezki, David Bouhadana, Abdulla Al Ameeri, Jeffrey Sioufi, Chakraborty Anindyo, Shawn Marhamati, Tiago Rodrigues, Brian Helfand, Mana Almuhaideb, Rakan Al Haidey, Juan Justo Quintas, Alexander Glaser, Hazem Elmansy, Kevin C. Zorn
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The WATER and WATER-II clinical trials of Aquablation demonstrated effectiveness for treatment of lower urinary tract symptoms secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) in men with prostate volumes (PV) 30-80 and 80-150 ml, respectively. In this study, we compare real-world Aquablation outcomes of men with similar PVs to results from WATER/WATER-II. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 1,946 consecutive men from the International Collaborative Aquablation Research Urology Society (ICARUS) database between 2018 and 2024 with PV≤150 ml who underwent Aquablation at one of four international centers. Baseline characteristics, functional outcomes and complications were compared to data from WATER/WATER-II using ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis tests. RESULTS: From the ICARUS database, 1,069 men (PV≤80 ml) were compared to 116 men (WATER), and 877 men (PV 80-150 ml) were compared to 101 men (WATER-II). As expected, there were slight differences in baseline characteristic between cohorts. Quality of Life and International Prostate Symptom Scores (IPSS) were slightly higher at some timepoints in the real-world (E. g. IPSS at 3-months: ICARUS-I 9.9±6.9 vs. WATER 7.0±5.7, p<0.001). Anejaculation rates, Qmax flow rates, and post-void residuals at 3 months were consistent across cohorts. Transfusion rates were significantly lower in the real-world large prostate dataset (ICARUS-II 1.3% vs. WATER-II 5.9%, p=0.01). CONCLUSIONS: Real-world outcomes of Aquablation are broadly comparable to those observed in the pivotal WATER/WATER-II trials. These findings support its generalizability and sustained effectiveness beyond the rigorous selection criteria of WATER/WATER-II, validating its role as a viable treatment for BPH in routine clinical practice. | | | --- | | |

title: REINTERVENTION RATES AND PATTERNS OF REOPERATION FOLLOWING SURGICAL MANAGEMENT OF BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Sahil H. Patel, Alka Tomar, Qiuchen Li, Smita De
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: There is currently a wide variety of surgical treatments available for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) that differ in invasiveness and durability. This study evaluates reintervention rates across frequently performed BPH procedures and identifies patterns of reoperative management for recurrent BPH. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using TriNetX, a multi-institutional network of deidentified electronic health records (January 2010 – October 2025). Male patients undergoing initial BPH surgery and subsequent reoperation were identified via CPT codes for the following procedures: simple prostatectomy (open, laparoscopic/robotic), transurethral resection of prostate (TURP), laser enucleation of the prostate (LEP), laser prostate vaporization (PVP), robotic waterjet therapy (RWT), water vapor thermal therapy (WVTT), prostatic urethral lift (PUL), transurethral needle ablation (TUNA), transurethral microwave therapy (TUMT), and balloon commissurotomy. Reoperation rates were assessed at 1, 3, and 5 years. Among patients with ≥ 5-year follow-up, secondary procedures were identified to characterize the distribution of reoperations by index surgery. RESULTS: We evaluated 112,091 patients with 1-year, 81,554 with 3-year, and 52,426 with 5-year follow-up ( Table 1). Simple prostatectomy and LEP had the lowest reoperation rates (0.9–1.4% and 1.5-6.0%, respectively) while less invasive modalities demonstrated higher reoperation rates (WVTT \[5.3–14.8%\], PUL \[4.3–16.6%\], and TUNA \[5.8–21.0%\]). Among reoperations, TURP (61%), PVP (22%), and LEP (8%) were the most common for recurrent BPH in patients with a minimum of 5 year follow up ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191296.28297.ff.07#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, TURP was the most popular BPH surgery but had a relatively high reoperation rate. LEP, a less invasive alternative to simple prostatectomy, demonstrated comparable low retreatment risk. Less invasive modalities (WVTT, PUL, and TUNA) showed higher reoperation rates and often required more invasive secondary procedures. Optimal surgical management of BPH requires balancing durability, invasiveness, and patient-specific factors. | | | --- | | |

title: COMPARATIVE OUTCOMES OF HOLMIUM LASER ENUCLEATION (HOLEP), PROSTATIC URETHRAL LIFT (UROLIFT), REZŪM, AND TRANSURETHRAL RESECTION OF THE PROSTATE (TURP): A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF EVIDENCE FROM 2015 TO 2025
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Waqas Khalil, Muhammad Mazhar Sheikh, Jawad Islam
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) has long been regarded as the surgical gold standard for men with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) caused by benign prostatic obstruction (BPO). In the past decade, minimally invasive surgical therapies (MISTs) such as the prostatic urethral lift (UroLift) and Rezūm water vapor therapy, as well as holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP), have emerged as alternatives with varying durability, recovery, and sexual function outcomes. Objective: To systematically compare efficacy, safety, and retreatment outcomes of HoLEP, UroLift, Rezūm, and TURP to determine whether TURP remains the current gold standard in the modern treatment landscape. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO-compliant methodology). Literature searches were performed in PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library for studies published between January 2015 and June 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), prospective comparative series, and meta-analyses reporting International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), peak urinary flow rate (Qmax), sexual function outcomes, and retreatment rates with ≥3 years of follow-up. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane ROB-2 and ROBINS-I tools. RESULTS: A total of 42 studies (15 RCTs, 12 prospective cohorts, 10 systematic reviews, and 5 meta-analyses) met inclusion criteria. HoLEP demonstrated the largest mean IPSS reduction (−18 to −21 points, 65–75% improvement) and the lowest retreatment rate (~6% at 5 years). TURP achieved durable symptom relief (mean IPSS reduction 13–15 points) with pooled retreatment ~7–8% at 5 years. Rezūm produced moderate improvement (IPSS −12 to −14; 45–50% improvement) with 4–5% reoperation at 4 years and minimal new sexual dysfunction. UroLift provided rapid recovery and ejaculatory preservation but smaller symptomatic gain (IPSS −11; 35–40% improvement) and higher retreatment (~13% at 5 years). Across RCTs, HoLEP and TURP yielded statistically equivalent IPSS and Qmax improvements at 12–60 months, while HoLEP reduced bleeding, catheterization time, and hospital stay. CONCLUSIONS: HoLEP demonstrates equal or superior long-term efficacy compared to TURP with lower morbidity and retreatment, positioning it as the new surgical benchmark where laser expertise exists. Rezūm and UroLift offer valuable, patient-centered MIST options for men prioritizing recovery and sexual function preservation. Contemporary evidence supports a transition toward HoLEP as the durable, size-independent gold standard in the surgical management of BPO.

title: DURABLE SYMPTOM RELIEF AND FUNCTIONAL PRESERVATION: FINAL 3-YEAR RESULTS FROM THE PINNACLE TRIAL OF THE OPTILUME BPH CATHETER SYSTEM
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Steven A. Kaplan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Optilume BPH is a novel minimally invasive surgical therapy (MIST) that combines mechanical dilation with the delivery of paclitaxel for the treatment of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) secondary to BPH. Mechanical dilation with Optilume BPH achieves an anterior commissurotomy, while delivery of paclitaxel is intended to maintain luminal patency during healing. The PINNACLE study was a randomized, sham controlled study evaluating Optilume BPH against a sham procedure, with long-term follow-up limited to the active (Optilume BPH) treatment group. METHODS: 148 subjects were randomized in a 2:1 fashion (100 Optilume BPH, 48 sham) at 18 centers in the US and Canada. Subjects and evaluating personnel were blinded to the treatment received through 12-months, subjects randomized to receive treatment with Optilume BPH continued follow-up through 2 years. Symptom improvement was measured utilizing the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), functional improvement measured by peak urinary flow rate (Qmax). Erectile and ejaculatory function were evaluated utilizing validated questionnaires. RESULTS: Sixty-nine subjects have completed the 3-year follow-up in the per-protocol set. A total of 6 subjects (6/100, 6%) pursued additional surgical management (PAE (1), TURP (2), laser ablation (2), prostatic urethral lift (PUL)(1)) through the 3-year timepoint. Improvement in IPSS was maintained through 3 years (23.4 vs 10.3; -12.9 improvement). Qmax improved from 8.9 ml/sec at baseline to 17.1 ml/sec through 3-year follow-up. Paired analysis showed minimal changes in IPSS and Qmax from 12 month to 3-year follow-up. There were no changes in perceived sexual or ejaculatory function. CONCLUSIONS: Treatment with Optilume BPH results in impressive and durable functional improvements in flow rate and symptomology. The peak flow rate nearly doubled from baseline and remained consistently above normal thresholds through 3 years, suggesting long term efficacy. Minimal surgical retreatment has occurred in the cohort of patients randomized to receive Optilume BPH as part of the pivotal randomized, sham controlled trial.

title: CLINICAL EVALUATION OF AI-BASED SOFTWARE FOR DIAGNOSING BLADDER OUTLET OBSTRUCTION AND DETRUSOR UNDERACTIVITY IN MEN WITH LOWER URINARY TRACT SYMPTOMS
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Michael J. Koo, Jihwan Lee, Sihyun Sung, Kwangjin Ko, Deok Hyun Han, Kyu Sung Lee
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) in men are commonly caused by bladder outlet obstruction (BOO) or detrusor underactivity (DU). The pressure–flow study (PFS) is the typical diagnostic reference but is invasive and not always available. This study aimed to validate an artificial-intelligence-based software (Esther Prostex 1™) that predicts BOO and DU non-invasively using uroflowmetry, symptom scores, laboratory data, and ultrasound images. METHODS: A retrospective study was conducted in 456 men aged ≥40 years presenting with LUTS between January 2021 and July 2023. Inclusion criteria were Qmax < 15 ml/s, transrectal ultrasound (TRUS), uroflometry, IPSS data, and available PFS results. The AI model integrated multimodal inputs (IPSS, uroflowmetry, and laboratory tests) to classify BOO and DU, with PFS-based diagnosis as the reference. Primary outcome was evaluated by the area under the ROC curve (AUC), and secondary outcomes included sensitivity, specificity, and overall accuracy. RESULTS: The AI model achieved high diagnostic accuracy for both BOO and DU. For BOO, AUC was 0.8995 (95% CI 0.8589–0.9401, p<0.001) and for DU, AUC was 0.8747 (95% CI 0.8366–0.9129, p<0.001). Five-level AUC interpretive criteria indicates that AUC over 0.8 is considered "good". The ROC curves ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191296.28297.ff.10#F1)) demonstrated excellent diagnostic accuracy for both disease types, with the BOO curve positioned slightly higher, reflecting superior overall specificity. Sensitivity and specificity analysis ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191296.28297.ff.10#F2)) showed complementary strengths: BOO exhibited sensitivity 78.6% and specificity 87.6%, whereas DU showed sensitivity 92.3% and specificity 66.3%. This pattern indicates that the AI system accurately differentiates obstructive cases while maintaining high sensitivity for underactive bladder identification. Both models exceeded the predefined lower 95% CI superiority margins, confirming statistically robust and clinically reproducible performance across subgroups. CONCLUSIONS: Esther Prostex 1™ demonstrated clinically meaningful diagnostic capability for identifying BOO and DU using only non-invasive data.
