High AUC values (> 0.87) and complementary sensitivity/specificity profiles support its utility as a practical AI-driven alternative to PFS for evaluating male LUTS.

title: EFFICACY AND SAFETY OF MIRABEGRON AND TAMSULOSIN COMBINATION THERAPY COMPARED TO TAUMSULOSIN MONOTHERAPY FOR LOWER URINARY TRACT SYMPTOMS DUE TO BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA: RESULTS OF MULTICENTER, RANDOMIZED, DOUBLE-BLIND, PHASE III CLINICAL TRIAL
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Tae Hyo Kim, Jun Hee Lee, Lee Ki Soo
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of mirabegron and tamsulosin combination therapy compared to tamsulosin monotherapy in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) patients with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). METHODS: This phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of mirabegron/tamsulosin combination therapy versus tamsulosin monotherapy in men with LUTS. The trial, conducted across 25 centers from July 2021 to October 2023. Eligible participants were randomly assigned to either the combination or monotherapy group for 12 weeks. Primary efficacy endpoints included changes in total urinary frequency score (TUFS) and International Prostate Symptom Scores (IPSS), with secondary endpoints evaluating various urinary symptoms and changes in post void residual volume (PVR), maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax), and quality of life scores. Safety assessments included adverse events, PVR, Qmax, vital signs, electrocardiogram, and laboratory tests. RESULTS: A total of 795 participants were randomized to monotherapy (n=397) and combination therapy (n=398) groups. After 12 weeks, 342 in the monotherapy and 339 in the combination therapy group completed the study, with no significant baseline differences. The combination therapy group showed a greater improvement in TUFS (-11.28) and IPSS (-10.85) scores compared to monotherapy (-8.30 and -9.85, respectively) with significant differences (p<0.0001, p=0.0325). Combination therapy showed significant improvements in storage symptoms and voiding diary variables, including daytime frequency, urgency, and incontinence, compared to monotherapy. The incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events was similar between the groups (13.10% vs 16.58%, p=0.1943), with no serious drug-related adverse events, confirming an acceptable safety profile for combination therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Combination therapy with mirabegron and tamsulosin is more effective than monotherapy in improving LUTS in patients with BPH, particularly storage symptoms, with a comparable safety profile. A fixed-dose combination formulation in the future may further improve patient adherence and quality of life. | | | --- | | |

title: BEYOND OPERATIVE TIME: NASA-TLX WORKLOAD SCORES REVEAL COGNITIVE AND PHYSICAL DEMANDS ACROSS THE HOLEP LEARNING CURVE
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Victor Sandoval, Raviraj Rege, Carl Ceraolo, Rajat Jain, Scott Quarrier, Nitin Sharma
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) has a steep learning curve which limits widespread adoption. Objective metrics to define surgical proficiency, efficiency, and perceived workload remain underexplored outside academic institutions. This study aimed to characterize the learning curve for HoLEP from a regional rural hospital. METHODS: A total of 103 patients underwent HoLEP for BPH between March 2024 and August 2025. Surgical cases were stratified into three sequential groups of 34, 34, and 35 cases, respectively, based on operative chronology. Operative characteristics were compared across groups: enucleation time, laser energy, fluid use, and enucleation speed (enucleation time/specimen weight). Perceived workload was assessed using NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), to evaluate perceived workload across several domains (mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance, effort, and frustration). Comparisons of outcome metrics were made for 90-day postoperative complications and urinary continence postoperatively. Univariable and multivariable multinomial logistic regression analyses were performed to examine associations between surgical characteristics and group classification. RESULTS: Progressive improvement was observed in operative time, enucleation time, laser energy, total fluid, enucleation speed, and NASA TLX, as seen in Table 1. No statistically significant associations were observed between group classification and 90-day postoperative complications or urinary continence outcomes at any follow-up interval. In multivariable multinomial logistic regression analysis, the NASA-TLX score (OR 0.84, 95%CI, 0.72-0.99, p=0.04) remained an independent predictor of higher learning curve classification. ( Table 2.) CONCLUSIONS: Progressive reductions in operative time, energy use, and perceived workload signify quantifiable improvement. The NASA-TLX score correlated independently with improvement in proficiency, outperforming traditional operative measures in defining the HoLEP learning curve. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: EJACULATION-SPARING THULIUM LASER ENUCLEATION OF THE PROSTATE (ES-THULEP): A FEASIBLE AND EFFECTIVE ALTERNATIVE FOR BPH TREATMENT
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Andrea Iannuzzi, Alberto Ragusa, Francesco Prata, Francesco Tedesco, Gianluca Muto, Rocco Papalia, Giovanni Muto
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is an age-related condition affecting approximately one-third of men over the age of 50, commonly leading to both storage and voiding lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). A major drawback of endoscopic treatments for BPH is the frequent occurrence of retrograde ejaculation. This study aims to assess the efficacy and feasibility of ejaculation-sparing thulium laser enucleation of the prostate (ES-ThuLEP) in managing LUTS due to BPH while preserving ejaculatory function. METHODS: Between June and September 2024, sexually active patients with BPH were enrolled and followed up at 3 and 6 months after surgery. Baseline data were collected, and two standardized questionnaires—the International Index of Erectile Function short form (IIEF-5) and the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)—were administered. In addition, all patients underwent uroflowmetry and an assessment of post-void residual volume (PVR). The surgical technique involves two key steps aimed at improving ejaculatory outcomes: preservation of bladder neck muscle fibers from the 7 o’clock to the 5 o’clock position; preservation of the entire posterior urethral plate from the colliculus seminalis to the bladder neck. The main differences compared to the conventional technique are illustrated in (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191296.28297.ff.13#F1). RESULTS: A total of 30 patients were enrolled. Median age was 60 yrs (IQR, 55-70). Median prostate volume was 65 ml (IQR, 50-70 ml). No patient presented with a large middle lobe. A statistically significant improvement in IPSS score, maximum flow (Qmax), and post-void residual volume (PVR) was observed at both 3 and 6 months postoperatively (p<0.05), while no statistically significant differences were found in IIEF-5 scores before and after surgery. All patients maintained ejaculation at 6 months postoperatively. However, some degree of hypospermia was reported by 43.7% and 30.6% of patients at 3 and 6 months, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: The ES-ThuLEP technique demonstrated good functional outcomes while preserving ejaculation in all patients, suggesting that it may represent a feasible option for the surgical management of BPH in sexually active men. However, further studies with larger patient cohorts and longer follow-up are warranted to confirm these findings.

title: DURABILITY OF HOLMIUM LASER ENUCLEATION OF THE PROSTATE: A 10-YEAR MULTI-INSTITUTIONAL COMPARISON USING THE COSMOS DATABASE
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Ryan M. Blake, Douglas Y. Sur, Tyler J. Sheetz, Thalia H. Bajakian, Manoj Monga, Roger L. Sur
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Holmium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate (HoLEP) is a size-independent, minimally invasive surgery for the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia which has gained significant popularity in the last decade. The durability of HoLEP lacks robust, long-term data. We aimed to examine durability and postoperative outcomes for HoLEP compared to other procedures. METHODS: We performed a retrospective, cross-sectional analysis using a multi-institutional electronic health record database (Epic Cosmos) from 2015 to 2025. We compared HoLEP to alternative prostate procedures (transurethral resection of prostate, prostatic urethral lift, photoselective vaporization, water vapor therapy, waterjet ablation, and microwave therapy) using CPT and ICD codes as well as de-identified data from Cosmos. Outcomes measured were durability (no subsequent prostate procedures), independence from medications (lack of filled prostate medication prescriptions following the procedure), immediate outcomes in the first 30 days, and early postoperative outcomes from 31 to 180 days. Categorical variables were compared using chi-squared tests, and all analyses were performed in R version 4.5.1. RESULTS: In total 60,352 patients underwent a HoLEP procedure while 506,959 patients underwent an alternative procedure. HoLEP showed superior surgical durability with 96.1% of patients remaining free of subsequent prostate procedures versus 88.5% in the non-HoLEP group (p<0.001). HoLEP demonstrated better independence from prostate medications with 65.6% of patients free of medications versus 41.8% (p<0.001) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191296.28297.ff.14#F1)). Perioperative (0-30 days) and early postoperative (31-180 days) outcomes were similar between HoLEP and non-HoLEP procedures with statistically significant but modest absolute differences ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191296.28297.ff.14#F2)). CONCLUSIONS: When compared to alternative prostate procedures for urinary symptoms, HoLEP demonstrated superior durability and independence from prostate medications. Postoperative outcomes were similar between the two groups. Our findings suggest that HoLEP can serve as a definitive treatment for patients deciding between surgical options.

title: HOW TO AVOID COMPLICATIONS DURING ROBOTIC WATERJET ABLATION THERAPY (AQUABLATION) IN BPH PATIENTS?
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Surgical Therapy & New Technology II (PD03)
authors: Dolev Perez, Ariel Mamber, Michael Pasherstnik, Dmitry Koulikov, Ala Eddin Natsheh, Ofer Shenfeld, Ilan Kafka, Adam Hen, Andres Malinger, Yehuda Warszawer, Avital Zeldin, Boris Chertin
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robotic Water-jet ablation has become an alternative to transurethral resection of the prostate to treat bladder outlet obstruction (BOO) in BPH patients. The significant advantages of this procedure are the ability to treat prostates of various sizes, reduced sexual side effects, and a shorter learning curve. However, some major complications such as higher post-procedural transfusion rates and recently reported 5% of post-procedure urethral stricture could not be brushed aside. We have aimed to identify predictive factors that could lead to serious complications during Aquablation to improve the durability and safety of the procedure. METHODS: We have reviewed the logs of all prospective patients who underwent Aquablation and presented with Clavien-Dindo (CD) Gr II-V complications. Deviations from the standard Aquablation protocol were recorded and analyzed about complications and their management. RESULTS: We have identified 87 (16.6%) out of 524 prospectively followed patients operated by a single surgeon between 2023- 2025. There were CD Gr II 66 (12.6%), Gr IIIa 12 (2.2%), and Gr IIIb 9 (1.7%) complications, respectively. None presented with Gr IV and V. False route passing of the hand piece of the Aquablation device was associated with urethral stricture and bladder neck undermining requiring longer indwelling catheter time in 47 (8.9%) patients, SPT in 5 (0.9%), and meatoplasty in the remaining 2 (0.3%) patients. Incorrect planning of the water jet alignment step at the bladder neck was associated with significant bleeding and a need for hemotransfusion, with a mean of 51+ 3.5 (SD) (blood PC). Incorrect nozzle position before placement of depth markers was associated with increased postoperative bleeding, but did not reach statistical significance. 6(1.1%) patients who required redo surgery due to failure of weaning the indwelling catheter underwent TUR-P of the apical tissue and voided spontaneously. Seventeen patients (3.2%) who required redosurgery 5.19 + 3.9 months due to de novo obstructive symptoms were diagnosed with cross-healing of the lateral distal prostatic lobes, obstructing the prostatic utricle. Two patients with severe postoperative hemorrhage were diagnosed with aberrant vessels of the prostatic artery and underwent successful PAE. CONCLUSIONS: Our data show that meticulous planning of the jet alignment at the bladder neck is crucial for avoiding significant bleeding. Verumontanum area preservation might lead to residual obstructive symptoms and the need for additional intervention. Patients with severe postoperative bleeding need PAE without delay.

title: CLINICAL DECISION SUPPORT AS A NUDGE TOWARDS IMPROVED PERIOPERATIVE CARE
session: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I (PD04)
authors: Walker C. Bailey, Suhong Tong, Duncan Wilcox, Kyle Rove
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Clinical Decision Support (CDS) systems seek to “nudge” provider behavior toward an intended goal. CDS comes in several forms such as pop up alerts, dynamic order sets, and others. We implemented perioperative CDS tools with the hypothesis that these interventions would increase adherence to target perioperative care goals over time. This study aims to assess the utility of these tools over a multi-year period to influence provider behavior. METHODS: Our department incorporated three CDS tools within our electronic medical record (EMR), and retrospectively studied the target outcome before and after implementation of each: To reduce postoperative opioid prescriptions, all opioid orders were removed from the urology discharge order set. Data regarding postoperative opioid prescriptions were gathered from 12,820 surgical cases over 94 months. To improve the number of electronic consents created prior to the day of surgery (DOS) so families could review ahead of time, a close visit validation warning was added to check for a surgical order and recommend the electronic consent be created if it was not. Data regarding consent creation prior to DOS were gathered from 5,707 surgical cases over 24 months. To improve preoperative urine culture (prUC) rates, pop-up recommended orders were added on when targeted procedures are ordered. Data regarding prUC orders were gathered for 193 target surgical procedures over 12 months. We summarized each data set for individual cases by month and analyzed the data via Statistical Process Control (SPC) chart with a cut-point representing the date of CDS intervention. RESULTS: The average monthly rate of postoperative opioid prescriptions dropped from 59% to 11% after intervention 1 (p<.0001). The average monthly rate of surgical consent forms prior to DOS climbed from 16% to 49% after intervention 2 (p<.0001). The average monthly rate of targeted prUC rose from 21% to 46% after intervention 3 (p=0.0060). Interventions 1 and 2 showed no seasonality after time series analysis; no interrupted time series modeling was performed for intervention 3 due to relative paucity of data. CONCLUSIONS: Our data show statistically significant improvements in adherence to perioperative goals after implementation of three targeted CDS interventions. However, it is important to acknowledge that these changes did not occur in isolation from departmental effort and intention. In light of the relative simplicity and cost-effectiveness of implementing these changes, we believe leveraging the functionality of CDS is a valuable tool to foster consistency in perioperative care and nudge providers towards desired departmental goals.

title: IMPACT OF NIGHTTIME CENTRALIZATION ON REFERRAL EFFICIENCY AND TESTICULAR SALVAGE IN PEDIATRIC ACUTE SCROTUM: A REGIONAL EXPERIENCE FROM JAPAN
session: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I (PD04)
authors: Takanori Mochizuki, Akira Abe, Hiroshi Shimura, Satoru Kira, Norifumi Sawada, Takahiko Mitsui
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Acute scrotum is a pediatric urological emergency that requires prompt diagnosis and timely surgical management to prevent testicular loss. However, in rural regions, timely care is often limited by the shortage of pediatric urologists and the absence of 24-hour surgical coverage. To address this problem, a nighttime centralization system was introduced in Yamanashi Prefecture, Japan, in October 2018. Under this policy, all pediatric patients presenting with suspected acute scrotum during nighttime hours (6:00 PM–8:00 AM) were directly referred to our hospital. This study aimed to evaluate whether this regional centralization improved referral efficiency and clinical outcomes for pediatric acute scrotum. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed electronic medical records of pediatric patients diagnosed with acute scrotum at the University of Yamanashi Hospital between January 2003 and December 2024. Patients were divided into two groups: before centralization (2003–September 2018) and after centralization (October 2018–2024). Cases lacking documented onset or consultation time, or those exceeding 24 hours (1,440 minutes) from symptom onset to consultation, were excluded. Annual case numbers, surgical rates, and testicular salvage rates were compared between the two groups. RESULTS: A total of 215 cases were identified. After October 2018, the number of nighttime consultations increased from 32 to 58, and surgical cases rose from 11 (26%) to 25 (43%). The testicular salvage rate improved from 71% to 88%. The median time from symptom onset to consultation decreased from 323 minutes (IQR 181–507) before centralization to 269 minutes (IQR 165–404) after implementation (p=0.0865). Among surgically treated patients, the median onset-to-surgery interval was significantly shorter in salvaged testes (258 \[170–455\] min) than in orchiectomy cases (434 \[281–1120\] min, p=0.032). CONCLUSIONS: Nighttime centralization improved the timeliness of care for pediatric acute scrotum, leading to increased surgical intervention and higher testicular salvage rates. Although the reduction in onset-to-consultation time did not reach statistical significance, the findings suggest that centralization effectively eliminated referral delays and enhanced regional coordination in pediatric urological emergencies.

title: EHR-INTEGRATED CLINICAL DECISION SUPPORT FOR PRIMARY CARE PROVIDER ENGAGEMENT FOR URINARY INCONTINENCE
session: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I (PD04)
authors: Sweta Parija, Abbas Bader, Elizabeth Hirschbeck, Jejo Koola, Jonathan Bergman, Richard Fantus, Tamara Grisales, Allison Mays, Tajnoos Yazdany, Emily Lukacz, Yahir Santiago-Lastra, Jennifer Singer, Colby Souders, Jennifer T. Anger, OPTIMA Author Group
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary incontinence (UI) affects nearly half of adult women, yet only ~20% receive guideline-concordant care. Embedding clinical decision support (CDS) tools into electronic health records (EHRs) may improve UI detection and management in primary care. The INTUIT trial evaluates whether a bundled CDS intervention enhances provider engagement and promotes evidence-based UI care. METHODS: Optimizing Primary Care Tools for Incontinence Management (OPTIMA) is a multi-site, cluster-randomized controlled trial across 60 primary care offices within four health systems. Providers were randomized to usual care vs. a bundled intervention including academic detailing and EHR-integrated CDS tools (order sets, note templates, and referral pathways). All providers received an interruptive Best Practice Advisory (BPA) when a patient with UI symptoms checked in; the intervention arm’s BPA linked to the order set. BPA engagement was defined as opening the order set (intervention) or selecting “Will address UI” (control). A chart review of 100 intervention encounters assessed CDS usage. Multivariable logistic regression examined predictors of BPA engagement and tool use. RESULTS: Between April 2023 and January 2025, the BPA fired 430 times (Table 1). Engagement was higher in the intervention arm (67.8% vs. 33.0%, p<0.001; (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191300.98315.e9.03#F1)). Engagement declined with repeat alerts but was positively associated with being in the intervention arm (OR 4.1, 95% CI 2.6–7.8) and provider (vs. assistant) encounters (OR 4.2, 95% CI 2.5–8.1). CDS tools were used in 20% of reviewed charts, and BPA engagement strongly predicted tool use (OR 12.0, 95% CI 1.5–94.4;Table 2). CONCLUSIONS: Bundled CDS interventions significantly increased provider engagement with EHR alerts for UI. Early interaction with interruptive alerts appears critical for sustained tool adoption, underscoring the role of thoughtful design and workflow alignment in CDS effectiveness.

title: CONSENSUS IS POSSIBLE: UTILIZATION OF A MODIFIED DELPHI ANALYSIS TO STANDARDIZE POSTOPERATIVE ORDERS AND EXPECTATIONS IN A MULTI-SITE PEDIATRIC UROLOGY PRACTICE
session: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I (PD04)
authors: Emily K. Clennon, Catalina Hwang, Alice Xiang, Jeffrey Campbell, Brian T. Caldwell, Nina Mikkilineni, Kelly T. Harris, Dan Wood, Nicholas G. Cost, Duncan T. Wilcox, Kyle O. Rove
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Inconsistencies in postoperative management and low-quality discharge instructions are associated with negative clinical outcomes and avoidable frustration for patients and families. Developing high quality instructions for pediatric urology practices is challenging given the wide range of procedure types and patient ages/development. This study aimed to use modified Delphi methodology to standardize post-operative instructions in a group of pediatric urologists and facilitate creation of a single postoperative discharge order set implementable across a large children’s health system. METHODS: Seven pediatric urologists and a transitional urologist in a single practice who perform surgeries at four locations were queried via REDCap survey using a two-round modified Delphi process between June 2024 and May 2025. Questions covered activity and travel restrictions, diet, bathing, swimming, dressings/wound care, medications, catheter management, and follow up for categories of pediatric urologic procedures including endoscopic, meatal, groin/scrotal, penile, kidney, ureteral reimplant, and lower tract reconstruction. Consensus was established for areas with ≥80% agreement. Outcomes of questioning were used to create a common post-operative discharge order set for ambulatory and inpatient surgery with branching logic based on procedure type, age, and— for areas without consensus— surgeon. RESULTS: After the first round, there was consensus in 21 of 106 (19.8%) areas queried. After the second round, consensus was reached for all activity restrictions, travel, diet, bathing/wound care, swimming, medications, catheter management, and routine follow up for all procedure categories. Consensus was not achieved for postoperative dressings (particularly those for penile surgery), and surgeon-specific dressing types were included in the order set. The order set was implemented successfully across all four locations, easing workflow for surgeons, surgical trainees, postoperative care unit staff, surgery schedulers providing anticipatory guidance regarding postoperative management, and clinic nurses fielding post-operative calls. CONCLUSIONS: Pediatric urologists have varied and individual preferences regarding postoperative instructions. A modified Delphi analysis brought these to light, yet consensus was achievable for most aspects of postoperative care, simplifying teaching for recovery and clinic nurses. Delphi process results may be implemented via order sets to standardize postoperative care, communication, and expectations across large health systems.

title: MULTI-DISCIPLINARY TRIAL OF VOID ALGORITHM REDUCES CATHETER-ASSOCIATED URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS: LONG-TERM OUTCOMES ON A SURGICAL UNIT
session: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I (PD04)
authors: David S. Han, Srinath-Reddi Pingle, Lovie M. Amolo, Maureen L. Roach, Maria S. Luga, Shelley-Ann Layne, David Kuang, Subhash Krishnamoorthy, Christopher B. Anderson, Gina M. Badalato, David M. Weiner
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prolonged indwelling urethral catheter use predisposes patients to catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs), an avoidable morbidity and healthcare expenditure. As such, efforts to minimize CAUTIs remain a priority for patients, providers, and hospital administration. We therefore sought to assess the long-term impact of a multi-disciplinary trial of void (TOV) algorithm on CAUTI rates and indwelling urethral catheter use on a surgical Step-Down Unit. METHODS: From April 2021 to March 2024, we performed an interrupted time series on a 36-bed surgical Step-Down Unit in a large urban academic medical center – with the TOV algorithm as the intervention ( Figure 1A). Our cohort included patients treated with intra-abdominal, thoracic, vascular, urologic, and gynecologic surgeries. The primary outcome was mean CAUTI rates 1.5 years before and after algorithm implementation. Secondary outcomes included mean rate of indwelling catheter use and mean total patient days before and after algorithm implementation. Given the low incidence of CAUTIs, our unit of analysis was a fiscal quarter. Univariable analysis was performed using Student's t-test. We compared outcomes on a surgical Step-Down Unit where the algorithm was implemented to a 34-bed surgical floor unit – where the algorithm was not implemented – to serve as a natural control. RESULTS: Over 12 fiscal quarters, there were 4124 indwelling urethral catheter days and 10 CAUTIs on the surgical Step-Down Unit. Average CAUTIs decreased from 1.3 per quarter to 0.3 (p=0.03, Figure 1B). Average indwelling urethral catheter days appeared to decrease after implementation of the TOV algorithm though this finding was not statistically significant (384.7 vs. 302.7, p=0.09). There was no difference in mean total patient days before and after algorithm implementation (2942.0 vs. 2991.0, p=0.27). During the same study period, the surgical floor unit experienced a decrease in catheter use (502.3 vs. 377.2, p<0.01) though CAUTI rates did not change (0.7 vs 0.2, p=0.09). CONCLUSIONS: Long-term implementation of a multi-disciplinary TOV algorithm to standardize catheter care is effective and appears to reduce CAUTIs without affecting patient care volume. Further investigations should assess what aspects of quality initiatives allow for sustained improvements to achieve superior patient care and hospital metrics.

title: FROM PROBLEM TO PRACTICE: LEARNING FROM A CATHETER SELF-IRRIGATION PROGRAM TO REDUCE PREVENTABLE EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT VISITS
session: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I (PD04)
authors: Saam Kazemi, Anthony Bettencourt, Kharen Palacio, Sarah Pate, Christopher S. Saigal, Kathy H. Huen
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: In prior work, we identified foley catheter malfunction as a major cause of preventable emergency department (ED) visits in postoperative urologic patients. Based on this, we implemented a program of catheter self-irrigation for patients who underwent surgery for benign prostatic hyperplasia. We aim to assess this program’s effectiveness. METHODS: Using the Institute for Healthcare Improvement’s Model for Improvement as a framework, we conducted 7 Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) learning cycles, starting June 2024. Process measures included: 1) intervention reach, defined as the proportion of patients who were discharged with catheters who received teaching, and 2) quality of teaching. Outcome measure was change in preventable ED visits, defined as a visit where patient was discharged home from the ED without imaging or urologic consultation. Statistical process control charts were used to measure changes over time. RESULTS: We conducted 7 PDSA cycles ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191300.98315.e9.06#F1)). A P chart illustrates how each PDSA cycle increased our intervention reach ( Figure 2A). By increasing the reliability of our intervention through creation of a default order set in the electronic medical record and integration of automatic patient education materials in cycle 6, intervention reach increased to 94%. 18% (15/83) of patients performed self-irrigation at home, and 60% of those (9/15) avoided an ED visit ( Figure 2B). Of the remaining 6, all represented appropriate escalations in care. Patients rated the teaching as valuable (median score 8/10) and reported confidence in performing self-irrigation (median score 8/10). CONCLUSIONS: Patient self-irrigation of catheter at home is a feasible alternative to the emergency department for catheter malfunction, and decreases preventable ED visits.

title: ENHANCING PROSTATE CANCER CARE WITH EDUCATIONAL VIDEOS: A QUALITY IMPROVEMENT INITIATIVE
session: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I (PD04)
authors: Dan Luca, Ailene E. Corona, Kian Kolahi Sohrabi, Wayne G. Brisbane
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate biopsy pathology reports are often too complex for patients to interpret despite their role in diagnosis and treatment decisions. We developed an instructional video to improve patient understanding of the biopsy report. We then evaluated the video's impact on patient anxiety, satisfaction, and comprehension. METHODS: On the day of biopsy, we presented 11 prostate cancer patients with a mock pathology report standardized for a patient (Mickey Mouse). Subsequently, we evaluated their understanding of the report as well as their anxiety, satisfaction, and comprehension (Scores 1–4). Approximately a week later, patients received their actual biopsy report, along with a supplemental educational video explaining it. Re-using the prior survey, we re-evaluated patient’s understanding of their report, anxiety, and satisfaction. We analyzed changes in these measured outcomes using Fisher’s Exact test and the Mann-Whitney U test. Educational Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c2e1VhhaUWc. RESULTS: Eleven patients completed the baseline survey, with a 45% response rate to the follow-up survey. Before presenting the educational video, only 55% of participants accurately identified “Mickey Mouse’s” cancer status and Gleason score. After watching the educational video and receiving their biopsy reports, 100% of patients accurately identified their cancer status and Gleason score. Furthermore, patient satisfaction scores significantly increased ( Figure A). There was a modest increase in understanding of next steps of care following review of the video. No change in anxiety levels pre-and-post video education was observed. CONCLUSIONS: Pathology reports are difficult to interpret. Providing patients with report specific explanatory videos improved comprehension, and satisfaction. Given the low cost and ease of implementation, video educational videos may play a role in prostate cancer care.

title: AT-HOME AND MAIL-IN SEMEN ANALYSIS: A CRITICAL REVIEW OF SCIENTIFIC VALIDATION, REGULATORY OVERSIGHT, AND MARKETING CLAIMS
session: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I (PD04)
authors: Juan P. Varela, Pablo Suarez, James F. Smith, Kevin J. Campbell
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: At-home and mail-in semen analysis (SA) platforms are expanding rapidly, marketed as convenient and private tools for fertility screening and post-vasectomy testing. However, many use clinical terminology without the regulatory or scientific backing required for diagnostic use. We aimed to critically evaluate major SA companies to determine their clinical purpose, regulatory status, validation evidence, and marketing accuracy. METHODS: A structured review was performed of 10 companies actively marketing SA services in the U. S. (Reprosource, Fellow Health, PVSA, Legacy, Trak, Yo, SpermCheck, CryoChoice, MaleFromHome, and Sapyen). Data sources included PubMed, FDA filings, and company documentation (January–April 2025). Each platform was assessed across four domains: (1) clinical purpose (diagnostic vs wellness), (2) regulatory oversight (CLIA \[New\ York State\], CAP, or FDA approval), (3) published analytical or usability validation, and (4) public-facing marketing claims. RESULTS: All mail-in fertility tests failed to meet NYS Department of Health standards and only Fellow Health had a NYS approved PVSA test, representing the current regulatory gold standard. Only Fellow Health and Reprosource demonstrated both CLIA certification and peer-reviewed validation for delayed mail-in analysis. Most other platforms, notably MaleFromHome, Legacy, and Sapyen, were marketed as diagnostic tools but lacked peer-reviewed validation or displayed legal-facing disclaimers citing wellness purposes in their Terms and Conditions. Consumer at-home tests (Trak, Yo, SpermCheck) showed good usability data yet remained qualitative or semi-quantitative, with labeling that risks consumer misinterpretation. Most companies lacked transparency regarding algorithmic adjustments involved in SA reporting. Marketing language frequently overstated diagnostic equivalency without disclosure of laboratory limitations. CONCLUSIONS: Few mail-in or at-home SA platforms meet criteria for true diagnostic-grade testing. High-Complexity, validated mail-in systems can safely expand access, whereas unverified at-home or “wellness” products may mislead consumers and providers. Greater regulatory transparency, peer-reviewed validation, and clinician integration are needed to ensure evidence-based adoption of these emerging reproductive technologies. | | | --- | | |

title: DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY OF PROSTATE MRI READS FROM NON-ACADEMIC VERSUS ACADEMIC CENTERS: IMPACT ON DETECTION OF CLINICALLY SIGNIFICANT PROSTATE CANCER AND AVOIDANCE OF UNNECESSARY BIOPSIES
session: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I (PD04)
authors: Omri F. Nativ, Adam Williams, Sabika Sadiq, Jessica Delgado, Gareth Reid, Hossein Sharifi, Nikolas Howell, Pedro Freitas, Dinno Mendiola, Archan Khandekar, Chad Ritch, Bruno Nahar, Dipen J. Parekh, Sanoj Punnen, Mark Gonzalgo
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) is integral to prostate cancer diagnosis but remains reader-dependent. Interpretation variability between non-academic and academic centers may affect detection of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) and lead to unnecessary biopsies. This study evaluated patients whose non-academic MRI showed a suspicious lesion that was deemed negative on academic re-read, comparing diagnostic accuracy and clinical impact between interpretations. METHODS: We prospectively analyzed 44 patients referred for mpMRI re-evaluation after non-academic imaging demonstrated one or more suspicious lesions not confirmed on academic re-read. Outside MRIs were performed using 3T scanners and interpreted per PI-RADS v2.1. Academic re-reads were performed by experienced genitourinary radiologists. All patients underwent MRI-targeted biopsies based on outside reads plus concurrent 12-core systematic biopsies. Pathology was categorized as benign, Grade Group (GG) 1, or GG≥2 (csPCa). Diagnostic performance and biopsy outcomes were compared. RESULTS: Median PSA was 5.7 ng/mL and prostate volume 60 g. Outside MRIs reported lesions as PI-RADS 3 (36%), 4 (52%), and 5 (11%). Overall cancer detection was 38.6%, and csPCa 16%. Targeted biopsies of non-academic MRI lesions yielded benign/GG1 results in 41/44 (94%) and csPCa in 3/44 (6.8%). Only one case (2%) represented csPCa detected solely within the MRI target. Academic re-reads classified all lesions as non-suspicious, which would have safely avoided biopsy in 36/44 (82%) cases. In 12 patients, the outside MRI was the only biopsy indication; of these, 3/12 (25%) had csPCa (two from systematic cores, one from target). Relying on academic reads would have missed 3/44 (6%), all detected by systematic sampling. CONCLUSIONS: Academic prostate MRI re-reads markedly improve diagnostic specificity and reduce unnecessary biopsies with minimal risk of missed csPCa. Centralized review by expert radiologists optimizes accuracy, decreases procedural morbidity, and enhances efficiency in prostate cancer diagnostic pathways.

title: CANCER SURGERY OUTCOMES AFTER IMPLEMENTATION OF A GLOBAL BUDGET MODEL IN RURAL HOSPITALS
session: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I (PD04)
authors: Jacob Whitman, Eric Roberts, Jonathan Yabes, Donald Bourne, Zhaojun Sun, Manisha Bhattacharya, Jeremy Khan, Bruce Jacobs, Lindsay Sabik
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Rural hospitals face increasing financial strain, threatening the sustainability of essential surgical services. The Pennsylvania Rural Health Model (PARHM), initiated in 2019, represents the first U. S. global budget program designed specifically for rural hospitals. The model aims to stabilize hospital finances and promote population health; however, its impact on the quality of complex surgical care remains uncertain. This study evaluated the association between PARHM implementation and short-term outcomes following inpatient cancer surgery among rural residents. METHODS: Analysis used a stacked difference-in-differences design leveraging the staggered implementation of PARHM across rural hospitals. Linked Pennsylvania Health Care Cost Containment Council (PHC4) discharge data and Pennsylvania Cancer Registry (PCR) records from 2016–2023 identified 17,048 patients residing in hospital service areas (HSAs) with a PARHM-participating hospital who underwent inpatient surgery for one of 11 cancers. Primary outcomes were 30- and 90-day mortality, readmission, and composite measures. Models applied HSA-level propensity score weights, adjusted for patient and area covariates, and clustered standard errors by HSA. RESULTS: Among 17,048 cancer surgery admissions, 3,537 occurred in PARHM HSAs and 13,511 in non-PARHM HSAs. In adjusted analyses, PARHM implementation was not associated with statistically significant changes in short-term surgical outcomes. The estimated effect on 90-day mortality was +1.1 percentage points (pp) (95% CI, −1.8 to 3.9; p=0.46) and on 90-day readmission was −1.6 pp (95% CI, −5.8 to 2.7; p=0.47). Findings for 30-day mortality, readmission, and composite outcomes were similarly nonsignificant. Cohort- and cancer site–specific analyses identified isolated significant estimates without consistent directional patterns. CONCLUSIONS: Implementation of PARHM was not associated with changes in short-term postoperative outcomes among rural residents undergoing cancer surgery. These results suggest that Pennsylvania’s global budget model did not measurably influence surgical oncology outcomes during the demonstration period. | | | --- | | |

title: UNPLANNED HEALTHCARE UTILIZATION AFTER BENIGN PROSTATE INTERVENTION IN MICHIGAN
session: Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I (PD04)
authors: John Michael Di Bianco, Michael Uy, Sabry Mansour, Stephanie Daignault-Newton, Naji Ayyash, Mahin Mirza, Jay Lonsway, Mark Bradshaw, Kushbu Narender Singh, Khurshid Ghani, Casey Dauw, Wilson Sui for the Michigan Urological Surgery Improvement Collaborative
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Randomized controlled trials have demonstrated the safety and efficacy of therapies for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). These common procedures are performed in a wide variety of patient populations and perioperative contexts in routine clinical practice. However, real-world data on perioperative outcomes are limited. Therefore, we sought to understand the incidence and predictors of emergency department (ED) visits after BPH procedures in a contemporary, real-world cohort. METHODS: Using Michigan statewide claims data, patients who underwent a BPH procedure between 2015 and 2023 were identified. Procedures included: water vapor thermal therapy (WVTT), transurethral resection of prostate (TURP), prostatic urethral lift (PUL), transurethral microwave thermotherapy (TUMT), laser photovaporization (PVP), simple prostatectomy (SP), robotic waterjet therapy (RWJT) and laser enucleation of prostate (LEP). ED visit rates were assessed within 30 days of index procedure and categorized by the primary ICD-9/10 diagnosis code. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to identify predictors of 30-day ED visits. RESULTS: A total of 55,693 procedures were identified. ED visit rates ranged from 10% to 17% by procedure ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191300.98315.e9.11#F1)) with an overall rate of 13.3%. The most common urologic reasons for ED visits were: urinary retention (39%), hematuria (29%), UTI/infection (21%), and catheter-related complications (17%). Patients experiencing an ED visit were older and more comorbid. On multivariable analysis, predictors of ED visits included: higher age (OR 1.01, 1.00-1.02), preoperative catheter use (OR 1.47, 1.29-1.67), and preoperative anticoagulation (OR 1.38, 1.22-1.55). Compared to TURP, patients undergoing RWJT had a higher risk of ED visits (OR 1.56, 1.12-2.17) and LEP a lower risk (OR 0.63, 0.51-0.78). CONCLUSIONS: Emergency department visits are common after BPH intervention particularly amongst older patients who are on anti-coagulation and are catheter dependent preoperatively. The most common causes of ED visits included hematuria, urinary retention, UTI and catheter-related complications. Further, the risk of unplanned ED visits differs by procedure with RWJT being the highest and LEP the lowest. Future work should develop strategies to reduce these visits.

title: BOTH OVER-PRESCRIPTION AND UNDER-PRESCRIPTION OF OPIOIDS AFTER INPATIENT UROLOGIC SURGERY INCREASES ODDS OF POSTSURGICAL OPIOID REFILLS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I (PD04)
authors: Walter R. Hsiang, Benjamin X. Guan, Patrick Hoang, Zhonghui Guan, Michelle Van Kuiken
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To assess the impact of mismatched (over-prescription and under-prescription) discharge opioid prescriptions on opioid refills up to 90 days after inpatient urologic surgery. METHODS: A retrospective single institutional cohort study examined 7,381 adult opioid-naïve and non-opioid-naïve patients discharged after inpatient urologic surgery between 2017 and 2024. Each patient’s daily dose of discharge opioid prescription was compared to their last inpatient daily opioid consumption before discharge. Discharge opioid prescriptions were categorized as matched, over-, and under-prescribed, defined as prescribed daily dose within 7.5 oral morphine equivalents \[OME\], ≥7.5 OME above, and ≤7.5 OME below of inpatient daily dose, respectively. Fisher’s test and multiple logistic regression analyses were used. RESULTS: 38.3% of patients were discharged with matched opioid prescriptions while 38.0% were over-prescribed and 23.7% were under-prescribed. Compared to the patients with matched prescriptions, patients with either over-prescription or under-prescription had higher opioid refill rates at 1-30, 31-60, and 61-90 days ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191300.98315.e9.12#F1)). Multiple logistic regression analyses revealed that when controlling for opioid-naïve status, type of surgical procedure, and other factors such as age, gender, and length of stay, opioid over-prescription independently increased the odds of refills at 1–30, 31-60, and 61–90 days after discharge by 85%, 49%, and 85%, respectively, while opioid under-prescription increased odds refills at 1–30 and 61–90 days by 47% and 33%, respectively ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191300.98315.e9.12#F2)). In contrast, the total dose of opioid prescriptions had minimal contribution to opioid refills. CONCLUSIONS: Both over-prescribing and under-prescribing of opioids, rather than the total dose of opioid prescriptions, independently contribute to increased odds of refills. Patient-centered, individualized discharge opioid dosing based on inpatient consumption may reduce prescription mismatch, enhance opioid stewardship and improve postoperative outcomes.

title: SPINAL ANESTHESIA IN UROLOGY FOR RESPONSIVE PEDIATRIC ANESTHESIA AND SATISFACTION IN SURGERY (SURPASS): A NOVEL PEDIATRIC SPINAL ANESTHETIC PROGRAM
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I (PD04)
authors: Marjorie M. Johnson, Alexander Radaoui, David Heap, Matthew M. Cao, Erin M. Mayeaux, Emmett M. Whitaker, Kelsey M. Davis, Heather M. Di Carlo, Charlotte M. Wu, Ming-Hsien M. Wang, Sapna M. Kudchadkar, Tricia M. Vecchione, Chad M. Crigger
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Children less than 12 months of age are at the greatest risk for complications associated with general anesthesia including hypoxia, hypotension, and cardiac arrest. Additionally, significant debate surrounds the lasting effects of general anesthesia on pediatric neurocognitive development. Spinal anesthesia (SA) offers an alternative that circumvents many risks associated with general anesthesia. We present our pilot program establishing an awake spinal anesthesia program for pediatric urologic procedures. METHODS: Initial implementation included distribution of educational materials regarding risks and benefits of spinal anesthesia to families in urology clinic. In parallel, the anesthesia department completed hands-on training with providers on performance of both tactile and ultrasound guided SA techniques. Operating room implementation began in August 2024. Pediatric urology patients were eligible for SA if they were 24 months or younger, planned for open outpatient procedure of 90 minutes or less, and had American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) status 1-3. Laparoscopic cases were excluded. The final anesthetic type was determined jointly by the anesthesiologist, surgeon, and patient’s guardian on the day of surgery. RESULTS: To date, 161 procedures have been attempted under SA. 141 procedures (87.58%) were successful, and 20 (12.42%) were converted to general anesthesia. Reasons for conversion included failed motor block resulting in partial anesthetic effects in 17 patients (85.00%), bronchospasm in 2 patients (10.00%), and vasovagal response in 1 patient (5.00%). The most common procedures successfully performed under SA were circumcision (58.87%), circumcision revision (23.40%), and penile torsion repair (23.40%). The median age for successful SA was 6 months (IQR: 4.00-8.00). The youngest patient was 1 month and the oldest was 20 months. The median weight of all patients was 7.90 kg (IQR: 6.94-9.10), with successful spinals weighing a median of 7.91 kg (IQR: 6.94-9.10) and converted patients weighing a median of 7.84 kg (IQR: 7.02-8.95). There was no statistically significant difference between the weight or age of successful spinals versus those that were converted to general anesthesia. CONCLUSIONS: Many pediatric urologic procedures performed on infants can be safely completed under spinal anesthesia. Beginning a successful and sustainable SA program requires a multidisciplinary approach. We hope to continue expanding this program to additional surgical specialties and procedures.

title: I’VE HAD A COUPLE OF SITUATIONS WHERE THEY’VE TALKED SUICIDE…”: A QUALITATIVE STUDY TO IMPROVE BEHAVIORAL HEALTH SUPPORT FOR PATIENTS UNDERGOING CYSTECTOMY
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Health Services Research: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety I (PD04)
authors: Zeeshan Zubair, Blashko Milenkovski, Malika Mian, Erin Costanzo, Kyle A. Richards
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Despite increasing recognition of the psychological burden of bladder cancer and cystectomy, behavioral health services are inconsistently implemented in uro-oncology. This study explored provider-perceived barriers to integrating behavioral health care throughout the perioperative cancer pathway and identified opportunities for system-level improvement and workflow-based solutions. METHODS: Four semi-structured focus groups were conducted with nurse navigators (two groups; n=7), ostomy nurses (n=4), and advanced-practice providers (total n=3). Guided discussions explored perceptions of patient distress, workflow barriers, and opportunities to integrate behavioral health services into routine care. Sessions were transcribed verbatim and analyzed in NVivo using the Sort & Sift, Think & Shift method. A hybrid deductive–inductive codebook guided analysis, and thematic summaries were developed through iterative synthesis and team consensus. RESULTS: Participants described multiple, interrelated barriers to addressing mental health needs in uro-oncology. Providers acknowledged the emotional toll of cystectomy but cited limited training and uncertainty about recognizing or responding to patient distress. Mental health was often addressed informally and outside of structured workflows, resulting in inconsistent screening and delayed referrals. Communication gaps across inpatient, outpatient, and behavioral health teams further fragmented care, with unclear referral ownership and poor coordination between oncology, primary care, and behavioral health services. Although behavioral health and other supportive care resources were available, their lack of standardization and visibility rendered them difficult to access. Providers emphasized that limited workforce capacity, competing demands, and the absence of clearly defined roles compounded these gaps, ultimately hindering consistent delivery of behavioral health care for cystectomy patients. CONCLUSIONS: Providers identified multilevel barriers—spanning knowledge, communication, and resource limitations—that impede integration of behavioral health services into uro-oncology care. Embedding structured psychosocial screening and designated behavioral health partnerships within the uro-oncology workflow may enhance patient outcomes and improve continuity of care. | | | --- | | |

title: CLINICAL EFFICACY OF THE AUTOMATIC TISSUE RECOGNITION FUNCTION IN A SUPER-PULSED THULIUM FIBER LASER: A MULTICENTER LITHOTRIPSY STUDY
session: Urolithiasis/Endourology (V02)
authors: Alexey Martov, Andrey Andronov, Magomed Adilhanov, Sergey Dutov, Zelimkhan Tokhtiev, Armais Kamalov, Nikolay Sorokin, Zare Gevorkyan, Daria Tsigura, Leonid Rapoport, Alim Dymov, Stanislav Ali, Temirlan Karakotov, Diana Khabib, Peter Glybochko
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Laser lithotripsy is the "gold standard" for urolithiasis treatment; however, risks of iatrogenic mucosal injury remain due to stone migration, calculus fracture, or poor endoscopic visibility. Thermal damage is particularly undesirable for ureteral stone treatment. These risks are exacerbated when inexperienced operators perform procedures. Automatic tissue recognition technologies integrated into laser systems and controlling on/off-target radiation have the potential to improve the safety of the procedure. The aim of this multicenter prospective study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the automatic tissue recognition feature (Tissue Sensor, TS) in a new-generation Super-pulsed thulium fiber laser (SP TFL) for lithotripsy of kidney and ureteral stones. METHODS: This multicenter prospective study, approved by the Ethics Committee, included 70 patients with 101 stones (22 ureteral, 48 renal). Lithotripsy was performed using a SP TFL Urolase+ Premium (VPG Laserone, Russia) with TS function. The duration of the procedure, laser time, pedal on time, energy parameters, ablation efficiency, and effectiveness were assessed. Safety was assessed using the Traxer-Sierra scale (thermal damage assessment) and the Clavien-Dindo classification (complications). The impact of TS on the effectiveness and safety of the procedure was recorded using a standardized surgeon questionnaire. RESULTS: The efficiency coefficient of TS (laser time/pedal on time) was 54% for the ureter and 69% for the kidney, demonstrating active intervention of the system to prevent off-target radiation. The incidence of thermal injuries was minimal: in the ureter group, no injuries were observed in 64% of cases (n=14), and grade 1 injuries were recorded in 36% (n=8). In the kidney group, grade 1 injuries were noted in 52% (n=25), grade 2 injuries in 10% (n=5), and no injuries in 38% (n=18) of cases. Complications (Clavien-Dindo ≥ IIIa) were absent. The stone-free rate was 100% for the ureter and 97% for the kidney. Most surgeons (73% for the ureter and 56% for the kidney) noted that TS does not significantly affect the duration of the operation. CONCLUSIONS: The automatic tissue recognition feature Tissue Sensor in the SP TFL significantly improves the safety of lithotripsy by reducing the incidence and severity of thermal mucosal injuries. The system effectively prevents off-target laser radiation in complex anatomical conditions without significantly affecting surgical duration or ablation efficacy. This technology is particularly valuable for ensuring the safety of procedures performed by surgeons of varying experience levels.

title: ALL-IN-ONE STONE MANAGEMENT: COMPLETE ENDOUROLOGICAL PROCEDURE USING ONLY A STEERABLE SUCTIONING URETEROSCOPE
session: Urolithiasis/Endourology (V02)
authors: Veda Malhotra, Shrinkhala Kaphle, Ziv Savin, Juan Serna, Blair Gallante, William M. Atallah, Mantu Gupta
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Definitive treatment of large renal calculi traditionally involves the use of percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL). However, this procedure carries significant risks, especially for patients with extensive comorbidities who may not be surgical candidates for PCNL. The new direct in scope suction (DISS) technology offers an opportunity to manage these large stone burdens in a less invasive way. The objective of this video presentation is to demonstrate the use of a DISS device as an “all-in-one” approach for cystoscopy, stent removal, renal access, stone fragmentation, and aspiration. METHODS: Definitive management of a 2.62 cm left renal stone for an 82 year old male patient was performed using the CVAC Aspiration System (Calyxo, Inc., Pleasanton, CA). The device was used to complete each procedural step, including cystoscopy, bilateral stent removal, ureteral and renal access, laser lithotripsy, and aspiration of stone fragments. The case was successfully completed without the use of a cystoscope, stent grasper, guidewire, ureteral access sheath, and ureteral stent. Only the floppy-tip introducer sheath was required to cannulate the ureteral orifice and advance into the kidney. This was replicated in four other cases. RESULTS: A total of 5 patients underwent the All-in-One Stone Management with the sole use of the DISS ureteroscope and nitinol basket. The average Charlson comorbidity index was 5.8 +/- 1.3 and average stone burden was 28 +/- 13 mm. 80% of patients were pre-stented and 80% of patients were left stent-free after the procedure. All surgeries were completed without intraoperative complications. Appropriate fluid irrigation and suction was maintained throughout the procedures without the use of ureteral access sheaths. CONCLUSIONS: In high-risk patients with large stone burdens who are poor candidates for PCNL, DISS systems offer an appropriate alternative treatment. We present the novel use of this system without the aid of cystoscopes, guidewires, or ureteral access sheaths showcasing the feasibility of this All-in-One stone management method. With this approach, patients can have a high likelihood to be left without a stent, significantly improving quality of life, and minimizing overall medical waste. | | | --- | | |

title: RETRO-MINI-PERCUTANEOUS NEPHROLITHOTOMY: DESCRIPTION OF THE TECHNIQUE, CASE SERIES, AND ADVANTAGES OF RETROPERITONEOSCOPIC ASSISTANCE IN THE TREATMENT OF PATIENTS WITH RETRO-RENAL ORGANS
session: Urolithiasis/Endourology (V02)
authors: Lucio Fila, Paolo Verri, Hernandez Pedro, Laura Más, Paula Izquierdo, Alejandra Bravo, Oriol Angerri
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: European guidelines recommend percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) as the first-line treatment for kidney stones >2 cm. However, injury to surrounding organs remains a possible complication, with colonic injury occurring in 0.3–1% of cases. A retro-renal colon, present in 0.6% of the population, represents the main risk factor. Treating patients with large stones and retro-renally located organs close to the puncture pathway remains a challenge. Techniques such as ultrasound- or laparoscopic-assisted puncture have proven effective in reducing injury risk. Retroperitoneoscopy-assisted Mini-PCNL is a less described but potentially valuable alternative. This study aims to describe the technique and outcomes of Retro-mini-percutaneous nephrolithotomy (Retro-Mini-PCNL). METHODS: We report a 45-year-old patient with a horseshoe kidney and a 2 cm, 1500 UH left renal stone associated with a retro-renal colon. The patient was positioned laterally at 45°, ensuring optimal C-arm orientation. A ureteral occlusion catheter was placed for retrograde pyelography. Retroperitoneal access was achieved using a balloon trocar, followed by fluoroscopy-guided puncture using the 0/90° technique. Tract dilation was performed up to 18 Ch, allowing access with a 12 Ch nephroscope. Lithotripsy was achieved using a Ho:YAG laser, and fragments were retrieved with a basket. The collecting system was inspected with a 16 Ch flexible nephroscope. A 6 Ch × 26 cm double-J stent and a 12 Ch Foley nephrostomy were placed. Subsequent cases were performed in a 30° modified Galdakao position, achieving both retroperitoneal access and percutaneous puncture from a single side using a split-screen view, reducing trocars from three to two and enabling an ECIRS approach. RESULTS: We present the first European case series of Retro-Mini-PCNL, including four patients (three left-sided, one right-sided). Mean operative time was 3 h 54 min, and mean hospital stay was 5 days. One patient developed a Clavien-Dindo I complication (postoperative leukocytosis), and one a Clavien-Dindo IV (septic shock requiring ICU admission). The stone-free rate was 75% (3/4). CONCLUSIONS: Retroperitoneoscopy-assisted Mini-PCNL is a feasible and safe option for patients with retro-renal organs, providing direct visualization during puncture, reduced risk of visceral injury, and favorable clinical outcomes.

title: ROBOTIC-ASSISTED MINI-PERCUTANEOUS NEPHROLITHOTOMY WITH THE MONARCH PLATFORM, UROLOGY
session: Urolithiasis/Endourology (V02)
authors: Margaret A. Knoedler, Emily C. Serrell
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) is the standard of care for treating large renal stones. The MONARCH™ Platform, Urology (Johnson & Johnson) is a novel FDA-cleared flexible robotic platform that combines robotic-assisted flexible ureteroscopy (URS) and mini-percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) with electromagnetically guided percutaneous access. METHODS: This is a 61-year-old male who presented with 2 cm lower pole stone and multiple interpolar stones for a total stone burden of 3.5 cm. The patient was taken to the operating room where a cystoscopy was performed and a ureteral access sheath placed. The robotic arms were positioned next to the patient and the ureteroscope advanced to the renal pelvis by using the handheld controller. An interpolar calyx was chosen for percutaneous access based on preoperative CT and intraoperative ureteroscopic evaluation. The electromagnetic guidance system was used to gain access into the intended calyx on the first attempt and a percutaneous sheath placed. The ureteroscope with a laser was used to fragment stones while a flexible percutaneous suction catheter removed stone fragments. The ureteroscope, laser, suction catheter as well as the fluidics system were controlled with a handheld controller. When the patient was deemed to be stone free by visual assessment of the collecting system the MONARCH™ system was undocked and a ureteral stent was placed. RESULTS: The operative time was 2 hours and 44 minutes. Imaging on POD1 showed no residual fragments and the patient was discharged from the hospital. The stent was removed one week later. The stone analysis showed calcium oxalate 82% and calcium phosphate 18%. The patient recovered without complications. CONCLUSIONS: Our initial experience suggests a future where MONARCH™ robot-assisted mini-PCNL may provide urologists with expanded capabilities for safe and effective treatment of select patients with nephrolithiasis.

title: SIMULTANEOUS BILATERAL ENDOSCOPIC SURGERY: MINI-PERCUTANEOUS NEPHROLITHOTOMY WITH PULSED THULIUM YAG AND FLEXIBLE URETEROSCOPE WITH THULIUM LASER FIBER
session: Urolithiasis/Endourology (V02)
authors: Lucio Fila, Paolo Verri, Hernandez Pedro, Laura Más, Paula Izquierdo, Alejandra Bravo, Andrés Kanashiro, Raúl Sánchez-Molina, Farré Alba, Oriol Angerri
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Simultaneous bilateral endoscopic surgery (SBES) is a well-described and evolving technique for the treatment of bilateral renal stones in a single surgical session. The advantages of this approach include fewer hospital admissions, reduced need for anesthesia, and optimized use of surgical and hospital resources—while maintaining patient safety and achieving high stone-free rates with minimal complications. Several modalities of SBES exist, including simultaneous PCNL, simultaneous ureteroscopy, or a combination of both performed concurrently on each renal unit. The optimal choice of laser energy remains undefined, highlighting the need for further studies with newer laser technologies. METHODS: A 70-year-old female with a history of bilateral nephrolithiasis was diagnosed with bilateral renal stones. On the right side, stones were located in the lower calyceal group (LCG), with the largest measuring 14 mm and 1400 HU. On the left, stones were present in the middle and lower calyceal groups, measuring 7 mm and 14 mm, respectively, with 1190 HU. After an episode of obstructive pyelonephritis, bilateral double-J stents were placed. Under general anesthesia and in the Galdakao-modified supine Valdivia position, simultaneous 18 CH mini-PCNL was performed using a 0–90° puncture technique and balloon dilation to 18 CH with a high-pressure balloon. A 12 CH rigid nephroscope (“M” mini-perc set) was used. Lithotripsy of the right renal stones was performed using a pulsed Thulium:YAG laser. Subsequently, a flexible 18 CH cystoscope was used to access stones in other locations. On the left side, retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS) was performed using a 9.5 CH LithoVue flexible ureteroscope with Thulium Fiber Laser (TFL) in dusting mode. Bilateral double-J stents were left in place, and no nephrostomy tube was placed on the right. RESULTS: Operative time was 120 minutes, with no intraoperative or postoperative complications. The patient was discharged 16 hours after surgery. A follow-up CT scan revealed mild right-sided pelvicalyceal ectasia with narrowing at the ureteropelvic junction suggestive of ostium syndrome, but no significant residual stone fragments. CONCLUSIONS: SBES is a promising option for managing bilateral nephrolithiasis in a single session. However, careful patient selection remains critical for its successful implementation.

title: FLUOROSCOPIC-FREE ULTRASOUND-GUIDED PERCUTANEOUS NEPHROLITHOTOMY: SURGICAL TECHNIQUE
session: Urolithiasis/Endourology (V02)
authors: Evan Garden, Ali Hamlani, Veda Malhotra, Juan Serna, Ziv Savin, Blair Gallante, Mantu Gupta, William Atallah
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Historically, percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) has been performed with fluoroscopic guidance to establish access in the collecting system. However, use of intraoperative ultrasonography (US) has provided comparable outcomes while safely reducing radiation exposure and minimizing costs associated with fluoroscopy. Here, we present our technique for fluoroscopic-free US-guided PCNL. METHODS: The patient is a 45-year-old-female with an obstructing 1.5 centimeter proximal ureteral stone with moderate hydronephrosis. Once general anesthesia is established, the patient is placed in the supine flank-free position. First, complete sonographic assessment of the kidney is performed; Doppler mode is used to identify areas of increased vascularity to avoid when obtaining access. Under US guidance, an 18-gauge needle is inserted into the collecting system, and the needle’s depth of advancement is noted. A sensor wire is advanced into the collecting system and once confirmed sonographically, the needle is removed. All instruments are marked to the appropriate depth of advancement. The percutaneous tract is established through serial dilation with a 10Fr fascial dilator, followed by balloon dilation, and finally a 24Fr sheath – at each step, proper placement and depth of advancement is confirmed both sonographically and via markings made on the instruments. PCNL is then performed and all stone fragments are removed. Upon completion, a double-J stent is placed and stent position is confirmed endoscopically. RESULTS: Patient was discharged home on postoperative day 0 and stent was removed on postoperative day 9. She suffered no postoperative complications. Stone analysis showed stone composition of 90% calcium oxalate dihydrate, 5% calcium oxalate monohydrate, and 5% calcium phosphate. Between August-October 2025, 53 patients underwent fluoroscopic-free US-guided PCNL at our institution, of which 77% (n=41) were ambulatory and 57% (n=30) were totally tubeless. The median operative time was 59.2 minutes and no intra-operative complications were noted. 11% (n=6) of patients visited the ER postoperatively, and 7% (n=4) required readmission. CONCLUSIONS: Fluoroscopic-free US-guided PCNL is a feasible and effective technique for the surgical management of stone disease.

title: MINIATURIZING URETEROSCOPY: NOVEL USE OF AN 8/10FR URETERAL DILATOR AS A URETERAL ACCESS SHEATH WITH A 6.3FR SINGLE-USE FLEXIBLE URETEROSCOPE
session: Urolithiasis/Endourology (V02)
authors: Juan S. Serna, Kenny Chin, Veda Malhotra, Ziv Savin, Shrinkhala Kaphle, William Atallah, Mantu Gupta
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The ureteral access sheath (UAS) is one of the most commonly employed tools during retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS). Flexible ureteroscope sizes have dictated UAS size, thus their relatively large size often raises concerns of ureteral wall ischemia and need for post-procedure stent placement. In some cases, insertion of the UAS is not possible or may cause ureteral injuries leading to case cancellations. The new 6.3Fr single-use flexible ureteroscopes offer new opportunities to miniaturize RIRS. The goal of this video is to demonstrate the feasibility of using an 8/10Fr ureteral dilator as a UAS with a 6.3Fr flexible ureteroscope in RIRS. METHODS: Definitive management of a right 11 mm renal stone for a 76 year old male patient was performed using the 6.3Fr single-use flexible ureteroscope (HugeMed, Inc., Shenzen, China). The ureteroscope is first used to place a sensor wire followed by passage of a standard 8/10Fr ureteral dilator. The wire and 8Fr dilator are then removed allowing easy passage of the 6.3Fr ureteroscope. The ureteral stone is fragmented in standard fashion and the renal stone is extracted through the 10Fr sheath without difficulty utilizing gravity irrigation. The case was successfully completed without the need for a post-procedure ureteral stent. This was replicated in five other cases. RESULTS: A total of 6 patients underwent the 8/10Fr UAS with a 6.3Fr flexible ureteroscope. Patients tended to be younger with an average age of 46.2 +/- 23.6 years and an average stone burden of 10.5 +/- 5.8 mm. All patients were not pre-stented and did not require stent placement at the conclusion of the procedure. All surgeries were completed without intraoperative complications with an average operative time of 31.2 +/- 8.3 minutes. CONCLUSIONS: We present the novel use of an 8/10Fr ureteral dilator as a UAS in conjunction with a 6.3Fr single-use flexible ureteroscope. This approach affords the benefits of a UAS while minimizing the trauma to the ureter that traditionally-sized UAS may cause and maintaining the 0.75 ureteroscope to sheath ratio described in the literature. Furthermore, this atraumatic approach reduces the need for post-procedure ureteral stent placement. Miniaturizing RIRS appears to be of special benefit for younger patients, patients with a history of ureteral stricture formation, or first-time stone formers who may have narrow ureters to begin with. | | | --- | | |

title: THE FAST AND THE FRICTIONLESS: CAPABILITIES OF A 6.3FR SINGLE-USE DIGITAL FLEXIBLE URETEROSCOPE
session: Urolithiasis/Endourology (V02)
authors: Michael Uy, Wilson Sui, Casey Dauw, Khurshid Ghani
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The advent of flexible ureteroscopy (URS) has transformed endourology, enabling safe and effective management of renal stones and upper tract urothelial carcinoma. However, traditional reusable ureteroscopes remain limited by progressive image degradation, instrument weight, and difficulty accessing narrow ureters due to scope diameter. The introduction of a thin single-use digital ureteroscope may potentially broaden clinical applications of URS. In this teaching video, we demonstrate the unique capabilities of a 6.3Fr flexible ureteroscope using real-world surgical scenarios. METHODS: Five representative clinical cases were collected to illustrate the range of performance of a 6.3Fr ureteroscope (HugeMed, China). All cases were performed by one of two surgeons at a tertiary academic center. Surgical footage was recorded and edited for educational presentation. Demonstrated applications included: wireless ureteric access and stent omission; upper tract tumor ablation; sheathless antegrade URS; office-based awake URS for oncologic surveillance; and endoscopic-guided percutaneous access for complex stone disease. Technical parameters such as operative feasibility, visual clarity, surgeon scope handling, were narratively reported. RESULTS: Across all five cases, the 6.3Fr ureteroscope demonstrated excellent image quality, maneuverability, and clinical versatility. 1. Stent omission for stones: surgical access was achieved without a guidewire or need for postoperative stent, with atraumatic passage under direct vision; 2. Tumor ablation: providing clear visualization and continuous irrigation through the 3.6Fr working channel; 3. Sheathless antegrade ureteroscopy for impacted ureteral stone: over a working wire without tract dilation or need for access sheath, allowing better two-handed control for fragmentation; 4. In-office awake URS: completed without general anesthesia, with the patient reporting minimal discomfort (pain score rated 0 - 1/10); and, 5. Endoscopic-guided percutaneous access: the slim profile allowed direct-vision puncture and tract dilation in the setting of a complete staghorn and tight space. No intraoperative complications occurred across all cases. CONCLUSIONS: The 6.3Fr single-use digital flexible ureteroscope demonstrates excellent visualization, ergonomics, and access capability across a wide spectrum of endourologic applications. Future work will clarify additional indications and technical limitations of these smaller diameter instruments, enabling more tailored, goal-directed surgical management.

title: TIPS AND TECHNIQUES FOR MAXIMIZING EFFICIENCY WITH FLEXIBLE AND NAVIGABLE SUCTION (FANS) URETERAL ACCESS SHEATHS
session: Urolithiasis/Endourology (V02)
authors: Veerain K. Gupta, Levi Bowers, Nicole L. Miller
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Flexible and Navigable Suction (FANS) ureteral access sheaths represent a significant advancement in retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS) by combining access and suction in a single device. The ClearPetra sheath is the first FANS system approved by the U. S. FDA (February 2024) and has been shown to have improved outcomes when compared to RIRS without suction and mini-percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL). This video demonstrates tips and technical maneuvers to maximize efficiency and safety when using the ClearPetra access sheath. METHODS: Through a series of example videos, we showcase advanced techniques that may improve surgeon efficiency while utilizing a ClearPetra sheath. We detail indications for use, sheath anatomy, appropriate setup, and stepwise surgical maneuvers. RESULTS: Key technical insights are demonstrated throughout this video. Proper setup and selection of an appropriately sized sheath are essential for the safe and effective use of the ClearPetra system. Lasering stones located distal to the sheath enables passive suction of fine fragments and stone dust. Intra-sheath lasering is a safe and effective technique for dislodging and removing stones trapped within the sheath itself. For stone debris embedded in blood clots or located in challenging anatomical locations, gentle manipulation of the sheath against the calyces and renal pelvis, referred to as the “raking” maneuver, facilitates clearance. In cases where the sheath cannot access all calyces, simultaneous irrigation via the ureteroscope and aspiration through the ClearPetra helps mobilize and evacuate residual fragments. When used synergistically, these techniques significantly enhance the sheath’s overall utility and procedural efficiency. CONCLUSIONS: The ClearPetra FANS ureteral access sheath integrates suction and flexibility to improve visualization, efficiency, and stone clearance during ureteroscopy. Achieving optimal outcomes requires a thorough understanding of sheath anatomy, careful selection of sheath size, and proficiency in suction modulation techniques. These practical insights may help urologists safely adopt and fully leverage the advantages of FANS technology in retrograde stone surgery.

title: ROBOTIC RETROGRADE INTRARENAL SURGERY USING FLEXIBLE AND NAVIGABLE SUCTION URETERAL ACCESS SHEATH (ROBOTIC FANS-RIRS): INITIAL FEASIBILITY ASSESSMENT WITH ZAMENIX ROBOTIC FLEXIBLE URETEROSCOPY PLATFORM IN A PORCINE MODEL
session: Urolithiasis/Endourology (V02)
authors: Sung Yong Cho, Jose Carlo Reyes Elises, Hyomyoung Lee, Hyunwoo Baek, Dong-Geol Lee, Jae Chul Kim, Kyu Seob Song, Joonhwan Kim, Dong-Soo Kwon, Dong-Ho Lee
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This study aims to evaluate the initial feasibility of robotic retrograde intrarenal surgery using a flexible and navigable suction ureteral access sheath (Robotic FANS-RIRS), with the Zamenix robotic flexible ureteroscopy platform. In this video, various robotic surgical techniques were assessed in a porcine model. METHODS: The Zamenix robotic system enables a single surgeon to control a ureteral access sheath (UAS), ureteroscope, and surgical tools (laser or basket) from a console. We enhanced the robot's capabilities by incorporating the flexible and navigable suction ureteral access sheath (FANS) and multiple control modes for both the FANS and ureteroscope. The following instruments were used: 7.5 Fr (HU30S), 9.5 Fr URS (Lithovue), 11/13 Fr FANS (ZSR), and a thulium fiber laser (EMS). We tested the accessibility to renal calyces, stone dusting, and the retrieval of stone fragments using active suction. An assistant controlled the vent slider on the FANS suction port during retrieval procedures. Ureteral injury was also assessed after the procedures. A total of eight artificial stones were used in this trial, distributed across three renal units in three pigs. RESULTS: Basic manipulation of the FANS and ureteroscope was successful, allowing access to all renal calyces. During the stone dusting procedure, stones were effectively trapped and pulverized while maintaining a stable position. A total of 26 active-suction extraction trials were performed, resulting in the removal of 35 stone fragments. All fragments were successfully extracted, with an average pull-out time of 37.3 seconds. One Grade I ureteral injury was observed postoperatively, likely related to initial ureteral dilation during FANS insertion. Insufficient suction pressure due to air leakage at the robot–FANS connector was identified as the primary factor limiting extraction efficiency. CONCLUSIONS: Robotic FANS-RIRS using the Zamenix robotic flexible ureteroscopy platform demonstrated technical feasibility in a porcine model, with all procedures successfully completed and no major safety issues identified. Further studies are needed to validate the efficacy of the system for clinical application.

title: FAST-PCNL (FLUOROSCOPY FREE, AMBULATORY, SUPINE, AND TOTALLY TUBELESS PERCUTANEOUS NEPHROLITHOTOMY)
session: Urolithiasis/Endourology (V02)
authors: Shrinkhala Kaphle
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) has evolved from a complex inpatient operation into a streamlined, minimally invasive procedure through steady progress in imaging, access, and instrumentation. The FAST-PCNL technique incorporates these modern refinements: ultrasound-guided access, supine positioning, a totally tubeless approach, and an ambulatory workflow into one cohesive system. The goal of this technique is to minimize radiation exposure, reduce operative time and hospital dependence, and simplify recovery, while maintaining the safety and stone-free outcomes of standard PCNL. METHODS: Between August and October 2025, 21 patients underwent FAST-PCNL. Procedures were performed entirely under ultrasound guidance in the modified supine position using endoscopic combined intrarenal surgery (ECIRS). After stone clearance was confirmed through dual antegrade and retrograde visualization, the tract was sealed with a hemostatic agent without nephrostomy or ureteral stent placement. All patients were monitored in PACU (Post Anesthesia Care Unit) and Phase 2 recovery before same-day discharge. Primary endpoints included intraoperative safety, operative time, and 30-day complications. RESULTS: There were no intraoperative complications and the mean operative time 54 minutes. All patients were discharged on the day of surgery with a mean total stay of 3 hours 50 minutes post-procedure.
