During the 30-day follow-up of 11 patients, one emergency visit and one hospital readmission were recorded. No secondary interventions were required. CONCLUSIONS: FAST-PCNL demonstrates that a radiation-free, supine, totally tubeless PCNL can be safely completed within a six-hour ambulatory window. By combining ultrasound guidance, ECIRS precision, and tubeless closure, this technique minimizes radiation exposure, hospital resource utilization, and postoperative morbidity while maintaining safety and efficiency in appropriately selected patients.

title: FLEXIBLE AND NAVIGABLE SUCTION URETERAL ACCESS SHEATH (FANS): TIPS AND TRICKS ON EFFECTIVE USAGE
session: Urolithiasis/Endourology (V02)
authors: Jenny N. Guo, Amir S. Patel, Nabila Khondakar, Amy E. Krambeck
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Flexible and navigable Suction Ureteral Access Sheaths (FANS) are a recent development in ureteral access sheaths that incorporate a suction mechanism along with a flexible tip allowing for more effective stone removal during flexible ureteroscopy (URS). In this video, we will describe the components of FANS and tips and tricks on how to effectively utilize a novel technique with FANS for treatment of renal and ureteral stones. METHODS: The FANS has several unique features. First, the flexible distal segment allows for full deflection into hard-to-reach calyces. The pressure vent has holes that allow for adjustment of aspiration pressure. The watertight rubber seal ensures air tightness and prevents leakage of irrigation fluid. The oblique side branch connects to a stone collection canister and vacuum suction that allows for aspiration of stone fragments. The canister has an on/off valve that allows for manual control of the suction pressure. RESULTS: For treatment of proximal ureteral stones using FANS, we recommend dusting at 0.3J and 60Hz while keeping the ventilation holes partially uncovered. We intermittently occlude the holes with our fingers to manually control the suction pressure. For treatment of renal stones, we recommend dusting at 0.3J and 120Hz with holmium pulse modulation for softer stones and fragmenting at 1-2J and 10-20Hz for harder stones. When extracting stone fragments after lasering, we recommend covering the ventilation holes completely with the tubing to allow for maximal suction. Keep the suction set between 150-200 mm Hg and irrigation pressure between 200 to 300 mm Hg. In general, try to use the shortest sheath length that can reach the calyces. Positioning the patient in slight reverse Trendelenburg can also aid in more efficient stone extraction. FANS can be very effective for small stones, which can be aspirated around the scope. Withdraw the scope only for larger stones which cannot be suctioned around the scope. This technique helps avoid the need for routine basketing. Intermittently switch the suction on and off to allow for effective suction while preserving good irrigation flow and visualization. If the stone fragments are too large or stuck inside the sheath, gently lasering while inside the sheath can assist with better suction and more efficient stone extraction. When withdrawing the scope, the tip of the scope should be deflected up or down to enhance the Venturi effect. CONCLUSIONS: FANS are the future of ureteroscopy and has several benefits including limiting intrarenal pressure while improving stone clearance rates and operative efficiency.

title: COMPARISON OF D-MANNOSE IN FOODS WITH URINE PH IN POST-MENOPAUSAL WOMEN WITH RECURRENT URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Juliann M. Chavez, Alana L. Christie, Philippe E. Zimmern
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: D-mannose supplementation and/or acidic pH in the bladder may prevent recurrent urinary tract infections (RUTIs) in women, but the mechanism supporting this effect is not well understood. Therefore, we investigated whether post-menopausal (PM) women with a history of RUTI and known urinary pH levels had different dietary regimens with regards to d-mannose intake, as reported and analyzed in diet and urine pH diaries. METHODS: Following internal review board approval, women used urinalysis reagent strips to record their urine pH four times per day and concurrently completed a three-day food diary. Two groups were identified based on urine pH: predominantly below pH 6, and predominantly above pH 6. Nutrient content of reported foods and supplements was analyzed and compared between the two urine pH groups. RESULTS: Fifty-seven women, ages 64-75 years were recruited. Patients tended to consume more d-mannose at breakfast compared to dinner. No significant differences were found in the amount of d-mannose or other nutrients consumed between the two urine pH groups. D-mannose-containing foods contained significantly more protein, carbohydrates, fat, calcium, iron, and water than non-d-mannose-containing foods (all p<0.01). Slight variations in consumptions of fiber, sugar, and sodium were found between groups. The amount of d-mannose foods consumed by weight was typically lower than found in recommended supplemental doses but was occasionally present in the diet at levels similar to the supplemental dose. CONCLUSIONS: In this limited single-institution study, we report no difference in dietary d-mannose levels consumed among PM women with a history of RUTI, regardless of their urinary pH level. Of note, when d-mannose supplementation is considered, it should be recommended at dinner given the low dietary intake at that meal.

title: UTI AND RECURRENT UTI-FREE SURVIVAL FOLLOWING ELECTROFULGURATION
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Stephanie V. Armstrong, Feras Alhalabi, Philippe E. Zimmern, Amyn A. Malik
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Recurrent UTIs (rUTI) contribute to significant morbidity and impaired quality of life. Electrofulguration (EF) of areas of chronic cystitis harboring deep seated bacteria (1) is an outpatient procedure increasingly used in antibiotic-recalcitrant rUTI cases; however, its long-term effectiveness and the impact of patient age and cystitis severity on outcomes remain to be fully characterized. METHODS: To evaluate UTI-free survival and recurrent UTI-free survival following EF and to assess the role of age and cystitis stage in predicting infection risk after EF we conducted a retrospective cohort study of 601 women with chronic, culture-confirmed UTIs who underwent EF between 2006 and 2024. Kaplan-Meier survival analyses and log-rank tests were used to compare survival outcomes by age group and cystitis stage (from 1-trigonitis to 4-pancystitis). Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models evaluated the independent associations of age and stage with each outcome. RESULTS: During follow up, 291 patients (48.4%) developed a post-EF UTI. The median time to first UTI was 50 months (95% CI: 40.8–64.8; (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191308.46584.7c.02#F1)). Increasing age was associated with higher risk of UTI (aHR=1.01 per year; 95% CI: 1.00–1.02; p=0.013), with median UTI-free survival time declining from 87.1 months in patients <50 years old to 24.1 months in patients who were ≥ 80 years old. Compared to patients with Stage 1 cystitis, patients with Stage 4 had a significantly shorter median UTI-free survival (24.5 vs. 69.3 months; aHR: 1.90, 95% CI: 1.33–2.71; p<0.001). Recurrent UTIs occurred in 87 (14.5%) patients, with a median time of recurrence at 153 months. Older age (aHR: 1.02; 95% CI: 1.00–1.04; p=0.019) and Stage 4 cystitis (aHR=3.23, 95% CI: 1.78–5.85; p<0.001) were again independently associated with higher risk of recurrent UTI. CONCLUSIONS: EF offers meaningful benefit in prolonging UTI-free survival among women with antibiotic-recalcitrant rUTI. However, its effectiveness is influenced by baseline cystitis severity and patient age. Ref 1 De Nisco NJ. et al. JMB 2019.

title: THE PREDICTIVE VALUE OF SERUM PROCALCITONIN FOR IDENTIFYING THERAPEUTIC FAILURE IN UROSEPSIS CAUSED BY MULTIDRUG-RESISTANT UROPATHOGENS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Alberto Saldivar Luna, Alan Rodrigo Perez Soriano, Rodrigo Perez Becerra, Victor Osornio Sanchez, Luis Trujillo Ortiz, Gerardo Garza Sainz, Ruben Miguel Santiago Gonzalez, Omar Vieyra Valdez, Genaro Arguelles Morales, Mario Alberto Toledo Diaz, Adrian Martinez Correa, Aaron Delgado Corral, Carina Nolasco, Gerardo Flores, Carlos A. Castro Fuentes, Montserrat Perez Rojas
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The rising prevalence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) uropathogens complicates urosepsis management, leading to increased therapeutic failure. This creates a clinical dilemma in identifying high-risk patients who need aggressive therapy, underscoring the need for objective biomarkers. This study aimed to rigorously evaluate the predictive ability of serial serum procalcitonin (PCT) to accurately identify patients with complicated pyelonephritis at high risk of an unfavorable clinical course. METHODS: A retrospective, observational study was conducted on a cohort of 40 patients (n=15 failure, n=25 success) hospitalized for complicated pyelonephritis. PCT levels were measured at admission, 48 hours, and day 5. Therapeutic failure was defined as the need for antibiotic escalation, unplanned urological intervention, or persistence of septic signs. The biomarker's discriminative ability was assessed using ROC curves, with optimal cutoffs determined by the Youden index. A multivariate logistic regression model was built to confirm PCT as an independent predictor. RESULTS: PCT levels were significantly higher in patients who experienced therapeutic failure at all three time points: admission (p=0.002), 48 hours (p=0.001), and most conclusively at day 5 (p<0.0001). The biomarker's predictive ability (AUC) improved over time, from 0.79 at admission to an excellent 0.93 on day 5. The optimal day 5 threshold of >1.11 ng/mL yielded a sensitivity of 87% and a specificity of 88%. In the multivariate logistic regression model, Day 5 PCT was the significant independent predictor of therapeutic failure. The odds of failure increased over six-fold for each 1 ng/mL rise in Day 5 PCT (Odds Ratio: 6.62; 95% CI: 1.85-23.6; p=0.004), confirming its robust predictive power irrespective of other clinical variables. CONCLUSIONS: Serial monitoring of procalcitonin is a high-value, dynamic tool for risk stratification and prediction of therapeutic failure in complex urosepsis. While an initial PCT level upon admission serves as an important early alert, a persistently elevated level above 1.11 ng/mL on day 5 is a highly accurate and independent indicator of an impending unfavorable outcome. This finding provides an objective, data-driven framework for evidence-based decisions at the bedside. It allows to personalize antimicrobial therapy, directly supporting modern stewardship goals by providing a rationale for safely de-escalating antibiotic therapy in the low-risk subgroup (PCT <1.11 ng/mL) and justifying the early, aggressive treatment for the confirmed high-risk subgroup.

title: RE-DEFINING MODIFIED NEWS2 SCORE FOR EMPHYSEMATOUS PYELONEPHRITIS (EPN): DEVELOPMENT OF A BIOCLINICAL HYBRID MODEL (MNEWS2-B) INTEGRATING SERUM LACTATE, NEUTROPHIL–LYMPHOCYTE RATIO, AND PROCALCITONIN FOR EARLY TRIAGE AND CLINICAL DECISION-MAKING
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Sriram Krishnamoorthy
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Emphysematous pyelonephritis (EPN) is a fulminant necrotizing infection where rapid triage dictates survival. The National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2) is ubiquitous for escalation, yet its broad upper tier (scores 7–20) conflates heterogeneous risk, potentially blunting triage precision. We hypothesized that re-binning NEWS2 into a modified, trichotomized scheme (mNEWS2-B) would sharpen prognostication and operational decision-making in EPN. METHODS: We conducted a single-centre cohort study of consecutive EPN admissions (July 2020–June 2025). Based on pilot overlap, we prespecified mNEWS2 strata: 0–6 (low), 7–14 (intermediate), 15–20 (critical). Group differences were analyzed using chi-square tests and ANOVA with post hoc testing. Discrimination for mortality was assessed using logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic analysis. Serum lactate, Neutrophil–Lymphocyte Ratio (NLR), and procalcitonin (PCT) were incorporated as biochemical markers to derive the bioclinical hybrid model (mNEWS2-B). RESULTS: Among 194 consecutive admissions, the distribution across mNEWS2 strata was: 0–6 (low) n=93 (47.9%), 7–14 (intermediate) n=89 (45.9%), and 15–20 (critical) n=12 (6.2%). Mortality was distinctly segregated across tiers: 0/93 (0%), 1/89 (1.12%), and 7/12 (58.33%), respectively (p<0.01). Escalation needs rose stepwise with severity: ICU care in 9.68%, 58.43%, and 100% (p<0.01); hemodialysis in 5.38%, 21.35%, and 91.67% (p<0.01). Procedural pathways diverged with risk; double-J stenting was needed in 56.9%, 94.4%, and 50% of cases (p<0.01); early nephrectomy was performed in 0%, 3.37%, and 50% of cases (p<0.01). Mean platelet count declined from 220,598/µL to 119,735/µL and 54,575/µL (p<0.001), serum sodium decreased from 131.7 to 131.7 and 123.6 mEq/L (p<0.001), and serum creatinine increased from 3.3 to 4.1 and 5.1 mg/dL (p=0.01). Using NEWS2 ≥15 to predict mortality maximized overall performance: sensitivity 87.5%, specificity 97.3%, PPV 58.3%, NPV 99.4%, accuracy 96.9%, with an AUC of 0.986. CONCLUSIONS: Modified NEWS2 enhances risk stratification, concentrating mortality and high-intensity care within the ≥15 stratum. Incorporating serum lactate, NLR, and procalcitonin into this framework (mNEWS2-B) amplifies discriminatory precision by aligning physiological instability with metabolic and inflammatory biomarkers. This bioclinical hybrid model demonstrates exceptional rule-out reliability, offering a pragmatic, evidence-based triage instrument to facilitate timely ICU transfer, renal support, and surgical decision-making in uroseptic emergencies.

title: NON-ANTIBIOTIC HERBAL THERAPY (BNO 1045) VERSUS ANTIBIOTIC THERAPY (NITROFURANTOIN) FOR THE TREATMENT OF LOCALISED URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS IN WOMEN: A RETROSPECTIVE, REAL-WORLD, MULTICENTRE STUDY
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Mustafa Kadihasanoglu, Emre Cinislioglu, Nazan Cinislioglu, Oner Odabas, Emre Uzun, Halil Lutfi Canat, Cagri Sevik, Alper Otunctemur, Eyyup Danis, Baris Altay, Nihat Ogut, Ates Kadioglu
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Localised urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most frequent infections in women and are traditionally managed with antibiotics. Increasing antimicrobial resistance has driven interest in non-antibiotic alternatives. This study aimed to retrospectively compare the clinical effectiveness and safety of the herbal combination BNO 1045 and nitrofurantoin in women treated for localised UTI in a real-world clinical setting. METHODS: Female patients aged ≥18 years diagnosed with localised UTI were retrospectively analysed. Group 1 received oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days, while Group 2 received BNO 1045 three times daily. Acute Cystitis Symptom Scores (ACSS) were assessed at baseline and on day 7 post-treatment. Treatment failure was defined as persistent symptoms requiring additional antibiotic therapy. Adverse events (AEs) were also recorded. RESULTS: A total of 511 patients were included in this interim analysis (226 in Group 1 and 285 in Group 2). Mean age was 32.8 ± 7.1 years in Group 1 and 30.2 ± 6.5 years in Group 2 (p=0.57). Baseline ACSS scores were comparable (12.85 ± 2.15 vs. 12.92 ± 1.78, p=0.68). On day 7, both groups showed significant improvement (mean ACSS 3.94 ± 0.30 vs. 4.03 ± 0.76, p=0.068). Clinical success rates were 91.6% for nitrofurantoin and 93.0% for BNO 1045, with an absolute difference of +1.39% (95% CI: –3.25% to +6.37%), remaining within the non-inferiority margin of 3.25%. AEs occurred in 6.2% and 6.3% of patients, respectively (p=0.093), all mild and non-serious (mainly abdominal pain and nausea). CONCLUSIONS: Both nitrofurantoin and BNO 1045 achieved significant symptom relief with comparable efficacy and safety. BNO 1045 may represent a suitable non-antibiotic alternative for selected women with localised UTI, potentially reducing unnecessary antibiotic exposure.

title: SERPINS AS MEDIATORS OF TUBULAR DAMAGE IN CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Mohammadreza Kasravi, Georgina Gyarmati, Rachael R. Wen, Janos Peti-Peterdi, Sargis Sedrakyan, Roger De Filippo, Laura Perin, Stefano Da Sacco
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: A hallmark of many chronic kidney diseases (CKDs) is the disruption of the glomerular filtration barrier (GFB). Persistent injury to GFB components triggers inflammatory cascades and glomerular–tubular crosstalk dysfunction, ultimately driving proteinuria and nephron loss. Despite its importance, the molecular mechanisms linking GFB injury to downstream urinary system and tubular compartment inflammation and fibrosis remain poorly understood. This study aims to elucidate the role of Serpin A3 as a mediator of renal inflammation and tubulovascular injury contributing to CKD progression using our model of CKD, Alport Syndrome (AS), a hereditary disease characterized by progressive glomerular injury leading to renal failure. METHODS: To characterize renal damage, Digital Spatial Profiling and scRNA-seq were performed on human biopsies. Using human renal cells derived from healthy individuals or Alport patients, we generated a glomerulus on a chip (GOAC) and an Alport glomerulus on a chip (AS-GOAC) and re-created the GFB in vitro. GOAC and AS-GOAC were characterized by immunofluorescence (IF). Filtrate was collected for proteomics analysis to identify molecular mediators of injury. To study glomerular tubular crosstalk, we generated a tubule on a chip (PTOAC), using human primary proximal tubular cells. Characterization was performed by IF. PTOACs were exposed to Serpin A3 for up to 7 days, and injury was evaluated by IF and by measuring Kidney Injury Molecule-1 (KIM-1) expression in the filtrates. RESULTS: Proteomic analysis of GOAC filtrates revealed significantly increased levels of Serpin A3, a protease inhibitor previously linked to inflammatory tissue injury. Digital Spatial Profiling and scRNA-seq data confirmed glomerular endothelial cell–specific upregulation of Serpin A3 and dysregulation of vascular integrity genes in human AS kidneys. In the PTOAC, Serpin A3 exposure induced tubular injury, evidenced by increased KIM-1 expression as well as loss of phenotype and function. CONCLUSIONS: Our data identify Serpins as key mediators linking glomerular injury to tubular damage in CKD. Multiomic and nephron-on-a-chip analyses show that Serpin A3 dysregulation disrupts tubulovascular homeostasis, while its elevated urinary levels in renal failure suggest a broader inflammatory role along the urinary system. Targeting Serpin A3 may offer a novel strategy to reduce renal inflammation and preserve kidney function.

title: DIFFERENCES IN THE PREVALENCE OF RECURRENT URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS IN WOMEN BASED ON DIETARY HABITS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Jacqueline Comiter, Christopher Elliott, Gary Fraser, Roy Mathew, Craig V. Comiter
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Different strains of bacteria may colonize the gut based on dietary factors. Over the past two decades, antibiotic consumption has doubled—70% of which is used in animal husbandry—allowing resistant bacteria to enter the food chain. As a result, individuals who consume meat may be more likely to harbor antibiotic-resistant bacteria as part of their fecal flora, with those who eat a plant-based diet harboring less virulent strains. We hypothesize that female vegetarians and vegans have a lower rate of recurrent UTI (rUTI) compared to non-vegetarians. METHODS: We performed a cross-sectional study of participants in the Adventist Health Study-2 (AHS-2) from whom detailed dietary and urinary history were collected. Participants were classified as vegan, lacto-ovo-vegetarian, pesco-vegetarian, and non-vegetarian. Within the AHS-2 study, there was also an assessment of UTI history. Other variables included were: age, BMI, race, diabetes and menopausal status. RESULTS: 57,252 women had complete data. Average age was 58 years. More than half (53.7%) of participants were non-vegetarian, 28.5% lacto-ovo-vegetarian, 10.3% pesco-vegetarian and 7.5% vegan. A history of rUTI was reported by 13.1%. Risk of rUTI increased with age, non-Black race, higher BMI, diabetes and menopause. The rate of reported rUTI significantly varied with diet: the highest prevalence of rUTI was in non-vegetarians (14.2%), followed by pesco-vegetarians (13.5%), lacto-ovo-vegetarians (11.6%) and vegans (10.3%, p<.001). On multivariate regression, age, race, diabetes and menopause remained significant factors associated with rUTI. Additionally, diet maintained a statistically significant association with rUTI, with lacto-ovo-vegetarians and vegans at lower risk than pesco-vegetarians and non-vegetarians. CONCLUSIONS: Compared to nonvegetarians, lacto-ovo-vegetarians and vegans have a 23% and 31% lower association of rUTI. In an age of increasing bacterial resistance, non-antibiotic prophylactic interventions with dietary modification to a more plant-based diet may add to the armamentarium for managing rUTI.

title: PEE-LEASE, NOT AGAIN! WOMEN TACKLING UTIS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Regine B. Sanchez, Bernadette M. M. Zwaans, Priya Padmanabhan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are common among females in the urology outpatient clinic. Over-the-counter testing and symptom relief products are more commonplace and available. We assess how women manage their UTIs and utilize preventative practices in their daily lives. METHODS: This is a cross-sectional study of women ≥18 with history of UTIs. An anonymous electronic survey was distributed using the ResearchMatchTM database. UTIs during pregnancies were excluded from the study. The questionnaire included 27 multiple-choice questions assessing patients’ history of UTIs, home remedies, and preventative practices. Consent to participate was implied with completion of the survey. RESULTS: 1186 women aged ≥18 completed the survey questionnaire. The majority of respondents (61.9%) are either peri- or post-menopausal. 20.3% of participants reported symptomatic UTIs, while 47% reported a history of asymptomatic bacteriuria. The most common UTI symptoms are urgency (79.8%), dysuria (77.6%) and frequency (74.1%). At onset of symptoms, 56.3% first use home remedies to alleviate symptoms, while 35.3% complete a urine culture. Only 15.7% see a specialist for their UTI symptoms. Cranberry extract (64.3%), increasing fluid intake (83.5%), and phenazopyridine (39.5%) are the most commonly used home practices. Elluraâ (0.5%) and PRVNTâ (0.2%) are the least likely to be used. Only 30.6% feel home practices are actually helpful. For UTI prevention, the top daily practices include: increased fluid intake (77.2%) and wiping from front to back (71.2%). Constipation exists in 25.8% yet 16.2% use a daily bowel regimen. 42.1% correlate sex with UTIs. 66.7% use sex toys. Of those, 79.1% associate their sex toy usage with UTIs. However, 57% reported cleaning sex toys prior to and 77.5% after sex. 6.8% use preventative antibiotics and 10.8% use vaginal estrogen for UTI prevention. CONCLUSIONS: Women commonly struggle with UTIs. Home remedies are the first course of treatment for most UTI symptoms. A vast majority associate sex and sex toy usage with UTIs. Most peri- and post-menopausal women are not using vaginal estrogen cream for prevention. Urology and urogynecology physicians are infrequently seen for management of UTIs. There is need for improved public education of UTI symptoms, prevention strategies, and importance of correct diagnosis and treatment.

title: PREDICTING SEPTIC SHOCK AFTER DECOMPRESSION OF AN INFECTED, OBSTRUCTED URINARY TRACT: AN ANALYSIS OF 25,131 ADULTS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Benjamin Coffey, Alexander Collins, Casey Dang, Jeffrey Villanueva
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prior studies have identified parameters associated with septic shock in patients with obstructed upper urinary tracts. However, they are limited by small sample sizes. This study validates predictors reported in prior literature and identifies additional laboratory, hemodynamic, and clinical factors associated with subsequent septic shock. METHODS: Using TriNetX, we identified adults who underwent decompression of an infected upper urinary tract obstruction. Patients were stratified into two groups: sepsis without shock or sepsis requiring vasopressors. Laboratory, hemodynamic, comorbidity, and demographic data were collected from the day of decompression. Continuous variables were compared using two-sample t-tests; categorical variables were compared using chi-square. RESULTS: 25,131 patients were identified (shock n=5,250, no shock n=19,881). The shock cohort had higher procalcitonin, international normalized ratio, blood urea nitrogen, white blood cell count, and heart rate, and lower C-reactive protein, albumin, glomerular filtration rate, platelet count, and systolic blood pressure ( Table 1). Shock was associated with increased age, female sex, and multiple comorbidities, whereas essential hypertension occurred less often. CONCLUSIONS: This is the largest study to date evaluating predictors of septic shock following upper urinary tract decompression. It confirms some previously reported predictors and identifies additional comorbidity associations. Values for both cohorts tend to deviate similarly from normal clinical ranges, demonstrating that individual abnormalities are insufficient for risk stratification. Considered together, these variables support development of a composite bedside model to estimate patient-level risk of shock at the time of decompression. | | | --- | | |

title: PREDICTIVE VALUE OF HYALURONAN FOR SEVERE ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY DEVELOPMENT IN UROSEPSIS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Naoki Fujita, Yuki Tobisawa, Tohru Yoneyama, Masaki Momota, Hirotaka Horiguchi, Hiroyuki Ito, Kazuaki Yoshikawa, Shingo Hatakeyama
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Hyaluronan is a major glycosaminoglycan component of the endothelial glycocalyx, which coats the luminal surface of vascular endothelial cells ( Fig. A). It plays a pivotal role in maintaining vascular homeostasis by regulating thrombogenicity, modulating inflammatory responses, and preserving endothelial barrier integrity. Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequent and life-threatening complication in patients with urosepsis, yet the association between hyaluronan degradation and AKI development in this context remains poorly understood. METHODS: This retrospective study included 145 patients with urosepsis who were treated between March 2017 and March 2019. AKI was defined according to the KDIGO criteria. Plasma hyaluronan levels were measured at admission using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to evaluate the association between glycocalyx injury and the development of severe AKI. Additionally, the predictive ability of elevated hyaluronan levels for severe AKI was assessed using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis and compared using net reclassification improvement (NRI) and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI). RESULTS: The median age of the cohort was 79 years. Of the 145 patients, 39 (27%) developed severe AKI (defined as KDIGO stage 2 or 3). Patients who developed severe AKI had significantly higher plasma hyaluronan levels than those who did not ( Fig. B). In univariable analyses, age, sex, qSOFA score, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and plasma hyaluronan levels were significantly associated with severe AKI development. In multivariable analysis, plasma hyaluronan level remained a significant independent risk factor for severe AKI (Table). Elevated plasma hyaluronan levels improved the predictive performance for severe AKI compared to conventional risk factors alone ( Fig. C). Furthermore, plasma hyaluronan levels were significantly correlated with serum E-selectin levels, a marker of endothelial dysfunction ( Fig. D). CONCLUSIONS: Endothelial glycocalyx injury was associated with endothelial dysfunction and served as a significant risk factor for severe AKI development in patients with urosepsis. These findings suggest that glycocalyx injury may represent a potential therapeutic target for preventing or mitigating severe AKI in this population.

title: METHENAMINE HIPPURATE VERSUS PROPHYLACTIC ANTIBIOTICS FOR PREVENTION OF RECURRENT URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS IN ADULTS: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Pedro Silva, Luis Campos Pinheiro, Miguel Gil, João Cunha, Luis Severo
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Recurrent urinary tract infection (rUTI) management traditionally relies on long-term antibiotic prophylaxis, which contributes to antimicrobial resistance. Methenamine hippurate, a urinary antiseptic, has emerged as a potential antibiotic-sparing alternative. This systematic review compares methenamine hippurate with standard prophylactic antibiotics for preventing rUTIs in adult patients, evaluating recurrence rates, resistance profiles, and safety. METHODS: A structured semantic search of Pubmed, Embase and Scopus identified 14 eligible studies (11 RCTs, 3 protocols; 1983–2025) including >2,000 adult women with recurrent UTIs. Comparators included low-dose continuous antibiotics (nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim, cefalexin). Primary outcome: UTI recurrence rate (episodes/person-year or 12-month recurrence). Secondary outcomes: post-treatment recurrence, antimicrobial resistance, and adverse events. Risk of bias was assessed qualitatively from study design and blinding data. RESULTS: Primary efficacy: Across four head-to-head RCTs (Harding et al. 2021–2022, Botros et al. 2021), recurrence rates were 1.38 vs. 0.89 episodes/person-year for methenamine vs. antibiotics (Δ 0.49; 90% CI 0.15–0.84; non-inferiority achieved). Botros et al. (2021): 65% recurrence in both groups (p=1.00). Non-inferiority confirmed in three trials, with no study showing antibiotic superiority. Post-treatment recurrence: At 6 months after discontinuation: 1.72 (methenamine) vs. 1.19 (antibiotics) episodes/year (Harding 2022a). Other RCTs reported similar recurrence rates post-treatment. Antimicrobial resistance: During treatment: E. coli resistance 56% (methenamine) vs. 72% (antibiotics). Post-treatment multidrug resistance higher with methenamine (20% vs. 5%), but not statistically significant. Methenamine did not induce new resistance in any study. Safety and tolerability: Adverse events mild and comparable (28% vs. 24%); serious events occurred only in antibiotic arms (2 cases). 18% of methenamine users switched to antibiotics due to perceived inefficacy; 6% vice versa. Patient convenience and adherence were higher with antibiotics (p < 0.05), but methenamine avoided antimicrobial exposure. Economic and population data: King et al. 2024: methenamine cost-effective alternative (incremental cost/QALY non-significant). Trials primarily in adult women (18–85 y); results consistent across secondary and primary care. CONCLUSIONS: Methenamine hippurate provides non-inferior prevention of recurrent UTIs compared with prophylactic antibiotics, with significantly lower antibiotic resistance during treatment and similar safety. While recurrence slightly increases post-discontinuation, methenamine represents a viable, antibiotic-sparing prophylaxis strategy for adult women with recurrent UTIs. Wider implementation could meaningfully reduce antimicrobial use in urological practice.

title: EVALUATING THE ROLE OF GENETIC MARKERS IN CHILDREN WITH NON-E. COLI INFECTIONS IN CHILDREN WITH AND WITHOUT VESICOURETERAL REFLUX: AN ANALYSIS OF RIVUR AND CUTIE COHORTS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Jin Kyu (Justin) Kim, Rosalia Misseri, Joshua Roth, Konrad Szymanski, Nikhil Batra, Martin Kaefer, Mark Cain, Richard Rink, Kirstan Meldrum, Benjamin Whittam, Pankaj Dangle, Shaobo Zhang, David Hains
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) in children are most often caused by Escherichia coli, whereas non-E. coli pathogens are linked with greater morbidity and higher recurrence risk. Host and anatomic factors such as vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) and bladder and bowel dysfunction (BBD) are well established, but the role of genetic variation is incompletely understood. The DEFA1A3 locus encodes neutrophil α-defensins, antimicrobial peptides central to innate immunity at mucosal surfaces. Copy number variation (CNV) at DEFA1A3 has been implicated in infection susceptibility, with higher copy number hypothesized to alter peptide expression and microbial clearance. We sought to evaluate the role of DEFA1A3 CNV, DMBT1 CNV, and RANSE7 polymorphism (rs1263872) in children with and without VUR, using data from the RIVUR and CUTIE cohorts. METHODS: We analyzed 303 RIVUR participants with available genetic data. Covariates included sex, age, BBD status, VUR grade (high vs. low), and genetic markers. Logistic regression identified independent predictors of non-E. coli UTI. Separately, 160 CUTIE children with genetic information were evaluated. Since CUTIE excluded VUR, regression included age, sex, BBD, and DEFA1A3 CNV. The outcome was pathogen type (E. coli vs. non-E. coli) at index UTI. RESULTS: In RIVUR, 11.2% of children had an index non-E. coli UTI. Multivariate regression identified significant predictors: female sex (OR 0.151, 95% CI 0.41–0.551, p=0.004), high-grade VUR (OR 2.487, 95% CI 1.116–5.544, p=0.026), and DEFA1A3 CNV ≥5 (OR 0.446, 95% CI 0.201–0.991, p=0.047). DMBT1 CNV and rs1263872 were not significant. In CUTIE, 8.75% presented with non-E. coli UTI. Regression showed no association between DEFA1A3 CNV and infection (OR 4.312, 95% CI 0.805–23.079, p=0.088) after adjusting for age (OR 1.066, 95% CI 1.019–1.114, p=0.005) and female sex (OR 0.137, 95% CI 0.030-0.625, p=0.021). CONCLUSIONS: Higher DEFA1A3 copy number, a marker of innate immune defense, was significantly associated with index non-E. coli UTI in children with VUR but not in those without reflux. These results suggest that the interaction between genetic predisposition and urinary tract anatomy modulates pathogen susceptibility. Integrating genetic markers with clinical features may enhance prediction of infection risk and inform tailored management strategies in pediatric UTI.

title: AI-BASED MODELLING OF UTI RISK USING AGE, GENDER, URINE PH, AND URINARY VITAMIN D
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Marta N. Monari, Fabio Grizzi, Mohamed A. A. A. Hegazi, Paola Petrillo, Sara Beltrame, Anita Stassi, Nicolò M. Buffi, Vittorio Fasulo, Rebecca Canneto, Benedetto Calabrese, Rodolfo Hurle, Paolo Vota, Matteo Zanoni, Cinzia Mazzieri, Nicola Frego, Enrico Marsili, Gianluigi Taverna
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To explore the performance of machine learning (ML) models that utilize urinary 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) levels, urine pH, gender, and age to predict the risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs). METHODS: A cohort of 358 subjects with an average age of 61 ± 21 years (ranging from 2 to 101 years) was investigated. For each subject, urinary vitamin D levels, urinalysis, and urine culture were evaluated. The performance of 12 ml models was determined in terms of accuracy, specificity, sensitivity, PPV, NPV, AUC-ROC and F1 score. RESULTS: A significant difference in urinary 25(OH)D levels was found between individuals with positive (1.33 ± 4.13 ng/mL) and negative (2.48 ± 4.52 ng/mL) urine cultures (p=0.02). Using urinary 25(OH)D, urine pH, age, and gender as predictors, 12 ml models showed accuracies of 65%–87%, sensitivities of 49%–79%, specificities of 53%–95%, PPVs of 63%–94%, NPVs of 62%–82%, AUC-ROC values of 0.656–0.909, and F1 scores of 0.597–0.859. A stacked model achieved 83% accuracy, 78% sensitivity, 87% specificity, 86% PPV, 79% NPV, AUC-ROC of 0.903, and an F1 score of 0.818. CONCLUSIONS: Significant differences in urinary 25(OH)D between positive and negative urine cultures suggest a link between low levels and higher UTI risk. Strong ML model performance using four predictors - urinary 25(OH)D, urine pH, gender, and age - supports validating a low-cost, non-invasive tool for early UTI management and reduced antibiotic use. The web-based platform will connect healthcare centers, broaden cohorts, and aid clinical decisions.

title: IN VITRO AND EX-VIVO MODELING OF RENAL RESPONSES TO MICROPLASTICS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Mohammadreza Kasravi, Charmi Dedhia, Raquel Rodriguez, Rachael Wen, Roger De Filippo, Laura Perin, Stefano Da Sacco
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Microplastics (MP), defined as synthetic polymer particles smaller than 5 millimeters, are increasingly recognized as environmental contaminants with potential health consequences. Recent studies have identified MP in human tissues, including the kidney, raising concerns about their role in renal injury. Given the kidney’s central role in filtration and waste elimination, this study aimed to evaluate the in vitro and ex vivo impact of MP exposure on renal cell phenotype and function, and to explore their potential contribution to kidney disease progression. METHODS: Primary human renal cells—podocytes, glomerular endothelial cells (GEC), mesangial cells and proximal tubular cells (PTC)—were exposed to fluorescently labeled polystyrene MP (1 µm) in vitro. MP uptake and cellular responses were assessed using live-cell imaging, flow cytometry, immunofluorescence, and protein array analysis. Functional effects were evaluated using microfluidic organ-on-chip platforms that model glomerular and tubular compartments. RESULTS: All renal cell types internalized MP, with podocytes showing the highest uptake. MP exposure led to phenotypic alterations, including cytoskeletal disruption, loss of endothelial markers, and re-expression of injury-associated proteins. Protein profiling revealed activation of oxidative stress and apoptosis pathways. Organ-on-chip studies demonstrated compromised glomerular barrier integrity, evidenced by increased albumin leakage and KIM-1 production. CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that MP are internalized by renal cells and disrupt their phenotype and function. MP exposure impairs glomerular and tubular integrity ex vivo and may contribute to renal injury and dysfunction. These results underscore the need for further investigation into the clinical implications of MP exposure and its role in renal pathophysiology, particularly in vulnerable patient populations.

title: CHRONIC MICROPLASTIC EXPOSURE ALTERS RENAL AND LOWER URINARY TRACT HOMEOSTASIS IN HEALTHY MICE
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Mohammadreza Kasravi, Velia Alcala, Rachael Wen, Roger De Filippo, Laura Perin, Stefano Da Sacco
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Microplastics (MP), synthetic particles <5 mm, are increasingly recognized as environmental contaminants with systemic health implications. While their presence in human kidneys has been documented, the impact of chronic MP exposure on renal and lower urinary tract physiology in healthy systems remains unclear. Given the kidney and bladder’s role in filtration and excretion, understanding MP biodistribution and toxicity is critical for urologic health. METHODS: Wild-type mice were exposed daily to fluorescently-labeled polystyrene MP for 45 days. MP biodistribution was assessed in blood, urine, kidney, and bladder tissues. Renal function was evaluated via albumin/creatinine ratio (ACR), histology, and immunofluorescence. Bladder tissue was analyzed for MP presence and structural changes. RESULTS: MP were detected in blood and urine within 2–4 weeks of exposure, confirming systemic absorption. Histological analysis revealed MP accumulation in glomerular and tubular compartments. ACR showed a trend toward increased proteinuria in exposed mice, suggesting early renal dysfunction. Notably, MP were also identified in bladder tissue, indicating lower urinary tract involvement. No overt histological damage was observed in the bladder, but MP localization suggests potential for long-term impact. CONCLUSIONS: Chronic MP exposure leads to systemic distribution, including the kidney and bladder, and induces early signs of renal dysfunction in healthy mice. These findings highlight the potential nephrotoxic and urologic risks of environmental MP exposure, warranting further investigation into their role in urinary tract health and disease.

title: METFORMIN ATTENUATES ISCHEMIC REPERFUSION INJURY-INDUCED ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY BY ENHANCING HISTONE LACTYLATION VIA UPREGULATING HK2 GENE EXPRESSION
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Nieke Zhang, Yi Xia, Guangyuan Zhang, Ming Chen
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Renal ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) is clinically prevalent, which can induce acute kidney injury (AKI) and even renal failure. Metformin has been proven to exert a protective effect against IRI in multiple vital organs. This study aims to investigate the specific mechanism underlying the protective effect of metformin on renal IRI. METHODS: Correlation between metformin and renal function was analyzed using NHANES database. HK-2 cells were pretreated with metformin (0.25, 1, 8, 64 mm) for 1/2 h, followed by hypoxia/reoxygenation. qRT-PCR and Western blot (WB) were used to assess mRNA and protein levels of apoptosis-related molecules. Cell supernatants were collected for further measurement. Cell apoptosis and proliferation were detected by flow cytometry and CCK-8 assay, respectively. Rats received intraperitoneal injections of metformin (50, 100, 300 mg/kg). After 24 h, the right kidney was resected, left kidney was subjected to I/R. Kidney tissues and serum were collected for further detection. Transcriptome sequencing was conducted to identify underlying mechanism. RESULTS: The retrospective cross-sectional study demonstrated a significant correlation between metformin and improved renal function. Annexin V/PI staining and CCK-8 assay showed that pretreatment of 1 mm metformin for 1 hour significantly reduce cell apoptosis and increase cell viability compared with other groups. qRT-PCR results indicated that this pretreatment method downregulate IL-6, TNF-, BAX, and Caspase3 mRNA expression, and upregulated Bcl2 mRNA expression, as well as increased the lactic acid level in the cell supernatant. Pathological examination revealed that 50 mg/kg/d metformin significantly alleviated renal IRI, reduced renal inflammation, and decreased the renal tubular injury score. TUNEL and Ki67 showed that this dose could reduce renal cell apoptosis and promote cell proliferation; ELISA assays confirmed decreased serum creatinine, urea nitrogen, IL-6, and TNF-. Lactic acid levels in the liver, spleen, lung, kidney, brain, and serum of rats were highest in the 50 mg/kg group. Transcriptome sequencing analysis revealed that metformin pretreatment upregulated glycolysis-related pathways, with increased HK2 expression (verified by qRT-PCR). WB results showed that pretreatment with metformin increased the level of pan-lactylation and the lactylation level at the histone H3K18 site. WB and qRT-PCR analyses confirmed that metformin treatment increased the protein and mRNA expression levels of Muc1. CONCLUSIONS: Metformin pretreatment attenuates IRI-induced AKI by enhancing histone lactylation which including H3K18 lactylation via promoting Muc1 and HK2 expression.

title: NOVEL APPLICATION OF THERAPEUTIC HYPOTHERMIA IN A RAT MODEL OF ABDOMINAL COMPARTMENT SYNDROME: A TREND TOWARD RENAL PROTECTION
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Hsuan Wei Ho
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS) impairs renal perfusion and leads to acute kidney injury (AKI). While therapeutic hypothermia (HypoT) is a potential renal-protective strategy. This study evaluated whether therapeutic hypothermia (HypoT) within the abdomen attenuates renal ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury in an ACS rat model. METHODS: Sprague-Dawley rats (n=27) were randomized into five groups: Control, ACS (Normal Temp, ~37°C), ACS+HypoT (32°C), ACS+HyperT (42°C), and ACS+Extreme HyperT (47°C). ACS was induced via intraperitoneal gelatin infusion to maintain IAP at 30 mmHg for 4 hours. Serum BUN, creatinine (Cre) were analyzed. Statistical significance was assessed using one-way ANOVA (p<0.05). RESULTS: Traditional renal markers (BUN, Cre) and the BUN/Cre ratio did not differ significantly among groups (p=0.2947). However, subgroup analysis revealed a trend toward renal protection in the hypothermia (HypoT) group compared with the hyperthermia (HyperT) group. In the HypoT group, serum creatinine decreased from 0.46 ± 0.05 to 0.43 ± 0.04 mg/dL, whereas in the HyperT group, creatinine increased from 0.50 ± 0.07 to 0.63 ± 0.33 mg/dL. The body temperature (BodyT) group also showed a mild decrease in creatinine (from 0.59 ± 0.00 to 0.50 ± 0.06 mg/dL), suggesting that the 4-hour ACS duration may have been insufficient to induce overt AKI. CONCLUSIONS: Therapeutic hypothermia demonstrated a trend toward renal protection, as evidenced by reduced serum creatinine levels compared with hyperthermic conditions. However, the lack of statistical significance likely reflects the limited ACS duration and small sample size, which constrained the ability to detect measurable renal impairment within this experimental setting.

title: IDENTIFICATION OF POTENTIAL INTRACELLULAR BACTERIAL COMMUNITIES IN THE HUMAN URINARY BLADDER
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Glenn Werneburg, Melanie Pearson, Surbhi Gupta, Shiuhyang Kuo, J. Quentin Clemens
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: About 50% of women and 14% of men will have a urinary tract infection (UTI) in their lifetime, and approximately a quarter of women with a UTI will develop recurrent UTI (rUTI). Evidence from rodent models supports that rUTIs may be due to intracellular bacterial communities (IBCs), large and dense intracellular aggregates of 104 to 106 bacteria, in bladder uroepithelium by uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) and other bacteria. Despite the strong evidence for IBCs in the pathophysiology of rUTI and chronic cystitis in rodent models, IBCs have never been demonstrated in the human urinary bladder. We sought to assess for the presence of intracellular bacterial communities (IBCs) in the human urinary bladder. We hypothesized that IBCs will be demonstrable in our patient cohort undergoing cystectomy. METHODS: Patients who were undergoing simple cystectomy for non-oncological indications were consented via IRB-approved protocol. Patient demographics were collected prospectively. Following bladder removal, a portion of bladder tissue was saved for laboratory analysis using scanning and transmission electron microscopy and immunohistochemistry (IHC). In addition, a urine specimen was collected from each patient prior to surgery. RESULTS: Twelve participants were enrolled in this prospective study. Median age was 65 years; 4 participants were female and 9 were male. Indications for cystectomy included end-stage bladder or upper tract deterioration in the context of neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction, recurrent urosepsis, and/or end-stage radiation cystitis. Each participant had matching bladder tissue and urine specimens available for analysis. Of the twelve bladder specimens analyzed, two had evidence consistent with IBCs on scanning electron microscopy (Figure left), or on IHC (Figure right), similar to those seen in rodent models. CONCLUSIONS: A subset of human urinary bladder had microscopic or immunohistochemical findings consistent with IBCs. Additional analysis of the present cohort, and corroborative laboratory investigations are ongoing. The identification of IBCs in human bladder tissue has major implications for preventative therapy and treatment of recurrent UTI, and may set the groundwork for targeting IBCs with adjunctive therapeutic or preventative strategies.

title: DEVELOPMENT AND EVALUATION OF NOVEL STAGE 5 CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE MODELS IN MICE AND THEIR APPLICATION IN KIDNEY REGENERATION RESEARCH
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Jae Sung Lim, Eun Hye Lee, Bo Hyun Yoon, Minji Jeon, Sang Hee Lee, Jun-Koo Kang, Jae-Wook Chung, Yun-Sok Ha, Seock Hwan Choi, Bum Soo Kim, Hyun Tae Kim, Tae-Hwan Kim, Eun Sang Yoo, Tae Gyun Kwon
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects 10-13% of the global population, often progressing to end-stage renal disease (ESRD), which demands dialysis or transplantation. Current treatments focus on slowing progression, highlighting a critical need for regenerative therapies. Developing effective therapies requires animal models that accurately replicate human CKD, as traditional models like conventional 5/6 nephrectomy (c5/6) have limitations. This study aimed to develop and characterize novel mouse models of stage 5 CKD to assess their suitability for kidney regeneration research. METHODS: We established two distinct models: a surgical approach using bilateral and bipolar 5/6 nephrectomy (bb) with or without scaffold implantation (bb+sca), and a medical approach combining cisplatin injections with unilateral nephrectomy (CP+Nx). C57/b6 mice were randomly assigned to control and experimental groups. Recovery was assessed through body weight monitoring and behavioral tests. Renal function was evaluated via serum creatinine and BUN measurements. Kidney tissues underwent histological analysis and qPCR for inflammatory and fibrotic markers. RESULTS: Both models demonstrated significant renal dysfunction. The surgical model showed elevated serum creatinine levels at one week post-surgery that partially recovered by eight weeks. The medical model exhibited progressive elevation of BUN and creatinine. Molecular analysis revealed increased pro-inflammatory markers (NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8) and fibrotic markers (TGF-β1, Col-1, vimentin) in both models, with the CP+Nx group showing the most pronounced changes. Histologically, inflammatory cell infiltration was observed at one week, with fibrosis developing by eight weeks. Notably, scaffold implantation in the surgical model (bb+sca) appeared to modulate the inflammatory response and reduce fibrosis compared to the bb group alone, suggesting potential benefits for regenerative approaches. CONCLUSIONS: These novel models reliably produce severe renal dysfunction and pathological changes consistent with advanced kidney disease, offering complementary strengths for investigating CKD pathophysiology and evaluating regenerative therapies. Our findings may contribute to the development of transformative treatments for patients with end-stage renal disease.

title: VERIFICATION OF RENAL TISSUE REGENERATION USING HUMAN PERINEPHRIC FAT-DERIVED COLLAGEN SHEET IN A PARTIALLY NEPHRECTOMIZED ANIMAL MODEL
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Jae Sung Lim, Eun Hye Lee, Bo Hyun Yoon, Minji Jeon, Sang Hee Lee, Jun-Koo Kang, Jae-Wook Chung, Yun-Sok Ha, Seock Hwan Choi, Bum Soo Kim, Hyun Tae Kim, Tae-Hwan Kim, Eun Sang Yoo, Tae Gyun Kwon
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Chronic kidney disease (CKD), a global health issue, affects approximately 10% of the population. However, limited treatment options, such as dialysis or transplantation, have significant drawbacks. Therefore, this study aims to investigate the potential of a collagen sheet derived from human perirenal adipose tissue for kidney regeneration. METHODS: Collagen sheets were derived from discarded perirenal adipose tissues and implanted into partially nephrectomized mice. The right kidneys were completely removed, and 2 mm of the upper and lower poles of the left kidneys were resected. A collagen sheet measuring 1×1×3 mm3 was implanted in the mid-pole of the left kidney following partial resection of renal parenchyme. Renal function, inflammation, and tissue regeneration were evaluated using serum analysis, PCR, histological staining, and immunohistochemistry to assess structural and functional improvements. RESULTS: The collagen sheet reduced pro-inflammatory markers, minimized fibrosis, and restored renal function indicators such as BUN and cystatin C, though creatinine levels remained unchanged. Regenerative markers, including PAX2 and Wt1, were significantly elevated, indicating enhanced tissue repair and structural recovery. CONCLUSIONS: The perirenal adipose tissue-derived collagen sheet demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects and promoted renal tissue regeneration. These findings suggest its potential as a biomaterial for renal injury management. However, further research is needed to evaluate long-term efficacy, optimize application methods, and ensure clinical safety.

title: NOVEL FOLEY CATHETER DESIGN PREVENTS ENCRUSTATION AND BLOCKAGE THROUGH ENHANCED BLADDER DRAINAGE: PRECLINICAL GLASS BLADDER MODEL STUDY
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Nikolai Hoffmann-Petersen, Niklas Herou, Nicola Morris, Ingrid Lönnstedt, Jesper M. Ganc-Petersen, Steven Kaplan, Marcus J. Drake
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTI) and encrustation-related blockage represent significant complications in long-term indwelling catheterization. Residual urine provides a nidus for planktonic bacteria forming crystalline biofilms, particularly Proteus mirabilis. We evaluated a novel Foley catheter designed to minimize residual volume through enhanced bladder neck positioning versus conventional all-silicone catheters in a validated infection model. METHODS: Eighteen 14-French catheters (nine Nowwell, nine all-silicone controls) were tested in glass bladder models at Bristol Urological Institute across three independent runs (n=3 per group per run). The novel catheter incorporates two additional drainage eyelets below the balloon with a bladder neck-anchoring skirt. Models were inoculated with Proteus mirabilis (8×108 CFU/mL) one hour before artificial urine flow (1 ml/min) up to 192 hours. Primary endpoint: time to blockage. Secondary endpoints: residual volume, biofilm formation. Statistical analysis: Cox proportional hazards model (adjusted for run), Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, linear mixed effects model. RESULTS: Zero of nine Nowwell catheters blocked versus nine of nine controls (100% versus 0% patency, p<0.001). Control blockage occurred at mean 109 hours (SD 9.75, range 90-120, median 108). Nowwell catheters reduced residual volume 93% (3 ml versus 42 ml, p<0.001) with minimal encrustation and maintained drainage, versus extensive crystalline biofilm with complete eyelet occlusion in all controls. Kaplan-Meier curves demonstrated 100% versus 0% patency at 192 hours (log-rank p<0.001). All models maintained urinary pH 9.0, confirming active bacterial urease activity. CONCLUSIONS: In this validated preclinical model, the Nowwell catheter prevented blockage in all tested units over eight days by reducing residual volume 93%, thereby preventing Proteus mirabilis biofilm formation through continuous bacterial washout. All conventional catheters failed by day five (mean 109 hours). This mechanical drainage enhancement represents a novel blockage prevention strategy distinct from antimicrobial coating approaches. Clinical trials are warranted to evaluate catheter lifespan extension, CAUTI reduction, and patient quality of life improvements in long-term catheterized populations.

title: COMPARISON OF 2 CATHETERS, 3 SOLUTIONS, AND 3 ORGANISMS IN HOPE OF REDUCING CAUTI: E. COLI BACTERIA LOAD REDUCTION NOTED
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Gerard D. Henry, Edward Karpman, Spencer Pringle, Lynn Tong, Carolyn Twomey
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTI) is a major health problem across the world. Clarke et al. state UTIs “are among the most common healthcare-associated infections, and 70%-80%” are CAUTI. Several of the isolates causing CAUTI have become more and more resistant to antibiotics. Catheters themselves are changing to become easier and less uncomfortable (hydrophilic coated, lubricous surfaces) to place into the bladder. The study is designed to evaluate the ability of antiseptics to kill bacteria after inoculation of various common UTI pathogenic species on sterile catheter disks with the protocol stimulating a real world self-cath patient situation. METHODS: An in-vitro Good Laboratory Practices (GLP) microbiological study done at Nelson Labs Bozeman (FDA and EPA registered, ISO 17025 certified)\] to compare outcomes of catheter activation with sterile water, 0.05% CHG solution (Irrisept® Antimicrobial Wound Lavage) or CHG lube (Cathejel C.5/ 1gram at 5 gram). Three (3) bacteria (Bacteroides fragilis, Enterococcus faecalis, and Escherichia coli) were inoculated onto 2 different catheter discs. The two different catheter discs to be utilized are from the Hydrophilic Cure Catheter® and the newer GentleCath® intermittent urinary catheter. For each challenge species, three 1 cm discs (carriers) of catheter material were dipped / activated in either of the 3 solutions for 2 minutes. Each disc was inoculated with 0.01 ml of an approximately 109 CFU/mL challenge suspension of 1 of the 3 bacterial strains for 2 to 3 minutes to mimic real life self-cath. Neutralization was done and the colonies on the plates were counted. RESULTS: Sterile water, used as a baseline, had the least effect on the three bacteria as compared to 0.05% CHG solution and CHG Lube. GC glide catheter reduced bacterial load better than hydrophilic coated catheter when using CHG solutions (see Table 1& 2). E. Coli had a 3-log reduction in bacterial load when using the combination of CHG lube and GC glide catheter. CONCLUSIONS: There appears to be a bacterial load reduction when using CHG activating solutions over sterile water and when using the GC glide over the hydrophilic coated catheters. E. Coli had a clinically significant reduction in bacteria counts with the combination of CHG activating solutions and GC glide catheter usage. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: NEUTROPHIL DEPLETION MITIGATES POST-IRRADIATION BLADDER INFLAMMATION AND TISSUE REMODELING RESPONSES
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Ryan D. Molony, Mahmudul Hasan Akash, Emma Ushchak, Angela Groves, Nicole Paris, Brian Marples, Yi-Fen Lee
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Acute post-radiotherapy (RT) bladder inflammation is common in prostate cancer (PCa). Up to 25% of patients develop delayed bladder radiotoxicity characterized by hematuria 6+ months post-RT. We have previously identified a pre-RT serum and urine neutrophil-related signature as a potential predictor of late hematuria. However, the functional role of neutrophils in the bladder following irradiation remains poorly understood, underscoring the need to directly characterize neutrophil responses in the post-RT bladder and their contributions to adverse tissue remodeling that may culminate in late radiation cystitis. METHODS: A murine model was established through the focal X-ray beam irradiation of the bladder in healthy male C57BL/6 mice (0 or 30 Gy) using a Small Animal Radiation Research Platform (SARRP, XStrahl). To deplete neutrophils, mice were intraperitoneally injected with anti-Ly6G (100 µg/mouse) every three days, beginning 4 days before irradiation. Bladders were collected 24 h or 7 days post-irradiation for flow cytometry-based analyses of monocytes/macrophages (CD14+) and neutrophils (Siglec-F–CD115–Gr-1+), and for qPCR. Urine samples were also collected to analyze extracellular vesicles and DNA content. RESULTS: In healthy mice, focal bladder irradiation triggered a time-dependent increase in bladder neutrophil-related effector gene (Mpo, Ctsg) expression. Flow cytometry confirmed this enhanced post-RT neutrophil infiltration of the bladder, which was still evident on day 7 after irradiation. Neutrophil depletion successfully reduced neutrophil frequencies in both whole blood and the bladder, suppressed the post-RT upregulation of inflammatory genes in the bladder, and altered the expression of genes associated with Notch signaling and other tissue remodeling-related pathways. Neutrophil depletion also reversed post-RT increases in urine EV counts and urine DNA levels. CONCLUSIONS: While whether neutrophil depletion can mitigate late post-RT outcomes is a focus of ongoing research, these analyses support a model wherein healthy bladder tissue irradiation, as occurs in PCa patients undergoing RT, elicits neutrophil activity that potentiates more intense inflammation and tissue remodeling in the bladder, potentially resulting in late radiation cystitis in a subset of patients.

title: INCIDENCE AND RISK FACTORS OF RADIATION CYSTITIS IN THE ERA OF INTENSITY-MODULATED RADIATION THERAPY FOR PROSTATE CANCER: A MULTICENTER RETROSPECTIVE STUDY
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Xiaoxiao Guo, Gangyue Hao, Fengbo Zhang
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Radiation cystitis (RC) is a clinically relevant late toxicity following prostate cancer (PCa) radiotherapy, yet its long-term incidence and modifiable risk factors in the era of intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) remain poorly defined. We aim to determine the cumulative incidence and identify independent risk factors for RC among PCa patients treated with IMRT. METHODS: This multicenter retrospective cohort study included 668 men with PCa who underwent IMRT between 2006 and 2020 at three medical centers. radiation parameters and patient factors were collected for analysis. Cumulative incidence was estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with between-group differences assessed by the log-rank test. Predictors of RC were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards models. Optimal cut-points for body mass index (BMI) and dietary inflammatory index (DII) were identified by maximally selected log-rank statistics. RESULTS: After a median follow-up of 96 months, 121 patients (18.1%) developed RC, including 7.5% with grade ≥ 2. The cumulative incidence of RC was 5.2%, 23.2%, and 28.3% at 5, 10, and 15 years, respectively, and 2.2%, 9.6%, and 13.1% for grade ≥ 2 events. On multivariable analysis, higher BMI (HR 1.16, 95% CI 1.09–1.25; p<0.001), higher DII (HR 1.10, 95% CI 1.01–1.23; p=0.048), and adjuvant radiotherapy (HR 2.66, 95% CI 1.70–4.17; p<0.001) were independently associated with increased RC risk. Age, tobacco use, ECOG performance status, anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy, radiation dose, and fractionation schedule were not significantly associated with RC risk. CONCLUSIONS: RC continues to accumulate beyond 10 years after IMRT. Patient-related factors, including BMI and DII, together with the radiotherapy setting, are major determinants of long-term RC risk. These findings emphasize the need for individualized survivorship care and highlight dietary modulation as a potential preventive approach.

title: BEYOND INFECTION: THE LONGITUDINAL IMPACT OF GENITOURINARY TUBERCULOSIS ON UROLOGIC AND REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Frances H. Kazal, Joshua J. Horns, Muyuan Zhang, Jeremy B. Myers, Jane T. Kurtzman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Genitourinary tuberculosis (GUTB) is a rare condition that poses significant challenges in both diagnosis and treatment. Despite its uncommon nature, it often affects younger individuals and can be associated with considerable morbidity. Diagnosing GUTB requires a high level of clinical suspicion due to its poorly understood natural history and tendency to mimic alternate diseases. Few studies track the course of GUTB, and none describe the clinical history preceding diagnosis. The purpose of this study is to characterize the clinical history and long-term risks in patients with GUTB before and after diagnosis. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective analysis of Merative MarketScan records from 2011-2021 to identify all patients with GUTB. Patients were followed throughout enrollment and diagnoses of concurrent diseases (pulmonary TB, HIV, infertility) and urologic adverse events (UAE) were captured. Events- and diagnoses-of-interest that occurred both prior and after GUTB diagnosis were included. UAEs were stratified as low- and high-grade events. Multivariable cox proportional hazards models compared risk of UAE and infertility with age- and comorbidity-matched controls. RESULTS: 1503 patients with GUTB were identified. Mean patient age was 43 years. Most patients were otherwise healthy (63% CCI ≤1). Only 3% of GUTB patients had pulmonary TB and 1% had HIV. Among GUTB patients, 46.4% experienced a low-grade UAE, 10.5% experienced a high-grade UAE, and 9.9% experienced infertility, compared to 24.0%, 3.5% and 3.9% of controls (all p-values < 0.001). Figure 1 demonstrates that GUTB was associated with 2.5-fold the risk of high-grade UAE prior to diagnosis (OR 2.5, p<0.001) and 2.7-fold the risk after diagnosis (OR 2.7, p<0.001). It was also associated with two-fold the risk of low-grade UAE prior to diagnosis (OR 2.0, p<0.001) and a 1.6-fold after diagnosis (OR 1.6, p<0.001) compared to controls. Infertility risk was significant among GUTB patients in the pre-diagnosis setting (HR 2.6, p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: We demonstrated GUTB is associated with an increased risk of infertility and UAEs both prior to and following diagnosis, highlighting the substantial long-term morbidity of the disease. Importantly, UAEs often precede the formal diagnosis of GUTB. Given this significant burden observed in the US, the impact on patients in low- and middle-income countries is likely greater.

title: CONTAMINATED VERSUS UROGENITAL SKIN FLORA ON PRE-OPERATIVE URINE CULTURE: CAN WE TREAT THESE THE SAME?
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Nabila Reem Khondakar, Yutai Li, Kendall Kling, Jenny Guo, Amy E. Krambeck, Perry Xu
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While collecting a pre-operative urine culture (UCx) prior to endoscopic urologic surgery is standard practice, the management of “contaminated” or “urogenital skin flora (USF)” results on UCx is unclear. This study compared pre-operative (pre-op) UCx results and post-operative (post-op) urinary tract infection (UTI) risk. We hypothesized that USF or contaminated pre-op UCx would not increase risk of post-op UTI compared to negative pre-op UCx. METHODS: The electronic medical record was queried for patients who had cystoscopy with ureteral stent, ureteroscopy (URS), percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), or holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) between 1/2022 and 8/2025. Pre-op UCx was categorized as positive, negative, USF (multiple urogenital skin flora present without uropathogen) or contaminated (\> three organisms with ≥ one uropathogen). Uropathogens were gram-negative bacilli, Enterococcus, Staph aureus, Staph saprophyticus, beta-hemolytic strep, Strep pneumo, and yeast. Outcomes included positive UCx within 90 days and UTI (ICD Code N39.0) or fever (T ≥ 100.4) within 60 days post-op. Chi-squared, Fisher’s exact tests, and multivariate logistic regression were performed. RESULTS: We analyzed 3386 urologic surgeries, of which 83% (2817/3386) were voided specimens. Overall, 30.4% of patients had post-op UTI. UTI rate was highest for positive (43.7%) and contaminated (34.6%) pre-op UCx compared to negative UCx (p<0.001) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191308.46584.7c.26#F1)). USF was not associated with UTI (18.2% vs negative: 19.5%, p=0.52). Only positive UCx was associated with fever (12.7% vs negative: 7.1%, p<0.001) although contaminated UCx trended (p=0.056). On multivariate analysis, positive straight catheter UCx (OR 1.61, 95% CI 1.21–2.15, p=0.001) and both positive and contaminated voided UCx were significant predictors of UTI (OR 3.23, 95% CI 2.69-3.90;OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.69–2.98). Adjusting for age, gender, and UCx, URS, stent, and PCNL significantly predicted higher UTI risk compared to HoLEP (p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In a cohort with predominantly voided specimens, contaminated pre-op UCx was associated with post-op UTI. USF demonstrated equivalence to negative pre-op Ucx. Voided and straight-catheterized cultures carried the greatest prognostic value. Contaminated UCx should warrant repeat collection, especially before upper tract surgery.

title: URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS AFTER BENIGN CYSTECTOMY: INCIDENCE, PATHOGENS, AND RISK FACTORS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Maxwell L. Sandberg, David Thole, Dylan Wolff, Gavin Underwood, Robert Evans, Soroush Rais-Bahrami, Alejandro Rodriguez
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are a well-known complication after cystectomy, most often understood in the setting of oncologic disease. However, there is an entirely different population of patients who undergo cystectomy for benign conditions not adequately researched. The purpose of this study was to quantify rates of UTIs after benign cystectomy (BC) and identify patient risk factors for UTI development. METHODS: All patients who underwent BC at our institution from 2012-2024 were reviewed, excluding any patients undergoing cystectomy for malignant disease. Cystectomy type (i. e. subtrigonal, supratrigonal, etc.) was noted as was urinary diversion selection. UTIs required urine culture confirmation with >105 colony forming units of an organism/high-powered field. UTIs were qualified as either in the immediate postoperative period prior to discharge or within 90-days of discharge from BC. Patient demographics and surgical information was collected and compared between those with and without a UTI both in the immediate postoperative period and within 90-days of discharge to assess risk factors for UTI development. RESULTS: 183 patients underwent BC, of which 27 (15%) had an immediate postoperative UTI and 35 (19%) had a UTI within 90-days of discharge ( Table 1a). 60 (33%) patients received postoperative antibiotic prophylaxis ( Table 1b). No association between prophylactic antibiotics and UTIs immediately after BC was observed and patients with a UTI 90-days from discharge were more likely to have received postoperative antibiotics (56% vs. 28%; p<0.05; Table 1a-c). Preoperative bladder capacity was not associated with the development of UTIs (p>0.05). Patients with a UTI immediately postoperatively had a longer mean procedure time (390 minutes versus 340 minutes; p<0.05). Patients with a UTI within 90-days of BC were more likely to be readmitted to the hospital (94% vs. 26%; p<0.05). Pathogen data was available on 90-day UTIs and the most common were Escherichia coli (N=10; 29%; Table 1d) and Klebsiella pneumoniae (N=7; 20%). CONCLUSIONS: UTIs after BC are common both in the immediate postoperative setting and within 90-days after discharge. Prophylactic postoperative antibiotics were not associated with a lower rate of immediate postoperative UTI and were associated with a greater likelihood of UTI within 90-days of discharge. The causes of these findings call for additional investigation. | | | --- | | |

title: VAGINAL LASER THERAPY AS A POTENTIAL TREATMENT OPTION FOR POSTMENOPAUSAL WOMEN WITH RECURRENT CYSTITIS: INITIAL EXPERIENCE FROM A SINGLE INSTITUTION
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Eriko Kasuya, Fumihiko Urabe, Yue Ogihara, Hirotaka Kondo, Ayaka Kawaharada, Mana Nakata, Minoru Nakazono, Takahiro Kimura, Hirokazu Abe
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Recurrent cystitis affects 20–40% of women, with 25–50% developing frequent recurrences, markedly impairing quality of life (QOL). Postmenopausal women are especially vulnerable due to genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM), which disrupts the vaginal microenvironment. Conventional management relies on antibiotics, raising concerns about resistance. Vaginal laser therapy (VLT) improves vaginal tissue health and microbiota in GSM, but its role in preventing recurrent cystitis is unknown. We evaluated the efficacy and safety of VLT in reducing cystitis recurrence and improving vaginal health in postmenopausal women. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 51 postmenopausal women with recurrent cystitis treated with VLT at a single pelvic floor clinic (Jan 2023–Jul 2024). Recurrent cystitis was defined as ≥3 episodes/year or ≥2 in 6 months requiring antibiotics. All had vaginal pH ≥5.5 and no urinary tract malignancy or pelvic infection. The protocol included three sessions of nonablative 2,940 nm Er:YAG laser in SMOOTH mode at 4-week intervals; 86% received concomitant vaginal estriol unless contraindicated. Outcomes included cystitis-free interval (CFI), infection frequency, vaginal health index (VHI), vaginal pH, and cystoscopic grading of atrophy. Safety was graded per Clavien–Dindo. RESULTS: Median age was 63; follow-up was 8 months. Median CFI was 9.2 months ( Figure 1A). Cystitis episodes fell from 4 to 0 in 6 months pre- vs post-treatment (p<0.001) ( Figure 1B). VHI improved from 10 to 18, pH from 8.0 to 5.5 (both p<0.001). Cystoscopic evaluation (n=40) showed significant improvement in vaginal/periurethral atrophy ( Figure 1C). Patients without estrogen (n=7) also had fewer infections, lower pH, and higher VHI. Adverse events occurred in 7.8%, all Grade 1 and resolved without intervention. CONCLUSIONS: This is the first clinical evidence demonstrating that VLT can substantially reduce cystitis recurrence in postmenopausal women, with concurrent improvements in vaginal tissue health and pH. The therapy was well tolerated, including in patients unable to receive estrogen. By directly targeting the underlying vaginal microenvironment, VLT offers a novel, non-antibiotic strategy for recurrent cystitis management, addressing a critical unmet need in this population. Prospective controlled studies are warranted to validate these findings and optimize patient selection.

title: THE UROME STUDY: UROLOGICAL MICROBES- EPIDEMIOLOGY OVER 7 YEARS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Kidney & Bladder I (IP07)
authors: Theresa Pachta, Eric Edison, Nneoma Okeke, Alero Ilawole, Ho Kwong Li, Kay Thomas
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major threat, with the WHO projecting 39 million associated deaths by 2050. Thus, surveillance is vital. Antimicrobial use increased substantially during the COVID-19 pandemic; while respiratory pathogens have been studied, resistance trends in urological microbes across this period were not. METHODS: This was a retrospective study of urinary cultures analysed within a tertiary referral centre June 2018-2025. Organism identity and antimicrobial susceptibility data were collected. Subgroup analyses compared urology inpatients (IP) and outpatients (OP). Prevalence trends were assessed using logistic regression and Chi-squared testing. RESULTS: A total of 49,624 cultures yielded 55,330 isolates; 91.2% (50,497) bacterial and 8.7% (4,833) fungal. The most common bacteria were Escherichia coli (E. coli) (44%), Enterococcus sp. (15%), Klebsiella pneumoniae(K. pneumoniae) (9%), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa) (6%) and Proteus mirabilis (P. mirabilis)(5%). Extended Beta Lactamase (ESBL) resistance increased in E. coli (7.5% to 17.9%), K. pneumoniae (9.1% to 28.4%) and P. mirabilis (0.42% to 4.0%) (all p<0.0001). E. coli gentamicin resistance was high (21.2%) and rose in K. pneumoniae (13.9% to 19.6%, p<0.001). Amikacin resistance remained low (E. coli 0.69%, K. pneumonia 1.3%, P. mirabilis 0.92% and P. aeruginosa 3.1%). ESBL resistance was higher for urology IP than OP, E. coli (23.8% vs 13.5% p<0.0001), and K. pneumoniae (28.1% vs 14.6%, p>0.0001). Meropenem resistance was low for E. coli (0.07%), K. pneumoniae (0.82%) and P. mirabilis (0.03%). Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) remained stable (10%); linezolid resistance (LRE) was rare (0.1%).Fungi comprised 14.9% of inpatient isolates (n=3377). Candida albicans (C. albicans) predominated (57.8%), followed by Nakaseomyces glabrata (N. glabrata) (13.9%) and Candida tropicalis (C. tropicalis) (5.4%). Candidozyma auris (C. auris) emerged in 2024 (n=7). Antifungal resistance remained stable for fluconazole and flucytosine respectively: C. albicans (1.92%, 3.9%), N. glabrata (25%, 4.7%) and C. auris (100%, 0%). CONCLUSIONS: AMR in urinary pathogens is increasing, particularly ESBL-mediated resistance, while carbapenems and amikacin retain activity. VRE rates are stable but LRE is of growing concern given limited treatment. Whilst Funguria with resistance to antifungals that penetrate the urinary tract remains stable, the emergence of C. auris highlights the need for vigilant fungal surveillance. Sustained stewardship and routine fungal speciation are essential in urological practice.

title: RETROSPECTIVE ANALYSIS OF MRI AND INTRAOPERATIVE CORRELATION IN THE LOCALISATION OF UNDESCENDED TESTES IN INDIAN POPULATION
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Shushant Shandilya, Devashish Kaushal, Kumar Madhavan, Ketan Mehra, Prasoon Jha, Aditya Sood, Amanpreet Guliani
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Undescended testes (UDT) affect 1–4% of full-term and up to 30% of preterm male infants.
