Non-palpable UDT comprise ~20% and require accurate localization for surgical planning. Ultrasound, though widely used, has limited sensitivity. MRI, particularly with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), offers superior soft-tissue contrast and may improve preoperative localization. This study is aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of MRI with DWI in localizing non-palpable UDT and to compare findings with intraoperative outcomes in Indian patients. METHODS: A retrospective analysis of 32 male patients (age 15–30 years) with clinically non-palpable UDT, managed at a tertiary center between January 2023 and December 2024, was performed. All underwent MRI abdomen (T1, T2, DWI sequences), and findings were correlated with laparoscopic exploration. Ethical clearance was obtained (IHEC-LOP/2025/IP077). Informed consent was taken from all patients. Diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and statistical significance (Chi-square test) were calculated. RESULTS: MRI correctly localized 29/30 intraoperatively confirmed testes (true positives), failed to detect one testis (false negative), and accurately identified absent/atrophic testes in 2 cases (true negatives). No false positives occurred. Testes typically appeared hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, and showed restricted diffusion on DWI. Diagnostic performance: Sensitivity 96.7%, Specificity 100%, Positive Predictive Value 100%, Negative Predictive Value 66.7%, Accuracy 96.9%. Chi-square analysis showed a statistically significant association between MRI and surgical findings (χ2=10.81, p=0.001). Right-sided UDT predominated. Distribution on MRI: intracanalicular (17), low abdominal (10), high abdominal (2), ectopic (1), non-visualised (2). CONCLUSIONS: MRI with DWI demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy in preoperative localization of non-palpable UDT and can reduce unnecessary diagnostic surgeries. However, a negative MRI does not exclude UDT, making diagnostic laparoscopy indispensable. In resource-constrained Indian settings, DWI-MRI should be considered an essential adjunct in managing non-palpable UDT, optimizing surgical planning, and minimizing morbidity.

title: IS PERI-RENAL FAT THICKNESS OF THE CONTRALATERAL KIDNEY AS MEASURED ON PRE-OPERATIVE IMAGING ASSOCIATED WITH PROGRESSION TO CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE AFTER RADICAL NEPHRECTOMY?
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Ankur Choksi, Andrew Williams, Gabriela Nieto Blanco, Graham Kupsaw, Sarah Duncan, Boris Gershman, Peter Chang, Andrew Wagner
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Peri-renal fat thickness (PRFT) has been associated with the development of chronic kidney disease (CKD) with metabolic disorders. The association of PRFT and the development of CKD in patients undergoing radical nephrectomy has not been explored. In this study, we analyzed whether greater PRFT on pre-operative imaging of the contralateral kidney, is a predictor of CKD Stage 3a (CKD3A) following radical nephrectomy. METHODS: Using our institutional database, we retrospectively identified CKD-naïve adults (≥18 years) who underwent radical nephrectomy for localized kidney cancer between 2007 and 2025 with at least 6 months of follow-up. Patients were excluded if they lacked pre-operative imaging or labwork, had a GFR < 60 at time of nephrectomy, had a solitary kidney, had renal cysts that distorted measurement, or had less than 6 months of follow up. Demographic and clinical data were abstracted from the database. PRFT was measured on the contralateral kidney, by summating the anterior, lateral and posterior distances between the edge of the renal parenchyma and Gerota's fascia at the mid-hilar axial slice on pre-operative scans. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was generated to determine the optimal PRFT cutoff value with maximal diagnostic utility. Kaplan–Meier curves were generated to assess CKD3A–free survival stratified by the cutoff value. Cox proportional hazards regression analysis was performed to identify predictors of CKD3A at 10 years postoperatively. RESULTS: Of the 609 patients who underwent radical nephrectomy, 266 patients met criteria for inclusion. ROC curve identified a cutoff of 33 mm (AUC=0.63) by the Youden index. The patient demographic and clinical information is summarized in Table 1, stratified by a cutoff of 33mm. Patients with PRFT ≥ 33 mm had greater BMI and were more likely to have diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Using a PRFT cutoff of 33 mm, Kaplan-Meier curves with 95% confidence intervals were generated to model CKD3A-free survival ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191312.43845.bb.02#F1)). Multivariable cox regression at 10 years postoperatively revealed PRFT ≥ 33 mm was associated with greater hazards of CKD3A (HR: 1.82, 95% CI: 1.11 – 3.02, p=0.019) adjusting for age, sex, race, BMI, GFR, laterality, and history of diabetes, hypertension, and smoking. CONCLUSIONS: Contralateral PRFT ≥ 33 mm measured on pre-operative imaging is associated with a higher risk of CKD3A at 10 years following radical nephrectomy.

title: MEMBRANOUS URETHRAL LENGTH AS A PREDICTOR FOR URINARY INCONTINENCE AFTER HOLMIUM ENUCLEATION OF THE PROSTATE FOR BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Nick J. Lee, Tarek Benzouak, David-Dan Nguyen, Sebastien Belliveau, Liam Murad, Lynda Kadi, Nathan Perlis, Rodney Breau, Dean Elterman, Bilal Chughtai, Dan Gralnek, Damien Olivie, Malek Meskawi, Cristina Negrean, Naeem Bhojani
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) is as an effective, size-independent treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) with durable outcomes. However, one of its adverse outcomes is post-operative stress urinary incontinence (SUI). We sought to determine if membranous urethral length (MUL) as measured on preoperative magnetic resonance imaging is a predictor for post-operative SUI in patients undergoing HoLEP for BPH. METHODS: A single-center, retrospective observational study was conducted on 147 consecutive patients who underwent HoLEP for BPH between 2018 and 2024. Preoperative baseline characteristics, perioperative details, and SUI outcomes at 1, 3, and 6 months were collected. Binary logistic regression was used to assess the association between MUL and SUI at each follow-up interval. RESULTS: Median MUL was 8.2 mm (IQR 6.1-11.0), and post-operative SUI incidences were 73 (49.7%), 36 (24.5%), and 16 (10.9%) at 1, 3, and 6 months respectively. Longer MUL was significantly associated with lower odds of SUI at 1 month (OR: 0.86, 95% CI: 0.77-0.96, p=0.009), 3 months (OR: 0.77, 95% CI: 0.65-0.91, p=0.002), and 6 months (OR: 0.65, 95% CI: 0.49-0.87, p=0.004). Internal validation demonstrated good discrimination (areas under the curve of 0.73, 0.75, and 0.83 at 1, 3, and 6 months) with well-calibrated models, and decision curve analysis confirmed clinical utility within prespecified risk thresholds. CONCLUSIONS: Longer MUL is significantly associated with lower rates of SUI following HoLEP at 1, 3, and 6 months. Longer MUL may serve as a valuable predictive factor for continence recovery and should be considered during preoperative counseling and surgical decision planning.

title: ASSESSMENT OF URINARY TURBULENCE IN THE RENAL PELVIS USING CINE MR UROGRAPHY WITH MSDE PREPARATION
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Masaki Kobayashi, Taro Takahara, Tomoaki Moroda, Motohiro Fujiwara, Soichiro Yoshida, Yasuhisa Fujii
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary stasis in the lower calyx has been suggested to contribute to the development of lower calyceal stones. However, urinary flow dynamics within the renal pelvis remain poorly understood. Motion-sensitized driven-equilibrium (MSDE) MRI suppresses signals from moving fluids and can visualize subtle flow differences. This study aimed to assess urinary turbulence within the renal pelvis using cine MR urography combined with MSDE and to evaluate differences according to pelvic morphology. METHODS: Five healthy male volunteers (10 kidneys) without a history of urolithiasis were enrolled. Manganese chloride tetrahydrate was orally administered as a negative contrast agent before MRI. Cine MR urography without flow sensitization was first performed, followed by cine MR urography with MSDE preparation (venc=0.7 cm/s in three orthogonal directions) under breath-holding, repeated 30 times. Turbulence was identified as areas of signal loss within the renal pelvis on MSDE images. The renal pelvis was divided into upper, middle, and lower sectors, and the frequency of turbulence in each sector was evaluated. Mean turbulence occurrence rates were compared between single and divided pelvises. Additionally, fusion images combining all turbulence events in each renal pelvis were generated to visualize the overall likelihood and spatial distribution of turbulence. RESULTS: Turbulence was observed in all kidneys. Single and divided pelvises were identified in five kidneys each. The mean turbulence occurrence rates in single and divided pelvises were 59.5% and 77.7% in the upper pelvis (p=0.144), 93.8% and 82.9% in the middle pelvis (p=0.074), and 67.4% and 40.1% in the lower pelvis (p=0.095), respectively. On fusion images, single pelvises showed a uniform distribution of turbulence, whereas divided pelvises exhibited turbulence predominantly concentrated in the upper and middle pelvises. CONCLUSIONS: Cine MR urography combined with MSDE enabled noninvasive visualization of urinary turbulence within the renal pelvis. In divided pelvises, infrequent turbulence was observed in the lower pelvis, indicating reduced flow activity and potential urinary stasis in this region. This imaging method provides a novel approach for investigating renal pelvic hydrodynamics and their role in the pathophysiology of urolithiasis.

title: URETERAL WALL THICKNESS IN PREDICTING NEED FOR SURGICAL INTERVENTION IN URETERIC CALCULI ≤7 MM: SINGLE CENTRE RETROSPECTIVE ANALYSIS
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Siddhant Kumar, Surag Kr, Anupam Choudhary, Sunil Pillai Bhaskara, Padmaraj Hegde, Arun Chawla
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ureteric calculi measuring ≤7 mm represent a therapeutic dilemma. Although these stones are generally considered amenable to conservative management, a clinically relevant proportion eventually necessitate surgical intervention. Accurately identifying such patients at initial presentation remains difficult. Ureteral wall thickness (UWT), measurable on non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT), may reflect localized edema and inflammatory response, serving as a surrogate marker for stone impaction and failure of MET. This study aimed to evaluate UWT as a predictive factor for surgical intervention and to identify an optimal threshold that can guide management decisions METHODS: In this retrospective analysis, 460 consecutive adult patients presenting with solitary ureteric calculi ≤7 mm between January 2024 and June 2025 were included. All underwent baseline NCCT at presentation. UWT was measured in axial view at the point of maximal thickening adjacent to the stone. Patients were stratified into three UWT groups:Group A: <1.0 mmGroup B: 1.0–3.0 mmGroup C: >3.0 mmPatients managed conservatively received standardized MET comprising: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg, Adequate oral hydration, Analgesics (NSAIDs) SOSFollow-up included repeat NCCT at 6 weeks or earlier if symptoms worsened. Patients who developed intractable pain, persistent vomiting, fever or worsening hydronephrosis despite MET were triaged for early surgical intervention and classified as part of the intervention group. Surgical intervention was defined as requirement of ureteroscopy or DJ stenting. Statistical analysis included univariate and multivariate regression adjusting for age, sex, stone size, location, HU, hydronephrosis and ROC analysis to identify an optimal UWT cutoff. RESULTS: Of the 460 patients:Surgical intervention rates were:15/124 (12.1%) in Group A86/211 (40.8%) in Group B97/125 (77.6%) in Group C(p<0.001 for trend) UWT >3 mm as a strong independent predictor of surgical intervention (OR: 13.2, 95% CI: 7.1–24.5, p<0.001).ROC analysis demonstrated an AUC of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.80–0.88).A UWT cutoff of 2.6 mm provided the best discriminatory power (sensitivity: 80%, specificity: 76%). CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative ureteral wall thickness measured on NCCT is a robust and independent predictor of need for surgical intervention in patients with ureteric calculi ≤7 mm. A UWT cutoff of 2.6 mm offers strong diagnostic accuracy for anticipating MET failure. Incorporating UWT into initial assessment protocols alongside traditional stone parameters can enhance early triage, facilitate patient counselling and potentially reduce time to definitive management.

title: REDEFINING RADIATION-FREE SURGERY: OUTCOMES OF ZERO-FLUORO PCNL AT A HIGH-VOLUME ENDOUROLOGY CENTER
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Mohamad Watfa, Alejandro Bautista-Pérez-Gavilán, Adam Cohen, José Agudelo, Sri Sivalingam
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Concerns of radiation exposure during percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) inspired alternative approaches for securing renal access and stone removal. Advances in ultrasound and scope technologies have enabled zero-fluoroscopy PCNL (ZF-PCNL) as a radiation-free alternative by combining ultrasonography (US) and endoscopic guidance. While feasibility has been previously reported, perioperative outcomes data for ZF-PCNL remain limited. We examined our outcomes on a novel ZF-PCNL technique in a high-volume endourology center. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed records of patients who underwent PCNL between January and September 2025, during which we performed ZF-PCNL. Demographic and perioperative outcomes were analyzed, with specific attention to cases that ultimately required fluoroscopy. These were stratified into those with planned fluoroscopic assistance and those where fluoroscopy was used as a rescue modality. RESULTS: A total of 97 consecutive patients underwent PCNL with our ZF-PCNL protocol during the study period. Mean linear stone burden was 27.5 mm. Fluoroscopy was employed in 22% of cases (18% planned, 5% converted), while 77% were completed without any fluoroscopy. Preemptive fluoroscopy was used in cases where retrograde ureteroscopic access was not deemed ideal, such as complex staghorn extending into UPJ, impacted stones, ureteral strictures, or urinary diversion. No intraoperative complications were observed, and mean length of stay was 23 hours. Postoperative fever/infection was noted in 5% of patients, and no blood transfusions or pleural complications occurred; 9% of patients presented to the emergency department within 30 days, with 5.2% requiring a secondary or staged procedure. Postoperative imaging was obtained in 82% of patients, and residual fragments ≤4 mm were identified in 66% of those who had CT. CONCLUSIONS: Zero-fluoro PCNL using our novel approach is a feasible technique for experienced endourologists. Our perioperative outcomes demonstrate ZF-PCNL to be a safe and effective technique for large renal stones, while providing ergonomic and safety advantages beyond radiation reduction alone. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: COMPARISON OF THE CHOKAI, STONE, AND NEW STONE SCORES FOR PREDICTING URETERAL STONES: EVIDENCE FROM A MULTICENTER PROSPECTIVE COHORT
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Hiroki Kusumoto, Hiroki Fukuhara, Osamu Ichiyanagi, Asumi Sugiura, Yuko Kawamura, Tadahiro Kobayashi, Tadahiro Kaneko, Toshihiro Tawara, Masaaki Tsukigi, Ryosuke Nomura, Kazunori Takahashi, Masaki Ushijima, Kento Morozumi, Yasuhiro Kaiho, Tomoyuki Endo, Norihiko Tsuchiya
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The CHOKAI and STONE scores are widely used for diagnosing ureteral stones. The STONE score includes race, whose clinical relevance has been questioned. The New STONE score replaced race with obvious hematuria ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191312.43845.bb.07#F1)), but its external validation against the CHOKAI score remains untested. This study aimed to compare the diagnostic accuracy of the CHOKAI and New STONE scores and to evaluate the New STONE score against the original STONE score in a Japanese multicenter cohort. METHODS: We analyzed 164 patients (98 with ureteral stones, 66 without) aged ≥15 years who presented to the emergency department with acute flank, back, or lower abdominal pain, from a multicenter prospective database collected during 2017–2018 and 2024–2025. Obvious hematuria was defined as (i) gross hematuria confirmed by medical staff or (ii) microscopic hematuria with ≥100 red blood cells per high-power field. Although data were prospectively collected, hematuria was retrospectively verified. Diagnostic performance was assessed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, calculating area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity for each scoring system. RESULTS: The CHOKAI score demonstrated significantly higher diagnostic accuracy than the New STONE score (AUC 0.944 vs. 0.837, p<0.001) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191312.43845.bb.07#F2)). The New STONE and original STONE scores showed similar performance (AUC 0.837 vs. 0.843, p=0.354). At optimal cutoffs, CHOKAI ≥6 achieved sensitivity 0.95 and specificity 0.88; New STONE ≥5 yielded 0.79 and 0.77; STONE ≥8 yielded 0.76 and 0.79, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: The CHOKAI score showed superior diagnostic accuracy compared with the New STONE score, while the New and original STONE scores performed comparably. These findings highlight the robustness of the CHOKAI score and support the New STONE score’s applicability to non-Western populations.

title: BMI-STRATIFIED CT DOSING PROTOCOL FOR POST-PCNL IMAGING: MINIMIZING RADIATION WHILE MAINTAINING DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Elizabeth A. Baldwin, Daniel Jhang, Erica Kinne, Kallan Richards, Jongwan Park, Ruben Crew, Gabriel E. Martin, Ali Albaghli, Zhamshid Okhunov, D. Duane Baldwin
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Current publication guidelines require computed tomography (CT) imaging following percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) to establish stone-free status. Current AUA guidelines recommend periodic imaging for stone surveillance. Current estimates predict that 5% of all new cancers are a result of CT imaging. The CT scan parameter most often adjusted to reduce CT dose is tube current–time product (milliampere seconds \[mAs\]). While low dose (LD) CT is routinely employed, certain factors may reduce image quality such as BMI, metal hardware, and arm positioning. This study aimed to develop a predictive model for determining the optimal CT dose required for adequate stone-free assessment at the lowest radiation dose based on patient characteristics. METHODS: We performed a retrospective review of 376 adult post-PCNL CTs at a single institution (2017 to 2024). Data collected included BMI, age, presence of metal hardware, patient arm positioning, mAs, and total radiation dose (dose length product \[DLP\]). Two attending endourologists and one radiologist blindly reviewed and rated the quality of deidentified CTs using a 5-point scale (1=inadequate, 2=marginally adequate, 3=ideal dose, 4=excessive dose, 5=extreme dose). A quartile regression model at the 25th percentile was performed for statistical analysis (p<0.05 considered significant). RESULTS: Mean patient age and BMI were 58 years and 30.7 kg/m2, respectively. Using the mean reviewer score (with target score 2-3.5), we developed BMI-stratified dosing guidelines: BMI <18.5 requires 30 mAs, BMI 18.5-29.9 requires 15 mAs, BMI 30-49.9 requires 30 mAs, BMI 50-59.9 requires 50 mAs, and BMI ≥60 requires 70 mAs. Quartile regression showed the presence of metal hardware required the greatest mAs increase for adequate imaging (β=83.2, p<0.001), followed by arms positioned within the field of scan (β=14.6, p=0.003). Patients whose arms cannot be removed from the imaging field, and those with metal hardware require mAs increases to meet minimal imaging standards. CONCLUSIONS: This BMI-stratified protocol provides the first evidence-based dosing guidelines to minimize radiation exposure while maintaining diagnostic accuracy for post-PCNL imaging. Utilization of these guidelines could significantly reduce cumulative radiation burden and potential future cancers in stone patients, without compromising detection of residual stones.

title: RESTORING BLADDER CONTROL VIA REPETITIVE TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION OF THE SUPPLEMENTARY MOTOR AREA AND DORSOLATERAL PREFRONTAL CORTEX IN IDIOPATHIC OVERACTIVE BLADDER
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Kristopher A. Hoffman, Betsy H. Salazar, Kevin Colbert, Rose Khavari, Rachel A. High
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) is associated with dysregulated activity within the bladder control network. Our repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) protocol targets two brain regions key in OAB by applying low-frequency (LF) rTMS to the pelvic supplementary motor area (pSMA) and high-frequency (HF) rTMS the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). We hypothesize this dual-site rTMS will reduce exaggerated urgency perception, improve pelvic floor control, and enhance voluntary suppression of the micturition reflex. METHODS: Adults with idiopathic OAB underwent resting-state functional MRI (fMRI) scans at baseline and after 5 sessions of rTMS to assess changes in functional connectivity within the brain-bladder control network. 40-minute rTMS sessions (once per day) delivered inhibitory 1 Hz stimulation (1,200 pulses) to the pSMA, then excitatory 10 Hz stimulation (2,000 pulses) to the right DLPFC. Bladder diary and symptom questionnaires measured at baseline, immediate post-rTMS, 3 weeks, and 6 weeks were compared with 1-way ANOVA. RESULTS: 14 participants (13 female, 1 male; mean age 63.8 ± 11.2 years) completed all rTMS sessions without serious adverse events. Bladder diary measures decreased post-rTMS and 3 weeks post-rTMS but returned to baseline at 6 weeks post-rTMS ( Figure 1A, B). At 3 weeks post-rTMS, symptom bother scores were significantly decreased (mean difference -30, p<0.02) and quality of life scores significantly increased (mean difference 11.4, p<0.02) at 3 weeks post-rTMS. Analyses of pre- and post-treatment fMRI data demonstrated emerging alterations in functional connectivity between the pSMA, DLPFC, and subcortical regions involved in bladder sensory and motor control ( Fig1 C, D). Although these findings are preliminary and not yet statistically significant, the observed directional trends support the hypothesis that rTMS induces adaptive neuroplasticity within supraspinal circuits governing lower urinary tract function. CONCLUSIONS: Preliminary findings suggest that rTMS targeting the pelvic SMA and right DLPFC may exert durable, beneficial effects on bladder function and symptom burden in idiopathic OAB.

title: AI-ASSISTED CYSTOSCOPIC DIAGNOSIS FOR CIS AND IC/HLD: STANDARDIZING VISUAL INTERPRETATION ACROSS MALIGNANT AND INFLAMMATORY LESIONS
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Taro Igarashi, Yuto Nukariya, Shota Kawano, Akira Furuta, Takahiro Kimura
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Differentiating carcinoma in situ (CIS) from interstitial cystitis with hunner lesion disease (IC/HLD) remains one of the most difficult challenges in cystoscopic diagnosis ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191312.43845.bb.10#F1): Representative cystoscopic findings of CIS and IC/HLD). Both present as flat erythematous mucosa under white light, yet their management differs completely—CIS requires oncologic therapy, while IC/HLD is treated symptomatically. Misclassification can lead to overtreatment or delayed cancer therapy. Despite advances in cystoscopic imaging, recent studies and expert reviews have highlighted major limitations in artificial intelligence (AI) research: heterogeneous datasets, uncertain labeling of Hunner versus non-Hunner phenotypes, limited external validation, and black-box interpretability issues. We aimed to evaluate whether AI can overcome these limitations, achieve reproducible diagnostic accuracy across both malignant and inflammatory lesions, and reduce interobserver variability among human specialists. METHODS: A PRISMA-guided meta-analysis included eight validated studies (2015–2025): six on bladder cancer (including CIS) and two on IC/HLD. Random-effects models estimated pooled diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity (95% CI). In parallel, diagnostic performance was compared among 20 board-certified urologists accredited by the Japanese Urological Association (JUA): 10 members of the Society of Interstitial Cystitis of Japan (SICJ) and 10 non-members from Jikei University Hospital. All had ≥4 years of post-residency training and independently reviewed 100 cystoscopic images (CIS, papillary tumors, IC/HLD). Variability among physicians was analyzed by disease type. Institutional ethics approval was obtained (Jikei University, No. 33-170). RESULTS: AI achieved a pooled diagnostic accuracy of 92.6% (95% CI 90.2–94.9), with balanced sensitivity (91.8%) and specificity (93.5%) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191312.43845.bb.10#F2): Diagnostic accuracy of AI-assisted cystoscopic diagnosis). Among human experts, diagnostic accuracy varied significantly by disease category. SICJ members outperformed non-members in IC/HLD (82.0% vs 46.0%, p=0.0066), while non-members showed relatively higher accuracy for CIS (78.0% vs 64.0%, p=0.111). Both groups achieved comparable precision for papillary tumors (96.0% vs 95.0%, p=0.34). These results confirm that AI can mitigate lesion-dependent diagnostic variability among specialists. CONCLUSIONS: This study integrates meta-analytic evidence from eight validated AI cystoscopy studies with comparative data from board-certified urologists. AI maintained over 90% diagnostic accuracy and demonstrated reproducibility across malignant and inflammatory conditions, whereas human specialists showed domain-specific variability. By addressing data heterogeneity, labeling ambiguity, and interpretability barriers highlighted in recent reviews, AI-assisted cystoscopy advances toward clinical translation. It equalizes diagnostic accuracy across expertise levels, standardizes endoscopic interpretation, and enhances precision in clinical decision-making. This technology represents a pivotal step toward globally reproducible and equitable cystoscopic diagnosis in urologic practice.

title: PLDAM: A MULTIMODAL AND INTERPRETABLE AI MODEL FOR ACCURATE DIAGNOSIS AND RISK STRATIFICATION OF PELVIC LIPOMATOSIS FROM CT AND MRI
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Mancheng Xia, Yiming Zhang, Liqing Xu, He Wang, Zihan Wang, Guoli Wang, Yiming Lin, Pengcheng Jiao, Kunlin Yang, Xiang Wang, Zhihua Li, Hongjian Zhu, Peng Zhang, Yaming Gu, Xicai Zhang, Jiaxin Xie, Chunlin Liu, Ruili Guan, Liqun Zhou, Kai Zhang, Xuesong Li
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Pelvic lipomatosis (PL) is a rare but clinically significant condition that can lead to progressive urinary obstruction and renal dysfunction, of which the diagnosis remains challenging due to nonspecific imaging features and substantial inter-reader variability. Our aim was to develop and validate a multimodal, interpretable artificial intelligence model—the Pelvic Lipomatosis Discriminant Analysis Model (PLDAM)—for accurate PL diagnosis from CT and MRI data, and to establish an imaging-based risk scoring system (PL-RS) to support individualized clinical decision-making. METHODS: This multicentre diagnostic study included 3,185 retrospective and 463 prospective urinary system CT and T1-weighted MRI scans collected from five Chinese hospitals between 2013 and 2024. After expert annotation and preprocessing, datasets were divided into training, internal, prospective, and external validation cohorts. Pelvic structures were automatically segmented using deep learning models, and radiomic and anatomical features were selected by combining least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression with the Boruta algorithm. Gradient Boosting Machine was used to construct PLDAM, whose interpretability and risk stratification were assessed using SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis and K-means clustering to derive the nine-feature PL-RS (score range, 0-13). RESULTS: PLDAM achieved outstanding diagnostic performance across all datasets (AUCs: training, 0.99; internal, 0.96; prospective, 0.96; external, 0.95), outperforming CT-only and MRI-only models. The model accurately identified both early-stage (PL I) and high-risk (PL IV) patients, demonstrating stable performance across the full clinical spectrum. The PL-RS correlated strongly with disease severity (p<0.001). In a reader study of 60 clinicians, PLDAM assistance significantly improved diagnostic accuracy and reduced interpretation time, particularly among less-experienced physicians. CONCLUSIONS: PLDAM is the first explainable, multimodal AI model for pelvic lipomatosis diagnosis, achieving expert-level accuracy and enhancing clinical efficiency. The accompanying PL-RS provides an interpretable, model-independent tool for early screening and risk-based management.

title: DOES THE PRESENCE OF BALLOON “WAISTING” DURING PACLITAXEL DRUG-COATED BALLOON DILATION AFFECT SUCCESS RATES?
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Vincent Hou, Helen H. Sun, Karen M. Doersch, Sasha Vereecken, Ty T. Higuchi, Brian J. Flynn
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Paclitaxel drug-coated balloon dilation (DCB) is an endoscopic therapy for urethral stricture disease (USD). Waisting, defined as a persistent indentation of the DCB during inflation, is an intraoperative finding that may reflect underlying fibrosis or rigidity, yet its clinical relevance remains unclear. Here, we aim to evaluate the relationship between DCB waisting and treatment outcomes. METHODS: We performed a retrospective review of patients who underwent DCB dilation at a single institution from 2024-2025. Pre-dilation was performed prior to DCB in all cases. Presence of intraoperative waisting was assessed independently by attending urologists. Treatment success was defined as the absence of recurrent stricture on cystoscopy, imaging, or patient-reported obstructive symptoms (weak stream, hesitancy). Clinical variables were compared between waisted/non-waisted groups using Fisher’s exact t-tests. RESULTS: 84 patients (including 16 patients with multiple DCB dilations) underwent 122 total DCB dilations. Median age and BMI were 67.6 years (range 21.1-92.8) and 27.4 kg/m2 (17.2-47.9). 41 patients had prior radiation (11 waisted, 30 non-waisted) and 79 patients had undergone a median of 1 prior treatment (1-9) for USD, including 33 prior urethroplasties. Out of 122 dilations, stricture types included bulbomembranous (n=64), bladder neck/vesicourethral anastomosis (VUA, n=52), and penile (n=6). Among patients with >3 months of follow-up, (15 waisted, 63 non-waisted), the waisted group demonstrated a trend toward higher treatment failure, though this did not reach significance (67% vs 42% failure, p=0.10). Waisting patients were more likely to have bladder neck/VUA strictures (71% waisting vs 36% non-waisting, p=0.01); radiation, age and prior stricture treatments were not significantly associated with waisting. There were no complications above Clavien-Dindo grade IIIa. CONCLUSIONS: Although DCB waisting was not significantly associated with treatment failure, a trend toward decreased success was observed in this cohort. This trend may have been influenced by the increased complexity of USD treated, with high incidence of pelvic radiation and prior stricture interventions. Further studies with larger samples and follow-up periods may validate waisting as a predictor of treatment failure.

title: DYNAMIC MRI ASSESSMENT OF URETHRAL STRICTURE: A NOVEL APPROACH TO NONINVASIVE ASSESSMENT OF LOWER URINARY TRACT BIOMECHANICS
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Ajinkya R. Limkar, Juan Pablo Gonzalez-Pereira, Madison Taychert, Alejandro Roldan-Alzate, Matthew D. Grimes
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Retrograde urethrogram (RUG) is the gold standard for diagnosing and staging urethral stricture disease (USD), but it is invasive and provides only 2D anatomical assessment of urethral caliber. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has been widely used in cardiovascular fluid dynamics, leading to significant scientific and clinical advances. Our group developed a noninvasive dynamic voiding MRI urethrogram (VMRU) protocol coupled with CFD that provides detailed anatomical information and quantitative biomechanical data in vivo. Here, we present a pilot study using VMRU in USD patients and hypothesize that regional variations in voiding urethral pressure, velocity, and wall shear stress (WSS) are higher in USD patients compared to healthy individuals. METHODS: Two subjects with bulbar USD scheduled for urethroplasty and two healthy volunteers underwent pelvic MRI on a clinical 3T scanner, and voiding dynamic volumetric images were acquired. The bladder and urethra were semi-automatically segmented, generating 3D models throughout voiding. Pressure, velocity, and WSS were calculated in SimVascular CFD using urethral 3D models and inflow rates derived from MRI-based bladder volume displacement. RESULTS: Sagittal VMRU images were compared to fluoroscopic RUG with similar appearance ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191312.43845.bb.14#F1)). Comparison of MRI-derived flow parameters demonstrated notable regional variation in USD compared to normal. Specifically, USD patients demonstrated higher urine velocities, increased wall shear stress, and pressure gradients across the strictured segment compared to non strictured urethras ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191312.43845.bb.14#F2)). CONCLUSIONS: We demonstrate the feasibility of VMRU coupled with CFD for in vivo assessment of urethral biomechanics in USD. We found that regional flow dynamics including pressure, velocity, and wall shear stress are altered in USD patients compared to non-strictured patients. These techniques have the potential be a powerful research tool enabling non-invasive and rigorous study of the impact of varying stricture characteristics on urethral biomechanics and how these are modulated with current repair techniques.

title: PHOTOACOUSTIC IMAGING FOR ASSESSMENT OF COLLAGEN REMODELING AND FIBROSIS IN A PARTIAL BLADDER OUTLET OBSTRUCTION RAT MODEL
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Alexander Koven, Eno Hysi, Xiaolin He, Monica Farcas, Darren Yuen
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Bladder fibrosis, predominantly driven by collagen remodeling, is a major contributor to bladder dysfunction. In partial bladder outlet obstruction (pBOO), such as that caused by benign prostatic enlargement, collagen remodeling and fibrosis play a central role in the progression to impaired bladder compliance and underactive bladder. Currently, no diagnostic tests exist to noninvasively monitor collagen remodeling in the bladder wall over time, limiting opportunities to optimize treatment before irreversible fibrosis and bladder decompensation develop. Our group has developed a novel photoacoustic (PA) imaging technique to quantitatively assess collagen. In this study, we investigate the application of PA imaging to measure changes in bladder collagen content in a pBOO rat model. METHODS: pBOO was induced in female Sprague-Dawley rats using a nerve-sparing mid-urethral obstruction technique and compared to weight-matched sham-operated controls. Rats were sacrificed at weeks 4 and 8 post-procedure. Prior to sacrifice, 24-hour urine output was measured in metabolic cages. At sacrifice, bladders were imaged with a VevoLAZR-X US/PA imaging system (680–930nm, 15MHz). A novel spectral unmixing algorithm was used to quantify a collagen contribution score (CCS) for each specimen. For the primary outcome, the PA-derived CCS values were correlated with collagen-to-muscle ratios (C:M) determined histologically from picrosirius red–stained biopsy sections. RESULTS: A total of 27 rats were analyzed (week 4: 4 sham, 8 pBOO; week 8: 4 sham, 11 pBOO). At both weeks 4 and 8 post-procedure, pBOO rats exhibited significantly lower C:M and CCS values compared to sham-operated controls (all p<0.05), consistent with compensatory muscle hypertrophy during remodeling. Metabolic cage testing showed no differences in urine output or urinary frequency between groups. Correlation analysis revealed a strong positive relationship between C:M and CCS across cohorts (r=0.75). CONCLUSIONS: This study is the first to apply PA imaging for the noninvasive measurement of bladder collagen. The findings validate the accuracy of PA imaging for collagen assessment and demonstrate its promise as a tool for detecting and monitoring bladder fibrosis, with the potential to enable earlier diagnosis, improve disease surveillance, and guide timely therapeutic interventions.

title: DETRUSOR OVERACTIVITY EFFECTS ON BLADDER WALL MICROMOTION: A NON-INVASIVE ULTRASOUND AND URODYNAMICS STUDY
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Mariam M. William, Sydney J. Smith, Mina P. Ghatas, Linda S. Burkett, John E. Speich, Adam P. Klausner
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) is a condition characterized by urinary urgency, often associated with detrusor overactivity (DO). Urodynamic (UDS) studies are the gold standard for assessing DO, which involve bladder catheterization and carry the risk of discomfort and urinary tract infection. Emerging evidence shows that bladder wall micromotion (BWM) plays a role in OAB and may be detectable non-invasively using ultrasound displacement imaging. This study aims to evaluate the relationship between ultrasound displacement patterns and DO events to determine whether micromotion characteristics change before and after a DO event. METHODS: Ultrasound anatomic M-mode cine-loops of the bladder were obtained from participants with OAB during clinically indicated UDS. The ICIq-OAB survey was used to evaluate the OAB severity. Ultrasound imaging was completed at ~50% cystometric capacity based on a pre-study void diary. DO events occurred before or after M-mode acquisition in subsets of patients. A custom texture correlation algorithm tracked temporal changes in bladder wall thickness. The peak micromotion amplitude, per participant, within 1–7 cycles/min from time segments before or after DO events was extracted using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) analysis. RESULTS: A total of 26 women were analyzed (8 DO (30.8%), 18 non-DO (69.2%)). The participants with DO detected on UDS were significantly older (69.6 vs. 59.7 years, p=0.04) and had higher BMI (34.6 vs. 28.1 kg/m2, p=0.006), while ICIQ-OAB scores did not differ (p=0.61). Micromotion amplitude was significantly higher after DO events (0.47 ± 0.10 a. u.) compared to before DO events (0.15 ± 0.06) and in the non-DO controls (0.05 ± 0.08, p0.017, Bonferroni-corrected), Figure 1. These results indicate increased synchronization of bladder wall motion following DO. Micromotion above the published significance threshold (≥ 0.1 a. u.) was present in 4/4 after DO, 3/4 before DO, and 3/18 controls. CONCLUSIONS: This work extends ultrasound techniques for detecting bladder wall micromotion by comparing micromotion amplitude before and after DO. Results show that micromotion was present in all subjects but increased following DO, suggesting enhanced bladder wall synchrony rather than a binary diagnostic marker. Ongoing studies will determine whether micromotion metrics can differentiate further OAB subtypes and support non-invasive urodynamic assessment.

title: CHARACTERIZATION OF NORMAL BLADDER PARAMETERS USING 3D MAGNETIC RESONANCE FINGERPRINTING
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Giulia M. Ippolito, Melis Ozkan, Vikas Gulani, Aruna Sarma, Anne P. Cameron, Shane Wells, Jesse Hamilton
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Magnetic Resonance Fingerprinting (MRF) is an emerging imaging framework that enables simultaneous quantitative mapping of multiple tissue properties. While MRF techniques have been developed and applied in several organ systems, their use in the bladder has been limited. We aimed to develop a high-resolution 3D MRF approach for whole-bladder and apply it to characterize normal bladder wall tissue properties values in healthy adults. METHODS: After voiding, MRF datasets were acquired at 1x1x3 mm3 resolution during an 11.8 min scan in a sagittal orientation. Global T1 and T2 values were measured over the entire bladder wall. Regional T1 and T2 values were measured within pre-established regions of interest (ROIs). Bladder wall thickness (BWT) was measured both globally and regionally using synthetic T2-weighted images derived from the MRF maps. The mean and standard deviation of T1, T2, and BWT were calculated across subjects, and associations with sex and age were investigated. RESULTS: A total of 29 participants were recruited (15 female; ages 18-78 years) and 17 participants underwent 1.5T and 3T MRI using the same MRF sequence. Some subjects only completed exams at one field strength (n=13 at 1.5T only, n=2 at 3T only). Global bladder T1 values were 984±53 ms at 1.5T and 1486±118 ms at 3T, and T2 values were 51.4±5.6 ms at 1.5T and 43.5±4.0 ms at 3T. Consistent with expected MRI physics, T1 values were significantly higher at 3T versus 1.5T (p0.001), while T2 values were significantly lower at 3T versus 1.5T (p0.001). Global BWT was 4.5±1.6 mm at 1.5T and 4.3±1.6 mm at 3T, with no significant differences between field strengths. Mean T1 and T2 values tended to be slightly higher in the dome and posterior wall compared to other bladder wall regions (e. g,. T1 1024 vs. 973 ms and T2 56 vs. 49 ms in anterior wall vs. dome at 1.5T).There were no statistical differences in T1 T2, or BWT values based on sex, although a trend was observed with higher BWT in men ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191312.43845.bb.17#F1)). Global T1 and BWT showed no correlation with age, while a weak positive correlation with age was identified for T2 values at both field strengths ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191312.43845.bb.17#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: We demonstrate the feasibility of high-resolution 3D bladder MRF at 1.5T and 3T, provide normative T1 and T2 relaxation measurements, and offer preliminary insights into age- and sex-related differences in healthy adults.

title: HIGH-FREQUENCY QUANTITATIVE MICRO-ULTRASOUND FOR NONINVASIVE CHARACTERIZATION OF RENAL CANCER SUBTYPES
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Laura Zuluaga, Alexander D. Gleed, Jewel Bamby, Cameron Hoerig, Kennedy Okhawere, Edward Zeltner, Jonathan Mamou, Ketan K. Badani
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Preoperative differentiation of renal cancer subtypes remains challenging. Renal mass biopsy is an invasive and underutilized procedure. Quantitative and micro-ultrasound (QUS/MUS) can assess tissue microstructure noninvasively. This study evaluated the feasibility of high-frequency ultrasound to classify benign and malignant renal tumors. METHODS: Renal tumors resected by partial or radical nephrectomy were scanned immediately after surgery using a 29-MHz ExactVu™ micro-ultrasound. In the initial cohort (n=137), cine loops were visually reviewed to identify echotextural patterns correlated with pathology across clear cell, papillary, chromophobe, oncocytoma, and angiomyolipoma subtypes. In the subsequent QUS cohort (n=44), parameters from radiofrequency data were analyzed to identify discriminating features; the homodyned K-distribution structure parameter (κ) and effective acoustic concentration (EAC) formed a linear classifier. RESULTS: Quantitative classification achieved 89% accuracy, 92% sensitivity, and 71% specificity ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191312.43845.bb.18#F1) and Table 1). Distinct imaging features were observed: clear cell RCC showed solid to cystic patterns; papillary RCC had granular heterogeneous texture; chromophobe RCC displayed punctate hyperechoic foci; oncocytoma appeared homogeneous with cyst-like regions; and angiomyolipoma was globally hyperechoic with small hypoechoic foci. CONCLUSIONS: High-frequency QUS/MUS enables differentiation of renal tumor subtypes using quantitative and architectural features. This noninvasive approach shows promise to guide diagnosis and reduce unnecessary surgery. Ongoing efforts include validation and in-vivo testing.

title: PREDICTING CLEAR CELL SUBTYPE FOR KIDNEY TUMORS FROM CROSS-SECTIONAL IMAGING USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Haya T. Abusafieh, Rikhil L. Seshadri, Sahil H. Patel, Rishi Jonnalagadda, Daniel Jevnikar, Salim Younis, Abdulrahman Al-Bayati, Nicolas Saputro, Jacob M. Knorr, Gagan Fervaha, Michal Ozery-Flato, Michal Rosen-Zvi, Robert Abouassaly, Erick Remer, Nicholas Heller, Christopher J. Weight
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common subtype of kidney cancer in adults. The standard of care for localized RCC is partial or radical nephrectomy or active surveillance for small tumors. Histologic diagnosis can assist shared decision-making, but is typically unavailable prior to renal mass biopsy, which has limitations due to tumor heterogeneity. This study explores whether histopathologic diagnoses can be predicted based on radiomic data. We present the application of artificial intelligence (AI) to predict the clear cell subtype directly from preoperative imaging. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent nephrectomy with available preoperative contrast-enhanced abdominal CT imaging from 10/2009 to 7/2024 at a single large health system. A ResNet-50 architecture was fine-tuned to predict ccRCC, using a 5-fold cross-validation. Additional models were trained on tumors sized 3-7 cm. The ensemble of 5 models was validated on an independent external dataset. AUC comparisons between the AI model and a tumor size-based prediction model were evaluated using DeLong’s test. RESULTS: Among 1642 nephrectomy patients with imaging and subtype classifications, 822 had tumors 3-7 cm. In the whole cohort, the model achieved an AUC of 0.71, significantly outperforming the tumor size AUC of 0.54 (p=6.6e-21). For the 3-7 cm subset, the model achieved an AUC of 0.81, outperforming tumor size (AUC of 0.49; p=2.1e-26). On the external validation cohort, the model also outperformed tumor size in the 3-7 cm subset (AUCs of 0.59 vs 0.44; p=0.009), but not significantly in the full external cohort. CONCLUSIONS: A computer-vision AI model can predict ccRCC from CT imaging more accurately than tumor size, offering a potential non-invasive alternative to biopsy for presurgical decision-making in kidney cancer. This may support treatment planning in cases where knowing the tumor subtype could influence the management approach. | | | --- | | |

title: EVALUATION OF RENAL IMAGING IN PATIENTS WITH BIRT-HOGG-DUBé SYNDROME
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Amalie Angel, Lilian Bomme Ousager, Annette Schuster, Tommy Hemmert Olesen, Jesper Rømhild Davidsen, Lars Lund
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome (BHD) is a rare genetic syndrome associated with lung, skin and kidney involvement with an increased risk of renal cell carcinoma (RCC). Clinical guidelines recommend renal Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) surveillance every 2 years. Aim: To evaluate renal imaging strategies in BHD patients. METHODS: All patients with BHD from the Region of Southern Denmark covering 1.3 mill. inhabitants were included in this single-center retrospective cohort study. Clinical and radiological data were extracted from medical records and radiology reports to assess renal morphology, RCC incidence, disease progression, and treatment decisions. RESULTS: A total of 151 patients (47% men, mean age at diagnosis, 48 years of age (18-86); women 50 years of age (19-77)) were included. 72 patients (48%) presented with benign renal cysts, 59 patients (39%) with no renal abnormalities while 20 patients (13%) had RCC. Renal status remained stable in 113 patients (75%) and 9 patients (12%) showed benign progression. Initial pathological imaging was significantly associated with RCC diagnosis (p<0.001), whereas patients with normal initial imaging showed a low likelihood of developing RCC. Furthermore, arterial hypertension was significantly associated with RCC (P=0.01). CONCLUSIONS: In a cohort of patients with BHD, renal imaging identified 13% with RCC, which supports a risk-adapted surveillance strategy. MRI surveillance intervals may be safely extended to 6 years in patients without renal abnormalities at first investigation. This approach could result in an estimated cost saving of approximately €69,000 over a 6-year period, while reducing healthcare burden and maintaining patient safety. Lifelong surveillance remains essential because of the increased lifetime risk of RCC in BHD patients.

title: PROGNOSTIC IMPACT OF SARCOPENIC OBESITY AND SYSTEMIC INFLAMMATION IN NON-METASTATIC RENAL CELL CARCINOMA AND RENAL ONCOCYTOMA
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Dario Garcia-Rojo, Marta Capdevila, Clara Centeno, Arturo Dominguez-Garcia, Leticia De Verdonces, Antoni Malet-Munte, Diana Fuertes, Olga Mayordomo, Carmina Pla, Anna Ferran, Paula Azuara, Silvia Cuadrench, Maria Eugenia Zegri, Anna Gavalda, Nuria Masip, Ayelen Millan, Eduardo Vicente, Jose Luis Gonzalez-Sala, Naim Hannaoui, Angel Prera, Jesus Muñoz-Rodriguez
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) and sarcopenia, a progressive skeletal muscle disorder, are both linked to an adverse prognosis in various malignancies. Sarcopenic obesity (SO), a condition characterized by a combination of high body fat and low muscle mass, and systemic inflammation has also been associated with poor survival. However, their prognostic impact on localized renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and renal oncocytoma has not been established. We therefore investigated the influence of SO and systemic inflammation on the prognosis of patients with non-metastatic RCC or renal oncocytoma. METHODS: We analyzed a retrospective cohort of 270 patients who had a partial or radical nephrectomy for non-metastatic RCC (n=251) or renal oncocytoma (n=19) between January 2005 and December 2015. The median follow-up was 126 months (IQR: 99.07-166.04). We used pre-operative CT scans to measure visceral adipose tissue (VAT) at the umbilicus level and total abdominal muscle area (TAM) at the L3 level (TAM includes the psoas, paraspinal, transversus abdominis, rectus abdominis, and internal and external oblique muscles). Sarcopenic obesity was defined as the ratio of VAT to TAM:(VAT/TAM). Systemic inflammation was assessed using pre-operative blood markers: the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and the lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR). We evaluated overall survival (OS), cancer-specific survival (CSS), and progression-free survival (PFS). Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox regression models were used to find factors linked to survival, with a p-value of <0.05 considered significant. RESULTS: Of the 270 patients, 134 (49.6%) had sarcopenic obesity. This group was older (OR: 1.07, 95%CI:1.04-1.09) and more obese (OR:1.07, 95%CI: 1.02-1.12), with a higher incidence of advanced pathological stage III (OR:2.37, 95%CI: 1.13-5.28) and histological grade II (OR:1.8, 95%CI: 1.08-3.04). Patients with sarcopenic obesity had significantly shorter OS (63.52% vs. 78.05%, p=0.00068). High NLR (65.24 versus 75.99%, p=0.022) and low LMR (62.9% versus 78.32% p=0.0051) were also independently linked to reduced OS. The worst survival was seen in patients with both sarcopenic obesity and adverse inflammatory markers: high SO and high NLR led to an OS of 52.75% versus 76.22% (p=0.00031), and high SO and low LMR resulted in an OS of 49.12% versus 78.15% (p<0.0001). Additionally, low LMR was significantly associated with a decrease in CSS (82.1% vs. 95.2%, p=0.028). CONCLUSIONS: Our findings show that sarcopenic obesity and adverse systemic inflammatory markers are strong, independent predictors of poor long-term prognosis in patients with non-metastatic RCC or oncocytoma. This is the first report to show the combined prognostic power of these factors in this patient population. These results suggest that interventions to increase muscle mass and reduce visceral fat could be valuable strategies to improve patient survival.

title: RADIOGRAPHIC RESPONSE TO NEOADJUVANT THERAPY FOR RENAL CELL CARCINOMA DOES NOT CORRELATE TO PATHOLOGIC RESPONSE USING IMMUNE-RELATED RESIDUAL VIABLE TUMOR (IRRVT)
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Benjamin J. Croll, Hafiz A. Yahya, Abigail Keller, Rainjade Chung, Shuanzeng Wei, Douglas Flieder, Fern Anari, Pooja Ghatalia, Matthew Zibelman, Andres Correa, Alexander Kutikov, Randall Lee, Marc Smaldone, Robert Uzzo, Rosalia Viterbo, Daniel Geynisman, David Y. T. Chen
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Immune-related residual viable tumor (irRVT) is a standardized measure of pathologic response to systemic therapy that captures distinct immune-mediated treatment effects not reflected by conventional pathologic reporting. Major response by irRVT has been associated with improved oncologic outcomes in other malignancies and has demonstrated discordance between radiographic change and tumor response. This study evaluated the relationship between radiographic size change and pathologic response in patients with localized and metastatic renal cell carcinoma (RCC). METHODS: A prospectively maintained RCC database was queried for patients undergoing surgery after systemic therapy. Pathology was re-reviewed to quantify %irRVT, defined as the proportion of residual viable tumor within the entire tumor bed, distinct from nonspecific necrosis and the regression bed consisting of immune-mediated cell death and immune activation components. Pre- and post-treatment imaging was assessed based on change in maximum tumor diameter. Correlation between radiographic and pathologic response was analyzed using linear regression. RESULTS: Thirty-seven patients were identified. Radiographic and pathologic responses were correlated (p=0.008), though several cases were discordant ( Table 1). The strength of correlation between size reduction and degree of pathologic response was modest (r2=0.34) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191312.43845.bb.22#F1)). Among six patients with complete pathologic response (irRVT=0; median residual mass 5.3 cm, range 2.4–7 cm), two had radiographically stable disease (diameter change 30%) despite absence of viable tumor. These patients had distinctly different tumor bed biology (one with 95% necrosis and the other with 90% tumor regression) despite similar treatment duration and regimen. CONCLUSIONS: While major pathologic response generally aligns with radiographic regression, correlation between irRVT and size change is weak. Radiographic response alone may underestimate true treatment effect following immune-based therapy in RCC.

title: RADIO-PATHOMIC FEATURES ASSOCIATED WITH RESPONSE TO NEOADJUVANT CABOZANTINIB IN LOCALLY ADVANCED RENAL CELL CARCINOMA
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: William Luke, Liping Li, Ahmet Yildirim, Gregory Palmateer, Edouard Nicaise, Benjamin Schmeusser, Reza Lahiji, Dattatraya Patil, Tilak Pathak, Kamal Hammouda, Sena Azamat, Krunal Pandav, BaoHan Vo, Amir Davarpanah, Bhakti Baheti, Haydn Kissick, Anant Madabhushi, Mehmet Bilen, Viraj Master, Rakesh Shiradkar
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: With a paucity of biomarkers for monitoring treatment response in patients with renal cell carcinoma (RCC), quantitative features from imaging (radiomics) and digitized pathology (pathomics) may offer critical information. A phase 2 clinical trial examining the use of neoadjuvant cabozantinib for locally advanced, unresectable RCC demonstrated an objective response. Patho-radiomic features and immunologic markers were available from this trial and warranted further investigation. METHODS: Seventeen treatment-naive patients with locally advanced non-metastatic clear cell RCC enrolled in a single-arm Phase 2 study received 12 weeks of neoadjuvant cabozantinib. Cross-sectional abdominal 3T-MRI T1-W imaging was obtained at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks. Treatment response was classified as per RECIST criteria. Within RCC lesions, first and second-order radiomic features were extracted and pathomic nuclear diversity features were analyzed on stained nephrectomy specimens. Pearson and bi-serial correlation were used to assess associations between radiomic-pathomic features and treatment response. RESULTS: Six patients had partial response in our cohort. Several radiomic features were significantly associated with PR on baseline, and baseline to six-week scans. Of these features, four had a point-biserial correlation > 0.50. We identified correlations between radiomic features and immune cell populations within nephrectomy and blood draw specimens. Pathomic features were also demonstrated to correlate with radiomic features. CONCLUSIONS: In patients receiving neoadjuvant cabozantinib, several baseline, and intra-treatment radiomic features were significantly associated with treatment response. Immune factors appear to correlate with final patho-radiomic results. Significant differences in radiomic feature order were detected when comparing immune and pathologic features in T1-W imaging. Further prospective modeling should confirm these results.

title: DEFINING USE CASES FOR GIRENTUXIMAB PET/CT IN UROLOGIC ONCOLOGY: INSIGHTS FROM AN SUO MEMBER SURVEY
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Gianpaolo Carpinito, Apoorv Dhir, Hung-Jui Tan, Mary E. Westerman, Zach S. Feuer, Marc A. Bjurlin
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Girentuximab PET/CT identifies localized and advanced clear cell renal cell carcinoma by targeting carbonic anhydrase 9 (CAIX) and is likely to become widely available. However, clinical uses remain undefined. To better understand potential use, we conducted a case-vignette survey of Society of Urologic Oncology (SUO) members to identify scenarios in which this novel diagnostic modality may offer the greatest clinical utility. METHODS: The survey was distributed to members of the SUO via Qualtrics software. Prior to dissemination, the survey was reviewed and vetted by the SUO to ensure clinical relevance and methodological soundness. It included nine clinical vignettes with related decision points: one addressing active surveillance (AS), four focusing on biopsy decisions, and four exploring scenarios with uncertain stage or pathology. Respondents rated their likelihood of making specific clinical decisions under three imaging conditions: (a) standard imaging (SI), (b) SI plus a PET-avid Girentuximab scan, and (c) SI plus a non-PET-avid Girentuximab scan. Responses were analyzed using paired-sample t-tests on coded Likert scale data to evaluate changes from baseline decision-making. RESULTS: We received 44 responses. For a small renal mass (V1), 68% were somewhat/very likely to choose AS based on SI, falling to 43% with PET-avidity (t(24)=4.67, p=0.00009) and increasing to 75% with non-PET avidity (t(43)=3.44, p<0.001) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191312.43845.bb.24#F1)). For borderline lymphadenopathy (V6), 84% were somewhat/very likely to perform RPLND with SI only, rising to 93% with PET-avidity (t(43)=-2.03, p=0.02) and falling to 41% with non-PET-avidity (t(43)=5.17, p<0.001). For equivocal post-ablation recurrence (V9), 43% were somewhat/very likely to intervene with SI only, increasing to 80% with PET-avidity (t(43)=-4.53, p<0.001), and falling to 21% with non-PET-avidity (t(43)=2.86, p=0.003). CONCLUSIONS: Girentuximab PET/CT results significantly polarized decisions for AS of a small renal mass (V1) and interventions for borderline lymphadenopathy (V6), mass of uncertain pathology (V8), and equivocal post-ablation recurrence (V9), suggesting high-value use cases. In other scenarios, PET results did not consistently augment management. These results likely reflect interplay between disease prevalence and procedural risk, stressing the need for further study of Girentuximab in various clinical contexts.

title: SUB-5-MINUTE DENOISED PET IMAGING OF INDETERMINATE RENAL MASSES USING 89Zr-DFO-Girentuximab: A FEASIBILITY STUDY
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Florence M. Muller, Margaret E. Daube-Witherspoon, Michael J. Parma, Joel Karp, Philipose Mulugeta
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Incidental renal masses (<7 cm) are increasingly detected on diagnostic images. While many small renal lesions are presumed to represent clear-cell renal cell carcinomas (ccRCC), up to 30% are benign at biopsy or surgery. Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging with 89Zr-DFO-girentuximab shows high sensitivity and specificity for ccRCC (>85%) \[1\]. However, the low administered dose (37 MBq) combined with delayed imaging (3-7 days post-injection, p. i.) required for clearance contributes to increased image noise and long scan times (~20 mins per bed position) on standard PET scanners. Advances in image denoising have shown potential to maintain diagnostic quality from noisy data in other clinical applications. METHODS: Five patients with a single renal mass ( 7 cm) were injected with 37 MBq (±10%) of 89Zr-DFO-girentuximab. Patients were scanned 5 ±2 days p. i. for 10 min on the PennPET Explorer (142 cm axial field-of-view, time-of-flight PET/CT). The 10-min list-mode data were sub-sampled and reconstructed into 5- and 1-min datasets. Each image was post-processed by a deep learning denoising (DL-DN) model \[2\], trained on 6,500 18F-FDG image slices. An additional image set was obtained by 5-mm Gaussian-filtering of the sub-sampled images. Signal-to-noise (SNR; mean lesion counts relative to background noise) and contrast-to-noise (CNR; lesion-to-background count difference relative to background noise) ratios were measured using the contralateral non-lesional kidney as background. A reader study is ongoing to assess image quality. RESULTS: Both DL-DN and Gaussian-filtering reduce noise in the 5- and 1-min images. Gaussian-filtering noticeably blurs lesion details, while DL-DN improves sharpness and lesion conspicuity. DL-DN achieved the highest SNR and CNR for both reduced durations, while Gaussian-filtering showed only moderate improvement over the non-denoised data. For 5-mins images, the DL-DN SNR and CNR values exceeded those of the 10-min reference (dashed line). CONCLUSIONS: These results support DL-DN as a feasible method for reducing scan times in 89Zr-PET imaging, enabling sub-5-min scans without diagnostic image quality loss for renal mass evaluation.

title: BP-VI-RADS COMBINED WITH NORMALIZED ADC ENHANCES DIAGNOSTIC EFFICACY FOR MUSCLE-INVASIVE BLADDER CANCER
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Zihan Hao, Danyan Li, Hongqian Guo, Rong Yang
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The diagnosis of Vesical Imaging-Reporting and Data System (VI-RADS) category 3 lesions persists as a diagnostic challenge, whereas the efficacy of normalized apparent diffusion coefficient (nADC) in evaluating muscle layer infiltration in bladder tumors remains indeterminate. This study seeks to examine whether the incorporation of quantitative nADC metrics into the VI-RADS scoring framework can substantially augment the diagnostic performance of conventional qualitative evaluations. METHODS: This study retrospectively enrolled 172 bladder cancer patients who underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) between January 2021 and March 2023. Three radiologists performed VI-RADS scoring on bp-MRI. Two of them manually delineated regions of interest (ROIs) on ADC maps via 3D Slicer software, calculating the mean ADC value (ADCmean) by measuring ROIs across three tumor sites. ROIs of bladder urine and the obturator internus muscle were used to normalize the data via the formula nADC=ADCmean(tumor)/ADC(reference). The Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to assess the association between nADC values and muscle invasion, whereas ROC analysis was used to determine thresholds. Composite models were constructed via binomial logistic regression. RESULTS: For bp-MRI VI-RADS (threshold ≥4), the area under the curve (AUC) was 0.87. Among the single ADC-based parameters, nADCurine performed best (AUC 0.82, cutoff 0.259). Notably, composite models integrating quantitative metrics with VI-RADS showed significant advantages (p<0.01). Model U (VI-RADS + nADCurine) demonstrated the highest diagnostic efficacy (AUC 0.93), significantly outperforming Model O (VI-RADS + nADCoim, normalized ADC of obturator internus muscle, P=0.046) and Model A (VI RADS + ADCmean, p<0.01). For the VI-RADS score 3 borderline cases, the nADCurine subgroup (VI-RADS 3U) achieved 100% sensitivity and negative predictive value (specificity 77.8%). Other normalization methods (e. g., nADCoim and raw ADC) presented significantly higher misclassification rates. CONCLUSIONS: Integrating nADC metrics into the VI-RADS framework improves the precision of assessing category 3 lesions and the overall diagnostic accuracy for muscle invasiveness. The findings indicate that nADC has the potential to refine preoperative staging in bladder cancer management, thereby guiding therapeutic planning.

title: CLINICAL UTILITY OF URETERAL OPTICAL COHERENCE TOMOGRAPHY FOR T STAGING OF URETERAL CANCER: TOWARD OPTIMAL KIDNEY-SPARING STRATEGY
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Makito Miyake, Takuto Shimizu, Nobutaka Nishimura, Kazuki Miyazaki, Yuki Oda, Yusuke Iemura, Kota Iida, Kiyohide Fujimoto
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: One of the major limitations of the current diagnostic techniques for upper urinary tract carcinoma (UTUC) is the risk of both understaging and overstaging, highlighting the need for real-time high-resolution intraoperative imaging. We evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and safety of ureteral optical coherence tomography (OCT) under uretero-renoscopy for T staging of UTUC. METHODS: In this study, 16 patients with suspected UTUC were prospectively enrolled. The diagnostic accuracy analysis set included 14 of 16 patients who had both ureteral OCT data and a final pathologic T (pT) stage from surgical specimens. The concordance, underdiagnosis, and overdiagnosis rates were compared between radiographic imaging-based T (cT) and OCT-based T (octT) diagnoses. The primary outcome was the diagnostic accuracy of ureteral OCT in discriminating between pTis/Ta/T1 (non-muscle invasive) and T2/T3 (muscle invasive) cancers. RESULTS: (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191312.43845.bb.27#F1) shows a representative case of a 74-year-old man with right middle to distal ureteral tumors. Perioperative octT staging was concordant with pT staging of cross-sectional RNU specimens. Concordance between cT-based and pT-based diagnoses was observed in 11 (79%) of the 14 patients, whereas a higher concordance rate (13/14, 93%) was noted for octT diagnosis. Additionally, the underdiagnosis and overdiagnosis rates of octT were 0% and 7.1%, respectively, which were lower than those of cT ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191312.43845.bb.27#F2); 7.1% and 14%, respectively). No safety signal including intra-procedural urinary injury was detected in addition to the routine uretero-renoscopy. Post-procedural complications included hematuria in five patients (31%), urinary tract pain in two (13%), and urinary tract infection in one patient (6.3%). CONCLUSIONS: Ureteral OCT exhibited a high diagnostic performance in discriminating between non-muscle invasive UTUC and muscle invasive UTUC with a safety profile. Further prospective trials with large sample sizes are necessary to determine the true diagnostic value and the wide use of ureteral OCT.

title: INCIDENTAL LUNG NODULES ON PSMA PET AND OPPORTUNITIES FOR EARLY LUNG CANCER DETECTION
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Luke W. Westrick, Anna Ochsner, Katherine Wainwright, Aaron Cleofas, John Scaringi, Anthony E. Mega, Elias S. Hyams
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET imaging is the current standard of care for staging higher-risk prostate cancer (PCa). We have anecdotally observed a high incidence of incidental lung nodules on these scans. Given the underscreening for lung cancer in older men, we hypothesized that PSMA PET could present an opportunity for early detection of this malignancy. METHODS: A retrospective chart review was performed for 664 patients who underwent PSMA PET imaging for PCa staging at Rhode Island Hospital (2022–2024). Data collected included the presence of metastatic disease and lung nodules (suspicious vs. equivocal). For patients with nodules, the number and size of nodules, as well as subsequent management (surveillance vs. biopsy), were recorded. Smoking history was categorized as current, former, or never, and pack-years were noted. Patients meeting USPSTF criteria for high-risk lung cancer screening (age 50–80 and ≥20 pack-years) were identified and analyzed. RESULTS: Among 664 patients, 352 (53.0%) had metastatic disease, including 180 (51.1%) osseous, 248 (70.5%) lymph node, and 108 (30.7%) other sites. 163 (24.5%) individuals had incidental lung nodules, of whom 85 (52.1%) had concomitant metastatic disease, 29 (17.8%) had equivocal metastatic findings, and 49 (30.1%) had no metastatic findings. Of 212 unique lung nodules with follow-up recommendations, 204 (96.2%) were recommended follow-up without biopsy and 8 (3.8%) with biopsy. Of those with biopsy recommendations, six biopsied nodules confirmed malignancy, none primary lung (3 prostate metastasis, 3 other, e. g. lymphoma); the other two elected for observation. Among high-risk lung cancer screening patients (n=23), 7 (30.4%) had lung nodules; among other patients (n=641), 156 (24.3%) had lung nodules (p=ns); see Table below for disposition and follow-up. Nodule number and size did not differ significantly by smoking status or pack-year history. CONCLUSIONS: Approximately a quarter of patients who underwent PSMA PET imaging had incidental lung nodules. There was no significant difference in nodule detection based on USPSTF screening criteria or smoking history. Despite the high rate of incidental lung nodules, PSMA PET does not appear to have utility for early detection of lung cancer. Additional follow-up and study in larger cohorts may clarify its value among high-risk patients. | | | --- | | |

title: QUANTIFYING CARBON AND ENERGY SAVINGS BETWEEN PROSTATE MRI PROTOCOLS
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Chengxuan Li, Nikhil Mayor, Jasmin Cooper, Hashim U. U. Ahmed, Andrea Rockall, Onesmus Mwabonje
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Pre-biopsy prostate MRI is now recommended in most major prostate cancer (PCa) guidelines and MRI may have a role in population-level PCa screening. Whilst the diagnostic accuracy of non-contrast MRI protocols is being assessed, environmental sustainability across MRI protocols has yet to be established. We aimed to assess the carbon and energy savings of biparametric (bp) compared to multiparametric (mp) MRI and explore the impact of field strength, equipment state management, and data storage policies. METHODS: We performed an ISO 14040/44-compliant life cycle assessment to quantify the carbon footprint and energy demand of prostate MRI. The model captured the full diagnostic process for a single MRI examination, including scanner electricity use, HVAC cooling, consumables, gadolinium contrast, and long-term data storage. Departmental data on scan duration and file size were used, with published emission factors applied for electricity and materials. We compared bpMRI and mpMRI protocols at both 1.5T and 3T field strengths. Additional analyses explored the influence of scanner power-saving policies and data storage. RESULTS: At 3T, a standard mpMRI examination generated approximately 5.9 kg CO2-eq and required 205 MJ per scan. Using a bpMRI protocol on the same scanner reduced emissions to 4.9 kg CO2-eq and 173 MJ (-17% carbon, -16% energy). Further reductions were achieved at 1.5T, where bpMRI emitted 4.4 kg CO2-eq and 164 MJ per scan (-25% CO2-eq, -20% energy versus 3T mpMRI). Implementing scanner power-saving or overnight shutdown policies lowered electricity consumption by a further 20-30%. PACS data storage was a major digital contributor: increasing file size from 1.2 GB (typical of bpMRI) to 1.8 GB (mpMRI) increased emissions by about 18% per examination. CONCLUSIONS: bpMRI offers a straightforward and scalable way to lower the environmental impact of PCa diagnostics. By omitting the dynamic contrast-enhanced sequence, bpMRI shortens scan time, avoids gadolinium use, and produces smaller image files, directly reducing both energy consumption and carbon emissions. Switching from 3T mpMRI to 1.5T bpMRI reduces carbon emissions by approximately one quarter, which is equivalent to the electricity used by an average UK household over five days.

title: EVALUATING THE POSITIVE PREDICTIVE VALUE OF PSMA PET FOLLOWING PRIMARY RADIATION THERAPY IN SUSPECTED RECURRENT PROSTATE CANCER
session: Imaging/Uroradiology I (IP08)
authors: Rainjade Chung, Abigail Keller, Benjamin J. Croll, Mark A. Hallman, Jian Q. Yu, Andres Correa, James R. Mark, David Chen, Randall A. Lee
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography (PSMA PET) has emerged as a highly sensitive imaging modality for detecting recurrent and metastatic prostate cancer. However, the evidence reporting its histopathologically confirmed diagnostic accuracy following definitive radiation therapy (RT) has not been robustly reported. False positives on PSMA PET in this setting may be due to treatment related stromal fibrosis and inflammation secondary to RT. Our objective was to report the positive predictive value (PPV) of PSMA PET in patients with suspected locally recurrent prostate cancer after primary radiation therapy using histopathologic confirmation. METHODS: We retrospectively identified patients at a single institution who had a PSMA PET scan between 2022-2025. Patients who received RT as initial treatment for prostate cancer with subsequent PSMA PET and lesion targeted prostate biopsy were included. Those who underwent prostatectomy or cryoablation as primary treatment or had diffuse metastatic disease on PSMA PET were excluded. The PPV was calculated. A paired t-test evaluated the correlation between positive PSMA PET results and subsequent positive prostate biopsies. RESULTS: We identified 1480 patients with a PSMA PET scan; 671 received radiation as primary treatment for their prostate cancer. We then identified 25 men who underwent a prostate biopsy for a PET avid lesion. The median age was 67 (IQR 72, 77) and the median PSA was 3.8 (IQR 2, 6.6). 19 biopsies were positive for prostate cancer. PSMA avid lesions significantly correlated with these positive results (p=0.011), however the PPV was only 76%. 7 patients had Grade Group 5 and 6 patients had Grade Group 4 disease ( Table 1). CONCLUSIONS: We report a pathologically confirmed PPV of 76% for PSMA PET avid lesions after primary RT for prostate cancer. Our findings indicate that the PPV in cases of locally recurrent prostate cancer is lower than the high fidelity observed in nodal metastases. This supports the idea that PSMA PET should not be used as the sole modality for clinical diagnosis and treatment decision making when considering salvage therapy for suspected locally recurrent prostate cancer after RT. | | | --- | | |

title: CONTINENCE DURABILITY FOR MALE SLING SURGERY AND SUBSEQUENT PELVIC RADIATION: A MULTICENTER ANALYSIS
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence (IP09)
authors: Chung Yon Lin, J. Nick Warner, Elizabeth N. Bearrick, Katherine T. Anderson, Christopher E. Wolter, Bridget L. Findlay
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: History of pelvic radiation therapy (RT) negatively impacts continence outcomes following male urethral sling surgery. While guidelines caution against use of slings in radiated patients, there is paucity of literature regarding the functional outcomes in patients who are exposed to RT after sling placement. We aim to evaluate urinary outcomes, need for re-intervention, and mesh complications in patients who undergo RT after sling placement. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 666 men who underwent sling placement for stress incontinence at three tertiary academic medical centers between 2010-2025. Patients who received pelvic radiation after sling placement were included for analysis. Demographics, radiation parameters, and functional outcomes were analyzed. Social continence was defined as ≤1 pad/day. Continuous variables were reported as median (IQR) or mean ± SD. Pre- vs post-radiation pad use was compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with p<0.05 significant. RESULTS: Of the 666 men who underwent sling surgery, 16 (2.4%) had radiation pre-sling and 17 (2.6%) had radiation post-sling. Median age at sling placement was 69 (65–73) years and median BMI was 29.7 (26.9–35.4) kg/m2. Most patients received Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT, 65%) for biochemical recurrence (88%) at a median total dose of 70 Gy (IQR 66–72). Median interval between sling and radiation was 14.9 (8.7–35.5) months. Median pad use declined from 2 (2–4) pre-sling to 0 (0–1) after sling (p0.01), then increased to 3 (2–5) post-radiation (p0.01) at a median follow-up of 21 months after radiation. Social continence (≤1 pad/day) decreased from 94% immediately post-sling to 12% after radiation (p0.001). No mesh erosions were identified. A total of 3/17 (17.6%) patients had subsequent anti-incontinence surgery after radiation (2 artificial urinary sphincter, 1 adjustable balloon device). Compared to literature benchmarks, non-RT sling cohorts maintain 65–80% continence at 2–3 years, and pre-sling RT patients show 40–50% success. The current post-sling irradiation group demonstrated markedly lower durability than either comparator. CONCLUSIONS: Post-sling pelvic RT adversely affects sling durability, with a significant decline in social continence to 12% within two years after radiation therapy. Patients should be counseled on high recurrence risk if adjuvant radiation is anticipated.

title: LONG-TERM OUTCOMES OF THE ADVANCE TRANSOBTURATOR SLING IN THE TREATMENT OF POST-PROSTATECTOMY INCONTINENCE
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Male Incontinence (IP09)
authors: Joshua Makary, Lewis Chan, David Habashy, Ruth Collins, Vincent Tse
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Transobturator slings are increasingly utilised in treatment of post-prostatectomy incontinence (PPI).
