Predictive accuracy was highest for calcium oxalate monohydrate. Prediction efficacy varied significantly depending on endoscope type and stone composition. CONCLUSIONS: We describe the first known study of an AI model developed to predict stone composition using real-time endoscopic images. Digital flexible endoscopes demonstrated the highest predictive accuracy to classify stone composition. While increased data is important for machine learning algorithms, consideration for endoscope type in data collection should be considered in how they will impact the algorithm and its efficacy. | | | --- | | |

title: A VALIDATED CUSTOM PIPELINE FOR THREE-DIMENSIONAL KIDNEY STONE RENDERINGS TO CREATE AN OPEN ACCESS REPOSITORY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Joao G. Porto, Kimberly Cortés Pérez, Lua Civetta, Sarvesh Saini, Julio Ojalvo, Ubbo Visser, Archan Khandekar, Hemendra Shah, Robert Marcovich, Jonathan E. Katz
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Three-dimensional (3D) rendering of urologic anatomy and pathology plays a crucial role in simulation and surgical training. However, no standardized library of accurate and reproducible 3D kidney stone models classified by composition currently exists. Our objective was to develop and validate a repository of high-fidelity 3D renderings of commonly encountered kidney stones. METHODS: We received kidney stones classified by the Louis C. Herring Laboratory including: calcium oxalate monohydrate (COM), cystine (Cyst), magnesium ammonium phosphate hexahydrate/carbonate apatite (MAPH/CA), and calcium hydrogen phosphate dihydrate (CHPD). Except for the fragmented MAPH/CA stone (80% MAPH, 20% CA) and the fragmented CHPD stone (which contained 1% hydroxyl apatite), all others were unfragmented and composed of a single material. Each stone was photographed on a custom rotating stage positioned between two fixed 4K UHD webcams, placed 7.5 cm apart and approximately 10 cm from the stone ( Figure 1A). The stage was rotated in 18° increments and 360° images were captured. The images were imported into Adobe Substance 3D Sampler for 3D renderings. To validate the renderings, five endourologists completed a Likert-scale survey evaluating model fidelity in terms of geometry and surface texture (1=Strongly Disagree, 5=Strongly Agree). RESULTS: 3D models were successfully generated for all uric acid (UA) stones (5/5), most COM stones (8/11), the MAPH/CA stone fragments (2/2), and the CHPD fragments (3/3), but not for any cystine stones (0/4) ( Figure 1B). Regarding the accuracy of the simulated stone morphology and texture, endourologists highly agreed for COM and UA stones (mean 4.4-4.6, median 5), moderately agreed for CHPD (mean 4.2-4.25, median 4), and were neutral regarding struvite stones (mean 3.2-3.4, median 3). CONCLUSIONS: This method produced accurate 3D kidney stone renderings for COM, UA and CHPD stones. Rendering failure or poor resolution in other stones was likely due to excessive surface reflectivity. Expanding this workflow with additional stone types and validation metrics could facilitate the creation of a robust, reproducible 3D kidney stone library for educational and research applications. All models are freely available at:https://github. com/Uro-GLiDER.

title: QUANTIFYING IMAGE QUALITY DURING FLEXIBLE URETEROSCOPY FOR KIDNEY STONE TREATMENT
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Charan S. Mohan, Daiwei Lu, Hao Li, Ipek Oguz, Nicholas L. Kavoussi
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Poor image quality during endoscopic stone surgery due to bleeding, debris, or technical factors can impact adequate visualization of the collecting system during kidney stone treatment. The aim of this work is to describe and quantify image quality during various parts of endoscopic stone surgery using standard image quality metrics. METHODS: We obtained 140 videos of flexible ureteroscopy (41 fiberoptic, 99 digital) for kidney stone treatment. We manually identified surgical tasks within each video which included: stone localization, laser ablation, basket retrieval, and residual dust assessment. We evaluated intraoperative image quality using standard image quality metrics throughout each video: a) noise variance (i. e., image blur), b) high-frequency variance (i. e., image contrast variation), c) image sharpness, and d) estimated signal-to-noise ratio (SNR, i. e., image clarity). We compared the means for these metrics for each surgical task to identify how image quality changes during fURS using an analysis of variance (ANOVA). RESULTS: Stone localization, laser ablation, basket retrieval, and dust assessment were seen in 71, 98, 52, and 40 of the videos, respectively. Significant between-group differences were seen across surgical tasks in noise variance (p=0.007), high-frequency variance (p=0.019), sharpness (p=0.018), and SNR (p=0.004). Image quality metrics demonstrated the poorest image quality during laser ablation (high noise variance and sharpness) and best image quality during dust assessment (low noise variance and high SNR) ( Table 1). For digital scope video, there was a significant difference in image quality between surgical tasks as measured by noise variance (p=0.02), sharpness (p=0.0005), and SNR (p=0.02). For fiberoptic scope video, there was only a difference in image quality between surgical tasks as measured by SNR (p=0.03). CONCLUSIONS: Image quality varies significantly across surgical tasks during ureteroscopy with the poorest image quality noted during stone lasering as measured by four different metrics. Future work will evaluate how these metrics associate with clinical outcomes. | | | --- | | |

title: AUTOMATION OF A REAL-TIME DIGITAL SOFTWARE FOR KIDNEY STONE MEASUREMENT DURING URETEROSCOPIC LITHOTRIPSY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Samiha Nasrin, Mark Lifson, David Holmes, Kevin Koo
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Accurate stone size estimation is an important aspect of ureteroscopic lithotripsy to ensure safe extraction or spontaneous passage of fragments and reduce the risk of ureteral injury. We have developed and validated a novel software that can provide accurate measurements of stone fragments visualized during ureteroscopy. However, the software requires additional personnel to operate, and it functions on paused video frames, which can add time and cost. We aimed to develop an automated software tool that can detect the outline of stones in endoscopic video frames to enable unassisted, real-time digital stone measurement. METHODS: The software tool was developed using Visual Studio Code and computer vision libraries (OpenCV). Several image processing techniques were used to analyze the endoscopic video frames before automating the stone outline. Frame operations such as CLAHE filters, gaussian blur, and morphology operations were applied to increase contrast, enhance edge preservation of the stone, and remove background noise that may be present. An OpenCV convex hull function was used to determine the smallest convex polygon that encloses the entirety of the stone boundary. The maximum ferret diameter was calculated using a “rotating calipers” algorithm. For the calibration, ureteroscopic images of black squares of known sizes (1-10.5 mm) were placed at defined distances (3-15 mm) from the ureteroscope. Pixel sizes of the checkerboard and x coordinates of the guidewire were measured using ImageJ. These two sets of measurement were fit into a multivariate linear model using Excel Solver and an evolutionary optimization algorithm RESULTS: The prototype software tool showed consistency automatically capturing the outline and ferret diameter of mock kidney stones during in vitro testing ( Figure). The software was able to account for clinical conditions such as low lighting and could detect mock kidney stones at different depths when placed into a simulated ureter. CONCLUSIONS: We developed a prototype software tool that can automatically detect the outline of mock stone fragments for real-time measurements of objects during simulated ureteroscopy. Future work will incorporate a calibration regression model into the stone-outline automation prototype for accurate detection and millimeter measurement of the stone during live ureteroscopy.

title: AUTONOMOUS ROBOT-ASSISTED URETEROSCOPY (ARA-URS) FOR NAVIGATING TO THE KIDNEY STONE
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Joao G. Porto, Sarvesh Saini, Julio Ojalvo, Archan Khandekar, Hemendra Shah, Robert Marcovich, Ubbo Visser, Jonathan E. Katz
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ureteroscopy (URS) is the gold standard for kidney stone treatment for stones <15-20 mm, but remains ergonomically demanding, operator-dependent, and limited by suboptimal stone-free rates. Robotic assistance improves precision and reproducibility, yet current systems lack autonomous capabilities. METHODS: We developed a supervised autonomous robot-assisted ureteroscopy (ARA-URS) platform integrated with a high-fidelity digital twin (DT). The robotic system actuates a Wolf RIWO ureteroscope through linear, rotational, and tip-bending mechanisms. A DT was rendered in NVIDIA Isaac Sim to replicate real-world kinematics and generate synthetic intraoperative scenarios for training vision and control models ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191320.09030.8b.05#F1)). We then assessed the system’s ability to navigate to the kidney stone by performing an experiment 30 times in both simulation and on a physical benchtop model. The tip of the ureteroscope was initially positioned in the renal pelvis approximately 2-3 cm from the kidney stone. Using color segmentation as a first test to estimate the stone position, we calculated inverse kinematics for autonomous navigation of the URS toward the stone. We then calculated the percentage of the screen occupied by the stone, considering > 50% of the screen a success. The Shapiro-Wilk test was used to assess the normality and then a non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test was used to determine statistical significance. RESULTS: In simulation the autonomous stone-targeting was very successful, with the stone occupying \> 50% of the final image in 100% of trials (30/30), while the benchtop model was successful in 56.7% of trials (17/30). In simulation the mean% of the screen occupied by the stone on final image was 67.3% ± 7.3% with a median of 69.8%, while on the benchtop model the mean was 59.0% ± 23.9%, with a median of 53.8% (U=612.0, p=0.017). CONCLUSIONS: This proof of concept demonstrates the feasibility of our DT-integrated ARA-URS for precise, reproducible, and partially autonomous navigation during ureteroscopy, though the system performed significantly better in simulation then on our benchtop model. The digital twin enables calibration, realistic validation, and cross-domain transfer between simulation and real environments, but further work to address the gap in performance is needed. Future work will optimize navigation and introduce laser lithotripsy to further enhance autonomy and clinical applicability.

title: OPTICAL TRACKING METRICS ASSOCIATE WITH SURGICAL TIME DURING FLEXIBLE URETEROSCOPY FOR KIDNEY STONE TREATMENT
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Durga Moorthy, Jumanh Atoum, Charan S. Mohan, Fangjie Li, Mai N. Bui, Matthieu Chabanas, Jie Ying Wu, Nicholas L. Kavoussi
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Eye gaze has previously demonstrated utility as an objective, intraoperative predictor of surgical experience during flexible ureteroscopy (fURS). However, gaze has yet to be associated with intraoperative outcomes. We sought to evaluate the potential for OT to be used as an objective assessment of intraoperative outcomes by associating eye gaze metrics with surgical times during fURS. METHODS: We prospectively collected eye gaze data from 25 ureteroscopic kidney stone surgeries performed by 5 endourologists. For each case, we obtained the surgeon’s eye gaze data using the optical tracking (OT) system integrated within Microsoft HoloLens 2 (Microsoft, 2019) during initial stone localization in the intrarenal collecting system. We collected standard eye gaze metrics, including: area of interest (AOI), gaze distance traveled, number of gaze fixation points, and gaze fixation dwell time. Surgical times were recorded and included localization of stone(s) time, stone laser ablation time, and total operative time. We then analyzed the relationship between eye gaze metrics and surgical times via linear regression. RESULTS: The total average surgical time was 40.8 minutes (standard deviation (SD) ± 22.8), with an average stone localization time of 1.7 minutes (SD ± 0.79) and stone ablation time of 17.9 minutes (SD ± 18.1). Average AOI among surgeons during stone localization was 797 cm2 (SD ± 452) with an average gaze distance traveled of 2484 cm (SD ± 1582). The median number of gaze fixation points was 85 (IQR: 17-136) with an average gaze fixation dwell time of 1.09 minutes (SD ±0.03) during stone localization. Eye gaze metrics were similar among experts. Linear regression analysis demonstrated a positive association between total operative time with AOI (r2=0.32, p<0.01, Fig. 1) and gaze distance traveled (r2=0.24, p=0.02). Additionally, there was a positive association between total operative time and number of fixation points (r2=0.25, p=0.02), but no association with fixation dwell time. There was no association between stone localization times or stone ablation times and any of the eye gaze metrics. CONCLUSIONS: Gaze metrics are associated with total surgical time during fURS for kidney stone treatment. This demonstrates the potential for gaze to be used as an objective assessment of intraoperative performance.

title: HELP UNDER PRESSURE: SIMPLE REAL-TIME ASSESSMENT OF URETERAL ACCESS SHEATH PLACEMENT FORCE
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Stephen J. Hassig, Mitchell Hoestermann, Rajat Jain
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The ureteral access sheath (UAS) is a common tool for the endourologist, though placement can lead to significant ureteral injuries in settings where narrow ureters require more force. Prior research in pigs has found that UAS placement requiring forces greater than 8N resulted in significantly higher rates of clinically relevant ureteral injury compared to <5N. To-date, pressure sensing materials have been expensive and difficult to obtain. Here we report the novel use of an off-the-shelf pressure sensor to provide force data during UAS placement. METHODS: A Compass Universal Hg (Centurion Medical Products, Williamston, MI) pressure gauge was zeroed, primed with a 3 ml, 5 ml, or 20 ml Becton Dickinson (BD) syringe containing saline, and occluded at the opposite end, producing a zero-mmHg closed chamber. Depression of the plunger creates pressure on the fixed volume of water in the gauge and the pressure is displayed on the LCD screen in mmHg. An Instron Universal Testing Machine was used to compress the closed systems to a maximum of 6N at a rate of 0.1 mm/second. Maximum gauge readings were recorded across five trials for each system and means with standard deviation (SD) were calculated. Force data from 4-8N was collected for the 5 ml system, as this system provided better ergonomic stability while also producing values in the middle range of the sensor (-199 to 999 mmHg). RESULTS: The 3 ml system setup is 21.5 cm long, 5 ml is 20.5 cm and 20 ml is 23.25 cm and all connect to the luer lock of the access sheath obturator. The mean maximum pressure displayed on the gauge at 6N was 736 mmHg (SD 11) for 3 ml, 376 (SD 16) for 5 ml, and 104 mmHg (SD 12) for 20 ml. For the 5 ml system, 4N testing showed 208 mmHg (+/- 22), 5N: 287 mmHg (+/- 7), 7N 416 mmHg (+/-2), 8N 468 mmHg (+/-7). CONCLUSIONS: The Centurion Compass Universal Hg device allows for rapid, legible, assessment of UAS placement forces as a function of pressure on a fixed volume of fluid. Using a 5 ml syringe system balance ergonomics and stability with the range of the gauge. In this system, we found that keeping pressure below 287 mmHg will avoid UAS placement forces above 5N.

title: DOES URETEROSCOPE MINIATURIZATION AFFECT THE EFFICACY OF THULIUM FIBER LASER FLEXIBLE URETEROSCOPY IN NON-PRE-STENTED PATIENTS? A RANDOMIZED COMPARATIVE STUDY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Federico Zorzi, Hubert Werth, Carlos Gonzalez Gonzalez, Nicola Nannola, Alejandra Bravo-Balado, Alberto Quarà, Marco Malvestiti, Stefano Moretto, Letizia Maria Ippolita Jannello, Luigi Candela, Steeve Doizi, Olivier Traxer, Frédéric Panthier
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The use of flexible ureteroscopy(FURS) for kidney stone treatment has markedly increased in recent years. Nevertheless, limitedaccess in non-pre-stented ureters remains a common challenge. Miniaturized single-use digital ureteroscopes may reduce ureteraltrauma and facilitate ureteral negotiation. However, comparative clinical data on lithotripsy efficacy with conventional platformsremain limited. This study aimed to evaluate whether ureteroscope miniaturization compromises the procedural and clinical efficacyor safety of Thulium Fiber Laser(TFL) lithotripsy. METHODS: Among 205 consecutive patients treated between September 2024 and October 2025, 112 without prior preoperative double-J(DJ)ureteral stent were randomized (1:1:1) to Storz 8.5Ch (n=37), Pusen 7.5Ch (n=37), or HugeMed 6.3Ch (n=38) ureteroscopes. Allprocedures were performed using TFL dusting settings (0.7–0.8J, 14–16Hz, ≤13W). A ureteral access sheath(UAS) was used whenrequired. The primary endpoint was failure to access the kidney. Secondary outcomes included stone-free rate(SFR), laser ablationrate(mm3/s), laser efficiency(mm3/kJ) and postoperative complications classified as Clavien–Dindo grade≥II. RESULTS: Patients in all groups showed similar demographic characteristics except for diabetes, which was more prevalent in the Storzgroup(p=0.02). Stone volume and density were comparable among groups(p=0.3 and 0.7, respectively). Failure to access the kidneydue to a narrow ureter occurred in 6 Storz(16.2%), 5 Pusen(13.5%), and 0 HugeMed(0%) cases(p0.01). A UAS was used in 35.1%,24.3%, and 21.1% of patients, respectively(p=0.4). Mean laser efficiency was 56.8, 65.7, and 47.2 mm3/kJ(p=0.7), while the meanablation rate was 0.50, 0.66, and 0.46 mm3/s(p=0.1), respectively. SFRs were 74.1%, 81.9%, and 86.3%(p=0.3), and complications occurred in 7.9%, 5.4%, and 2.6% of cases(p=0.7). Postoperative DJ was required in 83.8%, 78.4%, and 81.6%(p=0.4). CONCLUSIONS: FURS with the 6.3Ch ureteroscope achieved a significantly higher access rate to the upper urinary tract compared with larger-caliberplatforms, while maintaining equivalent efficacy and safety during TFL lithotripsy. Its smaller diameter and consistent performancemake it a valuable option for patients with narrow ureters, challenging anatomy, or ureteral sub-stenosis, reducing the need forpreoperative stenting.

title: IN VITRO COMPARISON OF TREATMENT EFFICIENCIES AND TEMPERATURE DYNAMICS AMONG HIGH POWER HOLMIUM:YAG, THULIUM FIBER, AND HIGH POWER THULIUM:YAG LASER PLATFORMS
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Ali S. Antar, Emily C. Serrell, Margaret A. Knoedler, Keegan Salah Steele, Shuang Li, Kristina L. Penniston, Dan R. Gralnek, Stephen Y. Nakada
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Multiple laser platforms—including Holmium:YAG, Thulium Fiber (TFL), and Thulium:YAG—are used for laser lithotripsy, each with distinct physical and thermal characteristics. This study compared stone ablation efficiency and temperature dynamics among three clinically available systems: the Moses Holmium:YAG (Boston Scientific), Soltive Thulium Fiber Laser (Olympus), and Thulio Thulium:YAG (Dornier). METHODS: An in vitro model was established in a 37°C water bath with continuous temperature monitoring via a K-type thermocouple. Synthetic 5:1 composition Begostones were treated for 7 minutes using 200 μm fibers under standardized irrigation using 0.9% saline, at 30°C and 150 mmHg with a Thermedx system (Stryker). Each laser underwent three trials under dusting and fragmenting settings. Post-treatment, stone fragments were filtered through a 200 μm mesh, dried, and weighed. Percentage weight change and mean intraoperative temperature were recorded and compared among systems. RESULTS: Under dusting settings, the Thulium Fiber Laser (TFL) achieved the greatest mean stone weight reduction after 7 minutes, followed by Holmium:YAG and Thulium:YAG. In contrast, under fragmenting settings, the Thulium:YAG produced the largest weight change, followed by Holmium:YAG and TFL. Differences were statistically significant between the Thulium:YAG and TFL systems, while no significant differences were observed with Holmium:YAG ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191320.09030.8b.09#F1)). Across both settings, the Holmium:YAG maintained a significantly lower mean temperature throughout treatment compared to the Thulium-based lasers ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191320.09030.8b.09#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: In a controlled in vitro model, Thulium:YAG and Thulium Fiber lasers exhibited distinct ablation characteristics. Thulium:YAG achieved superior fragmenting performance, while TFL excelled in dusting efficiency. The Holmium:YAG system maintained the lowest overall treatment temperature across both settings. These findings highlight important differences in ablation efficiency and thermal safety between platforms and support ongoing investigation into their clinical relevance for optimizing lithotripsy outcomes.

title: FIBER-TO-STONE DISTANCE AND FRAGMENT SIZE WITH HOLMIUM LASER LITHOTRIPSY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Leilane Glienke, Timothy L. Hall, Khurshid R. Ghani, William W. Roberts
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Control of stone fragment size during laser lithotripsy has taken on increasing importance with adoption of ureteroscopic aspiration technologies. Dusting may be preferred, but not all stones are amenable to dusting and fragmentation settings may be necessary in some scenarios. Thus, it is important to identify variables that influence the size of fragments produced during laser lithotripsy. The objective of this study was to characterize the relationship between laser-fiber-to-stone distance (FSD) and the size of stone fragments produced when using Ho:YAG laser with fragmentation settings. METHODS: Brushite crystalline aggregate model stones were treated with Ho:YAG laser (0.8 J x 10 Hz) with MOSESTM Distance (MD) and short pulse (SP) modes. A 200 µm laser fiber was positioned at 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, or 2.0 mm above the stone surface. Laser energy was delivered continuously while the fiber was automatically translated through a predetermined grid of points to cover the entire stone surface. Multiple passes were performed until ≥50% of each stone was ablated. Stone fragments were passed through sequential sieves to separate the fragments into size ranges of 0.25-0.5, 0.5-1.0, 1.0-2.0 and 2.0-4.0 mm. Five stones were treated for each set of parameters. One-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparison tests were performed. RESULTS: With MD mode, the percentage of ablated stone mass < 0.25 mm increased as FSD increased ( Fig). Similarly, the percentage of ablated stone mass > 0.5 mm and > 1.0 mm decreased as FSD increased ( Fig). Fragments > 2.0 mm were produced only with FSD of 0 mm. This trend demonstrates a more favorable fragment size distribution at greater FSD using MD mode. With SP mode there was no statistical difference in fragment size distribution for any FSD tested. Moreover, SP mode produced fragments > 2.0 mm for all FSDs. CONCLUSIONS: Increasing FSD resulted in a shift towards smaller size stone fragments when using Ho:YAG laser lithotripsy in MD mode with fragmentation settings. This discovery has potential impact on laser lithotripsy techniques and future technological developments to measure FSD during laser lithotripsy.

title: ASSESSING TISSUE INJURY IN LASER TREATMENT: PULSED SOLID‑STATE THULIUM VERSUS HOLMIUM:YTTRIUM‑ALUMINIUM‑GARNET LASERS IN A QUANTITATIVE PORCINE STUDY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Arkadiusz J. Miernik, Dennis Buente, Shane O'sullivan, Christian Gratzke, Ralf Petzold
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Lithotripsy using laser energy carries a risk of tissue injury. We compared the safety characteristics of two lithotripsy systems by quantifying their impact on porcine renal tissues: a holmium:yttrium‑aluminium‑garnet (Ho:YAG) laser and a pulsed solid‑state thulium:yttrium‑aluminium‑garnet (p‑Tm:YAG) laser. METHODS: Direct laser impacts were assessed using porcine renal parenchyma and pelvis in an automated setup. The setup comprised a 37 °C water bath, tissue holders and an XY‑plotter that guided the laser fibers. Ho:YAG and p‑Tm:YAG were tested at typical lithotripsy settings (0.2–3.5 J and 10–40 Hz) across comparable power ranges (2–40 W). Additional experiments for p‑Tm:YAG explored powers up to 80 W and frequencies up to 200 Hz. From 560 histological sections, coagulation zones and cut depths were measured, correlated with laser parameters, and automatically clustered to describe laser‑specific damage profiles. RESULTS: At identical power, p‑Tm:YAG delivered longer pulses and lower single‑pulse power (up to 3 362 W) than Ho:YAG (up to 7 777 W). Ho:YAG produced deeper cuts; in renal parenchyma the maximum depth reached 9.3 mm compared with 5.0 mm for p‑Tm:YAG. Cluster analysis delineated four impact profiles ranging from superficial coagulation to aggressive cutting. p‑Tm:YAG predominantly produced coagulative profiles with limited cut depth that persisted even at high power, whereas Ho:YAG was associated with deeper cutting, tissue detachment and thinner coagulation. In the renal pelvis this difference was reproduced: Ho:YAG achieved cut depths up to 3.6 mm, roughly twice as deep as those of p‑Tm:YAG. Histological analysis revealed distinct collagen fiber protrusion. CONCLUSIONS: Laser‑induced damage in lithotripsy depends strongly on laser type and settings. Medium power combined with longer pulse duration balances efficiency and safety. Beyond 20 W, p‑Tm:YAG yields superior damage profiles with shallower injury and enhanced coagulation, which may reduce adverse events during lithotripsy compared with Ho:YAG at similar power levels.

title: MODELING THE IMPACT OF OPERATOR DUTY CYCLE AND IRRIGATION FLOW RATE ON THERMAL SAFETY DURING HIGH-POWER LASER LITHOTRIPSY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Annika Singh, Arpit Mishra, Robert Medairos, Michael Lipkin, Pei Zhong, Charles Scales
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: High-power laser lithotripsy (LL) enables efficient stone fragmentation but may elevate intraluminal temperatures above 43°C, risking urothelial injury. This study extended the Williams er al. (2021) model to assess how increased irrigation flow rates (IFR) and operator duty cycle (ODC) can mitigate thermal injury risk by limiting temperatures rise during lasering. METHODS: A first-order convective model simulated temperature rise during LL for a 5.9 ml renal volume under varying IFR (0-39 ml/min) and powers (5-40 W). ODC (5/5, 10/10, 20/20 and 30/30 s on/off) and continuous lasing were modeled with equal total energy delivered (2400 J). Predicted absolute temperature and cumulative equivalent minutes at 43 °C (CEM43) were compared with in-vitro temperature profiles for model validation and to determine the thermal safety potential of different parameter combinations. RESULTS: Model predictions closely matched experimental temperature profiles, with maximum deviations of −0.9% and 0.5% for flows of 7.5 and 14.5 ml/min, respectively, confirming simulation accuracy ( Figs. A, D). Both peak temperature and CEM43 scaled inversely with flow and directly with power. At 40 W, all ODC modes produced markedly lower CEM43 values than continuous lasing, confirming reduced thermal dose at equal total energy ( Figs. B, E). Increasing IFR reduced maximum temperature rise (ΔTmax) by 4-100%, with IFR ≥ 14.5 ml/min halving temperature rise ( Fig. C). At 14.5 ml/min, ΔTmax decreased from 12.7 °C (continuous) to 4.4 °C (ODC 5/5, 65% reduction). With rising power, ΔTmax approximately doubled, but ODC reduced this rise by 19-91%, maintaining sub-injury temperatures ( Fig. F). CONCLUSIONS: Overall, these results suggest that combining ODC modulation with adequate irrigation flow can mitigate thermal load during high-power LL without reducing total energy delivered, thereby alleviating the risk of thermal injury. Incorporating real-time ODC management into laser systems could enhance procedural safety.

title: CHARACTERIZATION OF INTRARENAL TEMPERATURE AND PRESSURE DURING EX VIVO HIGH-ENERGY THULIUM LASER LITHOTRIPSY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Kantapon Tangwiwat, Jonathan Badin-Castro, Helen Gao, Carter Tu, Erika Martinez-Carcamo, Olga Derbeneva, Anastasiia Kovalenko, Igor Perchuk, Ilya Yaroslavsky, Gregory Altshuler, Aymon Ali, Bruce Gao, Sohrab Ali, Pengbo Jiang, Roshan Patel, Jaime Landman, Ralph Clayman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The thulium fiber laser (TFL) is a well-accepted modality for renal lithotripsy at low-power settings. Recently, interest has developed in special pulse modulation (Advanced Fragmentation Pulse – AFP) using high-energy settings in order to improve the efficiency of laser lithotripsy in fragmentation mode. The safety profile at high-energy settings (30 J) has yet to be characterized. Accordingly, we evaluated intrarenal temperature (IRT) and intrarenal pressure (IRP) during high-power thulium lithotripsy in porcine kidneys. METHODS: Two ex vivo porcine kidneys were implanted with three human calcium oxalate monohydrate stones (<10 mm) via a pyelostomy. Stones were placed in the renal pelvis and upper-pole calyx (total weights: 0.642 g and 0.693 g). Transparenchymal temperature and pressure probes were placed in the stone-bearing calyx and in the renal pelvis, respectively, for continuous recording. A 14 Fr 35 cm ureteral access sheath was placed above the ureteropelvic junction. Two separate retrograde intrarenal surgeries (RIRS) were performed (JB) in a 37 °C water bath: Advanced Fragmentation Pulse (AFP; 30 J × 1.0 Hz, 30 W) in one kidney and Regular Pulse (RP; 4.0 J × 8 Hz, 32 W) in the other kidney, each with a peak power of 500 W (prototype IPG TFL system, IPG Medical inc.). Room temperature (24 °C) normal saline irrigation at 150 mmHg was utilized. The procedural endpoint was stone fragmentation to visually <2 mm pieces. Fragments were sent for particle size distribution analysis. RESULTS: The total laser firing time was substantially shorter with the AFP mode (7.48 mins) compared to the RP mode (17.18 mins). The AFP mode exhibited a more favorable thermal and pressure profile, with a mean IRT of 23.35 ± 3.01 °C and a mean IRP of 10.11 ± 6.42 mmHg, along with peak values of 31°C and 56.3 mmHg, respectively. In contrast, the RP mode demonstrated consistently higher IRT and IRP, with a mean IRT of 38 ± 6.32 °C and a mean IRP of 52.82 ± 39.23 mmHg, and peak values of 56.3 °C and 159.5 mmHg, accordingly. Analysis of stone particle distribution demonstrated that the RP mode produced a higher proportion of fine fragments (<500 µm), whereas the AFP mode predominantly generated larger particles (1,500–2,000 µm) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191320.09030.8b.13#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: In an ex vivo porcine kidney, high-energy (AFP) TFL demonstrated improved efficiency for renal lithotripsy with lower transient temperature and lower pressure readings.

title: DUAL LASER LITHOTRIPSY: A NEW CONCEPT FOR MORE EFFICIENT STONE FRAGMENTATION
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Helen Gao, Jonathan Badin-Castro, Aymon Ali, Kantapon Tangwiwat, Ian Ong, Suraj Jayaraman, Bruce M. Gao, Sohrab N. Ali, Pengbo Jiang, Roshan M. Patel, Jaime Landman, Ralph V. Clayman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Thulium fiber laser (TFL) lithotripsy provides efficient lithotripsy with minimal retropulsion. Having developed a prototype triple lumen ureteroscope with two separate laser ports spaced 1 mm apart, we sought to compare the ablation efficiency of a single fiber vs. deploying two laser fibers via both of the laser ports simultaneously. METHODS: A 12 × 4 × 1 cm Bego stone slab submerged in 0.9% saline was mounted on an X-Y-Z motorized stage. Two 200-µm TFL fibers were fixed in a 3D-printed holder such that the fibers were spaced 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1.0 mm apart; both lasers were fired simultaneously while perpendicular to and 0.5 mm off the surface of the Bego stone at 1 J × 10 Hz (20 W total). Single-fiber controls were tested at 1 J × 10 Hz (10 W) and 2 J × 10 Hz (20 W). Each configuration was activated over a continuous 3 cm linear ablation at a traverse speed of 1 mm/s for 30 seconds. Crater and cut profiles were measured by 3D optical microscopy; ablation efficiency was assessed using mean crater depth (mm) and ablated volume per Joule (mm3/J). RESULTS: Dual-fiber ablation depth exceeded single-fiber controls across all spacings. Of note, the 0.25 mm configuration achieved the greatest mean depth (1.29 ± 0.13 mm), producing the most uniform trough. Wider spacings showed progressively reduced depth (0.45 ± 0.03 mm at 0.5 mm; 0.29 ± 0.03 mm at 0.75 mm; 0.26 ± 0.05 mm at 1.0 mm), whereas direct contact (0 mm) resulted in shallower craters (0.35 ± 0.02 mm). Single-fiber controls produced depths of 0.28 ± 0.04 mm (10 W) and 0.29 ± 0.02 mm (20 W). Ablation efficiency peaked at 0.25 mm spacing (0.057 ± 0.001 mm3/J) resulting in a fourfold increase in ablation depth and in ablation efficiency compared to a 1.0 mm spacing. CONCLUSIONS: Dual-fiber TFL lithotripsy achieved greater ablation depth and efficiency than the simultaneous firing of two single-fiber systems. A four-fold, synergistic effect was noted when the space between the two laser fibers was held at 0.25 mm.

title: ADVERSE EVENTS ASSOCIATED WITH LITHOTRIPTERS AND LASER FIBERS: A 5-YEAR ANALYSIS OF THE MANUFACTURER AND USER FACILITY DEVICE EXPERIENCE DATABASE
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Adam B. Cohen, Jacob Davis, Mahmoud Abou Zeinab, Smita De
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urolithiasis is a highly prevalent condition that often requires surgical management in the form of ureteroscopy or percutaneous nephrolithotomy. In the last few years, there has been significant innovation in the laser technology and lithotripters that are used to treat stones during these procedures. Our aim is to explore the spectrum of adverse events associated with use of current lasers and lithotripters in the management of urolithiasis. METHODS: The Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) database, maintained by the U. S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), was searched for entries related to stone lithotripters and laser technologies (i. e. High and low power holmium lasers, pulsed holmium lasers, thulium fiber lasers (TFL), and pulsed thulium lasers) between the years 2020-2024. All events related to kidney stones were included while those associated with stones outside of the urinary tract or other conditions were excluded. Patient complications and device-related problems were recorded and categorized. Incomplete entries or entries without any identifiable patient effect or device-associated concerns were excluded. RESULTS: There were 116 patient-related complications and 768 device-related problems associated with TFL, with the vast majority related to breakage (39.8%), communication errors (27%), and sparking/fires (23.2%). While the novel pulsed thulium laser did not have any formal patient or device complications per FDA criteria, almost all entries (n=10) were related to fiber breakage or dysfunction. For holmium lasers, there were 1107 total adverse events recorded, with 105 patient-related complications such as infections, bleeding, and trauma. The search for lithotripters yielded minimal adverse events affecting patients but over 500 device-related problems. CONCLUSIONS: Treatment of kidney stones continues to evolve with improving laser and lithotripter technologies. While these devices can be associated with complications, the majority did not cause significant patient harm. Though rare, urologists should be aware of dangerous situations such as fires or instrument breakage during lithotripsy. | | | --- | | |

title: IN-VITRO ASSESSMENT OF SUCTION PERFORMANCE AND BLOCKAGE RISK IN A 9.2/5.1CH DISS FLEXIBLE URETEROSCOPE
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Federico Zorzi, Carlos Gonzalez-Gonzalez, Alejandra Bravo-Balado, Nicola Nannola, Luigi Candela, Marie Chicaud, Letizia Maria Ippolita Jannello, Stessy Kutchukian, Marie-Lou Letouche, Stefano Moretto, Jordi Pena Lueza, Razvan Popescu, Aideen Madden, Alberto Quarà, Olivier Traxer
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Efficient intra-renal fragment evacuation remains a major challenge in flexible ureteroscopy. Recent advances in Direct-In-ScopeSuction (DISS) technology aim to overcome this limitation by integrating active suction within the working channel of flexibleureteroscopes. The newly developed 9.2 Ch DISS ureteroscope combines a large 5.1 Fr working channel with continuous suctioncapability, potentially improving visibility and reducing intrarenal pressure during lithotripsy. However, the effect of operative-channelobstruction caused by stone fragments has not been systematically evaluated. This study experimentally assessed the suctionperformance and blockage thresholds of the DISS channel using different laser-fiber diameters under standardized in-vitroconditions. METHODS: An in-vitro assessment of the PUSEN 9.2/5.1 Ch DISS ureteroscope was performed using standardized BegoStone fragments in sixparticle-size ranges (200–250, 250–300, 300–350, 350–400, 400–450, and 450–500 μm). Each test involved 2 g of fragments(≈1081 mm3) aspirated under a negative pressure of 450 mmHg, both with an empty working channel and with 150 μm, 200 μm, and 270 μm laser fibers inserted. Mean aspiration time (s ± SD) was recorded for complete evacuation. Partial or total blockages weredocumented, and test failure was defined as aspiration time > 5 minutes. RESULTS: Mean aspiration time increased with both particle size and fiber diameter. With an empty channel, particles up to 400–450 μm wereaspirated without obstruction (42 ± 4 s), while blockage occurred beyond 450–500 μm. With a 150 μm fiber, aspiration remainedeffective up to 350–400 μm (38.3 ± 4 s). With a 200 μm fiber, times ranged from 30 ± 4 s to 59 ± 12 s, and blockage appeared above400 μm. The 270 μm fiber configuration showed the slowest evacuation (46.7 ± 3 s to 99.3 ± 12 s) and partial blockage beyond 350–400 μm. CONCLUSIONS: The DISS 9.2/5.1 Ch ureteroscope enables effective fragment evacuation up to 350–400 μm with 150–270 μm laser fibers, and up to400–450 μm without fiber occupancy. Progressively larger fibers reduce suction efficiency while increasing the risk of channelobstruction above 400 μm. For optimal intra-renal pressure control and fragment clearance, dusting to ≤ 350 μm is recommended toensure maximum efficiency during DISS-assisted lithotripsy. | | | --- | | |

title: A PHYSICS-BASED SIMULATION OF INTRARENAL FLUID PRESSURE AND FLOW DURING SUCTION URETEROSCOPY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Tiange Li, Panagiotis L. Papalazarou, Shaikh Sufyan, Jonguk Lee, Brian Carrillo, Monica Farcas
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Suction during retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS) may lower intrarenal pressure (IRP) and improve fragment clearance, but optimal combinations of access sheath, scope, working channel size, and inflow remain undefined. We validated a physics-based model to 1) predict IRP and outflow velocity across device geometries, and 2) define safe and effective operating ranges. METHODS: We developed a benchtop ureteroscopy simulator using 3D printed collecting systems, and incorporated inline pressure transducers and flow sensors. We performed benchtop tests across combinations of irrigation pressures (50-500 mmHg), suction (0, -200 mmHg), sheath ID (10/11/12 Fr), scope OD (5.0-9.3 Fr), and working channel (2.4, 3.6 Fr), and evaluated extraction of artificial stone fragments. We then computationally modelled the urinary tract as a resistive pipe network to predict IRP and outflow velocities as a function of time and adjustable ureteroscopy parameters. Model predictions were validated against benchtop data across n=114 matched trials. We then simulated n=18 device geometries under a range of inflow and suction conditions. The primary efficacy criterion was the outflow fluid velocity associated with visible fragment extraction, and the primary safety criterion was maximum IRP < 40 mmHg. RESULTS: Across all benchtop trials and device geometries, the mean minimum fluid velocity required for visible fragment extraction was 15 cm/s (SD 2.6 cm/s). Predicted IRP closely matched benchtop measurements (R2=0.98; slope=0.90; mean absolute error 3.9 mmHg). To maintain IRP ≤ 40 mmHg, a ratio of endoscope to sheath ratio (RESD) of ≤ 0.75 without suction, or ≤ 0.85 with -200 mmHg suction, was required. Outflow velocity above the fragment extraction threshold (15 cm/s) was driven primarily by irrigation pressure and working channel size. Suction had limited impact on outflow velocity in cases above 200 mmHg of irrigation pressure. CONCLUSIONS: A physics-based model accurately predicts IRP and outflow during suction-enabled RIRS, and yields practical parameters for safe, effective operation. Our results demonstrate that the primary driver of effective fragment extraction is adequate inflow volume and working channel size, while suction is primarily useful in managing elevated IRP associated with high inflow volumes. This framework can evaluate novel device geometries and guide selection of effective operating parameters.

title: INTRARENAL PRESSURE RESPONSE TO SUCTION DURING URETEROSCOPY: IN VIVO PORCINE STUDIES
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Leilane Glienke, Anthony F. Bonzagni, Timothy L. Hall, Khurshid R. Ghani, William W. Roberts
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Suction can improve stone clearance during ureteroscopy but activation for too long can lower intrarenal pressure (IRP) and collapse the collecting system. The appropriate time to activate suction and the IRP at which the collecting system collapses have not been defined. We sought to apply short periods of suction and quantitatively assess IRP then correlate with the endoscopic appearance of the collecting system in an in vivo porcine model. METHODS: Ureteroscopy was performed in an anesthetized porcine subject using an 11/13Fr, 46 cm FANS device and a pressure measuring ureteroscope. Constant pressure irrigation was delivered from a prototype fluid management system to achieve baseline IRP of 40 cmH2O. Suction was activated for 1, 2, or 5 seconds by occluding the suction vent while IRP was recorded. Trials were conducted in triplicate. Longer periods of suction were also applied until complete collapse of the collecting system. Endoscopic video was synchronized with IRP measurements. RESULTS: Trials with 1, 2, or 5 seconds of suction activation produced a mean drop in intrarenal pressure from 40 cmH2O baseline to values of 18.3, 3.7, and -14.7 cmH2O, respectively. Upon release of suction, the mean time to return to baseline was 10.2, 21.8, and 41.3 seconds. With trials of longer suction activation IRP decreased in linear fashion until a mean of 10.7 cmH2O was reached at 2.2 seconds. At this point, the pressure-time curve flattened, with concomitant visual decrease in size of the collecting system volume. Full collapse of the collecting system occurred at mean IRP of 0.3 cmH2O after 9.8 seconds. Deactivation of suction resulted in immediate rise in IRP to a mean of 7.3 cmH2O, where the curve flattened, as the collecting system began to expand. IRP then gradually increased, reaching baseline after a mean of 35.2 seconds. CONCLUSIONS: Activation of suction during ureteroscopy produced a rapid drop in IRP. Visual contraction of the porcine collecting system was apparent when IRP decreased below 11 cmH2O. Understanding the relationships between IRP, suction, and the appearance of the collecting system can facilitate methods to better control and stabilize the ureteroscopic environment. Disclaimer: The prototype Fluid Management System used was a concept device further developed into the AsurysTM Fluid Management System, which is pending 510(k) clearance and not yet available for sale.

title: BUBBLE TROUBLE: COMPARISION OF INLINE AND PARALLEL AIR ELIMATION FILTERS TO A BUBBLE TRAP SYSTEM DURING ENDOSCOPY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Ye Na D. Lim, Elijah Haynal, Connor A. Church, Ye Jean Lim, Gabriel Martin, Ruben Crew, Elizabeth A. Baldwin, Frankis Almaguel, Ali Albaghli, D. Duane Baldwin
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: During laser lithotripsy, air bubbles are frequently introduced during endoscopic instrument insertion and irrigation. Even brief laser activation within these air bubbles can cause significant increases in temperature, leading to thermal injury. Air bubble accumulation further obstructs visualization, requiring continuous irrigation and drainage for clearance. This study evaluates the efficacy of various air elimination systems (AES) in reducing air bubbles in a benchtop endoscopic model. METHODS: A continuous irrigation flow system was connected to one of four AES: (1) control (no filter), (2) standard intravenous filter (1 or 10 in parallel), (3) high-flow intravenous filter (1 or 10 in parallel), and (4) a vertically orientated bubble trap (VOBT). Air boluses were injected upstream into each circuit at a rate of 5, 10, or 15 ml/min for 5 minutes (5 trials at each air rate). Real-time bubble detection was measured using a downstream AD-102 ultrasonic bubble sensor. Statistical significance was determined using ANOVA. RESULTS: Compared with control, all AES achieved significant reduction in air bubbles (100% filtered; p<0.05) with no significant differences between AES methods. Both IV filters showed declining flow performance with increasing air load (Standard IV filter: -24.1% per +5 ml air load; p<0.001; High-flow IV filter: -6.3% per +5 ml air load; p=0.03). In contrast, the VOBT demonstrated transient flow increases with higher air loads (+12.3% per +5 ml air load; p<0.001), indicating enhanced fluid transmission under higher air burden ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191320.09030.8b.19#F1)). Unlike the IV filters, the VOBT was demonstrated to reliably transmit manual irrigation pulses to the outflow without interruptions. CONCLUSIONS: While both filtrating and VOBT systems achieved complete air bubble elimination, the VOBT demonstrated higher flow rates, more reliable irrigation, and a simpler set up. The use of a VOBT during laser lithotripsy is a promising option for removing air bubbles, increasing visibility, and reducing the risk of thermal injury.

title: SMALLER OR SOFTER? A SINGLE CENTER RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL OF STENT DIAMETER AND MATERIAL EFFECTS ON URETERAL STENT SYMPTOMS
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Ali S. Antar, Emily C. Serrell, Margaret A. Knoedler, Andrew Z. Carey, Shuang Li, Kristina L. Penniston, Dan R. Gralnek, Stephen Y. Nakada
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ureteral stent–related discomfort remains a significant source of morbidity following ureteroscopy. The relative contribution of stent material versus caliber to patient comfort remains unclear. The novel Tria™ stent shares the Percuflex™ polymer base with an added PercuShield™ surface to enhance softness at body temperature (Boston Scientific). We performed a single-center randomized trial comparing Percuflex™ and Tria™ stents in both 4.8Fr and 6Fr sizes to determine their effects on patient-reported symptoms after ureteroscopy for stones <2 cm. METHODS: Patients undergoing surgery for stones <2 cm were prospectively randomized (1:1:1:1) to receive one of four ureteral stents: 4.8Fr Percuflex™, 6Fr Percuflex™, 4.8Fr Tria™, or 6 Fr Tria™. Primary outcomes included Ureteral Stent Symptoms Questionnaire (USSQ) and Wisconsin Stone Quality of Life (WiSQoL) scores at stent removal and 3 months post-procedure. Secondary outcomes were analgesic use, hematuria, stent migration, and adverse events. Comparisons were made using the Mann-Whitney U test with significance set at p<0.05. RESULTS: 70 patients were randomized, with 7 lost to follow-up. Baseline characteristics were similar. No significant differences were observed between Tria™ and Percuflex™ cohorts across primary endpoints. Within the Percuflex™ group, smaller diameter (4.8 Fr) stents were associated with better pain and general health scores on USSQ (p=0.015 and p=0.019, respectively) and higher WiSQoL scores (p=0.015) at the time of removal compared to 6Fr stents. The smaller Tria™ stent showed a similar, but non-significant trend. Analgesic use and complication rates were comparable among groups (p=0.354). At 3 months, USSQ and WiSQoL scores did not differ by stent type or diameter (all p>0.05). CONCLUSIONS: Stent material did not significantly affect patient-reported outcomes following ureteroscopy. In contrast, smaller-caliber stents were associated with improved short-term comfort and quality of life. These results suggest that stent diameter may exert a greater influence than material, supporting selective use of smaller stents when clinically appropriate.

title: THE OSU – OPTIMAL SAMPLING OF UPPER TRACT UROTHELIAL CARCINOMA (UTUC) BIOPSY INSTRUMENT
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Rajvi R. Goradia, Ian Rawdon, Mary Pancake, Ryan Brune, Maria DiVita, Kyle Van Koevering, Hamid Bhatti, Megan Malara, Firas Abdollah, Surena Matin, Akshay Sood
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: T stage is an important predictor of survival in UTUC and guides treatment decisions, but current biopsy tools provide inadequate information on T stage and histology of UTUC. In the era of precision oncology, robust pre-therapy tissue samples are essential to make decisions on radicality of surgery and choice of systemic therapy. We aimed to develop a proof-of-concept first-in-class endoscopic, tru-cut core-biopsy instrument. METHODS: A collaborative project including teams from OSU Urology and OSU CDME M4 Engineering Division was launched in 2023. Through re-iterative process, we sought to design, fabricate, and test a proof-of-concept prototype. Benchtop testing was conducted on 3D printed multilayered phantom tissue models that mimicked the anatomic and biomechanical properties of the ureter and renal pelvis ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191320.09030.8b.21#F1)). Key objective was to produce a long, narrow-caliber, flexible device capable of navigating the ureteroscope that was able to generate sufficient force at the tip to obtain full-thickness core biopsy of the phantom ureter. RESULTS: We were successfully able to develop a proof-of-concept device that is >115 cm, <3 Fr in caliber and is compatible with all existing flexible urology endoscopes. This device consists of three parts: a stylet, a cannula, and a handle. The stylet has a specimen notch that can collect up to a depth of 5 mm. Special focus was placed on designing an ergonomic handle that can help the surgeon maintain existing workflows. (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191320.09030.8b.21#F2) demonstrates the flexibility of this device. On high-speed camera analysis, the stylet has an average fire-rate of 2.0 m/s, which is comparable to rigid core-biopsy instruments, with little to minimal deflection. On benchtop phantom testing, we were able to reliably maneuver this device into a ureteroscope and collect a full-thickness biopsy sample. CONCLUSIONS: Our preliminary results support the successful building of a proof-of-concept endoscopic core-biopsy instrument. Future directions include benchtop user testing, cadaveric, and animal studies to demonstrate further efficacy and safety.

title: ANATOMICAL FOUNDATIONS, SURGICAL TECHNIQUE AND EARLY OUTCOME OF THE NO STRESS IN-CONTINENCE ENUCLEATION (NICE) TEMPLATE FOR HOLMIUM LASER ENUCLEATION OF THE PROSTATE (HOLEP)
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Aravindh Rathinam, Archan Khandekar, Adam Williams, Hasim Bakbak, Ansh Bhatia, Jonathan Elliot Katz, Robert Elliot Marcovich, Thomas R. W. Herrmann, Hemendra B. Shah
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Transient stress urinary incontinence (TSUI) remains a significant issue following Holmium laser enucleation of prostate (HoLEP). Herein we describe a novel technique called No stress-Incontience Enucleation (NIcE) designed to preserve both striated and smooth muscles within the anterior fibromuscular stroma and its overlying mucosa. The primary objective was to evaluate continence immediately after catheter removal. The secondary goal was to compare perioperative and early voiding outcomes in patients undergoing HoLEP using the NIcE technique vs standard en-bloc technique. METHODS: Patients undergoing HoLEP with NIcE modification from May 2024 were prospectively enrolled. The procedure used the Moses 2.0 holmium laser (2J, 30 Hz) with a specific template designed to preserve the anterior urethral mucosa between the 10 and 2 o’clock positions from the bladder neck to the external urethral sphincter. Perioperative data, complications, voiding outcomes and PSA at 3 months were retrospectively compared with a matched cohort of patients undergoing HoLEP with the standard en-bloc technique. RESULTS: 38 patients treated with NIcE were compared with 80 control patients treated with the en-bloc technique. Demographic and baseline characteristics were comparable. All patients in the NIcE group who had complete preservation of the anterior urethral mucosa were continent immediately after catheter removal. Postoperative Qmax, PVR, and PSA levels showed no significant differences between groups. CONCLUSIONS: NIcE HoLEP prevents TSUI immediately after catheter removal, providing safe and effective relief from benign prostatic obstruction (BPO). Early results suggest it may offer a viable alternative to standard HoLEP techniques.

title: SAFETY OUTCOMES OF A ROBOTIC PLATFORM FOR HOLMIUM LASER ENUCLEATION OF THE PROSTATE (HOLEP): PRIMARY RESULTS OF THE ASTRA STUDY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Peter Gilling, Rodrigo Ledezma, Ernesto Mohr, Tomás Olmedo, Gaston Astroza, Cristian Trucco, Giovanni Losco, Wikus Vermeulen, Fernando Gómez Sancha
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Holmium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate (HoLEP) is the gold-standard surgical treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), but its steep learning curve and ergonomic challenges limit widespread adoption. The Beacon platform (Andromeda Surgical) is a novel robotic system designed to improve precision, stability, and safety. The ASTRA Study is the first-in-human, multicenter evaluation of the safety and feasibility of robot-assisted HoLEP (RoLEP) using this system. METHODS: This prospective, open-label, multicenter pilot study enrolled men ≥ 45 years with symptomatic BPH indicated for HoLEP. Safety outcomes were assessed intraoperatively, and at 1 week and 1-month post-procedure. Adverse events (AEs) were graded using Clavien–Dindo. Device-related events, transfusions, and reinterventions were recorded. This interim analysis includes the first 26 subjects treated across five international sites. RESULTS: All procedures were completed robotically without conversion or device malfunction. No major (≥ Grade III) AEs, transfusions, or reinterventions occurred. Transient Grade I–II events included urgency, dysuria, mild hematuria with clot retention, and transient incontinence—all managed conservatively. Mean catheterization duration: 4.7 ± 2.6 days; mean hospital stays: 1.69 ± 0.62 days. Mean enucleation time: 2 h 24 min ± 1 h 23 min; morcellation time: 11 ± 15 minutes. In the most recent six cases, mean enucleation time improved to ~95 minutes with no increase in complications, demonstrating a favorable early learning and safety trajectory. No device-related safety issues were identified. CONCLUSIONS: Early multicenter experience with the Beacon robotic platform demonstrates a strong safety profile with no serious or device-related complications. RoLEP appears safe, feasible, and reproducible across sites, supporting further evaluation to validate long-term safety and potential to standardize HoLEP outcomes across surgeons and centers.

title: MECHANOPHYSIOLOGY OF THE LOWER URINARY TRACT: DETERMINING STRICTURE SEVERITY BY ESTIMATING TISSUE COMPLIANCE FROM RETROGRADE URETHROGRAMS
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Noah D. Roselli, Emily Ji, Diboro Kanabolo, Ziho Lee, Neelesh A. Patankar
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The proliferation of scar tissue in urethral strictures stiffens the urethral walls and decreases lumen diameter. A retrograde urethrogram (RUG), the most common diagnostic tool for urethral strictures, illuminates the lumen via X-ray to determine where the narrowing occurs. There is a large variability in the length and location of strictures determined by different physicians, as RUGs offer only static, geometric information and there is no direct indication of tissue quality. As such, patients are informed on multiple surgical outcomes that depend on the length and severity of the fibrosis. A novel technique was developed to locate the stricture by estimating the compliance of the tissue. METHODS: The urethra is modeled as a distensible tube, where fluid flow is governed by the conservation of mass and momentum equations, written in terms of tube area and fluid velocity. A neural network was trained to segment the urethra from the rest of the X-ray image, from which tube area can be calculated algorithmically. The equations are solved to determine what the compliance is at every location using the area measurements from the RUG. Regions of narrowing and stiffening are used in tandem to determine stricture location. A new metric, called the compliance ratio (CR), was defined to gauge the severity of the stricture. It measures, on average, how much stiffer the tissue is in the stricture as compared to the normal part of the urethra for a particular patient. RESULTS: A cohort of N=11 patients had their RUG images analyzed using the process defined here. The mean and standard deviation of the values for the compliance ratio (CR) in the cohort were found to be 2.62 and 1.11, respectively. The figure shows the relationship between the length of the stricture and the compliance ratio, where one patient is highlighted to show the algorithmically found start and end locations for the stricture. The algorithm tended to have higher values for the length compared to physician reads, as also shown in the figure. CONCLUSIONS: The method discussed here provides a way to algorithmically find strictures and is thus reproducible and objective. It also yields a natural way of defining the stricture severity by defining the compliance ratio for a patient. This can lead to stricture codex development in the future, defined in terms of tissue compliance and lumen diameter.

title: COMPARATIVE EFFECTIVENESS OF OPTILUME, OPTICAL URETHROTOMY, AND URETHRAL DILATION IN ANTERIOR URETHRAL STRICTURE: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS OF EFFICACY AND SAFETY
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Waqas Khalil, Muhammad Mazhar Sheikh, Jawad Islam
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Anterior urethral stricture disease (USD) is a common cause of lower urinary tract obstruction, historically managed with urethral dilation (UD) or optical urethrotomy (OU). Recurrence rates with these traditional techniques remain high, prompting interest in drug-coated balloon technology, such as the Optilume system (DCB). This meta-analysis aimed to compare efficacy, safety, and recurrence outcomes of Optilume versus OU and UD, with subgroup analyses based on stricture length and prior intervention status, to inform optimal minimally invasive management strategies. METHODS: A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science through June 2025 identified studies reporting clinical outcomes for Optilume, OU, or UD in adult anterior urethral strictures. Studies reporting stricture recurrence, patency, adverse events, or re-intervention rates were included. Data extraction was independently performed by two reviewers. The primary outcome was 12-month stricture recurrence. Secondary outcomes included time to recurrence, complication rates, and need for repeat intervention. Random-effects meta-analysis was used for pooled estimates, and heterogeneity assessed with I2. Subgroup analyses evaluated outcomes stratified by stricture length (2 cm vs ≥2 cm) and prior procedures (naïve vs recurrent). Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger’s test. RESULTS: Twelve studies involving 1,028 patients (Optilume n=312; OU n=452; UD n=264) were included. Twelve-month recurrence was significantly lower for Optilume (23.1%, 95% CI 17.2–30.3%) than OU (43.6%, 95% CI 37.1–50.3%) or UD (48.2%, 95% CI 40.5–56.0%). Time to recurrence was longer with Optilume (mean 10.7 months, 95% CI 9.2–12.2) compared to OU (6.4 months, 95% CI 5.1–7.7) and UD (5.9 months, 95% CI 4.8–7.0). Subgroup analysis showed Optilume superiority was most pronounced in naïve strictures 2 cm (recurrence 15.8%, 95% CI 10.2–23.3%), whereas benefits were attenuated in recurrent or longer strictures (32.4%, 95% CI 25.1–41.2%). Adverse events were mild and comparable across groups: hematuria (Optilume 8.3%, OU 10.1%, UD 9.5%) and urinary tract infection (Optilume 4.2%, OU 5.3%, UD 4.9%). Moderate heterogeneity was observed (I2=46%), and funnel plots indicated no significant publication bias (p=0.27). CONCLUSIONS: Optilume provides superior short-term patency and reduced recurrence compared with OU and UD, particularly in treatment-naïve, short anterior urethral strictures, with a safety profile comparable to conventional interventions. These findings support Optilume as a durable, minimally invasive alternative for selected patients. Ongoing randomized trials with extended follow-up are needed to assess long-term durability, cost-effectiveness, and broader applicability across stricture subtypes.

title: FURTHER VALIDATION OF THE TRANSURETHRAL CATHETERIZATION SAFETY VALVE (TUCSV) PRESSURE THRESHOLD IN A PORCINE MODEL
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Cathal Flood, Nikita R. Bhatt, Jay Budrewicz, Barry Rickman, Michael Walsh, Hugh Flood, Niall Davis
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Inadvertent inflation of a catheter anchoring ballon in the urethra can cause urethral rupture due to high balloon inflation pressures. Bleeding, urosepsis and late urethral stricture are common complications. A pressure relief valve has been developed to protect against catheter balloon injury (CBI). The TUCSV opening pressure is set at 150 kPa (range 140-170 kPa). The FDA has requested that the safety of the venting pressure window of 140-170 kPa be confirmed for the device by comparing, in an ex-vivo urethral model, the integrity of the urethra at an inflation pressure of 100 vs 170 kPa (15 vs 25 psi). The objective of this study was to confirm that inflation of the anchoring balloon of a urinary catheter at 25 psi produces no significant additional urethral tissue changes compared to inflation at 15 psi in a porcine model used in previous reports. METHODS: This study was run under Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) conditions. Proximal urethras from 5 male Yorkshire swine between 6 and 7 months old were harvested and utilized fresh to evaluate for any acute urethral injury after inflation of the 5cc anchoring balloon of a14 F, 100% silicone Foley catheter to a pressure of either 15 psi (control) or 25 psi (test). Test and control treatments were performed in each urethra at either proximal or distal locations according to a pre-determined treatment matrix. After testing, the urethra was evaluated and macroscopically scored for any tissue damage. Urethra sections from balloon treated sites and proximal and distal to the treated area were processed for histopathologic evaluation. Areas proximal and distal to the treated area had morphometric wall thickness measurements performed. RESULTS: Inflation of all catheters to their pre-determined balloon inflation pressures were successful. No noticeable external urethral damage upon balloon inflation, deflation or removal was observed. In all specimens, there was no macroscopic injury or evidence of tissue damage/tears within the urethra. No abnormal histologic findings including mucosal, submucosal, and muscular tears, or collagen and elastin fiber damage, tearing, or separation were observed in test (25 psi) or control (15 psi) groups. Urethral wall thickness was comparable for the two groups. CONCLUSIONS: The absence of any urethral injury at a TUCSV venting threshold pressure of 25psi (170kPa) combined with 60,000 units sold in Europe without reported CBI underlines the importance of this device in achieving safer urinary catheterization.

title: A NEW APPROACH TO DIFFICULT CATHETERIZATION: EVERTING DEVICE DEMONSTRATES TRACTION IN STRICTURE-MIMICKING MODELS
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Mitsuru Komeya, Kotaro Kishino, Rintaro Sasaki, Hiroyuki Yamanaka, Fumio Ito, Taro Nakamura, Kazuhide Makiyama
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Conventional urethral catheterization relies on manual pushing, which can shear the wall or impinge at bends/strictures, causing pain, bleeding, and injury. We developed a pressure-controlled, fluid-actuated mechanism that everts and advances a thin tube with minimal external sliding. We evaluated propulsion and catheter traction in gel urethral models reproducing urethral stiffness—normal anatomy and a pendulous-urethral stricture. METHODS: An inverting-extension actuator (OD 6 mm, length 280 mm, extendable 200 mm) was connected to a pressure chamber and driven at 90 kPa, with a 3.3-mm-OD catheter (length 280 mm) bonded to the tip. The mechanism is pressure-driven eversion: internal pressure turns the tube inside-out at an eversion front, which advances and pulls the catheter ( Fig.1). Motion was video-recorded and tip distance–time trajectories analyzed. The normal gel model (ID 6 mm, length 200 mm) reproduced geometry/compliance with a smooth 90–120° bend at the membranous-to-prostatic segment. The stricture model used the same bend plus a straight stenosis 30 mm long and 3 mm in ID. RESULTS: In the normal model, rapid propulsion occurred and the tip reached ~200 mm within 5–8 s; traction was established and no macroscopic lumen damage was seen. In the stricture model, maximum extension (~200 mm) was also achieved. Progression became temporarily gradual near a tip distance of ~50 mm, consistent with pressure-mediated dilation during stenosis traversal; after crossing, resistance decreased and acceleration resumed, with full extension at 47–52 s ( Fig.2). CONCLUSIONS: A pressure-controlled inverting-extension mechanism achieved reproducible propulsion and traction in stiffness-matched urethral models representing normal anatomy and pendulous-urethral stricture, while potentially reducing wall friction, local load, and operator dependence. Next steps include pressure-profile optimization, quantitative wall-load measurement, and definition of clinical use cases.

title: COST-BENEFIT OF A URETHRAL CATHETERISATION DEVICE (UCD®) FOR DIFFICULT CATHETER INSERTION IN THE EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Zoe Williams, Alyssa Chong, Song Kang, Alexander Combes, George McClintock, Jeremy Saad, Ramesh Shanmugasundaram, Varun Bhoopathy, Brayden March, Femi E. Ayeni, Isaac Thangasamy, Nicola Jeffery
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Catheter-associated urethral injury (CAUI) occurs in 13.4 per 1000 catheterised males. A urethral catheterisation device with an integrated guidewire (Urethrotech UCD®) can facilitate safe and successful urethral catheterisation by non-urologists when first-line techniques are unsuccessful. This study assesses the implementation of a protocol for difficult urethral catheterisation (DUC) incorporating the UCD® in an Australian metropolitan hospital Emergency Department and evaluates the cost-effectiveness of this approach. METHODS: A prospective trial was conducted over 12 months in an Australian tertiary hospital Emergency Department. For the first 6 months, referrals to urology for assistance with male DUC or management of CAUIs were audited. For the second 6 months, a protocol for male DUC was implemented and trialled. The protocol initiated UCD® use after failed male urethral catheterisation with a 16 Fr catheter. The cost of urology involvement for assistance with male DUC and CAUI care was obtained from the hospital Finance Department. RESULTS: In the 6-months without the DUC protocol, there were 13 referrals to urology for assistance with male DUC or CAUI management. Urology attended to perform urethral catheterisation over a guidewire in 9 patients using blind technique (n=5) or guided by bedside flexible cystoscopy (n=4). CAUIs during this period included urosepsis (n=3), false passages (n=2), urethral strictures (n=1), and periurethral bleeding (n=1). The complications required urology admission (n=7), a period of urethral catheterisation and outpatient trial of void (n=4), or rigid cystoscopy (n=1). After introduction of the DUC protocol, the UCD® was used in 12 patients and was successful in 10 patients (83%). Correspondingly, there were fewer referrals to urology for assistance with male DUC (n=2) and fewer cases of CAUI (n=2). Urology attended to perform urethral catheterisation aided by bedside flexible cystoscopy in 2 patients. CAUIs during this period included a bulbar urethral mucosal flap (n=1) and a prostatic urethra false passage (n=1). The mean cost of DUC-related care for patients for whom the UCD® was trialled (successfully or unsuccessfully) was $1266 per patient, compared with a mean cost of $2691 for DUC-related care when UCD® was not used. CONCLUSIONS: The UCD® is a successful urethral catheterisation technique and reduces patient morbidity, referrals to urology services, and health system costs.

title: A NEWLY DEVELOPED AI MULTI-MODAL IMAGE FUSION PRECISE INTERVENTION PLATFORM FOR SACRAL NERVE MODULATION
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Yan Li, Benkang Shi, Lipeng Chen
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Conventional sacral nerve modulation (SNM) procedures primarily depend on X-ray guidance, which exposes both patients and clinicians to radiation. Although several studies have demonstrated the feasibility of ultrasound-guided SNM electrode placement, traditional ultrasound techniques remain limited by the shield of the sacrum, especially in determining optimal insertion depth and trajectory. Here we developed an Artificial Intelligence (AI) multi-modal image fusion precise intervention platform for SNM electrode implantation. METHODS: The newly developed system integrates preoperative CT data of the lumbosacral region with real-time ultrasound imaging. During the procedure, an electromagnetic tracking system continuously monitors the spatial position of the ultrasound probe and puncture needle to guide precise electrode placement. Sensory responses and reflex activities were observed intraoperatively to verify appropriate stimulation. The final electrode position was confirmed with standard X-ray fluoroscopy. If fluoroscopy confirmed accurate placement, electrode implantation was completed. Operative duration and second-stage conversion rates were evaluated and the number of fluoroscopic sessions required was also recorded. RESULTS: Ten patients were enrolled in this study. Five underwent SNM using the AI multi-modal image fusion precise intervention platform, and five underwent conventional X-ray localization. The mean operative time in the multimodal group was 79.60 ± 7.72 min, compared with 83.80 ± 5.34 min in the control group (p=0.437). The number of fluoroscopy sessions was significantly lower in the multimodal group (4.80 ± 0.68) than in the X-ray group (8.20 ± 1.06; p=0.001). The rate of second-stage implantation was similar between the two groups (3/5 vs. 3/5). No postoperative complications were observed in either group during follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: The AI multi-modal image fusion precise intervention platform enhances the precision of SNM electrode placement, shortens operative time, and markedly reduces radiation exposure for both patients and surgeons. Further large-scale studies are warranted to validate these findings.

title: UNDER PRESSURE: A NOVEL CLOSED-LOOP IRRIGATION CONTROLLER TO REGULATE RENAL PRESSURE AND TEMPERATURE DURING PCNL
session: Surgical Technology & Simulation: Instrumentation & Technology I (IP10)
authors: Elijah Haynal, Connor A. Church, Ye Jean Lim, Ye Na Lim, Elizabeth A. Baldwin, Frankis Almaguel, Ruben Crew, Ali Albaghli, D. Duane Baldwin
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: During percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) elevations in intrarenal pressure (IRP), especially greater than 40 cm H2O (29.4 mmHg), greatly increase the risk of pyelovenous backflow and systemic infection. The risk of sepsis is further increased by urothelial trauma caused by instrumentation and suction under decreased visibility and increases in temperature. The ability to actively modulate these factors during PCNL has the potential to improve patient outcomes. The purpose of this study was to create a pressure regulated irrigation system for thermal and infection-free nephroscopic environment (PRISTINE) for pressure and temperature control and to test the feasibility of this system for optimizing these factors in a PCNL benchtop model. METHODS: The PRISTINE closed pressure control system utilizes a proportional-integral-derivative control scheme. The input data were pressure and temperature. These factors were controlled within specific set points using peristaltic pumps on the in- and outflow. To simulate PCNL and create a closed system for pressure control, a 3D printed kidney and ureter model was created which included a percutaneous access sheath sealed around a rigid nephroscope ( Figure 1a, 1b). The PRISTINE’s ability to maintain a set IRP of 20 mmHg and temperature of 37 °C were tested in trials pairing it with ultrasonic or laser lithotripsy compared against gravity bag irrigation (control). IRP and temperature were measured via the PRISTINE’s onboard sensors. Statistical significance was determined using Welch’s t-test and Levene’s test. RESULTS: During the use of an ultrasonic lithotripter, the PRISTINE maintained IRPs that were closer to goal of 20 mmHg than gravity irrigation (mean 19.78 vs. -1.79 mmHg, respectively; p<0.001). Additionally, the pressures maintained by the PRISTINE were significantly more stable than gravity irrigation (standard deviation 0.51 vs. 19.78 mmHg, respectively; p<0.001; Figure 1c). During the use of a laser lithotripter, the PRISTINE maintained lower intrarenal temperature (mean 38.81 vs. 40.74 °C, p<0.001; Figure 1d). CONCLUSIONS: The PRISTINE controller effectively controlled pressure and temperature within predetermined limits in this benchtop model. By optimizing intrarenal pressure and temperature and maintaining a clear working environment, the PRISTINE represents a promising option to improve efficiency and safety of PCNL.

title: LARGEST SINGLE CENTRE EXPERIENCE OF ROBOT ASSISTED RENAL TRANSPLANT: ANALYSIS OF 428 CASES
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Samit Chaturvedi, Rahul Agarawal, Shaunak Mitra, Mohammad Umar Khansherwani, Kumar Nishant, Anant Kumar
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robot-assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT) has evolved considerably in the past decade, yet large single-centre experiences from developing countries remain limited. We present outcomes from a high-volume tertiary centre in India, focusing on patient profile, operative details, complications, and short-term graft and patient survival. METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of all consecutive RAKT performed at a high-volume tertiary centre in India, between January 2016 and September 2025. All donor kidneys were retrieved laparoscopically. Data regarding recipient demographics, graft laterality, vascular anatomy, body mass index (BMI), etiology of chronic kidney disease (CKD), perioperative variables, and two-year outcomes were analysed. RESULTS: A total of 428 RAKT were performed during the study period. There were 310 males and 118 females (M:F=2.6:1) with a mean age of 40 years. Single-vessel grafts were used in 246 cases and multiple-vessel grafts in 182. Left-sided grafts predominated (394 left, 34 right). The mean BMI was 24.9 kg/m2, with 8 patients (1.9%) having BMI ≥ 35 kg/m2. The most common causes of CKD were hypertension (25%), diabetes mellitus (23%), and glomerular disease (16%). For graft insertion, a Pfannenstiel incision was employed in approximately 79% of cases and GelPort access in 21%. The mean vascular anastomosis time improved from about 55 minutes in the first 100 cases to 35 minutes in the last 100, indicating a clear learning curve. Immediate diuresis was observed in 98% of patients; the remainder voided within a few hours. Intraoperative bleeding occurred in 38 cases, all managed robotically without conversion. No patient required re-exploration for bleeding or primary graft non-function. Two patients were re-explored for subcapsular hematoma, and two required graft nephrectomy one week post-transplant for severe rejection. One-year graft survival was 95%, and one-year patient survival was 98%. The mean serum creatinine level at the time of discharge was 1.64 mg/dl, 1.42 after 1 month and 1.74 after 1 year.
