The two-year graft survival was 95%, and the two-year patient survival was 99%. CONCLUSIONS: This series represents the largest single-centre RAKT experience to date. The procedure demonstrated reproducible outcomes, low morbidity, and progressive improvement in efficiency with experience. With consistent laparoscopic donor retrieval, refined recipient access, and reliable robotic reconstruction, RAKT outcomes at our centre are comparable to those of open transplantation while retaining the advantages of a minimally invasive approach.

title: CURRENT PERSPECTIVES OF TRANSPLANT SURGEONS ON EVOLVING TECHNIQUES IN ROBOTIC TRANSPLANTATION
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Christina Delvalle, Hafiz Umair Siddiqui, Dylan Isaacson, Annaliese Ionson, Venkatesh Krishnamurthi, Alvin Wee, Mohamed Eltemamy, Yi-Chia Lin
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robotic transplantation has evolved rapidly in the past decade. Data suggests benefits such as less pain, shorter hospital stay and fewer wound complications, though barriers to broader adoption remain. We report the first multi‑organ survey of American Society of Transplant Surgeons (ASTS) members assessing their views on robotic transplantation. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was distributed via REDCap to 997 ASTS members. Demographics, experience, and perspectives on the future of robotic transplantation across all organ types were collected. Descriptive analyses examined trends by experience and organ type. RESULTS: A total of 122 surgeons responded (12%). Most were aged 35-44 (44%) and male (79%). Residency training was primarily in General Surgery (87%), then Urology (11%). Majority of respondents had over 5 years of transplant experience (73%). Primary organ practice was kidney/liver/pancreas (52%), followed by kidney/pancreas (16%) and kidney/liver (9%). Annual transplant volumes at respondents’ centers differed by organ: kidney 101-200/year, liver 101-150/year, and pancreas 5-10/year. Over half of respondents reported no robotic exposure during residency (53%) or fellowship (61%). Currently, 8% perform 11-20 robotic recipient transplants/year. Regarding perceived benefits: 33% viewed robotic kidney transplant as offering moderate advantage over open approaches; 73% rated liver transplant benefits as minimal (38%) or none (35%); 70% rated pancreas transplant benefits as minimal (32%) or none (38%). Among the stated disadvantages, learning curve and longer operative time were the most cited. Most respondents (75%) believe robotic surgery will be used in certain cases rather than universally; 13% expect it to become standard in 5‑10 years. Overall, 68% of surgeons perceived some level of institutional support for robotic transplantation. Key barriers for increased use included more supporting evidence (53%), robot availability (52%) and improved training (49%). CONCLUSIONS: Despite limited exposure during training, most surgeons anticipate selective integration of robotic transplantation into future practice. Perceived barriers include training, operative time, cost, and access to equipment. Overcoming these barriers and providing robust evidence of clinical benefit is critical to facilitating broader implementation.

title: ROBOTIC KIDNEY TRANSPLANTS FOR OBESE RECIPIENTS: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Lucinda Li, Zeyu Liu, Mehrnaz A. Siavoshi, Lorna C. Kwan, Nima Nassiri
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robotic kidney transplantation (RKT) has emerged as a promising alternative that may mitigate the high perioperative risks associated with morbidly obese patients. However, comprehensive assessments on its safety and efficacy are limited. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to examine the safety and efficacy of RKT in morbidly obese patients. METHODS: This review was conducted according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis regulations and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420250655777). PubMed and Web of Science were searched for peer-reviewed original research articles. Abstract and full-text screening were done on Excel. Data extracted included survival rates, kidney function metrics, and adverse outcomes. All analyses were performed in SAS 9.4. RESULTS: 40 studies were identified in preliminary searches with 8 included in full-text screening. 6 were eligible for inclusion in this review with 3 including an open kidney transplant (OKT) cohort. Overall, RKTs had high performance and consistency in survival metrics; patient survival was above 94% and graft survival above 95% 1-year post-transplant in all studies (I2=0-27.6%, p>0.05). Rejection rates, DGF incidence, eGFR rates (6 and 12 months), major complications, and length of hospital stay had high heterogeneity across studies (I250%, p0.05). Minor complications averaged around 30% with consistency in studies (I2=40, p>0.05). Readmissions at 30 days (average: 37.6% \[95%CI: 36.3-39.0\]) and 180 days (average: 44.8% \[95% CI: 44.5-45.0\]) were consistent across studies (I2=0, p>0.05). Compared to OKT cohorts, RKT patients had no significant differences in survival, kidney function, and complications. CONCLUSIONS: RKT is safe and effective in morbidly obese patients, demonstrating high survival rates. While there was considerable heterogeneity in kidney function metrics and complications, this likely reflecting institutional differences in peri- and post-operative care as no significant differences were found when compared to OKT cohorts. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: BODY-MASS INDEX AND POSTOPERATIVE RECOVERY AFTER ROBOTIC VERSUS OPEN DECEASED-DONOR KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION: A EUROPEAN MULTICENTER REGISTRY ANALYSIS
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Andre Belarmino, Angelo Territo, Francesco Di Bello, Giulio Avesani, Andrea Gallioli, Josep M. Gaya, Riccardo Campi, Luca Afferi, Alessio Pecoraro, Karel Decaestecker, Mireia Musquera, Begona Etcheverry, Joris Vangeneugden, Milla Ortved, Philip Zeuschner, Alessandro Volpe, Mirza Idu, Burak Kocak, Francesc Vigues, Antonio Alcaraz, Sergio Serni, Alberto Breda
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Obesity is a recognized risk factor for delayed recovery and wound morbidity after kidney transplantation. Robotic-assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT) may mitigate these effects by minimizing incision size and enhancing early mobilization, yet robotic access remains limited. Determining which recipients derive the greatest benefit is critical for case selection and resource allocation. This study evaluated whether increasing body-mass index (BMI) modifies the postoperative length-of-stay (LOS) advantage of RAKT compared with open deceased-donor kidney transplantation (DDKT). METHODS: All adult DDKT recipients (2018–2025) from a prospective European registry were analyzed. Living donors and conversions were excluded. LOS (days) was compared between open and robotic approaches using multivariable linear regression adjusted for age and metabolic comorbidities. An interaction term assessed whether BMI modified the LOS difference between approaches. Propensity weighting (BMI, age, comorbidity count) was used for confirmatory estimation of average treatment effects (ATEs) within BMI strata. RESULTS: Among 317 deceased-donor recipients (mean BMI 25.2 ± 3.7 kg/m2), RAKT was associated with shorter hospitalization at all BMI levels, with the benefit increasing in heavier recipients. Overall: RAKT shortened LOS by ~2 days (p=0.04). BMI effect: Each 1 kg/m2 increase prolonged LOS by 0.15 days (p=0.02). Interaction: The robotic advantage increased by 0.3 days per BMI unit (p=0.04). In open surgery, LOS rose steadily with BMI, whereas after RAKT it remained stable, yielding an estimated 15–20-day difference at BMI 40 kg/m2. Propensity-weighted analyses confirmed this pattern, showing little difference below BMI 25 but a 5–8-day shorter stay with RAKT among patients with BMI ≥30 ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191324.44573.90.04#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: In deceased-donor kidney transplantation, rising BMI markedly prolongs hospitalization after open surgery but not after RAKT. The robotic approach effectively neutralizes the obesity-related rise in LOS, translating to faster recovery, earlier ambulation, and reduced resource utilization. These findings suggest overweight and obese recipients derive the greatest benefit from RAKT and should be prioritized for robotic access in resource-limited programs. Conducted on behalf of the ERUS-RAKT Working Group, European Association of Urology Robotic Urology Section (ERUS).

title: ROBOT-ASSISTED KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION: THE ASSESSMENT OF LEARNING CURVE OVER THE YEARS IN A SINGLE-CENTRE
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Kishore TA, Atanu Kumar Pal, Jeni Mathew, Ramaprasad MK, Sandeep Prabhakaran, VN Unni
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The objective of this study was to evaluate the learning curve of robot-assisted kidney transplant (RAKT) and its influence over the perioperative and long-term outcomes of the recipients in a single centre. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was performed nine years after the start of the RAKT program (2015) at our institute. Each group had patients who were operated in a period of two years (2016-17: Group A; 2018-19 Group B; 2020-21 Group C; 2022-23: Group D). Patients with single-artery and double-artery reconstruction were analyzed separately. The patients who at least completed one year of follow-up were included in this study. Various clinico-demographic, intraoperative, and postoperative parameters were evaluated. Shewhart control charts and cumulative summation (CUSUM) graphs were generated to appraise learning curve. RESULTS: Out of 282 patients, group A, B, C, and D included 49, 49, 58, and 46 patients for single-artery (total 202 patients), and 21, 21, 12, and 26 patients for double-artery (total 80 patients). Warm ischemia time (WIT), setting-up time, console time, vein, and artery anastomosis time, ureteroneocystostomy time, total surgical time, blood loss, blood transfusion, hospital stay, Clavien-Dindo grade III, and IV complications decreased significantly over time from group A to group D ( Table 1). CUSUM analysis for single-artery-reconstruction showed initial high WITs, above the benchmark, with gradual improvement over time. For delayed graft function (DGF), there was a consistent downward trend. One-Year Graft Survival (OYGS) revealed a two-phase pattern: initial challenges reflected in downward steps, followed by a strong recovery and consistent improvement. One-Year Patient Survival (OYPS) showed a stepwise pattern, showing both downward and upward movements. For double-artery-reconstruction, WIT showed three distinct phases - initial challenges with higher WITs, stabilization, and eventual improvement. A better-than-benchmark performance was maintained for DGF. OYGS revealed early challenges followed by clear improvement, while OYPS showed stepwise changes, maybe because of the small sample size. CONCLUSIONS: The learning curve led to the development of a standardised reproducible protocol for RAKT. The perioperative parameters and graft function improve along the learning curve with more double-artery allografts can be transplanted robotically. | | | --- | | |

title: PREDICTORS AND POSTOPERATIVE OUTCOMES OF ICU ADMISSION FOLLOWING ROBOTIC-ASSISTED KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Hafiz Umair Siddiqui, Dylan Isaacson, Christina Delvalle, Venkatesh Krishnamurthi, Yi-Chia Lin, Alvin Wee, Mohamed Eltemamy
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Robot-assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT) is being increasingly utilized for more complex organs and recipients. Consequently, postoperative ICU admissions may rise as higher-risk recipients undergo RAKT. In this study, we evaluated the incidence and predictors of ICU admission after RAKT and compared graft and patient outcomes between ICU and non-ICU cohorts. METHODS: Patients in our prospectively maintained robotic kidney transplant database (RoKiT) transplanted from 10/2019 to 10/2025 were categorized based on postoperative ICU admission. Demographic, donor, intraoperative, and post-transplant variables were compared between groups. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify factors associated with ICU admission. RESULTS: Of 209 RAKT recipients, 32 (15.3%) required postoperative ICU admission, with a median ICU stay of 1 day. The most common indications were hemodynamic instability (12/32, 38%) and respiratory distress (7/32, 22%). Baseline demographics were comparable between groups. On univariate analysis, ICU admission was more common after deceased donor transplants (87.5% vs. 49.8%, p<0.001), transplants with kidneys with multiple arteries (31% vs. 12%, p=0.019), surgery with the multiport vs. the single port robot (88% vs. 66%, p=0.01), and the presence of delayed graft function (DGF, 44% vs. 10%, p=0.002). On multivariable analysis, multiport robotic surgery (OR 3.64, p=0.05), deceased donor transplantation (OR 4.36, p=0.02) and DGF (OR 3.09, p=0.035) were associated with increased odds of ICU admission. CONCLUSIONS: In our diverse series of RAKT recipients, use of the multiport robot, deceased donor transplantation, and DGF were associated with three-fourfold odds of ICU admission. These data may help inform future interventions to mitigate intraoperative cardiopulmonary stress and in organ-recipient matching. | | | --- | | |

title: SINGLE-PORT ROBOTIC-ASSISTED KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS ON THE DA VINCI PLATFORM
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Pierangelo Nitzkowski, Aaron Ouyang, Thriaksh Rajan, Farouq Alahmed, Ramy Abou Ghayda
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Single-port (SP) robotic platforms have emerged as a next-generation minimally invasive option for complex procedures, yet outcomes in robotic-assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT) remain poorly characterized. This systematic review and single-arm meta-analysis summarize perioperative and early graft outcomes from published SP-RAKT series. METHODS: Our protocol was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251086071) and followed PRISMA. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were queried on September 1, 2025. Only studies reporting outcomes with SP-RAKT in adult patients were included. Studies with SP robotic nephrectomy were excluded. Data were extracted on patient characteristics, complications, and outcomes. Weighted or simple pooled averages were calculated across studies. Study quality was assessed descriptively using the Joanna Briggs Institute and MINORS criteria. RESULTS: 17 studies published since September 20, 2019 encompassing 278 SP-RAKT procedures were identified. Mean recipient age was 49.3±5.7 years, and BMI 31.3±0.99 kg/m2, with living donors in 69% of cases. Mean operative time was 257.6±103.8 minutes, estimated blood loss 67.1 ml, vascular anastomosis time 53.2 minutes, and hospital stay 2.4 days. Delayed graft function occurred in 5% of patients, and no case required conversion to open surgery reported. Overall postoperative complication rate was 11%. Renal outcomes were favorable, with mean serum creatinine of 2.91 mg/dL at discharge and 1.75 mg/dL at last follow-up. No graft losses reported through 6 and 12 months in cohorts with available follow-up. Recovery-related outcomes included mean postoperative pain score 3.51, opioid consumption 61.2 morphine milligram equivalents, and readmission rate 27% within 90 days. Across studies, outcomes were comparable to conventional or multiport RAKT benchmarks, with reduced incision morbidity and acceptable warm ischemia times. CONCLUSIONS: Early experience with SP-RAKT suggests the approach is feasible and safe, with low rates of delayed graft function and complications. Operative times remain longer in initial cases but improve with surgeon experience. Current evidence is limited by small single-arm series and heterogeneity in reporting; prospective multi-center studies and standardized outcome reporting are needed. | | | --- | | |

title: SINGLE-PORT ROBOTIC AUTOTRANSPLANTATION: A MINIMALLY INVASIVE NOVEL SOLUTION FOR NUTCRACKER SYNDROME
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Hafiz Umair Siddiqui, Dylan Isaacson, Annaliese Ionson, Christina Delvalle, Yi-Chia Lin, Alvin Wee, Venkatesh Krishnamurthi, Mohamed Eltemamy
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Nutcracker syndrome (NCS) can present with left flank pain, pelvic congestion syndrome (PCS) and hematuria. Kidney autotransplantation (KAT) remains uncommon but can be definitive in a subset of patients. KAT is traditionally performed via open surgery with associated morbidity. We present the first institutional series of single-port (SP) robotic KAT for NCS, demonstrating the feasibility and outcomes of this minimally invasive approach. METHODS: Between August 2022 and October 2025, 22 consecutive patients with symptomatic Nutcracker syndrome underwent SP KAT through a peri-umbilical incision. A retrospective review was performed to collect demographic, clinical, operative, and postoperative data. Outcomes were summarized using descriptive statistics and reported as median \[IQR\] or number (%). RESULTS: Median age was 28 (23–34) years; 90% were female, and median BMI was 21.9 (20.5–24.2). Previous abdominal surgery occurred in 55%, and 41% had concomitant May–Thurner syndrome. Preoperative creatinine was 0.86 (0.69–0.96) mg/dL and hemoglobin 12.9 (11.7–13.6) g/dL. Two patients (9%) had prior renal vein transposition and two (9%) had gonadal vein transposition. Median operative time was 6 hr 14 min (IQR: 5 h14 min – 6 h 44 min), vascular anastomosis time 40 (35.5–48.5) minutes, estimated blood loss 62.5 (50–100) mL, and Δ hemoglobin 1.7 (0.72–2.17) g/dL. Most grafts had a single renal artery (74%), with two in 21% and three in 5%; implantation into the opposite iliac fossa occurred in 45%. No intraoperative complications or ICU admissions occurred. Postoperative creatinine was 0.81 (0.70–0.94) mg/dL, and median hospital stay was 3 (2–4) days. Postoperative day-1 pain score was 7 (6–8), and 30-day readmission occurred in three patients (13.6%). At last follow-up, 82% of patients reported complete or improved pain resolution, with stable renal function in all cases. CONCLUSIONS: Single-port robotic kidney autotransplantation is a safe and effective surgical option for Nutcracker syndrome. We report a high rate of pain relief, preserved renal function, and minimal morbidity. This represents a novel tool for treating this vascular disorder. | | | --- | | |

title: ROBOTIC SINGLE-PORT EXTRAPERITONEAL VERSUS MULTI-PORT LIVING DONOR KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Hafiz Umair Siddiqui, Dylan Isaacson, Christina Delvalle, Venkatesh Krishnamurthi, Yi-Chia Lin, Alvin Wee, Mohamed Eltemamy
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Kidney transplantation has evolved from an open approach to minimally invasive techniques with the introduction of multi-port (MP) robotic platforms. The emergence of single-port (SP) allows extraperitoneal graft placement without Trendelenburg positioning. We compared perioperative and early postoperative outcomes in recipients of living donor (LD) SP and MP robotic kidney transplants (RAKT). METHODS: We queried our prospectively maintained robotic kidney transplant database (RoKIT) for LD RAKT performed from October 2019 to October 2025. Baseline, transplant, and post-transplant characteristics were compared. Temporal trends of operative and anastomosis times were plotted to visualize our learning curves. RESULTS: A total of 46 SP and 47 MP RAKT were performed. Our first SP case was performed in 2019 and the first MP case in 2023. Baseline characteristics were similar. In the SP group, operative times (4:21 vs 3:58, hr:min, p=0.01) and anastomosis times (47 vs 36 min, p<0.001) were longer. Warm ischemia time was slightly longer in the MP group (4 vs 3 min, p=0.045). Multiple arteries were more frequent in MP (25.5% vs 0%, p<0.001). Postoperative pain was lower in SP (median 5 vs 7, p=0.005). Other postoperative outcomes were comparable. CONCLUSIONS: Single-port and multi-port robotic-assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT) demonstrated comparable outcomes in living donor recipients. The longer operative times observed with the SP approach likely reflect its adoption earlier in our learning curve rather than procedural limitations. With lower postoperative pain and comparable outcomes, SP appears to be a safe and viable alternative to the conventional multi-port approach.

title: FROM INNOVATION TO EXPERTISE: LEARNING CURVE AND OUTCOMES IN THE LARGEST SERIES OF SINGLE-PORT ROBOTIC KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Hafiz Umair Siddiqui, Dylan Isaacson, Christina Delvalle, Leen Akras, Venkatesh Krishnamurthi, Yi-Chia Lin, Alvin Wee, Mohamed Eltemamy
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Single-port robotic extraperitoneal kidney transplantation (SP-RAKT) is a novel, minimally invasive transplant approach, offering a single incision that enhances cosmesis and potentially accelerates recovery. Yet, data on its learning curve and clinical outcomes remain scarce. In this study, we present the world’s largest single-center experience with SP-RAKT, highlighting the procedural learning curve, perioperative safety, and early clinical outcomes. METHODS: We queried our prospectively maintained transplant database (RoKiT) and retrospectively analyzed the data. CUSUM analysis was used to assess learning curves for operative and anastomosis times. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize perioperative and graft outcomes. RESULTS: From October 2019 to October 2025, 65 SP-RAKT were performed by a single surgeon. Median age was 50.4 years, the median BMI was 31.5 kg/m2, and 40 (61%) were male. 46 (71%) were living-donor recipients. Two cases involved dual artery anastomosis, one was a simultaneous kidney–pancreas, and one was a dual kidney transplant. 28 (43.1%) patients were preemptive. Median operative time was 4 hours and 18 minutes, and anastomosis time was 48 minutes. CUSUM analysis demonstrated proficiency after 19 cases. Eight patients (12%) developed delayed graft function (6 deceased, 2 living), 4 (6%) required ICU admission, and 21 (32%) were readmitted within 30 days. Length of hospital stay was 2 days. Median creatinine improved from 2.58 mg/dL at discharge to 1.47 mg/dL at 3 months. One case was converted to open, and 2 patients developed lymphoceles. No graft loss or patient death was observed. CONCLUSIONS: Our experience demonstrates that SP-RAKT is technically feasible and associated with safe, reproducible outcomes. A learning curve of 19 cases was identified, beyond which operative efficiency plateaued. As the largest series reported to date, this study reinforces the potential for broader implementation of SP-robotic platforms in kidney transplantation. | | | --- | | |

title: PUSHING BOUNDARIES: SINGLE CENTER COMPARISON OF ROBOTIC AND OPEN DUAL KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Hafiz Umair Siddiqui, Dylan Isaacson, Christina Delvalle, Venkatesh Krishnamurthi, Yi-Chia Lin, Mohamed Eltemamy, Alvin Wee
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Dual kidney transplantation (DKT) allows the utilization of marginal donor kidneys, expanding the donor pool and decreasing organ discard. Traditionally performed through an open approach, it remains technically demanding and carries greater morbidity than standard kidney transplantation. Robotic kidney transplantation reduces surgical morbidity and offers a minimally invasive alternative. We present our early institutional experience comparing robotic and open DKT, demonstrating its feasibility and safety. METHODS: A retrospective review was performed of all DKT procedures conducted between January 2024 and July 2025. Donor and recipient demographics, operative details, perioperative outcomes, and graft function at discharge and follow-up were analyzed. A descriptive comparison between robotic and open cases was performed to assess feasibility and early outcomes. RESULTS: Ten DKTs were performed, 5 robotic and 5 open. Baseline characteristics were comparable, including recipient age (73 vs 67 years), BMI (26.8 vs 25.2 kg/m2), and KDPI (81 vs 96). Four robotic cases used a multi-port approach (two Pfannenstiel, two transvaginal insertions) and one single-port with a midline incision. Among robotic cases, two kidneys were transplanted bilaterally and three transplants ipsilateral, while in the open group, four cases were ipsilateral and one bilateral. In the open group, four used an extended right Gibson and one a bilateral anterior rectus sheath incision. Median operative time was longer in robotic cases (5 hr 18 min vs 3 hr 45 min), while blood loss (100 vs 200 ml) and hospital stay (4 vs 5 days) were lower. Median pain scores at day 1 were 6 in robotic vs 7 in open cases. Among open recipients, three required transfusions and one developed a lymphocele. One robotic recipient required readmission due to primary graft failure. CONCLUSIONS: Robotic dual kidney transplantation is a feasible alternative to the open approach, utilizing minimally invasive techniques that avoid extended or bilateral incisions. Ipsilateral graft placement is feasible, preserving the contralateral side for future use or when unsuitable due to calcification, prior grafts, or arterial disease. Our experience across varied incisions and robotic platforms highlights the versatility and expanding potential of robotics in kidney transplantation. | | | --- | | |

title: ROBOT ASSISTED KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION WITH DOUBLE ARTERY ALLOGRAFTS: PERIOPERATIVE AND GRAFT SURVIVAL OUTCOME COMPARISON OF DIFFERENT ANASTOMOTIC TECHNIQUES FROM A TERTIARY CENTRE
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Atanu Kumar Pal, Jeni Mathew, Chethan VN, Arun K, Ramaprasad MK, Sandeep Prabhakaran, VN Unni, Kishore TA
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The early concerns of multiple vessel grafts as a contraindication for robot assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT) have been largely dispelled by many evidences in recent literature. In this article, we described our experience with the different perioperative parameters and outcomes of RAKT with double artery allograft kidney. METHODS: This is a retrospective analysis of the patients who underwent RAKT with double artery reconstruction over six years. The patients with deceased renal transplantation, ABO incompatibilities, more than two arteries, and less than one-year follow-up were excluded. Three techniques were used: end-to-side anastomosis, double anastomosis to external iliac arteries and pantaloons anastomosis. RESULTS: Out of total 80 patients included in the study, end-to-side, trousering, and double anastomosis were done in 45, 11, and 24 patients. The mean age, body-mass-index (BMI), Charlson Comorbidity Index were similar in both groups. The cold ischemia time, arterial anastomosis time, and console time were significantly more in the patients with double anastomosis (32.11 ± 6.97, 35.64 ± 4.50, and 38.17 ± 5.36 minutes; 12.80 ± 4.34, 14.45 ± 3.21, and 19.38 ± 4.77 minutes; 156.09 ± 49.13, 169.91 ± 32.04, and 185.21 ± 57.78 minutes, respectively, p<0.05). The warm ischemia time, setting up time, total surgical time, blood loss, blood transfusion rate, postoperative hemodialysis, hospital stay, pain Score (Visual Analogue Score at postoperative day1,2, and 3), re-exploration, complication as per Clavien Dindo classification were comparable among all the three groups. Graft function in terms of serum creatinine, eGFR (Glomerular filtration Rate) for one, three months and one-year, delayed graft function, graft loss rates were similar (Table). 80 patients with double-arterial-anastomosis were compared with 194 patients who underwent single-arterial-anastomosis during the period. The console time, total surgical time, and arterial anastomosis time were significantly less (p<0.05). However, the other parameters like hospital stay, pain score, re-exploration, complication rate, graft function, graft loss were similar in both groups. CONCLUSIONS: Robot assisted kidney transplantation can be performed safely and effectively in recipients with double renal arteries with good results without increasing complications. | | | --- | | |

title: TRENDS IN ROBOTIC KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION: A SINGLE-CENTER EXPERIENCE OF INCREASING VOLUME AND EXPANDING COMPLEXITY
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Hafiz Umair Siddiqui, Dylan Isaacson, Christina Delvalle, Seema Casey, Venkatesh Krishnamurthi, Yi-Chia Lin, Alvin Wee, Mohamed Eltemamy
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Once considered experimental, robotic kidney transplantation (RAKT) is becoming more widely adopted. We describe the evolution of our RKT program since 2019, from our first case to one of the largest global experiences, highlighting both growth trajectory and expanding case complexity. METHODS: All RAKT performed from October 2019 to October 2025 were retrospectively analyzed. Annual data were categorized as open vs. robotic, and within robotic cases, by single-port (SP) vs. multi-port (MP) platforms. Complex robotic cases included deceased–donor (DDT), multiple renal arteries (MRA), recipient iliac vessel calcification, dual kidney transplant (DKT), or simultaneous kidney–pancreas (SKP) transplant. Temporal trends were visualized using time-series regression and cumulative trend plots to model robotic adoption. RESULTS: Between 2019 and 2025, 209 robotic kidney transplants (RKT) were performed (65 SP, 144 MP), including 115 deceased-donor (55%) cases. The median recipient age was 55.2 years (IQR, 44.6–62.9) and BMI was 31.8 (IQR, 28.1–36.9). The median operative time was 3 hours 52 min (IQR, 198–275) and anastomosis time was 44 minutes (IQR, 35–53). One case (0.4%) was converted to open surgery. The median hospital stay was 3 days (IQR, 2–4), and delayed graft function occurred in 41 patients (21.5%). The annual volume of RAKT increased from a single case in 2019 to 96 cases by October 2025. Progressive expansion in case complexity was observed over time; in 2025, DDT accounted for 52 cases, MRA grafts for 30 cases, and recipients with calcified vessels for 21 cases. Also, 5 DKT (3 in 2024 and 2 in 2025) and 4 SKP transplants (all in 2025) were performed robotically. Institutional transplant activity demonstrated a consistent annual increase, accompanied by a declining trend in open transplant procedures beginning in 2024. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates the evolution of a new robotic kidney transplant program into a high volume, complex practice within six years. Our findings support the feasibility and reproducibility of RAKT even in challenging scenarios.

title: AGE-STRATIFIED LENGTH OF STAY BENEFIT OF ROBOTIC VERSUS OPEN APPROACH IN DECEASED-DONOR KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION: EVIDENCE FROM A EUROPEAN MULTICENTER REGISTRY
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Andre Belarmino, Angelo Territo, Giulio Avesani, Francesco Di Bello, Andrea Gallioli, Josep M. Gaya, Riccardo Campi, Luca Afferi, Alessio Pecoraro, Karel Decaestecker, Mireia Musquera, Begona Etcheverry, Joris Vangeneugden, Milla Ortved, Philip Zeuschner, Alessandro Volpe, Mirza Idu, Burak Kocak, Francesc Vigues, Antonio Alcaraz, Sergio Serni, Alberto Breda
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prolonged hospitalization after kidney transplantation increases the risk of infection, deconditioning, and healthcare costs—particularly in older recipients. Robotic-assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT) may mitigate these risks by reducing wound burden and enhancing early mobilization, yet robotic access remains limited. Identifying which recipients derive the greatest benefit is therefore essential for case selection and resource allocation. This study evaluated whether increasing recipient age modifies the postoperative length-of-stay (LOS) advantage of RAKT compared with open deceased-donor kidney transplantation (DDKT). METHODS: All adult DDKT recipients (2018–2025) from a prospective European registry were analyzed. Living donors and conversions were excluded. LOS (days) was modeled as a function of surgical approach, age, BMI, and metabolic comorbidities. An interaction term tested whether age modified the LOS difference between techniques. Propensity weighting (age, BMI, comorbidity count) estimated confirmatory average treatment effects (ATEs) within age strata. RESULTS: Among 342 deceased-donor recipients, RAKT was associated with shorter hospitalization across all ages, with increasing benefit in older patients. Overall: RAKT reduced mean LOS by 2.2 days (p=0.04). Age effect: Each additional year prolonged LOS by 0.1 days (p=0.02). Interaction: The robotic advantage increased by ~0.25 days per year (p=0.09), yielding a 2–3-day gain per decade. Predicted LOS was similar below age 40 but diverged thereafter, reaching an 8–10-day shorter stay with RAKT by age 70. Propensity-weighted analyses confirmed this gradient (no difference <50 years; ~5 days shorter ≥60 years; (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191324.44573.90.14#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: In deceased-donor kidney transplantation, RAKT shortens hospitalization for all recipients, with a progressively greater advantage in older or comorbid patients. Because extended LOS increases exposure to nosocomial infection and mobility decline, minimizing hospitalization is particularly valuable in this group. Robotic access appears to offset the effect of aging on LOS, supporting its prioritization for elderly or frail recipients most likely to benefit from enhanced recovery and lower inpatient complication risk. Conducted on behalf of the ERUS-RAKT Working Group, European Association of Urology Robotic Urology Section (ERUS).

title: DOES ILIAC VESSEL CALCIFICATION PRECLUDE CANDIDACY FOR ROBOTIC KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION?
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Hafiz Umair Siddiqui, Dylan Isaacson, Ramsey Ugarte, Christina Delvalle, Venkatesh Krishnamurthi, Yi-Chia Lin, Alvin Wee, Mohamed Eltemamy
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Aorto-iliac vascular calcification is increasingly common among kidney transplant candidates and often considered a contraindication to robotic-assisted kidney transplantation (RAKT). Extensive vascular calcification poses technical challenges during recipient vessel dissection and anastomosis, often prolonging operative time and increasing the risk of complications. Data on the feasibility and outcomes of RAKT in this high-risk cohort are limited. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed all robotic deceased donor kidney transplants performed between July 2024 and June 2025. Preoperative recipient CT scans were manually reviewed to assess iliac vessel calcification, which was graded based on morphology and thickness (PMID: 40455172): grade 0=no calcification, grade 1=<1 mm, grade 2=1–2 mm, and grade 3=>3 mm. For this study, we included recipients with grade ≥1 (any measurable calcification). Demographic, intraoperative, and postoperative outcomes were analyzed. RESULTS: Among 205 RAKT recipients, 45 (22%) had CT-defined iliac vessel calcification. Compared with non-calcified recipients, those with calcification were older (64 vs 53.5 years, p<.001), received kidneys with higher Kidney Donor Profile Index scores (67% vs 44%, p=.002), and more frequently received deceased-donor kidneys (78% vs 49%, p<.001). Single-port RAKT was less common in the calcified group (64% vs 84%, p=.03). Median hospital stay was longer (4 vs 3 days, p<.001), and delayed graft function (DGF) occurred more in the calcified group (49% vs 12%, p<.001). In the setting of deceased donor recipients, logistic regression showed that DGF was independently associated with BMI, iliac calcification, and multiple arteries. Anastomosis times were similar between the groups. Rates of ICU admission, postoperative complications, readmission, and graft function at 3 months and 1 year were also comparable. CONCLUSIONS: RAKT in recipients with iliac vessel calcification is feasible and safe in carefully selected patients. Although the calcified group demonstrated higher rates of delayed graft function, perioperative parameters and graft outcomes at 3 months and 1 year were comparable to those of non-calcified recipients. The presence of iliac calcification should not be considered an absolute contraindication to RAKT but rather a factor warranting individualized preoperative evaluation and surgical planning. | | | --- | | |

title: ROBOTIC KIDNEY-PANCREAS TRANSPLANTATION – THE CLEVELAND CLINIC EXPERIENCE WITH IPSILATERAL ALLOGRAFT PLACEMENT AND SINGLE PORT APPROACH
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Dylan Isaacson, Ratib Mahfouz, Wei Kelly Wu, Sami Shoucair, Yasin Obeidat, Christina Delvalle, Hafiz Umair Siddiqui, Itunu Owoyemi, Alvin Wee, Venkatesh Krishnamurthi, Yi-Chia Lin, Mohamed Eltemamy
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Simultaneous kidney/pancreas transplantation (SPK) is the most definitive treatment for Type 1 diabetes with end-stage renal manifestations. Robot-assisted SPK may mitigate the morbidity of open SPK, however it has not yet been widely adopted. Reports of robotic SPK describe surgery with the multiport system and placement of the allografts on the bilateral iliac vessels, rendering a future second transplant more challenging. Here we present outcomes of our robotic SPK recipients. METHODS: Retrospective review of patients who underwent robotic SPK at our institution from 1/2025 – 10/2025. Donor/recipient variables, intraoperative data and postoperative outcomes were collected. RESULTS: Four patients underwent robotic SPK during the study period. Three had surgery using the multiport system, with four 8 mm robotic ports, 12 mm assistant port and Pfannenstiel incision to introduce the allografts. One was transplanted with the single port system, with graft introduction and implantation performed through a 5 cm periumbilical incision. Pancreata were prepared with iliac artery Y-graft anastomoses to the superior mesenteric and splenic arteries similar to the open approach. Our first patient had placement of the kidney on the left and pancreas on the right. The subsequent three had anastomosis of the kidney to the left external iliac vessels, kidney reperfusion, re-clamping distal to the kidney and pancreas implantation while maintaining kidney perfusion. Enzymatic drainage was enteric in all cases with robotic hand-sewn anastomosis of donor duodenum to recipient small bowel. Mean operative time was 5h 57 mins, with mean kidney and pancreas vascular anastomotic times of 30 and 41 minutes. Our first patient was admitted to the ICU intubated and extubated POD1. All four had otherwise unremarkable postoperative courses and were discharged after a median of four hospital days. None had major complications or needed reintervention. At most recent follow-up, all had good allograft function. CONCLUSIONS: Robot-assisted SPK is safe and feasible. We demonstrate excellent outcomes and short hospital length of stay, with operative and anastomotic times comparable to the open approach. We believe this to be the first description of ipsilateral graft placement, saving the contralateral iliac vessels for a future transplant, and the first report of SPK through a single micro-incision using the single-port robot.

title: PREDICTION AND EXPLANATION OF KIDNEY TRANSPLANT OUTCOMES WITH MULTIMODAL ANESTHESIA TIMESERIES DEEP LEARNING
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Rohit Malyala, Annudesh Liyanage, Anna-Lisa T. V. Nguyen, Alex Ng, Erika Escamilla, Christopher Nguan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: An increasing proportion of kidney transplants are sourced from deceased donors. However, deceased donor transplants have a higher risk of delayed graft function (DGF). We hypothesize that the complex interaction between operative parameters such as hemodynamics, fluid strategies, and medication use can impact perfusion to the newly transplanted kidney and influence DGF. Clinicians' limited capacity to analyze these intricate data poses a challenge in identifying subtle factors contributing to DGF, and in choosing optimal management strategies to mitigate these factors. METHODS: We have used time-series focused machine learning strategies to explain and predict DGF with multimodal inputs, incorporating tabular pre-transplant donor and recipient characteristics, with granular intraoperative anesthesia time-series from deceased-donor kidney transplant surgeries (n=424), both donation after cardiac death and neurologically-determined death (DCD and NDD). Two models were constructed: DGFpredict-time, based on a multimodal convolutional neural network, and DGFpredict-explain based on gradient-boosted trees. RESULTS: 121 DGF events were captured in our cohort derived from a single academic medical center (57/276 NDDs, 64/148 DCDs). DGFpredict-time predicts 80.07\\% (CI: 77.4-82.7\\% in 10-fold bootstrap) of DGF events in test splits, resulting in an AUROC of 0.87 (0.85-0.88). For DGFpredict-time, timeseries salience maps identified post-vascular anastomosis BP as the most influential feature of intraoperative management for DGF incidence in DCD kidneys, with normalized salience post anastomosis being 84.0\\% versus 37.8\\% pre-anastomosis (in DCDs). DGFpredict-explain was found to be 74.79\\% (CI 72.2-77.4\\%) accurate for DGF, AUROC 0.71 (0.69-0.72). In SHAP explanatory analyses, pre and post-anastomosis MAP was found to be within the top-5 predictors of DGF incidence. Dependency analysis indicated a MAP of 76.0 mmHg (or below) was identified as an optimal target at which to start pressors, and 37.3 cc/kg cumulative intraoperative crystalloid as an optimum for DGF prevention. Lastly, our gradient-boosted tree models were run in reverse with grid search to determine optimal recommendations for selected patient vignettes, showcasing personalized model recommendations for anesthesia targets, fluids, and pressor use based on donor or recipient preoperative characteristics. CONCLUSIONS: Our explanatory ML models help identify patients at risk of DGF, point to modifiable components of intraoperative management to prevent DGF, and demonstrate new methods to analyze complex timeseries data from the operating room.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE–BASED INTEGRATIVE MODEL FOR PREDICTING KIDNEY GRAFT LOSS: COMPARISON WITH THE ESTIMATED POST-TRANSPLANT SURVIVAL (EPTS) SCORE
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: William Fajardo, Mohammed Al-Toubat, Alejandra Galindo, Joseph Sanchez, Manuel Garzon, Samuel Serrano
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Traditional risk indices such as the Estimated Post-Transplant Survival (EPTS) score rely primarily on pre-transplant recipient characteristics and exclude dynamic post-operative and surgical variables. We developed and validated an artificial intelligence (AI)–based integrative model that incorporates early renal function, immunosuppressive intensity, and surgical parameters to predict kidney graft loss, and compared its performance with an EPTS-based logistic regression model. METHODS: A retrospective cohort of 207 kidney-transplant recipients (2010–2024) from a single tertiary center was analyzed. Variables included recipient age, BMI, diabetes status, donor type, ischemia time, and renal function (eGFR at 1 month and 1 year). Feature engineering added ΔeGFR (1-year – 1-month) and an immunosuppressive regimen-intensity score. A HistGradientBoostingClassifier (XGBoost-like) algorithm was trained using balanced bootstrap sampling (1:1), five-fold cross-validation, and a 70/30 hold-out validation split. Performance was compared against a logistic regression model based on EPTS variables. RESULTS: A total of 207 kidney transplant recipients were analyzed. Baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. Mean age was 49.4 ± 12.6 years, and 58.9 % were male. Diabetes was present in 66.6 % of recipients, and 12 % received a kidney from a living donor. 32 (15.5%) experienced graft loss. Patients with graft loss tended to be older (52.3 ± 11.8 years) and more frequently diabetic (78.1 %) compared to those with functioning grafts (48.8 ± 12.7 years; 64.6 %). The predominant immunosuppressive regimen was tacrolimus + mycophenolate \+ steroids (77.8 %) across all groups. The AI model achieved a cross-validated AUC=0.79 ± 0.04, outperforming the EPTS-based logistic regression model (AUC=0.60). CONCLUSIONS: This integrative AI model combines surgical, functional, and pharmacologic data to predict graft loss more accurately than EPTS alone. The model demonstrates robust discrimination and interpretability, supporting its potential for personalized risk stratification and clinical decision support in kidney transplantation.

title: AI-BASED QUANTIFICATION OF COLLAGEN MICROARCHITECTURE ON 3-MONTH PROTOCOL BIOPSY PREDICTS EARLY RENAL FUNCTION DECLINE AFTER KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Ajay Rajaraman Subramanian, Naoto Tokuyama, Yohei Abe, Anusha Krishnamoorthy, Fan Fan, Tilak Bahadur Pathak, Andrew Janowczyk, Alton B. Farris, Rikiya Taoka, Anant Madabhushi
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Early interstitial fibrosis is a key determinant of long-term graft function after kidney transplantation. However, at 3 months post-transplant, fibrotic changes are often subtle, and conventional histologic scores provide limited prognostic value. We evaluated whether AI-based quantification of collagen microarchitecture on 3-month protocol biopsies could predict early post-transplant renal function decline. METHODS: We analyzed 151 living-donor kidney transplant recipients at Kagawa University. Three-month protocol biopsies stained with Masson trichrome were processed using a computer vision–based pipeline for automated collagen segmentation and extraction of features including collagen area, thickness, fiber density, tortuosity, curvature, branching points, and orientation. Patients were divided into training and validation cohorts (2:1). Cox proportional hazards models were developed in the training cohort with five-fold cross-validation. Multivariate models combined features significant in univariate analysis with additional features improving model performance. The final model was validated in the hold-out validation cohort (N=52). The endpoint was ≥20% eGFR decline within 24 months from baseline. Survival curves were generated using the Kaplan-Meier method with log-rank testing. RESULTS: Among 151 recipients, 57 (37.7%) experienced ≥20% eGFR decline within 2 years. Disordered collagen orientation (HR=2.38, 95% CI 1.37 – 4.13, p<0.05) and increased branching (HR=1.71, 95% CI 1.01 – 2.90, p<0.05) were significantly associated with early eGFR decline. A multivariable Cox model integrating the significant features with fiber curvature (not independently significant) improved predictive performance in the validation cohort (HR=2.49, 95% CI 1.01–6.18, p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: AI-based quantification of collagen microarchitecture on 3-month protocol biopsies predicts early renal function decline after kidney transplantation, providing objective morphologic biomarkers for risk stratification and post-transplant surveillance.

title: MORE THAN KDPI: FAILURE TO ACHIEVE AN ESTIMATED GFR>30 ML/MIN WITHIN THREE MONTHS POST-KIDNEY TRANSPLANT
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Hafiz Umair Siddiqui, Yasin Obeidat, Dylan Isaacson, Christina Delvalle, Ratib Mahfouz, Venkatesh Krishnamurthi, Yi-Chia Lin, Emilio Poggio, Mohamed Eltemamy, Alvin Wee
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Kidney Donor Profile Index (KDPI) is widely used to predict post-transplant graft survival. Although higher values are associated with delayed graft function (DGF), there are significant limitations in predicting early graft function. In our study, we investigated donor and recipient factors associated with the inability to achieve an estimated GFR (eGFR) of 30 ml/min within 3 months post-transplant, and the subsequent impact on one-year outcomes. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 364 adult kidney transplant recipients at a single center. Recipients were divided into two groups: those who achieved an eGFR >30 ml/min (n=325) and those who did not (n=36). Continuous and categorical variables were compared using Student's t-test and chi-square analysis. RESULTS: Failure to achieve an eGFR >30 ml/min by 3 months was associated with increased donor age (51.4 years vs 41.3), increased recipient age (62.6 years vs 58.7 years), donor/recipient gender discrepancy (13.4% vs 7%), female donor, open-offer kidney, longer warm ischemia time (WIT) (30.2 vs 16.5 minutes), higher KDPI (62% vs 50%), donation after circulatory death (DCD), and a non-tacrolimus based regimen, all with statistical significance. This was also associated with a subsequently higher readmission rate (69% vs 40%) and an eGFR persistently <30 ml/min at 1 year. Multivariable regression analysis remained significant for older donor age (OR 0.889, p=0.002) and longer warm ischemia time (OR 0.979, p=0.008) as independent factors with decreased ability to achieve eGFR>30 ml/min by 3 months post-transplant, as well subsequent readmission within 90 days (OR 0.372, p=0.025). There was no statistically significant difference in achieving an eGFR>30 ml/min associated with donor/recipient age discrepancy (>10 years), blood loss, cold ischemia time, or recipient gender, BMI, race, operative time, or dialysis vintage. CONCLUSIONS: Failure to achieve an eGFR>30 ml/min within three months post-transplant can be predictive of diminished graft function at 1-year and is associated with higher readmission rates. Our study supports the relationship of high KDPI with worse early graft function; however, warm ischemia time can also be carefully considered when evaluating deceased donor kidneys in addition to KDPI. | | | --- | | |

title: MAYBE TWO IS BETTER THAN NONE: EVALUATING THE BENEFIT OF EXPANDED CRITERIA DONOR DUAL KIDNEY TRANSPLANTS
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Kaiying Wang, Rachel Z. C. Teo, Tianyuan Gu, Umer Khan, Bee Choo Tai, Anantharaman Vathsala, Ho Yee Tiong
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Marginal kidneys such as expanded criteria donor (ECD) kidneys and kidneys from donors with diabetes have been utilised increasingly to address the shortage of deceased donor kidneys. Although they present a higher risk of allograft failure, they may offer survival benefit over remaining on the waitlist. Dual kidney transplantation (DKT) is one way of utilising marginal ECD kidneys that would otherwise have been discarded. In this study, we present outcomes from our 16-year experience of performing dual kidney transplantation at our centre. Objective: to evaluate if ECD DKT provided any survival benefit to patients compared to remaining on the waitlist. METHODS: A retrospective analysis of dual kidney transplants performed at our centre between 2009-2024 was carried out to evaluate various surgical, graft and patient outcomes. ECD kidneys were considered for DKT if the Remuzzi score was between 4-6. Based on the waitlist in 2009, survival data of patients who received ECD DKT was compared to those of patients who remained waitlisted. Graft and patient outcomes were also specifically compared between diabetic and non-diabetic donor kidneys utilised for dual kidney transplantation. Additionally, target trial emulation was conducted to assess the effect of duration from waitlist to transplant on overall survival, taking into consideration patients' age, gender, and dialysis vintage. RESULTS: 241 patients were included, of which 38 (15.8%) were ECD DKT recipients and 203 (84.2%) received no transplant. 1-year and 5-year graft survival of dual kidney transplants were 87% and 71% respectively. ECD DKT recipients had 29% lower risk of mortality than waitlist patients, although this was not statistically significant (95% CI 0.32-1.64; p=0.38). This effect was persistent when overall survival was adjusted for gender, age and dialysis vintage (HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.38-1.86; p=0.68). On subgroup analysis among ECD DKT recipients, graft survival and overall survival was similar between donors with and without diabetes (HR 1.69; 95% CI 0.38-.86; p=0.46). Finally, on trial emulation, ECD DKT within 6 years of initial waitlisting was found to yield the greatest survival benefit compared to longer wait times. ECD DKT recipients who received a transplant within 6 years of waitlist had a 23% risk reduction in mortality (95% CI 0.11-0.38, p<0.05), and increased restricted mean survival time of 0.84 years (95%9 CI 0.25-1.46, p<0.05) compared to waitlist patients who did not receive a transplant. CONCLUSIONS: ECD DKT at our centre confer survival benefit, particularly with a 23% reduction in mortality if transplant is done within 6 years from date of waitlist. Donor diabetes was not a significant factor on survival post-transplant. This study supports the use of DKT in marginal ECD kidneys, which can also help to address the shortage of deceased donor kidneys.

title: OUTCOMES FOR LOCALIZED RENAL CELL CARCINOMA IN SOLID ORGAN TRANSPLANT RECIPIENTS IS COMPARABLE TO NON-TRANSPLANT RECIPIENTS
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Parth V. Shah, Edwin J. Abel, Joshua D. Mezrich, Andrew Z. Carey, Amy K. Taylor, Adam Bregman, David Al-Adra, David Aufhauser, Kelly M. Collins, Didier Mandelbrot, Glenn O. Allen, Paz Lotan, David F. Jarrard, Kyle A. Richards, Elizabeth L. Koehne, Michael C. Risk, Daniel D. Shapiro
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Solid organ transplant recipients (SOTRs) on chronic immunosuppression who develop localized renal cell carcinoma (RCC) present management challenges due to possible increased oncologic risk and comorbidity. Few data are available for RCC standard therapies (surgery, ablation, or surveillance) to demonstrate whether outcomes are comparable to non-SOTRs. This matched cohort study evaluated outcomes of SOTRs on chronic immunosuppressive therapy with localized RCC to a non-SOTR cohort. METHODS: Patients were identified with tissue diagnosis of localized RCC after transplantation between 2000-2020. Transplant patients were matched 1:2 as able to non-transplant patients based on treatment type (surgery, ablation, or surveillance), age, tumor size, and grade. Clinical variables and survival outcomes were compared. Cox models evaluated if transplant status was associated with survival across different treatment strategies adjusting for confounders. RESULTS: 81 SOTRs with localized RCC were matched to 161 non-SOTRs. Age, tumor size, stage and grade were similar between SOTR and non-SOTR cohorts (p>0.5 for all). Among SOTRs, median age was 57 years and initial treatments included surgery (65%), ablation (23%), and active surveillance (10%). Most common histologies were clear cell (43%) and papillary (41%) RCC. Median tumor size was 3.0 cm, and median follow-up was 68 months. Among all SOTRs, 3-year MFS and OS were 97% and 88%, respectively. In the surgical cohort (SOTR n=53; non-SOTR n=104), SOTRs had greater comorbidity and underwent radical nephrectomy more often (p<0.05 for both). Postsurgical complications were higher (11% vs 3%, P=0.04). Metastasis-free (MFS) and overall survival (OS) were similar to non-SOTR ( Fig A).In the ablation cohort (SOTR n=19; non-SOTR n=43), local recurrence free survival was higher in SOTRs compared to non-SOTRs (log-rank P=0.01). MFS and OS did not differ ( Fig B).In the active surveillance (SOTR n=9; non-SOTR n=14), SOTRs had comparable MFS and OS. Among SOTR, no metastasis occurred over a median follow-up of 89 months. CONCLUSIONS: SOTRs with localized RCC have similar oncologic outcomes compared to non-SOTR regardless of management strategy for localized RCC. Carefully selected SOTRs with localized RCC may be offered percutaneous ablation or active surveillance. Larger, prospective studies are warranted.

title: COMPREHENSIVE MANAGEMENT STRATEGIES AND CLINICAL OUTCOMES IN ABO-INCOMPATIBLE LIVING DONOR KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION: A SINGLE-CENTER COHORT STUDY OF HIGH-TITER (≥1:256) VERSUS LOW-TITER RECIPIENTS
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Yang Yang, Jian Zhang, Zhipeng Wang, Jun Lin, Lei Zhang, Yichen Zhu, Ye Tian
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: ABO-incompatible living donor kidney transplantation (ABOi-LDKT) is a critical pathway to expand the donor pool. However, recipients with high preformed ABO antibody titers (IgM/IgG ≥1:256) present significant perioperative challenges, including difficulties in antibody depletion, and increased risks of bleeding, antibody rebound, rejection, thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), and infection. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the comprehensive management strategy and clinical efficacy of our center's desensitization protocol—the "Friendship Protocol" in ABOi-LDKT recipients. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 29 ABOi-LDKT recipients between 2023 and 2025\. Patients were divided into a high-titer group (≥1:256, n=8) and a low-titer group (1:256, n=21) based on preoperative ABO antibody titers. Baseline characteristics included gender, age, BMI, PRA status, and plasma exchange (PE) strategies. Both groups received the "Friendship Protocol" for intensified desensitization: CD20 inhibitor (200 mg for weight ≥50kg; 100 mg for 50kg) combined with sequential PE (target titer ≤1:16), with conversion to or supplementation with AB plasma if needed. The preoperative immunosuppressive regimen consisted of Tacrolimus + MPA, followed by sequential administration of rATG and a single dose of Complement C5 inhibitor (900 mg) to prevent ABMR and TMA. Primary endpoints included renal function recovery, incidence of rejection, and complications. RESULTS: No significant differences were observed between the high-titer and low-titer groups in the baseline data. The high-titer group required significantly more PE sessions (median 6 vs. 2, P=0.002) and more frequently received combined compatible and AB PE (4 vs. 0 cases, P=0.003). All high-titer recipients achieved the target preoperative titer through flexible PE, including the use of AB plasma in 5 cases. Postoperatively, antibody rebound occurred in 5 cases (71.4%), with a peak titer of 1:128, but none developed clinical symptoms or rejection. Serum creatinine levels decreased significantly in both groups postoperatively, with a 100% dialysis discontinuation rate and no instances of DGF. Four cases of TCMR occurred (no intergroup difference), all of which were reversed after immunosuppressive adjustment. No ABMR or TMA events were recorded. In the high-titer group, 2 patients (28.6%) experienced hemoglobin decline related to bleeding, managed successfully with transfusion and coagulation correction. Two patients (28.6%) developed BK viruria, which subsided after adjustment of immunosuppression. No significant differences were found between groups regarding severe complications (bleeding, infection) or drug adverse events. CONCLUSIONS: The "Friendship Protocol," incorporating individualized antibody depletion (including AB plasma augmentation) and intensified immunosuppression (sequential Rituximab, rATG, and Eculizumab), successfully enabled safe transplantation in high-titer ABOi-LDKT recipients. Despite requiring more intensive plasma exchange, the high-titer group demonstrated comparable renal function recovery, rejection control, and overall safety to the low-titer group. This strategy provides a replicable perioperative management pathway for challenging ABOi-LDKT cases.

title: NOVEL USE OF A BREAST TISSUE EXPANDER IN KIDNEY RETRANSPLANTATION: A CASE REPORT
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Ali Hosseinzadeh, Anastasios Giannou, Christopher Nguan, David Harriman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Kidney transplantation remains the gold standard for treating patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD), offering superior survival and quality of life compared to dialysis. Despite a 5-year allograft survival rate of 77–88%, an increasing number of patients require repeat transplantation, now accounting for approximately 15% of kidney transplants in the United States. Allograft nephrectomy of a previous transplant is often leveraged to create room for a new graft in the original iliac fossa. Total resection of the allograft are major operative procedures which require dissection through dense scar, which then results in further scar deposition in the retransplant site. This case report describes a novel surgical approach using a tissue expander to maintain a potential space and minimize scar formation following kidney allograft nephrectomy. METHODS: A 37-year-old male with diabetes mellitus and ESRD had previously undergone simultaneous kidney-pancreas transplantation. The kidney graft later failed due to chronic rejection. During the left iliac fossa allograft nephrectomy, a tissue expander was placed within the resected fossa to preserve the surgical space and prevent scar formation before the anticipated living donor retransplantation. The expander remained in place for two months. RESULTS: At the time of the planned living donor kidney retransplantation, the tissue expander was removed, and the new graft was successfully implanted into the preserved iliac fossa. The procedure was uncomplicated, and the patient demonstrated immediate graft function postoperatively. Although the preserved space facilitated reoperation, a significant pseudocapsule was noted both around the fossa and enveloping the target recipient vessels, necessitating meticulous dissection. This intraoperative finding had not been previously described in similar contexts. CONCLUSIONS: This case represents the first documented use of a tissue expander to maintain an iliac fossa following kidney allograft nephrectomy prior to retransplantation. The technique effectively preserved surgical space and supported an uncomplicated graft implantation. However, the formation of a pseudocapsule indicates the need for further study to refine this approach and evaluate its long-term outcomes.

title: AN ISOCHORIC SUPERCOOLED PORCINE KIDNEY SUSTAINS LIFE UPON AUTOTRANSPLANTATION AND CONTRALATERAL NEPHRECTOMY
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Natalie R. Meyer, Jean Lee, Mustafa Saeed, Megill Stewart, Ronald Sellers, Brooke Chang, Allen Miller, Bradley Weegman, Jasper Noreiga, Anthony N. Consiglio, Elaheh Rahbar, Matthew J. Powell-Palm, Heiko Yang
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: There is a critical need to enhance preservation strategies for donor organs for transplantation. Isochoric supercooling – a cryoprotectant-free method by which graft temperature is lowered beneath 0 °C without ice formation – has shown promise for organ preservation in ex vivo models of multiple organs. However, it has not been demonstrated in large animal transplantation with long-term functional outcomes. Here we report a case study of a successful autotransplantation of a porcine kidney following multi-day supercooling with sustained long-term in vivo function. METHODS: The right kidney of a juvenile Yorkshire pig was surgically removed and flushed with clinical cold storage solution. The kidney was then placed in an isochoric chamber for controlled multi-day supercooling to -4 °C. On the day of autotransplantation, the kidney was rewarmed and kept on ice before implantation. Vascular anastomoses were performed to the aorta and inferior vena cava. A ureteral stent was placed across the ureterocystostomy. The animal was recovered for 5 days, simulating the clinical practice of providing dialysis to transplant recipients in the first days after transplantation, after which the left kidney was removed through a flank incision. The animal was then recovered and followed until 30 days after autotransplantation. Urine output was assessed semi-quantitatively using absorbent pads underneath the cage. Kidney functional panels were drawn at regular intervals through a jugular central venous catheter. RESULTS: Multi-day supercooling to -4 °C and autotransplantation with delayed contralateral nephrectomy were successfully performed. The animal survived for 30 days after autotransplantation, during which it continued to urinate and exhibited stabilization of blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and potassium. CONCLUSIONS: This case study demonstrates that isochoric supercooling can preserve porcine kidneys for multi-day durations with sustained post-transplant function, supporting its promise as a clinically translatable organ preservation strategy.

title: SILICON (SI)-BASED AGENT SUPPRESSES OXIDATIVE STRESS AND ANTIBODY-MEDIATED REJECTION, PROMOTING LONG-TERM GRAFT SURVIVAL AFTER KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Soichi Matsumura, Masataka Kawamura, Shota Fukae, Shigeaki Nakazawa, Yoichi Kakuta, Norio Nonomura
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR) is a major determinant of long-term graft survival after kidney transplantation. Ischemia–reperfusion injury (IRI) amplifies both innate and adaptive immune responses through the excessive production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), leading to oxidative tissue damage and contributing to the development of ABMR. We focused on molecular hydrogen, which possesses antioxidant properties and can suppress ROS production, and developed a novel orally administered silicon (Si)–based agent that continuously generates molecular hydrogen in the intestinal tract. In this study, we evaluated the efficacy of this Si-based hydrogen-generating agent as a novel therapeutic strategy to reduce oxidative stress and immune activation after kidney transplantation. METHODS: Male Lewis rats received kidney grafts from Fischer-344 (allogeneic) or Lewis (syngeneic) donors (F344→Lewis model). The Si-based agent was administered orally starting one week before transplantation and continued thereafter. Short-term (1 week) and long-term (3 months) models were used to evaluate early immune responses and chronic graft outcomes, respectively. Endpoints included oxidative stress markers, histopathology, immunostaining, graft gene expression, donor-specific antibody (DSA) levels, renal function, and safety. RESULTS: At 1 week, Si treatment significantly reduced serum malondialdehyde (MDA) levels and tended to lower urinary 8-OHdG, indicating attenuation of oxidative stress. CD3+ T-cell and peritubular inflammatory cell infiltration were decreased, and DSA binding to donor B cells was significantly reduced. At 3 months, graft survival improved (62% vs. 31%), accompanied by stable serum creatinine and lower urinary protein in the Si-treated group. Chronic graft injury was alleviated: serum MDA levels decreased, PPAR was upregulated, IL-6 and CCL2 were downregulated, macrophage infiltration was reduced, cg scores improved, and C4d deposition was suppressed. DSA levels remained lower at 3 months. No hepatotoxicity or electrolyte abnormalities were observed, and Si administration showed no adverse interaction with cyclosporine. CONCLUSIONS: The orally administered Si-based hydrogen-generating agent suppressed IRI-associated oxidative stress, attenuated both innate and adaptive immune activation, mitigated ABMR, and improved graft survival and function. Given its established safety profile and convenient oral administration, this approach represents a promising therapeutic strategy to prevent or ameliorate chronic ABMR and improve long-term kidney transplant outcomes.

title: NEUTROPHIL SUPPRESSION IN XENOTRANSPLANTATION USING GENETICALLY MODIFIED SWINE ENDOTHELIAL CELLS IN A NOVEL XENOTRANSPLANTATION MODEL
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Soichi Matsumura, Yoichi Kakuta, Shota Fukae, Masataka Kawamura, Shigeaki Nakazawa, Akira Maeda, Shuji Miyagawa, Norio Nonomura
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Recent clinical attempts of xenogeneic kidney transplantation from genetically engineered pigs to humans have drawn worldwide attention, demonstrating the potential feasibility of pig-to-human organ transplantation. However, early xenograft injury remains a major challenge, mainly driven by innate immune mechanisms such as neutrophil-mediated cytotoxicity. Although existing genetically modified pigs express human CD47 (hCD47), its effect on neutrophils is insufficient. PlexinB2, which suppresses neutrophil activity via SEMA4D, has been suggested to provide superior protective effects. In this study, we evaluated the role of human PlexinB2 (hPlexinB2) in xenotransplantation. METHODS: Human neutrophils were co-cultured with swine endothelial cells (SECs) expressing human CD47 (hCD47), human PlexinB2 (hPlexinB2), or wild type controls. Neutrophil-mediated cytotoxicity, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation were quantified using flow cytometry and WST-8 viability assays. For in vivo analysis, SECs were transplanted subcutaneously into humanized NOG mice (hG-CSF knock-in) reconstituted with human hematopoietic stem cells. Neutrophil infiltration into SEC grafts was assessed by flow cytometry and immunohistochemical staining for human markers, including CD66b and myeloperoxidase. RESULTS: Compared with wild-type SECs, both hCD47- and hPlexinB2-expressing SECs significantly suppressed neutrophil-mediated cytotoxicity (P=0.005 and P=0.002, respectively). Among them, hPlexinB2 induced greater reductions in ROS production (p<0.01) and NET formation (P=0.002). In vivo, SEC grafts were infiltrated by human neutrophils; however, in hPlexinB2 grafts, flow cytometry demonstrated a decreased number of CD66b-positive neutrophils (p<0.001), and myeloperoxidase staining revealed significantly fewer human neutrophils compared with WT (p<0.01). CONCLUSIONS: We established the first in vivo murine xenotransplantation model of human neutrophil responses to pigs. Using this model, we showed that hPlexinB2 markedly suppressed neutrophil activity in xenotransplantation, suggesting that hPlexinB2 expression in pigs may be a strategy to enhance xenograft survival.

title: CREATININE TRAJECTORIES, A DYNAMIC PREDICTOR OF POST KIDNEY TRANSPLANT RECOVERY AND DELAYED GRAFT FUNCTION
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Malik Muhammad Makki, Komal Kumar, Harutyun Davtyan, Jiro Kusakabe, Eduardo Fernandes, Antonio Pinna, Khaled Refaai
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Delayed Graft Function (DGF) remains a widely used outcome metric after kidney transplantation, yet binary definitions fail to capture the dynamic nature of early graft recovery. Creatinine trajectories offer a quantitative alternative, potentially improving prediction and guiding clinical decision-making METHODS: We analyzed 211 kidney transplant recipients (2024-2025) at Cleveland Clinic Weston: living donors (n=22), DBD (n=98), DCD with NRP (n=29), DCD without NRP (n=56). Creatinine slopes were derived via least-squares regression across three recovery phases (Day 1-7, 7-30, 30-90). Multivariable logistic regression assessed DGF predictors, adjusting for KDPI, ischemia time, and BMI. RESULTS: Phase 1 slopes demonstrated the fastest decline for DBD grafts (-0.71), intermediate for DCD-NRP (-0.57), and negligible for DCD non-NRP (+0.02). Phase 2 showed convergence of DCD-NRP with DBD (-0.035), while DCD non-NRP lagged (-0.087). Phase 3 demonstrated stabilization for DBD and DCD-NRP, but persistent variability for DCD non-NRP. Trajectory 2 (Days 7-30) showed the highest predictive performance for DGF (AUC=0.83; Pseudo R2=0.25), exceeding Phase 1 and 3 slopes. Living donors maintained favorable recovery across all phases. CONCLUSIONS: Dynamic creatinine trajectories provide a nuanced, phase-specific assessment of renal recovery and outperform traditional binary DGF definitions. The intermediate recovery phase (Day 7-30) is the most informative predictor, facilitating early risk stratification and clinical interventions. DCD-NRP grafts exhibit recovery kinetics comparable to DBD kidneys, supporting safe expansion of the donor pool. Integrating trajectory-based metrics into transplant practice may improve outcome prediction, reduce unnecessary organ discard, and optimize patient management.

title: USEFULNESS OF SCREENING FOR UROLOGICAL MALIGNANCIES AFTER KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION
session: Transplantation & Vascular Surgery (IP11)
authors: Yoichi Kakuta, Soichi Matsumura, Shota Fukae, Masataka Kawamura, Shigeaki Nakazawa, Norio Nonomura
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Advances in immunosuppressive therapy have prolonged the survival of kidney transplant recipients; however, they have also led to an increased risk of developing de novo malignancies. Under immunosuppression, the incidence of malignancies is higher than in the general population, and oncological outcomes tend to be poorer. The effectiveness of post-transplant cancer screening remains uncertain, largely due to the limited number of available studies. This study aimed to evaluate the usefulness of regular screening for urological malignancies after kidney transplantation, focusing on its impact on early detection, clinical course, and long-term survival. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 2,760 patients who underwent kidney transplantation within the Osaka University Kidney Transplant Group, identifying those with newly diagnosed urological malignancies. Clinical and pathological data at diagnosis, follow-up findings, and details of screening practices were collected. Overall survival (OS) and cancer-specific survival (CSS) were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method. RESULTS: Among the 2,760 recipients, 321 developed malignancies, corresponding to a cumulative incidence of approximately 40% at 40 years post-transplant. There was no significant difference in cumulative cancer incidence between urological malignancies and other malignancies ( Figure a). Urological malignancies included 47 cases of renal cell carcinoma, 20 of prostate cancer, and 15 of urothelial carcinoma. Recipients who underwent regular cancer screening had significantly better OS and CSS compared with those who did not undergo screening. The 20-year survival rates for patients with urological malignancies were 76.6% for renal cell carcinoma, 84.6% for urothelial carcinoma, and 92.9% for prostate cancer. Notably, patients with urological malignancies had better survival than those with other types of malignancies, and their survival did not differ significantly from recipients without malignancies ( Figure b). CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that regular screening for urological malignancies in kidney transplant recipients facilitates earlier diagnosis and contributes to improved long-term survival. Implementing individualized screening strategies tailored to each patient’s risk profile is essential for optimizing clinical outcomes in this population.

title: MORE THAN JUST SIZE: THE SEARCH FOR ACCURATE STONE VOLUME ASSESSMENT
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Seyed Amiryaghoub M. Lavasani, Aymon Ali, Yi Xi Wu, Yezan F. Hadidi, Grant Sajdak, Jacob C. Tsai, Andrei D. Cumpanas, Jaime Altamirano-Villarroel, Seyed Hossein H. Sharifi, Jonathan Badin-Castro, Bruce M. Gao, Zhamshid Okhunov, Sohrab N. Ali, Pengbo Jiang, Roshan M. Patel, Jaime Landman, Duane Baldwin, Ralph V. Clayman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Maximum linear measurement (MLM) and ellipsoid formulae (EF) poorly reflect true stone burden, prompting greater interest in direct volumetric analysis. Recent CT-based tools such as 3D Slicer®, Enterprise Imaging, and Visage Imaging® offer alternative approaches for determining stone volume. Herein for the first time, we compare prolate EF (stones <1.5 cm), scalene EF (stones >1.5 cm), 3D Slicer, Enterprise Imaging, and four Visage Imaging methods: Balloon Contour, 3D Segmentation, Balloon Contour + 3D Segmentation \[Multi\], and 3D Segmentation + Eraser tool against gas pycnometry, the gold standard for volume assessment. METHODS: A total of 64 air-dried human stones (Group 1: <1.5 cm; 0.415–1.288 cm) and 54 fabricated Bego stones (Group 2: >1.5 cm; 1.544–6.131 cm) were CT-scanned in air and within a phantom. Stone volumes were measured using all of the aforementioned methods, each of which was then compared to gas pycnometry using ANOVA with Dunnett’s post hoc analysis, stratified by stone MLM. RESULTS: When measured in air, Group 1 stone volumes measured with Enterprise Imaging and Visage Balloon Contour were not significantly different from gas pycnometry, overestimating volumes by 12% and 7%, respectively. In contrast, for the larger Group 2 stones, only the ellipsoid formulae differed significantly from gas pycnometry, overestimating volumes by 57% ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.01#F1)).When measured in the phantom, Group 1 volumes obtained using Enterprise Imaging, Visage Multi, and Visage Balloon Contour were not significantly different from gas pycnometry, with overestimations of 12%, 9%, and 9%, respectively. For the larger stones in Group 2, ellipsoid formulae overestimated volume by 75%. Notably, Visage 3D Segmentation in the phantom significantly overestimated Group 1 and Group 2 volumes by 189% and 933%, respectively; however, incorporation of the Eraser tool reduced these overestimations to 130% and 27% ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.01#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: Across all stone sizes and imaging conditions, only Enterprise Imaging and Visage with the Balloon Contour tool produced volume measurements equivalent to gas pycnometry.

title: FROM LENGTH TO TRUE BURDEN: MAKING SENSE OF LINEAR STONE MEASUREMENTS
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Benedikt M. Winzer, Carl Ceraolo, Jason Fairbourn, Ashley Li, Yadong Lu, Scott Quarrier, Rajat K. Jain
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Advances in software have enabled broader use of three-dimensional (3D) volumetric measurements in surgical planning for urolithiasis. However, stone volume remains less familiar to clinicians who have developed intuition around traditional linear measurements. We aimed to develop a reference tool that clarifies the relationship between commonly used linear benchmarks and 3D volume measurements. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed preoperative CTs for patients undergoing surgery for urolithiasis between 6/10-12/31/24. Using Spectra IDS7, we measured maximal stone length in any plane and calculated 3D volumes, summing them to obtain total length and volume. Number of stones and staghorn status were recorded. Volume distributions for common linear benchmarks were analyzed (5, 10, 15, 20 mm ± 2.5 mm). Stone length and volume were log-transformed to normalize their distributions and regression models were used to predict log(total stone volume) from log(total stone length), stone number, and binary staghorn status.
