RESULTS: A total of 653 stone procedures were analyzed. Figure 1a illustrates the distribution of 3D stone volumes among cumulative stone lengths at clinically relevant cutoffs. The interquartile range of stone volumes was narrow for small stones (5 mm: 77.7 mm3) but increased substantially and non-linearly as length increased (10 mm: 267.8 mm3; 15 mm: 571.9 mm3; 20 mm: 815.2 mm3), reflecting greater variability in stone number and morphology at higher stone burdens. In regression, stone volume was strongly predicted by stone length and was significantly influenced by stone number and the presence of staghorn morphology ( Figure 1b). Stones with greater length contributed disproportionately more to total volume, staghorn stones were roughly three times larger than non-staghorn stones, and cases with multiple smaller stones tended to have lower total volumes at similar cumulative lengths. CONCLUSIONS: We provide a reference tool for estimating stone volume from cumulative stone length. Variability in 3D volume increases nonlinearly with stone length and is significantly modulated by stone number and complex stone morphology. Incorporating these reference relationships into clinical workflows could improve preoperative planning.

title: MULTIMODAL INTEGRATION OF CT-DERIVED 3D MORPHOLOGY, RADIOMICS, AND DEEP LEARNING FEATURES FOR PREDICTING URINE CULTURE POSITIVITY AND CLINICAL STRATIFICATION IN URETERAL STONE PATIENTS
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Shunsuke Ikuma, Jun Akatsuka, Godai Kaneko, Hikaru Mikami, Kotaro Obayashi, Yuki Endo, Hayato Takeda, Go Kimura, Yukihiro Kondo
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: It is important to assess the risk of urinary tract infection and the need for intervention in patients with ureteral stones based on imaging. Although CT attenuation has been associated with urine culture positivity, it is unclear whether features of the segmented renal pelvis and bladder on CT can predict culture positivity. The aim of this study was to evaluate whether image features from multimodal imaging could predict urine culture positivity and stratify patients into risk groups. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 71 hospitalized patients with ureteral stones and hydronephrosis (2020–2024). Renal pelvis and bladder were manually segmented and morphology, radiomics, and deep learning features were extracted. LASSO regression selected predictors, and risk scores were calculated as weighted sums of coefficients. The ROC curve determined the optimal cut-off for predicting culture positive. Patients were stratified into risk groups by cut off value for clinical comparison. RESULTS: Among 71 patients, 28 had positive urine cultures. Coefficient contribution was 33.9% from morphology, 0.7% from radiomics, and 65.5% from deep learning. The risk score demonstrated high discrimination for culture positivity (AUC 0.986), with an optimal cut-off of 0.489. High-risk groups were older (p<0.001), had higher CRP (p<0.001), longer hospitalization (p<0.001), and more frequent stenting (p=0.036). CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrated that a multimodal risk score integrating CT-derived 3D morphology, radiomics, and deep learning features could predict voided urine culture positivity in patients with ureteral stones. The score enabled stratification into clinically distinct groups that differed in systemic inflammation, length of hospitalization, and need for ureteral stenting, thereby providing prognostic information beyond infection risk alone. This approach offers a non-invasive tool to support early risk assessment and guide personalized management strategies. | | | --- | | |

title: CT-DERIVED SKELETAL MUSCLE MASS AND VISCERAL ADIPOSITY METRICS INFLUENCE 24-HOUR URINE LITHOGENIC PARAMETERS IN STONE-FORMING PATIENTS
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Reza Lahiji, Lorenzo Storino Ramacciotti, Ernest A. Morton, Edouard H. Nicaise, Alexander Abdollahzadeh, Adam Braunschweig, Gregory Steven Palmateer, Benjamin Schmeusser, Maxwell Richardson, Frank Glover, Ethan Kearns, Aaron Lay, Viraj A. Master, Kenneth Ogan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urine composition is influenced by systemic and phenotypic factors, many of which are implicated in nephrolithiasis. While several urine constituents are known to promote or inhibit stone formation, the relationship between body composition and urinary lithogenic profiles remains poorly defined. The aim of this study is to evaluate associations between CT-derived body composition metrics and 24-hour urine parameters in a diverse stone-forming population. METHODS: A retrospective review of 443 stone-forming patients from the Emory Nephrolithiasis Database was conducted. All patients underwent 24-hour urine analysis via LithoLink and CT imaging within 120 days. Skeletal Muscle Index (SMI) and Visceral Adipose Tissue Index (VATI) values were calculated from axial CT images at the L3 vertebral level. Spearman correlations and multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted to analyze associations between body composition quartiles and urine abnormalities. RESULTS: Patients in the highest SMI quartile had significantly greater odds of elevated urinary volume defined as greater than 1.5 liters (OR 2.71, 95%CI 1.38-5.34), oxalate (OR 2.11, 95%CI 1.07-4.16), uric acid (OR 2.60, 95%CI 1.08-6.26), and sodium (OR 2.70, 95%CI 1.35-5.41) levels compared to the lowest quartile (all p<0.05). Patients in the 4th quartile of VATI values had significantly lower odds of urine volume (OR 0.44, 95%CI 0.20-0.98, p<0.05). Increasing age and black race were independently associated with lower odds of select stone-promoting abnormalities. Increasing age was associated with reduced risk of supersaturation of calcium phosphate (OR 0.97, 95%CI 0.95-0.99) and 24-hour uric acid (OR 0.96, 95%CI 0.94-0.98) (all p<0.05). Black race was associated with reduced odds of raised urinary volume (OR 0.44, 95%CI 0.25-0.77) and hypercalciuria (OR 0.50, 95% 0.26-0.96) on 24-hour measurements (all p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: CT-derived body composition metrics are associated with urinary lithogenic profiles in stone-forming patients. These findings support the integration of body composition assessment into routine stone risk evaluation and management.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE DERIVED BODY COMPOSITION IS ASSOCIATED WITH 24-HOUR URINE MARKERS USING ROUTINE CT IMAGING
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Reza Lahiji, William Luke, Dattatraya Patil, Edouard H. Nicaise, Benjamin Schmeusser, Ali Lahiji, Lorenzo Storino Ramacciotti, Rachel Kaufman, Ernest A. Morton, Mohammad Hajiha, Anant Madabhushi, Rakesh Shiradkar, Viraj A. Master, Kenneth Ogan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While 24-hour urine collections remain the gold standard for metabolic risk assessment in stone formers, their utility is limited by inaccuracy and poor completion rates. Body composition determined using routine imaging may offer a practical surrogate, but existing data is limited and segmentation times prolonged. We investigated whether artificial intelligence (AI) based CT segmentations predict skeletal muscle index (SMI. cm2/m2) accurately and whether this correlates with 24-hour urine markers and associated abnormalities. METHODS: Following IRB approval, our nephrolithiasis database was reviewed for patients ≥18 years who underwent 24-hour urine collections between 2010-2022 with pre-collection CT imaging. Patients on alkalinizing agents or inaccurate collections were excluded. SMI was calculated at L3 using human segmentation (ground truth) subsequently used to train a UNet deep learning (DL) model. Correlations between DL-based SMI and urine markers were assessed using Spearman analysis and multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors of lithogenic abnormalities. RESULTS: A total of 195 patients were included (median age 58 years, 44.6% female, 16.4% Black). DL segmentation achieved high concordance with human segmentation (DSC 0.90 ± 0.11) while reducing time-to-segment from 7.5 minutes to <1 second per scan. DL-based SMI correlated with nearly all 24-hour urine parameters. On multivariable analysis, higher SMI independently predicted hyperuricosuria (OR 11.49, 95%CI 2.00-65.89), lower risk of hypocitraturia (OR 0.22, 95%CI 0.07-0.71), and reduced odds of elevated urine pH (OR 0.33, 95%CI 0.12-0.89). CONCLUSIONS: AI-based CT body composition analysis strongly correlates with 24-hour urine abnormalities and may serve as a practical surrogate for metabolic evaluation in stone formers, offering a rapid, cost-effective alternative to urine collections. Further research is warranted to validate this study’s findings. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE DEEP LEARNING COMBINED WITH RADIOMICS IN PREOPERATIVE IMAGING DIAGNOSIS OF MEDULLARY SPONGE KIDNEY STONES
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Yubao Liu, Haifeng Song, Jianxing Li
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Medullary sponge kidney (MSK) is a rare congenital anomaly frequently associated with nephrolithiasis. Accurate preoperative differentiation between MSK stones and non-MSK multiple kidney stones remains challenging, yet it is essential for effective clinical decision-making. This study aims to develop a novel diagnostic model that integrates radiomics and deep learning features to improve the differentiation of MSK stones using CT imaging. METHODS: This single-center, retrospective study included patients who underwent surgical treatment for multiple kidney stones at Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital between 2022 and 2024\. All MSK and non-MSK cases were confirmed via endoscopic surgery. Radiomics features were extracted from manually delineated regions of interest (ROI) on nephrographic-phase CT images, while deep learning features were derived from a ResNet101-based model. Three diagnostic signatures—Radiomics (Rad), Deep Transfer Learning (DTL), and Deep Learning Radiomics (DLR)—were developed. A Combined model was constructed by integrating clinical variables with DLR features to further enhance diagnostic accuracy. Model performance was evaluated using AUC, calibration curves, Net Reclassification Index (NRI), and Integrated Discrimination Improvement (IDI) analyses. Additionally, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) visualization was employed to identify imaging regions critical to classification, improving interpretability. RESULTS: A total of 73 patients with multiple kidney stones were analyzed, comprising 34 MSK cases and 39 non-MSK cases, encompassing 110 kidneys in total. The DLR signature demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy, with AUCs of 0.96 in both the training and test cohorts. The Combined model further enhanced diagnostic performance, achieving AUCs of 0.98 in the training cohort and 0.95 in the test cohort. Calibration curves indicated strong agreement between predicted probabilities and observed outcomes. Furthermore, NRI and IDI analyses highlighted the superior predictive power of both the DLR and Combined models compared to other approaches. CONCLUSIONS: This study introduces an innovative approach for MSK stone diagnosis by integrating radiomics and deep learning features. The proposed model offers high diagnostic accuracy and promising clinical utility

title: NEPHROCALCINOSIS – A RADIOLOGICAL FINDING WORTHY OF GENETIC TESTING
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Wei-Jen Chen, Feres Camargo Maluf, Anne Roberts Crisler, John Corbin Norton, Vicente Elorrieta, Hannah Jarvis, Ethan Wan, John Thomas King, CH Wilfred Wu, Kazumi Taguchi, Thomas Chi, Joseph Crivelli, Kyle Wood
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Although nephrocalcinosis (NC) is traditionally considered an acquired condition, recent evidence suggests that monogenic causes account for a substantial proportion of cases. Despite that, there is poor evidence on the true impact of genetic mutations in NC prevalence and phenotype. This study aimed to analyze the results of genetic testing in patients with NC to understand how the testing may influence our comprehension of this clinical presentation. METHODS: NC patients were selected from our kidney stone disease (KSD) genetics database at a tertiary academic institution between May 2019 and May 2025. The genetic testing was done through Invitae® or PreventionGenetics® panels. NC diagnosis was made according to CT scan findings. Mild NC was defined as increased pyramidal density, while severe NC was defined as pyramids calcification. Demographic and laboratory parameters were also collected. Statistical analysis was performed via t-test and Chi-Square testing as appropriate. RESULTS: Out of 360 KSD patients with imaging data, NC was identified in 50 (13.9%) patients, out of which 29 (58%) had genetic mutations. The prevalence of NC was higher among patients with genetic abnormalities relative to those with negative tests (19.4% vs. 10%, p=0.01). NC patients were further categorized into mild (n=25) or severe (n=25) groups. There was no association between CKD and NC severity (p=0.31), although 5 out of the 6 patients with CKD stages 3b or higher were in the severe group. The rate of pathologic mutations was higher in the NC severe group, although marginally significant (32% vs. 12%, p=0.09). In the severe NC group, the most common mutated genes were SLC4A1 (n=5), CYP24A1 (n=3), SLC12A1 (n=3), while in the mild group were SLC26A1, ATP7B, and SLC22A12 with 2 mutations each ( Table 1, (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.07#T1)). CONCLUSIONS: Genetic testing demonstrates a high diagnostic yield in NC patients and improves our understanding of the NC phenotype. Distinct gene mutations were observed in patients with different severity of NC, suggesting that specific genetic mutations may lead to varying disease severity.

title: USING NON-DESTRUCTIVE 3D MICRO-CT IMAGING TO PREDICT RELATIVE CALCIUM OXALATE AND URIC ACID COMPOSITIONS IN KIDNEY STONES
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Abbas Hammoud, Gavin Hughes, Jonguk Lee, Rachel Wong, Mohamad Baker Berjaoui, Nikhile Mookerji, Toufic Safi, Brian Carrillo, Monica Farcas
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urologists try to predict kidney stone composition using indicators like Hounsfield units and urine pH. Definitive analysis relies on Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), a destructive technique that requires stone pulverization. However, the 3D spatial distribution of different materials may be relevant to the management of certain mixed composition stones. One example is a core of calcium oxalate (CaO) encased in a shell of uric acid (UA). Such information is completely lost in FTIR. In contrast, volumetric micro-CT (mCT) is a non-destructive modality with sufficient resolution to enable the separation of different stone materials, making it a promising tool for 3D, non-destructive compositional analysis of stones. Our study aimed to evaluate the ability of mCT to predict CaO:UA ratios in PCNL-derived stones and to validate predictions against FTIR analysis. METHODS: Kidney stone fragments were retrieved from 29 patients who underwent PCNL at St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto. A representative fraction of each stone was sent for FTIR, and the rest was scanned with mCT. On FTIR, 19/29 patients had pure CaO, 6/29 had pure UA, and 4/29 had both CaO/UA. Stones from 2 patients with pure CaO and UA (on both FTIR and mCT) were used for calibration. Pure CaO/UA intensity distributions were plotted and analyzed. Fisher's d' metric was used to assess histogram separability, and a ROC analysis was performed to determine the optimal intensity threshold for material classification. The threshold was then used to classify voxels in the remaining (test) stones as CaO or UA. Each material's relative composition was computed as the ratio of its voxel count to the total count. mCT-derived compositions of CaO and UA were compared to FTIR for each patient, and a visual inspection of incorrectly classified voxels was performed to investigate errors. RESULTS: Calibration histograms for CaO and UA demonstrated excellent separability, with Fisher's d'=4.2. ROC analysis yielded an intensity threshold with high discriminatory power (AUC=99%). The threshold achieved a 100% accuracy on test stones that were pure CaO on FTIR (n=18). When applied to test stones that were pure UA on FTIR (n=5), the threshold resulted in a mean error of 11±13% (i. e. on average, 11% of voxels in each pure UA stone were classified as CaO). On the mixed 4 mixed stones, the mean error was 24±22%. Visual inspection revealed that our classification separated CaO and UA well in all mixed test stones. This suggests that errors can be attributed to FTIR and mCT analyzing different fragments from each patient. CONCLUSIONS: Our study suggests that mCT can nondestructively compete with FTIR in kidney stone composition analysis.

title: VALIDATION OF THE DIMINISHED NEPHROGRAM AS AN INDICATOR OF RENAL OBSTRUCTION IN PATIENTS WITH ACUTE URETERAL STONES
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Satomi Kiriakedis, Resa Magill, Walton O'Connor, Jackson Schmidt, Nicholas Chakiryan, Ian Metzler, Marshall Strother
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The quantified diminished nephrogram has shown promise in distinguishing clinically significant obstruction from benign hydronephrosis without obstruction. We sought to validate the diminished nephrogram as an objective imaging marker of upper urinary tract obstruction by characterizing it in patients presenting with acutely obstructing ureteral calculi. METHODS: We reviewed records of patients who presented to our institution’s emergency department between January 2020 and July 2023 with an ICD-10 diagnosis indicative of nephrolithiasis and who underwent contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis. Diminished nephrogram was quantified separately in the renal cortex and medulla as the difference in renal attenuation (DRA) between the obstructed and unobstructed kidneys. Hydronephrosis was assessed using anterior-posterior renal pelvis diameter (APRPD) and maximal ureteral diameter. RESULTS: A total of 281 patients met inclusion criteria: 206 with obstructing ureteral stones (study group) and 75 with non-obstructing renal stones (control group). Differences in attenuation between kidneys in patients with obstructing stones were significantly greater than differences in patients with non-obstructing stones (cortical differences: -7 vs 1 HU p<0.001, medullary differences: -47 vs 1 HU p<0.0001). The previously reported very high specificity and modest sensitivity of a difference of -15 HU for identifying obstructed kidneys was confirmed in this cohort (Medullary: Specificity 97%, Sensitivity 75%; Cortical: Specificity 100%, Sensitivity 25%). CONCLUSIONS: We confirmed that a medullary DRA of 15 HU on contrast-enhanced CT as a highly specific indicator of renal obstruction. The diminished nephrogram is a reliable, objective marker of obstructive uropathy and may be useful in the evaluation of suspected ureteral obstruction. | | | --- | | |

title: VERY-LOW-DOSE CT WITH AUTOMATED ASSESSMENT: AN EX VIVO STUDY QUANTIFYING RESIDUAL SMALL STONES
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Naoto Tanaka, Akash Chitrakar, Satoshi Kitamura, Daiki Katsura, Fukashi Yamamichi, Yasuhiro Kaku, Yosuke Fukiishi, Masaichiro Fujita, Takaaki Inoue
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: We have reported CT characteristics that distinguish residual tiny fragments from dust on standard-dose CT (SDCT) (World Journal of Urology, 2025), also with 1 mSv low-dose CT (LDCT). Although radiation exposure is a major concern, postoperative CT is increasingly used as it can accurately detect and quantify very small residual stones after laser lithotripsy. Urinary stones exhibit inherently high contrast relative to the surrounding soft tissues, suggesting that radiation dose can be further reduced without compromising clinically meaningful information. To comply with the ALARA (as low as reasonably achievable) principle, this study aims to evaluate an even lower-dose protocol (effective dose ~0.2 mSv), hereafter referred to as very-low-dose CT (VLDCT), for accurately evaluating small-sized stones. METHODS: Calcium oxalate stone were sieved into three categories: small fragments (2.00-2.36 mm), tiny fragments (1.00-1.40 mm) or dust (< 250 µm). A uniform 0.25 g sample from each category was implanted into ex vivo porcine kidneys (n=24). CT images were acquired at three dose settings equivalent to SDCT, LDCT, and VLDCT (tube current: 250/50/10 mA, respectively; tube voltage: 120 kVp). Volumetric and attenuation values (maximum, mean and standard deviation \[SD\]) were calculated automatically using software. Intragroup comparison was performed. RESULTS: For dust, VLDCT produced volumetric and attenuation values that did not differ significantly from SDCT or LDCT. For tiny fragments, VLDCT slightly overestimated the volume compared with SDCT or LDCT (p<0.05), whereas all types of attenuation metrics remained comparable. For small fragments, VLDCT showed higher measured volume and mildly lower mean attenuation values (p<0.05), however, maximum and SD values were similar. CONCLUSIONS: VLDCT approaches the diagnostic performance of SDCT or LDCT for assessing residual small stones. However, as stone size increases, VLDCT tends to overestimate volume and to yield lower mean CT values. These findings suggest that effective postoperative surveillance can be achieved at radiation doses far below 1 mSv when using automated assessment.

title: GLP-1 RECEPTOR AGONISTS REDUCE KIDNEY STONE EVENTS IN OBESE PATIENTS: EVIDENCE FROM A REAL-WORLD COHORT
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Thomas Syphan, Quichen Li, Elsayed Desouky, Adam Cohen, Juan Calle, Sri Sivalingam
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1A) has surged in recent years. Originally intended for blood sugar control, they have been increasingly utilized for weight loss. The implications of this on urological health is poorly researched. There is an association between obesity and nephrolithiasis, and recent evidence suggests changes in urine chemistry (e. g. decreased urinary oxalate) associated with GLP-1A use may impact stone recurrence. We queried a real-world population dataset to assess the impact of GLP-1A on stone formation in nondiabetic obese patients. METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, we included nondiabetic adults >18 years old in the TriNetX US Collaborative Research Network (~ 130 million patients) diagnosed as obese/overweight within the last 20 years. Patients prescribed GLP-1A were identified. The primary outcome was the subsequent rate of stone events among patients with a history of nephrolithiasis, comparing those treated with GLP-1A versus non-users. Secondary analysis compared stone event rates in those without a history of stone disease. One-to-one propensity matching for demographics, comorbidities, insulin use, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors was performed to standardize cohorts. RESULTS: Among non-diabetic, obese patients with a history of nephrolithiasis, GLP-1A use was associated with significantly lower rates of stone events compared with non-users (27.1% vs 43.1%, p<0.001); This association remained after propensity matching (27.2% vs 30.8%, p<0.001). In patients without a prior history of nephrolithiasis, GLP-1A use was likewise associated with lower rates of new stone formation (0.59% vs 1.4%, respectively, p<0.001); persisting after propensity matching (0.60 vs 0.80%, p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In non-diabetic, obese patients, GLP-1A therapy was associated with a significantly lower incidence of kidney stone events, independent of prior stone history. While a definitive lithoprotective mechanism cannot be confirmed in the current study, these findings suggest that GLP-1A use may reduce the risk of nephrolithiasis. Given the widespread adoption of GLP-1A agents for weight management, further research is warranted to elucidate the biological and metabolic factors underlying this association. | | | --- | | |

title: DISTINCT URINARY MICROBIAL PROFILES IN CALCIUM OXALATE UROLITHIASIS: A 16S RRNA-BASED COMPARATIVE STUDY
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Won Ku Hwang, Tae Hyun Lee, Hyo Jong Kim, Seon Beom Jo, Sun Tae Ahn, Jong Wook Kim, Mi Mi Oh, Hong Seok Park, Du Geon Moon
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While urinary tract infections are well-established contributors to struvite stones, the role of the urinary microbiome in non-infectious stones such as calcium oxalate (CaOx) remains poorly defined. This study aimed to characterize the urinary microbiome in CaOx stone-forming patients using 16S rRNA sequencing and to compare it with that of healthy individuals. METHODS: Urine samples were collected prior to surgical intervention from 39 patients with confirmed CaOx urolithiasis and 37 age-matched healthy controls. Microbial DNA was extracted and analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Alpha diversity (Chao1, Shannon, Simpson, OTUs) and beta diversity (PCoA) were assessed. Differential taxonomic abundance was evaluated at the genus level. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Korea University Hospital. RESULTS: CaOx patients exhibited significantly increased richness (Chao1 and OTU indices), but significantly reduced diversity and evenness (Shannon and Simpson indices), suggesting microbial overgrowth with reduced ecological balance. Beta diversity analysis revealed distinct microbial clustering between the two groups. Uniquely, CaOx patients had a significant enrichment of environmental and biofilm-associated genera such as Ralstonia, Pelomonas, Sphingomonas, and Paracoccus, which are not commonly reported in previous stone microbiome studies ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.12#F1)). In contrast, beneficial genera with anti-inflammatory or barrier-protective roles—including Faecalibacterium, Bacteroides, and Bifidobacterium—were significantly depleted ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.12#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies a dysbiotic urinary microbiome profile in CaOx stone patients prior to treatment. Unlike infection-related stones, the CaOx-associated microbiome is characterized by non-traditional, biofilm-capable genera and a loss of protective commensals. These findings suggest that even in non-infectious stones, the urinary microbiome may play a mechanistic role, potentially offering new diagnostic and therapeutic targets.

title: DEVELOPMENT AND VALIDATION OF A PREDICTIVE MODEL FOR KIDNEY STONE RECURRENCE: INTEGRATING GUT MULTI-OMICS AND CLINICAL PROFILES
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Kai Dang, Teng Cui, Yang Yang, Xiangyu Wang, Qinxin Zhao, Yongan Zhou, Jinhua Liu, Xiao Jing
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Kidney stone recurrence remains a pervasive clinical challenge, yet prognostic tools leveraging integrated multi-omics approaches are still lacking. This study aimed to develop and validate an integrated model predicting kidney stone recurrence by combining gut multi-omics and clinical features. METHODS: We conducted a prospective study including patients undergoing surgical treatment for kidney stones at Beijing Friendship Hospital between July 2022 and April 2024. A comprehensive analytical approach was employed, combining 16S rDNA sequencing and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) of fecal samples with detailed clinical profiling. Variable selection was performed using univariate and multivariate logistic regression, followed by development of a clinically applicable nomogram. Model performance was rigorously assessed through receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis and calibration curves, with all statistical analyses executed in R software version 4.2.2 (release date: 31 October 2022). RESULTS: Among 203 enrolled patients, 100 (49.26%) experienced stone recurrence during follow-up. Gut microbiome analysis revealed significantly reduced alpha diversity in recurrent cases (Kruskal-Wallis test, p<0.05). LEfSe analysis identified distinct microbial signatures characterized by enriched _Proteobacteria_ and depleted _Firmicutes_ (LDA > 2.0, p<0.05). Multivariate analysis established Proteobacteria (OR=0.003, p=0.030) and Firmicutes (OR=36.003, p=0.025) as independent predictors of recurrence. The resulting nomogram demonstrated strong predictive performance, with AUCs of 0.883 (training) and 0.817 (validation). Calibration curves showed excellent agreement between predicted and observed outcomes (Hosmer-Lemeshow test: p=0.968 training, p=0.672 validation). CONCLUSIONS: _Firmicutes_ and _Proteobacteria_ serve as independent risk and protective factors for kidney stone recurrence. We developed and validated a novel predictive model that integrates gut multi-omics signatures with clinical parameters to accurately stratify recurrence risk in kidney stone patients.

title: GUT MICROBIOME AND METABOLOME SIGNATURES IN RENAL STONE RECURRENCE: A MULTI-OMICS STUDY
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Teng Cui, Yang Yang, Xiangyu Wang, Kai Dang, Yongan Zhou, Jinhua Liu, Jing Xiao
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This study explores the differential characteristics between single episode kidney stone patients and recurrent kidney stone patients from the perspective of differences in gut microbiota structure and metabolites, and identifies microbial markers that predict the occurrence and recurrence of kidney stones. METHODS: This study collected fecal samples from patients with recurrent stones (n=37), patients with initial stones (n=38), and healthy controls (n=39) for 16S rDNA sequencing, untargeted metabolomics sequencing and metagenomic sequencing to obtain differential microbial communities and metabolites, and analyzed their correlation. RESULTS: Compared to incident cases, recurrent stone patients exhibited further reduced gut microbial richness and diversity, with enrichment of Enterobacterales, Proteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, Enterobacteriaceae, Escherichia-Shigella, and Bacilli. In the recurrent kidney stone group, 27 metabolites were upregulated and 164 downregulated, primarily enriched in purine metabolism, phenylalanine/tyrosine/tryptophan biosynthesis, and caffeine metabolism pathways. We identified 10 metabolites as recurrence biomarkers and found significant correlations between Escherichia-Shigella and Asn-Tyr, Leu-Ala-Ile, Tyrosyl-Alanine, or 3'-hydroxyhexobarbital. Additionally, gender-specific gut microbiota signatures were observed. Oxalate decarboxylase and short-chain fatty acid-related enzymes decreased during stone formation but rebounded with recurrence. Caffeine and its metabolites were significantly downregulated in recurrent patients, supporting their potential role in inhibiting stone formation and recurrence. CONCLUSIONS: Recurrent kidney stone patients exhibit reduced gut microbiota diversity, evenness, and overall gut metabolism. We identified 10 biomarkers distinguishing initial from recurrent cases, and propose that caffeine metabolism and aromatic amino acid metabolism influence stone recurrence—potentially serving as clinical biomarkers for recurrence.

title: OPTIMAL PREOPERATIVE CULTURE TIMING: WITHIN 14-DAYS ASSOCIATED WITH REDUCED EARLY SEPSIS RISK IN UROLITHIASIS SURGERY
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Calvin C. Zhao, Audrey Lin, Elijah R. Sommer, Daniel G. Wong, Timothy C. Chang, Ryan R. Sun
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Despite positive cultures being linked to increased sepsis risk, the optimal latency between urine culture and surgery for urolithiasis remains unclear. We evaluated whether the timing of urine culture is associated with early sepsis, defined as ≤24 hours after surgery. METHODS: We performed a retrospective analysis of 4639 patients from a single institutional database who underwent ureteroscopy or percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) for urolithiasis between 2000-2025. We excluded patients who received IV antibiotics within 1 week before surgery and those without a urine culture 45 days before surgery. Comorbidity data was extracted from ICD codes and stone size was extracted from preoperative radiology reports using a HIPAA compliant large language model. Outliers were manually reviewed. We conducted four separate binary logistic regression and chi-squared analyses, stratifying patients by preoperative urine culture submission timing using cutoffs of ≤7 vs. >7 days, ≤14 vs. >14 days, ≤ 21 vs. >21 days, and ≤28 vs. >28 days prior to surgery. RESULTS: There were 2845 patients who met inclusion criteria of which 101 patients (3.6%) experienced sepsis within 30 days postoperatively and 31 (1.1%) experienced sepsis within 24 hours postoperatively. Only the 14-day cutoff showed a statistically significant association with early postoperative sepsis, conferring a protective effect. This remained consistent across subgroup analyses for stone-size, ureteroscopy procedures, UTI history and Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI). Multivariate and propensity score analysis showed similar protective effects when adjusting for demographics, CCI, prior urologic history, preoperative culture results, and procedure characteristics (adjusted OR=0.18-0.53 across models). There was additionally a non-significant trend towards increased likelihood of sepsis and longer culture-to-surgery latency, with the exclusion of the 7 day cutoff group. CONCLUSIONS: Lower rates of early sepsis was associated with obtaining cultures within 14 days prior to surgery. This effect was robust on subgroup, multivariate and propensity score analyses and offers evidence for optimal preoperative culture submission timing.

title: A NOVEL NOMOGRAM WITH AN EXTERNAL VALIDATION TO STRATIFY RISK OF SEPSIS IN PATIENTS UNDERGOING URETERAL STENT PLACEMENT FOR OBSTRUCTING STONES AND PRESUMED URINARY TRACT INFECTION
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Michal Segall, Juliana Villanueva Congote, David E. Hinojosa-Gonzalez, Christina S. Kottooran, Jason J. Lee, Jay Rollins, Alan J. Yaghoubian, Nikil Uppaluri, Dima Raskolnikov, Alexander Small, Brian H. Eisner
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Patients with obstructing ureteral stones and concomitant infection are at risk of developing urosepsis, even if adequately treated with emergent decompression. This study aimed to develop and externally validate a nomogram for predicting the risk of urosepsis after ureteral stent placement in this population. METHODS: A retrospective chart review was conducted on 187 patients from two centers (2016–2020) with obstructing ureteral stones, suspected UTI, and urgent stent placement. Septic shock was defined as qSOFA positivity plus vasopressor need >1 hour post-stenting. A training model was generated using multiple logistic regression based on previously identified risk factors. The model utilized a 76/24 partition, where age, purulent urine, UTI history, WBC, and lactate levels on presentation, along with a qSOFA score, were used to generate a nomogram. A validation of the nomogram was performed in a third center (2018–2023). RESULTS: In the nomogram cohort, 18 (9.6%) patients developed septic shock. The risk factors had the following point accrual potential: age (0-100), purulent urine (0,45), UTI history (0,35), WBC (0-50), lactate (0-100), qSOFA (0,50), with the total score ranging from 0-350. The lowest point accrual is 100 points, which correlates to an estimated risk of 10%. In the external validation cohort, 22 (9.7%) patients developed septic shock, with a receiver operating characteristic analysis revealing an area under the curve of 90.5% (p=0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Our nomogram offers a potentially useful clinical tool for predicting septic shock and guiding hospital resource allocation. Its strong performance suggests excellent generalizability. A prospective study is needed to determine whether the use of a nomogram may help identify patients most likely to benefit from ICU admission.

title: STONE TREATMENT FOR PATIENTS WITH RECURRENT UTIS AND CONCURRENT NON-OBSTRUCTING KIDNEY STONES: DOES IT MATTER?
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Amber S. Herbert, Matthew Kim, Calvin Z. Zhao, Daniel G. Wong, John T. Leppert, Simon Conti, Joseph C. Liao, Timothy C. Chang, Ryan R. Sun
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Recurrent urinary tract infections (rUTIs) have a profound impact on the healthcare system, accounting for nearly 7 million medical visits per year and $3.5 billion in medical spending. Patients with coexisting rUTIs and kidney stone disease (KSD) may benefit from definitive stone treatment, although the cure rate is not well-established. Our objectives were to assess and predict treatment response to stone clearance in patients with concurrent rUTIs and asymptomatic kidney stones. METHODS: Between 2019 to 2023, patients with rUTIs (defined as ≥3 culture proven UTIs in 12 months) and KSD who underwent surgical stone removal at a single tertiary center from were identified. Patient demographics, urine cultures, stone composition, stone and infection-free rates during a 12-month follow up period were reviewed. RESULTS: 112 patients met inclusion criteria with a mean age of 57 ± 16 years. The mean stone size was 12 ± 10 mm. Stone composition consisted of calcium oxalate monohydrate (45%), calcium oxalate dihydrate (27%), calcium phosphate (54%), struvite (21%), and uric acid (6%). During the one-year follow up period, 101 patients (91%) were free from rUTIs, 73 of which (61%) had no symptomatic UTI recurrence. Initial stone burden ≤ 5 mm, pre-op culture pattern inconsistent with bacterial persistence, and presence of Enterococcus or multiple organisms were less likely to experience complete resolution of rUTIs (p<0.05) ( Table 1). The presence of residual stones and multiple organisms on urine culture were independently predictive of unresolved recurrent UTI during follow up. CONCLUSIONS: Treatment of asymptomatic non-obstructive kidney stones in patients with rUTIs leads to significant reduction in symptomatic UTIs, with 91% of patients free from recurrent UTIs, 61% of which were completely infection-free at a one-year follow-up. Those with initial stone burden <5 mm, presence of residual stones, Enterococcus, and multi-organism preoperative urine cultures were less likely to experience cure after definitive stone surgery. These factors could aid in the counseling of patients with rUTIs being considered for stone surgeries with the primary goal of UTI prevention. | | | --- | | |

title: FROM 28 TO 6: EXTERNAL VALIDATION OF THE WISQOL SHORT FORM IN A LARGE TERTIARY STONE COHORT
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Yadong Lu, David Song, Carl Ceraolo, Zijing Cheng, Kristina Penniston, Rajat Jain, Scott Quarrier
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Wisconsin Stone Quality of Life questionnaire (WISQOL) is the first validated stone-specific health-related quality of life (HRQOL) instrument. A short form (WISQOL-SF, 6 items) was previously developed and internally validated, but external validation has not been performed. We aimed to externally validate the WISQOL-SF against the full 28-item WISQOL full form (FF) in a large real-world stone patient cohort. METHODS: We retrospectively identified 2,199 patients completing WISQOL-FF for the first time at the University of Rochester Medical Center from February 2020 to November 2023. All patients with suspected urolithiasis in our clinic were offered WISQOL at every clinic encounter. In addition to the 28 items in WISQOL, information about patients’ current stone status, symptoms, and recent ER and hospital encounters are gathered simultaneously. Standardized scores (0–100) were calculated separately for both WISQOL-FF and WISQOL-SF. Comparative analyses included paired t-tests, two one-sided tests (TOST) for equivalence (±3 points), Cronbach’s α for reliability, Pearson/Spearman correlations, subgroup discriminant validity (stone status, symptoms, ER visits, recent trauma, hospitalization, gender, age), and multivariable logistic regression (high vs low score by median split). RESULTS: Patients were 49.3% female with a mean age of 58.2 ± 15.8 years. The mean WISQOL-SF score was 77.9 vs 76.2 for the WISQOL-FF (mean diff +1.8, 95% CI 1.4–2.2, p<0.001). Despite statistical difference, equivalence testing confirmed scores were interchangeable within ±3 points. Internal consistency was high (Cronbach’s α: FF=0.965, SF=0.880). Agreement was excellent (Pearson r=0.94, Spearman ρ=0.90, ICC=0.94). Both WISQOL-FF and WISQOL-SF discriminated expected subgroups: lower HRQOL in patients with stones and/or symptoms, recent ER visits, trauma, and hospitalization, and higher HRQOL in men and older patients (all p<0.01). Multivariable regression demonstrated consistent independent predictors across WISQOL-FF and WISQOL-SF. CONCLUSIONS: The WISQOL-SF demonstrates equivalent psychometric performance to the full form in a large cross sectional external validation cohort. By reducing completion time from 5–6 minutes to ~1 minutes, the WISQOL-SF offers a practical, patient-friendly instrument for routine clinical and research use in stone disease. | | | --- | | |

title: LONGITUDINAL VALIDATION OF THE WISQOL-SHORT FORM: EQUIVALENT RESPONSIVENESS TO THE FULL INSTRUMENT IN A HIGH-VOLUME STONE CENTER
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Yadong Lu, Zijing Cheng, Soumya Konar, Carl Ceraolo, Kristina Penniston, Rajat Jain, Scott Quarrier
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Wisconsin Stone Quality of Life (WISQOL) questionnaire is the most widely used stone-specific patient-reported outcome measure (PROM). A short form (WISQOL-SF, 6 items) has recently shown strong cross-sectional performance in our prior external validation study, but its longitudinal responsiveness is unknown. We evaluated the ability of WISQOL-SF to capture temporal change relative to the full 28-item form (FF) in a large real-world stone cohort. METHODS: Adult patients with ≥2 WISQOL submissions from routine follow-up clinic encounters between Nov 2020-Jun 2025 were included. Standardized scores were calculated separately for both WISQOL-FF and WISQOL-SF. Rate of change in scores between consecutive submissions was calculated and correlated (Pearson and Spearman coefficients). A scatter plot was generated to demonstrate the strength and linearity of longitudinal relationship. Bland–Altman analysis assessed agreement in absolute scores across short, medium, and long intervals. A generalized estimating equation model evaluated if the SF–FF relationship remained robust after adjusting for clinical factors (stone status, symptoms, ER visit, traumatic event, hospitalization, sex, age) and time since baseline. RESULTS: Patients (n=1,203, 48.2% female) completed 4,152 WISQOL questionnaires (3.5 ± 2.1 per patient, range 2-16). SF and FF rate of change for total standardized score were strongly correlated (r=0.886; ρ=0.779; p<0.001). Tight clustering of data points around the identity line (Figure) confirmed strong alignment between SF and FF across follow-up intervals. Bland–Altman analysis showed a mean bias of 2.31 (95% LoA −14.40 to 19.02) with no systematic drift over time. In the GEE model, FF remained the dominant predictor of SF (β=1.132; 95% CI 1.105–1.159; p<0.001), with no significant effect of time since baseline (p=0.659). Female sex was associated with slightly higher SF scores (β=1.49; 95% CI 0.60–2.37; p=0.001), and the presence of stones at the time of WISQOL completion was associated with slightly lower scores (β=−0.79; 95% CI −1.49 to −0.08; p=0.029). All other covariates were non-significant. CONCLUSIONS: WISQOL-SF demonstrated excellent longitudinal validity, high agreement, and robust performance across time and clinical subgroups. These findings support the use of WISQOL-SF as a reliable and efficient PROM for longitudinal assessment in kidney stone patients.

title: ASSOCIATION OF SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH WITH POSTOPERATIVE COMPLICATIONS AND ACUTE CARE UTILIZATION AFTER STONE SURGERY: INSIGHTS FROM EPIC COSMOS
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Fikayo D. Akinbo, Felipe Antonio Pauchard, Stephen Rhodes, David Antonio Sheyn, Jose A. Salvado
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Social determinants of health (SDOH)—including insurance type, socioeconomic status, and access to care—may affect surgical outcomes. However, evidence assessing their relationship with stone surgery outcomes remains limited. We aimed to evaluate the association between adverse SDOH and postoperative complications and acute care utilization following definitive stone surgery using the multi-institutional COSMOS database. METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult patients undergoing ureteroscopy (URS), percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), or extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL) between 2015–2025 captured within Epic COSMOS. Surgery episodes were separated by 90 days. Patients were defined as SDOH-positive if, within 365 days before surgery, they had Medicaid, were uninsured/self-pay, or carried ICD-10 Z59 codes for adverse SDOH; SDOH-negative included those with commercial or Medicare coverage and no adverse SDOH codes. The primary outcome was any 30-day event (emergency department \[ED\] visit, readmission, or infectious complication). Secondary outcomes included each component and 90-day repeat stone intervention. RESULTS: Among 951,563 stone surgery episodes (859,470 SDOH-negative; 73,312 SDOH-positive), SDOH-positive patients were younger (median 44 vs 61 years), and more often female and Black or Hispanic. At 30 days, SDOH-positive patients showed higher risks of ED visits (18.7 % vs 10.3 %, p<0.001), readmissions (5.5 % vs 4.8 %, p<0.001), and infectious complications (12.2 % vs 9.7 %, p<0.001). Overall, 26.6 % of SDOH-positive vs 18.5 % of SDOH-negative patients experienced a composite 30-day event (p<0.001). Ninety-day repeat interventions were similar (13.6 % vs 13.8 %, p=0.2). Findings were consistent when restricted to first surgeries (25.8 % vs 18.3 %, p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Across a large national cohort, adverse SDOH were associated with increased short-term postoperative morbidity and acute care use after stone surgery, despite comparable 90-day reintervention rates. Integrating social risk factors into perioperative assessment may improve risk stratification and post-discharge follow-up in endourology.

title: INCIDENCE AND PREDICTORS OF OPIOID PRESCRIPTIONS 1–2 YEARS AFTER URETEROSCOPY
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Matthew W. Cole, Amanda Rubano, Raviraj J. Rege, Nitin Sharma, Scott Quarrier, Rajat Jain
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Although opioid-sparing approaches are increasingly common, practice patterns for postoperative pain management following ureteroscopy (URS) for urolithiasis remain highly variable. The extent to which perioperative exposure contributes to prolonged opioid use among otherwise opioid naive patients remains uncertain. This study aimed to characterize the incidence and determinants of opioid prescriptions 1–2 years after URS. METHODS: Using the TriNetX Research Network, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults undergoing URS between 2015 and 2024 with at least one outpatient encounter prior to the index procedure and documentation of continued follow-up beyond the defined 2-year observation period. Opioid prescriptions (codeine, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, morphine, oxycodone, and tramadol) occurring 1–2 years after URS were analyzed using two-proportion z-tests (Wald method), Kaplan–Meier estimation, and Cox proportional hazards modeling. Baseline confounders were balanced using 1:1 propensity score matching (greedy nearest-neighbor algorithm; caliper=0.1 SD). RESULTS: In a cohort of 17,256 opioid naive patients, opioid prescriptions occurring 1–2 years after URS were identified in 2,767 individuals (16.0%), of whom 1,092 (6.3%) had ≥2 encounters where an opioid was prescribed. Patients with perioperative opioid exposure had a higher adjusted incidence of subsequent prescriptions compared to those without exposure (17.73% vs 15.08%; weighted absolute risk difference 2.65%, 95% CI 0.78–4.52%; NNH=38, 95% CI 22–128). In the Cox proportional hazards model adjusting for the same covariates, perioperative exposure remained associated with a higher hazard of later opioid prescription (HR 1.12, 95% CI 1.01–1.24). Preoperative history of chronic ischemic heart disease, chronic kidney disease, affective mood disorders, and nicotine dependence were independently associated with increased hazard. CONCLUSIONS: Nearly one in five opioid naive patients undergoing URS received opioid prescriptions 1–2 years later. Perioperative exposure significantly increased the incidence of later opioid use. Further prospective studies are needed to clarify causal pathways and address this study’s limitations.

title: ASSOCIATION BETWEEN LOW BONE DENSITY, BISPHOSPHONATE THERAPY, AND URINARY STONE DISEASE: AN INTERNATIONAL RETROSPECTIVE REVIEW
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Matthew D. Mullen, Jacob Bleau, Benjamin Rubin, Nicholas Khoo, Aiden Masters, Sarah Kohl, Sidney Gregorek, Clara Goebel, Shane Cauley, Richard Grunert, Brian Irwin, Jenna Winebaum, Mohammad Mohaghegh
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The relationship between low bone density (LBD) and urinary stone disease has been described in prior studies, with evidence suggesting shared metabolic mechanisms involving calcium and phosphate homeostasis. Bisphosphonates (BPs) may mitigate stone risk by reducing bone resorption and urinary calcium excretion. However, existing data are limited by small sample sizes and single-center designs. Using a large multicenter database, we aimed to (1) compare urinary tract stone incidence between patients with and without LBD, (2) evaluate the effect of BP use on stone formation among patients with LBD, and (3) assess rates of stone-related procedures, including ureteroscopy (URS), percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), and extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL). METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was performed using the TriNetX database (2005–2025). Adults ≥18 years were included. LBD was defined using ICD-10 codes. Patients on oral bisphosphonate therapy for over one year were identified. Patients with urinary stones or BP initiation prior to LBD diagnosis were excluded. Subsequent analyses used 1:1 age- and sex-matched cohorts. Outcomes included urinary stone incidence and stone procedure rates and were identified based on ICD-10 and CPT codes. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. RESULTS: The initial comparison of LBD vs non-LBD patients included 145,949,059 individuals. Patients with LBD had higher stone incidence than controls (3.805% vs 1.643%; RR=2.316, 95% CI 2.305–2.327; p<0.0001). The LBD not using BPs cohort was 82.55% female, while the LBD with BP use cohort was 90.21% female. Among patients with LBD, BP users had lower stone incidence than non-users (2.028% vs 4.48%; RR=0.453, ARR=2.452%, 95% CI 0.441–0.465; p<0.0001). BP use was also associated with fewer stone procedures overall (0.46% vs 0.722%; RR=0.637, 95% CI 0.600–0.677; p<0.0001) in patients with LBD. By procedure type, BP users had lower rates of URS (0.439% vs 0.652%; RR=0.673, 95% CI 0.632–0.716), PCNL (0.016% vs 0.047%; RR=0.339, 95% CI 0.253–0.454), and ESWL (0.026% vs 0.09%; RR=0.287, 95% CI 0.229–0.360; all p<0.0001). CONCLUSIONS: LBD is associated with more than double the risk of urinary stone formation compared to patients without LBD. Among patients with LBD, bisphosphonate use is linked to significantly reduced stone incidence and lower rates of stone-related procedures. These findings suggest a potential protective role of bisphosphonates in urinary stone disease prevention. Limitations include a female-predominant cohort due to hormonal predisposition to low bone density.

title: URINARY PH FLUCTUATION TRIGGERS RAPID GROWTH AND PHASE TRANSITION OF CALCIUM PHOSPHATE STONES
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Mihoko Maruyama, Hiroto Takahashi, Yutaro Tanaka, Masashi Yoshimura, Hozumi Takahashi, Hiroshi Y. Yoshikawa, Kazufumi Takano, Yuki Sugiura, Rie Tajiri, Shuzo Hamamoto, Atsushi Okada, Takahiro Yasui, Yusuke Mori
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Calcium phosphate (CaP) kidney stones often grow rapidly and are clinically serious. Although high urinary pH due to bacterial infection is known to promote growth, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We obtained a CaP stone that had rapidly developed around a ureteral stent after surgery. The patient’s urinary pH fluctuated from 8 and 5.2 over 90 days. To elucidate the rapid growth process, we conducted in vitro experiments to evaluate the pH dependence of Brushite crystal growth and its phase transition to Apatite. Correlating experimental results with clinical data, including stone growth period and urinary pH profile, we revealed key factors driving rapid CaP stone formation. METHODS: Three experiments were performed:(1) Thin sections of the CaP stone were analyzed by polarized light microscopy and Raman spectroscopy to map crystal phases.(2) Synthesized Brushite powder was dispersed in a solution containing 2 mm phosphate and calcium ions (pH 5–6) and maintained under stirring. The time-dependent phase change was monitored by powder X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy, and the duration of the phase transition from Brushite to Apatite at 37 °C was determined.(3) Urine containing Brushite crystals obtained from a patient and about 1 ml of urine was placed into a vial. The pH was varied from 5 to 8 to estimate nucleation and growth rates under urinary conditions. RESULTS: (1) The CaP stone consisted mainly of metastable Brushite, while Apatite was deposited around the stent surface; partial transformation from Brushite to octacalcium phosphate (OCP) was observed.(2) At pH 6, Brushite transformed into Apatite via OCP, whereas at pH 5 it was estimated to be stable for several months at physiological temperature.(3) When urine pH was 6.5, Brushite size remained almost unchanged. At pH 5, it dissolved completely within 50 minutes, while at pH 8, Brushite nucleated and grew at approximately 60 μm/h. CONCLUSIONS: These findings demonstrate that urinary pH fluctuations strongly influence both growth and phase transition of CaP. Under alkaline conditions, Brushite grows rapidly, accelerating stone formation. Once formed, Brushite transforms around pH 6 into Apatite—a denser, harder, and more stable phase. These results suggest that proper urinary pH control could prevent rapid CaP stone formation, particularly after surgery when alkaline urine can accelerate growth around ureteral stents.

title: EQUIL SUPERSATURATION: A PRACTICAL WEB-BASED STONE RISK TOOL
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Jonathan Diah, Benjamin Canales, Siya Bhutani
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: In 1970, FORTRAN EQUIL2 was created to calculate groundwater mineral supersaturation (SS). Over a decade later, Dr. Birdwell Finlayson engineered the EQUIL algorithm to predict SS ratios for important urinary mineral components. Today, many commercial labs including Quest, ARUP, and Litholink use proprietary versions of EQUIL2 to calculate SS, and although useful in counseling, there has never been an accessible tool for physicians and patients to use to help visualize how altering 24-hour urine variables could affect future stone SS risk. Our goal was to develop an online EQUIL-based tool to fulfill this need. METHODS: Using older BASIC and R versions, EQUIL2 was ported into JavaScript™. Using the classic EQUIL equation, analytes from three different laboratory providers were input into our calculator. The Site presents SS values and normal ranges for CaOx, CaP, and UA computed by EQUIL2. After calculating, crystal SS are placed into stone risk categories of normal (green), moderate (brown), or high (red) risk depending on published ranges \[ (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.25#F1)\]. RESULTS: We found that means calculated using EQUIL, particularly for CaP, differed from those of commercial labs as much as 175%. We used a training set to modify the existing EQUIL program with a separate validation dataset to evaluate model performance. Once validated, we created parameters that can be adjusted to assess for corresponding SS changes. For example, a user can increase the volume parameter to immediately see how increasing urine output could reduce overall SS for stone types. CONCLUSIONS: We have developed an online version of EQUIL that is accessible to the public, allowing patients with physician guidance to better understand how to reduce future stone risk by varying their own laboratory results. Further work is needed to assess user interface, the impact of this tool on patient care and stone recurrence rates, and how this tool can be used in addition to dietary counseling to lower stone risk.

title: 24 HOUR URINE COLLECTION: PREDICTING STONE FORMERS VS. NON-STONE FORMERS BASED ON A COMPOSITE SCORE
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Sudarshan Srirangapatanam, David Bayne
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While 24-hour urine collection (24-hr-UA) has long guided clinical management of stone formers (SF), there still remains a controversy as to how to best alter its parameters to successfully reduce recurrence rates. We propose guidance with a new composite score to better differentiate SF from non-stone formers (NSF) clinically. METHODS: The Registry for Stones of the Kidney and Ureter (ReSKU), a prospective observational registry at UCSF, was queried to obtain the initial 24-hour urine collection (24-hr-UA) data following referral for stone diagnosis to define our stone-forming (SF) cohort. This data was augmented with non-stone-forming (NSF) data, utilizing 24-hr-UA from kidney donor registry participants within transplant clinics at UCSF who were confirmed to be stone-free as part of their donor evaluation. Individual parameters of the 24-hr-UA were first transformed into their respective normal curve equivalents to standardize all parameters. Orthogonal vectors were subsequently generated for each parameter using principal component analysis (PCA) to reduce overall noise in the dataset, given the known heterogeneity in the SF population. A linear discriminant analysis (LDA) was then performed on the outcomes of SF versus donors, and the resulting linear combination was designated as our composite score. RESULTS: The study population comprised a total of 183 donors and 414 stone formers (SF). The median age at urine collection was 47 for donors and 55 for SF. PCA revealed a heterogeneous population for both SF and donors, with significant overlap between the groups. Correlation analysis demonstrated expected patterns among individual 24-hour urine collection elements. LDA showed a clear separation of donors and SF ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.26#F1)) around a mean of 0. The urinary elements most positively contributing to the composite score were supersaturation of uric acid, calcium, oxalate, and pH. Conversely, the urinary elements most negatively contributing to the composite score were citrate, uric acid, sodium, and ammonium. CONCLUSIONS: Our proposed usage of 24-hr-UA composite score better distinguishes between SF and NSF than individual parameters alone. The next step is to determine the practical implication of using this method to predict for stone risk/recurrence in a population of exclusive stone formers. Nevertheless, this is an innovative adoption of a classic tool in the clinical management of stone disease.

title: ASSOCIATION BETWEEN LHRH AGONIST THERAPY AND URINARY STONE DISEASE IN MEN WITH PROSTATE CANCER: A LIVE DATABASE ANALYSIS
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Jacob Bleau, Benjamin Rubin, Matthew Mullen, Aiden Masters, Nicholas Khoo, Sarah Kohl, Clara Goebel, Sidney Gregorek, Shane Cauley, Brian Irwin, Jenna Winebaum, Mohammad Mohaghegh, Richard Grunert
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) with luteinizing hormone–releasing hormone (LHRH) agonists is a cornerstone of prostate cancer treatment but may impact calcium metabolism and thus urinary stone risk. This study explored the association between LHRH agonist use and urinary stone incidence in men with prostate cancer, and whether concomitant antiresorptive therapy modifies this risk. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was performed using the TriNetX US Network (2005–2025). Adult males (≥18 years) with prostate cancer were included; those with prior urinary stones were excluded. Exposure groups were defined by receipt of LHRH agonists (leuprolide, goserelin, or triptorelin) versus no LHRH therapy. A secondary analysis examined LHRH users receiving antiresorptive agents (bisphosphonates or denosumab) versus those not receiving them. All cohorts were propensity-score matched for age. Outcomes included urinary stone incidence and stone-related procedures identified by CPT codes. RESULTS: Among 86,799 matched patients per group, stone incidence was higher in those receiving LHRH agonists versus non-users (3.24% vs 1.64%; risk ratio \[RR\] 1.98, 95% CI 1.86–2.11, p<0.0001). When limited to stones ≥1 year after therapy initiation, the association remained significant (RR 2.23, p<0.0001). Stone-related procedures were 2.72 times more frequent in men receiving LHRH agonists (1.12% vs 0.41%, p<0.0001). Among LHRH users, antiresorptive therapy was associated with a lower stone incidence (1.75% vs 2.93%; RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.53-0.68, p<0.0001, n=22,567 per group). CONCLUSIONS: LHRH agonist therapy was associated with nearly double the risk of urinary stone disease and a greater need for stone-related procedures in men with prostate cancer. The risk attenuation observed with concomitant bisphosphonate or denosumab use suggests that preservation of bone mineral balance may mitigate ADT-related lithogenic changes. These findings highlight a potential lithogenic consequence of ADT and raise the possibility that antiresorptive therapy may confer protective effects against nephrolithiasis in this population.

title: ANDROGEN-DEPRIVATION THERAPY AND NEPHROLITHIASIS: DIVERGENT STONE RISK BY PRIOR STONE HISTORY IN PROSTATE CANCER
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Yi Shiou Tseng
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) is standard for prostate cancer, but its impact on kidney-stone risk is uncertain and may differ by prior nephrolithiasis. We assessed associations between ADT duration and nephrolithiasis, and secondarily osteoporosis, stratified by stone history. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study in the multi-institution TriNetX network including 512,489 men with prostate cancer (ICD-10 C61). To reduce immortal-time bias, follow-up began 6 months after diagnosis. ADT within 6 months was classified as long term (continuing ≥12 months), short term (no records after month 6), or ADT-naïve (no ADT); patients first exposed after month 6 were excluded. The primary outcome was first post–time-zero nephrolithiasis (N20–N23); the secondary outcome was incident osteoporosis (M80–M81). Within strata defined by prior nephrolithiasis, we performed 1:1 propensity-score–matched comparisons between exposure groups and estimated risks at 12, 24, and 36 months. RESULTS: In men with a stone history, long-term ADT showed the highest recurrence risk, with short-term ADT generally between long-term and naïve ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.29#F1)). In men without prior nephrolithiasis, long-term ADT was associated with the lowest cumulative stone risk, short-term ADT intermediate, and ADT-naïve the highest ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191328.95269.a6.29#F2)). Across strata, osteoporosis risk rose in a duration-related pattern (long > short \> naïve). CONCLUSIONS: In this large cohort, ADT was linked to heterogeneous kidney-stone risk—lower incident stones in men without prior nephrolithiasis but higher recurrence among stone-formers—while consistently increasing osteoporosis with longer exposure. These findings support proactive bone-health care for all patients on ADT and intensified stone-prevention strategies in those with a stone history.

title: WHICH NEUROGENIC BLADDER PATIENTS ARE AT HIGHER RISK OF SEPSIS AFTER PERCUTANEOUS NEPHROLITHOTOMY?
session: Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (IP12)
authors: Gustavo Monteiro Perrone De Oliveira, Alexandre Danilovic, Lucas Dias, Giovanni Marchini, Fabio Torricelli, Carlos Batagello, Fabio Vicentini, Rodrigo Perrella, William C. Nahas, Eduardo Mazzucchi
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Patients with neurogenic bladder are at increased risk of kidney stone formation, particularly infection stones, which puts them at risk for sepsis during stone manipulation. Our objective was to identify predictors of sepsis following percutaneous nephrolithotomy in this population, without investigating causal pathways. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed a consecutive sample of patients with neurogenic bladder who underwent percutaneous nephrolithotomy at our referral center between 2009 and 2020\. We also systematically searched PubMed until February 2025 for studies that investigated neurogenic patients undergoing this procedure. We then performed a single-arm meta-analysis of postoperative sepsis, including our own cohort, and meta-regressions to search for predictors. RESULTS: In our cohort, sepsis rate was 6% \[1%; 19%\], 2/36 patients. The Charlson Comorbidity Index was the only predictor (p=0.02). In the meta-cohort (13 cohorts, 2,369 patients), the combined sepsis rate was 12% \[7%; 17%\], despite high heterogeneity (I2=75%), with no evidence of publication bias (p=0.09). We identified younger age (p=0.04), non-urethral urinary diversions (p=0.04)—particularly ileal conduits (p0.001)—and non-traumatic etiologies (p=0.02), especially spina bifida (p=0.009), as predictors of sepsis. CONCLUSIONS: We recommend the development of a targeted antibiotic prophylaxis protocol, tailored to these predictors, for patients with neurogenic bladder undergoing percutaneous nephrolithotomy. We motivate further research on causal pathways.

title: SOCIOECONOMIC DEPRIVATION AND MALE FERTILITY: DECREASING PROSPERITY ASSOCIATED WITH LOWER SEMEN PARAMETERS IN A NATIONWIDE COHORT
session: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Juan P. Varela, Pablo Suarez, Siya Bhutani, Rafael Aldaya Bourricaudy, Daniel Nolte, Jospeh P. Alukal, James F. Smith, Kevin J. Campbell
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Socioeconomic disadvantage has been associated with disparities in nutrition, environment, and access to reproductive care, yet its relationship to semen quality has not been well quantified at a national level. We sought to evaluate the association between neighborhood socioeconomic deprivation, measured by the Area Deprivation Index (ADI), and semen quality parameters across adult men in the United States. METHODS: We conducted a population-based epidemiological study of adult men who ordered a mail-in semen analysis through Fellow Health between September 2020 and October 2024. Census tract code-level data enabled linkage to the ADI, a census-based metric of socioeconomic deprivation, and categorized by deciles (Q1=least deprived, Q10=most deprived). Demographic covariates included age, region, reason for ordering, and urbanization. Mean sperm concentration (million cells/mL), and total motile count (TMC, millions) were compared across ADI deciles using ANOVA tests. RESULTS: The total cohort included 29,071 adult men, with a mean age of 34.7 years. Men in the least prosperous decile (Q10) were younger, more likely to reside in the South or rural areas, and predominately ordered tests after trying to conceive for >1 year. Men in the most prosperous decile (Q1) were older, resided in the West or urban areas, and primarily ordered tests because they were planning to conceive in ≥1 year, (all p<0.001). Mean TMC across deciles (Q1-Q10) declined significantly ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191332.93827.7c.01#F1)). Increasing (decreasing prosperity) ADI was significantly associated with lower TMC (p<0.001). Concentration demonstrated a similar pattern, decreasing significantly from Q1 to Q10 ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191332.93827.7c.01#F2), p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Across a nationwide cohort, increasing socioeconomic deprivation was associated with significantly lower sperm concentration and TMC. This study supports a strong association between neighborhood disadvantage and male reproductive potential, emphasizing the role of social determinants in male fertility and the value of mail-in testing as a tool for population-level surveillance.

title: REVERSAL OR RETRIEVAL? COST-EFFECTIVENESS OF VASECTOMY REVERSAL VS IVF/ICSI UNDER EMPLOYER FERTILITY BENEFIT CAPS
session: Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Dhruv Puri, Achyutha Kodavatikanti, Eliad Amini, Garrett Peters, Ryan Nasseri, Tung-Chin Hsieh, Darshan Patel
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Many employers now offer capped fertility benefits, creating a practical choice for post-vasectomy couples: microsurgical vasectomy reversal or direct testicular sperm extraction (TESA) with IVF/ICSI. We developed an age-stratified decision model to compare pregnancy outcomes, total costs, and coverage thresholds for couples pursuing natural conception after reversal versus direct surgical sperm retrieval with ART. METHODS: A Monte Carlo microsimulation of 100,000 couples was conducted using parameters from AUA/ASRM guidelines and contemporary cohort studies. Female partner age distribution was modeled as 70% <40 years and 30% ≥40 years. Natural conception rates following VR were set at 58% for partners <40 and 14% for those ≥40. ICSI per-cycle pregnancy rates were 45% (<40) and 11% (≥40), allowing up to three cycles. Procedure costs included vasectomy reversal ($3,500–$17,000), testicular sperm retrieval ($1,000–$10,000), and ICSI ($14,500 per cycle). Employer fertility benefit caps of $30,000 and $40,000 were applied to estimate out-of-pocket and employer-paid costs. The primary outcome was successful pregnancy, with cost per additional pregnancy (ICER) as the secondary outcome. RESULTS: Overall, vasectomy reversal achieved higher pregnancy rates (75.8% vs 67.3%) and lower mean total costs ($32,114 vs $34,648) than TESA/ICSI, demonstrating cost dominance (ICER=–$29,601 per additional pregnancy). Among couples with female partners <40 years, reversal yielded pregnancy rates of 91.7% versus 83.2% for ART, with mean costs of $25,414 and $31,098, respectively (ICER=–$66,223; reversal dominant). For partners ≥40 years, reversal achieved 38.2% versus 29.7% pregnancy rates at mean costs of $47,960 and $43,043 (ICER=$58,816; marginal advantage for ART). Under employer fertility caps, 50% of reversal and 35% of ART couples achieved pregnancy within a $30k benefit, increasing to 61% and 55%, respectively, with a $40k cap. CONCLUSIONS: Vasectomy reversal is the most cost-effective first-line strategy for post-vasectomy couples, particularly when the female partner < 40 years. While ART approaches achieve comparable or slightly superior efficiency in older partners, the majority of couples under 40 can achieve pregnancy within typical $30,000–$40,000 employer fertility benefits, supporting routine consideration of reversal as the preferred initial approach.

title: ALCOHOL USE AND SEMEN QUALITY IN A NORTH AMERICAN PRECONCEPTION COHORT (PRESTO)
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Ashkan Pourabhari Langroudi, Chiyuan A. Zhang, Shufeng Li, Satvir S. Basran, Fausto Negri, Nicholas C. Sellke, Lauren A. Wise, Krystal E. Kuan, Amelia Wesselink, Eliza P. Pentz, Kenneth J. Rothman, Michael L. Eisenberg
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Men planning pregnancy often ask whether alcohol impairs semen quality, yet evidence at low-to-moderate intakes is inconsistent. We studied a large preconception cohort with repeated semen samples to estimate the association of baseline alcohol intake with standard semen parameters. METHODS: We analyzed men in Pregnancy Study Online (PRESTO) who provided ≥1 semen sample. Alcohol intake at enrollment was categorized as 0, 0.1-6.9, 7.0-13.9, and ≥14 drinks/week. Semen outcomes were volume, concentration, motility, total count, and total motile count (TMC); “low semen quality” was defined as volume ≤1.5 ml, concentration <16 million/mL, total count <39 million/ejaculate, motility <42%, or TMC <21 million. Missing data were addressed with multiple imputation. We fit generalized linear models to estimate adjusted percent differences and 95% confidence intervals and log-binomial regression with generalized estimating equations to estimate adjusted risk ratios (RRs) for low semen quality by alcohol intake. RESULTS: We analyzed data from 929 men (mean ± SD age was 32 ± 5 years) who provided 1,669 semen samples. The distribution of alcohol intake was 0 (22.1%), 0.1-6.9 (49.6%), 7.0-13.9 (19.2%), and ≥14 drinks/week (9.2%). In models using binary semen quality endpoints, ≥14 vs 0 drinks/week produced RRs of 0.67 (95% CI: 0.26-1.73) for low volume, 0.90 (0.52-1.56) for low concentration, 1.10 (0.56-2.16) for low total count, 1.19 (0.79-1.77) for low motility, and 1.40 (0.75-2.62) for low TMC. Among men 25 years, volume was higher at 0.1-6.9 (+12.9%, 95% CI: 2.6-23.2) and ≥14 (+15.3%, 0.7-29.9) drinks/week versus 0, and 7.0-13.9 vs 0 drinks/week was associated with higher risk of low motility (RR 2.23, 1.12-4.46); among men 30-34 years, ≥14 vs 0 drinks/week showed a moderately elevated but imprecisely estimated risk of low motility (RR 1.65, 0.98-2.77), while estimates in ≥35 years were near null. Among men with BMI 25-29.9 kg/m2, ≥14 vs 0 drinks/week suggested higher risks of low motility (RR 1.77, 0.94-3.34) and low TMC (RR 3.27, 1.22-8.80); RRs in other BMI subgroups were imprecise. CONCLUSIONS: Associations between baseline alcohol intake and semen volume, concentration, total count, motility, and TMC were generally modest, with isolated age- and BMI-specific elevations and no consistent dose-response pattern.

title: WHEN NORMAL ISN’T ENOUGH: THE EFFECT OF PATERNAL AGE IN NORMOSPERMIC MEN UNDERGOING ART
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Serena Maruccia, Stefano Terzoni, Daniele Tienforti, Mario Mignini Renzini, Ella Kinzikeeva, Cristian Ricci, Lucia Maragno, Giorgio Bozzini, Claudio Brigante, Mariabeatrice Dalcanto
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This study aims to investigate the impact of advanced paternal age on the outcomes of assisted reproductive technologies (ART) specifically in normospermic men. By concentrating on individuals with normal sperm parameters, we seek to isolate paternal age as the sole variable influencing fertility outcomes. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed all fresh ICSI/IVF cycles performed at Biogenesi Reproductive Medicine Centre in Monza between January 2028 and March 2024. Our focus was on normospermic males (as defined by WHO 2021 criteria), assessing the semen analysis performed on the day of embryo transfer, which was evaluated by the same team of experienced reproductive biologists. Female patients were then stratified into four groups based on maternal age and Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) levels: Group 1: <35 yo AMH≥1.2ng/ml; Group 2: ≥35 yo AMH ≥1.2ng/ml; Group 3: <35 yo AMH<1.2ng/ml; Group 4: ≥35 yo AMH<1.2ng/ml. The impact of APA on ART was assessed using the live birth (LB) rate per embryo transfer as the primary outcome, stratifying couples to control the interference of maternal variables. RESULTS: This retrospective study analyzed 6,262 ART cycles. Among 2,575 normospermic men, each additional year of paternal age was associated with a 2.6% reduction in live birth odds (adjusted OR=0.974; 95% CI 0.956–0.992; p=0.006), independent of maternal factors. The negative effect persisted across all female prognostic groups, including those with optimal reproductive potential. Similar findings were observed in dyspermic men (OR=0.973; p<0.001). Fertilization technique (IVF vs. ICSI) did not modify outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: Advancing paternal age is an independent predictor of reduced live birth even in men with normal semen parameters, highlighting that normospermia does not guarantee preserved fertility. The detrimental impact is consistent across maternal prognostic profiles and unaffected by fertilization method. Paternal age should be incorporated into prognostic counseling and ART outcome models.

title: SLEEP DISORDERS AND LONG-TERM RISK OF MALE INFERTILITY AND ENDOCRINE DYSFUNCTION: A NATIONAL RETROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Siddharth Ramanathan, Andrew Edgington, Tarak Davaluri, Grant Nelson, Paul Gabrial, Brayden Seliger, Vivek Aslot, Aidin Abedi, Puneet Sindhwani
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Sleep disruption has been implicated in impaired male reproductive health, but large-scale studies evaluating clinically diagnosed sleep disorders and infertility outcomes are limited. We investigated the long-term association between sleep disorders and male reproductive and endocrine dysfunction using a national database. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using TriNetX, identifying men aged 18–50 with and without documented sleep disorders from 2005 to 2020. Exclusion criteria removed known causes of infertility, including genetic, endocrine, infectious, neoplastic, and medication-related factors. Propensity score matching was performed 1:1 across more than 60 covariates, including demographic, metabolic, psychiatric, and reproductive variables. Outcomes included infertility diagnoses, testicular hypofunction, fertility-related encounters, and pharmacologic treatment. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated at 1-, 2-, 3-, 5-, and 10-year follow-up. Subgroups were stratified by age, body mass index (BMI), and disorder subtype (insomnia vs sleep apnea). RESULTS: The matched cohort included 117,154 men (58,577 per group).
