Sleep disorders were associated with a higher risk of the composite outcome across all follow-ups (1-year RR 1.40, 95% CI 1.26–1.56; 10-year RR 1.35, 95% CI 1.25–1.47). Testicular hypofunction emerged earliest and remained consistent (RR 1.55–1.60). Infertility treatment was also elevated (1-year RR 1.89, 95% CI 1.27–2.82; 10-year RR 1.65, 95% CI 1.34–2.02). Minimal signal was seen in men 18–25, with progressively stronger associations in ages 26–50, especially for infertility treatment (RR ~1.98 at 10 years in ages 36–45). Obese men showed the greatest risk. Sleep apnea conferred immediate and sustained elevations, while insomnia effects were modest and delayed. The composite findings are illustrated in the forest plot ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191332.93827.7c.05#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: Clinically diagnosed sleep disorders, particularly sleep apnea, are associated with increased long-term risk of male reproductive and endocrine dysfunction. Testicular hypofunction may represent an early indicator. These findings support the incorporation of sleep assessment into fertility evaluations and highlight the need for prospective studies to investigate whether treating sleep disorders can mitigate the risk.

title: REAL WORLD RESULTS OF POST-VASECTOMY SEMEN ANALYSIS: A LARGE NATIONAL SAMPLE OF OVER 100,000 MEN
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Tristan M. Nicholson, Dan Nolte, Scott Matson, Nahid Punjani, Stanton Honig, David Shin, John K. Amory, James F. Smith
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Mail-in testing has improved access and compliance with post-vasectomy semen analysis (PVSA). We aimed to characterize PVSA testing results among individuals undergoing multiple mail-in tests in a large nationwide cohort. METHODS: We evaluated the results of mail-in PVSA tests performed between 2020-2024 at Fellow Health by prospectively following men from the time of vasectomy to the time of PVSA sample submission within one year of their vasectomy. For individuals with sperm detected after vasectomy, additional tests were provided until azoospermia was achieved. For each individual, time to the first test was determined for the following categories: 0 sperm (azoospermia), 1-100k sperm, 100k-1M sperm and 1M or greater sperm. Due to the mail-in nature of the test, motility was not reported. RESULTS: Our cohort consisted of 103,592 individuals who underwent 117,826 PVSA tests. The majority (88.8%) underwent one PVSA test, 9.1% underwent two tests, and 2.1% underwent three or more tests. Incorporating all tests, 94.2% achieved azoospermia after vasectomy in our cohort. At 8 weeks post-vasectomy, 80% of men were azoospermic, and at 16 weeks, 87% were azoospermic; the percentage of men who achieved PVSA sperm clearance continued to increase until reaching a plateau at 42 weeks ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191332.93827.7c.06#F1)). At 6 months (26 weeks) 2% of men had at least 100k sperm detected, although motility could not be assessed due to the mail-in nature of the testing. CONCLUSIONS: Most individuals achieve PVSA sperm clearance 8-16 weeks post-vasectomy as recommended by American Urological Association guidelines. There was considerable variation in time to azoospermia with a small number of individuals achieving PVSA sperm clearance prior to 8 weeks and an increase in azoospermia rates observed until 42 weeks post-vasectomy. Detection of at least 100k sperm at and after 6 months post-vasectomy suggests a real world 2% rate of unsuccessful vasectomy in our cohort.

title: SECOND SEMEN ANALYSIS AFTER FIRST ASSESSMENT: CHALLENGING THE CURRENT AMERICAN UROLOGICAL ASSOCIATION GUIDELINES USING A TRIAL EMULATION DESIGN STUDY
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Fausto Negri, Edoardo Pozzi, Massimiliano Raffo, Alessandro Bertini, Ciro Piccolo, Marco Oddo, Christian Corsini, Gabriele Birolini, Simona De Luca, Luca Boeri, Richard Sucapuca, Rayan Matloob, Alessia D'Arma, Michael L. Eisenberg, Francesco Montorsi, Andrea Salonia
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The question of whether a single semen analysis suffices when initial parameters meet or exceed WHO reference thresholds remains contentious in the evaluation of male infertility. Current recommendations from AUA do not advise routine repetition of semen analysis when the first assessment demonstrates normozoospermia according to WHO criteria. We aimed to assess whether infertile men whose initial semen parameters meet or exceed the WHO reference thresholds should undergo a second semen analysis. METHODS: Data from 2070 infertile men were analyzed. All patients underwent at least one semen analysis, evaluated according to WHO 2021 criteria. Two groups were defined: i) normal, when all parameters meet or exceed reference thresholds; and, ii) abnormal, when at least one parameter was belowreference limits. We implemented a Synthpop-based trial simulation comprising 1000 iterations to evaluate two distinct scenarios: (i) universal testing of both groups, and (ii) adherence to current guidelines. This statistical analysis was used to estimate the diagnostic yield under both scenarios. RESULTS: Median (IQR) age was 37 (34-41) yrs and total motile sperm count (TMSC) 12 (1.5-46.9) mln. Men with abnormal semen analysis were older than those with normal semen analysis (37 \[34–41\] vs 36 \[32–40\] yrs, p=0.034), had higher BMI (25.2 \[23.4–27.4\] vs 24.7 \[22.8–26.6\], p=0.030), and higher rate of hypertension (9.2% vs 0.8%, p=0.003). Men with abnormal semen analysis also showed higher prevalence of chromosomal abnormalities (2% vs 0.8%, p=0.004), history of cryptorchidism (14.5% vs 1.7%, p<0.001) and reduced testicular volume (15 \[12-20\] vs 20 \[15-25\] Prader, p<0.001). To quantify the proportion of missed diagnoses, trial simulations estimated that adherence to guidelines recommendations would fail to identify 16.4% of semen abnormalities upon repeat analysis (95%CI 15.5–17.3%). Conversely, repeating the test when the initial semen analysis was altered resulted in a normal semen analysis in 2.5% (1.7-2.9%) of group 1 and 2.4% (1.8-3%) of group 2 ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191332.93827.7c.07#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: Re-testing only in case of abnormal semen analyses would result in missing approximately one in six cases of semen parameter deterioration on repeat analysis. These findings challenge existing recommendations and underscore the need to consider revised criteria for selected subgroups of infertile men.

title: MISSED KARYOTYPE ABNORMALITIES AND Y-CHROMOSOME MICRODELETIONS IN MALE INFERTILITY: TRIAL SIMULATION CHALLENGES CURRENT EUROPEAN ASSOCIATION OF UROLOGY GUIDELINES GENETIC TESTING THRESHOLDS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Edoardo Pozzi, Fausto Negri, Massimiliano Raffo, Alessandro Bertini, Marco Oddo, Ciro Piccolo, Gabriele Birolini, Simona De Luca, Luca Boeri, Richard Sucapuca, Alessia D'Arma, Francesco Montorsi, Andrea Salonia
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Current EAU guidelines recommend karyotyping for infertile men with sperm concentrations <5 million/mL and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing for ≤1 million/mL, with consideration for testing between 1-5 million/mL. The proportion of genetic diagnoses missed under guideline-adherent versus universal screening remains unknown. We used synthpop-based trial simulation to quantify diagnostic yield loss, providing robust estimates with confidence intervals unattainable from observational data alone. METHODS: We analyzed 641 consecutive white-European infertile men who all underwent comprehensive genetic screening (karyotype and Y-microdeletion testing). We employed trial simulation across 1000 iterations to model three scenarios: (1) testing all; (2) inclusive guideline adherence (Y-microdeletions for <5 million/mL); and, (3) strict guideline adherence (Y-microdeletions only for ≤1 million/mL, karyotype for <5 million/mL). This statistical approach was used to estimate the diagnostic yield under each scenario with quantified uncertainty through confidence intervals. RESULTS: Median (IQR) age was 36 years (33–40) and sperm concentration 1.8 mln/mL (0.3–6.7). Overall, 53 men (8.3%) had genetic abnormalities: 22 (3.4%) Y-microdeletions and 35 (5.5%) karyotype defects. Detection varied by sperm concentration: 12.6% (NOA), 8.9% (≤1 mln/mL), 10.4% (1–5 mln/mL), and 3.7% (≥5 mln/mL). Men with abnormalities had lower sperm concentration (1.0 vs 1.8 mln/mL, p=0.012) and smaller testicular volume (12 vs 12 ml, p=0.003). Trial simulation (1000 iterations) estimated strict guidelines would miss 20.6% of cases (95% CI 7.5–35.8%), while inclusive guidelines reduced missed diagnoses to 7.2% (95% CI 3.8–18.8%). CONCLUSIONS: Strict application of current guidelines (Y-microdeletions only for ≤1 million/mL, karyotype for <5 million/mL) would miss one in five genetic diagnoses. Expanding testing to <5 million/mL reduces this to one in fourteen. The current trial simulation methodology provides more robust estimates of missed diagnoses with quantified uncertainty. These findings challenge current threshold-based screening recommendations and suggest that revised cutoffs may be reconsidered.

title: CONCENTRATION MATTERS: PREVALENCE OF GENETIC DISORDERS IN OLIGOZOOSPERMIC AND AZOOSPERMIC MEN
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Jose I. Vinay, Ricardo Sobell, Mauricio Andriola, Joaquin Sanhueza
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Genetic factors, including chromosomal abnormalities and Y-chromosome microdeletions, represent established causes of male infertility. Current International guidelines recommend genetic screening based on sperm concentration thresholds. EAU/ASRM guidelines recommend karyotype analysis for men with concentration below 5 million/mL and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing particularly in patients below 1 million/mL. However, comprehensive data comparing genetic abnormalities prevalence across distinct concentration ranges in systematically screened cohorts remain limited. Understanding real life genetic disorders prevalence, could help clinical decision-making, resource allocation and correct patient counselling. The objective of the study is to determine the prevalence of genetic abnormalities (karyotype alterations and Y-chromosome microdeletions) in men presenting with azoospermia and severe oligozoospermia METHODS: Retrospective cohort study, analyzing 245 infertile men with severe oligozoospermia (sperm concentration ≤ 5 mill/mL) and azoospermia with palpable vas deferens, consulting at a tertiary andrological unit, between 2018 and 2025. Patients were stratified by sperm concentration: Azoospermia, ≤ 2 mill/mL and 2-5 mill/mL. All patients underwent standard G banding karyotyping and multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) based Y-chromosome microdeletion analysis targeting AZFa, AZFb and AZFc regions RESULTS: Among 245 patients, 18 presented genetic abnormalities (7.3%). Distribution by concentration revealed that in the azoospermic group (n=136), 15 patients presented genetic alterations (11.2%); of which 9 were Karyotype abnormalities (6.5%) including Klinefelter syndrome variants (47,XXY and mosaics, n=3), 47,XYY mosaicism (n=1), and balanced chromosomal translocations (n=4). In this group, 7 patients presentes Y-chromosome microdeletions (5.1%) including AZFc (n=4), multiple deletions (n=2), and AZFa (n=1)In the ≤2 million/mL group (n=70): 3 patients (4.3%) presented genetic alterations. Y-chromosome microdeletionswere found in 3 patients, including AZFc (n=2) and AZFb (n=1) regions. No karyotype abnormalities were detected. Lastly, in the 2-5 million/mL group(n=39), no patients presneted genetic abnormalities. Overall, patients presenting Y-chromosome microdeletions (n=10) slightly exceeded the number of patients with karyotype abnormalities (n=9), with one patient presenting both CONCLUSIONS: This study, of infertile men with seminal alterations, showed a concentration dependent gradient in genetic abnormalities prevalence. These findings validate current EAU/ASRM guidelines recommendations for genetic screening in azoospermia and severe oligozoospermia, while highlighting the diminishing diagnostic yield as sperm concentration increases. The absence of any genetic abnormalities in the 2-5 million/ml group could influence resource allocation within genetic testing protocols. Nevertheless, the 4.3% detection rate below 2 million/mL warrants extending systematic genetic evaluation in this patient group, particularly considering its implications for assisted reproductive technology planning and counselling

title: COMPARATIVE EFFECTS OF FINASTERIDE AND DUTASTERIDE ON SEMEN PARAMETERS IN YOUNG MEN WITH ANDROGENIC ALOPECIA: A RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED STUDY
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Hyun Jun Park
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To compare the impact of finasteride and dutasteride on semen parameters in young men treated for androgenic alopecia and to evaluate whether the duration of 5α-reductase inhibitor therapy affects sperm quality and hormonal profiles. METHODS: This single-center, randomized, controlled study enrolled 380 men aged 25–35 years who had been treated for androgenic alopecia with either finasteride 1 mg/day (n=190) or dutasteride 0.5 mg/day (n=190) for at least 3 months. Each drug group was further divided into five subgroups according to treatment duration: <6 months, 6–12 months, 13–18 months, 19–24 months, and >24 months. Serum total testosterone, FSH, and LH levels were measured, and semen analysis included semen volume, sperm concentration, total and progressive motility, morphology, vitality, and sperm DNA fragmentation. Statistical comparisons were performed using ANOVA and multivariate regression analyses, with p<0.05 considered significant. RESULTS: Semen volume, total motility, progressive motility, and vitality significantly decreased with longer treatment duration in both finasteride and dutasteride groups. DNA fragmentation index (DFI) increased progressively with treatment length. The decline in semen parameters was more pronounced among men taking dutasteride, particularly after 18 months of continuous therapy. No significant differences were observed in sperm concentration or morphology. Serum total testosterone remained stable across all groups, while FSH and LH showed mild, non-significant increases. CONCLUSIONS: Prolonged treatment with 5α-reductase inhibitors is associated with a time-dependent deterioration in semen quality, especially in sperm motility and DNA integrity. Dutasteride exerts a slightly greater suppressive effect than finasteride, likely due to its dual inhibition of type I and II 5α-reductase. Clinicians should exercise caution when prescribing these agents to young men who wish to maintain future fertility, and periodic semen monitoring is recommended during long-term therapy. | | | --- | | |

title: CANCER RISK AMONG MEN WITH AZOOSPERMIA: A MULTI-INSTITUTIONAL ANALYSIS USING THE COSMOS DATABASE
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Aymara Evans, Matthew Demasi, Stephen Rhodes, Nannan Thirumavalavan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Infertility affects about 4 million American men. Azoospermia, the absence of spermatozoa in semen, occurs in ~1% of all men and 15% of infertile men. Research has suggested an association between male infertility and long-term health risks, including increased cancer incidence. However, the degree to which azoospermic men differ in cancer risk from other infertile men remains unclear. Prior work by Eisenberg et al. demonstrated that men with azoospermia had nearly a threefold increased risk of cancer compared to the general population. We evaluated whether men with azoospermia have an increased risk of developing cancer compared to infertile men with oligospermia or normal semen parameters. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Epic Cosmos database, identifying men who underwent semen analysis between 2000 and 2025. We included men who had at least one reported sperm concentration value from a semen analysis. We excluded individuals who were non-male, younger than 18 or older than 70 years, had a history of cancer, testosterone or chemotherapy exposure, prior vasectomy or lacked sufficient follow-up activity. Men were categorized by sperm concentration as normal (>=15 mil/ml), oligospermic (<15 and > 0), or azoospermic (=0). The primary outcome was incident cancer diagnosis following semen analysis. Time-to-event analyses were performed using Kaplan-Meier survival estimates and Cox proportional hazards models. Hazard ratios (HRs) were reported before and after adjustment for age. RESULTS: A total of 56,880 men met inclusion criteria: 75% had normal semen parameters, 21% had oligospermia, and 5% azoospermia, with a median age of 34 years. Both oligospermic and azoospermic men exhibited higher rates of cancer compared with normospermic men. In unadjusted analyses, HRs for cancer were 1.58 (95% CI 1.37-1.80) for oligospermia, relative to normal, and 1.68 (1.32-2.13) for azoospermia (both p<0.001). After adjusting for age, the associations remained significant with HRs of 1.46 (1.27-1.67) for oligospermia and 1.39 (1.09-1.76) for azoospermia, relative to normal. CONCLUSIONS: Men with azoospermia and oligospermia had a significantly higher risk of developing cancer compared to those with normal semen parameters. However, cancer risk did not differ substantially between the two low-count groups, though this comparison was limited by the smaller size of the azoospermic cohort. Findings suggest impaired spermatogenesis may serve as a biomarker for future systemic disease. Further investigation is needed to explore the underlying mechanisms and evaluate whether enhanced cancer surveillance is warranted in this population.

title: ELEVATED CARDIOMETABOLIC AND MENTAL HEALTH COMORBIDITY BURDEN IN MEN WITH INFERTILITY: ANALYSIS FROM 7.2 MILLION PATIENTS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Jaxson Jeffery, Sandeep Voleti, Alex Theophilopoulos, Nahid Punjani
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Emerging evidence suggests male infertility may serve as an early clinical indicator for broader, underlying health issues, including but not limited to cardiovascular, metabolic, and musculoskeletal disorders. Large-scale, real-world data analysis is needed to comprehensively characterize the disease burden and comorbidities in this patient population. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used de-identified electronic health record data from several large healthcare platforms, encompassing over 16 million total patients using the Mayo Clinic Platform Discover. Two cohorts were created: Cohort A consisted of patients with a male infertility diagnosis by ICD code, and Cohort B consisted of patients defined by male sex alone. Primary outcomes measured included differences in demographics and the prevalence of comorbidities. Descriptive statistics, rate ratios (RR), chi-square tests, and p-values were used to compare cohorts. RESULTS: Cohort A consisted of 20,599 male patients compared to Cohort B which included 7.2 million male patients. Demographically, men in Cohort A presented at a significantly younger mean age (35.1 years) compared to men in Cohort B (39.6 years; Cohen's D=-0.25). Cohort A had significantly more patients identified as Asian (RR 1.5; p<0.001). Regarding systemic disease burden, men in Cohort A exhibited a substantially and statistically significant (all p<0.001) higher prevalence of multiple conditions, including obesity (RR 2.4), hyperlipidemia (RR 1.6), obstructive sleep apnea (RR 2.3), myocardial infarction (RR 1.2), essential hypertension (RR 1.2), liver disease (RR 1.6), and osteoporosis (RR 1.8). Type 2 diabetes mellitus (RR 1.0) and chronic kidney disease (RR 1.0) prevalence was similar. Cohort A also demonstrated an elevated mental health burden, with significantly higher prevalence of generalized anxiety disorder (RR 2.9), major depressive disorder (RR 2.9), alcohol use disorder (RR 2.2), and nicotine dependence (RR 2.1) (p<0.001 for all). CONCLUSIONS: This large-scale, real-world data analysis provides evidence that men diagnosed with infertility are captured at a younger age while simultaneously carrying a significantly greater burden of cardiometabolic, hepatic, musculoskeletal, and mental health comorbidities. These results validate the concept of male infertility as a risk stratification opportunity, underscoring need for comprehensive screening and integrated care to address systemic health risks in this population.

title: POOR METABOLIC HEALTH ASSOCIATED WITH LOWER SEMEN QUALITY AND HIGHER IVF RATES: ANALYSIS OF 25,000 US MEN
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Denise Asafu-Adjei, Ernesto Rojas, Jorge Arias, Daniel Nolte, Joseph Alukal, Tristan Nicholson, Milan Patel, Neel Shah, John Amory, James Smith
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The link between male fertility and metabolic health (MH) remains uncertain. Our main objective was to assess this relationship. We hypothesized that men residing in US counties with poorer MH have reduced semen quality and a greater reliance on assisted reproductive technologies, such as in vitro fertilization (IVF). Previous studies in the US have been limited by single-site sampling and a lack of clinical data connected to semen analysis (SA). METHODS: We used data from Fellow Health mail-in SA, US Census (USC) and CDC PLACES. The PLACES dataset contains prevalence estimates for chronic diseases for all U. S. counties, such as diabetes (DM), obesity, hypertension (HTN), and high cholesterol (HC). Prevalence of health conditions (quintiles) across counties were geocoded by county to link health conditions with SA variables and USC. We explored the relationship between MH and semen quality (Total Motile Count, TMC), and need for IVF (TMC < 5 M) while adjusting for geographic region, age, socioeconomic status, and urbanization. RESULTS: Our cohort (n-25,622) was distributed across the US (Mid-W 21%; NE: 7%; S: 36%; W: 36%). Most patients were aged 30-39 (61%), lived in urban areas (50%), and were trying to conceive or planning to in the next year (86%). Men in counties with the highest prevalence of DM, obesity, HTN, and HC had lower TMC and were more likely to require IVF. ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191332.93827.7c.13#F1), p<0.001). Mean TMC in the least healthy quintile for each parameter was at least 20 M lower than in the healthiest group. After adjusting for confounders, the odds of needing IVF for the least healthy versus the healthiest quintile was significantly higher ( Table 1): DM (OR 1.42), Obesity (OR 1.28), HTN (OR 1.39), and HC (OR 1.27). CONCLUSIONS: These data reveal a strong association between increased prevalence of metabolic disorders and diminished sperm quality. Prevalence of DM, obesity, HTN, and HC were associated with a 27% - 42% higher odds of needing IVF, reinforcing the link between semen quality, overall men’s health, and the need for fertility care. Semen analyses are an important window into metabolic health and may play a key role as the contemporary men’s health “vital sign”.

title: VALIDATION OF AN AI-GUIDED SPERM IDENTIFICATION SYSTEM IN POST-VASECTOMY PATIENTS DEEMED AZOOSPERMIC BY CONVENTIONAL SEMEN ANALYSIS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Aaron Brant, Laura C. Gemmell, Stephanie Morgan, Hemant Suryawanshi, Yejin Bann, Sajal Gupta, Alan Paniagua Cruz, Eric J. Forman, Zev Williams, Joseph P. Alukal
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Sperm Tracking and Recovery (STAR) system integrates artificial intelligence, high-speed imaging, and microfluidics to identify and isolate rare sperm in semen samples that have no sperm found with conventional analysis. To further validate its efficacy, STAR was used on a cohort of post-vasectomy patients whose samples were deemed azoospermic using conventional semen analysis. METHODS: Male patients who underwent vasectomy at a single institution between August 2024 and June 2025 provided on-site semen samples that were initially analyzed by an andrology-trained laboratory technician using 2021 World Health Organization criteria. Samples deemed azoospermic by conventional semen analysis were further analyzed by STAR. Patients who had sperm identified on their initial STAR analysis were invited to return for a repeat STAR. All samples were discarded after STAR analysis. Sperm motility was not assessed. RESULTS: Fourteen patients provided ejaculated samples at a median of 115 days post-vasectomy (range 24 to 165 days) wherein conventional semen analysis found no sperm. STAR identified sperm in 11 of 14 participants, with a median of 17 spermatozoa identified (range 1 to 1,000 sperm). Three of the 11 patients with sperm identified by STAR returned for a second collection, with sperm identified in two of three samples: one sample with 2 spermatozoa at 234 days and one with 9 spermatozoa at 339 days. CONCLUSIONS: The STAR system identified the presence of rare sperm in the majority of post-vasectomy samples in which no sperm were found using conventional semen analysis. Men deemed azoospermic by conventional semen analysis may benefit from more extensive sperm identification methods such as STAR. Continued prospective data collection will further validate the utility of this technology and may also enable more effective interrogation of surgically retrieved samples for the presence or absence of sperm.

title: FROM PI-RADS TO TE-RADS: TESTICULAR MRI BIOMARKERS PREDICTING SPERM RETRIEVAL IN NON-OBSTRUCTIVE AZOOSPERMIA
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infertility: Epidemiology & Evaluation I (PD05)
authors: Saturnino Luján, Rosa María Pacheco-Rendón, Irene Hervás, Javier Aquerreta, Amadeo Ten, Alberto Talaya, Luis Martí-Bonmatí, Maria Gil, Alberto Budia, Nicolas Garrido, Jose Remohí
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Microsurgical testicular sperm extraction (microTESE) is the standard treatment for men with non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA),although sperm retrieval (SR) rates remain limited. No validated biomarkers currently predict the presence of testicular sperm. This study aimed to identify magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) parameters associated with successful SR, proposing a non-invasive predictive model for NOA patients. METHODS: NOA patients who underwent testicular MRI and microTESE between 2022 and 2024 were included. MRI-derived parameters oftesticular architecture were quantified, including magnetization transfer ratio (MTR), fat fraction (FF), apparent diffusion coefficient(ADC), diffusion coefficient (D), pseudo-diffusion coefficient (D\*), and perfusion fraction (f). Partial Least Squares–DiscriminantAnalysis (PLS-DA) was used for dimensionality reduction and identification of variables associated with SR. Data were normalized using the Centered Log-Ratio transformation. Diagnostic performance was evaluated by ROC analysis, including sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and odds ratio (OR) RESULTS: Thirty-six NOA patients were analyzed; SR was positive in 38.9% (n=14) and negative in 61.1% (n=22). PLS-DA showed partial separation between SR-positive and SR-negative groups, with the first two components explaining 34.2% of total variance. HigherFF values were associated with negative SR. Logistic regression based on the first PLS-DA component achieved an AUC of 0.831 (p<0.001), with 85.7% sensitivity, 77.3% specificity, 89.5% negative predictive value, and 80.6% overall accuracy. A first-component value below −0.56759 strongly predicted successful SR (OR=20.4; 95% CI: 3.98–164.39; p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: MRI-derived biomarkers effectively discriminated between successful and unsuccessful SR in NOA. The proposed model demonstrated high sensitivity and predictive accuracy, particularly for identifying patients unlikely to benefit from microTESE. MRI-based predictive modeling could enhance patient selection and reduce unnecessary invasive procedures.

title: RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY WITHOUT PROSTATE BIOPSY BASED ON A NONINVASIVE DIAGNOSTIC STRATEGY: A PROSPECTIVE SINGLECENTER STUDY
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Tao Tao, Changming Wang, Yifan Ma
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate biopsy is the most common approach for diagnosing prostate cancer (PCa); however, it has inherent limitations, such as the invasive procedure, postoperative complications, and false negative results. We aimed to provide a noninvasive diagnostic strategy for patients with highly suspected PCa and to evaluate the feasibility of performing biopsy-spared radical prostatectomy. METHODS: This prospective study included a total of 86 patients between November 10, 2022, and October 1, 2025. All 86 patients underwent radical prostatectomy without prior prostate biopsy based on a noninvasive diagnostic strategy consisting of a diagnostic prediction model \[comprised of the prostate imaging-reporting and data system (PI-RADS)\ score and prostate-specific antigen density (PSAD)\] and the 18F-prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-1007 positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) examination. The primary endpoint was the positive predictive value (PPV) of clinically significant PCa\[the International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP)\ grade ≥2, Gleason score ≥3 + 4\]. The secondary endpoints were a PPV of any-grade PCa (ISUP grade ≥ 1, Gleason score ≥3 + 3) and high-grade PCa (ISUP grade ≥3, Gleason score ≥4 + 3), and the false positive rate of the diagnostic strategy. RESULTS: Of the 401 screened patients with clinically suspected PCa, 86 patients fulfilled the criteria and consented to participate in this study. The median PSAD level was 0.52ng/mL2; 22 (25.6%) patients were identified as having a PI-RADS score of 4, and 64 (74.4%) patients with a PI-RADS score of 5. The median SUVmax of 18F-PSMA-1007 PET/CT was 19.7. For the 86 enrolled patients who received radical prostatectomy directly, the PPV of clinically significant PCa was 97.7% \[84/86\]. Only 2.3% \[2/86\] of patients were diagnosed with clinically insignificant PCa (ISUP grade=1, Gleason score=3 + 3). The PPV of any-grade PCa and high-grade PCa were 100% and 72.1% (62/86), respectively. No one had a false positive result. CONCLUSIONS: We proposed a noninvasive diagnostic strategy consisting sequentially of a diagnostic prediction model and the 18F-PSMA-1007 PET/CT examination for diagnosing PCa. Despite some limitations, our initial findings suggest the potential feasibility of radical prostatectomy without prior prostate biopsy.

title: A DUAL-THRESHOLD STRATEGY FOR PREDICTING HIGH-RISK PROSTATE CANCER IN BIOPSY-FREE RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY COHORTS: A RETROSPECTIVE STUDY BASED ON CHINESE MULTICENTER CLINICAL DATA
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Yong Liang, Tao Tao
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Our previous study has suggested that biopsy-free radical prostatectomy reduces burdens for selected prostate cancer (PCa) patients based on a noninvasive diagnostic strategy(Prostate Cancer Prostatic Dis.2025 Jun;28(2):496-502.). However, the absence of pre-operative pathology precludes high-risk PCa (HRPCa) identification, crucial for determining the need for pelvic lymph node dissection (PLND). In this study, we try to explore a new non-invasive method for predicting HRPCa before surgery. METHODS: This retrospective diagnostic study included a development cohort of 93 patients from USTC center, as well as two external validation cohorts: one cohort of 83 patients from XYH Hospital and another cohort of 117 patients from XJH Hospital. All enrolled patients met the USTC model value≥0.6 criteria (https://ustcprostatecancerprediction.shinyapps.io/dynnomapp/) and obtained definitive pathological results within 4 weeks after 18F-PSMA-1007 PET/CT examination. Patients were stratified as HRPCa (D'Amico criteria: tPSA>20 ng/mL, GS≥8, or ≥cT2c) or non-high-risk (NHR). Maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) and target-to-background ratios (TBRs) of PSMA-PET/CT were quantified. Diagnostic performance for HRPCa was evaluated using ROC analysis. Multivariate logistic regression analysis identified independent predictors. RESULTS: Of 93 patients from development cohort, 63 (67.7%) had HRPCa. SUVmax (AUC=0.807, optimal cut-off=20.9) and tPSA (AUC=0.777, optimal cut-off=15.09 ng/mL) were independent HRPCa predictors (p<0.05). Patients meeting both thresholds (SUVmax>20.9 and tPSA>15.09 ng/mL, n=31) demonstrated a 100% HRPCa positive predictive value (PPV) and specificity (31/31), significantly outperforming single parameters (p<0.001). Patients below both thresholds (n=29) had only 31.0% HRPCa. In two external validation cohorts, similar diagnostic performance was observed. CONCLUSIONS: A dual-threshold non-invasive strategy is established for predicting HRPCa in biopsy-free radical prostatectomy cohorts, which can be used to decide whether PLND is needed.

title: SAFETY AND FEASIBILITY OF TRANSPERINEAL PROSTATE BIOPSY WITHOUT ANTIBIOTIC PROPHYLAXIS: A MULTICENTRIC RETROSPECTIVE STUDY
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Valerio Mallia, Vittorio Fasulo, Alessio Finocchiaro, Alessandro Tallari, Vincenzo Striano, Pieve Emanuele, Giuseppe Basile, Gianmarco Colandrea, Baiamonte Gianfranco, Pier Paolo Avolio, Marco Paciotti, Nicolò Maria Buffi, Giovanni Lughezzani, Riccardo Galli
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Transperineal prostate biopsy (TPBx) is increasingly adopted due to its favorable infectious risk profile. However, real-world data on its systematic use in a fully outpatient setting without antibiotic prophylaxis remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the safety and feasibility of TPBx performed without prophylactic antibiotics in routine urological practice. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 423 consecutive patients who underwent TPBx across three Italian urology centers between 2018 and 2024. All procedures were performed in an outpatient setting under local perineal anesthesia with lidocaine, without sedation or prophylactic antibiotics; skin preparation consisted of povidone-iodine only. The primary endpoint was the rate of infectious complications within 30 days (fever, culture-confirmed urinary tract infection \[UTI\], and sepsis). Secondary outcomes included complication grading according to the Clavien-Dindo classification. RESULTS: A total of 423 patients (mean age 65.4 ± 8.3 years) were included. Median prostate volume was 50 g (IQR 40–60). The mean number of biopsy cores was 10.2 ± 2.1, and the mean procedural time was 14.7 ± 1.1 minutes. Infectious complications were uncommon: 12 patients (2.8%) developed fever and 2 (0.5%) had culture-confirmed UTI. No cases of sepsis were observed. Overall, 292 patients (69%) had no complications. Grade I events occurred in 105 patients (24.8%), including hematuria (13.4%), hemospermia (13.4%) and transient LUTS (0.2%). Urinary retention was observed in 1.2% of cases and resolved with short-term catheterization. Grade II complications were recorded in 12 patients (2.8%), all of whom required oral antibiotics for fever or UTI. No Grade ≥III complications occurred. No emergency visits or readmissions were required. CONCLUSIONS: In this multicenter cohort, TPBx performed without antibiotic prophylaxis showed a low rate of infectious and clinically significant complications, and was feasible in an outpatient setting. These findings support the potential role of selective, risk-based antibiotic use in TPBx. Further prospective studies are warranted to confirm safety outcomes and better define patient selection strategies for prophylaxis-free pathways.

title: DETECTION RATE PLATEAU IN PROSTATE BIOPSY: HOW MANY CORES ARE ENOUGH? A RETROSPECTIVE ANALYSIS OF TWO THOUSAND BIOPSIES
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Flavia Proietti, Aldo Brassetti, Rocco Simone Flammia, Leslie Claire Licari, Eugenio Bologna, Alfredo Maria Bove, Giuseppe Chiacchio, Simone D'Annunzio, Gabriele Tuderti, Riccardo Mastroianni, Umberto Anceschi, Mariaconsiglia Ferriero, Leonardo Misuraca, Salvatore Guaglianone, Costantino Leonardo, Giuseppe Simone
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The optimal number of cores in prostate biopsy remains debated. Increasing sampling may improve cancer detection but also increases procedural time, patient discomfort, and complications. We aimed to evaluate whether detection rates (DR) continue to rise with the number of cores, and to identify a potential plateau beyond which additional samples provide negligible diagnostic benefit. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 2,089 consecutive prostate biopsies (2019-2024). Clinical, imaging, and pathological data were retrieved from an institutional database. DR were assessed for both overall prostate cancer (PCa) and clinically significant PCa (csPCa, ISUP 2–5). Analyses were restricted to cases with ≤25 cores. Crude DR were calculated by core number classes. Multivariable logistic regression models with restricted cubic splines (4 df) were used to estimate the adjusted probability of detection, adjusting for age, PSA density, PI-RADS score, previous biopsy, prostate volume, and biopsy approach (transperineal vs transrectal). A plateau was defined when the marginal gain per additional core was < 1% for ≥ 3 consecutive increments. RESULTS: Patients' characteristics are reported in Table 1. The crude DR for any PCa decreased from 97% (≤10 cores) to 52% (> 20 cores), reflecting a selection bias in highly suspicious cases ( Table 2, (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191336.68744.5b.04#F1)). After adjustment, the detection probability stabilised beyond 16–18 cores (≈ 70%). For csPCa, the adjusted probability plateaued at ≈ 17 cores, corresponding to a predicted detection probability of ≈ 70% ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191336.68744.5b.04#F2)). Beyond this threshold, additional cores increased detection by < 1% per core, indicating diminishing diagnostic returns. CONCLUSIONS: In prostate biopsy, both overall and clinically significant cancer DR a plateau around 17 cores. Sampling beyond this threshold provides minimal diagnostic gain while increasing procedural burden.

title: ASSOCIATION BETWEEN HETEROGENEITY OF PRIMARY PROSTATE CANCER ON PSMA PET/CT AND ONCOLOGICAL OUTCOMES IN LOCALIZED CASES: A WHOLE-MOUNT PATHOLOGY-BASED RETROSPECTIVE STUDY
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Yang Luo, Hongqian Guo, Xuefeng Qiu
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The heterogeneity of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) in the tumor has been implicated as a contributing factor in the limited efficacy of PSMA-targeted radioligand therapy for certain prostate cancer patients. Previous study has demonstrated that elevated PSMA heterogeneity correlates with circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) characteristics and abiraterone treatment responserates in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. However, the heterogeneity of PSMA in localized prostate cancer remains unexplored. This study aims to elucidate the spatial heterogeneity of PSMA uptake in localized prostate cancer and to examine its potential associations with adverse oncological outcomes and biochemical recurrence (BCR). METHODS: This retrospective analysis included 128 prostate cancer patients who underwent 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT prior to radicalprostatectomy (RP). We used SUVmax-mean (derived by subtracting SUVmean from SUVmax within the index lesion) to quantify intra-tumor PSMA uptake heterogeneity, while SUVhetero (the variance of SUVmean across all PSMA-positive lesions) captured inter-tumor heterogeneity. Adverse oncological outcomes were evaluated across PSMA heterogeneity subgroups. Kaplan–Meier analysis with log-rank test was used to test the ability of heterogeneity parameters to determine the survival probability. RESULTS: After excluding 10 patients had none PSMA positive lesion on PET/CT, a total of 118 patients were included for analysis. Patients with higher SUVmax-mean had greater initial serum PSA level (p<0.001), however, similar relation was not observed in patients with higher SUVhetero (p=0.401). Higher ISUP grade at RP, higher pathological T stage, more Positive Surgical Margin and Seminal Vesicle Invasion were found in patients with higher SUVmax-mean (all p<0.05). Only the ratio of Positive Surgical Margin was found to be significantly different in patients with different SUVhetero (p=0.036). Kaplan–Meier analysis revealed that patients with higher SUVmax-mean had shorter Biochemical Recurrence-free (BCR-free) survival compared to those with lower SUVmax-mean (log-rank p=0.003). There is no significant difference in BCR-free survival between patients with higher and lower SUVhetero (log-rank p=0.400) CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that heterogeneity in 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT uptake is associated with adverse oncological outcomes and increased risk of BCR in patients with localized prostate cancer, highlighting the potential of PSMA heterogeneity as a predictive marker for disease progression in localized prostate cancer.

title: A PROSPECTIVE STUDY ON THE VALUE OF CK5/6 RAPID IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY IN RAPID FROZEN SECTION DIAGNOSIS OF PROSTATE TARGETED BIOPSY SPECIMEN
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Miao Wang, Longteng Liu, Shuaitao Xiong, Wei Zhang, Ming Liu
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate biopsy remains the reference standard for preoperative diagnosis of prostate cancer (PCa). While recent studies have explored strategies for performing radical prostatectomy (RP) without prior biopsy, the issue of false positives results in imaging findings cannot be entirely avoided. The application of rapid frozen section (RFS) diagnosis to targeted biopsy specimens may reduce the number of biopsy cores required and potentially enable same-stage RP. This study investigated the feasibility of CK5/6 rapid immunohistochemistry (RIHC) as an adjunctive diagnostic tool and evaluated its accuracy and reliability. METHODS: This single-center prospective study enrolled 124 patients between October 2022 and September 2023. Eventually, clinical and pathological information from 116 patients was analyzed. For each patient, one biopsy core was obtained from both targeted and non-targeted regions for RFS diagnosis and CK5/6 RIHC testing. Two pathologists independently performed the diagnoses. The diagnostic accuracy of CK5/6 RIHC and its influencing factors were assessed using the remaining frozen tissue and conventional immunohistochemistry (IHC) as the reference standard. RESULTS: A total of 232 biopsy specimens from 116 patients were analyzed. Final pathological diagnosis confirmed PCa in 117 cases (50.4%). RFS alone identified 101 cases (43.5%) as PCa, 101 (43.5%) as benign, and 25 (10.8%) as indeterminate. Among CK5/6-negative cases by RIHC, all 115 (100%) were also negative on conventional IHC and were ultimately diagnosed as PCa. The concordance between RIHC and conventional IHC was excellent (Kappa=0.92, p<0.001). Junior pathologists diagnosed 102 cases (44.0%) as PCa, 95 (40.9%) as benign, and 35 (15.1%) as equivocal. With RIHC assistance, diagnostic certainty improved to 113 PCa cases (49.1%), 117 benign cases (50.4%), with only 1 (0.4%) remaining equivocal. Interobserver agreement between junior and senior pathologists significantly increased (Kappa=0.525, 95% CI 0.426-0.613 for RFS alone; Kappa=0.902, 95% CI 0.875-0.923 for RIHC) when incorporating RIHC (both p<0.001). Further multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed that tumor proportion in biopsy specimens may be an independent risk factor influencing diagnostic difficulty (likelihood of equivocal diagnosis) (p<0.001, 95% CI: 0.040 \[0.007–0.237\]). CONCLUSIONS: CK5/6 RIHC demonstrates clinical feasibility and high diagnostic accuracy in prostate targeted biopsy evaluation. Its incorporation significantly improves diagnostic confidence, particularly for less experienced pathologists. These findings support the potential of RIHC as a valuable adjunct to frozen section diagnosis. Further validation through multicenter studies with larger cohorts is warranted.

title: A PROSPECTIVE, PAIRED-COHORT, BLINDED, VALIDATION OF THE IBEX PROSTATE AI PATHOLOGY SYSTEM COMPARED TO EXPERT URO-PATHOLOGY REPORTING OF PROSTATE BIOPSIES: THE CANCER HISTOLOGY ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE RELIABILITY STUDY (IP6-CHAIROS)
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Hashim U. Ahmed, Johanna Sukumar, Hannah Markham, Salam Z. Al-Sam, Josephine Lloyd, Andrew Smith, Anna Silvanto, David Snead, Charles Tilley, Nesreen Magdy, Chaya Prasad, Preethi Gopinath, Alex Freeman, Emma Cullen, Francesca Rawlins, Ross Dalton, Thiagarajah Sasikaran, Natalia M. B. Klimowska-Nassa, Mathias Winkler, Chiwen Lin, Dawn Davies, Sean Mckee, Davina Hewitt, Amar Kansara, Marta Szajna, Bijan Khoubehi, Patricia Costa, Metod Oblak
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Artificial intelligence in assessment of digital prostate biopsy pathology has shown promise. We aimed to definitely assess the diagnostic accuracy of Ibex Prostate AI in a prospective paired-cohort blinded validation study. METHODS: Ibex Prostate AI pathology (index test) was compared to histopathology expert review (reference standard) with H&E pathology slides evaluated prospectively in consenting consecutive patients from 6 UK centres (8/Mar/2023-18/Mar/2025). Ibex Prostate AI pathology was evaluated within the pre-biopsy MRI pathway with those undergoing MRI-targeted and systematic biopsies eligible. The reference standard was determined using a first and second pathology review, and in cases of discrepancy, a third. The AI system was blind to all pathology reports. Patients, physicians and reporting pathologists were blind to the AI report. All pathologists were blinded to other pathology reports. The Ibex Prostate AI pre-specified algorithm thresholds in this study were set to give very high sensitivity with a view to potential use as a pre-screening tool for prostate biopsy. The primary endpoints were sensitivity and specificity for GG >/=2 at the patient level. These were compared against pre-specified thresholds of 94% and 75%, respectively, and success would be declared if both two-sided 95%CIs (Wilson's method) exceeded these. ClinicalTrials. gov NCT05228197. RESULTS: Of 712 eligible patients, 623 consented to participate. 26 subsequently withdrew consent. The analysis was based on 597. Median (IQR) age and PSA was 68.3 (61.50-74.10) and 7.40 (5.16-11.00). Any cancer was diagnosed in 425 (71.2%) and Grade Group >/=2 in 382 (64.0%).Primarily, sensitivity was 97.4% (372/382) (95%CI 95.2-98.6%) and specificity 89.8% (193/215) (95%CI 85.0-93.1). Success was declared according to pre-specified thresholds. Secondarily, positive and negative predictive values were 94.4% (91.7-96.3) and 95.1% (91.2-97.3). AUROC was 0.99 (0.978-0.993).For any cancer, Ibex Prostate AI had sensitivity 100.0 (99.1-100), specificity 69.2% (61.9-75.6), PPV 88.9% (85.8-91.4), NPV 100.0% (96.9-100.0) and AUROC 0.99 (0.987-0.997). CONCLUSIONS: Ibex Prostate AI has sufficiently high diagnostic accuracy in evaluating prostate biopsies for use in clinical practice. Ibex Prostate AI could also be used to triage cases suspicious of cancer for pathology review.

title: COMPARISON OF PROSTATE CANCER YIELD PER MRI TARGET LESION FOR LATP VERSUS TRUS PROSTATE BIOPSY: NEW INSIGHTS FROM THE TRANSLATE RANDOMISED CLINICAL TRIAL
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Nithesh M. S. Ranasinha, Alastair D. Lamb, Ioana R. Marian, Roxanne Williams, J. Francisco Lopez, Claudia Mercader, Mutie Raslan, Christopher Berridge, Jessica Whitburn, Teresa Campbell, Steve Tuck, Vicki S. Barber, Jessica Scaife, Aimi Hewitt, Amy Taylor, Alexander Ooms, Filipa Landeiro, Matthew Little, Jane Wolstenholme, Sukanya Ghosh, John M. Reynard, Freddie C. Hamdy, Matthew P. C. Liew, Tom A. Leslie, James W. F. Catto, Derek J. Rosario, Altan Omer, Daniel W. Good
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The TRANSLATE UK-wide multi-centre randomised clinical trial (RCT) detected a 5.7% uplift in detection of Gleason grade group ≥2 (GGG≥2) prostate cancer (PCa) in previously biopsy naïve individuals randomised to local anaesthetic transperineal (LATP) versus transrectal (TRUS) ultrasound guided prostate biopsy. All 1126 randomised participants in TRANSLATE underwent pre-biopsy MRI. We now test the hypothesis that increased detection of GGG≥2 PCa observed for LATP versus TRUS biopsy in TRANSLATE is due to better sampling of anterior and apical target lesions of the prostate. METHODS: We interrogated the positive diagnostic biopsies present in the 326 of 443 randomised participants recruited from the largest TRANSLATE UK centre and diagnosed with PCa. MRI lesion location was defined with the following categories: anterior, mid and posterior in the sagittal plane; base, mid or apex in the transverse plane; lateral or crossing midline. We considered each MRI-visible PIRADsv2 3-5 lesion and compared these against targeted prostate biopsy results for LATP and TRUS. Pairwise comparisons were analysed in SPSS using the chi-squared test. RESULTS: A total of 168/326 (51.5%) patients received LATP and 158/326 (48.5%) received TRUS biopsy. Of these, 323/326 (99%) patients had at least one MRI-visible lesion, with 423 lesions reported in total. Of these 423 MRI-visible lesions, 353 were PIRADs 4/5, and 70 PIRADs 3. Regarding location, 55 were restricted to the anterior gland, 280 were only posterior; 92 were basal, 241 mid, and 90 apical; 310 were lateral, and 113 crossing midline. GGG≥2 PCa was detected in lesions with an anterior component in 34/41 (82.9%) for LATP versus 35/47 (74.5%) TRUS (OR 1.67, 95%CI 0.59-4.73, p=0.336), posterior lesions in 114/149 (76.5%) LATP versus 106/146 (72.6%) TRUS (OR 1.23, 95%CI 0.73-2.08, p=0.441). For lesions located solely anteriorly, GGG≥2 was detected in 20/24 (83.3%) LATP versus 21/31 (67.7%) TRUS (OR 2.38, 95%CI 0.64-8.84, p=0.188) and for solely posteriorly 98/126 (77.7%) LATP versus 88/127 (69.3%) TRUS (OR 1.55, 95% 0.88-2.73, p=0.126). For apical lesions we observed GGG≥2 in 38/46 (82.6%) in LATP versus 22/38 (57.9%) in TRUS (OR 3.46, 95%CI 1.27-9.37, p=0.013). For basal lesions it was 31/43 (72.1%) LATP versus 27/41 (65.8%) TRUS (OR 1.34, 95% 0.53-3.39, p=0.536) and for mid-gland it was 81/104 (77.9%) LATP versus 87/113 (76.9%) TRUS (OR 1.05, 95%CI 0.56-1.99, p=0.875) lesions. Overall, LATP demonstrated higher detection in every location, but only apical lesions reached statistical significance in this cohort. CONCLUSIONS: Initial analysis of single centre data from the TRANSLATE RCT indicate MRI-visible apical prostate lesions are better sampled by LATP versus TRUS biopsy, when considering detection of GGG≥2 PCa.

title: DIAGNOSTIC PERFORMANCE OF PROSTATE MRI-BASED ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE MODELS IN DETECTING CANCER: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Jie Li, Pan Zang, Chao Liang, Lei Ding, Chesong Zhao, Zhentao Tang, Yibo Li, Zhisheng Guo, Jianrui Zeng
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Artificial intelligence (AI) is actively being explored as a transformative technology in modern medicine, particularly in MRI-based prostate cancer (PCa) prediction. The growing number of models demonstrating technical feasibility prompts the need for a comprehensive evaluation of their performance, generalizability and clinical utility. METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis was performed in accordance with the Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging (CLAIM-2024) and PRISMA-Diagnostic Test Accuracy (PRISMA-DTA) guidelines. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library on February 28, 2025 to identify English-language studies published starting from January 1, 2017, on the development of MRI-based machine learning (ML) or deep learning (DL) models with independent testing cohorts for predicting PCa. RESULTS: After screening 5090 retrieved articles, 50 studies involving 8078 patients were included in the meta-analysis. Compared with the clinically evaluated Prostate Imaging-Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS v2.1) score (SUCRA=0.247), AI prediction models, particularly DL models (SUCRA=0.966), exhibited superior efficacy in predicting PCa at the patient level (AUROC=0.95, 95%CI: 0.93-0.97). Furthermore, these models demonstrated diagnostic performance comparable to that of senior radiologists. When used independently, AI models exhibit excellent specificity (mean: 0.698±0.16); when deployed as a clinical adjunct, AI models can significantly improve radiologists’ sensitivity in detecting csPCa (mean: 0.907±0.03) (Figure). CONCLUSIONS: AI models demonstrate high accuracy in PCa detection, offering significant advantages for both large-scale, standalone screening and clinician-assisted diagnosis of aggressive disease. To fully realize this potential, future efforts should focus on the development of deep learning-based models by integrating multi-modal omics technologies, followed by their rigorous validation in multi-center, large-scale real-world datasets. This will facilitate the establishment of standardized AI-assisted diagnostic workflows of "AI-first read, physician-verification", thereby mitigating current challenges of both ”over-reliance” and ”under-utilization”.

title: DETECTION RATE OF PROSTATE CANCER USING PROSTATE-SPECIFIC MEMBRANE ANTIGEN/ULTRASOUND-FUSION BIOPSY IN PATIENTS WITH SUSPECTED RECURRENCE OR INCONCLUSIVE/NEGATIVE BIOPSIES: A SINGLE-CENTER RETROSPECTIVE STUDY
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Wayne G. Brisbane, Koichiro Kimura, Adrien Holzgreve, Vinicius Ludwig, Lena Unterrainer, Jacqueline De La Torre, Samantha Gonzalez, Johannes Czernin, Leonard S. Marks, Jeremie Calais
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)/ultrasound (US)-fusion biopsy may improve the detection of prostate cancer (PCa). This study evaluated its diagnostic performance, with the primary outcome being the PCa detection rate and the secondary outcome assessing the association between PSMA positron emission tomography (PET)–derived parameters and biopsy results. METHODS: We analyzed patients with suspected recurrent PCa or prior inconclusive/negative biopsies who underwent PSMA PET/CT as standard-of-care imaging to guide PSMA/US-fusion biopsy at UCLA (April 2021–April 2025). Lesion contouring was performed using dedicated software (ProFuse), and real-time fusion biopsy (Artemis) was conducted by an expert urologist. Detection rates were evaluated at the patient and lesion levels. SUVmax differences between PCa and non-PCa lesions and lesion-level detection across PRIMARY scores were retrospectively analyzed. Subgroup analyses compared detection rates by clinical background (post-non-surgical treatment vs. treatment-naïve). RESULTS: Sixty-two patients with 89 lesions were analyzed. Median PSA was 8.3 ng/dL (IQR, 4.2–13.8), and 36 (58%) were post-non-surgical treatment, most commonly cryoablation (36%). Twenty-six patients were treatment-naïve, and 13 were under active surveillance. Median Gleason grade found on biopsy was 3 (IQR, 2–3). Median SUVmax of target lesions was 6.35 (IQR, 5.33–8.41). Detection rates were 66% (41/62) at the patient level and 58% (52/89) at the lesion level. PCa lesions showed higher SUVmax (8.03 vs. 5.93; p<0.001) and higher PRIMARY scores, with detection increasing from 14% (score 2) to 80% (score 5) (p=0.0072, Cochran–Armitage trend test). Subgroup analysis suggested slightly lower detection in post-treatment lesions compared to treatment-naïve status (patient 64% vs. 69%, p=0.78; lesion 55% vs. 63%, p=0.52). CONCLUSIONS: PSMA/US-fusion biopsy shows favorable diagnostic performance and clinical utility in identifying PCa lesions in a more challenging subset of patients. Considering PSMA PET parameters and patient background may help optimize lesion targeting.

title: PREDICTING GLEASON GRADE GROUP AT RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY: A MACHINE LEARNING APPROACH FOR PROSTATE CANCER RISK STRATIFICATION
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Lampros Pantazis, Hersh H. Bendre, Madhur Nayan, Constantine Velmahos, Clemens An, Alexandra Hunter, Douglas M. Dahl, Chin-Lee Wu, Matthew Wszolek, Keyan Salari, Adam S. Feldman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate biopsy remains associated with significant rates of prostate cancer grade misclassification which can adversely impact risk stratification (RS) and clinical management. To address this limitation, we aimed to develop machine learning (ML) models to predict prostate cancer grade group (GG) at radical prostatectomy (RP). METHODS: Patients who underwent RP were identified in our institutional TRUS fusion prostate biopsy database (2014-2021). We defined a 3-class ordinal outcome measure: GG1, GG2-3, or GG4-5 on RP. The cohort was split into training and test sets (75/25%). Feature selection among the available demographic, clinical, imaging and pathology variables, was performed using the importance scores obtained from an ordinal LightGBM model. Seven ML models were trained and optimized using 5-fold cross-validation. Model performance was evaluated on the test set and compared with permutation tests against biopsy GG and NCCN Risk Group, where low, intermediate, and high risk predicted GG1, GG2-3, and GG4-5, respectively. Performance was assessed with the quadratic weighted kappa (QWK), mean absolute error (MAE), accuracy and macro F1 score. RESULTS: A total of 535 patients were identified, of which 82 (15.3%) had GG1, 368 (68.7%) GG2-3, and 85 (15.8%) GG4-5 prostate cancer at RP. The biopsy misclassification rate was 25.4% (136/535), with 15% (80) upgrading and 10.4% (56) downgrading at RP. Important predictive features included age, highest biopsy GG, primary biopsy target GG and maximum positive core length, PSA density, and a weighted score calculated as the sum of the number of biopsy regions per GG, each multiplied by its GG value. The best performance was achieved by the ExtraTrees and AdaBoost models adapted for ordinal outcomes with a QWK of 0.738 (95% CI: 0.619 - 0.832) and 0.734 (95% CI: 0.613 - 0.836), respectively. Both models significantly outperformed NCCN Risk Group (QWK=0.637 (0.483 \- 0.753), p=0.02, 0.026) and biopsy GG (QWK=0.632 (0.467 - 0.754), p=0.01, 0.037) (Figure). CONCLUSIONS: Our models demonstrated strong overall predictive ability outperforming biopsy GG and NCCN Risk Group in predicting prostate cancer GG at RP. These findings highlight the potential of ML models as future risk calculators to enhance RS and improve guidance of prostate cancer management.

title: MACHINE LEARNING-BASED RADIOMICS FOR PRECISION DIAGNOSIS IN REPEAT PROSTATE BIOPSIES
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Zhentao Tang, Jie Li, Chao Liang, Lei Ding, Pan Zang, Chesong Zhao, Yibo Li, Zhisheng Guo, Jianrui Zeng
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: A significant clinical challenge in current prostate cancer diagnosis is the risk of false-negative results from the initial biopsy. Following a negative initial biopsy, there is a lack of standardized assessment protocols for active surveillance strategies or for determining the necessity of a repeat biopsy. Furthermore, there is limited research on ML models that predict missed diagnoses based on MR imaging and biopsy pathology data. This study aims to address the need for precision diagnostics by developing a machine learning model that integrates radiomics features to provide early warning of missed diagnoses, predict high-risk regions, and guide the decision for repeat biopsies. METHODS: This study employed a single-center design. We enrolled patients with a PI-RADS score of ≤3, treated at Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital between 2019 and 2023, who had complete clinical data (including mp-MRI images and biopsy/radical prostatectomy pathology results). Patients who underwent repeat biopsies were specifically included. Collected data encompassed clinical information, laboratory test reports, prior medical records, imaging, and pathology data, including age, PSA levels, medical history, prostate volume, PI-RADS score (v2.0), and biopsy/radical prostatectomy pathology findings. All enrolled patients underwent mp-MRI examination prior to biopsy. The images were independently reviewed by two experienced radiologists who assigned PI-RADS scores. Radiomic features were then extracted from the manually delineated lesions on mp-MRI images. Patients were randomly allocated to the model's training set and internal validation set. A machine learning model was developed by integrating the extracted radiomic features with clinical data. Feature selection was performed to identify the most predictive features. The dataset was randomly split into training and testing sets in a 6:4 ratio. The model's diagnostic performance was evaluated on the test set, reporting the Area Under the Curve and the Youden index. Finally, the model's efficacy was validated using imaging data from the repeat biopsy cohort. RESULTS: The study enrolled 894 patients with PI-RADS scores ≤ 3 and complete clinical data, including 89 who underwent repeat biopsies. The machine learning model demonstrated robust performance in predicting prostate cancer diagnosis. In the validation set, it achieved an AUC of 0.922 (95% CI: 0.809-1.000), a sensitivity of 0.792, and a specificity of 1.000.; these results were confirmed in the test set with an AUC of 0.875 (95% CI: 0.850-0.950), a sensitivity of 0.858, and a specificity of 0.804 For diagnosing clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa), the model also showed high accuracy, with an AUC of 0.978 (95% CI: 0.975-0.981), sensitivity of 0.958, and specificity of 0.750 in the validation set, and an AUC of 0.877 (95% CI: 0.837-0.918), sensitivity of 0.813, and specificity of 0.814 in the test set. CONCLUSIONS: The machine learning model utilizing radiomics data from patients with PI-RADS scores ≤3 demonstrated superior performance in predicting repeat biopsy outcomes compared to traditional radiomics prediction models.

title: IMAGING-DERIVED RADIOMIC FEATURES AS PREDICTIVE MARKERS OF GLEASON SCORE ASSESSMENT IN PROSTATE CANCER
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Savannah R. Duenweg, Michael J. Barrett, Samuel A. Bobholz, Allison K. Lowman, Aleksandra Winiarz, Biprojit Nath, Hope M. Reecher, Fitzgerald Kyereme, Kenneth A. Iczkowski, Stephanie Vincent-Sheldon, Kathleen Bhatt, Katherine Troy, Michael Kim, Eric Fair, William A. Hall, Andrew S. Nencka, Peter S. La Violette
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate cancer (PCa) comprises one-third of new male cancers. While MP-MRI offers non-invasive tumor characterization, visual assessment shows limited concordance with pathology. Computational texture analysis from medical imaging offers extraction of quantitative information beyond human perception. This study sought to determine if MRI feature extraction could distinguish histological grade groups. METHODS: We analyzed 244 patients with PCa who underwent prostatectomy. T2WI and ADC maps were acquired; T2WI were z-score normalized using patient-specific prostate masks. Digitized whole slide images (n=732) were Gleason annotated (G3, G4, and G5), and non-linearly aligned to the T2WI. Mean MRI intensities and 107 radiomic features were extracted per grade and normal tissue. Kruskal-Wallis with post-hoc Dunn’s tests assessed inter-grade differences. Pearson correlations with FDR p<0.001, evaluated histology-MRI relationships. RESULTS: Kruskal-Wallis analyses revealed 104 (T2WI) and 106 (ADC) features significantly differing across Gleason grades (FDR< 0.001). Additionally, 102 and 104 features, respectively, significantly correlated with Gleason scores (T2WI/ADC median \|ρ\|=0.54, 0.57; both max ρ=0.80) ( Fig 1). Notably, T2WI intensity showed no correlation with Gleason grade, whereas ADC was negatively correlated (ρ=-0.28, Fig 2). CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that quantitative radiomic features extracted from MP-MRI correlate with Gleason patterns. Texture features captured biologically relevant tissue characteristics beyond visual assessment. The inverse ADC-Gleason relationship, coupled with non-significant T2WI intensity correlations, highlights the complementary value MP-MRI in characterizing PCa aggressiveness. These findings suggest radiomics can be used a non-invasive tool for predicting histopathological grade and improve prostate cancer assessment.

title: THE INFLUENCE OF GERMLINE PATHOGENIC VARIANTS IN DNA REPAIR GENES ON A COHORT OF PATIENTS WHO UNDERWENT CURATIVESURGERY FOR PROSTATE CANCER
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Benedetto Calabrese, Giuseppe Chiarelli, Alessio Finocchiaro, Pier Paolo Avolio, Marco Paciotti, Rosanna Asselta, Giulia Soldà, Pietro Cavalli, Miriam Cieri, Piergiuseppe Colombo, NicolòMaria Buffi, Giovanni Lughezzani, Vittorio Fasulo, Massimo Lazzeri
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Family history represents a significant risk factor for prostate cancer (PCa), emphasizing its genetic basis. Early identification ofgermline pathogenic variants (PVs) in DNA repair genes (DRGs) is crucial for timely PCa diagnosis, prognosis, and for informing at-risk relatives. Conversely, the presence of variants of uncertain significance (VUS) has been associated with worse clinicaloutcomes. This study aimed to assess how the presence of germline PVs and VUS affect clinical and pathological outcomes in amonocentric cohort of patients who underwent robot-assisted laparoscopic prostatectomy (RALP) for PCa. METHODS: This prospective study, supported by AIRC - Fondazione AIRC per la Ricerca sul Cancro (registered and emended with the numberID-IG-25027-V1.3), was conducted at a tertiary referral center in collaboration with the Departments of Oncology, Urology, Pathology,Radiology, and Medical Genetics. A total of 179 men aged 58–70 years who underwent RALP for localized PCa were screened forgermline PVs and VUS in DRGs prior to surgery. Patients were enrolled if they had an ISUP grade ≥3 at biopsy and/or a confirmedPCa diagnosis at ≤50 years of age. Individuals harboring a VUS or PVs were compared to those with negative genetic results. RESULTS: Of the 179 patients screened between 2021 and 2024, 162 shared the results of genetic testing. Median age at surgery did not differ between groups (65 years, IQR 59–70). Among them, 114 (69.9%) tested negative, while 39 (29.4%) and 9 (5%) carried a VUS orPVs in DRGs, respectively. The most frequent VUS involved ATM (22.2%), CHEK2 (15.6%), BRCA2 (13.3%), ATR (6.7%), NBN(6.7%), RAD51D (6.7%), and MSH6 (4.4%). The nine PVs identified were: BRCA2, PALB2 + NBN, PALB2 + BRCA2, BRCA1PALB2, CHEK2 + PMS2, CHEK2, and ATM. A family history of cancer was reported in 50% of VUS/PV carriers compared to 34.6%of non-carriers. High-grade PCa (ISUP > 3) was found in 46.3% of carriers versus 38.0% of non-carriers. A pathological stage ≥pT3a occurred in 53.6% of carriers versus 45.1% of non-carriers, while nodal involvement (pN1) was more frequent among carriers(21.4% vs 12.6%). Biochemical recurrence (BCR) occurred in 36.8% of carriers versus 30.4% of non-carriers. CONCLUSIONS: This study provides valuable insight into the role of germline VUS, by the first, and PVs in DRGs among PCa patients, suggestingthat such variants may confer a less favorable disease course. Although differences did not reach statistical significance, carrierstended to present with higher-grade and more advanced disease at final pathology. Genetic screening for PCa may therefore aid notonly in early detection among high-risk individuals but also in guiding clinical management and follow-up strategies.

title: DISCOVERY OF A RECURRENT FRAMESHIFT ASHKENAZI JEWISH FOUNDER MUTATION (F>2FS) IN THE PARPI-SENSITIVE MMS22L GENE ASSOCIATED WITH INCREASING RISK OF PROSTATE CANCER
session: Prostate Cancer: Detection & Screening I (PD06)
authors: Nathan Graham, William B. Isaacs, Jun Wei, Marta Gielzak, Qiang Wang, Nathan A. Snyder, S. Lilly Zheng, Guifang Yan, Lucy Lu, Valentina Engelmann, Daniel Rabizadeh, Polina Sysa-Shah, Brandon Cornell, Zhuqing Shi, Huy Tran, Shawn Lupold, Tamara Lotan, Oluwademilade Dairo, Patrick C. Walsh, Brian T. Helfand, Jim Lu, Jun Luo, Kathleen A. Cooney, Jianfeng Xu
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Most established prostate cancer (PCa) susceptibility genes (e. g., BRCA2) are involved in DNA repair with a subset involved in PARP inhibitor (PARPi). We systematically tested association of newly reported 65 genes in these pathways with PCa risk. METHODS: Ancestry-specific association between loss-of-function (LoF) germline variants in these genes and PCa risk was first tested between PCa patients from Johns Hopkins University (Hopkins) and population controls from the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD). Results were confirmed in additional three PCa patient cohorts and UK Biobank (UKB). RESULTS: Among men of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry (ASJ), the carrier rate of LoF mutations in MMS22L was significantly higher in 469 Hopkins cases than 5,573 gnomAD controls. The association was confirmed in the UKB. In the combined analysis of all cohorts, the carrier rate of F722fs, an ASJ founder mutation, was 1.5% in cases vs 0.31% in controls, Odds Ratio (OR)=4.9 (95% confidence interval: 2.1-10.6), PFisher=1.44E-04. Furthermore, carriers had a significantly higher proportion of aggressive disease (83%) than non-carriers (27%), OR=12.3 (2.2-132.5), PFirth=0.003. Another founder mutation in non-Finnish European (NFE), c.340+1G>A, was also significantly associated with PCa risk in the UKB; OR=7.7 (2.6-21.0), PFirth=5.10E-04. Somatic DNA analysis and response to therapeutic PARPi need to be characterized. CONCLUSIONS: We provide suggestive evidence that MMS22L is a novel major PCa susceptibility gene. Its carrier rate and effect size are similar to that of BRCA2. If validated, it can be used for risk stratification of PCa risk and aggressiveness.

title: THE SCALPEL AND SPOTLIGHT: HARRY W. MARTIN, THE UROLOGIST WHO TREATED HOLLYWOOD
session: History of Urology Forum (HF01)
authors: Dhruv Puri, William S. Azar, Aurora J. Grutman, Isaac E. Kim
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Dr. Harry W. Martin (1890-1951) was a Los Angeles urologist whose career bridged surgical innovation and the Golden Age of film. After a decade of academic work on bladder surgery and anesthesia, he became Medical Director of Twentieth Century Fox Studios in 1937, bringing urologic medicine to Hollywood. METHODS: Primary publications by Martin in JAMA and California and Western Medicine, along with contemporary news archives, studio-medicine accounts, and biographical records, were reviewed to reconstruct his transition from clinician to studio physician and analyze his contributions to early occupational health within the film industry. RESULTS: Martin’s early urologic career reflected the procedural rigor of interwar surgery, but his Hollywood tenure marked a new domain of clinical influence. At Twentieth Century Fox, Martin managed urinary and reproductive health for actors and production staff at a time when sexually transmitted infections threatened both employment and reputation. He instituted confidential screening programs, routine urinalysis, and early antibiotic therapy that paralleled the discipline’s emerging standards for venereal and genitourinary disease. Studio records and press accounts describe his discreet “sick call” system, including private house visits for leading actors, on-set hydration and recovery clinics, and consultation on scenes depicting medical treatment or fainting episodes. Martin also oversaw injury care for stagehands exposed to caustic film chemicals and devised rest protocols for male leads recovering from pelvic or hernia surgery before returning to set. His approach prefigured modern occupational medicine, embedding urologic practice into the entertainment industry’s welfare infrastructure. Through his marriage to gossip columnist Louella Parsons, Martin mediated the boundary between confidentiality and celebrity, shaping how illness and masculinity were portrayed in mid-century media. His dual identity – urologist and Hollywood physician – made urinary and sexual health a behind-the-scenes concern of the film industry. CONCLUSIONS: Dr. Harry W. Martin’s career illustrates how urology influenced cultural narratives of health, discretion, and performance in Hollywood.

title: ARNOLD M. BELKER: IN REMEMBRANCE OF ONE OF THE ARCHITECTS OF MODERN VASECTOMY REVERSAL AND MICROSURGICAL TRAINING
session: History of Urology Forum (HF01)
authors: Evan J. Panken, Daniel R. Greenberg, Hriday P. Bhambhvani, Nicholas A. Deebel, Joshua A. Halpern, Robert E. Brannigan
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Following the recent passing of Dr. Arnold M. Belker (1934-2023), a pioneer in male reproductive urology, we examine his work on microsurgical vasectomy reversal techniques, which marked a significant shift in male reproductive surgery. This paper explores the professional life and enduring legacy of Dr. Belker, whose work at the University of Louisville defined the technical standards and training methodologies for contemporary vasectomy reversal and other male reproductive microsurgeries. METHODS: We reviewed primary sources, including Dr. Belker’s seminal publications in _Fertility and Sterility_ and _The Journal of Urology_, institutional records from the professional societies of which he was a long-standing contributor, as well as secondary sources including biographical articles and obituaries. RESULTS: Dr. Belker was a thought leader in the field of male reproductive urology, championing the transition from macroscopic to microscopic vasectomy reversal. He made immense contributions throughout his career, including authoring numerous articles and book chapters, working as a member of three different AUA Guideline committees, and through his extensive work teaching microsurgical techniques to others. His seminal contributions were as head of the Vasovasostomy Study Group, a collaboration among five institutions reporting results from 1,469 microsurgical vasectomy reversals. This landmark paper demonstrated that microsurgical technique achieved high patency rates and highlighted the importance of the obstructive interval and intra-operative vasal fluid examination. This work encouraged interest in urologic microsurgery and helped establish microsurgical vasectomy reversal as the evidence-based gold standard. Dr. Belker was also instrumental in disseminating these complex microsurgical techniques through his formal, hands-on training courses for urologists, notably the course he taught at the annual AUA meeting for 30 years. CONCLUSIONS: Dr. Arnold Belker is remembered as an authoritative voice, mentor, innovator, and educator in the field of male reproduction. His work continues to shape current vasectomy reversal practices and standardized training. His lasting impact is underscored by the three distinguished service awards he received from the Society for the Study of Male Reproduction, the American Society of Andrology, and the Society of Reproductive Surgeons. We hope this brief history highlights a giant in the field of Urology who profoundly influenced both patients and practitioners.

title: HENRY BUGBEE’S EPONYMOUS ELECTRODE
session: History of Urology Forum (HF01)
authors: George K. Siodis, Trevor C. Hunt, Ronald Rabinowitz
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Bugbee electrode is used widely in urology for tasks such as basic fulguration and treating small bladder tumors, and its utility has even spread to other fields such as otolaryngology. Yet, few who use it today are familiar with the history of its origins or the man behind its name. Herein, we present the Bugbee electrode’s birth and evolution into a household name. METHODS: We performed a literature review, using online repositories and internet searches to identify pertinent sources such as book chapters and peer-reviewed articles, to inform this historical review. RESULTS: Therapeutic uses of electrical current are documented as early as the 18th and 19th centuries. However, in 1910, urologist Edwin Beer forever altered the course of urology by threading a monopolar Oudin cauterizer through his cystoscope. A flurry of innovation ensued, with early pioneers including Hugh H. Young using the technology to define new ways of treating urologic pathologies. Henry Bugbee himself ventured into the fray in 1913 when he began publishing extensively on his and others’ use of “high frequency spark” in treating prostatic obstruction. His seminal paper on the topic, published in 1917 and read at the AUA’s 16th annual meeting that year, was titled “The use of the high frequency spark in the treatment of median bar obstruction.” This remains the default citation in current works describing the origins of Bugbee’s now-ubiquitous electrode, though the eponym itself likely did not arise right away. In 1919, for example, Louis Jacobs wrote that he “followed the treatment of Bugbee” in describing fulguration with a small, insulated electrode inserted cystoscopically. While few primary sources exist to detail an exact timeline, it is likely that the term “Bugbee electrode” formally entered urology’s lexicon over the ensuing years as innovation continued and the electrode’s applications grew. For example, in 1926, Hermon Bumpus Jr. modified William Braasch’s cystoscope (itself a refinement of Young’s prostatic punch) to incorporate a Bugbee electrode for improved hemostasis and visualization. By the 1930s, accounts of the Braasch-Bumpus instrument were mentioning the Bugbee electrode by name when detailing the scope’s components. Written references continued through the 1940s, and now over 100 years later the Bugbee electrode remains a household name in urology. CONCLUSIONS: Alongside huge advances in urologic technology over the past century, Bugbee’s simple yet effective electrode has remained ubiquitous and, among his many other contributions and achievements, immortalized his name in urologic practice.

title: FORKED TONGUE CRUSHER OF STONE: A MYSTERY OF THE DIDUSCH MUSEUM
session: History of Urology Forum (HF01)
