authors: Soum D. Lokeshwar, Marjorie Johnson, Philipp Korn, Mark Essien, Craig Cronin, Carlos A. Rivera Lopez, Sunil H. Patel, Christian P. Pavlovich
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Surgical instruments span >2500 years and have rapidly evolved, with earlier instruments being almost unidentifiable in the modern day. Unidentified instruments are often donated to University museums and the Didusch Center for Urologic History. We sought to determine the purpose of one such donated instrument. METHODS: The instrument was loaned to us by the Didusch Museum head archivist. We surveyed urology faculty at Johns Hopkins, Yale and the University of Pennsylvania and queried the archives of Johns Hopkins History of Medicine Institute and relevant online catalogs. RESULTS: The instrument is a long nickel-plated steel straight shaft ending in a coude or angulated jaw, approximately 35-40 cm in length and 20 fr in outer diameter. The distal end is comprised of opposing jaws: the lower having a scoop shape with a right angle lip and the upper with a smaller lipped right angle jaw. A slightly curved “forked tongue” stylet can independently be advanced between the jaws. Proximally, the instrument has a palm plate, a finger guard and a thin knurled wheel. Construction is a three part concentric sliding system in a sheath fashion: the outer lower scooped jaw which contains the inscription “LÜER” along the palm plate, the upper scooped jaw and the innermost bifurcated stylet. Structure and comparators identify it as a late 19th – early 20th century LÜER lithotrite designed for cystolitholapaxy. The instrument was blindly inserted transurethrally where the jaws were then opened and within the jaws, the right angled lip would allow the stone to be trapped. Advancing the knurled wheel would allow for the jaws to close and the bifurcated stylet would engage and split the stone, similar to the Bigelow and the Weiss lithotrites. Georg Wilhelm Amatus Lüer (1802-1883) was a German born maker of surgical instruments who lived in Paris. His son-in-law Hermann Adolf Wulfing- Lüer advanced these designs and invented the precursor to the Luer-Lok. CONCLUSIONS: Detailed identification and archival review can highlight the historical and modern significance of surgical ingenuity and the timeless mission to decrease disease morbidity.

title: LEONARD PAUL WERSHUB, M. D. AND HISTORY OF UROLOGY
session: History of Urology Forum (HF01)
authors: Erin Schnell, Michael E. Moran
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Leonard Paul Wershub (1901-1969) was a New York City urologist and urohistorian. He chose to work at a homeopathic hospital and medical school but had a long and successful academic/clinical career at New York Medical College. METHODS: A review of all writings by and about Leonard Paul Wershub were pursued and the archivists at the New York Medical College were consulted and archives accessed. His five textbooks were also sought and all primary materials in urology were read. RESULTS: Dr. Wershub became a urologist at New York Medical College from 1925 till his death in 1968. The Archivist at NYMC was massively helpful in tracking down all personal materials on him and his urological practice. Dr. Wershub wrote five major textbooks, never rising to national prominence, possibly due to his clinical location. CONCLUSIONS: Wershub’s historical contribution was the first U. S. full textbook history of urology entitled Urology From Antiquity to the 20th Century. Published in 1970, a full two years prior to the much more heralded Leonard J. T. Murphy work. In 16 chapters we have a urologic history unique and different from others to come. Much thanks must be expressed to Nicholas Webb, Archivist at NYMC in New York City. He opened all of the archival collections for us to pursue the life and legacy of Dr. Wershub.

title: THE MAN BEHIND THE MANEUVER: ROBERT J. PRENTISS MD
session: History of Urology Forum (HF01)
authors: Joanna Orzel, Andrea Rossman, Ryan Steinberg
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The Prentiss surgical maneuver is ubiquitously known in any pediatric urology operating room; however, the man behind it is not. We highlight the life and career of Robert J. Prentiss M. D., including and beyond his initial publication of the Prentiss maneuver. METHODS: Primary and secondary sources were reviewed. The Prentiss Family Papers, which include personal correspondence, scientific writings, and memorabilia from his career are housed in the Iowa Women’s Archives and were assessed. RESULTS: Dr. Prentiss was born in Iowa City, IA, the youngest of five children to Lué Bradley and Dr. Henry Prentiss, founder of the Department of Anatomy. He attended the University of Iowa where he obtained his medical degree in 1934 and stayed to complete his residency (and later remained as faculty) under Dr. Nathaniel Alcock. He went on to the San Diego County Hospital where he was the acting chairman of the Division of Urology until 1968. During this time, he published on a variety of topics, including ureteral injury, Papanicolau smears for bladder cancer, and radical perineal prostatectomy. He also established a urology residency program using a community-based model. His eponymous publication, titled “Medical and Surgical Treatment of Cryptorchidism” was published in the American Medical Association (AMA) Archives of Surgery in 1955 and presented at the Section of Urology during the 103rd Annual Meeting of the AMA in San Francisco in 1954 on a trifold posterboard ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191340.67063.51.06#F1)). Besides berating his colleagues for “general disregard of basic principles and poor technical execution of the operation,” Prentiss described his approach to gain more length on the spermatic cord in 18 steps and through careful illustration. In his spare time, Prentiss enjoyed going on fishing trips filled with “imbibing of strong beverages.” His companions were known to document each day of the trip, mostly with descriptions on the quantity and type of alcohol they consumed. His role as a devoted father to his daughters is memorialized through his correspondence, advocating on their behalf. He gave talks, moderated panels, and attended conferences essentially through the year of his death in 1972. CONCLUSIONS: Although the eponym is associated with pediatric urology, Dr. Prentiss made many contributions to the early and burgeoning field of urology. His impact should not be minimized to only testicular descent.

title: OSWALD S. LOWSLEY, M. D.: A PIONEER IN PROSTATE ANATOMY AND UROLOGIC SURGICAL TECHNIQUE
session: History of Urology Forum (HF01)
authors: Megan M. Roedel, David R. Paolone
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Oswald S. Lowsley, M.D. (1884-1955) was an internationally known urologist whose work significantly advanced the anatomy, surgical treatment, and instrumentation of the prostate and urinary tract. METHODS: A review of all photos of and writings by and about Oswald Swinney Lowsley were sought and studied. Photos were provided by the AUA _William P. Didusch Center for Urologic History_. RESULTS: Oswald S. Lowsley completed his medical training at Johns Hopkins University in 1912, during which he began detailed studies of prostate anatomy, leading to publications in 1912 and 1915 on embryologic mapping of prostate lobular structure and growth during aging, which influenced later models of prostate zonal anatomy. He completed his internship at Bellevue Hospital and then served as a lieutenant surgeon in the U. S. Navy from 1917-1918 during the First World War before beginning his career in New York. During his time in practice, Dr. Lowsley developed several innovative operative techniques, including the use of ribbon gut for re-approximation of the renal capsule after nephrolithotomy. He also designed new surgical instruments such as the self-named Lowsley retractor, historically used in perineal prostatectomy for manipulation of the prostate gland. Dr. Lowsley was the author of several textbooks including “A Textbook of Urology” and “Embryology of the Prostate.” He was also a prominent leader in urology by serving as the first director of the department of urology at the New York Hospital and as the American Urological Association president from 1941-1942. He traveled extensively in the US and internationally to teach prior to his death in 1955 from a myocardial infarction. CONCLUSIONS: Oswald Swinney Lowsley was a pioneer in advancing the understanding of urologic anatomy, refining operative techniques, and furthering education in urology in the first half of the 20th century.

title: PROSTATE CANCER, WILLIAM H. WELCH AND UROLOGY
session: History of Urology Forum (HF01)
authors: Malone Locke, Michael E. Moran
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: William Henry Welch (Popsy, 1850-1934) lived and died in the “heroic age” of medicine at the Johns Hopkins Medical School. Welch was the first named Professor and became the first Dean of the Medical School. He also was pivotal in the appointment of Hugh Young as the second urologist at Johns Hopkins who consulted on Welch in his final illness from prostate cancer. We are interested here in the many interactions between Welch and urologists at the nascent Johns Hopkins. METHODS: We reviewed much biographic literature on all aspects of the life, writings, and terminal illness of William H. Welch, especially concerning his affiliation with urology at Johns Hopkins. Welch died of advanced prostate cancer at Johns Hopkins Hospital in 1934 following a long hospitalization. A Chesney Archive approved investigation of Welch’s personal medical records during his terminal illness from prostate cancer is the basis of this research project. RESULTS: The Welch hospital records during his final illness are very illuminating. He was admitted with a diagnosis of prostate cancer, he appears to have known this himself having been seen personally by Hugh Young prior to admission. There is no known family history of his multi-physician probands. Young wrote a letter to Harvey Cushing explaining his complex pathway to death, his acceptance of his illness and his urologic surgical interventions. CONCLUSIONS: Welch was admitted to his beloved Johns Hopkins Hospital, but sadly never left. He died quietly in the hospital that he had labored so mightily to make great. He had bouts of uremia, sepsis, and urinary retention throughout his slightly year-long hospitalization. His body, sadly with no autopsy, was returned to the family plot in Connecticut where his potentially bone-riddled metastatic skeleton lies alongside of his ancestors, many a generation of physicians. One cannot escape the irony that Welch himself, studied with F. D. Von Recklinghausen (1833-1910) who first reported osteoblastic bone metastases from prostate cancer.

title: FROM FATAL INJURY TO SURGICAL SUCCESS: THE EVOLUTION OF BLADDER RUPTURE MANAGEMENT
session: History of Urology Forum (HF01)
authors: Xiao J. Tong, Cairo F. Stanislaus, Daniela Diaz-Rubayo
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The earliest accessible reports of urinary bladder rupture following blunt abdominal trauma appeared in the London Medical and Physical Journal in 1826, marking the start of medical documentation of a once nearly fatal condition. This review traces the chronological evolution of the understanding of bladder rupture—from the first documented postmortem cases to the development of successful surgical repair and modern management principles. METHODS: A comprehensive historical review was conducted using primary medical literature from the early 19th to late 20th centuries. Case reports from the London Medical and Physical Journal, The Lancet, and other early sources were reviewed alongside analyses by MacCormac (1886), Carrol, and McAninch to outline the chronological progression in diagnosis and treatment of bladder rupture. RESULTS: In 1826, James Simpson, a 23-year-old man buried in a collapsed well, was found to have a pelvic fracture and bladder rupture during his autopsy. In early 1827, Thomas Doneghan, aged 22, sustained a similar injury after striking his lower abdomen against a post and subsequently died. Early management relied on intra-abdominal urine evacuation, which was largely unsuccessful. In 1886, Sir William MacCormac reported the first documented recoveries from intraperitoneal bladder rupture, marking a major turning point in urologic trauma care. With the advent of motor vehicles, mechanisms of injury shifted toward automobile-associated pelvic trauma. In 1929, Stirling and Belt described seven cases of traumatic bladder rupture with perivesical extravasation—five related to automobile accidents. Between 1976 and 1981, Carrol and McAninch’s work further clarified mechanisms and optimal repair strategies for intra- versus extraperitoneal ruptures, establishing principles that guide current management. CONCLUSIONS: Historically, understanding of bladder rupture advanced through keen observation and thoughtful investigation, as discoveries reshaped clinical management. The distinction between intra- and extra-peritoneal rupture became clearer with the rise of radiologic advancements, particularly retrograde urography in the early 20th century. These developments not only transformed a once-fatal condition into a readily repairable urologic emergency with excellent outcomes but also led to decreased social disruption, improved psychosocial recovery, and faster return to daily life, underscoring the vital role of radiology in modern urologic trauma care.

title: E. DARRACOTT VAUGHAN, JR, M. D. (1939-2016): BRIDGING SCIENCE AND SURGERY AS A PIONEERING LEADER IN UROLOGY
session: History of Urology Forum (HF01)
authors: Grace Chen, David Shin, Michael Stifelman, Ravi Munver
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: As April 2026 commemorates the 10-year anniversary of the passing of Dr. E. Darracott Vaughan, we aim to provide a brief life and career retrospective of a consummate gentleman and a pioneering leader in urology. METHODS: Research regarding Dr. Vaughan’s achievements was performed using sources from the AUA, PubMed which cataloged his extensive research endeavors, and testaments by his colleagues and mentees. RESULTS: Dr. Vaughan’s early life and career was situated in the Virginia amidst a medical family with a father, uncle, and two great grandfathers as physicians. He earned his B. A. from Washington and Lee University and his M. D. from University of Virginia School of Medicine. He completed residency at the University of Virginia, during which time he spent his first year in the laboratory studying renal physiology with emphasis on obstructive uropathy. That year changed his life as he realized that the lab year makes young physicians appreciate the literature, understand the scientific method, and practice better urology, particularly in this area of “evidence based decision making.” His interest in the renin and aldosterone system led him to a 2-year fellowship at Columbia Presbyterian Medical Center that was funded by the NIH. He would return to Virginia before he was asked to head the Division of Urology at what was then the New York Hospital-Cornell Medical Center in 1978 where he would maintain his role for over 20 years (1978-2001). In 1994, the division was elevated to department status. As the first Chairman of the Department of Urology at New York Presbyterian Hospital and Weill Cornell Medical College, holding the James J. Colt Professorship, Dr. Vaughan oversaw the transformation of his department into a national leader, as he forged himself as a true legend in the field nationally and internationally. Beyond his surgical and scientific accomplishments, Dr. Vaughan served in prominent leadership roles: President of the American Urological Association, the American Board of Urology, President Emeritus of the Urology Care Foundation (formerly the American Foundation for Urologic Disease), and Senior Associate Dean for Clinical Affairs at Weill Cornell. His prolific academic output—more than 250 peer-reviewed articles and over 70 book chapters—and his role as co-editor of the landmark text Campbell’s Urology underscore his commitment to knowledge dissemination. His accolades include the Gold Cystoscope Award, Hugh Hampton Young Award, Barringer Medal and Valentine Medal—each recognizing sustained excellence in the art and science of urology. While Dr. Vaughan’s extensive research portfolio, titles, and accoladed outline his vast contribution to urology, it is his dedication to his family and to mentoring the next generation of clinician-scientists that has cemented his legacy as a giant in the field. Under his tutelage, a number of distinguished academicians were able to ascertain prestigious positions throughout the country, including the current chair, vice chair, and vice chair of academics at our institution. CONCLUSIONS: E. Darracott Vaughan, Jr., MD, exemplified a rare blend of surgical mastery, research engagement, and institutional leadership. His legacy lives on not only in the department he shaped and the patients he treated, but in the many surgeons and scientists he inspired.

title: MANUFACTURING ANDROPAUSE: HOW MASCULINITY, MEDICINE, AND MARKETING MADE “LOW T”
session: History of Urology Forum (HF01)
authors: Stacy E. Piva, Ahmed Elauri, Jim K. Yee, Ha-Jung Kim, Jesse N. Mills, Sriram V. Eleswarapu
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Male aging involves no clear hormonal threshold. Testosterone often declines gradually, variably, and without dramatic physiological markers – a stark contrast to menopause, a universal and biologically programmed transition. The ambiguous role hormones play in the complex aging process has made declining testosterone levels irresistible to medical speculation, cultural anxiety, and commercial opportunity. This study traces the historical transformation of how the male climacteric, or andropause, evolved from a dubious endocrine diagnosis into a multi-billion-dollar market, and examines how this transformation shapes contemporary urologic practice. METHODS: We conducted a historical review and critical analysis of medical, epidemiologic, and sociocultural sources spanning 1813 through 2024, including early endocrinologic literature, the Massachusetts Male Aging Study, JAMA archives, pharmaceutical marketing campaigns, and FDA regulatory statements. We examined how language, diagnostic criteria, and cultural narratives surrounding testosterone and aging shifted over time. RESULTS: After synthetic testosterone was isolated in 1935, August A. Werner’s 1946 JAMA article proposed the male climacteric as a definable endocrine deficiency marked by fatigue, irritability, and diminished potency. Despite later research demonstrating that testosterone decline correlates more strongly with illness than normal aging, hormone replacement enthusiasm persisted. Postwar ideals linking masculinity to productivity and sexual vitality recast aging itself as a treatable condition. By the early 2000s, AbbVie’s “Is It Low T?” campaign reframed age-associated symptoms as evidence of hormonal deficiency, driving testosterone sales above $2 billion annually before FDA warnings restricted therapy to men with confirmed pathological hypogonadism. CONCLUSIONS: The andropause story reveals how cultural constructions of masculinity and market forces have long shaped and distorted definitions of male health. Understanding this history equips urologists to navigate patient expectations with evidence-based care, distinguishing the normal biology of aging from manufactured disease. This trajectory, from Werner’s “male climacteric” to AbbVie’s “Low T,” reflects a century-long negotiation between biology and belief, showing how medicine both mirrors and manufactures masculinity.

title: ORMOND’S DISEASE AND THE UROLOGISTS
session: History of Urology Forum (HF01)
authors: Mary Hunter Hyche, Michael E. Moran
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (RPF) is associated with two eponyms, Albarrán-Ormond’s disease. It was Albarrán that first noted the obstructive and destructive nature of this rare process, but Ormond clearly defined the peculiar, peri-aortic inflammatory manifestations, and tendency for ureteral involvement. METHODS: A review of all writings by and about retroperitoneal fibrosis since its first description by Albarrán in 1905 and Ormond’s cases in 1947 were pursued and studied. We also obtained modern knowledge of the now, widely known autoimmune nature of this process, and new innovative surgical methods of dealing with medical failures. RESULTS: About ½ of patients presenting with RPF have hydronephrosis that might require urinary diversion. Now about ½ of patients have abnormal IgG4 and these patients often have other autoimmune involvements. Medical therapy has become the first line of treatment still using non-specific corticosteroids, but rapidly expanding to other immune modifiers. A genetic abnormality has also been discovered and might lead to other medications. Though Albarrán is given first credit for recognizing this disease, Ormond also shares the prize of eponymous naming for his lucid explanations and correctly hypothesizing an ill-defined inflammatory etiology. CONCLUSIONS: Failures of medical therapy might still be broached by urologists as the ureterolysis and potential omental wrap can now be done robotically. Indocyanine green dye helps identify complex entrapments and vascular integrity of the ureter. We’ve come a long way since Albarrán and Ormond.

title: FIDELIS UDEH: EXPANDING THE LEGACY OF BLACK UROLOGISTS IN THE UNITED STATES
session: History of Urology Forum (HF01)
authors: Aurora J. Grutman, Arthur L. Burnett
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To reconstruct the career of Dr. Fidelis Nwankwo Udeh (1933–2007), a Nigerian-born urologist who trained at the Brady Urological Institute at Johns Hopkins in 1964, and situate his contributions within the broader, underacknowledged history of Black urologists in the United States and beyond. METHODS: This study draws on archival sources, published scholarship, and a conversation with Dr. Udeh’s son to document his professional trajectory and contributions. RESULTS: Udeh trained in the United States before returning to Nigeria, where he became a founding faculty member at the University of Nigeria School of Medicine and taught generations of physicians. His scholarly writings covered diverse urologic topics, but his lasting impact lay in institution-building and mentorship. His career illustrates how racism, segregation, and civil war shaped opportunities for African and African American urologists, while global networks of training and mentorship expanded the field’s reach. CONCLUSIONS: Recovering Udeh’s story challenges urologic histories that focus narrowly on the “firsts” and highlights the importance of diversity, resilience, and cross-border exchange in the development of urology.

title: THE EMERGENCE OF LABIAPLASTY IN UROLOGY
session: History of Urology Forum (HF01)
authors: Amanda Rubano, Dennis Phan, Matthew W. Cole, Ronald Rabinowitz
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urology has a long-standing history of modifying male genitalia, including piercing, pearling, and tattooing. In contrast, cosmetic female genital surgeries like labiaplasty have predominantly been conducted by gynecologists and plastic surgeons, with urology’s role being limited. This abstract examines the history of cosmetic female genital manipulation and the involvement of urologists in performing labiaplasty. METHODS: A historical literature review regarding cosmetic genital modification as far back as the 3rd century CE was carried out, focusing on cosmetic female genital manipulation, with emphasis on labiaplasty across different medical specialties. RESULTS: Urologic practice has an established history of cosmetic modifications to the male genitalia, as well as functional modifications, including penile prosthesis placement, with minimal opposition. Conversely, female aesthetic genital manipulation, especially labiaplasty, has faced controversy regarding its necessity, safety, and ethics for over 50 years. Cosmetic female genital manipulation has been documented as early as the 1950s in Germany with labial and clitoral piercings, whereas evidence of penile piercings date back to 3rd century CE in the Kama Sutra. Since the 1970s, labiaplasty has appeared in both plastic and gynecologic literature, but only recently in 2021, did it appear in a urologic context. In 1984, a case series documented women requesting labia minora reduction for aesthetic reasons. Refused by their gynecologists, some came to plastic surgeons, without mention of urologic participation, despite the specialty's area of expertise. A 2021 publication reported positive outcomes of labiaplasty performed by urogynecologists, marking a shift toward the procedure being performed by urologists. Despite these developments, research regarding the extent of urology’s role remains unknown. CONCLUSIONS: The expanding role of urologists in performing labiaplasty offers a promising opportunity to bridge aesthetic and functional management of external female genitalia within urology. Although under-explored, this emerging trend merits further investigation into safety and outcomes. Given urology’s historical acceptance of genital modifications in males, integrating female genital cosmetic procedures may transcend specialties and broaden the scope of urological practice.

title: RENAL STONES IN SPACE: ASTRONAUT PEGGY WHITSON'S LEGACY IN UROLOGIC RESEARCH
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Raeann M. Dalton, Stephanie Smith, David W. Sobel
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Dr. Peggy Annette Whitson, PhD (born Feb. 9, 1960), current astronaut at Axiom Space and former International Space Station (ISS) commander, is well known for her numerous accomplishments at NASA including the record of most cumulative days in space of any NASA astronaut. Less well known are her contributions to our current understanding of renal stone formation in the microgravity environment. Trained as a biochemist at Rice University earning a PhD in 1985, Whitson performed her early research in cell signaling and gene expression before transitioning to studies of human physiology and aerospace medicine at the Johnson Space Center, all while simultaneously working to achieve astronaut candidacy. One major area of focus was nephrolithiasis risk before, during, and after spaceflight, which has the ability to seriously disrupt and potentially abort spaceflight missions. Our objective is to reflect on Dr. Whitson’s contributions to urologic research and how it has set the groundwork for current projects in this field. METHODS: Biographical information was collected from primary and secondary sources. Whitson’s publication history from 1982-2025 was reviewed. RESULTS: Whitson has co-authored at least 13 original studies related to renal stone formation risk ranging from 1993-2009. Most studies were performed using 24-hour urine collection from human subjects before, during, and after spaceflight. Bedrest models were also implemented. Her studies demonstrate that increased stone formation risk occurs rapidly upon exposure to microgravity, and continues throughout space flights of 11-16 days duration and upon return. Potassium citrate has been shown to be an effective potential countermeasure to minimize risk of stone formation during missions. In addition, she has also been involved in early applications for diagnostic ultrasound on the ISS, which has demonstrated excellent anatomic fidelity and would allow remote clinical decision making. A series of studies performed by her research group on rat osteoblasts grown in microgravity published between 1996-2005 evaluated the impact of microgravity and vitamin D on cellular receptors and signaling indicated in bone resorption, which subsequently leads to hypercalciuria. CONCLUSIONS: Dr. Whitson’s work in understanding renal stone formation risk spans two decades and has helped to better characterize renal stone forming potential in astronauts during space flight. As interest in longer space missions grows, her research becomes increasingly relevant. Through her work, she advocates for the health and wellbeing of herself and her fellow crew members and the success of current and future space missions.

title: HISPANIC CONTRIBUTIONS TO THE FOUNDATIONS OF MODERN UROLOGY AND THEIR LASTING IMPACT ON THE EVOLUTION GENITOURINARY MEDICINE
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Rafael G. Bourricaudy, Juan Varela, Robert Carey, Hernan Carrion, Rafael Carrion, Victoria Bird
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The history of urology reflects a rich legacy of global contributions, with key milestones from Hispanic and Latin American physicians. Since the Spanish Golden Age, they advanced surgery, ethics, and anatomy, shaping the field through pioneering innovations. This study highlights major contributions by Hispanic urologists and advocates their inclusion in urologic history and training. METHODS: A historiographic review examined Hispanic physicians’ contributions to urology and genitourinary medicine from 1580–1980, tracing developments preceding formal establishment of the fields. Sources included PubMed, Google Scholar, and AUA archives. Materials analyzed included manuscripts, textbooks, biographies, and theses, examined across three themes: surgical and diagnostic advances; early genitourinary concepts; and academic leadership. Source triangulation ensured validity and rigor. RESULTS: Ten pioneering Hispanic urologists shaped modern urology and laid the foundation for today’s advances. Francisco Díaz (Spain,1588) wrote the first Spanish urology treatise integrating surgery and urologic care. Joaquín Albarrán (Cuba,1890s) transformed prostate surgery and emphasized genitourinary function. Ramón Guiteras (Cuba,1900s) founded the AUA and defined male genitourinary medicine. Isaac González Martínez (Puerto Rico, 1912) advanced cancer care with organ-sparing techniques. Aquilino Arreola (Mexico, 1920s) led in endourology and neurosexual preservation. Salvador Gil Vernet (Spain,1944) mapped prostatic zonal anatomy. Alejandro Palomo (Mexico,1949) introduced a lasting varicocele repair. Hernán Carrión (Peru,1975) developed the Small-Carrion prosthesis and intracavernous placement technique, foundational to modern prosthetic surgery.Álvaro Morales (Colombia, 1976) pioneered BCG therapy for bladder cancer. José Amén-Palma (Ecuador, 1970s) refined renal hemostasis methods. CONCLUSIONS: This review highlights the the impact of ten Hispanic urologists who advanced urology and genitourinary medicine before these fields were formally established. Their contributions from surgical innovation to academic leadership call for a more inclusive historical perspective. Recognizing their legacy enriches medical education and merits formal acknowledgment by the AUA, SMSNA, SAU, and integration into curricula and scholarship.

title: ALFRED BECQUEREL (1814-1862) AND HIS CONTRIBUTIONS TO UROLOGY
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Jasmin Katrin Badawi
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The term becquerel (Bq) is part of the global vocabulary and refers to the unit of radioactivity in the International System of Units. It was named after Henri Becquerel, a French physicist who shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with the Curies in 1903. Henri's uncle, the physician Alfred Becquerel, stands in the shadow of this achievement. The aim of this study was to examine Alfred Becquerel's contributions to urology. METHODS: Primary sources were analyzed like his original medical treatises, articles and archive material. In addition, relevant secondary literature was consulted. RESULTS: Louis Alfred Becquerel was born on June 3, 1814, in Paris, France, the eldest son of Aimée Cécile Darlu and physicist Antoine César Becquerel. He studied medicine. His postdoctoral thesis _De l\`empirisme en médecine_ was defended before the Medical Faculty of Paris and published in 1844. Of his numerous medical works, the 576-page _Traité de la séméiotique_ des urines published in 1841 contained a systematical classification of the various changes in urine to characterize different diseases. After describing the chemical and physical properties of urine and demonstrating the connections between them, he showed the modifications of urine under physiological and pathological conditions and developed the underlying principles. He then applied these general principles to a variety of diseases, including the formation of urinary stones. Finally, he systemically described “Bright's disease” in children and adults. This work, which also included numerous average values for urine parameters, was based on more than 6,000 urine analyses in more than 500 cases. In 1854, he and Rodier published a treatise on pathological chemistry, applied to practical medicine. In 1856, he and Vernois published On Albuminuria and Bright\`s disease. In 1857, Becquerel, who was already working as a doctor at the Hôpital de la Pitié and as a Professeur agrégé at the Faculty of Medicine in Paris, published a 376-page treatise on the use of electricity as a medical and surgical treatment method: Traité des applications de l\`électricité à la thérapeutique médicale et chirurgicale. In this book, Becquerel also critically examined the hypotheses of the time on the etiology of bladder emptying disorders and their possible electrotherapeutic treatment. In 1856, he had published a shorter version of this topic. CONCLUSIONS: Alfred Becquerel made a significant contribution to the newly developing field of urology through his comprehensive work on urine changes as a diagnostic tool, kidney diseases, and electrotherapy, which is still used today in a more advanced form, for example, as a neuromodulator for bladder dysfunctions.

title: EDITH POTTER AND THE BIRTH OF PEDIATRIC UROPATHOLOGY
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Veerain K. Gupta, Ronald Rabinowitz, Jennifer Gordetsky
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Edith Potter, M.D., PhD (1901-1993) was a clinician and pathologist whose work in pediatric autopsy pathology transformed the medical understanding of congenital and perinatal disease. Through meticulous examination, dissection, and research, Dr. Potter produced practice-changing observations that helped establish pediatric uropathology as a recognized discipline. We highlight Dr. Potter’s most notable contributions to the fields of pathology, urology, and embryologic malformations. METHODS: Publications by and about Edith Potter were reviewed. These included scientific manuscripts and textbooks by Dr. Potter, articles about her, and interviews related to her personal life as well as her professional achievements. RESULTS: Edith Potter began her pathology career at the Chicago Lying-in Hospital, the University of Chicago’s obstetrics–gynecology teaching unit, in 1934. She arrived in Chicago during a time of public health reform and was instrumental in identifying prematurity, birth trauma, and infection as leading modifiable causes of infant death. Another early breakthrough came through her work on hemolytic disease in newborns. By examining stillbirths and neonatal deaths, Dr. Potter recognized a pattern of kernicterus, hydrops fetalis, hepatosplenomegaly, and anemia that was ultimately linked to Rh incompatibility between mother and fetus. Her most defining contribution came with the description of bilateral renal agenesis and the collection of findings known as ‘Potter Sequence’. In the early 1940s, she began to explore the role of intrauterine respiration in fetal lung development. She showed that underdevelopment of the lungs often correlated with impaired intrauterine physiology. In 1946, she outlined the distinct constellation of findings associated with bilateral renal agenesis, including lung hypoplasia, cranial anomalies, and clubbed feet. By the end of her career, Dr. Potter completed over 10,000 autopsies, published more than 140 articles, and authored six textbooks. CONCLUSIONS: Dr. Edith Potter was the first pediatric uropathologist in the United States and was pivotal in shaping the understanding and treatment of congenital urinary tract disorders. She devoted her life to understanding diseases of the fetus, neonate, and infant, and bridged the fields of pathology with pediatric urology, gynecology, pediatrics, and embryology.

title: EARL F. NATION, M. D. (1910–2008): UROLOGY’S HISTORIAN-HUMANIST AND THE OSLERIAN SPIRIT OF THE AMERICAN WEST
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Hannah E. Moreland, Michael E. Moran
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Earl F. Nation, M. D. exemplified the union of clinical mastery, organizational leadership, and historical scholarship that defined twentieth-century American urology. A past President of both the American Urological Association (AUA) and the American Osler Society, Nation advanced not only the surgical craft but also the humanistic conscience of the profession. This study examines his formative experiences, professional milestones, and enduring contributions to urology’s collective memory. METHODS: A review of all of the writings by and about Nation were pursued and studied. Primary materials included Nation’s autobiographical essay “Saved by AΩA” (The Pharos, 2007); his 2006 San Diego State University oral history; and a personal interview recorded on October 23, 2002, by Drs. Sakti Das and Michael Moran, which explored his personal life and career. Additional data were drawn from the AUA Museum of Urologic History archives, the American Osler Society, and published commentaries by colleagues and trainees. RESULTS: Born in Zephyr, Texas, and educated at San Diego State and Western Reserve University, Nation graduated in 1935 amid the Great Depression. During his residency, he contracted tuberculous pneumonitis from a pathology exposure. His convalescence at the Barlow Sanitarium—spent reading Cushing’s Life of Osler—ignited his lifelong devotion to medical history. After recovery, he joined practice with H. C. Bumpus and Ben Massey in Pasadena, achieving Board Certification in 1944. As AUA President in 1977 and Treasurer for the preceding five years, Nation modernized the Association’s fiscal governance and advanced the creation of the AUA Office of Education. As a founding member of the American Osler Society in 1971 and President in 1978, he deepened the intellectual bridge between medicine and the humanities through four books and numerous historical essays chronicling urology’s pioneers. CONCLUSIONS: Through his scholarship and leadership, Nation institutionalized historical awareness within the AUA. The AUA Earl Nation Retrospectroscope Award stands as a testament to his conviction that the progress of urology depends as much on remembering its past as advancing its future.

title: DISSERTATION CULTURES IN UROLOGY - A COMPARISON BETWEEN GERMANY, FRANCE AND THE UNITED STATES 1850-1950
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Friedrich H. Moll, Thorsten Halling, Giacomo Padrini, Nils Hansson
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Medical doctoral dissertations (MD theses) played a major role within the process of professionalization of urology from a skilled craft into a medical specialty. In medical history research, the focus has often been placed on Renaissance topics and the early universities. As the major qualification work for academic physicians (in Prussia up to 1852 with the establishment of the “Aerztlicher Einheitsstand”, and later for physicians in general or in emerging specialties), this type of academic work was of central importance. Since urology has diverse roots, research must therefore take into account several medical fields, ranging from internal medicine and surgery to sexology. In addition, the regulations for dissertations differed between institutions both nationally and internationally. METHODS: We analyzed the newly digitized collections of the German Central Library of Medicine in Cologne, the holdings of the University of Vienna (Nominalkatalog Medizinhistorische Dissertationen 1700–1850), the catalogue of the University of Pennsylvania, and the collections of the DGU Library in Düsseldorf. RESULTS: For small medical specialties it is necessary to research in several collections, as urology-related topics appear only rarely. For each historical period, the prevailing level of academic knowledge must be considered (e. g., lithotripsy, cystoscopy, surgical procedures, conservative treatment options). Biographical information on the authors can often not be obtained from the dissertations themselves. The main research areas of early urologic or proto-urologic departments are reflected in the dissertation topics. Up to the 1980s, dissertations in urology are of limited use for gender studies, as topics related to gender (e. g., pediatrics, incontinence, female urology) are underrepresented. CONCLUSIONS: Historical medical dissertations represent a rich source for analyzing the development of the specialty, especially regarding professional networks, research priorities in defined periods, and scholarly exchange. The analysis shows that, due to the relatively low number of urologic topics in general collections, detailed research in still non-digitized archives remains essential for the history of urology.

title: AN AMERICAN PIONEER IN HYPOSPADIAS SURGERY: JOHN PETER METTAUER
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Craig Andrew Peters
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Most of the original methods for hypospadias surgery were considered to have evolved from European practice, and many of the eponyms reflect this. John Peter Mettauer (1787-1875) was a North American surgeon who should be considered amongst the pioneers in establishing the foundations of hypospadias surgery, who preceded many of his European counterparts. METHODS: Using direct review of his published writings and published reviews, a picture of his career and approaches was developed to explore his contributions in pediatric urology as well as general urology from an unpublished text at the Philadelphia College of Physicians Library. RESULTS: Mettauer the son of an Alsatian physician, practiced in Virginia from the 1810’s to the 1870s. He studies at Hampden-Sydney College and graduated from the University of Pennsylvania in 1809. His role in the early development of Pediatric Urology has been little explored. He is often considered one of the pioneers of Plastic Surgery, having developed methods to repair cleft palette and lip, as well as repair of vesicovaginal fistula. His contributions to hypospadias, included surgical techniques and insights into the anatomic configuration and origins of penile curvature. His description of distal urethral tubularization, often termed the Thiersch-Duplay repair today, preceded European description by several decades. Importantly, his procedures, techniques and results were all published in detail in the Boston Medical Journal the predecessor of the New England Journal of Medicine and are available for review today. It is also important to recognize that his surgeries for at least half of his career, were performed without the benefit of anesthesia. In his surgical descriptions, he discussed his techniques to reduce discomfort and describes postoperative care in great detail. He also describes the importance of timing of surgery, reflecting dependence on natural light, so the angle and intensity of sunlight played a role in the seasonal timing of surgical procedures. CONCLUSIONS: While hypospadias surgery continues to evolve and the current methods reflect decades of innovation and progress, many of the foundational surgical techniques originated in the 19th century. The contributions of JPM should be better recognized, and his work studied for its unique insights into urological reconstruction and pathophysiology.

title: LIGHT-YEARS TO MILLIMETERS: THE HISTORY OF NAVIGATION IN PROSTATE CANCER THERAPIES
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Lisa Teixeira, Sutchin Patel, David Paolone
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The early 16th century marked the first modern description of the prostate by Massa and the first circumnavigation of the Earth by Magellan. The history of prostate cancer treatment ran parallel with navigational improvements, but they now intersect with the integration of tracking beacons for high dose precision radiation therapy. METHODS: A review of the available literature pertaining to the history of prostate cancer treatments and global navigational techniques was performed. RESULTS: Modern radiation therapy is a complex web of procedural planning heavily reliant on the oncologist’s navigational prowess. Imbert and Imbert first used external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) for prostate cancer but wide margins and low doses were ineffective. Early brachytherapy is credited to Henri Minet, and refined by Henry Hampton Young and Octave Pasteau. Though without imaging, rods were passed blindly and often resulted in complications, causing radiation therapy to fall out of favor in the early 20th century. After Sputnik launched in 1957, researchers at Johns Hopkins University noted the Doppler effect allowed its location to be determined based on frequency at any time. The Department of Defense built on these findings and started the Global Positioning System (GPS) in 1973. In 1989, the first commercially available GPS device, Magellan NAV 1000, was released. As Sputnik orbited, the efforts of Flocks, Kaplan, Bragshaw, and Binzton to utilize new kilovoltage (kV) radiation therapies in prostate cancer renewed interest in EBRT. During the 1960-70s, scientists relied on x-ray imaging to define treatment areas by bony landmarks. Gold fiducial markers were first used in 1988. In the 1990s, the National Cancer Institute published on using CT imaging technology to define the treatment margins. Anders Brahme revolutionized care with Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT), a form of conformal RT that uses variable beam intensity and positioning to distribute high doses at the prostate and low doses peripherally. The Calypso 4D Localization System (Varian Medical Systems), introduced in 2003, relies on three intraprostatic beacons to continuously transmit non-ionizing positional information regarding interfraction and intrafraction gland motion to the receiver, similar to GPS device signaling. This allows the physician to reduce treatment margins further and allow expeditious adjustments. CONCLUSIONS: The connection between prostate and territorial borders may seem disparate, but the drive to discover has inspired the progress needed to advance navigational techniques critical to improving outcomes in successful treatment of prostate cancer patients.

title: THE CASE FOR A UROLOGIST TO BE ON THE FLIGHT CREW ON THE FIRST MANNED MISSION TO MARS: THE LEGACY OF ABE COCKETT
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Kevin R. Loughlin
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: NASA experts predict that it is likely there will be a successful manned mission to Mars sometime in the 2030s. The trip each way will take 18 months plus whatever time is devoted to Mars exploration itself. It has been recommended that one member of a proposed six member flight crew should be a physician. Dr. Abe Cockett identified early on, the increased risk of urolithiasis during space flight (J. Urol. 1964; 92(5):564-567). Since the flight crew will be composed of middle-aged, otherwise very fit individuals, a strong argument can be made that the physician should be a urologist. METHODS: A literature review in PubMed using search terms; medical aspects, space flight and space medicine was performed. RESULTS: Abe Cockett was prescient as he identified and anticipated the urologic problems that could occur during space travel and prolonged periods of weightlessness. He identified four factors that contributed to an increased risk of urolithiasis during extended space flights. These were: 1) effect of weightlessness and bone reabsorption with subsequent hypercalciuria,2) delayed voiding due to increased flight tasks and urinary stasis, 3) a relative lack of physical exercise that also contributes to hypercalciuria, 4) on a flight to Mars, the lack of fresh fruits and vegetables which can cause decreased dietary citrate and subsequent urinary citrate which is a known stone inhibitor, Preliminary reports have already confirmed Doctor Cockett's concern about the increased risk of urolithiasis associated with extended space flight (Whitson PA et al, Nephron2001;89 (3):264-70). CONCLUSIONS: During the nascent era of human space exploration, Abe Cockett correctly forecast the increased risk of urolithiasis with extended duration of weightlessness and prolonged space travel such as will occur during a journey to Mars. Now with the imminent manned exploration of Mars, it appears appropriate to urge that a urologist should be a member of the first Mars exploration flight crew.

title: FARM TO TABLE: THE STORY OF THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE FIRST SPERM BANK AND FROZEN SPERM PREGNANCIES
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Joanna Orzel, Andrea Rossman, Ryan Steinberg
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While most often thought of for Dr. Alcock’s development of the transurethral resection of the prostate and the invention of the Ellik evacuator, the University of Iowa (UI) has made a variety of additional contributions to the field of urology. In 1953, Dr. Raymond Bunge and zoology graduate student, Jerome Sherman, published their findings on the fertilizing capacity of frozen human spermatozoa in 3 women. Later, national news outlets reported the birth of these babies, leading to a major controversy regarding the ethical and moral implications of frozen-thawed sperm (FTS) for insemination. We present the journey that led to the first use of FTS for assisted reproductive technology (ART) and the response to their work. METHODS: A PubMed Search including the words “Bunge” and “sperm” was conducted to find primary sources. Secondary sources were also reviewed, including The Annals of Iowa, a history journal about Iowa’s past. RESULTS: Sherman was initially hired by the urology department as a research assistant to freeze-dry renal tissue. In this role, he became interested in the freezing process itself and stumbled upon British research using glycerol as a freezing agent for bovine insemination. Intrigued, he started to perform experiments with his own sperm to see how many were viable after freezing and thawing. While painting Dr. Bunge’s house, he shared his research ideas and the two men quickly formed an alliance. Bunge and Sherman recruited an obstetrician-gynecologist collaborator, Dr. William Keetell, who had just helped to open an infertility clinic in 1952. The group performed 3 FTS inseminations for infertile married couples in 1953 with resulting pregnancies (confirmed by lack of menses, physical exam and positive Ascheim-Zondek test) and live births. After the results were published in Nature, the New York Times ran a story about the results, leading to public outcry on the grounds of ethical and religious concerns. The research collaboration quickly dissolved. Bunge remained at UI and only years later, would discuss his role in FTS. Sherman, conversely, left UI to work at the University of Arkansas Department of Anatomy and spent his career working in cryobiology, honing freezing techniques and writing certification standards for frozen human sperm banks. Only after commercial sperm banks were widely accepted and established did the two men gain accolades for their work. CONCLUSIONS: Since the founding of the department, UI has played a large role in advancing urologic care. The impacts of the contributions made by Dr. Raymond Bunge and Jerome Sherman ultimately revolutionized ART and will continue to be felt for generations.

title: FROM FORM TO FUNCTION: A HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE ON THE EMERGENCE OF FUNCTIONAL & RECONSTRUCTIVE UROLOGY
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Sasha J. Vereecken, Kieran J. Moore, Brian J. Flynn
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: For much of the 20th century, urologic reconstruction focused on restoring anatomy rather than function. The advent of urodynamics and video-urodynamics catalyzed a paradigm shift toward functional urology (FU) restoring continence, bladder emptying, and pelvic floor function. This historical review traces key milestones, contributors, and organizational shifts that established FU/FRU (Functional Reconstructive Urology) as a distinct subspecialty. METHODS: We conducted a comprehensive review of academic and historical literature on functional urology from 1914 to 2025. Using PubMed and open search engines, we identified key primary studies, surgical textbooks, patents, and professional society documents (AUA, ICS, EAU, BAUS) that contributed to the field’s evolution. RESULTS: Foundations (1920s–1960s): Barrington’s neurophysiology and Von Garrelts’ pressure/flow studies enabled objective functional assessment. Cine and video-urodynamics, pioneered by Turner-Warwick, Whiteside, Caine, and Edwards, introduced routine functional evaluation and laid the groundwork for “functional reconstruction.” Conceptual consolidation (1970s–2000s): Turner-Warwick’s Functional Reconstruction of the Urinary Tract emphasized physiological restoration over symptom relief. The International Continence Society (founded 1971) standardized terminology and incorporated neurourology, embedding functional concepts globally. Organizational Recognition and Modern Champions (2000s–): The European Association of Urology recognized “functional urology” in 2008 through its Functional Urology section. That same year, the University of Colorado launched the first FRU fellowship. In 2016, Sender Herschorn advanced the field as Canada’s first endowed Chair in Functional Urology. The first International Functional & Reconstructive Urology Update, held in Denver in 2024, further cemented the field’s global identity. CONCLUSIONS: Functional urology emerged as technological innovation reframed from surgical goals from anatomical resemblance to physiologic restoration. Professional societies, institutional programs, and contemporary leaders cemented FU/FRU as a patient-centered discipline. This evolution underpins current advances in neuromodulation, robotics, and collaborative education.

title: PROSTATECTOMY MORTALITY AT THE TURN OF THE CENTURY: AN EXPLORATION OF DOCUMENTATION AND TECHNIQUE
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Soum D. Lokeshwar, Mark Essien, Shayan Smani, Tyler Garman, Jack Campbell, Sunil H. Patel, Michael Leapman, Thomas V. Martin
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prior to the modern era, there is a paucity of information on prostatectomy morbidity. We describe and compare the post operative mortality of prostatectomies at the turn of the 20th century, using a direct surgeon’s experience, to that of the modern day. METHODS: Sources from the Yale Historical archives were analyzed and included the primary sources of Dr. Oliver Smith, a prominent CT Urologist, who detailed prostatectomies he performed from 1902-1912 in his 1912 work “Conclusions Drawn from One Hundred Prostatectomies”. These were then compared to the most recent 1000 prostatectomies performed at Yale from 5/2021-9/2024. RESULTS: Dr. Oliver C. Smith (1859-1915) served as the Senior Surgeon at Hartford Hospital where he focused on Urologic surgery. He rose to national prominence and was the primary prostate surgeon in the region. As a surgical instructor he shaped urologic teaching in the northeast to this day. Dr. Smith detailed his prostatectomies with intricate detail and subdivided his experience in fourths by technique. The first 25 were performed using a median perineal incision, the next using Dr. Young’s technique of an inverted V incision and traction of the bladder neck, the third using a perineal route with “ungloved” finger enucleation, and the final series using an extraperitoneal suprapubic approach. He also included an overview of the patient population, complications, and details of each death. In Dr. Smith’s series, the average age was 67.6 and the majority of patients were given Ether for anesthesia (94%). The primary surgical route was perineal (83%). The primary gross pathology was benign 79%, however the unspecified majority of specimens were not analyzed microscopically. The 30 day mortality was 16% with the most common cause being infection (25%). The average age in the modern cohort was 65.1 and the 30 day mortality was significantly less at 1 death (0.1%) from a cardiovascular event. CONCLUSIONS: Prostatectomy mortality has declined significantly in the last 112 years. The meticulous documentation of Dr. Smith and other early Urologists has allowed for the improvement in surgery to this day.

title: DEVELOPMENT AND EVOLUTION OF THE URETERAL ACCESS SHEATH: FROM EARLY “GUIDETUBES” TO NAVIGABLE SUCTION SHEATHS
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Adam Schwartz
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Although ureteral access sheaths (UAS) are a current focus of endourologic debate, their origin dates back over fifty years. This study provides one of the first detailed analyses of their historical development from early “guidetubes” to modern flexible and navigable suction systems (FANS UAS). METHODS: A literature review was conducted to identify major device milestones, associated clinical outcomes, and key studies relevant to the development and evolution of the ureteral access sheath. RESULTS: The earliest UAS like device, a guidetube introduced in the 1970s, facilitated insertion of early passively flexible fiber optic ureteroscopes and prevented buckling in the intravesical segment (Takaysu, 1974). Despite success in preliminary testing (19/19 vs 40/50 without), limited scope availability and diagnostic function curtailed adoption. In the 1980s, a dilator sheathing system was developed to overcome mucosal edema and bleeding after balloon dilation by maintaining a tract for repeated instrument access, but perforations in 12 of 43 cases limited use (Newman, 1987). Concurrently, peel away introducer sheaths, originally for antegrade stent delivery, were repurposed for retrograde stone basketing, stent placement, and stone flushing (Rich, 1987). They also served as antegrade working conduits for flexible ureteroscopy, enabling evaluation and fragment removal through a percutaneous tract and bridging percutaneous with later retrograde UAS designs. Throughout the 1990s, miniaturization of ureteroscopes and the advent of holmium laser fibers and nitinol baskets yielded the first modern UAS; consisting of an inner dilator and outer sheath placed over a guidewire (Kourambas, 2001). Global use expanded through the 2000s–2010s amid debate over ischemic injury and stricture risk. Flexible and navigable suction UAS, first available in the United States in 2024, feature atraumatic flexible tips that follow the ureteroscope into the renal pelvis and calyces. Integrated suction enables continuous irrigation, dust evacuation, and modulation of intrarenal pressure and temperature, while scope withdrawal allows aspiration of larger fragments. A multicenter randomized trial showed higher stone free rates, fewer fevers, and reduced basket use versus conventional UAS (Zhang, 2024). CONCLUSIONS: Across five decades, the UAS has evolved from a passive conduit into an active platform for fluid control, visualization, and stone evacuation. Flexible and navigable suction systems represent the latest chapter and may define future endourology through integration of real-time pressure and temperature monitoring and continuous irrigation.

title: PHALLUS, FLOW, AND THE FUTURE: REAWAKENING MOCHE SEX POTS FOR MODERN MEN’S HEALTH
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Fionna Sun, Kezia Reji Thomas, Kaitlin L. Berry, Kenneth G. Sands
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Nearly two millennia ago, on Peru’s northern coast, the Moche civilization (100–800 CE) molded vessels that spoke of power, fertility, and the sanctity of bodily fluids. Their erotic ceramics—often called “sex pots”—depicted the penis, ejaculation, and urination with striking anatomical precision. These subjects so freely portrayed by the Moche remain difficult to discuss in modern Peru, where prostate and testicular cancer screening is hindered by stigma. In recent years, however, Moche iconography has been reimagined as an innovative tool linking cultural heritage with public health awareness. This study explores how ancient Moche art has been adapted to promote men’s genitourinary health and how historical imagery can inform modern urologic education. METHODS: A comprehensive review was performed using search terms: Moche, sex pot, urology, and genitourinary health. We focused on historical and anthropologic texts, reviews of Moche collections (e. g., Museo Larco, Lima; Princeton University Art Museum; Brooklyn Museum), and contemporary public-health initiatives employing ancient iconography. RESULTS: Reframing Moche ceramics through a health-communication lens transformed ritual imagery into a powerful educational medium. Campaigns displaying erotic vessels with prostate-screening messages gained national and international visibility through museum exhibitions, media, and digital platforms, attracting over 100,000 visitors and broadening audience engagement. Their anatomical fidelity reinforces understanding of male genital structure, while recurring motifs of ejaculation, urination, and ritual cleansing echo urology’s enduring principles of flow, function, and fertility. Collaboration between historians and clinicians shows that culturally grounded outreach can enhance education and destigmatize discussion of sexual and urinary health more effectively than conventional messaging. CONCLUSIONS: Reawakening Moche “sex pots” bridges art and anatomy, transforming ancient expressions of virility into modern instruments of men’s health. Though quantitative outcomes remain unstudied, these efforts highlight how historical art can catalyze dialogue, improve comfort discussing genitourinary symptoms, and inspire renewed engagement with preventive screening—reminding us that the story of urology began long before the scalpel, written instead in clay.

title: LHRH IN PROSTATE CANCER TREATMENT: FROM BREAKTHROUGH DISCOVERY TO MODERN THERAPEUTIC APPROACHES
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Samuel Benisti, Fred Saad, Guila Delouya, Daniel Taussky
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: This project highlights the key scientific discoveries that led to the isolation of luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH). We describe the scientists behind this breakthrough, Andrew Schally and Roger Guillemin, whose biochemical refinement and competitive research led to the Nobel Prize in 1977. METHODS: A review of the main scientific steps that led to the discovery of LHRH. Peer-reviewed articles, Nobel lectures, and oral history transcripts were consulted. RESULTS: G. W. Harris was the first to show that the anterior pituitary is regulated by the hypothalamus in 1937. His work established the principles of Schally and Guillemin. He was also part of the scientific race to characterize hypothalamic releasing factors but lacked funds to succeed. Charles Huggins discovered in 1941 that prostate cancer is androgen-dependent, which highlights the breakthroughs that led to the isolation of LHRH. Both Schally and Guillemin independently isolated thyrotropin-releasing factor (TRF) in 1969. TRH consists of only 3 amino acids. Due to rapid degradation and lack of sensitive detection techniques, hormone extraction required over 160,000 porcine hypothalami. Both then turned to LHRH, operating in secrecy because of their rivalry. The structure of LHRH was not elucidated until 1971, when both isolated it independently within a few weeks. For their discovery, they developed advanced biochemical techniques and used 240,000 porcine brains. These methods were also integral to the synthesis of LHRH analogs, later tested in prostate cancer models. In 1971, Schally demonstrated that LHRH could suppress gonadotropin secretion through continuous intravenous infusion of synthetic LHRH (GnRH) in rhesus monkeys. This induced a rapid LH surge within the first hour, followed by a decline to baseline in 4–6 hours, and suppression lasting over 24 hours. It was shown that LHRH can desensitize pituitary GnRH receptors, creating a negative feedback loop, which laid the groundwork for using LHRH analogs to treat hormone-sensitive conditions, such as prostate cancer, endometriosis, and precocious puberty. The first clinical trial was conducted by Schally in Mexico and published in 1972. The first clinical study of LHRH agonists in prostate cancer, organized by Schally, took place in Montreal and was published in PNAS in 1982. CONCLUSIONS: Intense competition drove researchers to discover LHRH and prove the negative feedback loop, earning both Nobel Prizes. Their research laid the foundation for the development of agonist analogs that continue to inform the core principles of managing advanced prostate cancer.

title: NECROPHAGES FROM ANTIQUITY: THE EVOLVING HISTORY OF MAGGOTS AS AN ADJUNCTIVE DEBRIDEMENT THERAPY FOR GENITOPERINEAL WOUNDS
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Paramjot S. Gogia, Lauren M. Nesi, Kristina D. Suson
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Maggot Debridement Therapy (MDT), also known as larval therapy or biosurgery, is a non-operative treatment involving the application of live, sterile blowfly larvae (Lucilia sericata) to selectively digest devitalized tissue, decrease bioburden, and promote granulation. While MDT has largely been used for chronic ulcers, burns, and diabetic foot disease, the historical origins and evolution of its application for genitoperineal wounds remain unclear. METHODS: Major medical databases were systematically queried for primary and secondary literature sources discussing the history of MDT and its application in urology. A timeline was established following chronological review of historical and clinical evidence for MDT use in postoperative genitourinary wounds. RESULTS: The therapeutic use of maggots in colonized wounds has ancient origins, with accounts among Mayan healers in Central America, Aboriginal tribes in Australia, and hill communities of Myanmar. These practices predate principles later formalized by modern biotherapists. In the late 1920s, after treating wound myiasis during World War I, surgeon William S. Baer introduced sterile maggot therapy for chronic osteomyelitis, demonstrating complete resolution of infection and establishing the first controlled medical use of larvae in contemporary wound management. With a post-1940s decline in MDT, few clinicians continued to document the biotherapy. Well-established in non-healing wounds, its modern role in urology is concentrated in contaminated genitoperineal wounds and necrotizing infections. Scattered evidence demonstrated successful debridement using larvae as post-excisional adjunct therapy for both penoscrotal necrosis and Fournier’s gangrene. Independent cases showed that larvae could safely be used on delicate scrotal and perineal tissues after initial debridement. MDT was also reported in gynecology for post-vulvectomy wound dehiscence with evolving tools such as a maggot-filled BioBag system introduced in 2002, allowing proteolytic larval secretions to debride necrotic tissue without direct contact. Novel biosurgical modalities continue to emerge. CONCLUSIONS: From antiquity to a popular 1930s remedy, through mid-century obscurity, and back to the 21st century, larval therapy reflects cyclical innovation in medicine. By the early 2000s, it regained credibility where conventional therapies fell short. Historical literature shows MDT’s metamorphosis as a specialized tool, its urologic niche clearest in Fournier’s gangrene and select genitoperineal wounds. Today, clinical acceptance of maggots has grown as part of the modern therapeutic armamentarium.

title: FROM BATTLEFIELD ANESTHETIC TO PUBLIC-HEALTH CHALLENGE: A HISTORICAL REVIEW OF KETAMINE AND ITS GENITOURINARY SEQUELAE (1960S–PRESENT)
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Christopher Edwards, Michael West, Gina DeMeo, Katiana Vazquez-Rivera, Elie Kaplan-Marans, Edward Wu, Ariel Schulman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Created to replace its analog, phencyclidine, ketamine maintained anesthetic potency but with shorter, safer action and less psychotic effects. Over six decades, it has been used in anesthesia, psychiatry, and recreationally. With increasing involvement as a drug of abuse, ketamine uropathy (KU) has emerged as a major consequence. We trace ketamine’s historical trajectory and chart how urologist recognized and managed KU. METHODS: A narrative review of medical literature, regulatory documents, and case series (1962–2025) was conducted to trace ketamine’s historical milestones and its evolving urological implications. RESULTS: Following its synthesis in 1962, ketamine’s safety and efficacy were demonstrated in 1964 human trials by Domino and Corssen. This led to FDA approval in 1970 and widespread military use during the Vietnam War. Its hemodynamic stability made it indispensable for trauma and pediatric anesthesia, particularly in low-resource and field settings. By 1985, it was added to the WHO Essential Medicines List as a critical anesthetic. Recreational use peaked by the 1990s, prompting U. S. Schedule III classification in 1999. Around the same period, low-dose infusions showed rapid antidepressant effects, culminating in FDA approval of intranasal esketamine in 2019. Concurrently, urologists began recognizing a new complication among chronic and excessive abusers. The first case reports from Canada and Hong Kong described severe lower urinary tract symptoms including frequency (77%), urgency (70%), pain (60%), and hematuria. By 2007, these cases defined ketamine-induced cystitis, characterized by ulcerated, contracted bladders with capacities often <150 ml. Histopathology reveals urothelial loss, mast-cell infiltration, and submucosal fibrosis, sometimes progressing to hydronephrosis, ureteral strictures, and renal dysfunction. Ketamine’s urinary metabolites appear directly toxic to the urothelium, inciting inflammatory cascades. Cessation remains essential, but refractory cases may require intravesical therapy. Furthermore, end-stage ketamine bladders may require augmentation cystectomy, or diversion. Recognition of this syndrome led to the 2024 British Association of Urological Surgeons (BAUS) consensus guidelines outlining diagnostic and management algorithms. CONCLUSIONS: Ketamine’s evolution from anesthetic innovation to public health concern underscores its dual legacy. As use expands, urologists must recognize, prevent, and manage its genitourinary sequelae.

title: JOHN DAVY\`S EXTENSIVE RESEARCH IN MEDICINE AND BEYOND IN SRI LANKA (1816-1820)
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Jasmin Katrin Badawi
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: In 1816, Cornish physician John Davy (1790-1868), who was serving as an officer in the British medical department of the army at the time, was sent to Sri Lanka (formerly Ceylon), where he worked until 1820. This historical study examined his research there, particularly on medical and urological topics. METHODS: Primary sources such as his original books, articles and personal notices were analyzed. In addition, secondary literature was included. RESULTS: During his stay in Sri Lanka, Davy collected original material and conducted research, which was published in 1821 by a London publisher in his book “An account of the interior of Ceylon and of its inhabitants, with Travels in that island”. This work comprised more than 500 pages and covered a wide range of topics such as the “physical state of the Island in general”, animals, political conditions, religion, architecture, and history. Davy rounded off his work with a “medical sketch relative to the climate and its diseases, and the preservation of health”. He began with descriptions of the effects of the tropical climate on the human body and described typical illnesses in newly arrived people. In addition, he conducted studies on the temperature of adult residents and of children at an orphan school near Colombo. He also specified various diseases affecting Europeans living in Sri Lanka or locals, particularly skin, abdominal, liver, urological, pulmonary, infectious, and febrile diseases. Davy stated that urinary organs diseases occurred much less frequently in hot climates than in temperate climates. During his entire time in Sri Lanka, he encountered only three cases of renal gravel, all in English officers who also suffered from dyspepsia. In 2 cases, the chemical composition of the stones consisted of magnesium ammonium phosphate. Furthermore, he discovered that the locals had been acquainted with diabetes and the “peculiar property of the urine characteristic since time immemorial”. In his medical considerations, Davy took into account not only the extreme climatic conditions, but also the predominantly vegetarian diet of the local population. Further studies in Sri Lanka, later published in another book, focused on the urinary organs of amphibians and reptiles and included a chemical analysis of their urine as well as a comparison with human urine. CONCLUSIONS: John Davy advanced medicine through his extensive research in Sri Lanka. He contributed to a better understanding of the human body's adaptation processes under extreme climatic conditions and expanded knowledge about diseases in tropical regions. In addition, his systematic detailed research into the urinary organs and urine enriched the field of urology.

title: ALESSANDRI MASSARIAE _PRAELECTIONES DE MORBIS MULIERUM_, CONCEPTUS ET PARTUS: MASSARIA’S CONTRIBUTION TO UROGYNECOLOGY IN SEVENTEENTH-CENTURY ITALY BETWEEN TRADITION AND INNOVATION
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Carolina D'Elia, Daniela Marrone, Armin Pycha
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: In 16th and 17th century Italy, women’s health and anatomy were predominantly a male domain, while gynecology emerged as a specialized field already within the Hippocratic medical tradition. Around 1600, the Italian physician and philosopher Alessandro Massaria published the Praelectiones de morbis mulierum (Lectures on the Diseases of Women), a exhaustive treatise on women’s diseases, conception, and childbirth, written in Latin and never translated into Italian. The objective of our study was to produce a translation of the work into Italian, which required a continuous comparison with the ancient and historical scientific sources employed by Massaria, in order to reconstruct the state of contemporary knowledge on the subject. METHODS: The text under examination is the result of the university lectures delivered by Alessandro Massaria, at the University of Padua in 1591, where he had graduated. Born in Vicenza between 1510 and 1524, Massaria, in fact, attended the Studium Patavinum during Gabriele Falloppia’s tenure and followed his course. In 1587, the Venetian Senate appointed him to the first Chair of Practical Medicine. Our research is based on the first printed edition published in Leipzig in 1600, used as the source for our translation. In the Praelectiones, Massaria—fully aware of the breadth of the subject—addresses a wide range of topics, organizing the material into 13 chapters: the first 4 discuss the menstrual cycle; the next 2 concern conception and infertility; the seventh and eighth deal with the pathological products of conception; the ninth and tenth examine uterine pathologies; and the last 3 are devoted to childbirth and the puerperium. RESULTS: One may observe that Massaria agrees with Aristotle and Galen regarding “embryology” and the anatomy of the genital organs. He also concurs with the physiological theories found in Aristotle, Galen and Avicenna concerning the physiology of the menstrual cycle. As for therapy, Massaria draws on the humoral theory of dyscrasias, following Hippocrates and especially Galen, particularly in his discussion of “derivation” and “revulsion”. He also devotes great attention to the detailed description of simple remedies and pharmaceutical recipes CONCLUSIONS: Massaria combined philosophical reflection, medical practice, and humanistic culture. Faithful to Hippocratic and especially Galenic theory, he approached the study of female diseases in a comprehensive and didactic manner, offering a synthesis of classical medicine and Renaissance scholarship, situating himself within a research context that, at that historical moment, still required further extensive investigation

title: HISTORY OF THE UROLOGY SERVICE IN THE CENTRAL LISBON HOSPITAL UNIVERSITY CENTRE
session: History of Urology Forum (HF02)
authors: Pedro Silva, Luis Campos Pinheiro, Luis Severo, João Cunha, Miguel Gil
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The evolution of Portuguese urology is deeply rooted in Lisbon’s historic hospitals, where independent urology units developed over the past century into the integrated academic structure of the Central Lisbon University Hospital Centre (CHULC). This study aims to trace the institutional, technological, and academic milestones that shaped the formation of CHULC’s Urology Service, highlighting the progression from early 20th-century pioneers to the present-day robotic and multidisciplinary era. METHODS: A historical review was conducted using archival materials, institutional documents, and published historiographic sources spanning 1900–2025. Primary sources included: Archival records from Hospital do Desterro, Hospital Curry Cabral, and Hospital de São José. Official ministerial decrees and hospital annual reports. Centenary publications of the Associação Portuguesa de Urologia and internal chronicles from the Urology Service. Historical milestones were analyzed in relation to service development, technological innovation, and integration processes within the Lisbon hospital network. RESULTS: Early foundation (1902–1950): In 1902, Artur Ravara founded Portugal’s first dedicated urology consultation at Hospital do Desterro, introducing cystoscopy and establishing urology as an independent specialty. Mid-century expansion (1970s–2000): The Curry Cabral Urology Service, created in 1973 under Alberto Matos Ferreira, became a national reference center for surgical training and innovation—introducing several procedural “firsts” in Portugal and pioneering prostate-cancer management. Under Fernando Calais da Silva, the Desterro service advanced public-hospital brachytherapy and early PSA-based screening before relocating to Hospital de São José in 2006. Integration and modernization (2007–present): The formation of the Centro Hospitalar de Lisboa Central (CHLC) in 2007, later expanded into CHULC, unified Lisbon’s legacy urology services.
