Patients in the fourth ADI-quartile were younger, less frequently NHW, and more frequently without insurance compared to those in the first. Patients were predominantly diagnosed as stage I and on MVA, the odds of stage II and stage III testicular cancer was noted to be higher for higher ADI. The 15-year survival estimates based on their ADI quartile was 97.9% for ADI 0-24, 93.0% for ADI 25-49, 91.5% for ADI 50-74, and 87.8% for ADI ≥75 (p<0.0001). On MVA, all quartiles were significantly different from quartile 1. The 15-year cancer-specific mortality incidence based on their ADI quartile was 0.4% for ADI 0-24, 2.1% for ADI 25-49, 1.6% for ADI 50-74, and 2.9% for ADI ≥75 (Gray’s test p-value 0.1234). ADI was not significantly associated with testicular cancer specific mortality. CONCLUSIONS: Our study is a one of the first studies to evaluate the association between neighborhood deprivation and TCa outcomes in a contemporary North American cohort. While all-cause mortality and stage at diagnosis appears to be impacted by ADI, testicular cancer-specific mortality does not. Current management may potentially be one of the factors mitigating some of the effect on cancer-specific mortality. However, a delay in diagnosis and potential treatment-associated morbidity compel us to better understand disparities affecting this subset of patients.

title: PERIOPERATIVE ANTIBIOTIC PROPHYLAXIS DOES NOT AFFECT INFECTION RATES AFTER TRANSPERINEAL PROSTATE BIOPSY
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Maxwell L. Sandberg, Robert Smith, Randall Bissette, Madeline Sandberg, Alejandro Rodriguez, Matvey Tsivian
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Transperineal prostate biopsy (TPB) is a modality to adequately sample the prostate gland for cancer with low infection rates postoperatively. There is still debate as to whether perioperative antibiotics are required as infection prophylaxis with TPB. Further, while infection rates \[urinary tract infections (UTIs)\] are felt to be low, acute urinary retention (AUR) after TPB is a known complication. The purpose of this study was to compare perioperative antibiotics versus no antibiotics for patients undergoing TPB. Secondarily, this study aimed to assess rates of AUR after TPB and its relation to prostate size. METHODS: This was a multi-institutional retrospective analysis of all patients undergoing TPB for elevated prostate specific antigen (PSA) or as confirmatory biopsies on active surveillance between 2012-2025. Patients were divided into two groupings based on whether they received perioperative antibiotics (second or third-generation cephalosporin) versus no antibiotics. Post TPB infection was defined as at least one of the following: fever (≥ 38.3°C) with/without symptoms of UTI or positive urine culture (>105 colony forming units) within 5 days post biopsy. AUR was defined as an inability to urinate within 72 hours of TPB requiring catheter. Independent samples t-test and chi squared test were used to compare patients based on antibiotic prophylaxis, presence infection, and AUR. RESULTS: 904 patients were included in the analysis (771 antibiotics and 133 no antibiotics; Table 1a). Age at TPB was equivalent between groups (p>0.05). Mean PSA at TPB and PSA density were greater in the no antibiotic group (13.5 ng/mL and 0.24 ng/mL/cm3) versus antibiotic group (3.6 ng/mL and 0.07 ng/mL/cm3; p<0.01). A total of 18 (2.0%) UTIs were observed after TPB and no difference in rate of infection was observed based on use of antibiotics (p>0.05; Table 1b). 2/18 (11%) patients, both of which received antibiotics, experienced urosepsis requiring readmission. Patients who developed a UTI after TPB were older than those who did not (71.1 years versus 66.4 years; p<0.01). 44 (4.9%) patients went into AUR after TPB. Mean prostate volume on magnetic resonance imaging was significantly greater in patients who went into AUR (77.1 cc) than those who did not (52.4 cc; p<0.01; Table 1c). CONCLUSIONS: Use of perioperative antibiotics does not appear to influence UTI rate after TPB. Older age at TPB is associated with developing an infection after TPB. Larger prostate size is associated with risk of developing AUR after TPB. | | | --- | | |

title: INCIDENCE AND RISK FACTORS OF PERIOPERATIVE INFECTIONS FOLLOWING ROBOT-ASSISTED RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY: A MULTICENTER RETROSPECTIVE ANALYSIS
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Takuhisa Nukaya, Kiyohito Ishikawa, Kiyoshi Takahara
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To clarify the incidence and risk factors of surgical site, urinary tract, and remote infections following robot-assisted radical prostatectomy in Japan and to examine their association with prophylactic antibiotic regimens. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 6,600 robot-assisted radical prostatectomy procedures performed at 13 institutions between 2009 and 2021. Eligible cases included those who were administered prophylactic antibiotics recommended by the guidelines: cefazolin, ampicillin/sulbactam, or second-generation cephalosporins. The incidence of surgical site, urinary tract, and remote infections within 30 days postoperatively was compared by antibiotic type and administration duration (≤24 h vs. >24 h). Multivariate analyses identified independent risk factors. RESULTS: The incidence rates of surgical site, urinary tract, and remote infections were 1.2%, 1.4%, and 0.3%, respectively. Bowel injury, particularly deep and organ or space infections, was a surgical site infection risk factor. Second-generation cephalosporins were associated with a lower surgical site infection rate than that of cefazolin. Prolonged urethral catheterization (≥8 days) was a risk factor for urinary tract and remote infections. Urinary tract infection incidence was higher with ampicillin/sulbactam than with cefazolin (no duration difference). Remote infection incidence did not differ by antibiotic regimen. CONCLUSIONS: Perioperative infection incidence following robot-assisted radical prostatectomy was low. Bowel injury and prolonged urethral catheterization were surgical site infection and urinary tract and remote infections risk factors, respectively. Early urethral catheter removal may prevent infection. Prophylaxis with first- or second-generation cephalosporins within 24 h is recommended, and broad-spectrum antibiotics may be appropriate bowel injury-complicated cases.

title: VALUE OF URINE CULTURE BEFORE RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Franck Bruyere, Tanguy Maurice, Stessy Kutchukian, Antoine Vincentelli, Jerome Rigaud, Humphrey Robin, Omar Karray, Maxime Vallee, Ali Bourgi
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Post-operative urinary tract infections (UTIs) are a notable complication of radical prostatectomy, contributing to prolonged hospital stays, increased healthcare costs, and diminished patient quality of life. Despite international guideline recommendations of European Association of Urology regarding the use of pre-operative urine cultures and antibiotic prophylaxis (AP) before radical prostatectomy, the role of pre-operative urine cultures in mitigating UTI risk remains uncertain. METHODS: This multi-center prospective cohort study analyzed data from six French urology departments. Patients who underwent radical prostatectomy between January 2019 and June 2023, with variable inclusion periods across centers, were included if pre-operative urine cultures were performed. Patients were stratified into subgroups based on the occurrence of post-operative UTIs. Uni-variable and multi-variable logistic regressions, as well as receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, were used. RESULTS: A total of 467 patients were analyzed, among whom post-operative UTIs developed in 30 patients. Among peri-operative factors, only the ASA (American Society of Anesthesiologists) score (p=0.014) and the duration of post-operative catheterization (p=0.001) were significantly associated with UTI occurrence in uni-variable analyses. Multi-variable logistic regression confirmed both factors as independent predictors of post-operative infections, with a model area under the ROC curve for catheterization duration of 0.789. A seven-day threshold for catheterization duration was identified as the optimal cutoff for predicting infection risk. Notably, neither pre-operative urine bacterial cultures nor AP reduced the incidence of post-operative UTIs. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that pre-operative urine cultures and prophylactic antibiotic agents do not mitigate UTI risk following radical prostatectomy, underscoring the need for optimized infection prevention tactics. The findings challenge the clinical utility of routine pre-operative urine cultures and highlight the critical roles of ASA score and post-operative catheterization duration in predicting infections.

title: EPIDIDYMO-ORCHITIS A “RARE” COMPLICATION AFTER LASER ENUCLEATION OF THE PROSTATE: A PROSTATE ENUCLEATION COLLABORATIVE INITIATIVE
session: Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Matthew W. Cole, Adil Ali, Amanda Rubano, Smita De, Deepak Agarwal, Dan Gralnek, Eric Ghiraldi, Scott V. Wiener, Rajat Jain, Scott Quarrier
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Infectious events after Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) are recognized, however epididymo-orchitis is rarely reported as a discrete endpoint despite clear clinical impact. Most series aggregate scrotal infections under “soft-tissue” complications, leaving procedure-specific rates and risk profiles undefined. This study aimed to characterize the incidence of epididymo-orchitis after HoLEP and the corresponding impact on unplanned healthcare utilization. METHODS: Using the TriNetX Research Network, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults undergoing HoLEP between 2015 and 2024 with at least one outpatient encounter prior to the index procedure and documentation of continued follow-up beyond the defined 1-year observation period. First time epididymo-orchitis occurring within 1 year after HoLEP were analyzed using two-proportion z-tests (Wald method), Kaplan-Meier estimation, and Cox proportional hazards modeling. Baseline confounders were balanced using 1:1 propensity score matching (greedy nearest-neighbor algorithm; caliper=0.1 SD). RESULTS: In a cohort of 10,357 patients who underwent HoLEP between 2015 and 2024, incident epididymo-orchitis occurred in 146 individuals (1.4%), with a median time to diagnosis of 62 days (95% CI 54-81). Patients with a prior urinary tract infection had a higher adjusted incidence compared to men without a history of urinary tract infection (2.12% vs 1.10%; weighted absolute risk difference 1.02%, 95% CI 0.48-1.56%). Previous antibiotic resistant infection (HR 2.57, 95% CI 1.18-5.60) ≥14 days before the index procedure, was also independently associated with increased hazard. Among affected patients, most cases were successfully managed in the outpatient setting; however, 38% required an unplanned emergency department evaluation and 11% were admitted for inpatient care or observation. CONCLUSIONS: Epididymo-orchitis after HoLEP carries meaningful morbidity, frequently prompting emergency evaluation or hospital admission. A history of urinary tract or antibiotic-resistant infection identifies a subset of patients at higher risk, suggesting opportunities for targeted perioperative prophylaxis and tailored follow-up strategies. Further prospective research is indicated to validate these findings and determine whether enhanced perioperative infection control can mitigate risk.

title: INFECTION RISK ASSOCIATED WITH SODIUM-GLUCOSE COTRANSPORTER 2 INHIBITORS IN PATIENTS WITH CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Zi-Jun Xiao, Shang-Jen Chang, Jeff Shih-Chieh Chueh, Shin-Mei Wong
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Recent researches established that Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2 inhibitors) exhibit cardiovascular and renal protective effect in heart failure and chronic kidney disease (CKD) population regardless of their DM status. However, the associated adverse events remain a pronounced concern, particularly urinary tract infections (UTIs) and genital infections (GIs). While CKD patients were at higher infection potential due to impaired immunity or present genitourinary tract anomalies, it is imperative to investigate the infection risk associated with SGLT2 inhibitors used in CKD populations. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) enrolling patients with chronic kidney disease who received SGLT2 inhibitors or placebo/standard care. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane databases were searched up to July 2025. Eligible trials reported incidence of urinary tract infections (UTIs) and/or Genital infections (GIs) as safety outcomes. The study followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, and the selection process was summarized in a PRISMA flow diagram. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using ‘fixed- and random-effects’ models. Subgroup analyses were conducted for individual SGLT2 inhibitors in UTI category. RESULTS: Eighteen RCTs involving 30,308 participants were included. For genital infections, 381 events occurred among 16,023 patients receiving SGLT2i compared with 100 events among 14,440 controls, yielding a significantly increased risk with SGLT2i (OR 2.95, 95% CI 2.36–3.68; p0.001; I2=0%), favoring the control group. In contrast, for urinary tract infections, 1,620 events occurred among 15,868 patients receiving SGLT2i versus 1,301 among 14,440 controls, with no significant difference between groups (OR 1.07, 95% CI 0.95–1.21; p=0.27; I2=29.7%). CONCLUSIONS: In our study, SGLT2 inhibitors are associated with significant increased risk of genital infections rather than UTIs in CKD patients. The increased UTI risk observed with canagliflozin warrants further evaluation. These findings support careful monitoring of infection-related adverse events in CKD patients initiating SGLT2 inhibitors while recognizing the substantial cardio-renal benefits.

title: HIGH PREVALENCE OF UREAPLASMA IN GONORRHEA-NEGATIVE MALE PATIENTS: 40-YEAR RETROSPECTIVE ANALYSIS SUPPORTING ROUTINE DUAL TESTING
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Anthony J. Tundo, Jack Considine, Ali Dabaja
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ureaplasma urealyticum (UU) causes 3-11% of non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU). For symptomatic urethritis, it is recommended to test for and treat the more common pathogens (such as Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae (GC), and Mycoplasma genitalium) rather than routinely include Ureaplasma testing. We aimed to quantify the prevalence of UU in men tested for GC over four decades, hypothesizing that a meaningful proportion of GC-negative men harbor UU, warranting broader dual-testing protocols. METHODS: A retrospective chart review of all male patients (n=83,489) tested for GC by point-of-care, Nucleic Acid Amplification Test, or culture at a tertiary health care center in Detroit, Michigan from January 1st, 1985, to October 9th, 2025. We identified all men who presented with symptoms and tested for GC alone and simultaneous GC and UU and then evaluated the positive rates in each group. RESULTS: Of 83,489 males tested for GC, 80,662 (96.6%) were negative and 6,441 (7.7%) were positive. Among GC-negative patients, only 492 (0.6%) underwent simultaneous UU testing, with 79 (16.1%) testing positive for UU and 430 testing negative (see (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191352.93132.27.07#F1)). Among the 6,441 GC-positive patients, only 22 (0.3%) were simultaneously tested for UU, and 3 (13.6%) were positive. CONCLUSIONS: In this 40-year retrospective analysis, a notable prevalence of UU (16.1%) was identified among the subset of GC-negative males who underwent simultaneous testing. Despite this, only 0.6% of GC-negative and 0.3% of GC-positive patients were tested for UU, underscoring a substantial diagnostic gap. These findings suggest that selective dual testing in men with persistent or recurrent urethritis could improve diagnostic accuracy, guide targeted therapy, and reduce unnecessary empiric antibiotic use.

title: EVALUATING THE ROLE OF THE 9-VALENT HPV VACCINE IN PREVENTING RECURRENCE OF GENITAL WARTS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Etan Eigner, Kamil Malshy, Nicola Fazza, Ameer Nsair, Melissa Atallah, Gilad E. Amiel, Michael Mullerad
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection worldwide. Although the 9-valent vaccine (Gardasil 9) prevents primary infection, its role in secondary prevention after condyloma acuminatum is uncertain. We evaluated whether post-treatment HPV vaccination lowers recurrence risk and identified predictors of recurrence among men treated with carbon dioxide (CO2) laser ablation. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed men ≥17 years treated with CO2 laser ablation for genital condyloma at a tertiary center (June 2016–June 2025). The primary outcome was recurrence after documented clearance. Logistic and mixed-effects regression models tested associations between post-treatment vaccination and recurrence, adjusting for demographic and clinical factors. RESULTS: Among 560 patients (722 sessions), recurrence occurred in 28.4%. Those with recurrence were younger (32 ± 10 vs 37 ± 13 years; p<0.001) and more likely to need ≥2 sessions (18.6% vs 11.6%; p=0.02). Post-recurrence vaccination showed no significant association with reduced risk (aOR 0.49; 95% CI 0.14–1.69; p=0.26). Independent predictors were younger age (aOR 0.96 per year; p<0.001) and ≥2 sessions (aOR 2.44; p=0.003). Table 1. Baseline Characteristics by Future Recurrence Status. Table 2. Mixed-Effects Logistic Regression: Effect of Post-Recurrence HPV Vaccination on Future Recurrence. CONCLUSIONS: Post-treatment HPV vaccination did not reduce recurrence of genital condyloma. Younger age and multiple treatment sessions independently predicted recurrence, reinforcing vaccination’s role primarily in primary prevention. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: HIDDEN MOLECULAR BURDEN OF SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED PATHOGENS: AN IMPERATIVE FOR UROLOGISTS IN ONCOLOGIC SCREENING AND PREVENTION
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Alberto Saldivar, Alan Rodrigo Perez Soriano, Rodrigo Perez Becerra, Victor Osornio Sanchez, Luis Trujillo Ortiz, Gerardo Garza Sainz, Ruben Miguel Santiago Gonzalez, Omar Vieyra Valdez, Genaro Arguelles Morales, Mario Alberto Toledo Diaz, Adrian Martinez Correa, Aaron Delgado Corral, Carina Nolasco, Gerardo Flores, Carlos A. Castro Fuentes, Monica Sierra
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: A dangerous, outdated paradigm persists in urology: equating the absence of symptoms with no risk for Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) in men. This approach, often prioritizing BPH, creates a diagnostic blind spot that conceals a large pathogen reservoir. Our objective was to dismantle this assumption using high-sensitivity molecular biology. We aimed to illuminate the true prevalence of the molecular infectious burden (HPV and bacterial pathogens) in this "asymptomatic" population and to quantify coinfection as a sentinel for active, unrecognized high-risk behaviors. METHODS: A descriptive, cross-sectional study was conducted on 102 male patients (age range: 23-84 years; mean: 56.17) from a general urology clinic. After obtaining informed consent, a standardized questionnaire on sexual risk behavior was administered, and a urethral swab sample was collected. Molecular analysis was performed using a multiplex PCR panel for the detection and genotyping of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) and the specific identification of three key bacterial pathogens: Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma hominis, and Ureaplasma spp. RESULTS: Molecular analysis revealed an overall infectious burden in 27.45% (1 in 4 men) of the cohort. The bacterial load was the most prominent, with a prevalence of 11.76% for Mycoplasma hominis (n=12) and 11.76% for Ureaplasma spp. (n=12). Chlamydia trachomatis was detected in 3.92% (n=4) of cases. HPV prevalence was 7.84% (n=8), with the identification of both high-risk (including HPV 51) and low-risk (HPV 6) genotypes. The pattern of coinfection proved to be the most clinically impactful finding: 100% of HPV-positive patients (both oncogenic and low-risk) were simultaneously harboring multiple bacterial pathogens. Notably, carriers of high-risk HPV were consistently positive for both M. hominis and Ureaplasma spp., establishing a synergistic, high-risk infectious profile. Consistent with the underlying risk, 100% of the patients with a positive molecular test result reported null or inconsistent condom use. CONCLUSIONS: The urology clinic is a silent risk epicenter that demands the immediate abandonment of symptom-based diagnosis. The high prevalence (27.45%) and the pattern of coinfection of oncogenic HPV with bacteria serve as a potent biological alarm, suggesting pro-inflammatory synergy that can enhance viral persistence and potentially accelerate anogenital carcinogenesis. This redefines the Urologist's role. Therefore, the implementation of molecular screening is a public health and oncologic imperative that must be embraced by modern urology, positioning the specialist on the front lines of prevention.

title: SEX-BASED EPIDEMIOLOGIC DIFFERENCES IN LICHEN SCLEROSUS: A MULTICENTER TRINETX COHORT STUDY (2018–2024)
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Paige Richards, Kyra Van Kirk, Cameron Coakes, Zenya Yanoff, Lakshaye Anand, Prabhjot Singh
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Lichen sclerosus (LS) is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis with distinct male and female manifestations. Autoimmune, atopic, infectious, and mechanical factors contribute to sex-specific LS risk, but quantification of fixed versus modifiable risk factors and protective effects, like HPV vaccination, require further definition between sexes. This study quantified the incidence and association of these factors with LS development after adjusting for sex. METHODS: A retrospective, cohort study was conducted using the TriNetX Research Network (2018–2024). Adults ≥18 years without prior LS were followed for incident LS (ICD-10: L90.0, N90.4, N48.0). Multivariable Cox regression adjusted for sex, age, and autoimmune, atopic, metabolic, psychiatric, and viral covariates identified independent predictors. A 1:1 propensity score-matched comparison evaluated adjusted hazard difference by sex (balance <0.1). Significance defined as two-sided p<0.05. RESULTS: Among 1,118,878 adults (466,434 men; 652,444 women), LS incidence was higher in women (1.14%) than men (0.08%). Male sex was protective (HR 0.07, 95% CI 0.06–0.08, p<0.001). Each year of age increased hazard by 2.9% (HR 1.03). Significant predictors included obesity (1.09), autoimmune and atopic conditions: vitiligo (2.18), alopecia areata (1.76), autoimmune thyroiditis (1.62), psoriasis (1.57), Crohn’s disease (1.28), atopic dermatitis (1.26), asthma (1.17), and allergic rhinitis (1.14), viral infections: HSV (1.49), HPV (1.44), psychiatric disorders: depressive episode (1.18) and anxiety (1.11). Quadrivalent HPV vaccination was protective (0.52). Tobacco use (0.66) likely reflected detection bias. Type 1 and 2 diabetes were not independently significant after adjusting for obesity ( Table 1). After matching (455,923 per sex), female hazard remained significantly >10× higher (0.068). CONCLUSIONS: Across 1.1 million adults, LS risk was driven by autoimmune, atopic, viral, and psychiatric comorbidities, with female hazard remaining markedly higher after adjustment. Autoimmune and atopic diseases conferred the strongest risk, whereas HPV vaccination was protective. These findings underscore biologically distinct yet overlapping autoimmune–viral pathways and support coordinated, sex-specific interdisciplinary care to optimize disease prevention, management, reconstructive planning, and long-term outcomes. | | | --- | | |

title: WHO’S AT RISK? AUTOIMMUNE AND METABOLIC PREDICTORS OF LICHEN SCLEROSUS IN EPIC COSMOS
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Neil Vyas, Justin LaClair, Elise De, Brian Masao Inouye
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Lichen sclerosus (LS) is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis associated with both autoimmune and metabolic dysregulation. Population based studies estimate an annual incidence of 50–80 cases per 100,000 person-years and a prevalence of only 0.1–0.3% in the general population. Leveraging the Epic Cosmos electronic health record network, which aggregates data from over 300 million patients nationwide, this study sought to quantify the 2- and 5-year risk of developing LS across major autoimmune and metabolic comorbidities. By comparing large scale, disease specific incidence estimates with established population baselines, we provide a contemporary, real world assessment of LS risk and its relationship to systemic immune and metabolic pathways. METHODS: Retrospective cohort of adults ≥18 years in Epic Cosmos (2017–2025). Inclusion required multiple clinical encounters and ≥1 year of follow-up. Autoimmune (psoriasis, type 1 DM, RA, MS, SLE, celiac, vitiligo) and metabolic (type 2 DM, obesity, HTN, dyslipidemia) cohorts were defined by ICD-10 codes. Diagnosis of LS by ICD-10 code within 2 and 5 years was the primary outcome. Cumulative incidence and adjusted odds ratios (OR, 95% CI) were calculated. Our IRB deemed the study exempt. RESULTS: Among 1,654,627 patients, 56,265 autoimmune and 447,881 metabolic patients developed LS within 2 years; by 5 years, 68,010 and 582,993 cases, respectively. LS prevalence within these cohorts reached 0.53% for autoimmune and 0.35% for metabolic, several fold higher than the reported 0.1–0.3% general population rate. Autoimmune conditions were associated with nearly threefold higher odds of LS at 2 years (OR=2.90, 95% CI 2.87–2.92, p<0.0001) and remained significantly elevated at 5 years (OR=1.51, 95% CI 1.49–1.52, p<0.0001), indicating an early and sustained autoimmune-linked risk pattern. CONCLUSIONS: Patients with autoimmune diseases exhibit substantially greater LS risk compared with those with metabolic disorders. While both groups show progressive incidence over time, autoimmune conditions demonstrate a disproportionate early rise, supporting immune mediated pathogenesis and emphasizing the need for targeted dermatologic screening in autoimmune populations.

title: UNDERSTANDING THE CLINICAL PRESENTATION OF PATIENTS WITH UROGENITAL TUBERCULOSIS IN A SUB-SAHARAN TERTIARY CARE SETTING
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Edouard Ngendahayo, Charles Niyotwiringiye, Princess R. N. Umunyurwa, Patience Mukundirukuri, Francis Rubagumya, Frances Kazal, Jane T. Kurtzman, Theophile Ndayishimye
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Tuberculosis remains the second leading infectious killer worldwide. Extrapulmonary tuberculosis represents 15%-40% of all cases, with urogenital tuberculosis (UGTB) as the second most common form. UG-TB can cause severe urologic complications - including obstructive uropathy, renal failure, and infertility - due to inflammation and scarring. This study describes the presentation of UG-TB at a tertiary hospital in a low- and middle-income country (LMIC), aiming to raise clinical suspicion among providers. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional study of patients diagnosed with UG-TB at a semi-private, tertiary referral hospital with a 160-bed capacity in Kigali, Rwanda between 2015 and 2023. We collated patient logs from the hospital’s inpatient and laboratory's tuberculosis registry to identify all cases of UG-TB. RESULTS: Thirty-two patients were diagnosed and treated for UG-TB. Nearly all were male (96.9%), Rwandan nationals (90.6%), and younger than 55 years old (90.6%). Most had no known medical comorbidities (87.5%) and none were HIV positive. The majority (75%) presented with a scrotal mass, typically a unilateral epididymal nodule (83%); and the remaining presented with upper urinary tract and/or bladder TB. Nearly half (41%) of the patients required surgical intervention for their disease. Three patients required nephrectomy, one underwent bladder augmentation with bilateral ureteroneocystostomy, and one required unilateral nephroureterectomy with contralateral ileal ureter. CONCLUSIONS: UG-TB imposes a high surgical burden in otherwise young, healthy men. Expanding subspecialty training in complex urinary reconstruction is essential to equip urologists to manage these challenging cases. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: PATHWAYS OF PAIN: INCIDENCE OF VARICOCELE, ORCHIALGIA, AND PROSTATITIS IN MALES WITH PELVIC FLOOR DYSFUNCTION
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Olivia Copelan, Aurora Grutman, Amin Herati
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The pelvic floor is a crucial but often overlooked determinant of male urologic health. Pelvic floor dysfunction (PFD) may manifest as chronic pelvic pain, voiding issues, and sexual dysfunction. However, its broader relationship to other genitourinary pain syndromes remains poorly characterized. While varicocele, orchialgia, and prostatitis are traditionally viewed as distinct pain conditions, they may share common pathophysiologic mechanisms. This study leverages a large, multi-institutional dataset to explore the incidence of these conditions among males with and without PFD, offering new insights into mechanisms of male pelvic pain. METHODS: Data were derived from the TriNetX Research Network, which aggregates de-identified electronic health records from participating health systems. Data from 2005-2025 were analyzed. Male patients currently aged ≥ 18 years old were classified as having PFD if they received a diagnosis of either pelvic/perineal pain (ICD-10 R10.2) or segmental/somatic dysfunction of the pelvic region (ICD-10 M99.05). Controls were defined as those who used healthcare services and did not receive either diagnosis. Using the TriNetX analytic platform, incidence proportions and rates (cases/person-day) were calculated for outcomes of interest. Analyses were stratified by age and race. RESULTS: This study included 798,868 patients with and 24,309,831 without PFD. Among those with PFD, the incidence proportions were 2.2% for varicocele (0.000005 cases/person-day), 8.2% for orchialgia (0.000019), and 6.6% for prostatitis (0.000015). In patients without PFD, corresponding proportions were 0.53%, 1.2%, and 0.91%, respectively. Incidence proportions were highest among PFD patients aged 10-14 and 20-24 for varicocele, 0-14 for orchialgia, and 50-59 for prostatitis. For patients without PFD, similar patterns were observed by age but with lower proportions. By race, varicocele was proportionally more common among Black and White males, orchialgia among American Indian/Alaska Native males, and prostatitis among White and Asian males. CONCLUSIONS: Males with clinical indicators of pelvic floor dysfunction appear to have higher burden of varicocele, orchialgia, and prostatitis compared to those without PFD. These findings suggest that pelvic floor pathophysiology may play a broader role in the pathogenesis of male urologic pain syndromes than previously recognized. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal and mechanistic relationships to develop targeted interventions that reduce the burden of chronic pelvic pain.

title: FROM SCROTAL PAIN TO SEROTONIN PATHWAYS: DULOXETINE IN CHRONIC ORCHIALGIA
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Amogh Pande, Susan MacDonald
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Chronic orchialgia is persistent scrotal pain lasting at least 3 months and impairing the patient’s quality of life. There is no standard algorithm for treatment. Neuropathic pain medications often have side effects. The SNRI Duloxetine (Cymbalta) has been well studied and utilized off label by anesthesiologists to treat chronic neuropathic pain. This study evaluates the effectiveness of Duloxetine for chronic orchialgia. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study that analyzed 30 patients (>18yrs) diagnosed with chronic orchialgia between 2016 to present. Ten patients were excluded from final analysis due to loss of follow up. Data collected included patient demographics, Cymbalta prescription, duration of therapy and reported outcomes with side effects. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize baseline characteristics and treatment responses. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test was applied to compare pre- and post- prescription pain scores, assessing the significance of Cymbalta’s effect. RESULTS: For the 20 patients taking duloxetine, the mean pain score pre-treatment was 7.3 ± 2.5 on a pain scale form 0-10, which decreased to 3.6 ± 2.7 with treatment (p=0.0004). Mean pain reduction was 3.7 points (95% CI 2.44-4.96) indicating a clinically meaningful improvement. The effect size calculated using Cohen’s d, was 1.37, indicating a large treatment effect. Among the 19 patients with available side effects data, 11(58%) reported experiencing side effects. Patients who did not report side effects had a higher average of pain reduction (4.8 ± 2.4) compared to those who did not (2.7 ± 2.8) p=0.083, though not statistically significant. The reported side effects include constipation, hypertension and overall fatigue. Upon prescription of duloxetine, every patient was given a black box warning of increased risk of suicidal thoughts as issued by FDA. However, to our knowledge no patient quit because of increased thoughts of suicide and self-harm. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort of patients with chronic orchialgia, treatment with Duloxetine resulted in a statistically and clinically significant reduction in pain scores with mild side effects reported. These findings warrant a prospective clinical trial.

title: PHYSICO-ENZYMATIC APPROACH FOR CHRONIC PROSTATITIS MANAGEMENT: LONG-TERM RESULTS OF ESWT COMBINED WITH BOVHYALURONIDASE AZOXIMER
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Maya Epifanova, Elena Slavkina, Sergey Artemenko, Andrey Kostin, Alexander Epifanov
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Modern medicine faces the pressing challenge of treating chronic prostatitis (CP) and chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CPPS) due to the lack of treatment standards and their detrimental impact on quality of life. The aim of the study was to evaluate the long-term effect of the combined use of extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT) and bovhyaluronidase azoximer (BA) in the comprehensive treatment of patients with CP II and CPPS IIIA–IIIB. METHODS: This open-label, randomized, placebo-uncontrolled study included 116 patients (mean age 45.5±9.5 years, disease duration 20.8±7.7 months) with CP and CPPS. According to the NIDDK/NIH classification, bacterial CP (II) was verified in 37 cases (32%), inflammatory CPPS IIIA in 39 cases (33.6%), and non-inflammatory CPPS IIIB in 40 cases (34.4%). Three groups were identified: Group 1 with CP II (n=37) - ESWT, "3-As" therapy; Group 2 with CPPS IIIA-IIIB (n=38) - ESWT monotherapy; Group 3 with CPPS IIIA-IIIB (n=41) - ESWT, BA. ESWT (Dornier Aries) sessions of 2,000 to 4,000 shocks were administered to the perineum twice weekly for a course of 12 procedures. At weeks 0, 7, 10, 18, 30, and 54, the following were assessed: NIH-CPSI, IPSS, IIEF-5, VAS, uroflowmetry (UFM) data, TRUS with elastography, Doppler ultrasonography, and laboratory tests. RESULTS: All patients completed the full course of treatment without adverse effects. At week 7, a more significant improvement was observed in Group 1 for NIH-CPSI, IPSS, VAS, and UFM (p<0.05). From weeks 10–54, a positive effect was noted in all groups, with a more consistent and significant effect in Group 3, which saw a reduction in the size of fibrotic zones and the number of calcinates, an increase in normal elastic zones, and improved blood flow (p<0.05). Between-group analysis confirmed the superiority of Groups 1 and 3 over Group 2 (p<0.05), with no significant differences between Groups 1 and 3 for NIH-CPSI, IPSS, or VAS (p>0.05). Patients with non-inflammatory CP/CPPS (IIIB) also showed an improvement in erectile function according to IIEF-5 (p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: The presented treatment methods for CP and CPPS demonstrate safety. Effectiveness in eliminating clinical symptoms and improving the morpho-functional parameters of the pancreas. In long-term follow-up, ESWT and the drug BA demonstrate high efficacy in lysing fibrotic areas and pancreatic calcifications, and relieving symptoms of CP/CPPS.

title: CLINICAL CHARACTERISTICS AND OUTCOMES OF MEN WITH CHRONIC PELVIC PAIN AND GENITOURINARY PAIN: A SINGLE-SPECIALIST RETROSPECTIVE REVIEW
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Aidan J. Kennedy, Ethan Aweitzman, Bernadette M. M. Zwaans, Kenneth M. Peters
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome/chronic prostatitis (CPPS/CP) is a heterogeneous disease process affecting 2-6% of men and severely impacting quality of life. AUA Guidelines on the Diagnosis and Management of Male CPPS recommend a multimodal treatment strategy, including medical therapy, psychological treatment, neuromodulation, and pelvic floor physical therapy (PFPT). As a major referral center for CPPS, we sought to review the presenting symptoms, prior evaluation and treatments from outside providers, our evaluation and management strategies, and clinical outcomes. METHODS: A retrospective review of male patients with ICD codes related to pelvic pain evaluated by a single subspecialty-trained urologist at our institution between February 2023 and July 2025 was done. Demographic data, presenting and associated symptoms, initial and most recent visual analog scale (VAS) pain scores, and prior interventions were collected. Interventions initiated after consultation with the male pelvic pain specialist were also recorded. RESULTS: 158 men were included (mean age 46.9 years, range 20-89; mean follow-up 301 days). 26 did not return after the initial visit. Urine cultures were obtained in 27.8%, of which 11.3% were positive. Mean initial 10-point VAS pain score was 3.4 (range 0-9), improving to a mean of 2.5 at most recent follow-up. Common associated symptoms included overactive bladder (45.5%), incomplete emptying (22.2%), and dysuria (12.7%); 5.7% of patients had Hunner’s lesions. Pain was most often diffuse (51.4%), followed by penile (14.6%) and rectal (12.0%). Bike riding/perineal compression (22.2%) and intercourse/masturbation (15.8%) were the most identified pain triggers, though 39.8% of patients could not identify their pain trigger. Prior to specialist consultation, 52.5% had undergone PFPT and 23.4% had received local anesthetic blocks. Most common treatments offered by the urologist were PFPT with therapists trained in intrarectal myofascial release (44.3%), local anesthetic/steroid blocks (pudendal, penile, spermatic cord, levator trigger point injections) (41.8%), and low intensity shockwave therapy (47.5%). Neuromodulation was performed in 8.2% of patients. CONCLUSIONS: Men with CPPS present with heterogeneous symptoms, frequently without clear pain triggers, and demonstrate low rates of urinary tract infection. Many patients have already pursued pelvic floor physical therapy or procedural interventions before further specialist evaluation. Modest improvements in pain scores over follow-up highlight the need for individualized, multimodal management strategies and further study of optimized treatment pathways.

title: CLUES TO PAIN RELIEF: TREATMENT AND SYMPTOM PATTERNS IN MEN WITH CHRONIC PELVIC PAIN
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Aidan J. Kennedy, Ethan A. Weitzman, Bernadette M. M. Zwaans, Kenneth M. Peters
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome/chronic prostatitis (CPPS/CP) is a complex syndrome affecting 2-6% of men and severely impacting quality of life. A multimodal treatment strategy is recommended by the AUA Guidelines. As a major referral center for CPPS, we examined differences between patients that had improvement in their pain scores compared to those who did not. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective review of male pelvic pain patients evaluated by a single subspecialty-trained urologist at our institution between February 2023 and July 2025. We included patients that had a baseline and follow up visual analog scale (VAS) pain score. Demographic data, presenting and associated symptoms, initial and most recent VAS pain scores, and prior interventions were collected. Interventions initiated after consultation with the male pelvic pain specialist were also recorded. Patients were stratified into two groups based on change in VAS scores: those with improvement and those without improvement or worsening scores. RESULTS: 103 patients had baseline and recent VAS scores with a mean follow-up of 311 days. 65 (63.1%) demonstrated improvement in VAS scores (mean improvement 3.1 points; follow-up 315 days), while 38 (36.9%) had stable or worsened pain (mean decline 1.2 points; follow-up 305 days). Patients who improved were slightly younger (mean age 44.4 vs. 47 years). Although not statistically significant, responders tended to report more overactive bladder symptoms (47.7% vs. 44.7%, p=0.77) and dysuria (13.8% vs. 7.9%, p=0.36), but less frequently reported incomplete emptying (18.5% vs. 23.7%, p=0.52). Rates of new pelvic floor physical therapy with intrarectal myofascial release were similar between groups; however, patients that improved more often received a peripheral nerve block (69.2% vs 44.7%, p=0.01) and neuromodulation (12.3% vs 7.9%, p=0.48). Analgesic and antispasmodic medication use was generally comparable, although responders more often received agents targeting obstructive voiding symptoms (15.4% vs. 2.7%, p=0.04). CONCLUSIONS: Younger age and differences in baseline urinary symptoms may distinguish men with CPPS who experienced pain improvement. Responders more often received peripheral nerve blocks, neuromodulation, and medications for obstructive voiding symptoms. These findings suggest that patient age, symptom profile, and treatment selection may influence outcomes and highlight the need for further investigation into tailored management strategies.

title: IGG4-RELATED PROSTATITIS: PROPOSAL FOR ITS DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Hajime Kido, Terumi Kamisawa, Shin-Ichiro Horiguchi, Keigo Setoguchi, Masaya Ito, Masahiro Toide, Takahiko Soma, Fumitaka Koga
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is an immune-mediated fibro-inflammatory disorder that can affect multiple organs, characterized by elevated serum IgG4 levels and mass formation in various organs with infiltration of dense IgG4-positive plasma cells. Corticosteroid (CS) therapy is generally effective, but relapse is not uncommon. While any organs can be involved, IgG4-related prostatitis (IgG4-RP) has been scantly reported and lacks standardized diagnostic criteria. The utility of FDG-PET and Diffusion-weighted Whole-body Imaging with Background body signal suppression (DWIBS) has been reported in assessing organs involved by IgG4-RD. We experienced 2 IgG4-RP cases where IgG4-RD was pathologically confirmed by prostate biopsy. We aimed to propose diagnostic criteria for IgG4-RP and evaluate its incidence using DWIBS findings in male patients with histologically confirmed IgG4-RD. METHODS: Histological criteria were proposed based on the 2 biopsy-proven cases and previous case reports. The study cohort included 30 male IgG4-RD patients who underwent DWIBS. Positive DWIBS findings were defined as high signal intensity on DWIBS + inflammatory changes on T2-weighted MRI. We assessed the incidence of positive DWIBS findings and relations of CS response with changes in DWIBS and serum IgG4 levels. LUTS were assessed in a subset of cases and was defined as IPSS ≥8. RESULTS: We propose histological criteria of IgG4-RP as follows: the presence of dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration with >10 IgG4-positive plasma cells/HPF or an IgG4/IgG-positive cell ratio of >40%. Among 14 patients underwent DWIBS before CS, DWIBS was positive in 9 (64%) including the 2 biopsy-proven cases. Of 6 patients re-evaluated after CS, 5 (83%) showed DWIBS improvement along with serum IgG4 decline. LUTS were found in 3 of 4 IPSS-assessed, DWIBS-positive patients before CS; post-CS IPSS was assessed in a biopsy-proven IgG4-RP case where IPSS normalized along with DWIBS and serum IgG4 levels. CONCLUSIONS: We propose the diagnostic criteria for IgG4-RP: histologically, the presence of dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration with >10 IgG4-positive plasma cells/HPF or an IgG4/IgG-positive cell ratio of >40%, and clinically, positive findings on DWIBS or FDG-PET as well as elevated serum IgG4 levels. DWIBS evaluation suggests prostatitis in the majority of male IgG4-RD patients.

title: COMPARISON OF NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING DNA VERSUS TRADITIONAL CULTURES IN PENILE IMPLANT REVISION CASES: “WHAT AM I MISSING USING ONLY CULTURES”
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Jaimy Joji, Jacob Ancira, Niccole Diaz, Lynn Tong, Andy Bennett, Spencer Pringle, Anthony Stuart, Paul Chung, Gerard Dhenry
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Traditional cultures are used to diagnose penile prosthesis (PP) infections and guide antibiotic therapy. However, false negative results are common, due to biased growth media, non-cultivable organisms, antibiotic usage, or insufficient sample volumes. Next generation sequencing (NGS) circumvents these issues by sequencing DNA directly from the samples. NGS allows for more sensitive and comprehensive identification of microorganisms, which in turn can guide antimicrobial treatment and surgical decision-making. Our goal is to evaluate the performance of NGS-based diagnostics compared to traditional culture in detecting bacteria on infected PPs. Our hypothesis is that NGS will be more sensitive and identify more isolates than traditional cultures. METHODS: 322 PPs removed for any reason from 2015 to July 2025 were included in the study. During revision surgery, two swab specimens were collected from the pump space if an inflatable PP / corporal space if rod: 1) sent for traditional culture testing at the institutional laboratory, and 2) for NGS testing (MicroGenDx, Lubbock, TX, USA), including targeted 16s rRNA and ITS gene sequencing. Positivity rates, numbers of species, and organism profiles per test were compared. RESULTS: NGS had a significantly higher rate of positive detections (n=111, 34.47%) compared to culture results (n=40, 12.42%, p<0.001). NGS identified significantly more bacterial species than culture (NGS mean=1.35 (2.55), Culture mean=0.30 (0.65), p<0.001). NGS found 3 fungal species and 55 bacterial species in comparison to the 1 fungal species and 16 bacterial species identified by traditional culture ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191352.93132.27.20#F1)). Unique species found by NGS included many fastidious organisms likely to be missed by culture including various anaerobes, Mycoplasma, and Ureaplasma. CONCLUSIONS: NGS offers a more sensitive and comprehensive characterization of the organisms contributing to PP microbiome, which may be a useful aid in diagnosis and treatment.

title: HARNESSING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TO PREDICT POST-OPERATIVE INFECTION AFTER INFLATABLE PENILE PROSTHESIS IMPLANTATION: A MACHINE LEARNING PREDICTION MODEL
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Muhammed A. M. Hammad, Faysal A. Yafi, Justin Schneider, Jonathan Prunean, Elia Abou Chawareb, David Han, Babak Azad, Daniel Swerdloff, Jake A. Miller, Robert Andrianne, Arthur L. Burnett, Kelli Gross, Georgios Hatzichristodoulou, James M. Hotaling, Tung-Chin Hsieh, James M. Jones, Aaron Lentz, Vaibhav Modgil, Daniar Osmonov, Sung Hun Park, Ian Pearce, Paul Perito, Hossein Sadeghi-Nejad, Maxime Sempels, Alfredo Suarez-sarmiento, Jr, Koenraad Van Renterghem, J. Nicholas Warner, Matthew Ziegelmann
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Post-operative infection following inflatable penile prosthesis (IPP) surgery remains one of the most serious complications despite advances in antiseptic techniques. Current infection-risk assessment relies on surgeon experience rather than objective tools. We developed and validated a machine learning–based model using a unified complication taxonomy to enable preoperative infection risk stratification. METHODS: A total of 5,815 multicenter IPP cases (primary, revision, and infection-salvage) were analyzed. Unstructured operative entries were standardized into a 38-feature taxonomy encompassing demographics, comorbidities, surgical variables, prosthesis type, and intraoperative details. Among these, 117 cases (2%) were complication-positive for post-operative infection. We compared 80 model configurations (10 classifiers × 4 resampling strategies × 2 data splits). Model performance was evaluated using macro-averaged precision, recall, F1 score, and precision–recall area under the curve (PR-AUC). Feature interpretability was assessed with SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations). RESULTS: Gradient Boosting with Random Undersampling (RUS) achieved the best standard-split performance (Precision=0.52, Recall=0.75, F1=0.46, PR-AUC=0.10). Logistic Regression without resampling performed best on temporal validation (Precision=0.52, Recall=0.63, F1=0.51, PR-AUC=0.06). SHAP analysis ( Fig 1) identified diabetes, coronary/peripheral vascular disease, and history of prior IPP infection as the strongest positive predictors of infection, with maximum SHAP contributions of +0.21, +0.67, and +0.83, respectively. Additional risk factors included intra-operative complications and older age. Protective associations were observed for AMS LGX prosthesis use and combined peri-operative antifungal + vancomycin prophylaxis. CONCLUSIONS: A gradient-boosting model integrating pre- and intra-operative variables achieved 75% sensitivity for post-operative infection prediction, supporting its role as a preoperative screening tool. SHAP interpretability highlights patient comorbidities and infection history as dominant drivers of infection risk, while combination antifungal-antibiotic prophylaxis may confer measurable protection. External validation is underway to optimize model calibration and clinical deployment.

title: UROPRIME (UROLOGICAL PROSTHETIC INFECTION MODEL EVALUATION): DEVELOPMENT OF A EUROPEAN MULTICENTER NOMOGRAM PREDICTING PERIOPERATIVE INFECTIOUS RISK IN UROLOGICAL PROSTHETIC SURGERY
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Bruno Bucca, Rocco Simone Flammia, Mattia Lo Re, Andrea Cocci, Marco Falcone, Wai Gin Lee, Andrea Gobbo, Shiv Sarna, Luca Matteo Gobbi, Greta Basile, Roberto Acanfora, Martina Scavone, Eleonora Sollazzi, Anna Ricapito, Borja Garcia Gomez, Julio Cesar Ramon Calderon, Manuel Alonso Isa, Claudia Zaccaro, Christian Gozzi, Miroslav L. Djordjevic, Ignacio Moncada, Giorgio Franco, Carlo Bettocchi, David Ralph
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Postoperative prosthesis infection is a severe complication. Accurate, early risk stratification is essential to guide preventive strategies. We aimed to develop and externally validate a clinical nomogram to predict the 90-day risk of postoperative prosthesis infection in a large European cohort. METHODS: We conducted a multicenter retrospective study of patients undergoing urogenital prosthetic surgery. The cohort was randomly divided into a training (2/3, n=541) and test (1/3, n=271) dataset. The primary outcome was 90-day postoperative infection. A stepwise logistic regression model was developed on the training set to best combination of predictors. The final model was displayed as a nomogram. Model performance was evaluated for accuracy (C-index) and calibration plot plots). Clinical usefulness was determined using Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) on the validation dataset test. RESULTS: Of the 812 patients, 40 (4.9%) experienced an infection. The final model included Age at Surgery (OR 1.03, 95% CI: 0.99–1.08; p=0.124), Obesity (OR 2.28, 95% CI: 0.88–5.53; (p=0.075), Time of Surgery (OR 1.01, 95% CI: 1.00–1.02; p=0.001), and n° of days of prophylaxis antibiotics (OR 0.88, 95% CI: 0.74–1.04; p=0.145). In the internal validation, the model demonstrated good discrimination with a C-index of 0.72 and excellent calibration. In the split validation, the model retained acceptable discrimination with a C- Index of 0.69. The split calibration plot showed good agreement between predicted and observed probabilities. Decision curve analysis confirmed that using the nomogram provided a greater net benefit than the “treat all” or “treat none” strategies across a wide range of clinically relevant risk thresholds (approx. 2.5% to 10%). Based on Youden test a nomogram cut-off of 6% was identified showing a sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV of 63, 76.5, 12,3 and 97.5% respectively. CONCLUSIONS: We have developed and externally validated a simple nomogram that provides good predictive accuracy for 90-day postoperative prosthesis infection. This tool can assist clinicians in identifying high-risk patients who may benefit from targeted preventive measures.

title: CYSTOSCOPY AND RISK OF URINARY TRACT INFECTION. A NATIONWIDE 5-YEAR COHORT STUDY
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Lars Lund, Christoffer Froekjaer, Szimonetta Szépligeti, Mette Noergaard
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to examine the 7-day risk of urinary tract infection (UTI) following cystoscopy in an outpatient clinic. METHODS: This nationwide population-based cohort study included all adult patients (age ≥18 years), who underwent a cystoscopy in an outpatient setting in Denmark in the period 2018-2023. We identified the patients through the Danish National Patient Registry (DNPR) using procedure codes KUKC0O2 or KKCD02. We defined UTI as a hospital diagnosis recorded in DNPR and/or redemption of at least one prescription for urinary tract infection-specific antibiotics (sulfamethizole, trimethoprim, pivmecillinam or nitrofurantoin) (ATC codes J01EB02, J01EA, J01CA08, and J01XE01) within one week after cystoscopy. From DNPR we obtained information on patients’ comorbidities registered before date of cystoscopy including by using Charlson Comorbidity index. We characterized the patients at date of cystoscopy including the prevalence of UTI within 5 years before date of cystoscopy and followed the individuals within the first week after the procedure. Among patients without UTI at the index date, we computed the 7-day risk of UTI overall and stratified by age, sex and underlying comorbidities. RESULTS: We included 294,075 patients who underwent cystoscopy in an outpatient setting in the period 2018-2023. Of these, 70% were men and 75% were 50 years or older (See table 1). A total of 49,855 (17%) had a UTI registered within 5 years before cystoscopy based on hospital diagnoses and redeemed prescriptions and 38% had no registered comorbidity according to the Charlson comorbidity Index. Within 7 days after cystoscopy, 2.6% (95% CI, 2.55–2.67) experienced an UTI (Table 2). Individuals aged 18-39 years had the highest risk, 4.19% (95% CI, 3.91–4.48) CONCLUSIONS: We conclude, based on this robust 5-year national study in a time when there is a large overuse of antibiotics, that it is NOT necessary to use antibiotics during outpatient cystoscopies except in selected patients e. g. such as patients with heart valve surgery or immunosuppressed patients.

title: AI-BASED CT ANALYSIS OF MYOSTEATOSIS PREDICTS MORTALITY IN FOURNIER GANGRENE
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Byeong Jin Kang, Kyung Hwan Kim, Chan Ho Lee, Ja Yoon Ku, Hong Koo Ha, Hyun Jun Park
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Fournier’s gangrene (FG) is a fatal necrotizing infection with high mortality. Existing indices such as the Fournier Gangrene Severity Index (FGSI) rely on static parameters and may not reflect baseline metabolic status. Myosteatosis, or fat infiltration within skeletal muscle, is linked to poor outcomes in cancer and critical illness. This study evaluated the prognostic significance of myosteatosis in FG using artificial intelligence (AI)-based computed tomography (CT) analysis. METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of 40 patients with Fournier’s gangrene treated between 2012 and 2022. Preoperative L3-level CT scans were analyzed using AI software (ClariSarco, ClariPi, Seoul, Korea) to quantify skeletal muscle quality. Parameters including normal attenuation muscle area (NAMA) were automatically extracted to assess myosteatosis, which was defined by sex-specific NAMA/TAMA cutoffs. Clinical characteristics, FGSI, septic shock, and mortality were compared, and predictors of mortality were evaluated by multivariate logistic regression. RESULTS: Among 40 patients, 22 (55 percent) had myosteatosis. These patients exhibited higher rates of septic shock (45.5 percent vs 11.1 percent, p<0.05) and mortality (31.8 percent vs 5.6 percent, p<0.05) than those without myosteatosis. Survivors had higher NAMA (79.1 ± 31.5 vs 46.2 ± 22.3, p<0.05) and lower myosteatosis percentage (37.9 ± 16.8 percent vs 56.5 ± 15.2 percent, p<0.05). Multivariate analysis revealed that myosteatosis percentage (odds ratio 1.11, 95 percent confidence interval 1.01–1.23, p=0.03), FGSI >9 (odds ratio 62.9, p=0.026), and cardiovascular disease (odds ratio 53.5, p=0.018) were independent predictors of mortality. CONCLUSIONS: AI-based CT analysis provides an objective and reproducible assessment of muscle quality in FG. Myosteatosis independently predicted septic shock and mortality, outperforming traditional measures such as BMI and FGSI. Incorporating AI-derived myosteatosis evaluation into clinical workflows may enable early risk stratification and individualized treatment planning for high-risk FG patients.

title: AUTONOMIC OVERDRIVE UNMASKED: PERIPHERAL COLD HYPERSENSITIVITY REVEALS A NEUROVASCULAR PATHWAY TO PREMATURE EJACULATION
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: H. Y. Sun, Chang Chi Chang, Yi Chun Chiu, Wei Ming Cheng
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Cold hypersensitivity in the hands and feet (CHHF) reflects sympathetic overactivity and endothelial dysfunction affecting peripheral blood flow. Although associated with erectile dysfunction, its role in premature ejaculation (PE)—a disorder characterized by autonomic hyperexcitability—remains unclear. This study aims to investigate the independent association between CHHF and PE in men with preserved erectile function, isolating autonomic influences on ejaculatory control. METHODS: An anonymous web-based survey conducted in December 2022 enrolled 1,008 sexually active Taiwanese men aged 20–40 years. Those with erectile dysfunction (IIEF-5 ≤ 21) or phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor use were excluded. CHHF was defined by persistent cold sensations in both hands and feet lasting ≥6 months. PE was identified by Premature Ejaculation Diagnostic Tool (PEDT) scores ≥9. Multivariate logistic regression adjusted for age, smoking, insomnia, and exercise to assess CHHF-PE association. RESULTS: Among participants (mean age 31.6 ± 5.2), 22.5% reported CHHF. Compared to non-CHHF men, CHHF-positive men had higher smoking prevalence (21.6% vs. 14.5%; p=0.018) and insomnia rates (13.2% vs. 7.0%; p=0.009). PE prevalence was significantly greater in CHHF men (25.1% vs. 18.3%; p=0.029). CHHF independently predicted PE with adjusted odds ratio 1.64 (95% CI 1.00–2.69; p=0.048). Item-level PEDT analysis revealed “ejaculation occurs too early” as the dominant symptom driving this link (odds ratio 2.03; p=0.011), implicating accelerated ejaculatory reflex over psychological distress. CONCLUSIONS: Peripheral cold hypersensitivity independently associates with premature ejaculation despite normal erectile function, unveiling a shared autonomic-vascular pathway. CHHF serves as an easily reportable sensory biomarker of systemic dysautonomia impacting male sexual health. This “cold–rapid” connection reframes PE within an autonomic-vascular continuum, highlighting the potential of interventions targeting microcirculatory and autonomic balance—such as aerobic exercise, stress reduction, and biofeedback—to complement pharmacotherapy. | | | --- | | |

title: POST-VASECTOMY PAIN SYNDROME AND VASECTOMY COMPLICATIONS: REAL-LIFE DATA FROM A SINGLE TERTIARY REFERRAL CENTER
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Massimiliano Raffo, Maurizio De Rocco Ponce, Paula Izquierdo, Jashua Haddad Baldassari, Julio Cesar Murillo Pinto, Doron Vantman Luft, Francesco Montorsi, Andrea Salonia, Eduard Ruiz-Castane
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Vasectomy is an increasingly utilized method of permanent male contraception. No-scalpel vasectomy (NSV) is the preferred technique due to its favorable safety profile and low complication rates. However, complications such as infection, hematoma, and chronic post-vasectomy pain syndrome (PVPS) can occur. The true incidence and risk factors for PVPS remain uncertain. This study aims to evaluate the rates of PVPS and other complications following vasectomy, as well as to identify associated risk factors. METHODS: This retrospective study evaluated 1,774 sexually active men undergoing vasectomy between 2016 and 2024 at a single tertiary-referral center. Baseline data, including age, number of children, and BMI, were collected preoperatively. Postoperative follow-up assessed complications, need for repeat surgery, and results of post-vasectomy semen analysis (PVSA) performed three months after the procedure. Statistical analysis utilized nonparametric tests and multivariate logistic regression to identify independent risk factors for complications (significance: p<0.05). RESULTS: Patients had a median age of 42 years (IQR 7.0), median BMI 26.95 (IQR 4.96), and median follow-up of 101 months (IQR 97–104). Most (90%) completed PVSA; 94.9% achieved azoospermia at first analysis, with 2% requiring re-vasectomy, and 0.2% undergoing vasovasostomy or TESE for regret. Postoperative recovery was uneventful in 97.3% of cases; infection and hematoma rates were 1.5% and 1.1%, respectively. PVPS occurred in 0.7% (n=14); most were managed with NSAIDs, a minority (n=3) required escalated treatment, including one surgical re-intervention. Multivariate analysis identified postoperative complications (p<0.001) and higher BMI (p=0.012) as independent risk factors for PVPS; age was not significant. CONCLUSIONS: No-scalpel vasectomy offers high efficacy and safety for male sterilization, with rare complications and a low PVPS incidence. Postoperative complications and elevated BMI independently increase PVPS risk and may merit consideration during preoperative counseling and risk stratification.

title: EARLY FOLLOW-UP OF DECOMPRESSIVE EPIDIDYMECTOMY: SAFETY AND OUTCOME PROFILES
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Chase William Mallory, Austin Krishingner, Rachel Lin, Rohan Arora, Anirudth Venkatesh, Kevin Campbell
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Epididymectomy is an underutilized, yet effective intervention for scrotal content pain localized to the epididymis. Referral to a surgeon experienced in scrotal surgery is often valuable given possible injury to the testicle or gonadal vasculature which reside close to the epididymis. At our tertiary referral center, epididymectomy is offered to men with pinpoint, reproduceable, epididymal tenderness who present for scrotal content pain refractory to NSAIDs and conservative management. We describe a novel surgical approach which involves opening of the epididymal sheath and disarticulating the epididymis off the underlying posterior epididymal fascia which is kept in-situ overlying the testis and gonadal vasculature, and its early safety and outcome profiles. METHODS: Patients were assessed for chronic scrotal content pain who underwent decompression epididymectomy at a tertiary referral center from July, 2022 to October, 2025. Pain had to be present for greater than 30 days, reproducible on exam, and localized to epididymis. Men without post-operative follow up were excluded. Patients were assessed for laterality, prior surgeries, origin of pain, post-operative pain assessment and 90-day complications. Chi-square analysis was used for sub-group analysis. RESULTS: Fifty-four men underwent decompression epididymectomy. Forty-five men were included in the final cohort. Mean time to initial follow up was 3.9 weeks. Scrotal content pain improved in 74.1% (n=40) men, resolved in 26.2% (n=12), unchanged in 7.4% (n=4) and worsened in 2.2% (n=1) of men. Post-operative pain response improved when stratified by patients undergoing epididymectomy only, without concomitant scrotal surgery ( Table 1). Pain improvement was not associated with prior penoscrotal surgery (p-0.67), bilateral nature (p-0.47) or chronic narcotic pain medication (p-0.21). Surgical site inflammation (7%), scrotal hematoma (4%) and superficial wound dehiscence (2%) were noted 90 days post-operatively. Pain response did not corelate with prior genitourinary or scrotal surgical history. CONCLUSIONS: Our case series demonstrates that decompression epididymectomy is a safe and effective approach to epididymal resection for scrotal content pain. Our approach may help minimize potential complications and risk to the gonadal vessels, while optimizing pain relief. | | | --- | | |

title: VARICOCELECTOMY WITH PERI-VASAL DENERVATION IS A SAFE INTERVENTION IN SETTING OF IDIOPATHIC ORCHALGIA
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Patrick Martin-Tuite, Luke Brawer, Joel Vetter, Alethea Paradis, Dane Johnson
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Subinguinal microscopic varicocelectomy is a well-established treatment for men with varicoceles and chronic orchalgia. Peri-vasal veins are typically preserved to protect fertility and avert testicular atrophy. Incorporation of peri-vasal denervation (PVD) with varicocelectomy may be an appropriate surgical option for patients with varicoceles and orchalgia that does not align with typical varicocele symptoms. This study aimed to evaluate whether combining standard varicocelectomy with PVD is a safe operative intervention for men with varicocles and idiopathic orchalgia. METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of men undergoing subinguinal microscopic varicocelectomy for the primary indication of orchalgia between July 2017 and December 2024 at our institution. Patient demographics, varicocele characteristics, surgical findings, and pre- and post-intervention pain severity scores (scale of 1–10) were collected. Inclusion required a palpable varicocele and ≥ 3 months of orchalgia, including typical varicocele pain and atypical symptoms more consistent with idiopathic orchalgia. Men desiring future fertility were excluded. PVD was performed only when the deferential artery was identified. RESULTS: We evaluated 91 patients who underwent varicocelectomy for the primary indication of orchalgia, with 21 patients undergoing PVD at time of varicocelectomy. Mean post-operative follow-up time of 4.73 months. No independent factors including varicocele grade or laterality, patient BMI, or comorbidities were associated with severity of pre-operative pain. Mean pre-operative pain severity was 6.7 (SD 2.7) and mean post-operative pain severity was 2.5 (SD 2.8). Pain improved in 19 (90.5%) patients, including resolution of pain in 9 (42.9%) patients. Two (9.5%) patients saw no change or worsening pain. No post-operative complications at the level of Clavien-Dindo Grade II or above were observed. CONCLUSIONS: Incorporation of PVD with varicocelectomy is a safe, viable intervention for men with varicoceles and orchalgia when the deferential artery is identified. Consideration of this surgical approach is appropriate for men with idiopathic orchalgia, with atypical symptom patterns suggestive of a neuropathic component. Further investigations of varicocelectomy with PVD are warranted to refine patient selection and compare outcomes with standard varicocelectomy. | | | --- | | |

title: COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF MINIMAL-INCISION MODIFIED FENESTRATION TECHNIQUE AND STANDARD HYDROCELECTOMY: REDUCED BLEEDING AND HEALTHCARE UTILIZATION
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Chloe Shi, Nancy Wei, Matthew Ziegelmann, Tobias Köhler, Landon Trost, Sevann Helo
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Hydrocelectomy is typically a low-risk operation, but minimally invasive approaches may offer added benefits for patients and providers. The minimal-incision modified fenestration technique (MIMFeT), performed in-office under local anesthesia, may reduce complications and healthcare utilization. We compared postoperative outcomes of MIMFeT with standard hydrocelectomy. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent hydrocelectomy at our institution from January 2018 to July 2024. Technique selection was based on surgeon preference. Primary outcomes were 30-day postoperative complications (bleeding, infection, reoperation). Secondary outcomes included unplanned patient contacts within 90 days and hydrocele recurrence within 1 year. Fisher’s exact test was used for categorical comparisons. RESULTS: Among 311 patients (130 MIMFeT; 181 standard), recurrence outcomes were available for 300. Overall 30-day complication rates were lower with MIMFeT (6.2%) versus standard (12.7%), though not statistically significant (OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.17–1.09; p=0.083). Rates of infection and reoperation were comparable. Notably, bleeding occurred in 6.1% of standard cases but in none of the MIMFeT cases (OR 0, 95% CI 0–0.53; p=0.003). MIMFeT patients also had fewer unplanned postoperative contacts (43.8% vs 58.6%; OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.34–0.89; p=0.011). One-year recurrence did not differ significantly between groups ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191352.93132.27.29#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: MIMFeT demonstrated comparable safety and recurrence rates to standard hydrocelectomy while eliminating bleeding events and reducing postoperative healthcare utilization. These findings suggest MIMFeT may be particularly advantageous for patients at elevated bleeding risk and offer a practical, office-based alternative for those seeking to minimize perioperative morbidity and follow-up needs.

title: THE UTILITY OF AUTOLOGOUS TUNICA VAGINALIS GRAFT REPAIR ON VARYING TESTICULAR PATHOLOGIES
session: (https://www.auajournals.org/journal/juro "Journal of Urology")Infections/Inflammation/Cystic Disease of the Genitourinary Tract: Prostate & Genitalia (IP14)
authors: Yara Elgindy, Anthony-Joe Nassour, Darius Ashrafi, Paul Sved, David Eisinger
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The use of tunica vaginalis grafts has been incompletely described in the current literature. This surgical method could have potential benefits in patients with varying testicular pathologies. This includes testicular compartment syndrome due to torsion or epididymo-orchitis and for patients with large defects after testicular rupture. Our aim was to demonstrate the versatility and applicability of tension free autologous tunica vaginalis graft repair (aTVGR). METHODS: We conducted a retrospective case series of two surgeons. 68 patients underwent scrotal exploration between April 2017 and February 2021 for various indications. 11 patients received a TVGR and were included in this case series. Patient demographics, clinical history and indications were collected retrospectively. Written consent was obtained for the use of intraoperative images. All patients had post-operative follow-up at 2 and 6 weeks with a repeat ultrasound. RESULTS: 11 patients underwent TVGR. 6/11 (55%) for ruptured testicular tunica albuginea following blunt trauma, 3/11 (18%) epididymo-orchitis induced testicular compartment syndrome with post-operative ultrasound confirming good flow. 2/11 (27%) were re-do scrotal explorations for tension ischemia following primary repair of ruptured testicle with post-operative ultrasound confirming good flow. There were no post-operative complications at 2 or 6 weeks. CONCLUSIONS: TVGR should be considered in traumatic testicular rupture with extensive tunica albuginea defect or if tension-free primary closure cannot be achieved. TVGR is a safe and viable management solution for the treatment of testicular compartment syndrome of varying aetiology. Future prospective comparative studies with long term follow-up would help guide management.

title: EASYVOID: A NOVEL PORTABLE UROFLOWMETER FOR HOME-BASED, CONTAINER-FREE URINARY FLOW TESTING ON ANY TOILET
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Ray Chang, Yu-Chen Chen, Hao-Wei Chen, Ruei-Hong Zeng, Manu Prakash
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Conventional uroflowmetry requires patients to void into collection funnels or devices within clinics, often altering their natural voiding behavior and limiting access. Existing sound- or sensor-based systems attempt home use but face challenges of acoustic variability, calibration drift, and toilet incompatibility. We developed EasyVoid, a novel portable uroflowmeter that enables accurate, home-based, container-free urinary flow testing on any toilet, leveraging the Coandă effect to capture real-time flow without microphones, pressure sensors, or urine collection. METHODS: EasyVoid incorporates a passive novel helical rotor that converts urinary stream momentum into rotational velocity through the Coandă effect ( Fig. A). A Hall effect sensor detects rotor spin, transmitting data wirelessly for signal processing. Flow rate is calculated via a polynomial calibration model integrating noise filtering, Hilbert transform, and phase unwrapping ( Fig. B). The system was evaluated using simulated voiding across five standard flow patterns (bell-shaped, bell-with-tail, plateau, intermittent, and low-volume) and compared with a clinical uroflowmeter (MMS Flowmaster). Four key parameters—Qmax, Qave, voided volume, and voiding time—were analyzed. Six board-certified urologists also performed a single-blind review of 90 randomized flow curves to assess diagnostic concordance between EasyVoid and standard uroflowmetry. RESULTS: Across 45 simulated voids, EasyVoid demonstrated strong agreement with standard uroflowmetry: Qmax (R2=0.81), Qave (R2=0.89), voided volume (R2=0.73), and voiding time (R2=0.99) ( Fig. C). In the reader validation task, diagnostic interpretations between EasyVoid and standard uroflowmetry achieved 91% concordance (κ=0.84) ( Fig. D), consistent with expert-level inter-rater reliability. CONCLUSIONS: EasyVoid enables accurate, naturalistic uroflowmetry at home or in any restroom—without urine collection, calibration, or specialized hardware. Its low-cost, passive design supports longitudinal LUTS monitoring and postoperative follow-up in real-world settings. This technology represents a clinically ready step toward democratizing access to objective urinary flow assessment beyond hospital walls. Patent pending: PCT/US2025/034459.

title: NOCTURNAL BLADDER CAPACITY INDEX ASSESSMENT TO IMPROVE NOCTURIA MANAGEMENT IN PATIENTS WITH LOWER URINARY TRACT SYMPTOMS RELATED TO BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Manfredi Bruno Sequi, Fabio Maria Valenzi, Andrea Fuschi, Paolo Pietro Suraci, Yazan Al Salhi, Onofrio Antonio Rera, Alice Antonioni, Damiano Graziani, Filippo Gianfrancesco, Giuseppe Candita, Giorgio Martino, Paolo Benanti, Giovanni Di Gregorio, Luca Erra, Gaia Vivarelli, Salvatore Viola, Hila Rogozinski, Riccardo Lombardo, Cosimo De Nunzio, Antonio Carbone, Antonio Luigi Pastore
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Nocturia is a prevalent and disruptive symptom in men with BPH. The Nocturnal Bladder Capacity Index (NBCI) is a diagnostic toolthat helps differentiate between nocturia subtypes, such as nocturnal polyuria (NP) and reduced nocturnal bladder capacity (NBC),guiding targeted treatments.
