This study compares the clinical outcomes of NBCI-guided management versus non-stratified standardtreatment approaches in men with BPH-associated nocturia. METHODS: This prospective study included men between 45 and 65 years old with significant nocturia (≥3 voids/night) and LUTS related toBPH. Participants were divided into the NBCI guided and non NBCI groups. The NBCI-guided group underwent differential diagnosisbased on NBCI values. Patients with NBCI >1.3, indicating reduced NBC, were treated with tamsulosin (0.4 mg/day) and solifenacin(5 mg/day). Patients with NBCI ≤1.3 underwent frequency-volume charts and nocturnal urine volume (NUV) assessment todetermine the presence of NP or other bladder dysfunctions. Patients with NP were treated with desmopressin (0.2 mg/day); thosewithout NP were treated according to their specific diagnosis. The non-NBCI group received treatment with tamsulosin (0.4 mg/day).Outcomes were assessed at 6 months, including nocturnal void frequency (NVF) and IPSS. RESULTS: A total of 150 men were included (75 in the NBCI-guided group and 75 in the non-NBCI group). The NBCI-guided group achieved a55% reduction in NVF (from 3.6 to 1.6, p<0.001), compared to a 30% reduction in the non-NBCI group (from 3.5 to 2.5, p<0.001).IPSS scores improved in the NBCI-guided group, decreasing from 22.6 to 13.7 (p<0.001). The non-NBCI group showed a smallerimprovement from 22.4 to 17.2 (p<0.09). In patients with NBCI≤1.3, 73% were diagnosed with NP and experienced a 58% reductionin NVF (from 3.5 to 1.5, p<0.001) with desmopressin (0.2 mg/day). The remaining 27% without NP achieved a 48% reduction in NVF(from 3.4 to 1.8, p<0.01) when treated according to the diagnosis. Patients with NBCI>1.3 treated with tamsulosin (0.4 mg/day) andsolifenacin (5 mg/day) showed a 41% reduction in NVF (from 3.8 to 2.2, p<0.01). CONCLUSIONS: The results demonstrate that NBCI-guided management is significantly more effective than non-stratified approaches in reducing NVF and improving IPSS. By distinguishing between NP and other bladder dysfunctions, NBCI-guided treatment enabled targeted interventions. Desmopressin was highly effective for NP. These findings highlight the clinical value of NBCI in optimizing treatmentfor nocturia and reducing symptom burden in men with BPH. NBCI-guided management outperformed non-stratified treatmentapproaches in reducing NVF, improving IPSS scores, and enhancing patient QoL. This study underscores the importance of NBCI as a diagnostic tool for tailored treatment in BPH-associated nocturia.

title: PERCEPTIONS OF EJACULATION AMONG PATIENTS PRESENTING TO UROLOGY CLINIC FOR LOWER URINARY TRACT SYMPTOMS
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Amir S. Patel, Jenny Guo, Alyssa McDonald, Allaa Fadl-Alla, Amy Krambeck, Perry Xu
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Loss of ejaculatory function (EjF) is a risk for men undergoing treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). A prior study assessing the perceived importance of EjF was performed at a state fair and included patients as young as 18 years of age. The objective of our study is to assess the perception of EjF among the population of men presenting to the urology clinic for BPH management. METHODS: A survey assessing EjF and perception was handed out to patients and their partners when they were seen for their consultation at our BPH clinic or in the pre-operative area for their BPH procedure. The questionnaire asked about baseline demographics and BPH medication use. Patients noted their current EjF and its importance to them and their partner through Likert scales (1 is strongly disagree, 5 is strongly agree). Responses were tallied and multiple linear regression was performed to determine factors that impacted ejaculation and their response to the statement: “Preserving ejaculation is more important than improving urination”. RESULTS: There were 203 surveys completed: 190 by the patients and 13 by their partners. The median age of patients and partners were 69 and 67, respectively. (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191356.52697.6d.03#F1) shows patient and partner responses in which they agreed or strongly agreed(scored 4 or 5 on the Likert scale) with the statements presented. 62% of patients agreed that EjF is important for pleasure but only 13% agreed that preservation of EjF is more important than improving urination. On multiple linear regression, alpha-blocker use was not associated with EjF. Increased age correlated with worsening EjF. Patients with a better EjF were more likely to agree that preserving EjF is more important than improving urination, as shown in (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191356.52697.6d.03#F2). CONCLUSIONS: Our study finds that ejaculation remains important at an older age, but when presented with the decision between treating BPH and preserving ejaculation: few patients or partners would favor ejaculation over urination.

title: THE LURN SI-10 QUESTIONNAIRE: A VALID AND CLINICALLY MEANINGFUL TOOL THAT EXTENDS THE IPSS IN LUTS ASSESSMENT
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Rodrigo Espana-Navarro, Enrique Gomez-Gomez, Javier De La Torre, Luis Ortega-Polledo, Javier Fernandez-Siles, Daniel Carrasco-Gomez, Emilio Garcia-Galisteo, Borja García-Gómez, Fernando Gómez-Sancha, Eduardo Albers, Manuel Saavedra Centeno
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the psychometric performance and clinical utility of the Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction Research Network Symptom Index-10 (LURN SI-10) in men with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) and to explore its correlation with the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS). METHODS: A cross-sectional multicenter study was performed in 212 men with LUTS across four university hospitals. Participants completed both the IPSS and the LURN SI-10. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha. Construct validity was analyzed by exploratory factor analysis (principal component extraction, Promax rotation). Convergent validity was evaluated by Spearman correlation between total scores. Discriminant validity was examined across IPSS severity strata and in patients with vs without urinary incontinence. ROC analysis determined optimal cut-off values, and multiple linear regression identified symptom domains independently associated with IPSS severity. RESULTS: Median total scores were 14 for IPSS and 9 for LURN SI-10. Internal consistency was high (α=0.85 and 0.82, respectively). Factor analysis confirmed two correlated components explaining 54% of variance (KMO=0.831; p<0.001). LURN SI-10 correlated strongly with IPSS (ρ=0.76, p<0.001). It discriminated across IPSS-defined severity groups (Welch F=84.85, p<0.001) and between patients with and without urinary incontinence (p<0.001). ROC analysis demonstrated excellent discrimination (AUC=0.86; 95% CI 0.81–0.91), with a cut-off ≥8 yielding 72% sensitivity and 87% specificity. Regression identified bladder pain (β=0.283, p<0.001), urgency incontinence (β=0.192, p=0.009), and post-micturition dribble (β=0.153, p=0.043) as independent predictors of higher IPSS scores. CONCLUSIONS: The LURN SI-10 demonstrated robust reliability and strong clinical concordance with the IPSS. By capturing additional domains such as incontinence, bladder pain, and post-micturition dribble, it provides a broader, patient-centered evaluation of LUTS that complements and extends the clinical scope of the IPSS.

title: FROM IPSS TO LURN SI-10: EMPIRIC CUTOFFS ALIGNING MILD/MODERATE/SEVERE BPH SYMPTOMS USING 6,382 SAME-DAY ASSESSMENTS
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Alexander P. Glaser, Padraig Carolan, Dacey Maglaque, Pooja Talaty, Rowida Mohamed, Francesca R. Farina, Melissa Marquez, Grace Bardwick, Michael Bass, James T. Kearns, Andrew M. Higgins, Hayley Silver, Brian Thelfand, James W. Griffith, Abigail R. Smith
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The LURN SI-10 is a one-page questionnaire developed by the NIH Symptoms of Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction Research Network that captures additional symptoms such as incontinence and pain not queried by the IPSS. For men with BPH, we sought to (1) quantify association between SI-10 and IPSS in a large real-world dataset and (2) evaluate SI-10 severity bands that correspond to IPSS mild, moderate, and severe categories to support clinical interpretation and future trial endpoints. METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study at a single integrated health system of adult men with a diagnosis of LUTS/BPH (N40.1) who completed both IPSS and SI-10 on the same calendar day. Pearson correlation quantified association between continuous IPSS and SI-10 scores. Differences in mean SI-10 scores across IPSS categories were tested using one-way ANOVA. Based on the observed SI-10 distributions within IPSS strata we derived candidate SI-10 ranges aligned with IPSS “mild,” “moderate,” and “severe.” RESULTS: Among 6,382 paired assessments, mean (SD) age was 71.8 (9.8) years, and mean (SD) IPSS and SI-10 scores were 11.2 (7.1) and 7.7 (4.5), respectively. Scores demonstrated strong correlation (r=0.77, 95% CI \[0.76-0.78\]). IPSS severity was mild, moderate, and severe in 36%, 50%, and 14%, respectively, with median (IQR) SI-10 scores of 4 (3, 6), 8 (6, 10), and 13 (10, 16), respectively (ANOVA p<0.001, Figure). Based on these empirical distributions, we propose preliminary SI-10 score ranges of 0–5 (mild), 6–9 (moderate), and ≥10 (severe) as thresholds mapping to the central tendency of each IPSS category in this real-world sample. CONCLUSIONS: In a large single-institution cohort of men with BPH, SI-10 demonstrated strong correlation with IPSS and showed stepwise increases across IPSS severity levels. The proposed SI-10 severity bands (0–5 mild, 6–9 moderate, ≥10 severe) offer an interpretable framework that preserves content advantages of SI-10 (continence and pain) while harmonizing with widely used IPSS categories. These real-world data provide an empirical foundation for clinical decision thresholds to be tested via rigorous prospective data collection in NCT05898932.

title: PROSTATE TRANSITION ZONE STIFFNESS MEASURED BY ULTRASOUND SHEAR WAVE ELASTOGRAPHY VARIES ACROSS CLINICAL BPH/LUTS PHENOTYPES: A FEASIBILITY STUDY
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Kourosh Kalayeh, Wilson Sui, Man Zhang, Christopher L. Brace, Matthew D. Grimes, Priyadarshini Tripathy, Timothy J. Hall, Ivan Rosado Mendez, J. Brian Fowlkes, Shane A. Wells
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Shear wave elastography (SWE) is a non-invasive method to characterize tissue stiffness. We hypothesize that elevated transition zone (TZ) stiffness alters prostatic urethra caliber during voiding altering flow dynamics, contributing to BPH/LUTS and the development of bladder outlet obstruction (BOO). Therefore, the purpose of this study was to demonstrate feasibility of prostate SWE in men without and with BPH/LUTS and BOO. METHODS: Transrectal prostate SWE was performed using a Siemens Sequoia ultrasound system with a modified 18H6 hockey stick probe. TZ stiffness (modulus of elasticity in kPa) was measured using 15 regions of interest on the midgland right and left periurethral TZ ( figure). Clinical data included age, International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), prostatic urethral length (PUL), uroflowmetry, and post-void residual (PVR). BOO was defined as peak flow 15 ml/s or PVR > 100 ml and bothersome LUTS (IPSS > 19). Participants were categorized as: 1) classic BPH (men > 50 years old with prostate mass > 40 g and BOO or bothersome LUTS), 2) normal (no BOO or LUTS), and 3) high risk (BOO or bothersome LUTS with prostate mass 40 g or age 50 years). The Kruskal-Wallis test was used to compare stiffness across phenotypes with post-hoc Mann-Whitney U tests for pairwise comparisons. Relationships between TZ stiffness and clinical parameters were assessed. RESULTS: In 15 men (median age: 48 years, range: 30–74), mean TZ stiffness (mean±SEM) differed significantly across phenotypes (p=0.02, figure). Classic BPH (n=4) demonstrated the lowest TZ stiffness (5.75±0.89 kPa), normal/reference (n=6) intermediate (15.96±4.77 kPa), and high-risk (n=5) the highest (29.09±4.35 kPa). Post-hoc analysis revealed significantly lower stiffness in classic BPH compared to high-risk patients (p=0.016). TZ stiffness correlated with phenotype severity when treated as an ordinal variable. Additionally, TZ stiffness showed a trend with IPSS severity, although not statistically significant. CONCLUSIONS: Transrectal prostate SWE reveals distinct stiffness patterns across clinical BPH/LUTS phenotypes. Higher stiffness in high-risk patients suggests tissue stiffness contributes to BOO, independent of prostate size.

title: RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN PROSTATE MRI MORPHOLOGY AND LOWER URINARY TRACT SYMPTOMS
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Chai Kam, Jakob Waryas, Hailey Travis, Desirea Harder, Aman Burji, Charles Welliver, Jr
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Increasing use of prostate MRI (pMRI) for prostate cancer detection offers a unique opportunity to evaluate prostate morphology including prostate volume (PV), intravesical prostatic protrusion (IPP), urethral angle, and bladder neck angle (BNA). Previous works have looked at prostate imaging and lower urinary tract symptoms due to benign prostatic hyperplasia (LUTS/BPH) but this has not been comprehensively evaluated in the MRI era. METHODS: Patients with a pMRI were eligible for inclusion. For this study they needed to have an American Urological Association Symptom Scores (AUASS) obtained within 6 months of their prostate MRI. PV, IPP, urethral angle, and BNA were measured by a single trained reviewer on pMRIs performed from 2015–2025. Multiple linear regression assessed associations between MRI variables and total AUASS and symptom subscores. Significance was defined as p<0.05. RESULTS: We analyzed 324 MRIs from 138 men. AUASS were taken an average of 29 days from pMRI (SD 74, range 180 days before to 177 days after). Mean AUASS was 9.8 ± 6.5 (Median 9, IQR 4.8-14, range 0-31) and mean PV was 69.3 ± 37.2 cc. Median IPP was 11.5 mm (IQR 8.4-16.4). IPP length was independently associated with higher AUASS (p<0.001; R2 ≈ 8.9%), while PV, urethral angle, and BNA were not independently associated with LUTS (p>0.05).When looking at LUTS subscores, IPP length also correlated with urgency (p=0.003), frequency (p=0.015), and weak stream (p=0.001). BNA was associated with frequency (p<0.001). No other MRI features predicted LUTS subscores. CONCLUSIONS: While PV, urethral angle, and BNA were not predictive of symptoms, IPP length demonstrated the strongest independent association with LUTS/BPH severity, particularly urgency, frequency, and weak stream. These findings reinforce IPP as a clinically relevant marker for LUTS burden and warrant routine reporting in men undergoing prostate MRI.

title: THE MICROSCOPIC STRUCTURAL CHANGES OF PROSTATE REFLECTED BY THE APPARENT DIFFUSION COEFFICIENT VALUE AFFECT LOWER URINARY TRACT FUNCTION
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Hidenori Akaihata, Masahiro Maruya, Risa Hagino, Takahiro Tsumori, Yuki Harigane, Yusuke Hakozaki, Yusuke Kirihana, Tomoyuki Kumekawa, Akihisa Hasegawa, Hitomi Imai, Ryo Tanji, Ruriko Takinami, Junya Hata, Yuichi Sato, Soichiro Ogawa, Yoshiyuki Kojima
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The prostate volume and morphological features of the prostate are well known to be associated with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) in the male patients. However, whether microscopic structural changes of prostate contribute to LUTS and lower urinary tract dysfunction (LUTD) has not been established. On the other hand, recent attention has focused on the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) which is a non-invasive functional MRI technique that can assess changes in diffusion of water molecules due to microscopic structural changes. We considered that the ADC can provide the quantitative information about the microscopic structural changes of the prostate. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of microscopic structural changes of prostate on LUTS and LUTD by evaluating the association between ADC values and LUTS and lower urinary tract function. METHODS: Patients who underwent MRI before random transrectal ultrasonography–guided prostate biopsy and had a diagnosis of benign by the biopsy at our hospital between May 2019 and January 2022 were included in this study. Before the biopsy, uroflowmetry parameter, bladder voiding efficiency (BVE); (voided volume/total bladder capacity) × 100, International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) and overactive bladder symptom score (OABSS) were evaluated. The voiding and storage IPSS sub-score (IPSS-V and IPSS-S, respectively) were recorded separately. We measured mean ADC value at the base of the prostate by MRI. The relationship between the mean ADC value and the parameters evaluated before the biopsy was analyzed. All values were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. A linear regression analysis was used for continuous variables. P-values of <0.05 were considered to be statistically significant. RESULTS: A total of 111 patients (68.9 ± 6.3 years) entered the study. The mean ADC value at the base of prostate was 1,468 ± 190 mm2/sec. The mean ADC value was significantly positively correlated with IPSS-S (C. C=0.22, P=0.03) and OABSS (C. C=0.25, P=0.02). The mean ADC value was significantly negatively associated with BVE (C. C=-0.22, P=0.04). The IPSS-V, maximum flow rate and bladder capacity were not significantly associated with the mean ADC value. CONCLUSIONS: We demonstrated that high ADC value at the base of prostate caused storage symptoms and decreased the BVE. The microscopic structural changes of prostate reflected by high ADC value may affect lower urinary tract function through the different mechanism from the prostate volume and morphological features of prostate. The evaluating ADC value of prostate may provide individualized treatment options for patients.

title: PSA KINETICS FOLLOWING BENIGN PROSTATE BIOPSY: TEMPORAL PATTERNS AND CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Blake R. Baer, Tully A. Tully, Sri S. Manivasagam, Jay D. Raman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Transient elevations in prostate specific antigen (PSA) levels occur following prostate procedures such as prostate needle biopsy (PNB). After PNB, normalization of PSA back to baseline could be a function of prostatic inflammation, natural PSA progression, and PSA half-life kinetics. Understanding such timing has important implications for subsequent laboratory testing. Here, we evaluate the timeline of PSA normalization following PNB in men with benign prostate biopsy to guide best practice of retesting PSA following the procedure. METHODS: A retrospective cohort review of TriNetX research database using ICD10, LOINC, CPT codes from 2005-2025 was conducted. Males with a PSA value within 6 months before and 6 months following PNB were evaluated. Exclusion criteria included multiple PNB, lifetime diagnosis of prostate cancer (PCa) or lifetime treatment of PCa including radiation, surgical, androgen deprivation, or ablative therapy. Primary endpoint was return to baseline PSA following PNB, defined as PSA less than or equal to pre-PNB PSA. RESULTS: Of 751 patients who met criteria, 629 patients (83.8%) returned to pre-PNB baseline PSA in follow up. Median time to normalization was 161 days (95% CI 155-168). 61.4% of patients returned to pre-PNB baseline by 180 days and 74.2% by 1 year. Patients who normalized had less frequent PSA checks (mean 1.42 vs. 2.91, p<0.001) and higher pre-PNB PSA (6.5 vs. 5.38, p<0.001) but were not significantly different in age at biopsy, race, ethnicity, geographic region, 5-alpha reductase inhibitor therapy, or diagnosis of BPH. Higher baseline PSA showed faster normalization than lower PSA (HR 1.46, 95% CI 1.29–1.66). Of the patients without PSA resolution by 1 year, 37% ultimately normalized by end of recorded follow up. CONCLUSIONS: PSA trend demonstrates transient elevation immediately after PNB with a median normalization time of almost 6 months. A majority (74.2%) of patients return to baseline within 1 year following PNB. We recommend that PSA should not be rechecked before 3 months after PNB to maximize chance of clinical resolution of PSA and minimize potential for patient anxiety and frequent retesting.

title: COMPREHENSIVE IDENTIFICATION OF FACTORS ASSOCIATED WITH WORSENING MALE LOWER URINARY TRACT SYMPTOMS VIA META-16S ANALYSIS USING A LARGE HUMAN GUT MICROBIOTA DATABASE
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Junya Hata, Saizo Fujimoto, Toshiki Oka, Makoto Matsushita, Mitsugu Kanehira, Koji Hatano, Takuji Yamada, Shinichi Yachida, Tetsuya Takao, Shingo Takada, Akira Tsujimura, Norio Nonomura, Kazutoshi Fujita, Yoshiyuki Kojima
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The factors underlying the progression of male lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) remain unclear. Recent research has highlighted the role of various microbiomes, including those in the gut, urine, and oral cavity, in contributing to different diseases. Therefore, we sought to identify gut taxa associated with LUTS severity and prostate volume (Pvol), with emphasis on a malignancy-negative subcohort, and to explore lifestyle correlates. METHODS: Rectal swabs from 723 Japanese men undergoing prostate biopsy were profiled by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. Associations between genera and LUTS parameters-International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), Overactive Bladder Symptom Score (OABSS), and Pvol-were evaluated using Spearman’s correlation and nonparametric tests. Strong associations were highlighted using predefined thresholds (\|ρ\| ≥ 0.60, R2 ≥ 0.30, ≥5 non-zero samples). The association between lifestyle factors and identified genera were assessed via standardized questionnaires, and results were visualized with volcano plots. RESULTS: In the overall cohort, several genera were significantly correlated with LUTS parameters and Pvol. In the cancer-negative subcohort (n=262), Anaerofilum showed the strongest positive correlation with IPSS, while Lachnospiraceae showed negative correlations, suggesting a protective role. Bergeyella abundance was positively correlated with OABSS. For Pvol, Lachnospiraceae UCG-002, Eubacterium xylanophilum group, Asteroleplasma, and vadinBBE97 exhibited strong positive associations. Lifestyle analyses indicated that Anaerofilum abundance was positively associated with wine intake, overall alcohol consumption, fruit juices (melon/orange), and smoking. Bergeyella abundance was associated with recent cardiac infarction, urinary stone disease within one year, longer time spent fast walking, and birthplace variables (all FDR < 0.05). Lachnospiraceae showed no significant lifestyle associations after correction. CONCLUSIONS: This large-scale study identified specific gut microbial taxa associated with LUTS severity and Pvol in Japanese men, with consistent findings in a malignancy-negative subcohort. In addition, lifestyle factors might affect several specific taxa, which have the possibility to lead the protective strategy for male LUTS.

title: TISSUE-LEVEL EVIDENCE OF MICROPLASTICS IN BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Seyed Sajjad Tabei, J. Patrick Mershon, Ozan Akkus, Shiv Verma, Grahame J. Kidd, Sanjay Gupta, Shubham Gupta
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Microplastics, defined as plastic particles smaller than 5 mm, have emerged as pervasive environmental contaminants. Recent evidence suggests their accumulation in urogenital tissues, raising concerns about potential clinical effects. Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), one of the most common urologic disorders, has not been extensively investigated in relation to microplastic exposure within the United States. The study aimed to characterize the chemical composition and spatial distribution of microplastics in BPH tissue samples obtained from a de-identified U. S.-based biorepository. METHODS: Prostate tissues from eight patients were analyzed using non-plastic equipment to prevent cross-contamination. Samples were digested following published protocol for corpus cavernosal tissue, incubating 5 ml of a solution (50 g KOH, 160 ml 13% NaOCl, 1 ml 10% Tween-20, 340 ml Milli-Q water) for 24 hours. Digested material was filtered through 0.8 µm gold-coated membrane filters to isolate microplastics. Particle composition was analyzed by Raman spectroscopy and morphology visualized by scanning electron microscopy. A reagent-only blank was included to control contamination. RESULTS: A total of 21 microplastic particles were identified in samples from 5 of 8 patients. Polystyrene was the predominant polymer, comprising 19 particles (90.5%), followed by single particles of polyacrylonitrile (4.8%) and polyvinyl chloride (4.8%). No contamination was detected in the reagent-only blanks. CONCLUSIONS: This pilot study provides the first U. S.-based evidence of microplastics in BPH tissue, identifying particle types not previously reported. These findings underscore the need for larger investigations to elucidate the sources and potential clinical implications of microplastic exposure.

title: SPATIAL TRANSCRIPTOMIC REVEALS STROMAL HETEROGENEITY AND SRD5A2-INDEPENDENT METABOLIC NICHES UNDERLYING 5ARI RESISTANCE IN BPH
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Xingbo Long, Danyu Chen, Heidi J. Rayala, Ruslan Korets, Boris Gershman, Zongwei Wang, Olumi F. Aria
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: SRD5A2 is the therapeutic target of 5α-reductase inhibitors (5ARIs) widely used for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). However, its expression exhibits substantial inter-individual heterogeneity, with approximately 30% of patients showing low or absent SRD5A2 expression in prostatic tissues. This variability likely contributes to the heterogeneous clinical response to 5ARI therapy. Elucidating the molecular drivers of SRD5A2-deficient BPH is essential to understanding 5ARI treatment failure and identifying novel therapeutic targets. METHODS: Using tissue microarray technology, we performed Xenium spatial transcriptomic profiling on 142 prostatic tissue regions from 63 patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), generating spatial transcriptomic profiles across prostatic areas exhibiting variable SRD5A2 expression levels. RESULTS: We observed pronounced heterogeneity in SRD5A2 expression not only among patients but also across distinct regions within the same prostate. This intra-patient heterogeneity was more pronounced in men over 60 years (P=0.052). Spatial transcriptomic analysis identified two SRD5A2high expression fibroblast subtypes (Fib1 and Fib2) and one SRD5A2low subtype (Fib3) within the prostatic stroma. These fibroblasts, together with other stromal components, formed distinct spatially organized niches with divergent functional characteristics in SRD5A2-high and SRD5A2-low prostatic regions. The Fib1/2-dominant niches were SRD5A2-dependent, characterized by activation of androgen, WNT, and mTOR signaling pathways, and constituted the predominant stromal spatial architecture in SRD5A2-high areas. In contrast, Fib3-dominant niches were SRD5A2-independent, enriched for metabolic and EGFR–KRAS signaling pathways, and maintained these features regardless of SRD5A2 levels, constituting the dominant stromal spatial configuration in SRD5A2-low regions. Notably, patients with a BMI > 28 exhibited a trend toward a higher proportion of Fib3-dominant niches (P=0.09), supporting their metabolically driven nature. CONCLUSIONS: SRD5A2-high and SRD5A2-low regions exhibited distinct stromal composition and spatial organization. The SRD5A2-independent, metabolically driven Fib3-dominant niches may underlie 5ARI resistance and highlight metabolic and EGFR–KRAS pathways as potential therapeutic targets.

title: MMP7-TRIGGERED MITOPHAGY VIA REGULATING PARKIN-MEDIATED UBIQUITINATION OF VDAC1 CONFERRED ANOIKIS RESISTANCE IN THE EPITHELIUM OF HYPERPLASTIC PROSTATE
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Yongying Zhou, Xinhua Zhang
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), prevalently disturbing aging men, is characterized by aberrant cell death of prostate cells. Anoikis, a particular branch of apoptosis, is triggered when cells are detached from the extracellular matrix, whereas those with anoikis resistance (AR) are susceptible to various pathological conditions including abnormal cell death and proliferation. However, whether AR plays a role in BPH is still scarcely understood. METHODS: Bulk RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data and single cell RNA‑seq data of prostate tissues from normal individuals and BPH patients were analyzed. Immunoprecipitation-mass spectrum (IP-MS) analysis was performed to identify the proteins interacted with Matrix metalloproteinase 7 (MMP7). In vitro approaches including diverse staining strategies, transmission electron microscopy, flow cytometry, mitochondrial cell stress assay, immunoblotting, co-IP and ChIP analysis together with in vivo experiments on testosterone propionate-induced BPH (TP-BPH) rats were employed to ascertain the underlying functional mechanisms. RESULTS: In this study, elevated AR level was observed in BPH tissues compared to normal prostates. Furthermore, MMP7 was identified as a critical regulator of AR in hyperplastic prostatic epithelium. Under anoikis-inducing conditions, MMP7 promoted mitophagy via the PINK1-Parkin pathway, alleviated mitochondrial stress damage, and enhances AR in BPH-1 cells. Mechanistically, MMP7 interacted with VDAC1 and bond specifically at lysine residues K109 and K110, thereby inhibiting VDAC1 oligomerization and increasing the accumulation of VDAC1 monomers, which served as additional binding sites for Parkin-mediated polyubiquitination. Moreover, clinical data revealed that MMP7 expression levels correlated significantly with International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) and nocturia frequency. Additionally, in vivo experiments demonstrated that inhibition of MMP7 suppressed mitophagy and markedly attenuated prostatic epithelial hyperplasia in BPH model rats. CONCLUSIONS: Collectively, our findings elucidated the functional significance of the MMP7-VDAC1 axis in BPH pathogenesis and highlighted its potential as a therapeutic target for the management of BPH.

title: DISTINCT SRD5A2-REDUCED SUBTYPES OF BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA EXHIBIT P-AMPK/RAB9A/PLIN3-MEDIATED LIPOPHAGIC COMPENSATION FOR ANDROGEN SIGNALING DEFECTS
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Zhemin Lin, Zhanliang Liu, Yinong Niu
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: 5-α-reductase inhibitors (5-ARIs) are among the standard pharmacologic therapies for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). However, patients with BPH subtypes characterized by reduced 5-α-reductase 2 (SRD5A2) expression often show poor responsiveness to 5-ARIs, and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to elucidate the alterations in lipid droplet metabolism in SRD5A2-reduced BPH and identify key molecular events that may serve as potential therapeutic targets. METHODS: Testosterone and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) levels in BPH tissues were determined using high-performance liquid chromatography. SRD5A2, perilipin-3 (PLIN3), Rab9a, AMPK, phosphorylated AMPK (p-AMPK), and autophagy-related markers were assessed by immunohistochemistry (IHC), RT-qPCR, and Western blotting. Lipid droplets (LDs) distribution and morphology in BPH tissues and prostatic epithelial cells were evaluated by Oil Red O (ORO) staining and microscopy. Immunofluorescence staining (IF) was performed to examine the distribution of perilipin on LDs. Cell proliferation following DHT, oleic acid (OA), or chloroquine treatment was analyzed using the CCK-8 assay. RESULTS: IHC analysis of prostate tissues from 72 BPH patients revealed decreased (33%, 24/72) or nearly absent (14%, 10/72) SRD5A2 expression (experiment group) in a subset of cases. DHT were markedly reduced in experiment group. In these tissues, LDs were smaller but more numerous, indicating enhanced lipid turnover. Compared with control group, experiment group exhibited increased LC3 expression, decreased p62 levels, and elevated PLIN3 and AMPK phosphorylation. In vitro, androgen deprivation induced autophagy and AMPK phosphorylation in prostatic epithelial cells, while autophagy inhibition impaired LDs utilization and slowed or arrested cell proliferation. PLIN3 is the predominant perilipin responsible for regulating LDs metabolism in prostatic epithelial cells. PLIN3 expression was inversely correlated with DHT levels and shown to interact with Rab9a. CONCLUSIONS: Distinct BPH subtypes exist according to SRD5A2 expression. In SRD5A2-reduced BPH, activation of the p-AMPK/Rab9a/PLIN3 axis triggers lipophagy, compensating for impaired androgen receptor signaling to sustain epithelial cell proliferation and drive hyperplastic progression.

title: REVISIT EMBRYONIC REAWAKENING IN BPH THROUGH HAYFLICK ANALYSIS OF PROSTATIC STROMAL CELLS
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Mohammad Reza Askarpour, Wang Zhou
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a non-cancerous proliferation of epithelial and stromal cells primarily within the prostate’s transitional zone. While aging, androgens, and inflammation are recognized contributors, the potential role of embryonic reawakening and cellular senescence in BPH pathogenesis remains to be clarified. The increased stromal-to-epithelial ratio observed in BPH underscores the pivotal involvement of stromal cells in disease progression. Whether this imbalance arises from reactivation of developmental stromal–epithelial signaling (“embryonic reawakening”) or from the paracrine influence of senescent cells remains uncertain. We revisited the Hayflick principle by culturing patient-derived primary stromal cells from BPH and normal adjacent prostate (NAP) tissues to assess whether BPH stromal cells exhibit features of extended proliferative capacity, consistent with embryonic characteristics, or reduced proliferative capacity, reflecting a senescence phenotype. METHODS: Four cancer-free matched pairs of BPH and normal adjacent prostate (NAP) tissues were obtained from patients with low-volume prostate cancer and BPH under IRB approval. Minced tissues were digested with Dispase II for 2 h at 37 °C on a rocker, centrifuged, and resuspended in PDE medium. Cells were cultured in T75 flasks at 37 °C, 5% CO2 for 5 days, then supplemented with fresh medium to reach confluence. Then, the stromal cells were serially passaged in T25 Flasks using trypsin–EDTA until the Hayflick limit, with cell counts recorded throughout the experiment. For the first patient, only two repeat NAP and one BPH flasks were available, whereas for the remaining three patients, NAP and BPH triplicate flasks were established once sufficient cell numbers were obtained. Cell morphology and proliferation were monitored microscopically, and immunofluorescent staining was used to verify the stromal cell population, and -galactosidase staining was used to reconfirm senescence in flasks. RESULTS: BPH stromal cells reached the Hayflick limit much sooner than the NAP counterparts in three of the four paired samples. In the last paired sample, the BPH and NAP stromal cells reached the Hayflick limit after similar numbers of doublings. CONCLUSIONS: The lower proliferative capacity of BPH-derived stromal cells compared to their NAP counterparts challenges the notion that BPH stromal cells regain embryonic proliferative features. Our findings warrant further investigation into role of stromal cells senescence in BPH.

title: PROSTATE-SPECIFIC PLASMA PROTEOMIC AGING CLOCKS FOR DISEASE PREDICTION
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Kai Ma, Shengzhuo Liu, Xiaoyang Liu, Xin Yan, Pan Song, Luchen Yang, Xianding Wang, Qiang Dong
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Aging proceeds heterogeneously across organs, and organ-specific plasma proteomic clocks have shown promise for predicting tissue-relevant disease risk. The prostate, a leading source of age-related morbidity in men, has not been characterized with this approach. METHODS: Using plasma proteomes from 20,346 male participants in the UK Biobank, we identified prostate-enriched proteins and trained two elastic-net–based prostate aging models: Model 1 calibrated to chronological age and Model 2 trained using mortality via Cox regression. We compared model performance for predicting prostate cancer, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), and all-cause mortality against a conventional global proteomic age and other organ-specific proteomic ages. We also examined associations between prostate age acceleration and modifiable environmental factors using multivariable linear regression. RESULTS: We report a prostate-specific plasma proteomic clock. Model 1 (chronological-age trained) outperformed Model 2 in discriminating prostate disease endpoints. The prostate-specific proteomic age exceeded a global proteomic age and other organ-specific ages in predicting prostate-related conditions. Prostate age acceleration correlated with several modifiable exposures. CONCLUSIONS: A prostate-focused plasma proteomic clock captures organ-relevant biological aging and improves prediction of prostate disease risk beyond existing proteomic aging measures. External validation and mechanistic studies are warranted.

title: STEM-LIKE PROSTATE REMODELING IN OBESITY MEDIATES RESISTANCE TO 5Α-REDUCTASE INHIBITION THERAPY IN BPH
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Xingbo Long, Christina Sharkey, Rongbin Ge, Shuoshuo Wang, Yao Tang, Aaron Fleishman, Boqing Gu, Ruslan Korets, Boris Gershman, Heidi J. Rayala, Zongwei Wang, Aria F. Olumi
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Obesity and metabolic syndrome are significant risk factors for the development and progression of BPH. Although 5α-reductase inhibitors (5ARIs) are widely used to treat BPH, their effectiveness varies significantly, particularly in obese patients. The mechanisms by which obesity promotes prostate growth and modulates therapeutic responses remain poorly understood. METHODS: Prostate tissues from Srd5a2‑null and control mice fed regular‑fat or high‑fat diet (HFD) for 3 months underwent scRNA‑seq. Clinical human validation integrated Xenium spatial transcriptomics from institutional transurethral resection prostate specimens and bulk transcriptomics from the Medical Therapy of Prostatic Symptoms (MTOPS) trial, integrated with MTOPS longitudinal clinical data. RESULTS: In mice, HFD increased prostate weight and induced SRD5A2-independent epithelial remodeling with expansion of proximal urethral luminal epithelial cells. ScRNA-seq showed enrichment of proximal stem-like populations, reduced androgen signaling, and activation of WNT and NOTCH pathways via heightened stromal-epithelial crosstalk. Clinically, BMI gain, regardless of 5ARI use, correlated with transition zone growth, stronger activity of stem-cell signatures, and reduced SRD5A2, androgen signaling. Spatial profiling indicated that BMI gain expands stem-like epithelial populations and a NOTCH‑enriched periepithelial stromal niche surrounding epithelial compartments, supporting stemness. MTOPS patients with substantial BMI gain were less responsive to 5ARI, whereas weight control plus 5ARI therapy synergistically improved outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: BMI gain promotes proximal prostate enlargement through an SRD5A2-independent stem-like cell mediated pathway that blunts 5ARI efficacy. Combining pharmacotherapy with weight control yields superior efficacy and supports individualized management of BPH.

title: RETHINKING LONG-TERM MONITORING OF BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA: DOES SERIAL UROFLOWMETRY PREDICT CLINICAL PROGRESSION?
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Austin Martin, Andy Parzych, Brian Linder, Kevin Wymer, Jamie O. Byrne, Daniel Elliott
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Current guidelines recommend medical therapy for initial management of bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) due to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Many patients elect to remain on medical therapy for years, with unknown long-term effects on bladder function. In this study, we utilize serial uroflowmetry to assess long-term changes in voiding parameters and the risk of progression to acute urinary retention (AUR) or outlet surgery in men with medically managed LUTS due to BPH. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective review of patients who presented to our institution from 2008-2015 with a diagnosis of BPH (ICD 10 code N40.1). Patients were included if they had at least three uroflowmetry studies performed, each at least one year apart. Uroflowmetry parameters evaluated included Qmax, post void residual (PVR), and voiding efficiency \[voided volume/(voided volume + PVR)\]. Patients with a history of prostate surgery, pelvic radiation, urethral stricture disease, and neurogenic bladder were excluded. Univariable and mixed effects logistic regression was utilized to determine the association between changes in uroflowmetry parameters, type of medical therapy, international prostate symptom score (IPSS), prostate size, PSA, patient comorbidities, and progression to AUR or outlet procedure. RESULTS: A total of 142 patients were included in the analysis. Median age at first uroflowmetry was 69.0 years (IQR: 64.0, 74.0) and median international prostate symptom score (IPSS) was 13 (IQR 9-19). At initial uroflowmetry, 55 men (38.7%) were on no medications and 43 men (30.3%) were on alpha blockers alone. There was no significant change in Qmax, voiding efficiency (VE), or post-void residual (PVR) over the seven-year study period. The use of alpha-blockers was associated with an increase in PVR (p=0.04). Changes in IPSS and uroflowmetry parameters were weakly correlated over time (all R values <0.3). A total of 21.8% of patients developed AUR and 25.4% underwent outlet surgery. Increasing PVR was associated with an increased risk of outlet surgery (p=0.04). Median time from first uroflowmetry to outlet surgery was 8.7 years (IQR 6.9-12.2). Changes PVR, Qmax, and VE were not predictive of AUR. CONCLUSIONS: Serial uroflowmetry parameters did not significantly change over time in men with medically managed BPH and were poorly associated with subjective measures of voiding. None of the uroflowmetry parameters evaluated were associated with progression to acute urinary retention and only increases in PVR were associated with progression to outlet surgery.

title: ASSOCIATION BETWEEN GLUCAGON-LIKE PEPTIDE-1 AGONIST USE AND ESCALATION TO SURGICAL TREATMENT FOR BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA: A NATIONWIDE CLAIMS DATABASE STUDY
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Devin M. Dishong, Brendan K. Wallace, Andrew J. Cohen
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is typically medically managed for many patients with alpha-blockers and/or 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (5-ARIs) prior to surgical intervention. Previous research has suggested reduced prostate cancer risk with Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) agonist use, but little is known about their association with BPH and its progression. This study investigates the impact of GLP-1 agonist use on the incidence of BPH-related surgery. METHODS: Using the TriNetX national claims database, we identified BPH patients aged 40-75 on alpha-blockers alone, 5-ARIs alone, or combination therapy. Within each cohort, patients actively using GLP-1 agonists were compared to a control group with no GLP-1 exposure. The primary outcome was BPH surgery at 1, 3, and 5 years post-GLP-1 initiation. Patients with prior prostatectomy or BPH surgery were excluded. Propensity score matching (PSM) was utilized on demographics, type II diabetes mellitus, hypertensive disorders, hyperlipidemia, obesity, inflammatory diseases of the prostate, personal and family history of prostate neoplasm to address the association between GLP-1 use and progression to BPH surgery. RESULTS: Following PSM, the study arms included 17,232 (alpha-blocker), 807 (5-ARI), and 6,257 (combination therapy) patients per matched group (i. e., GLP-1 users and non-users), respectively. For patients with or without GLP-1, no statistically significant difference in rates of BPH surgery was observed in the alpha-blocker or combination therapy arms at any time point ( Table 1). However, the 5-ARI cohort demonstrated a significant reduction in BPH surgery risk at 3, and 5 years after initiating GLP-1 agonist use (p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: The use of GLP-1 agonists is associated with a reduced risk of surgical intervention for BPH in patients treated with 5-ARIs alone, suggesting that GLP-1 agonists may augment the therapeutic effects of 5-ARIs on the prostate in patients with BPH or patients on 5-ARI and GLP-1 seek surgery at decreased rates. Further laboratory research should focus on GLP-1 receptor expression in the non-malignant prostate tissue and its potential therapeutic value. | | | --- | | |

title: EFFICACY AND SAFETY OF VIBEGRON IN MEN ≥75 YEARS OF AGE WITH SYMPTOMS OF OVERACTIVE BLADDER ON PHARMACOTHERAPY FOR BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA: A SUBGROUP ANALYSIS OF THE COURAGE TRIAL
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Sender Herschorn, Kenneth M. Peters, Monisha S. Crisell, David Staskin, Eric S. Rovner, Laleh Abedinzadeh, Aanika Das, Jingmei Lu, Janet Owens-Grillo
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Vibegron is a selective β3-adrenergic receptor agonist approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of overactive bladder (OAB) symptoms in adults and adult males on pharmacological therapy for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). We report efficacy and safety of vibegron from the COURAGE trial in the subgroup of men ≥75 y with persistent OAB symptoms on pharmacotherapy for BPH. METHODS: COURAGE (NCT03902080) was a phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial that evaluated efficacy and safety of once-daily vibegron 75 mg vs placebo. Men ≥45 y with OAB and BPH receiving a stable dose of α-blocker ± 5α-reductase inhibitors were randomized 1:1 to vibegron or placebo for 24 weeks. This subanalysis assessed change from baseline in the mean number of daily micturitions, urgency episodes, and nightly nocturia episodes and adverse events (AEs) in patients ≥75 y and <75 y. RESULTS: Of the 1080 participants included in the COURAGE trial efficacy analyses, 192 were ≥75 y (92 received vibegron, 100 received placebo). Demographics and baseline clinical characteristics were generally similar between ≥75 y and <75 y subgroups; however, respectively, 96.4% and 85.7% were White, 75.0% and 63.7% had preexisting hypertension, 37.5% and 26% had urinary incontinence, and patients ≥75 y were more likely to have had prior therapies. Clinically significant reductions from baseline at week 12 and 24 were observed in average daily number of micturitions, urgency episodes, and nocturia episodes with vibegron vs placebo (Figure). These results were comparable to outcomes in men <75 y. For men ≥75 y, 52.1% of patients receiving vibegron had ≥1 treatment-emergent AE (TEAE), compared with 43.5% for men <75. The most common TEAEs in men ≥75 y receiving vibegron were hypertension (5.2%), hematuria (4.2%), and upper respiratory tract infection (4.2%). For men <75 y, these TEAEs were reported in 9.8%, 1.5%, and 1.3% of patients receiving vibegron, respectively. TEAEs were similar to placebo in both subgroups. CONCLUSIONS: Vibegron was associated with substantial improvements in clinical efficacy outcomes vs placebo and was safe and well tolerated in men ≥75 y with persistent OAB symptoms on pharmacotherapy for BPH, comparable to men <75 y.

title: THE ASSOCIATION OF FINASTERIDE FOR BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA WITH DEVELOPMENT OF MALE BREAST CANCER IN THE UNITED STATES: A RETROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY OF TRINETX DATABASE
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Renil S. Titus, Ansh Bhatia, Archan Khandekar, Hemendra N. Shah
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: 5-α reductase inhibitors (5AI: finasteride, dutasteride) inhibit the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, reducing the overall androgenic stimulus to growth of the prostate and is used as medical therapy for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). 5AI class is associated with gynecomastia and erectile dysfunction(ED) as adverse events but it’s association with breast cancer in males (MBC) has been controversial. To address this, we conducted a retrospective cohort study comparing the association of 5AI for BPH with MBC, gynecomastia and ED in the United States (US). METHODS: We queried the U. S. collaborative network of TriNetX database. We included patients ≥ 18 years of age diagnosed with BPH. The exposure of interest was 5AI for BPH. We propensity score matched (PSM) for demographic features, comorbidities and breast cancer risk factors. Balance between the 5AI cohort and non-5AI cohort was assessed by standardized mean difference (SMD) <0.1. Outcomes of interest included diagnosis of MBC at 1-yesr, 2 years and beyond, gynecomastia and ED defined using ICD-10-CM diagnostic codes and procedural codes (ICD-10-PCS, CPT). Further to assess the differential risk associated with either finasteride or dutasteride, we conducted subgroup analysis for either medication. Outcomes were reported as risk ratio (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). All statistical analysis were done using software built within TriNetX. RESULTS: 5-AI cohort and non-5AI cohort included: 637,804 and 2,426,442 patients, respectively before PSM and 273,403 patients each after PSM. Both cohorts were well balanced after PSM (SMD<0.1). Follow up of median 2.69 years and interquartile range (IQR) of 5.05 years in the 5AI cohort versus median 2.56 years (IQR: 4.98 years) in the non-5AI cohort. Patients in the 5AI cohort were not associated with a statistically significant increased risk of MBC (RR 1.07; 95%CI: 0.86-1.32). There was an increased risk of gynecomastia (RR 1.36, 95%CI: 1.28-1.44) and ED (RR 1.07, 95%CI: 1.05-1.09) associated with the use of 5AI. ( Table-1) CONCLUSIONS: In this multi-institutional retrospective cohort study, we did not find an increased risk of MBC associated with the use of 5AI for BPH. | | | --- | | |

title: LENALIDOMIDE: AN ANTIFIBROTIC REDUCES OUTPATIENT VISITS RELATED TO LOWER URINARY TRACT SYMPTOMS/BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Matthew S. Lee, Ajinkya R. Limkar, Kevin T. McVary, William Ricke, James Burke, Amanda Gusovsky Chevalier
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Medical treatment of lower urinary tract symptoms secondary to BPH (LUTS/BPH) primarily consists of alpha blocker therapy, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, or combination therapy. Still, over 20% of men have clinical progression of LUTS/BPH despite being on maximum medical treatment. Animal and human pathologic studies supports the hypothesis that prostate fibrosis contributes to LUTS and is an untargeted mechanism. Lenalidomide, a thalidomide analogue is an anti-fibrotic and FDA-approved for the treatment of multiple myeloma (MM). Thus, our objective was to determine whether lenalidomide reduces the risk of LUTS/BPH-related outpatient visits compared to non-antifibrotic therapy. METHODS: We analyzed the Merative Marketscan database between 2016-2023 for men who were newly diagnosed with MM, had ≥ 6 months of continuous enrollment prior to first MM diagnosis, and a prescription for lenalidomide (experimental group) or cyclophosphamide (non-antifibrotic MM treatment, control group) within 30 days of MM diagnosis. Men with any oncologic diagnosis other than MM were excluded. Inverse probability weighting was applied to balance baseline characteristics (age, U. S. region, rurality, Medicare Advantage plan, Charlson index, baseline inpatient and ED visits, and Index year) between experimental and control groups, reducing potential confounding. Our primary outcome was time to first BPH-related outpatient visit up to 5 years. We performed Kaplan-Meier probability analyses and Cox regression to adjust for residual confounding. RESULTS: A total of 1,834 patients met the study criteria (1,665 experimental and 169 controls). On average patients were 64 years old, 43% resided in the U. S. South, and 36% had a Medicare Advantage plan. The hazard ratio for a LUTS/BPH-related outpatient visit for men treated with lenalidomide was 0.44 (95% CI: 0.40-0.48, p<.0001) compared to the control group ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191356.52697.6d.22#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: Men treated with lenalidomide had a significantly reduced risk of LUTS/BPH-related outpatient visits compared to those treated with cyclophosphamide. These results support exploring antifibrotics as a novel treatment for LUTS/BPH. Randomized trials are needed to explore these findings in a non-MM population.

title: DOES BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA AFFECT THE RISK OF REPEAT TURBT?
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Nicholas Khoo, Shane Cauley, Clara Goebel, Ben Rubin, Jake Bleau, Mark Plante, Jenna Winebaum, Richard Grunert, Seyed Mohammad Mohaghegh Poor, Brian Irwin
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) is one of the most challenging urological cancers to treat. These patients need to be closely followed with periodic cystoscopy and imaging due to the highly recurrent nature of this disease. Independently, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a highly prevalent condition in aging men. Bladder outlet obstruction is associated with urinary stasis, poor bladder emptying, and increased chronic inflammation and mucosal irritation, all of which are potential contributors to carcinogenesis. This investigation aims to determine whether the diagnosis of BPH has an appreciable effect on the risk of requiring a repeat transurethral bladder tumor resection (TURBT). METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study using the TriNetX Diamond database. The cohorts included men with an initial diagnosis of NMIBC who underwent TURBT. The cohort was then separated into two groups: those diagnosed with BPH before undergoing their TURBT and those who were not. For men with BPH, we excluded patients who underwent BPH surgeries. The risk of requiring a repeat TURBT was determined for both groups to determine the risk difference between the groups. An absolute risk reduction between the cohorts was calculated with TriNetX’s statistical analysis. Statistical significance was defined as p<0.05. RESULTS: 7927 men with a mean age of 67.8 did not have BPH at the time of TURBT, and 7869 men with a mean age of 72.9 had BPH at the time of TURBT. The distribution of T1, Ta, and Tis for patients without BPH was 55.6%, 33.3%, and 11.1%, and for those with BPH was 50.0%, 37.5%, and 12.5%, respectively. For patients without BPH, there was a 35.7% risk for requiring a repeat TURBT within 1 year, 43.5% within 5 years. For patients with BPH, the risk of requiring a repeat TURBT was found to be 40.2% and 51.2% within 1 and 5 years, respectively. The risk difference between the cohorts for repeat TURBT within 1 and 5 years are -4.51% (95% CI: -3.00 - -6.02%) and -7.74% (95% CI: -6.12 \- -9.30%), respectively, showing a lower risk for the group without the BPH co-diagnosis (p<0.0001). CONCLUSIONS: This preliminary, large sample population investigation demonstrates that there may be a relationship between BPH that is not surgically treated and repeat TURBT given that we saw up to a 7.74% risk increase of a repeat TURBT in patients who had BPH at the time of their index TURBT. These findings raise interesting questions about the importance of treating BPH in patients with NMIBC and require further prospective validation.

title: INCIDENCE AND PREDICTORS OF THE COMPLICATIONS OF CATHETER-DEPENDENT BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA WAIT-TIMES: A MULTI-CENTRE RETROSPECTIVE STUDY
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Noushin Miandashti, Kaiden Jobin, Ali Hosseinzadeh, Vanay Verma, Connor Forbes, Mark Assmus, Nicholas Dean
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Surgical wait times are a key quality indicator in healthcare. Recent literature has focused on reducing delays for oncological surgeries, while non-oncological surgeries have received little to no attention. Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) affects nearly 80% of men by their eighties, often causing lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) and urinary retention, leading to reduced quality of life and financial burden. Treatment options for moderate-to-severe LUTS-BPH range from medical therapy to minimally invasive and invasive surgeries. This study aims to examine surgical wait times for BPH and identify predictors of complications related to catheter dependence. METHODS: A retrospective review was undertaken to identify catheter dependent BPH patients who underwent surgical treatment in the form of transurethral resection of prostate (TURP), Green Light Laser of prostate (GLLP), simple prostatectomy and Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) from May 1, 2022 to May 1, 2024 in Western Canada. Collected data included patient characteristics (BMI, ASA classification, pre-operative anti-coagulation use, prior BPH surgery, pre-operative 5-alpha reductase inhibitor use, prostate volume), catheter dependent period until surgery and preoperative complications. RESULTS: Of 494 catheter-dependent patients, 332 (67.2%) underwent TURP, 85 (17.2%) GLLP, 19 (3.8%) simple prostatectomy, and 58 (11.8%) underwent HOLEP. Excluding patients with comorbidities delaying surgery, the mean time from catheter insertion to OR was 109 days (median: 85 days). Preoperative complications occurred in 281 patients (56.9%), including ER visits for UTI (63.3%), recurrent UTIs (19.2%), hematuria (40.2%), epididymitis (2.5%), catheter-related issues (40.2%), and hospital admissions for urosepsis or hematuria (13.9%). Binary regression on a subset of patients with complications identified catheter duration as the only significant predictor (OR=1.013, p<0.001), representing a 1.3% increase in the odds of complications per additional day with catheter. Mean time to complication in this group was 43 days (median: 30 days). CONCLUSIONS: More than half of the patients experienced complications associated with prolonged catheterization. Alarmingly 13.9% of patients required admission for catheter-related complications while waiting for bladder outlet surgery. These findings highlight the significant impact of delayed surgical intervention, emphasizing the need for targeted strategies to reduce wait times and enhance patient care.

title: TOTAL SLEEP DURATION AND RAPID EYE MOVEMENT SLEEP FOLLOWING SURGICAL INTERVENTION FOR BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA: A COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS USING WEARABLE DEVICE DATA
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Yash H. Kadakia, Muhammed A. M. Hammad, Elia Abou Chawareb, Mohammed Mahdi, David I. Lee, Akhil Das, Faysal A. Yafi, Mohammed Shahait
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is associated with nocturia, which can reduce sleep quality and contribute to fragmented sleep. Specifically, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is a critical restorative sleep phase linked to cognitive function, mood regulation, and overall health. This study investigates whether surgical management with transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) or holmium laser enucleation (HoLEP) influences total and REM sleep duration compared with patients experiencing nocturia from BPH on conservative management. METHODS: Data were obtained from the NIH All of Us Research Program Controlled Tier v8 database. Three cohorts were defined using standardized concept IDs: (1) conservative management (CM), (2) TURP, and (3) HoLEP. Fitbit Sleep Daily Summary data were analyzed to quantify nightly total sleep duration and REM sleep duration in minutes, with each sleep record representing one night of sleep. For each cohort, the average total sleep, average REM sleep, and standard deviation were calculate using Python. Group differences were tested using Welch’s t-tests. Statistical comparisons were made between surgical intervention vs. CM for both sleep metrics, and between TURP vs. HoLEP to assess procedure-specific differences. RESULTS: For total sleep duration, a total of 10,005 sleep records were identified for CM and 25,123 for surgical intervention. For total sleep duration, the record-level mean was 322.44 min (CM) and 346.56 min (surgical intervention), with surgical patients sleeping 24 minutes longer (p<0.001). When comparing procedure types, HoLEP patients (349.42 min) slept longer than TURP patients (329.78 min) (p<0.001). Table 1. REM sleep characteristics across treatment groups. Surgical intervention vs CM (p<0.001); TURP vs HoLEP (p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Surgical intervention for BPH was associated with significantly longer total sleep duration and REM sleep duration compared to CM, highlighting the positive impact of surgical intervention for patients with BPH. These results highlight the physiological connection between urological intervention and sleep physiology, suggesting that sleep quality is an important factor to consider when making decisions in BPH management. | | | --- | | |

title: COST-EFFECTIVENESS OF SURGICAL OPTIONS FOR LARGE GLAND BPH DEPENDS ON PATIENT PRIORITIES: A COMPARISON OF HOLEP, AQUABLATION, AND SIMPLE PROSTATECTOMY
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Hannah Botkin, Vidit Sharma, Grace Ratcliff, Bijan Borah, Dan Kelleher, Kelly Lehner, Connor Forbes, Mitchell Humphreys, Daniel Joyce, Kevin Wymer
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: For patients requiring surgical intervention for BPH with a large gland (>80-150cc), guideline options include HoLEP and simple prostatectomy (SP). Robotic waterjet therapy (RWT) is also being increasingly utilized. These treatments vary in their costs and outcomes, as do individual patient priorities. In this study, we assessed cost effectiveness (CE) for these three BPH treatments for large glands, and the sensitivity to relative weighting of different outcomes. METHODS: Using a microsimulation model, a CEA was performed comparing HoLEP, SP, and RWT. Model probabilities were based on published values, and effectiveness was calculated using post-operative complication severity, sexual function, and urinary symptom scores (IPSS). The model was performed from a U. S. Medicare payer perspective, with quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) used to assess cost-effectiveness at a willingness-to-pay threshold of $100,000/QALY. Univariate and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were performed. RESULTS: Over a patient’s lifetime, HoLEP and SP resulted in nearly identical effectiveness (12.25 vs. 12.26 QALYs), but HoLEP had a significantly lower lifetime BPH cost per patient ($8,361 vs. $19,012) and was therefore CE (SP ICER > $2,000,000). RWT was the least effective (12.19 QALYs) with intermediate cost ($11,969). The model was found to be sensitive to changes in multiple input parameters. Specifically, SP became more CE if the cost decreased significantly, whereas RWT was more CE if the utility value (effectiveness) assigned to post-operative ejaculatory dysfunction increased, the cost of RWT decreased, or the relative post-operative symptom improvement of HoLEP decreased ( Figure 1-2). CONCLUSIONS: At baseline assumptions, HoLEP is the most cost-effective surgical option for patients with a gland size 80-150cc. However, this was dependent upon procedure cost and patient priorities. Such findings highlight the benefit of HoLEP on a systems-level, while emphasizing the importance of surgical selection driven by individual patient priorities.

title: HIGH PATIENT ADHERENCE TO SMARTPHONE-BASED HOME UROFLOWMETRY: REAL-WORLD EVIDENCE FROM A LARGE COMMERCIAL DATABASE
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Bilal Chughtai, Jennifer Polo, Naeem Bhojani, Kevin C. Zorn, Dean Elterman, Catherine Song, Karen Doo
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Patient adherence to digital health monitoring is often cited as a barrier to adoption in chronic urological care. Smartphone-based home uroflowmetry provides non-invasive, high-frequency monitoring of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) between clinic visits. This study evaluated real-world adherence and engagement patterns in a large voluntary cohort using physician-referred home uroflowmetry. METHODS: This retrospective analysis examined de-identified data from a commercial smartphone-based uroflowmetry service database (proudP, FDA Class II) comprising 3,332 male patients who enrolled between November 2020 and October 2025. Patients were referred by urologists from 33 US urology practices and paid directly for the self-directed monitoring service. Data were extracted from a HIPAA-compliant database; patients consented to research use of de-identified data per service terms. Practices included in this analysis had at least 3 active service users. Patients were predominantly monitored for BPH/LUTS, with additional voiding conditions including urethral stricture. Analysis included total tests, monthly monitoring frequency, and uroflow parameters (Qmax and VT). Correlation between baseline symptom severity and monitoring frequency was investigated. RESULTS: The cohort conducted 209,718 home uroflowmetry tests over the 5-year study period. Patients demonstrated sustained engagement with a median monitoring frequency of 5.0 days per month (mean: 7.5 days). Analysis showed 80.9% of patients tested on 2-15 days monthly, while only 7.6% tested on a single day. Median Q\_max was 14.2 ml/s (mean: 14.8 ml/s, SD: 5.9) and median VT was 29.6 seconds (mean: 37.0 s, SD: 26.3 s). The 25th percentile Qmax of 10.5 ml/s confirmed most patients had flow compromise consistent with mild-to-severe LUTS. Baseline symptom severity (Qmax) showed no significant correlation with monitoring frequency or daily measurement frequency (p>0.05). CONCLUSIONS: This large real-world study demonstrates sustained patient adherence to smartphone-based home uroflowmetry over a 5-year period across diverse urology practices, with consistent monitoring regardless of symptom severity. These findings provide evidence that digital LUTS monitoring can achieve meaningful patient engagement in routine urological practice and may facilitate more frequent assessment between clinic visits.

title: ALCOHOL CONSUMPTION AND HISTOLOGIC PROSTATIC INFLAMMATION: A POST-HOC ANALYSIS OF THE REDUCE TRIAL
session: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: Epidemiology, Evaluation & Medical Non-surgical Therapy (IP15)
authors: Alexander Hernandez-Tirado, Nadine A. Friedrich, Maria P. Mogollon, Daniel M. Moreira, Stephen J. Freedland, Farnoosh Nik-Ahd
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostatic inflammation has been linked to both prostate cancer (PC) and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), yet its underlying drivers remain poorly understood. Alcohol intake has been linked to increased PC risk in some studies, but decreased BPH risk in other studies. We hypothesized that these associations may, in part, be mediated by altered prostatic inflammation. To test this, we evaluated the association between alcohol intake, known to promote inflammation in multiple organ systems, and histologic prostatic inflammation in patients from the REDUCE trial. METHODS: We included patients from the REDUCE efficacy population with complete data on alcohol intake and baseline prostate inflammation. Alcohol use (units/week) was divided into quartiles (Q1: 0, Q2: 1–3, Q3: 4–8, Q4: >8). Baseline prostate biopsies were performed prior to study start and were reread centrally to confirm negative results. Acute and chronic inflammation were graded histologically (none, mild, moderate, or marked), and subsequently collapsed into binary variables (presence vs. absence of inflammation). Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were compared across alcohol quartiles using the Kruskal–Wallis test for continuous variables and chi-square tests for categorical variables. Binary logistic regression models evaluated associations between alcohol quartiles and inflammation, adjusting for age, race, region, prostate-specific antigen (PSA), body mass index (BMI), international prostate symptom score (IPSS), smoking status, and prostate volume. RESULTS: Among 8,053 patients (mean age 63 years), 26% reported no alcohol use, while 28%, 22%, and 23% were in quartiles Q2–Q4, respectively. Most patients exhibited no acute inflammation (84-85%), with no significant differences across quartiles in unadjusted analysis (p-value=0.7). In contrast, chronic inflammation was highly prevalent and demonstrated a modest but statistically significant difference across quartiles in unadjusted analysis (p-value=0.007). The proportion with chronic inflammation decreased steadily from Q1 (80%) to Q4 (76%). In adjusted models, alcohol quartile was not associated with acute inflammation (global p-value=0.8) or with chronic inflammation (global p-value=0.3). CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort of patients from the REDUCE trial, alcohol intake was not independently associated with the presence of histologic acute and chronic prostatic inflammation. These findings suggest that alcohol consumption’s effect on BPH may be through pathways outside of prostatic inflammation.

title: COMPARING URINARY URGENCY PATIENTS WITH AND WITHOUT PAIN — A LURN II STUDY
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: H. Henry Lai, Jon Wiseman, Brian Bieber, Cindy Amundsen, Eric Jelovsek, Anne Cameron, J. Quentin Clemens, Catherine Bradley, Karl Kreder, Claire Yang, Brian Helfand, Alexander Glaser, Kimberly Kenton, Ziya Kirkali
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary urgency (the cardinal symptom of OAB) and pain are both subjective noxious sensations. Some OAB patients experience pain in addition to urinary urgency. 54% of adult women with OAB symptoms stated that their urge to urinate was associated with pain, pressure, or discomfort (Reynolds et al 2017). The objective of this study was to phenotype urinary urgency patients with pain, and to compare to urgency patients without pain. METHODS: Adults seeking treatment for bothersome urinary urgency, without or with urgency urinary incontinence, were enrolled in the LURN II Study. A sex-matched control group without urinary symptoms was also enrolled. Urgency was assessed using the LURN SI-29s? subscale. Urologic pain was assessed using the GUPI (genitourinary pain index) pain subscale and LURN SI-29 pain subscale. Widespread pain was defined as pain involving 3 or more body regions on a pain map. Urologic and widespread pain were compared urgency patients and controls. Patients with a diagnosis of IC/BPS were excluded. RESULTS: Urgency patients (n=742) were significantly more likely to report any urologic pain on GUPI (49% vs. 11%, p<0.01) and LURN SI-29 (56% vs. 23%, p<0.01) compared to controls without urgency (n=139). GUPI pain subscale scores were higher among urgency patients compared to controls (mean 4.3 vs. 0.7, p<0.01). LURN SI-29 pain subscale scores were also higher among urgency patients compared to controls (13.3. vs. 2.3, p<0.01). Urgency patients were also more likely to report widespread pain on the pain map than controls (32% vs. 14%, p<0.01). There were significant positive correlations between worsening LURN SI-29 pain scores and OAB-q scores, LURN SI-29 urgency subscale scores, and LURN SI-29 incontinence subscale scores (see Figure). \\* \[means p<0.05; number in figure=correlation coefficient\]. CONCLUSIONS: In care-seeking patients with urinary urgency, over half reported mild urologic pain and one-third reported widespread pain. There were positive correlations between their OAB and pain symptoms. These data support the concept that OAB patients may have heightened sensitivity to noxious stimulation and/or central sensitization. Studies are needed to examine if urgency patients with pain might represent a distinct phenotype.

title: COMPARING SYMPTOM PRESENTATION, TREATMENT PATTERNS, AND SYMPTOM TRAJECTORIES BETWEEN MEN AND WOMEN WITH URINARY URGENCY — A LURN II STUDY
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: H. Henry Lai, Alan Fossa, Brian Bieber, Cindy Amundsen, Eric Jelovsek, Anne Cameron, J. Quentin Clemens, Catherine Bradley, Karl Kreder, Claire Yang, Brian Helfand, Alexander Glaser, Kimberly Kenton, Ziya Kirkali
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) in men is poorly understood and under-studied. The co-occurrence of storage and voiding symptoms makes it challenging to recognize and manage. The objectives of this study were to compare the symptom presentation, treatment patterns, and symptom trajectories between men and women with urinary urgency, the cardinal symptom of OAB. METHODS: Adult men and women seeking treatment for bothersome urinary urgency, without or with urgency urinary incontinence, were enrolled in the LURN II Study. Patients with a clinical impression of bladder outlet obstruction or pain as a primary diagnosis were excluded. LUTS were assessed using the OAB-q and LURN SI-29 questionnaires at baseline, 3, 6, 9, and 12-month. Treatment data were queried during study visits. RESULTS: 272 men and 339 women with urinary urgency were enrolled. Men were older and reported less severe OAB-q symptoms and better HRQL at baseline compared to women. Men also had lower LURN SI-29 total scores, urgency scores, and incontinence scores compared to women. Conversely, men reported higher nocturia and voiding scores compared to women. In terms of treatment patterns, more men used BPH medications (61% alpha blockers, 19% 5-alpha reductase) than OAB medications (40% anticholinergics, 22% beta-agonists). It was uncommon for men to do pelvic floor muscle exercises (3.1%) or pelvic floor physical therapy (4.2%) to manage their urgency (see Table). Although men had less severe OAB symptoms at baseline, there was greater improvement in OAB symptoms and HRQL over time among women, such that there were no differences between them at follow-up (see Figure). CONCLUSIONS: At baseline, women reported more severe urgency, incontinence, and overall OAB burden, whereas men had higher nocturia and voiding scores. Despite these sex-specific differences, women experienced greater improvement in urgency and quality-of-life measures over time. At study end, there were no significant differences in OAB outcomes between men and women.

title: A PROSPECTIVE LONGITUDINAL STUDY OF URINARY METABOLITES AMONG WOMEN WITH AND WITHOUT OVERACTIVE BLADDER
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Ashley Harrie, Joanna Marantidis, Maureen Kachman, Abraham Raskind, Annapurna Kuppa, J. Quentin Clemens, Anne P. Cameron, Aruna Sarma, Giulia M. Ippolito
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: There has been little research evaluating the urinary metabolome and its relationship to overactive bladder (OAB). We aim to bridge this gap by evaluating the urinary metabolome in postmenopausal women with and without OAB. METHODS: This is a prospective observational study of postmenopausal women with clinical OAB, defined by LURN Symptom Index-10 responses, who were not managed with medications or recent procedures, and controls. LURN Symptom Index-29 (LURN-SI-29) and catheterized urine specimens were collected at baseline and 5-weeks. Untargeted metabolomics using reverse phase negative ionization (RP-neg) and ion pairing negative ionization (IP-neg) assays were performed at the University of Michigan Metabolomics Core. Peak intensity of metabolites was compared between groups and over time. RESULTS: Urine at baseline and 5 weeks was available for all cases (n=25) and controls (n=11). The mean age was similar between the OAB and control groups (65 vs 61 years, respectively). LURN-SI-29 scores discriminated between cases (x̄=25.7, IQR 21-31) vs controls (x̄=7.6, IQR 3.8).RP-neg assays found that 19 metabolites, primarily bile acids, had statistically significant higher peak intensity among cases vs controls. Examples include Taurohyocholic acid (p<0.001) and Tauroursodeoxycholic acid and Taurohyodeoxycholic acid (p=0.003, Figure 1a, 1b). The excitatory neurotransmitter Glutaric acid was also higher in urine of cases (p=0.003, Figure 1c). IP-neg found that 11 metabolites showed statistically significantly higher peak intensity among cases vs controls, several of these were amino acid or caffeine metabolites. Examples included Alanine (p=0.003), 1,7-Dimethyluric acid (p=0.005), and 1,3,7-Trimethyluric acid (p=0.010, Figures 2a-c). CONCLUSIONS: Post-menopausal women with OAB have distinct urine metabolites compared to controls. Specifically, we found higher peak intensity among urine bile acid levels, including primary, secondary and conjugated bile acids. These represent multiple steps in bile acid metabolism, suggesting these pathways as potential therapeutic targets.

title: PROTEOMIC ANALYSIS OF HUMAN UROTHELIUM REVEALS DISTINCT MOLECULAR MECHANISMS UNDERLYING OVERACTIVE BLADDER DUE TO BLADDER OUTLET OBSTRUCTION
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Gun Hwa Kim, Dong Yeon Lee, Hyoseok Kang, Jae Sung Lim, Ki Hak Song, Chang Sik Yoon, Ji Yong Lee, Chung Lyul Lee, Jaegeun Lee, Yong Gil Na, Khae-hawn Kim, Ju Hyun Shin
