abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) in men with bladder outlet obstruction (BOO) due to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) represents a major therapeutic challenge, as symptoms often persist even after surgical relief of obstruction. The underlying molecular mechanisms, however, remain poorly defined. The aim of this study was to identify differentially expressed proteins in the urothelial tissues of patients with BOO-related OAB using a proteomic approach. METHODS: Bladder urothelial tissues were obtained via cold-cup biopsy during transurethral resection of the prostate from 11 male patients with BPH (6 OAB, 5 non-OAB). Patients with hematuria, neurogenic bladder, active urinary tract infection, urological malignancy, or prior pelvic radiation were excluded. Proteomic profiling was conducted using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Differential expression analysis utilized MaxQuant and Perseus software. Functional annotation and pathway enrichment were performed using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis and Gene Ontology tools. RESULTS: Proteomic analysis identified 1,510 proteins, of which 133 were differentially expressed proteins in patients with OAB compared with the non-OAB group. Dysregulated pathways included cytoskeletal remodeling, Rho GTPase signaling, serotonergic signaling, and immune responses. Structural proteins such as ACTA2, CFL2, MYLK, and PPP1R12B were markedly downregulated, whereas GNA13 and multiple inflammatory mediators were upregulated. Functional analysis confirmed the enrichment of neurotransmitter catabolic processes, immune responses, and impaired cell–cell contact, suggesting structural disorganization and aberrant epithelial signaling in the OAB group. CONCLUSIONS: BOO-related OAB exhibits distinct proteomic signatures characterized by cytoskeletal disorganization, aberrant neurotransmitter signaling, and chronic inflammatory responses. Downregulation of structural proteins alongside upregulation of inflammatory mediators suggests impaired mechanotransduction and barrier dysfunction in OAB pathophysiology. These findings provide novel molecular insights and identify potential therapeutic targets for biomarker discovery and precision medicine approaches in OAB management.

title: URINE IN INDIVIDUALS WITH OVERACTIVE BLADDER HARBORS GREATER ABUNDANCE OF CALCIUM- AND FAD-BINDING PEPTIDES RELATIVE TO HEALTHY CONTROLS
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Glenn Werneburg, Stacy Jeong, Sean McSweeney, Aaron Miller, Sandip Vasavada
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary peptide composition remains poorly understood both in the physiological state and in the overactive bladder state. We sought to investigate and compare the urinary peptidome of individuals with and without overactive bladder (OAB). We hypothesized that urine from individuals with OAB would harbor unique peptide signatures relative to those of healthy controls. METHODS: Adult female patients with and without overactive bladder were included. Urine specimens were prospectively obtained via midstream clean catch collection. Samples were analyzed for peptide composition following standard fractionation techniques and isolation from the peptide-rich supernatant. Data were analyzed by PEAKS Online V11 using all spectra to search against the human UniProtKB protein sequence databases in addition to Deep Novo peptide identification for peptide identification and quantitative values. RESULTS: 102 patients with OAB and 54 healthy controls were included. Peptide composition and concentration differed between OAB and control groups (p=0.001). Peptides associated with calcium binding and FAD binding were more abundant in OAB, and peptides associated with cAMP metabolism and mitochondrial translocation were more abundant in controls (false discovery rate corrected p-values <0.05 and log2 fold changes >2, Figure). Machine learning classifiers were generated and the greatest explainers in the models were a human mitochondrial ribosomal protein (more abundant in OAB) and extracellular superoxide dismutase (more abundant in healthy controls), a secreted antioxidant. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that the urinary peptidome differs between individuals with overactive bladder and healthy controls, revealing biologically plausible peptide signatures that may reflect underlying pathophysiology. Enrichment of peptides related to calcium and FAD binding in the OAB cohort suggests altered cellular signaling and oxidative pathways. The identification of mitochondrial ribosome- and extracellular superoxide dismutase-derived peptides as discriminators highlights potential mechanistic links between oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and bladder overactivity. The findings establish urinary peptidomics as a promising noninvasive approach to uncover molecular correlates and candidate biomarkers of overactive bladder.

title: SERUM URIC ACID PARTIALLY MEDIATES NOCTURIA-ASSOCIATED MORTALITY: NHANES ANALYSIS
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Sung Tae Cho, Sung Jin Kim
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Nocturia is linked to increased mortality risk, potentially via metabolic pathways. This study evaluates serum uric acid (sUA) as a mediator in the nocturia-mortality association using nationally representative data. METHODS: We analyzed NHANES data (2005–2014) from 12,522 adults aged ≥40 years with complete nocturia, sUA, and follow-up data (median 107.3 months; mortality via National Death Index linkage). Nocturia was defined as ≥2 nighttime voids. sUA was categorized into quartiles (Q1–Q4) and modeled continuously. Cox proportional hazards regression assessed associations with all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, BMI, smoking, alcohol, sleep duration, hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia. Hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) models evaluated nonlinear relationships. Mediation analysis quantified direct/indirect effects of nocturia via sUA using the regmedint package. RESULTS: Higher sUA quartiles were associated with older age, greater nocturia prevalence (41.3% in Q4 vs. 35.4% in Q1), and elevated mortality (all-cause: 24.3% vs. 12.9%; cardiovascular: 7.2% vs. 2.9%). In fully adjusted models, nocturia predicted all-cause (HR 1.984, 95% CI 1.803–2.182) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.915, 95% CI 1.617–2.267). RCS revealed J-shaped associations for sUA with both outcomes (p for nonlinearity <0.001). Mediation analysis showed partial mediation by sUA: for all-cause mortality, total indirect effect HR 1.031 (95% CI 1.018–1.044); direct effect HR 1.909 (95% CI 1.736–2.101). Similar patterns held for cardiovascular mortality. CONCLUSIONS: Nocturia independently predicts all-cause and cardiovascular mortality. sUA partially mediates this pathway, suggesting integrated management targeting hyperuricemia and metabolic risks to mitigate nocturia-associated mortality.

title: SKIN SYMPATHETIC NERVE ACTIVITY REFLECTS SYMPATHETIC OVERACTIVATION IN A RAT MODEL OF OVERACTIVE BLADDER INDUCED BY PARTIAL BLADDER OUTLET OBSTRUCTION
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Yu-Chen Chen, Hao-Wei Chen, Ping-Hsuan Shih, Shiou-Lan Chen, Yung-Shun Juan, Wei-Chung Tsai
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) has been increasingly linked to autonomic dysregulation. However, direct measurement of sympathetic drive in vivo remains technically challenging. This study aimed to validate whether skin sympathetic nerve activity (SKNA), recorded from body surface sites, accurately reflects the underlying sympathetic hyperactivity in a rat model of OAB induced by partial bladder outlet obstruction (pBOO). METHODS: Eight female Sprague–Dawley rats were included (Sham=4; pBOO=4). pBOO was induced by partial urethral ligation, while Sham rats underwent urethral exposure only. Sympathetic activity was simultaneously recorded at thoracic and abdominal skin and directly from the sympathetic ganglion inside a Faraday cage. Mean signal amplitude (µV) was quantified at each site. Between-group differences were analyzed using one-tailed Welch’s t-tests (pBOO > Sham), and effect sizes were calculated as Cohen’s d. A composite sympathetic index was computed by averaging z-scores across the three sites. Fisher’s method was used to integrate site-specific p-values. RESULTS: Compared with Sham, pBOO rats demonstrated classic OAB features, including increased voiding frequency, reduced voided volume, and higher bladder weight (all p<0.05) ( Fig. A). Sympathetic nerve activity was consistently elevated in pBOO rats across thoracic skin, abdominal skin, and ganglionic recordings ( Fig. B). Fisher’s combined analysis confirmed global sympathetic overactivation (p=0.045). The composite three-site index demonstrated significant sympathetic hyperactivation in the pBOO group (p=0.013) ( Fig. C). Importantly, even when restricted to the two skin electrodes only, the non-invasive composite index remained significantly elevated (p=0.027) ( Fig. D), confirming that skin SNA reliably reflects sympathetic drive. CONCLUSIONS: This animal study provides physiological validation that skin-derived sympathetic nerve activity faithfully mirrors autonomic hyperactivation in a rat model of overactive bladder. The strong concordance between skin and direct ganglionic recordings establishes SKNA as a reliable surrogate of sympathetic drive. These findings lay the experimental foundation for future translational development of surface SKNA as an objective biomarker to diagnose and monitor autonomic dysfunction in overactive bladder.

title: REGIONAL WHITE MATTER DIFFERENCES IN OVERACTIVE BLADDER IDENTIFIED BY DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING: FIVE DISTINCT CLUSTERS INCLUDING TWO ACCESSIBLE TO BRAIN OPTICAL TECHNOLOGIES
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Lynn Stothers, Benjamin Ellingson, John Speich, Linda Burkett, Andrew Macnab, Kyle Zuniga, Adam Klausner
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Recent MRI studies have identified overactive bladder (OAB) associated with alterations in brain white matter microstructure. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) quantifies these changes through fractional anisotropy (FA) reflecting white matter integrity and connectivity. This study aimed to a) identify regional FA differences between individuals with OAB and healthy controls (HC), and b) to determine whether DTI areas of interest were accessible to optical monitoring systems such as brain functional near-infrared spectroscopy specifications. METHODS: Participants were classified by ICIQ-OAB responses (HC ≤1 on all questions; OAB ≥2 on the “urgency” question). All participants were cognitively intact and completed a standardized hydration protocol. DTI data were processed using MRtrix3 and FSL pipelines, including denoising, eddy-current and motion correction, skull stripping, and registration to the Johns Hopkins University DTI atlas (ICBM-DTI-81 1 mm). Voxel-wise FA maps were analyzed within a mask combining white and deep gray matter (basal ganglia and thalamus) derived from the Harvard-Oxford subcortical atlas. Group differences and correlations between FA and ICIQ scores were evaluated using a general linear model (p<0.05, FDR q<0.05). Geography was mapped to subjects also underlying fNIRS with natural bladder filling protocols. RESULTS: Twenty-one females (6 HC, 15 OAB; ages 24–80) were included. Compared to HCs, OAB participants exhibited significantly reduced FA across multiple white matter tracts involved in sensory integration and urgency perception, including the corpus callosum (body and genu), internal and external capsules, and corona radiata. Five discrete clusters showed lower FA in OAB relative to controls, consistent with disrupted interhemispheric and thalamocortical communication. Notably, two of these clusters were in cortical regions within optical penetration depth and thus targetable by non-invasive brain imaging modalities such as fNIRS. CONCLUSIONS: OAB is associated with reduced white matter integrity across five specific brain regions, supporting the concept that bladder dysfunction involves central connectivity changes. Two of these regions are accessible using superficial optical technologies, establishing a foundation for future fNIRS-based optical correlations or biomarker studies.

title: A NON-INVASIVE APPROACH TO DETECTNG DETRUSOR OVERACTIVITY IN PATIENTS WITH OVERACTIVE BLADDER VIA BLADDER NEAR-INFRARED SPECTROSCOPY
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Vandanaa Jayaprakash, Sydney J. Smith, Ishika Singh, Roshni M. Patel, Joseph E. Schultz, Mina P. Ghatas, Ethan S. Casto, Kaitlyn M. Maddra, Nyasia Jones, Julie A. Suyama, Linda S. Burkett, John E. Speich, Adam P. Klausner
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Detrusor overactivity (DO) is characterized by involuntary bladder contractions that may cause overactive bladder (OAB) symptoms, such as urination and incontinence. While Urodynamics (UDS) is the established gold standard test for diagnosis of DO, Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) measures tissue hemodynamics non-invasively, offering a potential cost-effective imaging alternative to UDS. This study evaluates bladder NIRS as a potential non-invasive alternative for detecting DO in individuals with OAB. METHODS: OAB patients participated in simultaneous bladder NIRS and UDS studies. Peak and area-under-the-curve (AUC) values were calculated during DO events using detrusor pressure (pDet) and bladder NIRS (oxygenated hemoglobin (O2Hb)). NIRS segments during DO events were compared within subjects to control segments without DO (internal control), and externally to segments from participants without DO (external control). To account for data drift, a normalized AUC for NIRS data over the testing period was computed after motion artifact correction and subtraction of the area under a linear fit. RESULTS: Among 44 enrolled female OAB participants, four experienced demonstratable DO, producing a total of 39 DO events. During DO events, pDet peaks were significantly higher (51.8 ± 7.3 cm H2O) compared to internal (3.7 ± 0.5 cm H2O), and external control periods (5.4 ± 1.2 cm H2O) (p0.001). Likewise, NIRS O2Hb peaks were higher during DO events (p0.001). pDet AUC was 30,988 ± 7,318.2 (DO), 444.5 ± 86.7 (internal control), and 1,036.6 ± 352.9 (external control), with similar outcomes seen with NIRS O2Hb (p0.001). Normalized NIRS AUC was greater in patients with DO (0.56 ± 0.11) than in external controls (0.09 ± 0.01, p0.001). Using a threshold AUC value of 0.146, provides clear separation between urodynamic segments with and without DO, p0.05 ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191360.00345.d8.09#F1)). CONCLUSIONS: DO events were consistently associated with marked increases in both pDet and NIRS O2Hb values when compared to control segments. These findings support the potential use of bladder NIRS as a non-invasive tool for detecting DO in OAB patients.

title: ALTERATIONS IN BLADDER HEMODYNAMICS USING NEAR-INFRARED SPECTROSCOPY IN FEMALES WITH OVERACTIVE BLADDER AND NORMAL HEALTHY CONTROLS
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Joseph E. Schultz, Mina P. Ghatas, Ethan S. Casto, Tiffany Wong, Mariam M. William, Justin Dare, Peter T. Daniels, Helen Query, Michael K. Shields, Gabriela Grob, Lynn Stothers, Linda S. Burkett, John E. Speich, Adam P. Klausner
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: A common condition, overactive bladder (OAB) is characterized by urinary urgency, frequency, and incontinence. While alterations in bladder hemodynamics are suspected to contribute to OAB pathophysiology, current diagnostic methods lack the ability to directly assess bladder hemodynamics. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether a noninvasive imaging modality, near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), could detect differences in bladder hemodynamic patterns between healthy females and those with OAB during bladder filling. METHODS: A total of 22 female participants (13 with OAB and 9 healthy controls) completed a natural filling protocol while a bladder-mounted NIRS device measured oxygenated hemoglobin (O2Hb) levels. Real-time bladder sensation of fullness was recorded using a previously published and validated “Sensation Meter”. Data were segmented into low and high sensation phases using “first desire to void” as the cutoff threshold. Comparisons were made between the last 10% and first 10% of the high sensation phase, defined as the difference in mean O2Hb (ΔO2Hb). Motion artifacts were corrected using a head-mounted inertial measurement unit (IMU) for detection, and then the data were processed using a custom MATLAB algorithm. RESULTS: Participants with OAB showed significantly lower ΔO2Hb levels during bladder filling compared to controls (−1.2 ± 0.8 vs. 0.7 ± 0.18, p0.05). The slopes of linear fit lines (ΔO2Hb/%time) were significantly higher in the normal control group compared to the OAB group (0.008 ± 0.002 vs. -0.016 ± 0.01, p=0.01. A ΔO2Hb threshold of 0.26 correctly identified OAB participants in 90% of participants, (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191360.00345.d8.10#F1). CONCLUSIONS: Our study demonstrates that bladder NIRS can non-invasively identify altered hemodynamics in females with OAB. These findings, particularly with threshold identification, highlight the potential of NIRS to serve as an objective diagnostic and stratification tool for OAB. Future studies are needed to validate its clinical utility.

title: PEOPLE WITH URGENCY HAVE DIFFERENT SENSATIONS TO URINATE: A LURN II STUDY
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Joanna Marantidis, Giulia Mippolito, J. Quentin Clemens, John Graff, Ziya Kirkali, Brian Bieber, Glenn Werneburg, Emi C. Bretschneider, Tara Morgan, Victor Andreev, Anna Kirby, Michael Odom, Aruna Sarma, Nathan Goodrich, Anne P. Cameron
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The sensation of the need to urinate (NTU) and the sensation of urinary urgency varies. Using the Symptoms of Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction Research Network (LURN II) dataset, we aimed to identify the variety of bladder sensations to void, including the character, location and temporal description. We assessed if these vary based on symptom severity or if distinct sensations to void are interpreted by people with urinary urgency (URG) and urinary urgency incontinence (UUI). METHODS: Six LURN research sites enrolled men and women with bothersome URG or UUI as well as controls without symptoms. Bladder questionnaires were administered. Percentages of participants indicating specific sensations and locations were calculated by sex and patient type and, differences were tested with Chi-square tests. RESULTS: There were 819 symptomatic participants (218 URG and 466 UUI) and 135 controls. Of these 54% were female and the vast majority were white (82%). While most participants localized the sensation of NTU to the “bladder area” (74-90%), more people with URG or UUI localized sensation to the urethra (33-65% URG/UUI vs 9-26% Control, p≤0.001) or penis/scrotum/vagina compared to controls (39-58% URG/UUI vs 8-15% Control, p≤0.001). ( FIGURE) Both control and URG/UUI participants described the sensation of NTU as “pressure” (47-88%) or “fullness” (47-78%). Compared to controls, those with URG/UUI had larger proportions describing the sensation as “tingling” (20-42% vs 7-11%), “urgency” (88-94% vs 28-34%), “discomfort” (67-78% vs 14-20%) or “stinging” (6-11% vs 0-1%). CONCLUSIONS: The sensations and locations of the need to urinate is felt differently among controls versus people with URG and/or UUI. Higher proportions of people with URG report sensation of NTU as discomfort, stinging, pressure or fullness and localize this to areas beyond the bladder.

title: IS THERE A CENTRAL SENSITIZATION PHENOTYPE IN FEMALES WITH OVERACTIVE BLADDER?
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: William Furuyama, Stephen Bruehl, Lindsey McKernan, Benjamin Johnson, John E. Speich, Adam Klausner, Aaron X. Lee, Tatsuki Koyama, Roger Dmochowski, A. Grace Kelly, Elisabeth Sebesta
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) is challenging to treat due to its broad symptomatology and absent unifying pathophysiologic mechanism. Central sensitization (CS) may be an underlying mechanism affecting up to 48% of individuals with OAB. This study evaluated potential phenotypic characteristics associated with CS in OAB involving affect, pain, and co-occurring conditions. We hypothesized that CS would be elevated in OAB compared to controls and associated with increased psychosocial burden, co-morbidity, and urinary symptoms in OAB. METHODS: We recruited adult females with OAB (OABv3≥4) to complete validated symptom measures and a sensory sensitivity protocol, including quantitative sensory testing evaluating average pain threshold, tolerance, and temporal summation of pain (TSP) at 48 degrees C. TSP slopes were calculated using regression, compared between groups, and correlated with proposed phenotypic features within OAB. RESULTS: N=202 with OAB and N=27 controls were recruited, of whom 183 OAB and 23 controls completed TSP testing. 26 (12.6%) with OAB had positive TSP slopes, suggesting CS, versus 1 control (0.5%). There was no difference in pain threshold and tolerance levels, but significant differences in TSP slopes (p=.005, Table). Within the OAB group, there was no association between self-reported emotional distress, sensory sensitivity, increased pain comorbidity, or urinary symptoms based on TSP ( Table). CONCLUSIONS: Results are inconclusive regarding OAB-CS phenotypes. Individuals with OAB may have more difficulty habituating to pain stimuli. Results contradict prior OAB work, including our own, with both lower rates of CS and no association between TSP and putative phenotypic characteristics in OAB. Sample differences and study methodology may partially explain disparate findings between investigations. We highlight the importance of objective measures of bladder hypersensitivity in identifying CS in those with OAB. | | | --- | | |

title: HIDDEN VOIDING DYSFUNCTION IN REFRACTORY FEMALE OVERACTIVE BLADDER: INSIGHTS FROM REAL-WORLD URODYNAMIC PROFILING
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Yoshihisa Matsukawa, Yushi Naito, Yuta Sano, Kazuna Matsuo, Shohei Ishida, Satoshi Inoue, Tomokazu Kimura, Shusuke Akamatsu
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Up to 20% of patients with overactive bladder (OAB) remain refractory to conventional therapy, representing a growing clinical challenge, particularly among elderly women. While recent reports question the clinical utility of urodynamic studies (UDS) in refractory OAB, the underlying bladder pathophysiology in these patients remains poorly defined. This study aimed to characterize the urodynamic features of women with refractory OAB to uncover potential mechanisms of treatment resistance. METHODS: Female patients with idiopathic OAB who failed to improve after ≥12 weeks of behavioral and pharmacological therapy and were referred for surgical consideration underwent standardized UDS. Those with known neurological disease were excluded. Storage and voiding phase parameters were analyzed to identify distinct urodynamic phenotypes. RESULTS: A total of 184 women (mean age, 65.7 years) were analyzed. The mean OAB symptom score was 7.8, and 85.3% reported urgency urinary incontinence. In the UDS, detrusor overactivity (DO) was identified in 71.2% of patients, whereas 19% demonstrated no abnormality in the storage phase, including urinary sensation. Notably, in voiding phase, 32.6% exhibited urodynamic evidence of detrusor underactivity (DU; maximum urinary flow rate \[Qmax\] 10 ml/s and detrusor pressure at Qmax \[PdetQmax\] 30 cmH2O), often voiding by abdominal straining. The coexistence of DO and DU was found in 23.3% of cases, with a higher mean age (75.1 years). Furthermore, one-fourth of patients showed poor voiding bladder efficiency (70%). CONCLUSIONS: Nearly one-third of women with refractory OAB exhibit detrusor underactivity, and coexistence of DO and DU is common among the elderly—findings that are often undetectable without UDS. These results highlight that in refractory female OAB, particularly in older patients, UDS remains an indispensable tool for uncovering hidden voiding dysfunction and guiding individualized therapeutic strategies.

title: URODYNAMIC CORRELATES OF ANTICHOLINERGIC BURDEN: EVIDENCE FOR CHOLINERGIC SATURATION AND DETRUSOR OVERACTIVITY SUPRESSION
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: João P. F. Oliveira, Simão Abreu, Luis Vale, Carlos Ferreira, Joao Silva, Tiago Antunes-Lopes
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder syndrome (OAB) is a prevalent and bothersome condition for which detrusor overactivity (DO) is a key urodynamic correlate. Anticholinergic drugs (AC) remain a cornerstone of treatment; however, many patients are exposed to other medications with anticholinergic properties, contributing to the overall anticholinergic burden (ABu). The Drug Burden Index (DBI) quantifies this cumulative exposure and has been associated with reduced response to OAB antimuscarinic therapy. Whether this observation reflects a true pathophysiological effect at the bladder level or identifies a distinct patient phenotype remains unclear. Elevated anticholinergic burden may suppress detrusor contractility through peripheral muscarinic blockade, while central or sensory pathways sustaining urgency remain unaffected. We aimed to investigate the relationship between DBI and urodynamic findings, exploring a potential mechanistic link between systemic anticholinergic load and detrusor overactivity. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed all urodynamic studies performed at our tertiary center over a 7-month period (n=200). Children and patients with neurological disease, structural genitourinary malformations, or prior botulinum toxin injection within six months were excluded. Demographic and clinical data, including medication history, were collected from medical records. Anticholinergic burden was quantified using the Drug Burden Index (DBI). The primary outcome was the presence of detrusor overactivity (DO) on urodynamic testing. RESULTS: After exclusions, 134 non-neurogenic studies were analyzed. Median age was 64 years (IQR 19.5; 29–87), and 61% were female. Patients were taking a median of two medications (IQR 5; 0–15), with a median DBI of 0.5 (IQR 0.7; 0–3.6). Overall, 34% showed DO. The frequency of DO decreased with increasing DBI: 45% for DBI=0, 33% for DBI 0–1, and 10% for DBI≥1 (p=0.0037). Among patients reporting urgency (n=45), DO was observed in 87.5% with DBI=0 but only in 10% with DBI≥1 (p=0.0026). Logistic regression confirmed the inverse association between DBI and DO. In symptomatic patients, each unit increase in DBI reduced the odds of DO by 85% (OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.05–0.45, p=0.0007). The effect was strongest in urgency patients not treated with OABspecific medication, where each DBI unit decreased the likelihood of DO by 95% (OR 0.05, 95% CI 0.008–0.30, p=0.001) CONCLUSIONS: Higher ABu is strongly associated with the absence of DO, particularly in urgency patients not receiving OAB-specific therapy. Cumulative AC exposure may saturate muscarinic pathways, suppressing detrusor excitability despite persistent urgency. These findings provide mechanistic support for reduced antimuscarinic responsiveness in patients with high DBI and underscore the importance of considering ABu when interpreting urodynamic studies and tailoring OAB treatment.

title: A COMPARISON OF UROGYNECOLOGY AND RECONSTRUCTIVE PELVIC SURGERY (URPS) VS NON-URPS-INTERPRETED URODYNAMIC STUDIES (UDS): DIFFERENCES IN COMPLETENESS AND OUTCOMES
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Chaoyang Wang, Mashtura Hasan, Maya Srinath, Iyla Bagheri, Samir Derisavifard
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urodynamic studies (UDS) help provide valuable information that guides clinical practice, but testing is costly, time consuming, and not without risks. Our aim is to compare UDS studies interpreted by URPS-trained vs non-URPS-trained urologists for completeness and secondarily assess differences in objective outcomes. METHODS: Patients with CPT code of 52718 were queried between 2024-2025 at a single institution and divided into a URPS and non-URPS reading group. Assuming a 25% difference in our primary outcome between groups with an α of 0.05 and a power of 80%, 33 patients need to be included in each group. A random sample of 101 patients was ultimately assessed: 13 patients from 4 current URPS attendings and 5 patients from each of the 10 non-URPS attendings who performed the most UDS. Chi square and Fisher’s exact test were performed to compare completeness in documenting capacity, compliance, course sensation, cough stress test, detrusor overactivity, contractility, complete emptying, clinical obstruction, EMG findings, and flow curve shape, as well as differences in whether an intervention occurred after UDS. RESULTS: A total of 101 UDS (51 URPS and 50 non-URPS) were analyzed. UDS ordered by URPS-trained attendings were significantly more complete; URPS UDS document compliance, contractility, cough stress testing, PVR, and EMG findings significantly more (all p<0.01) compared to non-URPS UDS ( Table 1). URPS UDS were more frequently ordered based off AUA UDS guidelines (98% URPS vs 74% non-URPS, p<0.01), and were more likely to document a new diagnosis compared to non-URPS read studies (52.9% URPS vs 30% non-URPS, p=0.02). There were no statistically significant differences in whether an intervention occurred after UDS (88% URPS vs 76% non-URPS, p=0.1) or whether the intervention was indicated between these groups (98% URPS vs 91% non-URPS, p=0.36). CONCLUSIONS: URPS-read UDS reports were more complete and more commonly ordered based on UDS guidelines. Additionally, URPS-read studies were more likely to document a new diagnosis compared to non-URPS reports. The rate of guideline-indicated intervention that occurred after UDS between the two groups is similar. These data suggest URPS-read UDS are of higher quality and provide greater clinical value compared to non-URPS read studies. | | | --- | | |

title: WHAT LEVEL OF BENEFIT JUSTIFIES BETA-3 AGONIST THERAPY FOR OVERACTIVE BLADDER? ESTIMATING THE PATIENT-PERCEIVED TREATMENT THRESHOLD USING THE SMALLEST WORTHWHILE DIFFERENCE APPROACH
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Kenji Omae, Yan Luo, Ethan Sahker, Aran Tajika, Yuki Kataoka, Noritoshi Sekido, Toshi A. Furukawa
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The smallest worthwhile difference (SWD) represents the minimal beneficial effect of an intervention that patients consider valuable when weighed against its burdens, including potential harms, costs, and inconveniences. We aimed to determine the SWD for overactive bladder (OAB) treatment with beta-3 agonists and to evaluate the impact of trust in physicians on the SWD. METHODS: We recruited participants with symptoms suggestive of OAB in February 2025 through a research crowdsourcing service. The SWD for beta-3 agonists was estimated as a patient-required improvement in response rate to lifestyle modifications after three months using a benefit-harm trade-off approach. Trust in physicians was measured using the five-item Wake Forest Physician Trust Scale. RESULTS: Of 630 respondents, 472 who had symptom-related distress but were medication-naïve were included. Of these, 261 (55%) did not consider beta-3 agonist treatment worthwhile even if it achieved a 100% response. For the 211 participants willing to consider beta-3 agonists, the median SWD was a 20% improvement in response rate, with a wide IQR (5 to 40) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191360.00345.d8.16#F1)). Multivariable generalized linear model analysis showed that higher levels of trust in physicians were associated with smaller SWDs (mean difference per SD, -4.11; 95% CI, -7.00 to -1.22) ( Table 1). CONCLUSIONS: More than half of participants with symptoms suggestive of OAB and associated distress did not consider that beta-3 agonist treatment would be worthwhile given its burdens, even if there was a 100% response. Even among those willing to consider beta-3 agonists, the SWD varied substantially between individuals. Trust in physicians may influence SWD.

title: BEYOND GLYCEMIC CONTROL: CONCURRENT GLP-1 RECEPTOR AGONIST USE IS ASSOCIATED WITH REDUCED URINARY ADVERSE EVENTS FOLLOWING ONABOTULINUMTOXINA TREATMENT IN NON-DIABETIC ADULTS WITH OVERACTIVE BLADDER
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Muhammed Hammad, Sophia Quesada, Aimee Belczyk, Gamal Ghoniem
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) affects nearly 20% of adults and is strongly associated with obesity. OnabotulinumtoxinA (BTX-A) is an established treatment for refractory OAB but carries risks of urinary retention and urinary tract infection (UTI). Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), such as semaglutide, have demonstrated metabolic and anti-inflammatory benefits beyond weight loss. We investigated whether concurrent GLP-1 RA use reduces urinary adverse events among non-diabetic OAB patients treated with BTX-A. METHODS: Using the TriNetX Research Network, we conducted a retrospective, propensity-matched cohort study of non-diabetic adults with OAB who received BTX-A alone or BTX-A plus a GLP-1 RA. Matching (1:1) adjusted for age, race, ethnicity, hypertension, and obesity/BMI. Primary outcomes included incidence of urinary retention, UTI, and new antispasmodic use following BTX-A. Kaplan–Meier survival analyses were performed for one-year event-free survival. RESULTS: After matching, 992 patients were included per group with comparable demographics. GLP-1 RA use was associated with significantly lower urinary retention (4.9% vs. 8.6%; risk difference 3.7%; p=0.0044) and UTI incidence (8.8% vs. 13.3%; risk difference 4.5%; p=0.0224). One-year retention-free (log-rank p=0.0064; HR 1.74) and UTI-free survival (log-rank p=0.0420; HR 1.48) were higher with combination therapy. No differences were observed in new antispasmodic initiation (10.3% vs. 11.8%; p=0.69). Increased antiemetic and laxative use reflected known gastrointestinal side effects of GLP-1 RAs. CONCLUSIONS: In this large, real-world analysis of non-diabetic OAB patients, concurrent GLP-1 RA therapy was associated with reduced risks of urinary retention and UTI following BTX-A treatment, independent of weight loss. These findings suggest potential anti-inflammatory or neuromodulatory effects of GLP-1 signaling on bladder function and warrant prospective studies to evaluate its role as an adjunctive therapy in OAB management.

title: INTRADETRUSOR ONABOTULINUMTOXIN A IS SAFE AND EFFECTIVE IN MEN WITH OVERACTIVE BLADDER FOLLOWING STRESS URINARY INCONTINENCE SURGERY
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Randy G. Tsai, Lauren Muramoto, Victor W. Nitti
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Men with stress urinary incontinence (SUI) treated with artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) or male sling (MS) may develop overactive bladder (OAB). Intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA (onabotA) is effective for refractory OAB, but safety and long-term outcomes in this population are poorly defined. This study evaluates safety, success, and persistence of onabotA therapy in men with and without prior AUS or MS. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective review of men with prior AUS or MS treated with intradetrusor onabotA for OAB at a single center from January 2018 to September 2025. Safety outcomes included new clean intermittent catheterization (CIC), elevated post-void residual (PVR ≥200cc), and escalation to advanced therapy. Persistence was assessed by total number of injections and by Kaplan-Meier analysis of time to discontinuation or escalation. Group comparisons were performed using Fisher’s exact and Mann-Whitney U tests. RESULTS: 126 men met inclusion criteria, 23 with prior SUI surgery (19 AUS, 7 MS, 3 both) and 103 without. Most with AUS/MS (19/23) had prior prostate surgery. No patient with AUS or MS required new CIC or experienced elevated PVR after onabotA compared to 6% and 19% of men without AUS or MS (p=0.591 and p=0.023, respectively). Therapy escalation occurred in 13% of men with AUS or MS and 15% of mean without. Mean number of injections was higher in the AUS/MS group (3.50 ± 2.48 vs 2.66 ± 2.29; p=0.059). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed similar 36-month continuation rates among men with AUS or MS and men without (70.9% vs 68.1%; log-rank p=0.970). CONCLUSIONS: Intradetrusor onabotA for OAB is well tolerated in men with prior AUS or MS. No post-AUS or MS patient required CIC or developed elevated PVR, highlighting a favorable safety profile. Success rates and persistence were comparable or higher than in men without SUI surgery. These findings support onabotA as a safe and effective treatment for refractory OAB in men with prior SUI surgery.

title: INITIATION OF DE-NOVO MEDICAL THERAPY FOR OVERACTIVE BLADDER AFTER BLADDER OUTLET PROCEDURES
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Michael Uy, John Michael Di Bianco, Sabry Mansour, Stephanie Daignault-Newton, Naji Ayyash, Giulia Ippolito, Mahin Mirza, Jay Lonsway, Mark Bradshaw, Kushbu Narender Singh, Khurshid Ghani, Casey Dauw, Wilson Sui
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Despite mechanical relief of bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), some men have persistent or de-novo storage symptoms necessitating pharmacologic therapy, resulting in patient dissatisfaction. Identifying clinical or procedural factors that may identify these men preoperatively could better inform shared decision making, especially as the BPH procedural portfolio continues to grow. We sought to report the rates and factors associated with overactive bladder (OAB) prescriptions following BPH surgery. METHODS: Using Michigan statewide claims data (2017–2023), we identified patients who had BPH surgery without OAB prescriptions (β3-agonist or anticholinergic) within 90 days preoperatively. Procedures included water vapor thermal therapy (WVTT), transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), prostatic urethral lift (PUL), laser photovaporization (PVP), simple prostatectomy (SP), robotic waterjet therapy (RWJT), transurethral microwave thermotherapy (TUMT), and laser enucleation of the prostate (LEP). Medication initiation was defined as a prescription between 3 months and 12 months after surgery. Cox proportional hazards models, adjusted for demographic and clinical factors, were used to identify predictors of medication initiation. RESULTS: 11,926 patients underwent BPH surgery and were OAB medication naive. At 6 months, the initiation rates of OAB medications ranged from 3-8% and by 12 months, ranged from 5-12% ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191360.00345.d8.20#F1)). On multivariable analysis, predictors of OAB medication initiation included increasing patient comorbidity as measured by the Elixhauser score (HR 1.02, 95% CI 1.0-1.05). Compared to TURP, only PVP was associated with higher risk of medication initiation (HR 1.5, 95% CI 1.3-1.8). In contrast, preoperative catheterization was associated with a lower risk (HR 0.7, 95% CI 0.6-0.9). CONCLUSIONS: OAB medication initiation occurs in 5-12% of patients after BPH surgery and varies by procedure type. Compared to TURP, PVP demonstrated the highest rate of medication initiation, indicating a procedure-related risk for postoperative irritative symptoms. Patients who were catheter-dependent prior to surgery were at lower risk, likely reflecting that bladder outlet obstruction, rather than detrusor overactivity, was the predominant underlying pathology.

title: INCIDENCE OF AND TIME TO MINIMALLY INVASIVE THERAPY AMONG PATIENTS WITH IDIOPATHIC OVERACTIVE BLADDER
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Andria Li, Rachna Sridhar, Wilson Sui, Caitlin Seibel, Evan Goldfischer, Robert Dowling, Giulia Ippolito
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Overactive bladder (OAB) is a common condition affecting up to 43% of adults, yet adoption of minimally invasive therapies (MIT), including percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS), botulinum toxin (BTX), and sacral neuromodulation (SNM), remains low. There is limited data describing whether physician practice models influence MIT uptake. This study compares rates and time to MIT in large, community-based practices within the Large Urology Group Practice Association (LUGPA) and at a single academic institution. METHODS: This retrospective study evaluated rate of progression to MIT and time to progression to MIT in two cohorts: 1) the claims of patients with an encounter for overactive bladder from 2020 to 2023 in 41 independent Large Urology Group Practice Association (LUGPA) practices and 2) the medical records of patients with an encounter for OAB between 2012 and 2021 from an academic tertiary care center, University of Michigan (UM). Descriptive statistics, Kaplan-Meier analyses, and Cox proportional hazards models assessed MIT adoption and predictors of progression. RESULTS: During the study period, 42,633 of 419,041 patients in the LUGPA cohort and 1,013 of 15,655 patients in the UM cohort progressed to MIT. In LUGPA, the MIT most often utilized was BTX (52%), followed by SNM (42%) and PTNS (17%). At UM, the MIT most often utilized was PTNS (46%), followed by BTX (34%) and SNM (20%). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed cumulative MIT uptake at 1, 2, and 3 years of 9.6%, 13.7%, and 17.3% in LUGPA, compared with 9.1%, 10.9%, and 12.8% in UM. Across both cohorts, MIT was more common among female and older patients. In LUGPA, Medicare insurance and smaller practice size (<50 providers) were associated with higher uptake, while in UM, commercially insured patients were more likely to undergo MIT. CONCLUSIONS: We found that progression to MIT was more common and more rapid in independently owned private urology practices compared to a single academic center. Practice model-specific factors, such as the presence of nurse navigators, may play a critical role in long-term uptake. Broader evaluation across academic centers is warranted to define best practices for optimizing patient access to MIT.

title: COMPARATIVE OUTCOMES FOR MINIMALLY INVASIVE THERAPIES FOR IDIOPATHIC OVERACTIVE BLADDER IN OLDER ADULTS: A NATIONAL STUDY OF MEDICARE BENEFICIARIES
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Unwanaobong Nseyo, Stephanie Zuo, Lufan Wang, Adam Crow, Abigail Shatkin-Margolis, John Boscardin, Anne Suskind
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: To compare 2-year treatment continuation outcomes among minimally invasive therapies \[onabotulinumtoxinA injections (BTX-A), sacral neuromodulation (SNM), and percutaneous\ tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS)\] for idiopathic overactive bladder (OAB) in older adults. METHODS: This is a retrospective cohort study of a 100% sample of fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries who underwent minimally invasive therapy for idiopathic OAB from 2015-2020. Therapies were identified by Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes and included intravesical BTX-A, SNM, and PTNS. The primary outcome was continuation of therapy, which was defined as follows for each treatment: BTX-A: at least one repeat injection within 2 years; SNM: progression to implantable pulse generator (IPG) within 90 days of initial implant and no explant at 2 years; PTNS: completion of induction PTNS (11 treatments in 15 weeks) followed by at least 9 maintenance PTNS treatments within 2 years (definitions based on prior research from our group). Propensity score weighting and modified Poisson regression were used to compare outcomes between therapies. RESULTS: A total of 111,494 Medicare beneficiaries initiated a minimally invasive OAB therapy during the study period, and 34.5% (n=38,502) demonstrated continuation of therapy over 2 years. Rates of therapy continuation were as follows: BTX-A 58%, SNM 36.3%, PTNS 9.9%. On weighted regression analyses, beneficiaries undergoing BTX-A were 5.9 times more likely to continue treatment compared to PTNS (95% CI 5.71-6.10) and 1.63 times more likely to continue treatment compared to SNM (95% CI 1.60-1.65). Beneficiaries undergoing SNM were 3.63 times more likely to continue treatment compared to PTNS (95% CI 3.57-3.68). CONCLUSIONS: Older adults with idiopathic OAB undergoing minimally invasive therapy are most likely to continue BTX-A and least likely to continue PTNS over 2 years of follow-up. However, rates for continuation of any type of minimally invasive OAB therapy are low. Further research is needed to determine reasons for discontinuation of minimally invasive OAB therapy in older adults.

title: REAL-WORLD EXPERIENCE WITH IMPLANTABLE TIBIAL NERVE STIMULATION IN PATIENTS WITH AND WITHOUT PRIOR FAILED NEUROMODULATION FOR OVERACTIVE BLADDER
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Francis A. Jefferson, Christina Sze, Christine Herforth, Ramy S. Goueli, Gary E. Lemack, Maude E. Carmel
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The BlueWind Revi system is an implantable tibial nerve stimulator for overactive bladder (OAB). This study reports institutional outcomes, focusing on patients with prior failed sacral neuromodulation (SNS) or percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS). METHODS: A retrospective chart review was performed for all patients undergoing Revi implantation between May 2024 and April 2025. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 3-month, and 6-month follow-up. Statistical comparisons were made between patients with and without prior neuromodulation. RESULTS: Twenty-one patients (median age 73, 71% female, 5% neurogenic) were included. Most had previously used anticholinergics (81%), beta-3 agonists (24%), PTNS (52%), and/or SNS (10%). All prior PTNS patients were responders. Comparing preoperative symptoms to first (median 3.5 months) and second (median 6.1 months) follow-up: Median daily voids decreased from 9 (IQR 7–12) to 6 (IQR 5–8) at first (p=0.002), and to 7 (IQR 5–9) at second (p=0.004). Median nocturia decreased from 2 (IQR 1–3) to 1 (IQR 0–2) at first (p=0.01) and remained at 1 (IQR 0–2) at second (p=0.02). Median UUI episodes/day dropped from 1 (IQR 0–1) to 0.5 (IQR 0–1) at first (p=0.03), and to 0.5 (IQR 0–1) at second (p=0.04). Median pads/day decreased from 1 (IQR 0–1) to 0.5 (IQR 0–1) at both follow-ups (p ≤ 0.05). Median UDI-6 improved from 45 (IQR 35–62) to 29 (IQR 25–33) at first (p=0.002), and to 27 (IQR 25–33) at second (p=0.003). ≥50% reduction in UUI was achieved by 69% at first and 70% at second follow-up (McNemar’s p<0.05). No serious device- or procedure-related adverse events occurred. Subgroup analysis (n=8 prior neuromodulation \[1 SNS, 7 PTNS\] vs. n=13 without) showed no significant differences in baseline or outcomes at either follow-up (all p>0.05; Table 1). CONCLUSIONS: In this small, real-world cohort, Revi implantation resulted in significant, durable improvements in OAB symptoms and quality of life, with similar efficacy in patients regardless of prior failed neuromodulation. | | | --- | | |

title: EXPLORING PATIENT PERSPECTIVES ON SACRAL NEUROMODULATION: A QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS OF ONLINE DISCUSSIONS
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Ahmed Albakr, Mohamed Elkhashab, Mazen Mansour, Maria D'Amico, Alexander Koven, Howard Goldman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Sacral neuromodulation (SNM) is an established treatment for refractory overactive bladder and urinary incontinence, yet patient perceptions and understanding of this therapy remain underexplored. Online forums increasingly serve as major sources of peer-to-peer education and informal health advice. This study qualitatively analyzed patient discussions about SNM on Reddit to characterize shared experiences, identify misconceptions, and assess the educational value of online discourse. METHODS: A qualitative content analysis was conducted using public posts and comments from the subreddits r/OveractiveBladder and r/Incontinence. Entries containing the terms “sacral neuromodulation,” “InterStim,” “Axonics,” or “sacral nerve stimulation” were included. Two independent reviewers performed systematic, line-by-line coding, applying Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis framework. Coding reliability was evaluated using Cohen’s kappa. Non-relevant posts were excluded. RESULTS: A total of 464 threads comprising 3,413 comments were analyzed. Five overarching themes emerged: (1) Expectations and Decision-Making, (2) Postoperative Experiences, (3) Device Function and Performance, (4) Emotional and Psychosocial Responses, and (5) System- and Industry-Related Concerns. Patients frequently expressed anxiety about candidacy, surgical risks, and long-term outcomes, often comparing SNM to other third-line therapies. Postoperative accounts ranged from life-changing improvement to persistent discomfort or loss of efficacy. Users discussed differences between InterStim and Axonics devices, battery life, MRI compatibility, and programming challenges. Emotional responses varied from hope and gratitude to frustration and distrust of medical providers. Cost, insurance coverage, and company support were additional recurrent issues. CONCLUSIONS: Reddit discussions about SNM reveal a complex landscape of patient expectations, lived experiences, and misconceptions. While many describe substantial benefits, others express uncertainty and disappointment, reflecting ongoing gaps in patient education and clinical communication. Social media analysis offers a valuable lens for understanding patient perspectives and improving educational outreach around advanced bladder therapies.

title: OCCUPATIONAL VOIDING RESTRICTIONS ASSOCIATED WITH OVERACTIVE BLADDER SYMPTOMS: LOW INCOME INDIVIDUALS MOST AFFECTED
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Arshia Aalami Harandi, Jason Kim
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prior studies suggest that overactive bladder (OAB) may be associated with certain occupations, such as healthcare, transportation, and education. They propose that these occupations limit natural voiding patterns and thereby lead to OAB. This study aims to determine the association between overactive bladder symptoms and occupational voiding restrictions and to identify healthcare disparities. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey of employed adults was conducted via ResearchMatch. Participants were asked about demographics, income level, OAB symptoms via OAB symptom score (OABSS) and occupational voiding restrictions via a novel survey. Differences in median reported occupational voiding restrictions was determined via Kruskal-Wallis H test and post-hoc Dunn test. Spearman’s Rank-Sum correlations were conducted to determine associations between OABSS and occupational voiding restrictions scale. RESULTS: Three hundred and forty one participants completed the survey with median age of 35-44 years old, predominantly female gender (76.0%), predominantly white ethnicity (87.1%), and median household income of $60-80K. As shown in (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191360.00345.d8.25#F1), low-income participants reported significantly higher occupational voiding restrictions than high-income participants (H(2)=6.52, p=0.038). As shown in Table 1, weak correlations were found between OABSS and occupational voiding restrictions (r=0.16, p<.01). When stratified by income, low income individuals had a moderate association between OABSS scores and distress caused by occupational voiding restrictions (r=0.40, p<.01). CONCLUSIONS: Occupational voiding restrictions are associated with OAB symptoms in a large sample of employed adults. Low-income individuals are most affected by occupational voiding restrictions and experience greater association between restrictions and distress. Physicians should advocate for healthy toileting behaviors at the workplace.

title: UNDERSTANDING PRIMARY CARE PROVIDER URINARY INCONTINENCE KNOWLEDGE
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Sweta Parija, Abbas Bader, Gaurav Bhushan, Jonathan Bergman, Richard Fantus, Tamara Grisales, Allison Mays, Jejo Koola, Emily Lukacz, Yahir Santiago-Lastra, Jennifer Singer, Colby Souders
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urinary incontinence (UI) places a substantial social and economic burden on women, with its prevalence rising alongside an aging population. We are conducting a study to improve the quality of care for women with UI. As part of this effort, we assessed baseline knowledge of primary care providers (PCPs) regarding UI using a validated questionnaire. Here, we present the findings from our baseline assessment. METHODS: This is an ongoing a multi-site cluster randomized comparative effectiveness trial at three academic institutions: University of California of San Diego, University of California Los Angeles, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and University of Kansas. As part of the baseline assessment, participating PCPs complete the Pelvic Floor Awareness Knowledge Survey (PFAKS), a validated 31-item knowledge questionnaire with three domains: stress urinary incontinence (10 items), overactive bladder (10 items), and pelvic organ prolapse (11 items), with questions on condition pathophysiology, management, and quality of life. Responses from the PFAKS will undergo thorough analysis to evaluate PCPs’ knowledge levels across the three topics. RESULTS: Results from 158 UI knowledge questionnaires were reviewed. The average number of years in practice is 7.17 years. For 15 of the 20 questions related to OAB/UI, PCPs had the correct answer more than 60% of the time (See (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191360.00345.d8.26#F1)). More than a third (28.4%) of PCPs incorrectly indicated that medications could cure pure stress urinary incontinence (SUI), with the highest rate of incorrect responses. In addition, PCPs were given the option to indicate whether they did not know the answer to a question. The top two questions with the highest rate of uncertainty were understanding whether surgery could cure urinary incontinence and the relationship between overactive bladder and fluid intake. CONCLUSIONS: Although most PCPs have strong overall knowledge of UI pathophysiology, treatment, and quality of life, significant knowledge gaps remain. These data have informed our targeted education and custom clinical decision support tools to enhance PCPs’ UI knowledge as part of our ongoing UI quality improvement work.

title: POST-MICTURITION DRIBBLING: NEW INSIGHTS INTO THE ROLE OF POST-VOID RESIDUAL VOLUME AND AFTER-CONTRACTIONS — A PROSPECTIVE STUDY
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Yonatan Yacobi, Ilia Beberashvili, Amnon Zisman, Kobi Stav
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Post-micturition dribbling (PMD) is defined as passive urinary leakage immediately following voiding. Despite its high prevalence among men, affecting up to 58%, and its significant impact on quality of life, research on its etiological and clinical aspects remains limited. Notably, PMD is not included in the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) questionnaire. We aimed to search for clinical risk factors for PMD, perhaps providing clues about its possible etiology. METHODS: A prospective study was conducted with systematic data collection. Male patients aged 18 and above referred for urodynamic evaluation for any indication were asked to complete a structured form incorporating the IPSS and specific questions regarding PMD. Additional clinical parameters were recorded, including PSA levels, US data, age, comorbidities, medications, and prior surgeries. Data was collected from a total of 160 patients. Statistical analysis was performed to assess correlations between clinical variables and the presence of PMD ( Table 1). RESULTS: Univariate analysis revealed a statistically significant correlation between post-void residual (PVR) volume and PMD, as well as between after-contractions and PMD. Multivariate logistic regression ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191360.00345.d8.27#F1)) demonstrated a linear association between increasing PVR volume and PMD, with an odds ratio (OR) of 1.08 for every 10 ml increase in residual volume (95% CI: 1.03–1.14). The strongest association was observed in patients with PVR exceeding 85 ml (AUC=0.63). This correlation persisted after adjustment for additional clinical variables, including diabetes, prior surgeries, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), age, detrusor overactivity (DO), bladder outlet obstruction (BOO), and after-contractions. No significant correlation was found between PMD and the presence of BOO or DO on urodynamic testing. CONCLUSIONS: Elevated post-void residual volume and after-contractions are independent and significant risk factors for post-micturition dribbling. These findings suggest a pathophysiological link that warrants further investigation to elucidate the underlying mechanisms and to develop targeted diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. | | | --- | | |

title: COMPARATIVE ASSESSMENT OF TWO STANDARD OF CARE PAIN MANAGEMENT PROTOCOLS FOR INTRADETRUSOR ONABOTULINUMTOXINA INJECTIONS IN A DIVERSE URBAN PATIENT POPULATION
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Grace Khaner, Nancy De Grezia, Alexander Del Vlahos, Akash Sharma, Gregory Vurture, Whitney Clearwater, Nitya Abraham, Melissa Laudano
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Intravesical alkalinized lidocaine instillation prior to intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA (BTX-A) injection for refractory overactive bladder (OAB) may be undesirable to some patients due to prolonged appointment time and associated discomfort. This study evaluates the utility of oral phenazopyridine as a feasible alternative to intravesical instillation for periprocedural pain control. METHODS: This ongoing prospective, non-randomized study includes nonpregnant women aged ≥18 years undergoing BTX-A for idiopathic, refractory OAB. Patients received either oral phenazopyridine two hours pre-procedure or a 20-minute intravesical alkalinized lidocaine instillation for pain control. The primary outcome was post-procedure pain measured using a 100 mm visual analog scale (VAS). Secondary outcomes included overall satisfaction and preference for future pain control. Preliminary statistical analysis was performed by Mann-Whitney (Wilcoxon) tests with p<0.05 considered significant. RESULTS: Eighty-six patients were recruited; 60 received intravesical lidocaine and 26 received oral phenazopyridine. Participants represent a racially and socially diverse population; 51.4% percent self-identified as Hispanic and 32.4% as Black, and 51.1% live in areas where over 27.7% of women live below the poverty level. There were no differences in sample demographics between groups. Most patients (73.3%) had previously received BTX-A. Post-procedure pain scores and overall satisfaction were not significantly different between groups (p=0.212 and p=0.359, respectively). Among phenazopyridine recipients, 13/14 reported they would choose it again for future injections. CONCLUSIONS: Oral phenazopyridine represents a feasible alternative for periprocedural pain control prior to intravesical onabotulinumtoxinA injections when patients prefer a less invasive or quicker option. These findings highlight an important opportunity for shared decision-making and operational efficiency in the outpatient procedure setting. | | | --- | | |

title: INTRADETRUSOR ONABOTULINUMTOXINA IS SAFE AND EFFECTIVE IN MEN WITH OVERACTIVE BLADDER FOLLOWING RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY OR OUTLET SURGERY
session: Urodynamics/Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction/Female Pelvic Medicine: Overactive Bladder (IP16)
authors: Randy G. Tsai, Lauren Muramoto, Victor W. Nitti
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: After radical prostatectomy (RP) or outlet surgery (OS), men often experience overactive bladder (OAB) and may be offered intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA (onabotA) for refractory symptoms. Efficacy and safety of onabotA are well established in the general population, but outcomes in men with surgically altered lower urinary tracts remain poorly characterized. This study evaluated safety and persistence of onabotA in men with and without prior RP or OS. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective review of men treated with intradetrusor onabotA for OAB at a single center from January 2018 to September 2025. Patients were categorized into 3 groups: (1) prior RP (n=33), (2) prior OS (TURP, HoLEP, TURBN, GreenLight, or Aquablation) (n=42), and (3) no prior OS or RP (n=51). Outcomes included new clean intermittent catheterization (CIC), elevated post-void residual (PVR ≥200cc), escalation of therapy (sacral neuromodulation or augmentation cystoplasty), and persistence of therapy by Kaplan-Meier analysis. Group comparisons were performed using Fisher’s exact and log-rank tests. RESULTS: Table 1 compares CIC, elevated PVR, and escalation rates in the 3 groups. Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated 36-month continuation rates of 85.8% for prior RP, 38.4% for prior OS, and 81.5% for no OS or RP. Pairwise comparisons showed lower persistence in the OS group compared to without (p=0.045) but no difference between prior RP and no OS or RP (p=1.000). CONCLUSIONS: Intradetrusor onabotA for OAB is safe and well tolerated in men with or without prior prostate surgery. Men with prior RP had no new catheterizations and lower rates of adverse outcomes compared with those without prior OS or RP, while also demonstrating long-term persistence. In contrast, patients with prior OS had comparable safety outcomes to patients with no prior OS or RP but exhibited reduced persistence. | | | --- | | |

title: IMPACT OF INTRAVESICAL PROSTATIC PROTRUSION ON CONTINENCE OUTCOMES FOLLOWING SINGLE-PORT TRANSVESICAL RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Lin Wang, Nicolas Soputro, Karim Daher, Abdulrahman Al-Bayati, Rui Miguel Marques Bernardino, Salim Younis, Riccardo Autorino, Jihad Kaouk
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The effect of intravesical prostatic protrusion (IPP) on continence recovery after radical prostatectomy is not well established. Previous studies relied on intraoperative assessment and categorized IPP only as present or absent. We sought to evaluate IPP quantitatively on preoperative MRI using a validated grading system and to assess its impact on continence recovery following single-port transvesical radical prostatectomy (SP-TV RARP). METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed a prospectively maintained database of patients who underwent SP-TV RARP between November 2020 and August 2024. IPP was measured on mid-sagittal T2-weighted MRI as the perpendicular distance from the tip of the protruding prostatic tissue into the bladder to the bladder circumference at the prostate base. IPP was graded as: 0 (none), I (≤5 mm), II (>5–10 mm), or III (>10 mm). Continence, defined as <2 pads/day, was assessed immediately (≤1 week), and at 6 weeks, 3, 6, 9, and 12 months after Foley removal. Kaplan–Meier analysis and chi-square tests compared outcomes across IPP groups (Python 3.11, Python Software Foundation, Wilmington, DE). RESULTS: Of 208 eligible patients with complete MRI and continence data ( Table 1), immediate continence rates were 46.8%, 43.5%, 25.5%, and 25.0% in IPP 0, I, II, and III groups, respectively. There is no significant difference among IPP groups in BMI. Older age is associated only with IPP grade 3 compared to grade 0. Prostate volume is significantly larger in IPP grade 2 and 3 compared to grade 0, and larger in grade 3 compared to grade 1. Higher IPP grades were associated with lower immediate continence, though the difference approached but did not reach statistical significance (P=0.052). Patients with grade II–III IPP demonstrated delayed recovery, yet continence exceeded 95% in all groups by 9–12 months (p>0.05) ( (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191364.82577.9a.01#F2)). CONCLUSIONS: While IPP may create a wider bladder neck defect, it does not seem to adversely affect short or long-term continence outcomes of SP-TV RARP.

title: OPTIMIZING PSA FOLLOW-UP AFTER RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY: A POPULATION-BASED ANALYSIS OF BIOCHEMICAL RECURRENCE PATTERNS
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Francesco Pellegrino, Ugo Giovanni Falagario, Olof Akre, Markus Aly, Tobias Nordström, Henrik Grönberg, Lars Egevad, Matteo Ferro, Anna Lantz, Peter Wiklund
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The oncological follow-up of patients with prostate cancer treated with radical prostatectomy (RP) is based on serial PSA measurements. However, the optimal duration and frequency of PSA testing during follow-up remain debated. In this context, we evaluated the incidence and patterns of biochemical recurrence (BCR) following RP. METHODS: This population-based study utilized data from the STHLM0 register. We included only patients undergoing RP between 2003 and 2023, resulting in a final cohort of 11,070 patients. All PSA values during their lifetime were available. We calculated the annual incidence of BCR (defined as PSA ≥0.2 ng/mL on two consecutive measurements) for patients grouped according to CAPRA risk categories. In addition, we plotted BCR incidence using the LOWESS smoothing function. The same analyses were performed for high-risk (HR) and low-risk (LR) BCR, defined according to EAU criteria. RESULTS: The median preoperative PSA was 7.3 (interquartile range \[IQR\]: 5.0–11.0). Overall, 2696 (30%) patients had pT3 disease, and 4328 (39%) and 985 (9%) patients had ISUP 3 and 4-5 at final pathology, respectively. According to CAPRA risk stratification, 4575 (41%), 5170 (47%), and 1325 (12%) patients were classified as low-, intermediate-, and high-risk, respectively. After a median follow-up of 85 months (IQR: 51–136) among patients without BCR, 2392 (22%) experienced recurrence. Among these, 1439 had HR-BCR. (https://www.auajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1097/01.JU.0001191364.82577.9a.02#F1) illustrates the annual incidence of BCR by year of follow-up. The incidence of BCR and HR-BCR was highest in the CAPRA high-risk group (≈13% in the first year), decreasing steadily during the first 5 years of follow-up before stabilizing thereafter (≈1%, Figure 1b). Similar patterns were observed among patients in the low- and intermediate-risk groups. Conversely, the incidence of LR-BCR remained relatively stable throughout follow-up ( Figure 1c); for example, LR-BCR incidence ranged from 3% to 2% among patients in the CAPRA high-risk group. CONCLUSIONS: Most BCR after RP occur within the first 5 years after treatment, particularly among high-risk patients. Similarly, the incidence of HR-BCR after 5 years of follow-up is very low. PSA follow-up schedules after RP should be guided by patient-specific risk factors. Given that most recurrences arise within 5 years after surgery, a de-intensified surveillance strategy may be appropriate beyond this period, especially for low-risk patients.

title: INTEGRATING PREOPERATIVE PSMA-PET AND MRI FINDINGS TO PREDICT NODAL METASTASIS IN PROSTATE CANCER PATIENTS UNDERGOING PROSTATECTOMY
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Nadim Alame, Jad Najdi, Riad Khouzami, Abdallah El Kasti, Mohammad Ali Mazloum, Albert El Hajj
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: PSMA-PET scan and MRI are increasingly utilized in prostate cancer staging, particularly in differentiating between localized and metastatic disease and in predicting regional lymph node involvement. We aimed to evaluate the accuracy of PSMA-PET in predicting lymph node involvement among patients undergoing prostatectomy, and to assess other predictors of lymph node positivity. METHODS: Patients who underwent robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy at our center between 2018 and 2024, with available preoperative PSMA-PET and MRI scans were included. Patients with positive lymph nodes on pathology were compared to those without using t-tests for continuous variables and Chi-Square or Fisher’s Exact tests for categorical variables. The index prostate lesion was defined as the one with the highest PIRADS score (or largest size if equal) on MRI and the highest SUVmax on PSMA-PET. MRI was used to measure index lesion size. PSMA-PET sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV for predicting nodal positivity were calculated. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression identified predictors of nodal metastasis. RESULTS: A total of 190 patients were included. 17 patients (8.9%) had positive lymph nodes on pathology, and 22 patients (11.6%) had positive lymph nodes on PSMA-PET scan, resulting in a sensitivity of 41.2%, specificity of 90.5%, PPV of 31.8% and NPV of 93.5%. Patients with positive lymph nodes on pathology had a higher probability of having PSA>10 ng/dL (p=0.01), higher SUVmax of index lesion (p=0.049), higher proportion of higher gleason grade group on biopsy (p=0.001), and a larger index lesion size on MRI (p=0.007). After adjusting for age, BMI, preoperative PSA and SUVmax of index lesion, we found that index lesion size was significantly associated with increased odds of having positive lymph nodes on pathology (OR 2.91, p=0.045). Alternatively, SUVmax of index lesion failed to show a statistically significant association after adjusting for age, BMI, preoperative PSA and index lesion size. CONCLUSIONS: PSMA-PET demonstrates high specificity but limited sensitivity for detecting lymph node metastasis, suggesting it should not be solely relied upon to omit lymph node dissection during prostatectomy. Index lesion size is a strong predictor of nodal positivity, while other PSMA-PET parameters such as index lesion SUVmax may also be associated, warranting further exploration in other cohorts. | | | --- | | |

title: SALINE-ASSISTED FASCIAL ENGORGEMENT (SAFE) NERVE PRESERVATION GUIDED BY MICRO-ULTRASOUND DURING ROBOTIC RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY: INTERIM ANALYSIS OF A PHASE III RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Adriana Marcela Pedraza Bermeo, Monali Fatterpekar, Himanshu Joshi, Manish Choudhary, Neeraja Tillu, Coskun Kacagan, Arora Chahat, Daniel Ajabshir, Yashaswini Agarwal, Cristina Pasat-Karasik, Mani Menon, Ash Tewari
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Erectile dysfunction remains a major morbidity after radical prostatectomy. The Saline-Assisted Fascial Engorgement (SAFE) technique, first described by our group (BJU Int, 2023), uses real-time 29-MHz micro-ultrasound–guided low-pressure hydrodissection to achieve atraumatic fascial separation and enhance visualization of the neurovascular bundle. This randomized controlled trial (RCT) compared the functional and oncologic outcomes of SAFE and standard robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP). METHODS: In this single-center RCT, patients were randomized 1:1 using permuted blocks, stratified by age (<60 vs ≥60 years) and baseline SHIM score (<22 vs ≥22). Patients and outcome assessors remained blinded. The primary endpoint was 6-month erectile function recovery (SHIM ≥17). Secondary outcomes included SHIM/EHS (Erection Hardness Score) trajectories, urinary continence, and oncologic parameters. The primary endpoint was analyzed using a one-sided pooled z-test (α=0.15), and secondary outcomes were evaluated descriptively. This report presents the planned interim analysis. RESULTS: A total of 107 patients were included (SAFE=54, Control=53). At 6 months, erectile function recovery occurred in 51.9% of SAFE vs 43.4% of controls (Δ=8.5%, 95% CI –10 to 27; one-sided p=0.22). SAFE showed higher early recovery at 6 weeks (37.0% vs 20.8%; p=0.032) and a trend at 3 months (44.4% vs 37.7%; p=0.24). Linear mixed models demonstrated faster early SHIM and EHS improvement in the SAFE group (+2 SHIM, +0.5 EHS; p ≈ 0.04), converging by 6 months. Urinary continence and oncologic outcomes were similar (PSM 9.3% vs 11.3%; BCR 3.7% vs 5.7%; p>0.6). No technique-related complications occurred. CONCLUSIONS: Although the primary endpoint of 6-month erectile function recovery was not statistically significant, the SAFE technique achieved faster early recovery at 6 weeks, with no differences in complication rates or oncologic outcomes. These findings suggest that SAFE may enhance early neurovascular recovery without compromising safety or cancer control.

title: ERECTILE FUNCTION OUTCOMES AFTER MENON PRECISION PROSTATECTOMY: ANALYZING PREDICTORS OF FUNCTIONAL RECOVERY AND EVIDENCE OF REPRODUCIBILITY OF OUTCOMES
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Kaushik P. Kolanukuduru, Wooju Jeong, Akshay Sood, Firas Abdollah, Craig C. Rogers, Ashutosh K. Tewari, Mani Menon
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Menon Precision Prostatectomy (MPP) is a subtotal surgical treatment for localized prostate cancer (PCa) that involves preserving the unilateral capsule and seminal vesicle on the side opposite the dominant nodule. We sought to assess potency rates after MPP, identify predictors of potency recovery, and explore the reproducibility of outcomes. METHODS: MPP was offered to patients with intermediate-risk PCa who prioritized maintaining erectile function. Four surgeons performed MPP at three different centers with different surgical teams. Potency was defined as SHIM≥17 both preoperatively and postoperatively. The primary study measure was the potency rate at 12 months. Multivariable Cox regression was used to identify predictors of potency recovery. RESULTS: A total of 175 patients underwent MPP for intermediate-risk PCa. The median age and preoperative SHIM score were 61 years (IQR 56-66) and 22 (IQR 18-24.5) respectively, with 79% reporting SHIM≥17 prior to surgery. At 12 months, 90% of preoperatively potent patients regained erectile function. Cox regression analysis showed that age (>60 yr vs. ≤60 yr: HR=0.53) and preoperative potency status (Preoperative SHIM≥17 vs. SHIM<17: HR=8.3) were significant predictors of potency recovery. The type of nerve-sparing on the radical side did not influence postoperative recovery. There was no difference in potency recovery between surgeons. CONCLUSIONS: Nearly 90% of patients undergoing MPP recover erectile function by 12 months. While age and preoperative functional status are the primary determinants of postoperative function, nerve-sparing on the radical side does not impact erectile recovery. The technique was reproducible across multiple surgeons with varying levels of experience. Further studies are required to support these findings.

title: OMITTING PELVIC LYMPH NODE DISSECTION IN PROSTATE CANCER PATIENTS WITH NEGATIVE PSMA-PET/CT: A MULTICENTER STUDY CHALLENGING CURRENT NOMOGRAM RECOMMENDATIONS
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Fabio Zattoni, Giuseppe Reitano, Felix Preisser, Shah Taimur, Nicolas Bonanno, Francesco Barletta, Daniele Amparore, Enrico Checcucci, Campobasso Davide, Rossella Nicoletti, Giorgio Ivan Russo, Felice Crocetto, Junlong Zhuang, Vera Sweere, Matthijs Scheltema, Jereny Y. C. Teoh, Steven Leung, Matteo Bauckneht, Fiona Page, Shomik Sengupta, Nikhil Vasdev, Elaina Gubbay, Jeffrey R. Karnes, Veeru Kasivisvanathan, Timo F. W. Soeterik, Giacomo Novara, Pawel Rajwa, Paolo Gontero
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Pelvic lymph node dissection (PLND) remains controversial in prostate cancer (PCa) patients with nodes-negative preoperative PSMA-PET/CT imaging. This study aimed to evaluate the oncological outcomes of performing versus omitting PLND in PSMA-negative PCa patients with a high risk of lymph-node invasion, undergoing radical prostatectomy. METHODS: From an initial cohort of 1713 high (HR) and intermediate (IR) PCa patients, miN0M0 at preoperative PSMA-PET, we retrieved those with lymph node invasion (LNI) probability exceeding the threshold defined by the Briganti 2023 score. Patients were divided into PLND and no-PLND. Outcomes were PSA persistence, biochemical recurrence (BCR) and radiological recurrence (RR)-free survival (FS). Kaplan-Meier analysis was used for survival outcomes. Multivariable regression analyses were performed to identify preoperative and postoperative predictors of disease persistence or progression, adjusting for PLND status and covariates encompassed by the UCSF-CAPRA and postoperative S-CAPRA scoring systems. RESULTS: A total of 963 patients were included, comprising 208 without ePLND and 755 with ePLND. PLND was associated with increased 90-day postoperative complications (n=97,18.7% vs n=20, 10%), especially high-grade complications (n=54, 10.4% vs n=12,6% p=0.02). No significant differences were found between PLND (n=755) and no-PLND (n=208) in PSA persistence (11.6% vs 8.7%, p=0.23), BCR (19.7% vs 16.4%, p=0.29) and RR (8.4% vs 10.2%, p=0.41) rates after a median follow up of 25 months. Survival analyses showed that BCR-FS and RR-FS were comparable between groups (p>0.05). In the multivariable analyses avoiding PLND was not predictive of PSA persistence, BCR and RR. Limitations of the study include the retrospective design. CONCLUSIONS: PLND did not provide significant oncological benefit in PCa patients with a node-negative PSMA-PET/CT scan but a high risk of LNI. Avoiding PLND in this setting seems not to compromise short-to-medium term oncological outcomes but has a significant impact in reducing perioperative complications. | | | --- | | |

title: THE ROBOSLING RANDOMISED CONTROLLED TRIAL - CONTINENCE OUTCOMES WITH AUTOLOGOUS VASCULARISED BLADDER NECK SLING DURING ROBOTIC RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
