authors: Darius Ashrafi, Juliette Cotte, Patrick Julien-Treacy, Dhiya Suresh, Kate Alexander, Sascha Karunaratne, Lewis Chan, Paul Sved, Arthur Vasilaras, Nariman Ahmadi, Daniel Steffens, Ruban Thanigasalam, Scott Leslie
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The morbidity of robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) is often secondary to functional complications i. e. post-prostatectomy incontinence and sexual dysfunction. The gold standard surgical treatment for PPI succeeds by strengthening the urethral-sphincter mechanism with a sling or an artificial sphincter. Intra-operative methods to do the same are a crucial knowledge gap in the RARP era. This study evaluates the use of a novel well-vascularised, autologous intra-operative sling to support the bladder neck and the urethra – the ‘RoboSling’. A retrospective cohort study evaluating this technique in our institution has demonstrated improved continence outcomes. METHODS: In this phase 3 study, adult men with localised prostate cancer who underwent RARP were randomised, and blinded, to RARP with RoboSling (intervention) or RARP alone (control) in a 1:1 fashion following a strict inclusion criteria. RARP and RoboSling techniques were standardised with only clinically indicated variations taking place to the prostatectomy portion. Sample size and power calculations (90% power, α=0.05) were based upon institutional continence data and pilot study results. The primary outcomes were early (3 month) and late (12 month) urinary incontinence measured via pad-free rate, mean pad number and 24-hour pad weight. Secondary endpoints included functional urinary parameters, peri-operative outcomes, oncological outcomes and patient reported outcomes. The trial was protocoled by the SLHD Human Research Ethics Committee (No. X16-0294&HREC/16/RPAH/377) and registered with the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ACTRN12618002058257). RESULTS: 123 patients were recruited between April 2019 and October 2024 (RoboSling: 62, Control: 61). There was no cross-over. 123 patients have reached 3-month follow-up, 12-month analysis is ongoing and will be completed in November 2025. At 6 weeks, of patients who did require continence pads, there were fewer mean number of pads in RoboSling arm (p=0.04) At 3 months, the complete pad-free rate was 42% in RoboSling and 41% in controls with no significant difference. There were no significant differences found with mean 24-hour pad weight or mean number of pads between the groups. There were no differences in secondary outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: The RoboSling at time of RARP was well tolerated with no adverse clinical or oncological outcomes. However, the RoboSling failed to demonstrate improvement in early continence compared to RARP alone. At 6 weeks, incontinent patients required fewer pads with RoboSling. Late continence outcomes are pending.

title: EVALUATING EFFICACY OF SURGICAL INTERVENTION AGAINST COMBINATION RADIATION AND ANDROGEN DEPRIVATION THERAPY FOR MEN WITH LOCALLY ADVANCED PROSTATE CANCER: AN NCDB ANALYSIS
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Francis Ryan, Mohammad G. Deameh, Michael Whalen
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Locally advanced prostate cancer (LAPCa), defined as cT3-4N0-1M0 prostate adenocarcinoma, remains a challenge in urologic oncology management. Although radiation therapy with androgen deprivation therapy (RT+ADT) is widely recommended as first-line treatment, radical prostatectomy (RP) +/- extended pelvic lymph node dissection has gained interest as an effective definitive treatment for this advanced disease. This study aims to compare overall survival (OS) between an RP-first approach and definitive RT+ADT in a large, contemporary cohort of patients with LAPCa. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the National Cancer Database (NCDB) for patients diagnosed from 2010 to 2022. We identified men with cT3-4N0-1M0 LAPCa who received either an RP-first strategy or definitive RT+ADT. After exclusions, 1:1 propensity score matching was performed to balance baseline characteristics and yielded n=4,271 patients in each treatment arm. The primary outcome was OS, analyzed using Kaplan-Meier curves and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models on the matched cohort, along with subgroup analyses. RESULTS: Definitive RT+ADT demonstrated superior OS compared with a surgery-first approach, with clear separation of Kaplan-Meier curves and an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.770. Subgroup analyses showed the survival benefit of RT+ADT was confined to node-negative patients (cN0 HR 0.748; p<0.001) and was concentrated in patients with Gleason Grade Group ≥ 4 (HR 0.726; p<0.001), with no significant advantage observed for node-positive or lower-grade subgroups, and the treatment effect was consistent across age (<70 and ≥70 years). In comparative Cox models using RP Alone as the reference, definitive RT+ADT had the best survival (HR 0.783; p<0.001), RP followed by postoperative radiation alone showed improved survival (HR 0.856; p=0.009), and patients who required RP with multimodal postop therapy (RP + postop RT + ADT) experienced the worst survival (HR 1.201; p=0.003). CONCLUSIONS: The survival advantage of RT+ADT over RP was strongest for N0, high-grade tumors and was consistent across age groups. Therefore, our findings support prioritizing RT+ADT for appropriate patients with cT3-4, N0, high Gleason grade disease and highlight the prognostic importance of nodal status, tumor grade, and comorbidity. However, how these results fare in the modern PSMA PET era remains to be seen.

title: MORTALITY AFTER RADICAL TREATMENT OF NON-METASTATIC PROSTATE CANCER: A POPULATION-BASED COHORT STUDY
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Ahmad Abbadi, Alessio Crippa, Olof Akre, Anna Lantz, Andrea Discacciati, Margaux Mariaz, Ugo Falagario, Peter Wiklund, Henrik Grönberg, Markus Aly, Tobias Nordström
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The comparative effectiveness of radical prostatectomy (RP) and radiotherapy (RT) for localized and locally advanced prostate cancer remains a topic of debate, particularly regarding prostate cancer–specific mortality (PCSM). We aimed to compare PCSM after RP and RT, stratified by biochemical recurrence-risk group, using long-term registry-based data. METHODS: We conducted a population-based cohort study including all men in Stockholm, Sweden, treated with curative intent for non-metastatic prostate cancer between July 2005 and December 2023, as identified through Swedish national registers. Flexible parametric survival models (Royston-Parmar) were used to estimate cumulative incidence and risk differences (RD), accounting for death from other causes as a competing risk. Models were adjusted for age, civil status, income, education, country of birth, year of treatment, healthcare utilization in the preceding year, Charlson comorbidity index, family history of prostate cancer, neoadjuvant hormonal therapy, prostate-specific antigen (PSA), Gleason grade, T-stage, and biochemical recurrence-risk group (low-, intermediate-, high-risk localized, and high-risk locally advanced) unless otherwise stratified. RESULTS: During the study, 17,794 men were treated radically for non-metastatic prostate cancer. Of them, 11,332 (63.7%) underwent RP, while 6,462 (36.3%) received RT. 3,597 (20.2%) men were < 60 years at time of treatment, 8.531 (47.9%) men aged 60-69, 5,320 (29.9%) men aged 70-79, and 346 (1.9%) were ≥80 years. Biochemical recurrence-risk distribution was 13.7% low-risk, 54.0% intermediate-risk, 16.5% high-risk localized, and 15.8% high-risk locally advanced disease. Over follow-up, 107 men (0.9%) died from prostate cancer after RP and 254 (3.9%) after RT. At 18-years, the cumulative incidence of PCSM was 1.8% (95% CI 1.4%, 2.4%) for RP and 4.7% (95% CI 3.8%, 6.0%) for RT, corresponding to an RD of 2.9% (95% CI 1.6%, 4.2%) favoring RP. Among men with low-risk disease, 9 deaths occurred during the follow-up (six among men treated with RP, and three after RT). At 18-years, the RD for PCSM favored RP with 2.1% (95% CI 0.4%, 3.7%) for intermediate-risk, 6.4% (95% CI 1.0%, 11.9%) for high-risk localized, and 11.6% (95% CI 4.8%, 18.3%) for high-risk locally advanced disease. CONCLUSIONS: Prostate cancer–specific mortality following radical treatment is low at 18-years. Comparing the radical treatment modality, RP was associated with a lower risk of PCSM compared with RT, improving with higher risk-group. While the non-randomized design limits causal interpretation, these results may inform shared decision-making alongside consideration of treatment-related adverse events.

title: INITIAL OUTCOMES ASSESSING MARGIN STATUS AFTER ROBOT-ASSISTED PROSTATECTOMY USING A REAL-TIME DIGITAL MICROSCOPY DEVICE
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Jacob O'Hara, Robert Chang, Allison Horn, Patrice Hassoun, Michael Stifelman, Aaron Sohn
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: In patients with prostate cancer undergoing robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP), positive margins occur in approximately 11-38% of cases. Intraoperative frozen sections have been used for margin evaluation, but are limited to select regions, time-consuming, and resource-intensive. SamanTree Medical’s Histolog Scanner is a digital microscopy (DM) tool that enables rapid visualization and comprehensive margin assessment of much larger areas of the prostate directly in the operating room. This study evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of DM after RARP. METHODS: Specimens from RARPs performed from June 2025 to August 2025 were collected fresh, sent to pathology, and scanned in 5 quadrants (apex, left/right lateral, posterior, and base) using a DM unit. Each quadrant was recorded as being negative or suspicious for adenocarcinoma and compared to margin status on the final pathology report. Initially, five pathologists analyzed DM images. In a second evaluation, one pathologist who underwent advanced technical training reviewed all DM images independently. True negatives (TN) were defined as negative for adenocarcinoma on DM and positive for adenocarcinoma on final pathology. False negatives (FN) were negative on DM and positive on final pathology. True positives (TP) were positive on DM and positive on final pathology. False positives (FP) were positive on DM and negative on final pathology. Data from both phases were aggregated and diagnostic accuracy statistics were calculated. RESULTS: 31 RARPs were performed with 154 prostate locations analyzed for the presence of adenocarcinoma using DM. Results summarized in Tables 1 and 2. CONCLUSIONS: Our initial experience with DM demonstrates an excellent negative predictive value for ruling out positive margins after robot assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP). These results indicate that DM may be a useful tool for the efficient assessment of negative margin status during RARP. Future study should focus on optimizing the ability to accurately detect positive margins using DM and to investigate potential benefits in OR time and perioperative outcomes from its use. | | | --- | | | | | | --- | | |

title: ACCURACY OF INDOCYANINE GREEN FLUORESCENCE IN DETECTING LYMPH NODE METASTASES IN HIGH-RISK PROSTATE CANCER
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Arnaldo Fazoli, Rafael Coelho, Giuliano Guglielmetti, Guilherme Garcia Barros, Gilberto Rodrigues, Leonardo Cardili, Carlos Alberto Buchpiguel, Publio Viana, José Pontes Junior, William Nahas
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Prostate cancer is the most common solid malignancy in men worldwide. Although PSA screening and multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) enable early diagnosis and curative radical prostatectomy, accurately identifying nodal metastasis remains difficult. Extended pelvic lymphadenectomy (ePLND) is the staging gold standard but adds morbidity. Fluorescence-guided lymph node mapping with indocyanine green (ICG) offers a less invasive alternative. This study evaluated lesion-targeted ICG fluorescence (ICG-F), achieved by mpMRI–ultrasound fusion injection into the index lesion, to detect node metastasis. METHODS: This prospective, non-randomized study included 50 men with high-risk prostate cancer undergoing robotic prostatectomy. ICG was injected into the mpMRI-defined index lesion using fusion guidance, and fluorescence was visualized intraoperatively with the Firefly® system. All patients also underwent ePLND, and every lymph node was examined histologically. The primary endpoint was sensitivity for fluorescent node identification on a per-patient basis; secondary endpoints included specificity, positive and negative predictive values (PPV/NPV), and overall diagnostic accuracy. Statistical analyses were conducted in R using logistic regression, McNemar’s test, and the weighted kappa coefficient. RESULTS: The cohort’s mean age was 67 years (61–84) with BMI 25.4 kg/m2 (18.0–27.6). Median Charlson comorbidity index was 4.0 (3.0–5.0). Initial PSA averaged 20.52 ng/mL (9.6–23.2). Histology showed high-risk distribution: ISUP 4 in 48.2% and ISUP 5 in 30.4%. Most were ASA II (80%) and ECOG 0 (73.2%). Median Briganti score was 50% (21.2–72.0). Concordance between positive fluorescence and pathologic nodal metastasis occurred in 23 of 25 pN1 cases. Per-patient performance was: sensitivity 100% (95% CI 86–100), specificity 92% (74–99), PPV 93% (76–99), NPV 98% (85–100), and accuracy 96% (86–99). No adverse events related to ICG were observed. On lymph-node chain analysis, ICG-F showed sensitivity 0.66 and specificity 0.64 with NPV 0.93, outperforming mpMRI (sensitivity 0.04; specificity 0.99) and PET-PSMA (0.13;0.98, respectively). CONCLUSIONS: Lesion-targeted ICG-F achieved 96% accuracy for detecting nodal metastases in high-risk cases, outperforming PSMA PET/CT and mpMRI and providing real-time anatomic guidance. Given its high NPV, deferring completion ePLND after a positive fluorescence but negative intraoperative pathology seems safe in most patients, with ≈4% risk of missed nodal disease. The technique is safe and may support selective, anatomy-guided lymphadenectomy that lowers morbidity without compromising oncologic control.

title: REFINING PATIENT SELECTION FOR SALVAGE RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY BEYOND EAU RECOMMENDATIONS: DEVELOPMENT OF A NOMOGRAM TO ESTIMATE METASTASIS-FREE SURVIVAL
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Giorgio Calleris, Francesco Barletta, Giancarlo Marra, Alessandro Marquis, Pawel Rajwa, Mohamed Ahmed, Alireza Ghoreifi, Luis Ribeiro, Nicole Benfant, Simone Albisinni, Yannic Raskin, Joseph A. Smith, Raj Persad, Henk Van Der Poel, Steven Joniau, Rafael Sanchez-Salas, Alexander Kretschmer, Paul Cathcart, Inderbir Gill, Giovanni Cacciamani, Andre Abreu, Robert J. Karnes, Derya Tilki, Giorgio Gandaglia, Shahrokh F. Shariat, Karim Touijer, Paolo Gontero
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Salvage radical prostatectomy (sRP) represents a potentially curative treatment for locally recurrent prostate cancer (PCa), though it is associated with substantial morbidity. According to EAU recommendations, sRP should be reserved for patients in good condition and with favorable recurrence profiles, primarily defined by biochemical recurrence risk. Our objective was to construct a more precise predictive model for metastasis-free survival (MFS) to optimize candidate selection for sRP. METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated 1,265 men who underwent sRP between 2000 and 2021 across 14 high-volume centers. We excluded men with metastatic or castration-resistant disease, or with incomplete clinical data. Independent predictors of MFS were identified through multivariable Cox regression and used to generate a nomogram. The optimal threshold distinguishing low- and high-risk progression groups was established by maximizing the C-index for 10-year MFS. RESULTS: A total of 408 patients satisfied inclusion criteria. Preoperative PSA, clinical T stage, Gleason score, and time interval to sRP emerged as independent predictors of MFS (all p<0.05). Only 30% fulfilled EAU eligibility criteria (C-index 0.61; 10-year MFS for EAU-compliant men=84% \[95% CI: 76–93\]). Using a 75% 10-year MFS cut-off, our model stratified 60% of patients as high-risk and 40% as low-risk, enhancing discrimination (C-index 0.68). Kaplan–Meier analysis (p<0.001) demonstrated clear separation between high-risk (10y-MFS=51% \[95% CI: 42–63\]) and low-risk groups (10y-MFS=86% \[95% CI:\ 80–93\]), expanding the pool of potential surgical candidates by 33% (N=41). CONCLUSIONS: Conventional selection criteria may overlook patients suitable for curative surgery. Our Cox regression–based nomogram provides improved prognostic accuracy and supports individualized counselling, potentially extending access to local curative treatment. Further external validation and integration with novel imaging strategies are recommended.

title: NEGATIVE PREOPERATIVE PSMA PET DOES NOT RULE OUT NODAL METASTASIS IDENTIFICATION BY PELVIC LYMPHADENECTOMY
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Ronney Abaza, Benjamin Carey, Daniel Frommeyer, Sam Carey
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: With the improved staging of prostate cancer afforded by prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography (PSMA-PET), the role of pelvic lymphadenectomy (PLND) at the time of prostatectomy has been called into question. We evaluated patients with negative preoperative PSMA-PET scans who underwent PLND to determine how often nodal metastasis was detected to inform whether PLND is still warranted in such patients. METHODS: We reviewed our prospective database of 1,231 prostatectomies between February 2023-October 2025 performed by a single surgeon (RA) and identified 501 patients who had undergone preoperative PSMA-PET scanning since it became available in our region. Of these patients, 478 had negative scans, and 23 had oligometastatic disease or suspicion of nodal metastasis on PSMA-PET and underwent prostatectomy but were excluded from analysis. All patients had identical PLND including external iliac, obturator and internal iliac nodes (Zones I-III). RESULTS: Among the 478 patients with negative preoperative PSMA-PET, 63% had Gleason 6 or 7 disease on biopsy and 37% had Gleason 8, 9 or 10. Mean PSA was 10.1 (0.2-122). A total of 38 patients (8%) with negative preoperative PSMA-PET had nodal metastasis identified on PLND with 1 to 3 nodes involved. Among these, 22 (58%) had Gleason 7 disease on biopsy with only 2 upgraded on final pathology (to Gleason 9). Mean preoperative PSA in this group was 14.2ng/mL with only 7 patients having a PSA greater than 20ng/mL. Sixteen patients had Gleason 7 on biopsy and PSA of 10ng/mL or less yet had nodal metastasis on PLND despite negative PSMA-PET. CONCLUSIONS: PSMA-PET failed to identify nodal metastasis in 8% of patients found to have involved nodes on PLND, which suggests that PLND is still warranted in these patients. Omission of PLND based on PSMA-PET would have understaged a significant number of patients, including many who did not have high-risk disease preoperatively.

title: COMPARATIVE OUTCOMES OF ROBOTIC RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY TECHNIQUES: A NETWORK META-ANALYSIS OF 5,641 PATIENTS
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Tarek Mohamed, Abdelrahman Abdelshafi, Mohammad G. Deameh, Hamza Mohamed, Mohamed Ramez
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Single-port (SP) robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) aims to minimize invasiveness while maintaining oncological and functional outcomes comparable to conventional multi-port (MP) surgery. This network meta-analysis compared perioperative, functional, and oncological results across five RARP techniques: transvesical single-port (TV-SP), extraperitoneal single-port (EXTRA-SP), intraperitoneal single-port (INTRA-SP), extraperitoneal multi-port (EXTRA-MP), and transperitoneal multi-port (TP-MP). METHODS: Nineteen comparative studies (n=5,641) were analyzed using random-effects network meta-analysis. Primary endpoints were 3-month continence, potency, and positive surgical margins (PSM). Secondary outcomes included estimated blood loss (EBL), catheter duration, length of stay (LOS), operative time, complications, nerve-sparing, and pelvic lymph node dissection (PLND) rates. Treatments were ranked using SUCRA probabilities. RESULTS: Functional outcomes: Early continence recovery favored EXTRA-SP (RR 1.80, p=0.003) and TV-SP (RR 1.67, p=0.01) over multi-port approaches. At 6 months, continence equalized. Potency was highest with EXTRA-SP (RR 1.15, p=0.007) and INTRA-SP (SUCRA 0.90), while MP approaches ranked lower but not significantly different. PSM rates were equivalent across all groups (p>0.05). Perioperative outcomes: SP approaches achieved significantly lower EBL (TV-SP –101 mL; EXTRA-SP –62 mL, p < 0.01), shorter LOS (EXTRA-SP –1.25 days; INTRA-SP –1.11 days, p < 0.01), and earlier catheter removal (TV-SP –4.3 days; INTRA-SP –2.8 days, p < 0.05). Operative time was modestly longer for SP (TV-SP +22 min; EXTRA-SP +11 min, p < 0.05). Complication rates and nerve-sparing frequency were comparable between SP and MP groups. PLND was performed less often in TV-SP (RR 0.34, p < 0.001) than in MP RARP. CONCLUSIONS: Across 19 studies, SP RARP provides equivalent oncological safety and superior early functional recovery compared with MP RARP. SP techniques—particularly TV-SP and EXTRA-SP—achieve faster continence and shorter hospitalization, while INTRA-SP yields the highest potency ranking. MP approaches remain advantageous when extended PLND is required. These data support SP RARP as a safe, effective, and recovery-enhancing alternative to traditional MP approaches in experienced hands.

title: EVALUATING THE IMPACT OF CALCULATED FREE TESTOSTERONE ON ONCOLOGICAL OUTCOMES IN PROSTATE CANCER MEN POST RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Yeagyeong Hwang, Mai Xuan Nguyen, Chloe T. Yang, Linda My Huynh, Catherine Fung, Thomas E. Ahlering
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Recent studies have shown that low testosterone levels have been associated with decreased libido, diminished energy, and increased mortality from cardiovascular disease and cancer. Calculated free testosterone (cFT), which reflects the biologically available portion of testosterone, is a more precise marker than total testosterone (TT) alone. This study evaluates the association between preoperative cFT and oncological outcomes, specifically biochemical recurrence (BCR), in men undergoing radical prostatectomy (RP). METHODS: Retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data of 1,299 men who underwent RP by a single surgeon between October 2005 and June 2025. Preoperative TT and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) levels were collected, and cFT was calculated using the Vermeulen equation. Patients were stratified into cFT quartiles: Group 1 (≤4.65), Group 2 (4.66–6.01), Group 3 (6.02–7.56), and Group 4 (>7.56). Kaplan–Meier analysis was used to assess time to BCR, and multivariate regression identified independent predictors of recurrence. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics significantly differed across cFT quartiles for age, prostate weight, preoperative PSA, TT, SHBG, and Gleason Grade Group (all p<0.05). Men in the lowest cFT quartile (≤4.65) had higher rates of adverse pathology (pT3/4 disease 42.7%; p=0.0146), positive surgical margins (25.0%, p=0.0402), and BCR (36.0%; p<0.001) compared to higher quartiles. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed significantly worse BCR-free survival among men with lower cFT levels (p=0.0012). On multivariate analysis, independent predictors of BCR included age (OR 1.03, p=0.003), preoperative PSA (OR 1.14, p<0.001), BMI (OR 1.07, p<0.001), prostate weight (OR 0.99, p=0.008), and cFT (OR 0.88, p=0.003). CONCLUSIONS: Lower preoperative cFT was independently associated with increased risk of BCR after RP. These findings suggest that integrating cFT into preoperative risk stratification could enhance prediction of oncologic outcomes and support a more personalized postoperative management approach. | | | --- | | |

title: IMPACT OF PRIMARY TREATMENT MODALITIES ON SURVIVAL IN DUCTAL AND INTRADUCTAL PROSTATE CARCINOMA
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Arjun Pon Avudaiappan, Mohammad Arfat Ganiyani, Hiba Narvel, Murugesan Manoharan, Rohan Garje
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Ductal and Intraductal prostate carcinoma (DIPC) are rare, aggressive variants with limited disease-specific management guidelines. Based on risk stratification, treatment for localized DIPC varies between radical prostatectomy (RP), radiation ± androgen deprivation therapy (RT±ADT), and observation. A few studies in the literature evaluate survival outcomes across different treatment modalities. To evaluate this, we used the national cancer registry to compare survival outcomes between different treatment modalities in localized DIPC. METHODS: We identified patients diagnosed with localized DPC between 2004 and 2020. The analytical cohort included 3 groups: the RP cohort, comprising patients who underwent RP; the RT±ADT cohort, comprising patients who underwent RT±ADT; and the observation cohort, comprising patients under observation. We performed a Kaplan-Meier survival analysis to evaluate overall survival (OS). We also conducted a multivariate Cox proportional hazards model adjusting for age, race, NCCN risk classification, comorbidities, socioeconomic factors, and facility type to evaluate survival hazards. RESULTS: Among 2,650 patients with localized DIPC, 1,586 (59.8%), 785 (29.6%), and 279 (10.6%) underwent RP, RT±ADT, and observation, respectively. 2-year OS for RP, RT±ADT, and Observation was 98%, 94%, and 78% respectively (p<0.001). Similarly, 5-year OS was 92%, 81%, and 54% respectively (p<0.001). Multivariate Cox regression showed that RT±ADT was associated with increased mortality compared to RP (HR: 2.27; p<0.001). 2-year OS for patients with PSA ≤4ng/dL and >4ng/dL was 89.9% and 97.2%, respectively. Similarly, 5-year OS were 75.8% and 88.8%, respectively. Multivariate Cox regression showed that PSA ≤4 was associated with an increased risk of mortality compared with PSA >4 (HR: 1.27; p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: In our study on localized DIPC, we observed that RP, with or without salvage therapy, had better OS than RT±ADT. The association of low PSA with worse prognosis could be due to dedifferentiation-driven aggressiveness. Therefore, based on risk stratification, a multimodal approach with RP as the initial treatment and RT±ADT could provide additional survival benefits.

title: POSITIVE SURGICAL MARGINS ARE NOT INDEPENDENTLY ASSOCIATED WITH BIOCHEMICAL RECURRENCE AFTER SINGLE PORT ROBOT-ASSISTED RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY: A MULTI-INSTITUTIONAL ANALYSIS FROM THE SINGLE PORT ADVANCED RESEARCH CONSORTIUM (SPARC)
session: Prostate Cancer: Localized: Surgical Therapy I (IP17)
authors: Abdulrahman Al-Bayati, Jacob Hershenhouse, Sam Cole, Jacob O’hara, Jack Considine, Mehr Nasir-Moin, Narmina Khanmammadova, Yeonsoo Lee, Ruben Sauer Calvo, Karim Daher, Simon Kim, Alissa Elanjian, Anastasia Mavridis, Nicolas Soputro, Sean Horan, Lin Wang, Dattatraya Patil, Rui Bernardino, Shamsunnahar Imtiaz, Firas Abdollah, Adam Lorentz, David I. Lee, Ram Pathak, Kshitij Hemal, Jullet Han, Jaschar Shakuri-Rad, Ryan J. Nelson, Bertram Yuh
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: While prior studies have shown that positive surgical margins (PSMs) are not consistently associated with biochemical recurrence (BCR) after robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP), evidence specific to the Single Port (SP) platform remains limited. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the relationship between PSMs and BCR following SP-RARP and to identify independent predictors of recurrence using data from the multi-institutional SP Advanced Research Consortium (SPARC). METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted using the prospectively maintained, IRB-approved database of the SPARC to identify all consecutive patients who underwent SP RARP across participating centers. Patients without postoperative PSA data or with less than 6 months of follow-up were excluded. BCR was defined according to the AUA guidelines. Kaplan–Meier analysis with log-rank testing and multivariable Cox regression were performed to evaluate predictors of BCR, including margin status. Grade Group, and pathologic stage. RESULTS: A total of 2,825 patients were identified across participating centers, of whom 1,473 met inclusion criteria for analysis. Among these, 396 (26.9%) had PSMs. Median follow-up was 27 months, during which 42 patients (2.9%) developed BCR. In multivariable Cox regression, PSM was not independently predictive of BCR (HR 1.24, 95% CI 0.74–2.08, p=0.42). Higher pathologic stage (pT3/4 vs pT2: HR 3.00 (95% CI 1.49–6.04), p=0.002) and higher Grade Group (GG 4–5 vs 1–3: HR 2.59 (95% CI 1.35–4.98), p=0.004) were independently associated with recurrence. The proportional hazards assumption was met (global p=0.269), and model robustness was confirmed with a site-level frailty analysis, which demonstrated similar findings. CONCLUSIONS: In this large multi-institutional analysis, PSMs were not independently associated with BCR following SP RARP. Pathologic stage and tumor grade were the primary determinants of recurrence. These findings suggest that margin status alone does not appear to confer additional prognostic significance beyond established pathologic factors. | | | --- | | |

title: EXTENDED FOLLOW-UP SHOWS ACCUMULATING BENEFIT FOR PATIENTS TREATED WITH AGLATIMAGENE BESADENOVEC (CAN-2409) +PRODRUG IN COMBINATION WITH STANDARD OF CARE EXTERNAL BEAM RADIATION (EBRT) IN MEN WITH LOCALIZED PROSTATE CANCER: UPDATE FROM A RANDOMIZED PLACEBO-CONTROLLED PHASE 3 CLINICAL TRIAL
session: P2s: Practice-changing, Paradigm-shifting Clinical Trials in Urology (P2)
authors: Mark Garzotto, John Sylvester, Thomas Wheeler, Thomas Schroeder, Glen Gejerman, Gregory Chesnut, Thomas Facelle, Ronald Tutrone, Christopher Pieczonka, Michael A. Liss, Stephen J. Savage, Bryan Mehlhaff, Steven Sukin, Maximiliano Sorbellini, Jenessa Vogt, Shangbang Rao, Maria Lucia Silva Polanco, Andrea Manzanera, Francesca Barone, Garrett Nichols, Theodore L. DeWeese, Paul P. Tak
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Current standard of care (SoC) for localized prostate cancer (PCa) treated with curative intent includes surgery or EBRT±ADT. Still, ∼ 30% of men experience disease recurrence, leading to salvage therapies associated with reduced quality of life. Aglatimagene, a replication-defective adenovirus encoding HSV-tk, combined with valacyclovir (prodrug), induces immunogenic cell death. Topline results from the phase 3 NCT01436968 randomized, double-blind, placebo (PBO)- controlled trial in intermediate- (IR) and high-risk PCa patients (pts) demonstrated that aglatimagene added to SoC EBRT+/- ADT (≤6 mos) improved disease-free survival (DFS) by 30% compared to PBO (p=0.0155, HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.52, 0.94; data as of Aug 30,2024), supported by secondary endpoints (median follow-up 50.3 months, CI 45.4, 51.3) (All CI represents 95% CI). Here we report PCa-specific outcomes after extended follow-up. METHODS: 745 pts were randomized 2:1 (496 to aglatimagene and 249 to PBO) and stratified by NCCN risk group and ADT use; 635 had IR PCa (422 into aglatimagene arm and 213 in to PBO arm). Three intraprostatic injections of aglatimagene CAN-2409 (5×10 11vp/2 mL) or PBO were administered, each followed by 14 days of prodrug. We evaluated PCa-specific DFS (time from randomization to PCa recurrence or PCa death) in the total intent-to-treat population (ITT) and in the IR subset as of March 15, 2026. Secondary and exploratory endpoints included time to biochemical failure (TTBF), time to metastasis (TTM), and time to new therapy (TTNT). PCa-specific DFS median follow-up was 58.0 mos, CI 56.6, 60.2. RESULTS: The aglatimagene arm exhibited 39% improvement in PCa-specific DFS vs PBO (HR=0.61; CI: 0.44, 0.85; p=0.0031). There were only 2 PCa-specific deaths, one in each arm. Trends consistently favor aglatimagene vs PBO for TTBF (HR 0.72, CI 0.40, 1.31), rate of metastasis (1.6% (8/496) vs PBO 2.8% (7/249)), TTM (HR 0.58, CI 0.21, 1.59), and TTNT (HR 0.72, CI 0.39, 1.31); curves are still immature. Within the IR subgroup, aglatimagene shows an even greater eWect: 41% improvement in PCa-specific DFS vs PBO (HR 0.59, CI 0.41, 0.84; p=0.0034). We observed improvement in TTBF (HR 0.48, CI 0.22, 1.03), rate of metastasis (0.24% (1/422) vs 2.35% (5/213)), TTM (HR 0.1, CI 0.01, 0.85), and TTNT (HR 0.51, CI 0.24, 1.1), comparing the aglatimagene arm vs PBO. CONCLUSIONS: Aglatimagene significantly improved PCa-specific DFS when added to SoC EBRT±ADT. Further exploratory analyses after extended follow-up show accumulating benefit for PCa-specific clinical outcomes. If approved, aglatimagene could represent a new therapy for pts treated with EBRT with curative intent for localized PCa.

title: LONG-TERM ONCOLOGICAL OUTCOMES OF EXTENDED VERSUS LIMITED PELVIC LYMPH NODE DISSECTION DURING RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY FOR INTERMEDIATE- AND HIGH-RISK PROSTATE CANCER: PHASE 3 RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL
session: P2s: Practice-changing, Paradigm-shifting Clinical Trials in Urology (P2)
authors: Matheus T. Ruggeri, Jose Pontes, Jr, Giuliano B. Guglielmetti, Mauricio D. Cordeiro, Rafael F. Coelho, William C. Nahas, Jean F. P. Lestingi
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: The oncological value of extended pelvic lymph node dissection (ePLND) during radical prostatectomy remains debated, mainly due to the limited number of randomized studies with long-term follow-up. After our previous publication reporting early outcomes from a randomized trial comparing limited pelvic lymph node dissection (lPLND) and ePLND, we now present the updated long-term results. The primary endpoint was biochemical recurrence-free survival (BCRFS); secondary endpoints included metastasis-free survival (MFS) and cancer-specific survival (CSS). METHODS: From May 2012 to December 2016, 300 patients with intermediate- or high-risk prostate cancer (≥cT2b, PSA≥10 ng/mL, and/or Gleason≥7), without metastases or prior treatment, were randomized 1:1 to undergo ePLND (bilateral obturator, external, internal, common iliac, and presacral nodes) or lPLND (bilateral obturator nodes only). The trial was designed to demonstrate a minimum 15% advantage in 5-year BRFS with ePLND. (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01812902). RESULTS: Mean and median follow-up were 123 and 112 months, respectively. BCR rates were comparable between groups (HR 0.93; 95% CI 0.66–1.31; p=0.681). No significant differences were observed in MFS (HR 0.93; 95% CI 0.7–2.89; p=0.32), CSS (HR 0.97; 95% CI 0.6–1.57; p=0.892), or overall survival (HR 1.01; 95% CI 0.29–3.49; p=0.988). However, patients with preoperative ISUP grade 3–5 disease who underwent ePLND maintained improved BCRFS (HR 1.92; 95% CI 1.04–3.57; p=0.034; NNT=5), confirming the benefit seen at 5 years. In this high-grade subgroup, MFS was also significantly longer with ePLND (HR 5.12; 95% CI 1.12–23.42; p=0.035; NNT=4), supporting a durable oncological advantage in selected cases. CONCLUSIONS: This phase 3 randomized trial showed no overall survival or oncologic superiority of ePLND over lPLND. Nevertheless, in patients with high-grade (ISUP 3–5) tumors, extended dissection sustained long-term benefits in BCRFS and MFS, suggesting a potential role for ePLND in this specific subgroup.

title: BREAK WAVE LITHOTRIPSY: FDA-CLEARED, ANESTHESIA-FREE POINT-OF-CARE TECHNOLOGY REDEFINING STONE MANAGEMENT (S.O.U.N.D. PIVOTAL TRIAL)
session: P2s: Practice-changing, Paradigm-shifting Clinical Trials in Urology (P2)
authors: Ben H. Chew, Jonathan D. Harper, Justin Ahn, Helena Chang, James R. Johannes, Roger L. Sur, Nicholas L. Kavoussi, Shubha De, Kenneth T. Pace, Amy E. Krambeck, Connor M. Forbes, Ryan F. Paterson, Anne R. Buckley, Victor K. F. Wong, Kennedy Hall, Ross Kessler, Sarah Gartner, Lisa Gill, Ralph Wang, Leo Chen, David Guo, Errin Hoffman, Seth K. Bechis, Jason R. Woo, Tyler Sheetz, Rahim Samji, Derek Bochinski, Trevor D. Schuler
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Break Wave lithotripsy enables truly anesthesia-free, point-of-care stone treatment that can be delivered almost anywhere, positioning it as a disruptive new platform for urolithiasis treatment. Break Wave is a compact, ultrasound-guided lithotripsy system designed to fragment upper tract stones in a non-invasive fashion without fluoroscopy. METHODS: In this multicenter pivotal trial (10 U.S. and Canadian sites, NCT05701098), adults with ureteral or renal stones (4–10 mm) underwent a 30-minute session performed entirely outside the operating room without any anesthesia or sedation. The primary endpoint at 10±2 weeks (CT or KUB) defined success as stone-free or residual fragments ≤4 mm. RESULTS: Among 64 treated patients, 94% of procedures (60/64) were completed in clinic settings, underscoring the device’s portability and workflow flexibility. All patients tolerated treatment without anesthesia or sedation, eliminating pre-op clearance, PACU recovery, and anesthesiology support. Overall, 70% (45/64) achieved the primary efficacy endpoint, with 48% completely stone-free; distal ureter/UVJ stones (mean 7.3±1.4 mm) achieved 90% success, including 72% stone-free. 83% of Adverse events were mild (hematuria) and transient (84% resolved within one week), and no sepsis, renal hematoma, or arrhythmia occurred over 90 days of follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: Patients strongly endorsed this paradigm shift: 97% would choose Break Wave again for a future stone, including those with prior ureteroscopy or shock wave lithotripsy (92% each). Meeting all pivotal non-inferiority endpoints for safety and effectiveness, this trial directly supported FDA clearance in January 2026. Break Wave lithotripsy introduces a new care model—non-invasive, anesthesia-free stone treatment that can be delivered in virtually any clinical environment, redefining how and where stones are treated. | | | --- | | |

title: A NON-VIRAL INTRAVESICAL GENE THERAPY FOR BCG-UNRESPONSIVE NMIBC WITH CIS, WITH OR WITHOUT PAPILLARY DISEASE: PIVOTAL PHASE 2 INTERIM RESULTS OF DETALIMOGENE VORAPLASMID
session: P2s: Practice-changing, Paradigm-shifting Clinical Trials in Urology (P2)
authors: Ashish M. Kamat, Mark Tyson, Ricardo Rendon, Félix Guerrero-Ramos, Jen-Jane Liu, Shreyas Joshi, Paras H. Shah, Grégoire Robert, Giuseppe Simone, Bogdana Schmidt, Gautier Marcq, Wassim Kassouf, John A. Taylor, III, Christine Tosone, Mahima Agochiya, Anthony Cheung, Katherine Chan, Hussein Sweiti, Sam S. Chang
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Detalimogene voraplasmid (EG-70) is a novel, non-viral investigational intravesical gene therapy, designed to induce local innate and adaptive immunity via sustained interleukin-12 expression and retinoic acid-inducible gene I pathway stimulation. In Phase 1 of the LEGEND study (NCT04752722), detalimogene was well tolerated with preliminary efficacy results in patients (pts) with Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG)-unresponsive carcinoma in situ (CIS) ± papillary disease. Cohort 1 is a pivotal Phase 2 cohort evaluating efficacy and safety in this population. METHODS: Cohort 1 enrolled adults (≥18 yrs) with BCG-unresponsive CIS ± papillary (Ta/T1) tumors who were either ineligible for or declined cystectomy. Pts received four 50-mL intravesical doses of detalimogene at weeks 1, 2, 5 and 6 of each 12-week cycle during Year (Yr) 1\. Pts with persistent or recurrent disease after Cycle 1 were eligible for re-induction. Those achieving a complete response (CR) at Yr 1 transitioned to maintenance treatment: doses at weeks 1 and 2 of each cycle for up to two yrs. Efficacy assessments included quarterly urine cytology and cystoscopy, mandatory templated biopsies at the 12-month (mo) assessment, and as clinically indicated. The primary endpoint is CR rate at any time. Secondary endpoints are duration of response (DOR), landmark CR rates and safety. RESULTS: A total of 125 pts were enrolled (median age 71.0 years (35.0-90.0); 80.8% male. Pts received a median of 12 prior BCG doses (6-50); 24.8% received additional prior therapies; 39.2% had CIS + papillary disease. Median number of prior recurrences was 2 (0-11). CR rate was 54.0% (95% CI 44.9-63.0) at any time and 43.0% (95% CI 34.0-52.3) at 6 mo. Median time to CR was 2.1 mo (1.5-6.2); with 91.0% of CRs occurring at first assessment. At data cut-off, 96.8% remained free from progression to ≥T2 disease. Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) occurred in 55.2% of pts, predominantly Grades 1-2 (91.3%). Common TRAEs included fatigue (21.6%), dysuria (13.6%), micturition urgency (12.0%), pollakiuria (12.0%) and bladder spasm (11.2%). Grade \\x{2265}3 TRAEs (4.8%) and serious TRAEs (1.6%) were infrequent. TRAEs led to dose interruption in 2.4% and discontinuation in 2.4% of pts. CONCLUSIONS: Interim results of LEGEND Cohort 1 demonstrate encouraging activity of detalimogene in a heavily pre-treated BCG-unresponsive NMIBC population. The rapid onset of response, non-viral platform, and favorable safety profile support detalimogene voraplasmid as a promising bladder-sparing option in this setting.

title: DURVALUMAB IN COMBINATION WITH BACILLUS CALMETTE-GUÉRIN INDUCTION AND MAINTENANCE THERAPY FOR BACILLUS CALMETTE-GUÉRIN-NAÏVE, HIGH-RISK NON-MUSCLE-INVASIVE BLADDER CANCER: EXPANDED EFFICACY AND SAFETY ANALYSES FROM POTOMAC
session: P2s: Practice-changing, Paradigm-shifting Clinical Trials in Urology (P2)
authors: Neal D. Shore, Maria De Santis, Joan Palou Redorta, Michał Krawczyński, Artur Seyitkuliev, Andrey Novikov, Félix Guerrero-Ramos, Minoru Kato, Lieven Goeman, Eva Hellmis, Thomas Powles, Kilian M. Gust, Robert Zielinski, Julien Deturmeny, Girish Kulkarni, Jarmo Hunting, Purnima Rao-Melacini, Suliman Boulos, Angie K. Marsh, Hiroyuki Nishiyama
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: One year of durvalumab (D) plus BCG induction (I) + maintenance (M) vs BCG (I+M) alone demonstrated a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in disease-free survival (DFS) in patients (pts) with BCG-naïve, high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC; POTOMAC, NCT03528694). Early recurrence is associated with worse outcomes and BCG unresponsive disease is an indication for radical cystectomy. Papillary tumors constitute the majority of NMIBC, and their prognosis depends on disease stage and grade. This was also the largest pt subgroup in POTOMAC. We report in-depth additional efficacy and safety analyses for D+BCG (I+M) vs BCG (I+M). METHODS: Eligible pts who had TURBT (complete resection; including residual carcinoma in situ \[CIS\]) were randomized 1:1:1 to D+BCG (I+M), D+BCG (I), or BCG (I+M). For D+BCG (I+M) vs BCG (I+M), we report time to cystectomy (secondary endpoint) and post-hoc exploratory analyses of time to high-risk disease event, BCG-unresponsive disease per FDA guidelines, median time to cystectomy, cystectomy-free survival (time from randomization to cystectomy/death), and outcomes in pts with papillary tumors. RESULTS: Fewer high-risk disease events (high-risk NMIBC recurrence \[high-grade Ta/T1/CIS\], persistent CIS at 6 mo, or MIBC/metastasis) occurred with D+BCG (I+M) (53/339) vs BCG (I+M) (69/340). Median time to high-risk event was 14.1 vs 8.3 mo; 45% (24/53) vs 61% (42/69) of pts had early high-risk events (≤1 year from randomization). At recurrence, 65% (24/37; D+BCG \[I+M\]) vs 81% (44/54; BCG \[I+M\]) met BCG-unresponsive criteria. Time to cystectomy in ITT resulted in a HR of 0.63 (95% CI 0.31–1.24) with D+BCG (I+M) vs BCG (I+M), with medians not reached in either arm. Among pts who underwent cystectomy, median time to cystectomy was 19.0 vs 14.1 mo. The cystectomy-free survival HR was 0.69 (95% CI 0.48–0.99) with D+BCG (I+M) vs BCG (I+M). Outcomes in papillary subgroups are summarised (Table). Safety in pts with papillary tumors was consistent with the overall population. CONCLUSIONS: Fewer early high-risk events occurred with D+BCG (I+M) vs BCG (I+M), as well as a delayed time to high-risk events, and fewer BCG-unresponsive recurrences. Time to cystectomy and cystectomy-free survival showed a trend in favor of D+BCG (I+M) vs BCG (I+M). Notably, a DFS benefit was observed across papillary subgroups with D+BCG (I+M). These data further support D+BCG (I+M) as a potential new treatment in this setting. | | | --- | | |

title: A PROSPECTIVE RANDOMIZED STUDY OF SEXUAL AND EJACULATORY OUTCOMES FOLLOWING WATER VAPOR THERAPY VERSUS HOLMIUM LASER ENUCLEATION FOR LARGE-VOLUME BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA
session: P2s: Practice-changing, Paradigm-shifting Clinical Trials in Urology (P2)
authors: Hany F. Fathy Badawy, Akram A. Almarakby, Rabee M. Abdallah, Mohamed Salem, Jeffrey Mangel, Kevin Miller
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia usually require procedural therapy when symptoms are refractory to medical management, and sexual outcomes influence treatment selection. We prospectively compared 12-month sexual, ejaculatory, and urinary outcomes after water vapor therapy versus holmium laser enucleation in sexually active men with large-volume benign prostatic hyperplasia. METHODS: In a prospective randomized trial (April 2024-October 2025), 110 sexually active men aged≥50 years with benign prostatic hyperplasia (prostate volume 80-120 mL, International Prostate Symptom Score>13, maximum flow rate<15 mL/s) were randomized 1:1 to water vapor therapy or holmium laser enucleation of the prostate. Sexual outcomes were assessed using the 15-item International Index of Erectile Function and the ejaculatory domain of the Male Sexual Health Questionnaire. Urinary outcomes included International Prostate Symptom Score, maximum flow rate, and post-void residual. Adjusted p values were reported using Benjamini-Hochberg. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics were comparable (all p≥0.05). At 12 months, holmium laser enucleation of the prostate was associated with worse orgasmic function (6.8±1.6 vs 7.6±1.3; p\_adj=0.018) and intercourse satisfaction (8.3±1.7 vs 9.4±2.6; p\_adj=0.045), with a greater decline in ejaculatory function (-3.0±2.5 vs -0.7±2.6; p\_adj<0.001). Erectile function and overall sexual satisfaction did not differ. Urinary outcomes favored holmium laser enucleation: International Prostate Symptom Score 6.0 vs 11.0, maximum flow rate 22.1±3.1 vs 13.7±2.8 mL/s, and post-void residual 24.1±12.3 vs 42.0±12.8 mL (all p\_adj<0.001). Operative time and hemoglobin drop were greater, while catheter duration was shorter. Reintervention rates were similar. CONCLUSIONS: In sexually active men with large-volume benign prostatic hyperplasia, water vapor therapy better preserves ejaculatory and orgasmic outcomes at 12 months, while holmium laser enucleation of the prostate provides substantially greater improvement in lower urinary tract symptoms and objective flow measures. These data support individualized, shared decision-making that balances sexual priorities against the magnitude and speed of symptom relief.

title: RANDOMIZED, CONTROLLED, DOUBLE-BLIND TRIAL IN PATIENTS WITH URGENCY URINARY INCONTINENCE: QUALITY OF LIFE OUTCOMES WITH THE INTIBIA SYSTEM
session: P2s: Practice-changing, Paradigm-shifting Clinical Trials in Urology (P2)
authors: Jeffrey Mangel, Kevin Miller, Ty Erickson, Alexis Dieter, Jan-Paul Roovers, Cathrine A. Matthews
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Implantable Tibial Nerve Stimulation (ITNS) offers promising benefits for patients with urgency urinary incontinence (UUI); however, no comparisons have been conducted between ITNS and sham controls which remains a critical need considering the historically high placebo response rates with OAB neuromodulation. The objective of this analysis was to determine the impact of the Intibia System ITNS device on quality-of-life (QoL) in patients with UUI and to compare to a sham control. METHODS: The Intibia Pivotal Study was a prospective, randomized, sham-controlled, double-blind trial in adult male and female subjects with UUI. Subjects across 23 sites in the United States and the Netherlands were randomized to an ITNS-treatment group (ITNS-ON) or a sham control group (ITNS-SHAM) in a 2:1 ratio and implanted with the Intibia System. After 3 months, subjects were unblinded and sham subjects had their devices turned on. Follow-ups occurred at 3, 6, and 12 months. Secondary analyses reported here include the Overactive Bladder Questionnaire (OABq-SF), the International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire (ICIQ-UI SF), and the Patient Global Impression of Improvement (PGI-I). RESULTS: Overall, 208 subjects were randomized and implanted (n=139 ITNS-ON and n=69 ITNS-SHAM). Significantly more ITNS-ON subjects reported feeling “Much better” or “Very much better” on the PGI-I after 3 months compared to ITNS-SHAM subjects (29.2% vs. 13.4%; p=0.0133), and 83% of ITNS-ON subjects reported any level of improvement on the PGI-I after 12 months. Significantly more ITNS-ON subjects exceeded the Minimally Clinically Important Difference (MCID) for improvement in the OABq-SF Symptom Bother Score (62.8% vs. 41.8%; p=0.0046) and the Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQL) Total Score (57.4% vs. 42.4%; p=0.0463) at 3 months relative to baseline compared to ITNS-SHAM subjects. After 12 months, 71.5% and 74.2% of ITNS-ON subjects exceeded the MCID for the Symptom Bother and HRQL scales, respectively. ITNS-ON and ITNS-SHAM groups improved similarly in their ICIQ-UI SF total scores at 3 months relative to baseline (-2.5±4.2 ITNS-ON vs -1.9±3.8 ITNS-SHAM; p=0.3687), while 71.5% of ITNS-ON subjects exceeded the ICIQ-UI SF MCID by 12 months. CONCLUSIONS: The Intibia Pivotal Study is the first randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial with an ITNS device assessing quality-of-life outcomes in patients with UUI. Significant and clinically meaningful improvements in QoL were observed after 3 months of ITNS treatment compared to a sham control and benefits were observed through 12 months of therapy.

title: DAROLUTAMIDE PLUS ANDROGEN DEPRIVATION THERAPY (ADT) IN METASTATIC HORMONE-SENSITIVE PROSTATE CANCER (MHSPC): ARASEC – US PROSPECTIVE, OPEN-LABEL PHASE 2 STUDY WITH AN EXTERNAL CONTROL ARM
session: P2s: Practice-changing, Paradigm-shifting Clinical Trials in Urology (P2)
authors: Rana R. McKay, Ashley E. Ross, Mark A. Preston, Justin R. Gregg, Simpa S. Salami, Fred Saad, Christopher M. Pieczonka, Ronald F. Tutrone, Joelle Hamilton, David S. Morris, Laurence H. Belkoff, Raymond S. Lance, Natasha Littleton, Niculae Constantinovici, Shankar Srinivasan, Frank Verholen, Neal D. Shore
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Darolutamide+ADT has FDA and EMA approval for mHSPC based on the global phase 3 ARANOTE study, in which darolutamide significantly improved radiological progression-free survival (rPFS) vs placebo (HR 0.54; 95% CI 0.41–0.71; p<0.0001) with favorable safety and tolerability. ARASEC (NCT05059236) was designed using a novel, pragmatic design that leveraged propensity score matching to compare darolutamide+ADT in a prospective investigational arm vs an external ADT control arm derived from CHAARTED, as a prospective ADT arm was not possible. METHODS: US patients with mHSPC were enrolled to receive darolutamide 600 mg BID+ADT (n=223) and were matched 1:1 to patients in the CHAARTED ADT arm (n=393) using propensity scores based on baseline prognostic characteristics: age, performance status, extent of disease, prior local therapy, Gleason score, and PSA. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS) defined per CHAARTED. Secondary endpoints were overall survival (OS), time to metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), rPFS, PSA <0.2 ng/mL response rates, and safety. A sensitivity analysis compared the two trial cohorts including all match-eligible patients, applying inverse probability of treatment weighting to adjust for baseline differences between ARASEC and CHAARTED. A second sensitivity analysis compared the ARASEC darolutamide arm with the contemporary ARANOTE ADT arm using propensity score matching, as in the primary analysis. RESULTS: In the primary analysis, propensity score matching identified 160 patients/arm with similar baseline characteristics. At the primary data cutoff (median follow-up: darolutamide arm 26 months; ADT arm 28 months), darolutamide+ADT significantly improved PFS vs ADT (HR 0.29, 95% CI 0.20–0.40; p<0.001). Darolutamide+ADT was also associated with significant improvements in OS (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.30–0.82; p=0.003), time to mCRPC (0.26, 0.18–0.38; p<0.001), and rPFS (0.30, 0.19–0.48; p<0.001) vs ADT. PSA<0.2 ng/mL response rates were 59% in the darolutamide arm and 23% in the ADT arm at 6 months (p<0.001) and 68% and 33%, respectively, at any time (p<0.001). The sensitivity analyses support these findings: the PFS HRs were 0.28 (95% CI 0.23–0.33) in the ARASEC–CHAARTED match-eligible population and 0.30 (0.21–0.44) in the ARASEC–ARANOTE propensity score matched population. In the darolutamide arm (n=223), treatment-emergent adverse events were mostly grade 1/2 (58%) and led to discontinuation in 8%. CONCLUSIONS: In US patients with mHSPC, ARASEC demonstrates significantly improved efficacy with darolutamide+ADT vs. ADT control arms derived from phase 3 trials. To our knowledge, ARASEC is the first mHSPC study comparing a prospectively enrolled cohort with matched cohorts from previous and contemporary trials. This innovative design demonstrates a feasible approach to accelerate enrollment, enhance operational efficiency, and expedite patient access to emerging therapies in a rapidly evolving treatment landscape.

title: EFFICACY AND SAFETY OF ZENFLOW PROSTATIC SPRING FOR TREATMENT OF LOWER URINARY TRACT SYMPTOMS SECONDARY TO BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA; RESULTS FROM A PIVOTAL IDE CLINICAL TRIAL
session: P2s: Practice-changing, Paradigm-shifting Clinical Trials in Urology (P2)
authors: Dean Elterman, Susan Kalota, Andrew Wright, Mohamed Bidair, Osvaldo Padron, Michael Trotter, Tyler McClintock, Brian Mazzarella, Edward Matsumoto, Kevin Zorn, Malek Meskawi, Premal Patel, Brian Neuman, Ricardo Gonzalez, Neal Shore, Jeffrey Campbell, Ahmed Zakaria, Hazem Elmansy, Mark Jalkut, Bilal Chughtai, James Young, Gregg Eure, Mitchell Efros, David Cahn, Brian Helfand, Alexander Glaser, John Kowalczyk, Sheldon Freedman
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is the leading cause of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) in males and is associated with significant reductions in quality of life (QoL). The Zenflow Spring is a small, minimally invasive implant indicated for reducing LUTS due to BPH. The objective of the present study is to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the novel Zenflow Spring. METHODS: In this prospective, multi-center, multinational, randomized, single-blinded controlled clinical trial, 205 male subjects aged 45+ years with LUTS associated with BPH and baseline International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)≥13 were enrolled and randomized 2:1 to Zenflow Spring (Spring) or Sham with follow-up at 2 weeks, 1, 3, 6, and 12 months. The co-primary efficacy endpoints (statistical tests) were: percent of subjects who experienced≥30% improvement in IPSS at 3 months (chi-square test); mean percent change in IPSS of 30% or more among Spring subjects from baseline to 12 months (t-test). The co-primary safety endpoints included: rate of extended post-operative urinary catheterization (> 7 days from treatment) for inability to void; incidence of device or procedure-related serious adverse events (SAEs) through 12 months. QoL and peak urinary flow rate (Qmax) were also measured. RESULTS: There were 137 subjects in Spring and 68 in Sham intent-to-treat population (ITT). Post-treatment, 38 subjects (27 Spring and 11 Sham) were erroneously enrolled in the ITT population and should have been excluded due to the presence of intravesical prostatic protrusion >10mm and/or obstructive median prostatic lobe protrusion. A second analysis of the effectiveness endpoints was completed excluding the subjects who did not meet this eligibility criterion in a modified ITT (mITT), which reflects the actual intended use population for the device, resulting in 166 subjects (109 Spring, 57 Sham). A higher proportion of subjects in the Spring arm achieved 30% improvement in IPSS total score at 3 months than in Sham (59.6% vs. 33.3%, p=0.001). The mean percent change (95% CI) in IPSS total score at 12 months in the Spring arm was 37.2% (31.0% -43.4%), exceeding the pre-specified clinical success threshold of 30% (p=0.012).There were no reports of extended post-operative urinary catheterization (> 7 days from treatment) for inability to void, and no device or procedure related SAEs reported through 12 months of follow-up in ITT. Qmax showed immediate improvement sustained through 12 months, and QoL improved from 4.5 at baseline to 2.5 at 12 months. CONCLUSIONS: The Zenflow Spring is effective, safe, and well tolerated for treating LUTS due to BPH.

title: INTRAVENOUS PEMBROLIZUMAB COMBINED WITH INTRAVESICAL BACILLUS CALMETTE–GUÉRIN (BCG) FOR PATIENTS WITH BCG-NA&IUML;VE &LDQUO;VERY HIGH-RISK&RDQUO; T1 NON-MUSCLE INVASIVE BLADDER CANCER TRADITIONALLY RECOMMENDED FOR RADICAL CYSTECTOMY
session: P2s: Practice-changing, Paradigm-shifting Clinical Trials in Urology (P2)
authors: Eugene Pietzak, Emily Feld, Noah Frydenlund, Maria Ponomarev-Cannon, Natasha Reyes, Divya Ajay, Ashley Regazzi, Bernard Bochner, Jonathan Rosenberg, Niamh Keegan, Han Xiao, Neil J. Shah, Robert Smith, Samuel Funt, David Aggen, Alvin Goh, Judy Sarungbam, Irina Ostrovnaya, Hikmat Al-Ahmadie, Dean Bajorin, Gopakumar Iyer
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Patients with BCG-naïve high-grade T1 (HGT1) and concomitant carcinoma in situ (CIS) with additional adverse features have poor outcomes with bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) and are often treated with immediate radical cystectomy (RC). We evaluated pembrolizumab+BCG in patients with BCG-naive “very high risk” HGT1. METHODS: This investigator-initiated, single-center phase II trial enrolled adults with BCG-naïve HGT1+CIS and≥1 additional high-risk feature who declined RC. Patients received pembrolizumab 400 mg IV every 6 weeks (up to 48 weeks) with intravesical BCG (induction & 1 year maintenance). A Simon two-stage design was used (planned N=37). The primary endpoint was 6-month complete response rate; secondary endpoints included RFS, PFS, RC-free survival, and safety (CTCAE v5.0). RESULTS: Between 6/2022 and 6/2025, 37 patients were enrolled (median age 67 years, range 34–86; 86% male). All patients had≥1 adverse risk feature, including tumor size≥3 cm (68%), extensive lamina propria invasion (57%), multiple T1 tumors (43%), deep lamina propria invasion (T1b; 37%), persistent/residual T1 on re-TUR (30%), prostatic urethral involvement (24%), and variant histology (22%). Notably, 76% had ≥2 adverse features and 70% had diffuse or multifocal CIS. The 6-month complete response rate was 92% (34/37, 95% CI 79%–97%) and surpassed the prespecified number of responses. At a median follow-up of 20.8 months, no patient progressed to muscle-invasive disease (MIBC), four experienced recurrence (2 T1, 1 CIS, 1 prostatic urethral CIS), and 2 underwent RC. HG-RFS at 12-months was 89%, median not reached. Grade ≥3 immune-related adverse events occurred in 21%, consistent with known immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) toxicity. One death possibly related to pembrolizumab occurred. No new safety signals emerged related to combination therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Pembrolizumab+BCG achieved a 92% 6-month complete response rate in an exceptionally high-risk cohort, with low rates of RC and no progression to MIBC at current follow-up. The expected toxicities of ICB were seen. Although longer follow-up is needed, given historically poor outcomes with BCG alone in this population, our findings support pembrolizumab+BCG as a bladder-preserving option for carefully selected patients with the highest-risk NMIBC who decline or are unfit for RC.

title: A PIVOTAL, RANDOMIZED, SHAM-CONTROLLED TRIAL OF THE UROCROSS EXPANDER SYSTEM FOR TREATMENT OF LOWER URINARY TRACT SYMPTOMS DUE TO BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA: 30 MONTH SAFETY AND DURABILITY INTERIM RESULTS FROM THE EXPANDER-2 TRIAL
session: P2s: Practice-changing, Paradigm-shifting Clinical Trials in Urology (P2)
authors: Kevin T. McVary, Daniel Rukstalis, The Expander-2 Investigators, Jonathan Harper
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Urocross Expander System is a non-permanent prostatic urethral implant technology designed to indwell for up to 6 months and intentionally retrieved, leaving no permanent foreign body behind. When indwelling, the Urocross is designed to remodel the obstructing prostatic outlet to relieve LUTS. This FDA approved pivotal RCT evaluated safety and effectiveness of the investigational Urocross technology as compared to sham (cystoscopy) and to access outcomes through 3.5 years (3-yrs post-retrieval/PR). This analysis provides interim results for up to 30 mos. METHODS: Expander-2 was a 2:1 randomized, blinded, prospective, multi-center trial involving men ≥45 years with symptomatic BPH (IPSS≥13). Urocross subjects underwent implantation followed by intentional retrieval at 6 mos. Sham subjects underwent cystoscopy and were blinded through 3 mos. Primary safety was post-operative extended (>7 days) catheterization rate due to inability to void. Effectiveness metrics (IPSS, QoL, Uroflowmetry) were assessed throughout the duration of the study. RESULTS: 240 men (160 Urocross, 80 sham) at 23 sites (US and Canada) were randomized. The Urocross arm exhibited a reduction in IPSS of 8.2±8.0 points (-32.0%, n=155) at 6 mos, prior to Urocross retrieval from the ITT analysis. Incremental IPSS improvement was observed immediately and sustained after Urocross retrieval, with 11.3±7.8 points (-45.2%, n=146) at 7 mo (1 mo PR), 12.0±8.0 points (-49.0%, n=133) at 12-mos (6-mos PR), 10.0±8.2 points (-40.6%, n=88) at 18-mos (12-mos PR) and 13.2±6.8 points (-56.8%, n=19) at 30 mos (24-mos PR), validating the intended remodeling mechanism with intentional retrieval. Treatment response (≥ 30% IPSS improvement) was 74.4% at 12 mos (6-mos PR). QoL improved from 4.6 to 2.2 (+48.7%), and Qmax increased from 8.8 to 12.5 ml/s (+44.5%). Extended catheterization was low (0.6% post-implant; 2.5% post-retrieval). No device/procedural-related serious adverse events occurred. Related AEs (36.9% implant; 18.8% retrieval) were mostly Clavien-Dindo Grade I/II. To date, all subjects underwent successful implant retrieval and no retreatments with Urocross have occurred. Cystoscopy at 12 mos after retrieval exhibited a visible degree of prostatic remodeling. CONCLUSIONS: The intermediate clinical follow-up of the FDA pivotal trial exhibited visible prostatic urethral remodeling and sustained improvement of voiding symptoms lasting through 24 mos after Urocross retrieval. The results have been accomplished without subsequent placement of an additional Urocross and support safety and effectiveness for Urocross, as a potential first-line treatment option to relieve LUTS/BPH.

title: URINE VOLUME AND URINE OSMOLALITY AND RISK OF RECURRENT STONE EVENTS: RESULTS FROM THE PREVENTION OF URINARY STONES WITH HYDRATION (PUSH) TRIAL
session: P2s: Practice-changing, Paradigm-shifting Clinical Trials in Urology (P2)
authors: Jonathan Harper, John Lieske, Alana Desai, Gregory Tasian, Miloni Shah, Charles Scales, Peter Reese, Sri Sivalingam, Hussein Al-Khalidi, Ziya Kirkali, Naim Maalouf
abstract_text: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Increasing hydration is fundamental to prevent urinary stone recurrences, but the optimal measure and amount of sufficient hydration are uncertain. Our objective was to investigate the association of urine volume (Uvol) with stone recurrence and to evaluate the role of urine osmolality (Uosm) in determining risk of future stone events. METHODS: This analysis included data from adult participants in the Prevention of Urinary Stones with Hydration randomized controlled trial. 24-hr urine collections were performed at baseline, 2 weeks, 6, 12, 18, and 24 months. We defined achieved Uvol and Uosm as each participant’s mean on all collections from 2 weeks to 24 months. We examined change in Uvol from baseline and classified clusters by baseline and achieved Uvol (above or below median for each). Outcomes were time to first symptomatic stone event and a composite outcome of symptomatic or radiographic stone recurrence at 2 years. Stone events were calculated by quintiles of achieved Uvol and Uosm, and examined by Uvol change from baseline and Uvol clusters. Cox models were used to estimate hazard ratios for symptomatic stone events, while a logistic regression model was used for the composite outcome. RESULTS: Among the 1461 participants, median age was 48 years, 56% were female and 30% were first-time stone formers. Mean baseline and achieved 24-hr Uvol and Uosm were 1.3 and 1.8 L/day, and 647 and 577 mOsm/kg, respectively. The median change in Uvol from baseline was +438 ml/day. Those who increased Uvol by greater than this median experienced a 24% lower odds of a symptomatic or radiographic stone recurrence compared to those who did not (OR 0.76 \[95% CI 0.59, 0.98\]; p=0.04), after adjusting for age, sex, BMI, race, recurrent stone former, treatment arm and baseline Uvol. The incidence of symptomatic stone events was less across lower quintiles of achieved 24-hr Uosm (p=0.04, figure) but showed no significant association across achieved 24-hr Uvol quintiles (p=0.12). Finally, the Uvol cluster that maintained higher Uvol from baseline through follow-up (high baseline-high achieved) experienced 49% less symptomatic stone recurrence (multivariable adjusted HR 0.51(95% CI 0.31, 0.83), p<0.01) and 33% less symptomatic and/or radiographic stone recurrence (adjusted OR 0.67 (0.51–0.87), p<0.01) compared to the low baseline–low achieved Uvol cluster. CONCLUSIONS: A greater increase in Uvol from baseline was associated with a lower risk of recurrent stone events, even when the increase did not meet the guideline-based goal of 2.5 L/day. Thus, even modest increases in Uvol may be meaningful for many with stones. Since lower achieved Uosm was associated with fewer stone recurrences, monitoring Uosm may provide additional context to 24-hr urine measures in clinical practice.
